# TJS Platform
[docs](https://tjs.tosijs.net) | [playground](https://tjs-platform.web.app) | [github](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang#readme) | [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tjs-lang) | [discord](https://discord.gg/ramJ9rgky5) ## What is TJS? **TJS is a language.** It's what JavaScript always promised, but never quite delivered. Indeed it's what Apple's Dylan promised and never delivered. Instead of "a lot of the power of Lisp", _all_ the power of Lisp. Instead of C-like Syntax, actual JavaScript syntax. Instead of easy to learn but with weird corner cases, dangerous gotchas, and problems at scale, we fix the corner cases, remove the gotchas, and provide the tools that let you scale. **TJS is also a runtime.** A runtime that remembers your function declarations and can check whether parameter types are what they ought to be. It can guarantee safety by default, and speed when it's needed (including inline WASM). **AJS is another language.** It's a language for safe evaluation with injected capabilities and a gas limit. It's the language tjs allows you to Eval and use to create a SafeFunction. It also has its own VM and runtime to allow you to build **universal endpoints**. It's a language that's easy for agents to write and comprehend. It can be converted into an AST and run remotely. **TJS is also a toolchain.** It transpiles its own source into JavaScript — the transpiler is written in TypeScript, and running it through its own TS→TJS→JS pipeline yields a bootstrapped transpiler whose output matches the native one exactly (`src/use-cases/bootstrap.test.ts`). That's a compiler that processes its own source, not (yet) a compiler written in its own language. It transpiles TypeScript into TJS and then into JS. It turns function definitions into runtime contracts, documentation, and simple tests. It uses types both as contracts and examples. It allows inline tests of private module internals that disappear at runtime. It compresses transpilation, linting, testing, and documentation generation into a single fast pass. As for bundling? It allows it but it targets an unbundled web. ![TJS Platform Overview](docs/diagrams/platform-overview.svg) ## The Problem **TypeScript is fragile.** It pretends to be a superset of JavaScript, but it isn't. It pretends to be typesafe, but it isn't. Its Turing-complete type system is harder to reason about than the code it supposedly documents—and then it all disappears at runtime. TypeScript is also _difficult to transpile_. Your browser can run entire [full virtual machines](https://infinitemac.org/) in JavaScript, but most TypeScript playgrounds either fake transpilation by stripping type declarations or use a server backend to do the real work. **JavaScript is dangerous.** `eval()` and `Function()` are so powerful they're forbidden almost everywhere—blocked by CSP in most production environments. The industry's answer? The **Container Fallacy**: shipping a 200MB Linux OS just to run a 1KB function safely. We ship buildings to deliver letters. **Security is a mess.** Every layer validates. Gateway validates. Auth validates. Business logic validates. Database validates. We spend 90% of our time building pipelines to move data to code, re-checking it at every hop. ## What If? What if your language were: - **Honest** — types that actually exist at runtime, not fiction that evaporates - **Safe** — a gas-metered VM where infinite loops are impossible, no container required - **Mobile** — logic that travels to data, not oceans of data dragged to logic - **Unified** — one source of truth, not TypeScript interfaces _plus_ Zod schemas _plus_ JSDoc That's what TJS Platform provides: **TJS** for writing your infrastructure, and **AJS** for shipping logic that runs anywhere. ## TJS — Types That Survive Write typed JavaScript where the type _is_ an example. No split-brain validation. ```typescript // TJS: The type is an example AND a test function greet(name: 'World'): 'Hello, World!' { return `Hello, ${name}!` } // At transpile time: greet('World') is called and checked against 'Hello, World!' // Runtime: The type becomes a contract console.log(greet.__tjs.params) // { name: { type: { kind: 'string' }, required: true, … } } // Safety: Errors are values, not crashes const result = greet(123) // MonadicError: Expected string for '…greet.name', got number ``` **Why it matters:** - **One source of truth** — no more TS interfaces + Zod schemas + JSDoc comments - **Types as examples** — `name: 'Alice'` means "required string, like 'Alice'" - **Runtime metadata** — `__tjs` enables reflection, autocomplete, documentation from live objects - **Monadic errors** — type failures return values, never throw - **Zero build step** — transpiles in the browser, no webpack/Vite/Babel - **The compiler _is_ the client** — TJS transpiles itself _and_ TypeScript entirely client-side ![Compile Time and Runtime Flow](docs/diagrams/compile-runtime.svg) ## AJS — Code That Travels Write logic that compiles to JSON and runs in a gas-limited sandbox. Send agents to data instead of shipping data to code. ```typescript const agent = ajs` function research(topic: 'AI') { let data = httpFetch({ url: '/search?q=' + topic }) let summary = llmPredict({ prompt: 'Summarize: ' + JSON.stringify(data) }) return { topic, summary } } ` // Run it safely—no Docker required const result = await vm.run( agent, { topic: 'Agents' }, { fuel: 500, // Strict CPU budget capabilities: { fetch: http }, // YOUR fetch wrapper: the only network access (see guides/safe-eval.md) } ) ``` **Why it matters:** - **Safe eval** — run untrusted code without containers - **Code is JSON** — store in databases, diff, version, transmit - **Fuel metering** — every operation costs gas, infinite loops impossible - **Capability-based** — zero I/O by default, grant only what's needed - **LLM-native** — simple enough for small models to generate correctly ## The Architecture Shift ![Architecture Shift: Data-to-Code vs Code-to-Data](docs/diagrams/architecture-shift.svg) The agent carries its own validation. The server grants capabilities. Caching happens automatically because the query _is_ the code. ## Safe Eval `eval()` that is safe to hand untrusted code: fuel-metered so it always halts, and with no way out except the capabilities you give it. ```js import { Eval } from 'tjs-lang/eval' const { result } = await Eval({ code: 'items.filter(x => x.price < budget)', context: { items: [{ price: 40 }, { price: 250 }], budget: 100 }, fuel: 1000, }) console.log(result) // → [{"price":40}] ``` No CSP violations, no infinite loops, no access to anything you did not grant. **[Safe Eval](guides/safe-eval.md)** covers `SafeFunction`, network access through an injected `fetch`, and exactly what the sandbox guarantees and what it does not. ![Safe Eval: Capability-Based Security](docs/diagrams/safe-eval.svg) ## Quick Start ```bash npm install tjs-lang ``` ### Run an Agent ```typescript import { ajs, AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang' const agent = ajs` function double(value: 21) { return { result: value * 2 } } ` const vm = new AgentVM() const { result } = await vm.run(agent, { value: 21 }) console.log(result) // { result: 42 } ``` ### Write Typed Code ```typescript import { tjs } from 'tjs-lang' const { code, metadata } = tjs` function add(a: 0, b: 0): 0 { return a + b } ` // code: JavaScript with __tjs metadata attached // metadata: { add: { params: { a: { type: { kind: 'integer' }, example: 0, … }, b: { … } }, returns: { kind: 'integer' } } } ``` ### Try it in your browser Since TJS compiles itself, the full engine runs in the page. The documentation site runs its examples live, and you can edit them: **[tjs.tosijs.net](https://tjs.tosijs.net)** The older playground, [tjs-platform.web.app](https://tjs-platform.web.app), is still up for the multi-file examples that need it. ## At a Glance | | TypeScript | TJS | AJS | | --------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------- | | **Purpose** | Write your platform | Write your platform | Write your agents | | **Trust level** | Your code | Your code | Anyone's code | | **Compiles to** | JavaScript + `.d.ts` | JavaScript (with runtime checks + introspection) | JSON AST | | **Runs in** | Browser, Node, Bun | Browser, Node, Bun | Sandboxed VM | | **Types** | Static only (erased at runtime) | Examples → runtime validation | Schemas for I/O | | **Errors** | Exceptions | Monadic (values, not exceptions) | Monadic | | **Build step** | `tsc` → JS + `.d.ts` | Runs tests, builds docs, produces JS | None | > **Note:** TJS can transpile TypeScript into JS (via TJS) using `tjs convert`, giving your existing TS code > runtime type checks and introspection. You can even add inline tests using `/*test ...*/` comments > that run automatically during the build. ## Bundle Size The cost of "safe eval"—compare to a 200MB Docker image. **Measured at v0.14.0-rc.10 (main, 2026-11-11)**; each row is a standalone entry point, not an increment (import only what you need): | Entry point | Bundle | Size | Gzipped | | ----------------------------- | ---------------- | ------ | --------- | | `tjs-lang/vm-ast` (VM, no parser — recommended) | tjs-vm-ast.js | 137 KB | **43 KB** | | `tjs-lang/vm` (VM + transpiler) | tjs-vm.js | 321 KB | 99 KB | | `tjs-lang/eval` (safe eval) | tjs-eval.js | 201 KB | 64 KB | | `tjs-lang/batteries` | tjs-batteries.js | 11 KB | 4 KB | | `tjs-lang/lang` (transpiler) | tjs-lang.js | 411 KB | 132 KB | | `tjs-lang` (full, TS support) | index.js | 558 KB | 181 KB | | `tjs-lang/runtime` (runtime for emitted code) | tjs-runtime.js | 45 KB | 15 KB | | `tjs-lang/schema` (tosijs-schema + `$predicate`) | tjs-schema.js | 41 KB | 12 KB | | `tjs-lang/lang/from-ts` (TS converter; needs `typescript`) | tjs-from-ts.js | 49 KB | 16 KB | | `tjs-lang/browser` (self-contained, any CDN) | tjs-browser.js | 664 KB | 205 KB | | `tjs-lang/browser/from-ts` (lazy-loads `typescript`) | tjs-browser-from-ts.js | 51 KB | 16 KB | | `tjs-lang/css` (CSS validators) | tjs-css.js | 54 KB | 17 KB | | `tjs-lang/linalg` (SIMD kernels) | tjs-linalg.js | 14 KB | 4 KB | | `tjs-lang/import-resolver` (bare imports, no bundler) | tjs-import-resolver.js | 7 KB | 3 KB | | `tjs-lang/rbac` (rule primitives) | tjs-rbac.js | 5 KB | 2 KB | The transpiler grew ~11% in 0.14.0 — `Type` examples are now read for what they mean (floats, unions, recursive references) and checked by a real fixed-point solver, and it carries the linear regex engine (regex literals are checked at transpile time; `compilePredicate` runs on it). The VM without a parser roughly DOUBLED since rc.1 (21 KB to 41 KB gzipped, measured against the published rc.1; with the transpiler 71 KB to 93 KB; the regex engine is about 7 KB) for its budgets and its two membranes: every method guest code can call declares the exact type of each argument and what a call may allocate, and is charged for it before it runs; and guest regexes run on the VM's own linear-time engine instead of the host's backtracking one, so no pattern can hang a run ([`docs/vm-budgets.md`](docs/vm-budgets.md)). The VM and eval bundles got **23%** and **40%** smaller in 0.13.10, and not by optimising anything: giving AJS its own parser (`parseAgentSource`, see the CHANGELOG) meant the VM stopped bundling ~26 TJS-only source transforms it had no business running. Less code on the path that compiles untrusted input is a security property before it is a size one. > These numbers are **verified by `src/bundle-size.test.ts`**, which re-measures the built > bundles and fails if this table drifts — so they can go stale by at most one release. **Dependencies:** `acorn` + `acorn-walk`/`acorn-loose` (JS parsing), `tosijs-schema` (validation). All have zero transitive dependencies. ## Documentation - **[Documentation site](https://tjs.tosijs.net)** — Everything below, with live examples, plus the books as ePub - **[TJS Language Guide](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/blob/main/DOCS-TJS.md)** — Types, syntax, runtime - **[AJS Runtime Guide](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/blob/main/DOCS-AJS.md)** — VM, atoms, capabilities - **[WASM Quick Start](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/blob/main/docs/WASM-QUICKSTART.md)** — Build WASM-accelerated libraries with zero toolchain setup - **[Architecture Deep Dive](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/blob/main/CONTEXT.md)** — How it all fits together - **[Playground](https://tjs-platform.web.app)** — Try it now ## Installation ```bash # npm npm install tjs-lang # bun bun add tjs-lang # pnpm pnpm add tjs-lang ``` ### If you re-export a tjs-lang type from your own package A trap worth knowing about before you hit it — reported from `tosijs-ui` ([#28](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/issues/28)). `import type` is erased from emitted **JavaScript** but **not** from emitted **`.d.ts`**. So if your package does the natural thing: ```ts import type { AutocompleteConfig } from 'tjs-lang/editors/codemirror' export type MyConfig = AutocompleteConfig ``` your published `.d.ts` still contains that import — and every consumer of _your_ package now needs `tjs-lang` installed to typecheck, even if they never touch TJS: ``` error TS2307: Cannot find module 'tjs-lang/editors/codemirror' ``` **Declaring tjs-lang as an optional peer does not help.** Optionality governs installation, not type resolution; `tsc` still has to find the module to check the declaration. Three ways out, roughly in order of preference: 1. **Do not re-export the type.** Structurally duplicate what you need in your own declaration. Verbose, but your public API stops depending on ours. 2. **Make the dependency real** — a regular `dependency`, not an optional peer — if your package genuinely requires tjs-lang at type level. 3. **Inline the shape at the boundary** (`export type MyConfig = { … }`) so the import never reaches your `.d.ts`. This is not specific to tjs-lang; it catches any package that re-exports a type from an optional peer. It is documented here because we ship the types that invite it. ## Credits Logo animation by [@anicoremotion](https://pro.fiverr.com/freelancers/anicoremotion). ## License Apache 2.0

# TJS Interactive Examples

Try these examples in the playground! Each demonstrates a key TJS feature.

## In this section

<!-- prettier-ignore-start -->

<!-- toc -->
- [Featured](/tjs-featured/)
- [Basics](/tjs-basics/)
- [Patterns](/tjs-patterns/)
- [Advanced](/tjs-advanced/)
- [Full Stack](/tjs-fullstack/)
- [Unbundled](/tjs-unbundled/)
- [WASM Libraries](/tjs-wasmlib/)
<!-- /toc -->

<!-- prettier-ignore-end -->

## Types by Example

TJS types ARE example values - self-documenting and runtime-checkable:

```javascript
// The example IS the type AND the documentation
function greet(name: 'World', times: 3): '' {
  let result = ''
  for (let i = 0; i < times; i++) {
    result = result + `Hello, ${name}! `
  }
  return result.trim()
}

// greet.__tjs shows: name: string, times: number -> string
console.log(greet('TJS', 2)) // "Hello, TJS! Hello, TJS!"
```

## Type Declarations with Defaults

Define reusable types with the `Type` keyword:

```javascript
// Type with default value
Type Name = 'Anonymous'
Type Count = 0
Type PositiveAge = +18  // positive number

// Use types as parameter annotations
function introduce(name: Name, age: PositiveAge): '' {
  return `Hi, I'm ${name} and I'm ${age} years old`
}

console.log(introduce('Alice', 30))
console.log(Name.default)  // 'Anonymous'
```

## Generic Types

Runtime-checkable generics:

```javascript
// Define a generic Box<T> type
Generic Box<T> {
  description: 'a boxed value'
  predicate(obj, T) {
    return typeof obj === 'object' &&
           obj !== null &&
           'value' in obj &&
           T(obj.value)
  }
}

// Instantiate with different types
const StringBox = Box('')
const NumberBox = Box(0)

console.log(StringBox.check({ value: 'hello' }))  // true
console.log(StringBox.check({ value: 123 }))      // false
console.log(NumberBox.check({ value: 42 }))       // true
```

## Compile-Time Tests

Tests run during transpilation and evaporate from output:

```javascript
Type Email {
  example: 'test@example.com'
  predicate(x) {
    return typeof x === 'string' && x.includes('@')
  }
}

// This test runs at transpile time, not runtime
test 'email validation' {
  if (!Email.check('user@example.com')) {
    throw new Error('valid email should pass')
  }
  if (Email.check('not-an-email')) {
    throw new Error('invalid email should fail')
  }
}

// The test code is stripped from the transpiled output
function sendEmail(to: Email): { sent: true } {
  return { sent: true }
}
```

## Safety Markers

Control validation with `(!)` and `(?)`:

```javascript
// Default: safe function with validation
function safeAdd(a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  return a + b
}

// (!) Unsafe: skip input validation for performance
function fastAdd(! a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  return a + b
}

// (?) Force safe: always validate even if module is unsafe
function alwaysSafe(? data: { x: 0 }): 0 {
  return data.x * 2
}

console.log(safeAdd(1, 2))   // 3
console.log(fastAdd(1, 2))   // 3 (faster, no validation)
```

## SafeFunction and Eval

Safe replacements for `new Function()` and `eval()`. See **[Safe Eval](./safe-eval.md)**.

## Monadic Error Handling

Errors are values, not exceptions:

```javascript
function divide(a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  if (b === 0) {
    return error('Division by zero')
  }
  return a / b
}

const result = divide(10, 0)

if (isError(result)) {
  console.log('Error:', result.message)
} else {
  console.log('Result:', result)
}

// Errors propagate automatically through function chains
```

## Native Type Checking

Check platform types pragmatically:

```javascript
// typeOf returns constructor names for objects
console.log(typeOf(new Map())) // 'Map'
console.log(typeOf(new Date())) // 'Date'
console.log(typeOf([1, 2, 3])) // 'array'
console.log(typeOf(null)) // 'null'

// isNativeType checks prototype chain
console.log(isNativeType(new TypeError('oops'), 'Error')) // true
console.log(isNativeType(new Map(), 'Map')) // true
```

## Union Types

Use `||` for union types:

```javascript
Union Status 'task status' {
  'pending' | 'active' | 'done'
}

function updateTask(id: '', status: Status): { updated: true } {
  console.log(`Task ${id} -> ${status}`)
  return { updated: true }
}

updateTask('task-1', 'active')
```

## Unbundled Integration

TJS runs directly in the browser with no build step. Compare React (which requires bundling) with tosijs (which doesn't):

### React Todo App

This would be easier with JSX, but we're not supporting JSX build magic (yet).

```javascript
import { useState, createElement as h } from 'react'
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'

// Without JSX, we use createElement (aliased as h for brevity)
// h(type, props, ...children)

function TodoApp() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState(['bathe the cat', 'buy milk'])
  const [newItem, setNewItem] = useState('')

  const addItem = () => {
    if (newItem !== '') {
      setItems([...items, newItem])
      setNewItem('')
    }
  }

  return h(
    'div',
    null,
    h('h1', null, 'To Do'),
    h(
      'ul',
      null,
      items.map((item, i) => h('li', { key: i }, item))
    ),
    h(
      'label',
      null,
      'New item',
      h('input', {
        placeholder: 'enter thing to do',
        value: newItem,
        onChange: (e) => setNewItem(e.target.value),
      }),
      h(
        'button',
        {
          disabled: !newItem,
          onClick: addItem,
        },
        'Add'
      )
    )
  )
}

const root = document.createElement('div')
root.setAttribute('id', 'root')
document.body.append(root)
createRoot(root).render(h(TodoApp))
```

### tosijs Todo App

```javascript
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

const { todoApp } = tosi({
  todoApp: {
    items: ['bathe the cat', 'buy milk'],
    newItem: '',
    addItem() {
      if (todoApp.newItem !== '') {
        todoApp.items.push(String(todoApp.newItem))
        todoApp.newItem = ''
      }
    },
  },
})

const { h1, ul, template, li, label, input, button } = elements

document.body.append(
  h1('To Do'),
  ul(
    {
      bindList: {
        value: todoApp.items,
      },
    },
    template(li({ bindText: '^' }))
  ),
  label(
    'New item',
    input({ placeholder: 'enter thing to do', bindValue: todoApp.newItem }),
    button({ bindEnabled: todoApp.newItem, onClick: todoApp.addItem }, 'Add')
  )
)
```

The tosijs version:

- No JSX, no transpilation, no bundler
- Reactive bindings built-in
- Runs directly in browser via ES modules
- ~30KB total (vs React's 140KB+ minified)

## Running TJS

```bash
# CLI commands
tjs check file.tjs      # Type check
tjs run file.tjs        # Execute
tjs emit file.tjs       # Output JavaScript
tjs emit --debug file.tjs  # Include source locations

# Or use the Bun plugin for native support
bun --preload ./src/bun-plugin/tjs-plugin.ts file.tjs
```

# Learn to Program

Programming from scratch, in TJS, in your browser. You need nothing installed and no
experience.

If you already program, skip this part and start at [For Programmers](/for-programmers/),
which is written for working developers and has a chapter for JavaScript and one for
TypeScript.

**TJS** is a programming language built on JavaScript, the language every web browser runs.
Nearly everything you learn here is also JavaScript, so it carries over to the programs you
will meet anywhere on the web. TJS adds checks that catch your mistakes and explain them,
which makes it a good first language: when something goes wrong, it tells you.

## How the examples work

Every chapter is full of small programs that run on the page. You can change any of them, and
the result shows beside the program (or above it, on a phone) as you type. You cannot damage
anything: if a change goes badly, the example's undo button or its menu puts the original
back.

Most examples end with a **test**: a few lines that say what the program should do. The line
under the result turns green when the program does it and red when it does not, so you can
see when you have it right. The first chapter, How This Book Works, shows you all of this
before you need it, and Checking Your Work teaches you to write tests of your own.

## What you will learn

There are sixteen chapters, starting with How This Book Works. After it, you learn to:

- put words, headings and paragraphs on a page (Hello, Screen)
- work with numbers and text, and give them names so you can use them again (Values and
  Names)
- write **functions**: named pieces of program you can run as often as you like (Functions)
- write tests that check your programs (Checking Your Work)
- make a program choose what to do (Decisions)
- repeat work without writing it out every time (Repetition)
- keep lists of things (Lists)
- describe one thing with several named parts, such as a person's name and birth year
  (Things with Parts)
- respond when someone clicks a button or types (Responding to the Reader)
- find and fix mistakes (When Things Go Wrong)
- wait for something slow, such as a timer or information fetched from another computer
  (Things That Take Time)

A Calculator puts all of that together into a working pocket calculator. Three chapters
follow it:

- write a function that calls itself, and draw with it (Recursion)
- make a program that runs on a clock and is steered by the keyboard (Time and Events)
- build a game of Tetris, step by step, from everything before it (Tetris)

That is not a watered-down version of programming. Every program you will ever write is made
of the same few ideas: values (pieces of information, like numbers and words), names for
them, decisions, repetition, lists, things with parts, and functions. Real programs use more
of them, in bigger combinations, but nothing fundamentally different.

Some things this part leaves out. Classes (templates for making many similar things) and
modules (splitting a program across files) are covered later in this book. Servers (programs
that run on another computer, not in the page) are not in this book; the tjs-lang website has
a [Full Stack](/tjs-fullstack/) section about them. When you finish Tetris, go on to
[The TJS Language](/the-tjs-language/), which takes each feature in depth. Those chapters are
written for people who already program, so they move faster, but by then that is you.

## How to read this part

Read the chapters in order. Each one uses what came before, and each is short enough to
finish in a sitting.

Do the examples, not just read them. Change a number and see what happens; change it back.
Every chapter ends with a few **Try it** exercises, done in the examples on the page; where an
exercise has a test, the test tells you when you have it. If you get stuck, go back to the
last example that made sense and change one thing at a time. The exercises matter more than
the prose: reading about programming teaches you about as much as reading about swimming.

Expect to make mistakes. Programmers make them all day; the skill is noticing and fixing
them quickly. When you make one, TJS tells you what went wrong and where: for example, that
you gave it a word where it needed a number. You will see those messages often, and by the
end of the part you will read them the way you read a road sign.

For a one-page overview of the whole language, see [TJS: Typed JavaScript](/tjs/), the quick
start on the tjs-lang website. It is not part of this book and is written for programmers.

# TJS: Typed JavaScript

TJS is a typed superset of JavaScript where **types are examples**.

```javascript
function greet(name: 'World', times: 3): 'Hello, World! Hello, World! Hello, World!' {
  let result = ''
  let i = 0
  while (i < times) {
    result = result + `Hello, ${name}! `
    i = i + 1
  }
  return result.trim()
}
```

## In this section

<!-- prettier-ignore-start -->

<!-- toc -->
- [TJS Interactive Examples](/tjs-examples/)
- [TJS: Typed JavaScript](/DOCS-TJS/)
- [TJS for JavaScript Programmers](/TJS-FOR-JS/)
- [JS Footguns That TJS Quietly Fixes](/footguns/)
- [AJS Patterns](/patterns/)
- [WASM in TJS](/DOCS-WASM/)
- [WASM Quick Start](/WASM-QUICKSTART/)
- [Playground Imports](/playground-imports/)
- [Context: Working with tosijs-schema](/tosijs-schema/)
- [TJS Performance Guide](/performance/)
<!-- /toc -->

<!-- prettier-ignore-end -->

## Philosophy

TJS takes a different approach to typing than TypeScript:

| Aspect         | TypeScript                              | TJS                           |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Types          | Abstract declarations                   | Concrete examples             |
| Runtime        | Erased completely                       | Preserved as metadata         |
| Validation     | Compile-time only                       | Runtime optional              |
| Learning curve | Learn type syntax                       | Use values you know           |
| Error messages | "Type 'string' is not assignable to..." | "Expected string, got number" |

### Why Examples?

Consider how you'd explain a function to another developer:

> "This function takes a name like 'World' and a count like 3, and returns a greeting string"

That's exactly how TJS works. The example _is_ the type:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```javascript
// TypeScript
function greet(name: string, times: number): string

// TJS - the example IS the documentation
function greet(name: 'World', times: 3): ''
```

## Core Concepts

### 1. Types by Example

Instead of abstract type names, use example values:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```javascript
// Strings
name: ''           // any string
name: 'default'    // string with default value

// Numbers
count: 0           // any number
port: 8080         // number with default

// Booleans
enabled: true      // boolean (default true)
disabled: false    // boolean (default false)

// Arrays
items: ['']        // array of strings
numbers: [0]       // array of numbers
mixed: [0, '']     // tuple: number, string

// Objects
user: { name: '', age: 0 }  // object with shape

// Null/Undefined
nullable: null
optional: undefined
```

### 2. Required vs Optional (`:` vs `=`)

The colon `:` means required, equals `=` means optional:

```javascript
function createUser(
  name: 'Anonymous', // required string
  email: 'user@example.com', // required string
  age = 0, // optional number (defaults to 0)
  role = 'user' // optional string (defaults to 'user')
):! { id: '', name: '', email: '', age: 0, role: '' } {
  return {
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),
    name,
    email,
    age,
    role,
  }
}

// Valid calls:
createUser('Alice', 'alice@example.com')
createUser('Bob', 'bob@example.com', 30)
createUser('Carol', 'carol@example.com', 25, 'admin')

// Invalid - missing required params:
createUser('Dave') // Error: missing required parameter 'email'
```

### 3. Return Type Annotation

Use `:` to declare the return type:

```javascript
function add(a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  return a + b
}

function getUser(id: ''): { name: '', email: '' } | null {
  // Returns user object or null
}
```

### 4. Union Types

Use `|` for unions (same as TypeScript):

```javascript
function parseInput(value: '' | 0 | null):! '' {
  if (value === null) return 'null'
  if (typeof value === 'number') return `number: ${value}`
  return `string: ${value}`
}
```

### 5. The `any` Type

When you genuinely don't know the type:

```javascript
function identity(x: any): any {
  return x
}
```

Generics from TypeScript become `any` but preserve metadata:

```javascript
// TypeScript: function identity<T>(x: T): T
// TJS: any, but __tjs.typeParams captures the generic info
function identity(x: any): any {
  return x
}
// identity.__tjs.typeParams = { T: {} }
```

### 6. Type Declarations

Define reusable types with the `Type` keyword:

```javascript
// Type with default value (= syntax)
Type Name = 'Alice'
Type Count = 0
Type Age = +18              // positive number

// Type with description and example
Type User {
  description: 'a registered user'
  example: { name: '', age: 0 }
}

// Type with predicate (auto-generates type guard from example)
Type EvenNumber {
  example: 2
  predicate(x) { return x % 2 === 0 }
}

// Complex validation with predicate
Type Email {
  example: 'test@example.com'
  predicate(x) { return /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(x) }
}
```

**Default vs Example:**

- `= value` sets a **default** for instantiation
- `example:` in block sets an **example** for testing/documentation
- When both are present, they serve different purposes

When `example` and `predicate` are provided, the type guard auto-checks the example's shape, then your predicate refines it.

### 7. Generic Declarations

Define parameterized types with the `Generic` keyword:

```javascript
// Simple generic
Generic Box<T> {
  description: 'a boxed value'
  predicate(x, T) {
    return typeof x === 'object' && x !== null && 'value' in x && T(x.value)
  }
}

// Generic with default type parameter
Generic Container<T, U = ''> {
  description: 'container with label'
  predicate(obj, T, U) {
    return T(obj.item) && U(obj.label)
  }
}
```

In the predicate, `T` and `U` are type-checking functions that validate values against the provided type parameters.

### 8. Bare Assignments

Uppercase identifiers automatically get `const`:

```javascript
// These are equivalent:
Foo = Type('test', 'example')
const Foo = Type('test', 'example')

// Works for any uppercase identifier
MyConfig = { debug: true }
const MyConfig = { debug: true }
```

Native-TJS only — off for plain JS (`dialect: 'js'`),
TS, and VM code. Fires only on the **first** assignment of an undeclared
uppercase name; a reassignment of an already-declared binding
(`let B = null; … B = 2`) is untouched. Because the first assignment becomes
`const`, declare `let Foo` if you need `Foo` to change later.

## Runtime Features

### Monadic Error Handling

TJS functions propagate errors automatically — when a `MonadicError` arrives where it does
not fit the parameter's type:

```javascript
// processData(input: { rows: [0] }) — a MonadicError is not { rows: [0] }
const result = processData(maybeError)
// If maybeError is a MonadicError, result is that same error (the body does not run)

// Check for errors
if (isMonadicError(result)) {
  console.log(result.message)
}
```

The rule is decided at the type check. A function that declares it takes anything
(`x: any`, `x: unknown`) receives the error and runs; that is how a handler works. A
plain `Error` (from `new Error()` or a `catch`) where something else is expected is an
ordinary type error, not a pass-through.

### The Flight Recorder

Since monadic errors don't throw, they can silently vanish. TJS keeps a bounded ring of what the runtime noticed, so you always know what failed:

```javascript
greet(42) // returns MonadicError, caller ignores it

// Find it later
__tjs.errors() // → recent type errors (newest last, max 64)
__tjs.clearErrors() // → clear and return them
__tjs.getErrorCount() // → total since last clear

// Testing pattern: clear → run → check
__tjs.clearErrors()
runMyCode()
if (__tjs.errors().length > 0) {
  console.log('Unexpected type errors!')
}
```

On by default. Zero cost on the happy path — only writes when something happens.

#### It records more than errors

The failures that cost you a week are rarely the loud ones. A `wasm{}` block that quietly fell back to JavaScript is _fine_ — until your page claims "⚡ SIMD" and is running plain JS. A typed array passed without `wasmBuffer()` is _fine_ — except it's copied in and out on every call, and can be **slower** than the JS it replaced. Nothing throws. Every test is green.

So the runtime records those too, and `records()` gives you the whole flight:

```javascript
__tjs.records() // → everything: type errors, wasm fallbacks, VM failures…
__tjs.records({ source: 'wasm' }) // → filter by source…
__tjs.records({ severity: 'notice' }) // → …and/or severity

// Your own code can report. Record what you'd want after an incident,
// not just what you're certain is broken.
__tjs.record({
  source: 'app',
  severity: 'notice',
  message: 'cache miss on user lookup',
  data: { userId: 42 },
})

__tjs.getRecordCount() // → total, every severity
__tjs.getDroppedCount() // → how many were lost to ring wrap
```

Each entry carries a `source` (`type`, `wasm`, `vm`, `predicate`, `app`, …) and a `severity` (`error`, `warning`, `notice`).

Two rules make it trustworthy:

- **`errors()` stays narrow.** It returns type errors and _only_ type errors. If notices leaked into it, every `clearErrors() → run → expect none` test would start failing on things that aren't errors.
- **Recording never changes behavior.** It doesn't throw, doesn't log unbidden, and doesn't touch control flow — a recorder that alters the flight isn't a recorder. It also fires once per site, never once per call, so it can't become the performance problem it exists to detect.

The bias is deliberate: a false alarm costs one slot in a ring buffer, while a missing entry costs a debugging session with no evidence. When in doubt, it records.

### Safe by Default

TJS functions are wrapped with runtime type validation by default:

```javascript
function add(a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  return a + b
}

add(1, 2) // 3
add('1', 2) // Error: expected number, got string
add(null, 2) // Error: expected number, got null
```

This provides excellent error messages and catches type mismatches at runtime.

### Safety Markers

`(! a: 0)` turns off validation for the function. `: 2` is a worked example, tested at
transpile time. `:! 0` declares the return type only. `:? 2` tests the example and checks
every result at run time.

See the [TJS Syntax Reference](/TJS-SYNTAX/) and [Safety and Validation](/safety-markers/).

### There Is No `unsafe { }` Block

There is no `unsafe` block, and the old `unsafe <expr>` prefix is deprecated. The wrapper
decision is made at transpile time, so a block could not skip anything a marker does not
already skip.

Mark the whole function `!` when it is a hot path over trusted data:

```javascript
function sum(! numbers: [0]): 0 {
  let total = 0
  for (let i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {
    total += numbers[i]
  }
  return total
}
```

### Performance Characteristics

| Mode              | Overhead   | Use Case                                 |
| ----------------- | ---------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `safety none`     | 1.0x       | Metadata only, no wrappers               |
| `safety inputs`   | ~1.15-1.3x | Production with validation               |
| `safety all`      | ~14x       | Debug — validates inputs and outputs     |
| `(!)` function    | 1.0x       | Hot paths — explicit opt-out             |
| `(!)` on a helper | 1.0x       | Hot loops — mark the helper, not a block |

Use `(!)` for internal functions that are called frequently with known-good data. Keep public APIs safe.

### SafeFunction and Eval

Safe replacements for `eval()` and `new Function()` — fuel-metered, time-limited, and with no
ambient authority: the code can reach only what you pass it. See **[Safe Eval](./safe-eval.md)**, which covers the API, what the
sandbox guarantees, and what it does not.

## Testing

### Compile-Time Tests

Tests run at **transpile time** and are stripped from output:

```javascript
Type Email {
  example: 'test@example.com'
  predicate(x) { return x.includes('@') }
}

// This test runs during transpilation
test 'email validation' {
  if (!Email.check('user@example.com')) {
    throw new Error('valid email should pass')
  }
  if (Email.check('invalid')) {
    throw new Error('invalid email should fail')
  }
}

function sendEmail(to: Email) {
  // ...
}
```

The transpiled output contains only:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```javascript
const Email = Type('Email', ...)
function sendEmail(to) { ... }
```

The test code **evaporates** - it verified correctness at build time.

### Emitting When Tests Fail

`tjs emit --jfdi file.tjs` emits even when tests fail.

## Differences from JavaScript

### Removed/Discouraged

| Feature  | Reason                                                       |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `var`    | Use `let` or `const` — `var` is an error in `.tjs`           |
| `new`    | Classes are callable without `new`                           |
| `throw`  | Return errors as values (monadic errors)                     |
| `eval()` | Use `Eval()` or `SafeFunction()` — bare `eval()` is an error |
| `Date`   | Use `Timestamp`/`LegalDate`, or `LegacyDate(x)`              |

### Added

| Feature           | Purpose                                                        |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `: example`       | Required parameter with type                                   |
| `= example`       | Optional parameter with default                                |
| `: example`       | Return worked example, tested at transpile time                |
| `:? example`      | Return worked example, plus a runtime check                    |
| `:! example`      | Return type only                                               |
| `(!)`             | Skip input validation for the function                         |
| `test 'name' {}`  | Compile-time test block (evaporates)                           |
| `mock {}`         | Test setup block                                               |
| `\|` in types    | Union types                                                    |
| `Type Name = val` | Define runtime type with default                               |
| `Generic<T>`      | Define a parameterized runtime type                            |
| `Foo = ...`       | Bare assignment — auto-`const` (native TJS, first assign only) |
| `SafeFunction`    | Safe typed async replacement for `Function`                    |
| `Eval`            | Safe typed async replacement for `eval()`                      |

## Differences from TypeScript

### Types are Values

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```typescript
// TypeScript - abstract type
interface User {
  name: string
  age: number
  email?: string
}

// TJS - concrete example
Type User {
  example: { name: '', age: 0, email: '' }
}
```

### Runtime Preservation

TypeScript erases types at compile time. TJS preserves them:

```javascript
function greet(name: 'World'): 'Hello, World!' {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`
}

// At runtime:
greet.__tjs = {
  params: { name: { type: 'string', required: true } },
  returns: { type: 'string' },
}
```

This enables:

- Runtime validation
- Auto-generated documentation
- API schema generation
- Better error messages

### Generics

TypeScript generics become `any` in TJS, but constraints are preserved:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```typescript
// TypeScript
function process<T extends { id: number }>(item: T): T

// TJS - constraint becomes validatable schema
function process(item: any): any
// process.__tjs.typeParams = { T: { constraint: '{ id: 0 }' } }
```

The constraint `{ id: number }` becomes the example `{ id: 0 }` - and can be validated at runtime!

### No Type Gymnastics

TJS doesn't support:

- Conditional types
- Mapped types
- Template literal types
- `infer` keyword

If you need these, you probably need to rethink your approach. TJS favors simple, explicit types over clever type-level programming.

## The `__tjs` Metadata

Every TJS function has attached metadata:

```javascript
function createUser(name: 'Anonymous', age = 0):! { id: '', name: '', age: 0 } {
  return { id: crypto.randomUUID(), name, age }
}

createUser.__tjs = {
  params: {
    name: { type: 'string', required: true, default: 'Anonymous' },
    age: { type: 'number', required: false, default: 0 },
  },
  returns: {
    type: 'object',
    shape: { id: 'string', name: 'string', age: 'number' },
  },
  // For generic functions:
  typeParams: {
    T: { constraint: '{ id: 0 }', default: null },
  },
}
```

This metadata enables:

1. **Runtime validation** via `wrap()`
2. **Documentation generation** via `generateDocs()`
3. **API schema export** (OpenAPI, JSON Schema)
4. **IDE autocompletion**
5. **Version-safe serialization**

## CLI Tools

### `tjs` - The TJS Compiler

```bash
tjs check file.tjs      # Parse and type check
tjs emit file.tjs       # Output transpiled JavaScript
tjs run file.tjs        # Transpile and execute
tjs types file.tjs      # Output type metadata as JSON
```

### `tjsx` - Quick Execution

```bash
tjsx script.tjs                    # Run a TJS file
tjsx script.tjs --name=value       # Pass arguments
tjsx -e "function f() { return 42 }"  # Evaluate inline
echo '{"x": 1}' | tjsx script.tjs --json  # JSON from stdin
```

### Bun Plugin - Native `.tjs` Support

Run `.tjs` files directly with Bun using the preload plugin:

```bash
# Run a single file
bun --preload ./src/bun-plugin/tjs-plugin.ts script.tjs

# Enable globally in bunfig.toml
[run]
preload = ["./src/bun-plugin/tjs-plugin.ts"]
```

The plugin transpiles `.tjs` files on-the-fly with full runtime support (Type, Generic, Union, etc.).

## Best Practices

### 1. Use Examples That Document

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```javascript
// Bad - meaningless example
function send(to: '', subject: '', body: '') {}

// Good - self-documenting
function send(
  to: 'user@example.com',
  subject: 'Hello!',
  body: 'Message content here...'
) {}
```

### 2. Validate at Boundaries

```javascript
// Public API - safe by default
export function createUser(name: '', email: ''):! { id: '', name: '', email: '' } {
  return createUserImpl(name, email)
}

// Internal - mark as unsafe for speed
function createUserImpl(! name: '', email: ''):! { id: '', name: '', email: '' } {
  return { id: crypto.randomUUID(), name, email }
}
```

### 3. Return Errors, Don't Throw

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```javascript
// Bad
function divide(a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  if (b === 0) throw new Error('Division by zero')
  return a / b
}

// Good
function divide(a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  if (b === 0) return error('Division by zero')
  return a / b
}
```

### 4. Keep Types Simple

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```javascript
// Bad - over-engineered
function process(data: {
  items: [{ id: '', meta: { created: 0, tags: [''] } }],
}) {}

// Good - extract complex types
const Item = { id: '', meta: { created: 0, tags: [''] } }
function process(data: { items: [Item] }) {}
```

## Transpilation

TJS transpiles to standard JavaScript:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```javascript
// Input (TJS)
function greet(name: 'World'): '' {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`
}

// Output (JavaScript)
function greet(name = 'World') {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`
}
greet.__tjs = {
  params: { name: { type: 'string', required: true, default: 'World' } },
  returns: { type: 'string' },
}
```

The output is valid ES modules that work with any bundler (Vite, esbuild, webpack, Bun).

## Further Reading

- [Performance guide](./performance.md) - Performance characteristics
- [ajs.md](./ajs.md) - The sandboxed agent language
- [API Documentation](./docs/) - Generated from source

# AJS: Code That Travels to Data

AJS is a subset of JavaScript for code you do not trust: agents written by a language model,
scripts submitted by users, logic sent from another service. It is the familiar syntax with
the dangerous parts left out, and it never runs as JavaScript.

An AJS program goes through three steps:

1. **Transpile.** The source is parsed and checked on the side that owns it, and becomes a
   versioned JSON AST. Mistakes are refused here, with a message that says what to write
   instead.
2. **Ship.** The AST is plain JSON, so it can be stored in a database, sent over the network,
   or inspected before anything runs it. This is what the title means: instead of pulling the
   data out to wherever the code lives, you send the program to the service that holds the
   data. The data stays put, the host decides what the program may touch, and the program can
   be read before it runs.
3. **Run.** The AJS VM executes the AST. Every step costs fuel, so a runaway agent stops. The
   VM can reach nothing by default: no network, no storage, no model. The host passes each
   one in for this run as a capability, an object of functions given to `vm.run` (the
   quickstart below passes `capabilities: { llm: { predict } }`).

Fuel is counted in small units. An expression node costs 0.01, a variable write 0.1, an
`httpFetch` 5 and a model call 100; a run's default budget is 1000.

The VM is the security boundary, and it only has to be correct and safe. Being helpful is the
transpiler's job: it rejects bad programs before they reach the VM and explains the fix.

The built-in operations an agent calls, such as `llmPredict`, `httpFetch` or `storeGet`, are
**atoms**. An atom takes one object of named inputs, `storeSet({ key, value })`, and the
transpiler refuses a positional call, `storeSet('k', v)` (refused). Some JavaScript is left out, and
each refusal names the replacement: there is no C-style `for` (use `for...of`, or `while` with
a counter), and no `throw`, because an error is a value, not an exception that could escape
into the host (call `Error('message')`, which a `try`/`catch` can take). [The language
guide](/DOCS-AJS/) lists every rule.

## Who this book is for

- **Embedders** run AJS inside an application or a service. You decide what an agent may do:
  which capabilities it gets, how much fuel, how many model calls. Start with the quickstart
  below, then [Embedding the AJS VM](/ajs-host/), [Capabilities and Custom
  Atoms](/ajs-capabilities/) and [Safe Eval](/safe-eval/) (the same VM as a drop-in for
  `eval`).
- **Agent authors**, people or models, write the programs. You need the language rules and
  the atom list. Start with the first agent below, then [the language guide](/DOCS-AJS/),
  [the examples](/ajs-examples/) and the [Atom Reference](/ajs-atoms/). The [LLM system
  prompt](/ajs-llm-prompt/) is the same material written for a model.

## A first agent

On the doc site this agent runs in the page, called with no arguments, and its result appears
below the code:

```ajs
function shortlist({ items = [
  { name: 'kettle', price: 40 },
  { name: 'toaster', price: 25 },
  { name: 'blender', price: 90 },
], maxPrice = 50 }) {
  let affordable = items.filter((item) => item.price <= maxPrice)
  let names = affordable.map((item) => item.name)
  let total = affordable.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0)
  return { names, total }
}
```

It returns `{ names: ['kettle', 'toaster'], total: 65 }` for about 5 fuel. The shape is the
one every agent has: one destructured object in, one plain object out, so agents compose.

A parameter's value sets its type. `maxPrice = 50` is a default, used when the caller leaves
`maxPrice` out, and it makes `maxPrice` an integer: `{ maxPrice: 49.5 }` is refused. Write
`50.0` to accept any number. A colon (`maxPrice: 50`) would make the argument required, with
`50` as an example of its type.

## Quickstart for embedders

The host transpiles the agent, then runs the AST on `tjs-lang/vm-ast`, the VM build with no
parser in it. This agent asks a model for a summary, so the host grants it a model, here a
stand-in function, and allows exactly one call:

```typescript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang' // where the source is handled
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast' // where the agent runs

const source = `
/**
 * Summarize a list of notes in one line.
 * @param notes - the notes to summarize
 */
function summarize({ notes = ['buy milk'], style = 'terse' }): { summary: '', count: 0 } {
  if (notes.length == 0) {
    return { summary: '', count: 0 }
  }
  let summary = llmPredict({
    prompt: \`Summarize, \${style}: \${notes.join('; ')}\`,
  })
  return { summary, count: notes.length }
}
`

// Model-written source is untrusted input to the parser too, so cap its size.
// A bad program throws here (see below); catch it where you accept submissions.
const { ast } = transpile(source, { maxSourceBytes: 64 * 1024 })

const vm = new AgentVM()
const { result, error, fuelUsed } = await vm.run(
  ast,
  { notes: ['ship the release', 'write the docs'] },
  {
    fuel: 1000, // the time budget: every step costs fuel
    capabilities: {
      // the only model this agent can reach; a real host calls its LLM here
      llm: { predict: async (prompt) => `summary of: ${prompt}` },
    },
    quotas: { llmPredict: 1 }, // at most one model call, whatever the fuel allows
  }
)

if (error) console.log(error.op, error.message)
else console.log(result, fuelUsed)
// { summary: 'summary of: Summarize, terse: ship the release; write the docs',
//   count: 2 }  101.4  (the model call is 100 fuel; the rest is about 1.4)
```

**Transpiling** reports a bad program by throwing. Had the agent used `throw`, `transpile`
would throw a `TranspileError` with `'throw' is not supported in AsyncJS. Use
Error('message') to trigger error flow`, plus the line and column. Source over
`maxSourceBytes` is refused the same way, before it is parsed.

**Running** never throws for a failing agent. `vm.run` returns `{ result, error, fuelUsed }`,
and on failure `error` is an `AgentError` naming the step that failed (`error.op`) and why
(`error.message`). `result` then holds the same error object, so check `error` first.
Changing one thing above shows each guard:

| Change                                | `error.op`   | `error.message`                                              |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| leave out `capabilities`              | `llmPredict` | `Capability 'llm.predict' missing`                           |
| `fuel: 1`                             | `varAssign`  | `Out of Fuel`                                                |
| call `llmPredict` twice in the agent  | `llmPredict` | `Quota exceeded for 'llmPredict': 1 call allowed`            |
| `{ notes: 'x' }` as the arguments     | `vm.run`     | `Input validation failed: args do not match expected schema` |
| return `{ summary, count, debug: 1 }` | `vm.run`     | `Result does not match the declared result type`             |

With `fuel: 1`, `error.op` is whichever step was running when the fuel ran out; here that is
the first assignment. The fourth row is the parameters at work: they are the agent's input
contract, checked before it runs. The declared result after the parameter list,
`: { summary: '', count: 0 }`, is the output contract, checked when the agent returns.

The `llmPredict` atom calls `capabilities.llm.predict`, and quotas are keyed by atom name. The
[Atom Reference](/ajs-atoms/) lists the capability every atom needs.

Two more things the quickstart relies on:

- **Transpile outside the VM.** `tjs-lang/vm-ast` refuses source, with a message saying where
  to transpile, and a VM that cannot parse has no parser defect for a payload to reach.
  Passing source to `vm.run` on `tjs-lang/vm` still works and is deprecated. For agents you
  wrote yourself, the `ajs` tagged template (from `tjs-lang`) turns source into an AST in one
  step, with no `signature` and no size cap.
- **The other limits have safe defaults.** Wall-clock time, live memory and the size of a
  value crossing a capability are all bounded; [Run options](/ajs-host/#run-options) lists
  them.

## Agents as tools

`transpile` also returns a `signature`: the entry function's name, its JSDoc description and
its parameters. `createAgent` wraps an agent as an async function, and `getToolDefinitions`
turns such functions into OpenAI-style tool definitions. When the model answers with a tool
call, dispatch it by name:

```javascript
const tools = { shortlist: createAgent(shortlistSource, new AgentVM(), { fuel: 1000 }) }
const definitions = getToolDefinitions(tools) // offer these to the model

// the model replies with a tool call
const call = { function: { name: 'shortlist', arguments: '{"maxPrice":30}' } }
await tools[call.function.name](JSON.parse(call.function.arguments))
// { names: ['toaster'], total: 25 }
```

Here `shortlistSource` is the first agent's source as a string. The function `createAgent`
returns resolves to the run's `result`, which on failure is the `AgentError`. It also parses
where it runs, with no size cap, so use it only for agents you wrote. The full version is in
[Agents as tools](/ajs-host/#agents-as-tools).

## Reading path

1. **The language.** [The AJS Language](/DOCS-AJS/): what is allowed and forbidden, the
   input and output contract, builtins, errors, and the JSON AST format.
2. **Examples.** [AJS Examples](/ajs-examples/): runnable agents, from string handling to API
   calls and model pipelines.
3. **Patterns.** [AJS Patterns](/patterns/): what to write instead of `break`, `switch`,
   retries and parallel calls, and which of those belong to the host.
4. **Safe Eval.** [Safe Eval](/safe-eval/): the same VM as `Eval` and `SafeFunction`, for
   running snippets in place of `eval()` and `new Function()`.
5. **Embedding.** [Embedding the AJS VM](/ajs-host/): run options, fuel, timeouts, the heap
   ceiling, quotas, and what `vm.run` returns.
6. **Capabilities.** [Capabilities and Custom Atoms](/ajs-capabilities/), then [The universal
   endpoint](/universal-endpoint/) for one capability model shared by browser and server.
7. **Atom reference.** [Atom Reference](/ajs-atoms/): every atom, including the batteries
   (optional atoms for a local model and vector search).
8. **The LLM prompt.** [AJS LLM System Prompt](/ajs-llm-prompt/): a system prompt for models
   that write AJS.
9. **Internals.** [VM budgets](/vm-budgets/) (how fuel and the heap ceiling stay true) and
   [Technical Context](/CONTEXT/) (the VM's architecture).

**Design notes, not yet shipped:** the [native VM](/ajs-native-vm/) (Rust compiled to wasm),
the [Lean specification](/ajs-lean-spec/), and [Pattern](/pattern/), the planned replacement
for regex. AJS supports regex today, on the VM's own linear-time engine; see [Regular
expressions](/DOCS-AJS/#regular-expressions).

To run the model examples on your own machine, see [Running a local model (LM
Studio)](/lm-studio-setup/) or [Local models with MLX](/mlx-setup/).

# TypeScript: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly

What TypeScript gets right, where it leaks, and what TJS does about it.

TypeScript won, and it deserved to. This chapter opens the TypeScript book, and the book
is not an argument against TypeScript. It is an argument about one decision at its core,
that types are erased before the program runs, and about what follows from that decision:
what it makes cheap, what it makes impossible, and what grew up around the gap.

The argument in one sentence: **a TypeScript type is a claim about a value that nobody
checks when the value arrives.** TJS keeps the claim, writes it as an example, and checks
it at run time. In TJS, `a: 2` means "an integer, for example 2", not the literal type
`2`; [Examples as contracts](#examples-as-contracts), below, explains it before any TJS
code appears. Everything else in this chapter is a consequence of that difference.

Most claims here come with a program you can run. The `ts` examples are real TypeScript:
the page converts them with the same converter you would use on your own code
(`fromTS`) and runs the result. The `tjs` examples are TJS. Edit any of them and run it
again. A block marked `typescript` (there is one, in The Ugly) is for reading only. Each
`console.log` is followed by a comment showing what it prints.

## Who this book is for

The book is for TypeScript programmers deciding whether TJS is worth their time, and for
those who have decided and want to move code across. There are two ways to use TJS, and
the rest of the book follows the split:

- **Stay in TypeScript and use TJS at the edges.** Your code stays `.ts` and you keep
  `tsc`. You call TJS's libraries from it: safe eval (run code you did not write, with a
  budget and no access to anything you did not hand it), the agent VM (AJS, which runs
  untrusted programs under a fuel limit), and runtime-checked types where data comes in.
  You can also turn on runtime checks file by file without leaving TypeScript.
- **Migrate.** You convert `.ts` files to TJS, one file at a time. Conversion is a
  faithful translation: a converted file behaves exactly as `tsc`'s output would. The
  checks this chapter describes start when you mark a file `TjsStrict` or graduate it to
  native TJS (both are defined [below](#four-states-of-a-file)).

[TJS for TypeScript Programmers](../../TJS-FOR-TS.md) is organized the same way: Part 1
is the first path, Part 2 the second. Read this chapter first either way; it explains why
the second path exists.

## The Good

TypeScript solved real problems, and TJS keeps as many of those solutions as it can.

- **Your editor knows what things are.** Autocomplete, go-to-definition, rename across a
  codebase. This is the reason most teams adopt it, and it is worth the price.
- **Intent is written down.** A signature like `function ship(order: Order): Receipt` is
  documentation that cannot drift out of the file, because it is the file.
- **Refactoring is safer.** Change a field name and the compiler lists every place that
  used it.
- **Adoption is gradual.** You can rename one `.js` file to `.ts` and stop there.
- **It is still JavaScript.** Remove the annotations and you have the program. Nothing
  new happens at run time, so nothing new can go wrong at run time.

TJS reads TypeScript rather than replacing it. The converter turns `.ts` files into TJS,
and TJS emits `.d.ts` files so TypeScript consumers keep their types (with one gap for
generics, covered in [What TJS does not fix](#what-tjs-does-not-fix)). Plain TypeScript
keeps its meaning. The example below has nothing TJS-specific in it, and that is the point:
it goes through the converter and prints what `tsc`'s output would print.

```ts:inline
interface Item {
  name: string
  price: number
}

function total(items: Item[]): number {
  return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0)
}

const cart: Item[] = [
  { name: 'pen', price: 1.5 },
  { name: 'pad', price: 3.25 },
]
console.log('total:', total(cart)) // total: 4.75
```

The last item on that list, nothing new happens at run time, is also the root of
everything in The Bad. First, what TJS keeps in place of an erased type.

## Examples as contracts

What TJS keeps instead of an erased type is an example. One example does four jobs:

```tjs:inline
function add(a: 2, b: 3): 5 {
  return a + b
}

console.log(add(10, 20)) // 30
console.log(add('10', 20)) // MonadicError: Expected integer for '…add.a', got string
console.log(add(1.5, 2)) // MonadicError: Expected integer for '…add.a', got number
```

- **Type.** `2` is an integer, so `a` accepts integers. `add('10', 20)` returns an error
  instead of `'1020'`.
- **Documentation.** The signature shows a real call and its real result.
- **Test.** The return annotation is a worked example. At build time TJS calls
  `add(2, 3)` and compares the result with `5`. Change the body to `a - b` and the build
  fails, with no test file and no test runner.
- **Metadata.** The function carries its signature at run time (`add.__tjs`), so
  documentation, JSON Schema and editor tooling read it from the value itself.

This is the most common misreading of TJS, so it is worth saying plainly: `: 5` is not
the literal type `5`. It is an example, and `a: 2` accepts every integer.

How a number is written decides which numbers it accepts. `42` is an integer, so
`add(1.5, 2)` above is refused. `3.14`, or `0.0`, is a float and accepts any number. `+0`
is a non-negative integer. The converter maps TypeScript's `number` to `0.0`, the widest
of the three, so converted code keeps accepting `1.5`. That is why the TJS examples below
write prices as `80.0`: a price is not always whole.

Two markers change what TJS does with a signature:

| Marker                             | Where                         | Meaning                                                                              |
| ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `!` (`function hot(! x: 0)`)       | first, inside the parameters  | skip input validation for this function                                              |
| `:!` (`function f(x: 0):! 0 { }`) | in place of the return colon  | the return example is a type only, not a worked test; the converter writes this for a TypeScript return type |

### Four states of a file

The rest of the chapter refers to a file being in one of these states:

- **TypeScript.** A `.ts` file, compiled by `tsc` as usual.
- **Converted.** The same file run through the converter (`fromTS`, or `tjs convert`). It
  keeps JavaScript's semantics: `==` coerces and parameters are not checked.
- **`TjsStrict`.** A `.ts` file whose first line is `/* @tjs TjsStrict */`. To `tsc` it is
  a comment and changes nothing. To the converter it says "make this full TJS", so every
  parameter is checked. Only code that goes through the converter gets the checks; the
  `tsc` output of the same file has none.
- **Native TJS (graduated).** A `.tjs` file. Graduation is the step that turns a converted
  file into one; [Converting a TypeScript Project](ts-converting-a-project.md) covers it.

Most examples in this chapter use `TjsStrict`, because it is the shortest way to see the
checks on TypeScript source.

## The Bad

### Types are erased

The compiler checks the code it can see. It cannot see what arrives from a network, a
form, a file, `localStorage` or `postMessage`. Those values are typed by assertion, and the
assertion is gone by the time the value shows up.

Here the price comes from a form, as a string. Every annotation is correct and the program
compiles under `--strict`. It prints a wrong answer and keeps going:

```ts:inline
function total(price: number, shipping: number): number {
  return price + shipping
}

// The price arrives as JSON from a form or an API, as a string.
const form = JSON.parse('{"price": "20"}')

console.log('total:', total(form.price, 5)) // total: 205
```

`205` is not a crash. A crash would at least be reported. It is a plausible number that
goes into a database. The converted version, which is what this page runs, prints `205`
too, because conversion keeps JavaScript's behaviour.

Now the same function with one line added. `/* @tjs TjsStrict */` makes the file full TJS,
and the `number` annotation becomes a check that runs on every call:

```ts:inline
/* @tjs TjsStrict */

function total(price: number, shipping: number): number {
  return price + shipping
}

const form = JSON.parse('{"price": "20"}')

console.log('total:', total(20, 5)) // total: 25
const result = total(form.price, 5)
console.log(isMonadicError(result)) // true
console.log(result.message) // Expected number for '…total.price', got string
```

The bad call does not throw. It returns a `MonadicError`: an `Error` object, returned as
the function's result instead of thrown, that says which parameter was wrong and what it
received. `isMonadicError(value)` tests for one. Errors in TJS are values, and they pass
through: a checked function that receives a `MonadicError` as an argument returns that
same error without running its body. So the error surfaces where you look at the result,
not somewhere in the middle. TypeScript code that calls a TJS function and does not check
gets the error object back as an ordinary value, so test results at the boundary.

### `as` and `any` lie

TypeScript has two ways to make the compiler stop asking, and both are routine. `any`
turns checking off for a value. `as` tells the compiler what a value is, and the compiler
believes it. `JSON.parse` returns `any`, so `JSON.parse(text) as User` is how most
TypeScript code reads data, and it is a promise nobody keeps:

```ts:inline
/* @tjs TjsStrict */

interface User {
  name: string
  email: string
}

function greeting(user: User): string {
  return `Hello, ${user.name} <${user.email}>`
}

const user = JSON.parse('{"name": "Ada"}') as User // the compiler believes this

console.log(greeting({ name: 'Grace', email: 'grace@navy.mil' }))
// Hello, Grace <grace@navy.mil>
console.log(greeting(user))
// MonadicError: Expected User for '…greeting.user', got object
```

Under `tsc` the second call prints `Hello, Ada <undefined>`. In TJS the assertion still
compiles, because TJS does not need to argue with it. Conversion turns `interface User`
into a TJS `Type` with the example `{ name: '', email: '' }`, so a value that is missing
`email`, or has a number where `name` should be, fails it. The value is checked where it
is used, against the type the function declared, and the second call returns an error
that says `user` was not a `User`.

### Structural types accept anything shaped right

TypeScript's types are structural: a value fits a type if it has the right members. That
is usually what you want, and it is why TypeScript can describe JavaScript at all. It also
means two types with the same shape are the same type:

```ts:inline
interface Celsius {
  degrees: number
}
interface Fahrenheit {
  degrees: number
}

function boils(t: Celsius): boolean {
  return t.degrees >= 100
}

const warmWater: Fahrenheit = { degrees: 150 } // well below boiling (212 F)
console.log('150 F water boils?', boils(warmWater)) // 150 F water boils? true
```

TJS does not pretend to fix this. A TJS `Type` built from an example is structural too,
and it would accept the Fahrenheit value just the same. The honest answer is to make the
difference visible in the data, so the two shapes differ:

```tjs:inline
Type Celsius {
  description: 'a temperature in degrees Celsius'
  example: { celsius: 0.0 }
}

function boils(t: Celsius): false {
  return t.celsius >= 100
}

console.log(boils({ celsius: 100 })) // true
console.log(boils({ fahrenheit: 150 }))
// MonadicError: Expected Celsius for '…boils.t', got object
```

A `Type` block has up to three fields: `description` (for documentation), `example` (a
value of the type, which gives it its shape) and an optional `predicate` (a function that
must return true). Here the example says a `Celsius` is an object with a numeric `celsius`
field, so `{ fahrenheit: 150 }` is refused. The return example `: false` is a worked
example like `add`'s: TJS calls `boils({ celsius: 0.0 })` at build time and expects
`false`.

For what a shape cannot say at all, TypeScript's tool is the branded type, which is a
compile-time fiction again. TJS's tool is a predicate, which runs:

```tjs:inline
Type Percent {
  description: 'a percentage, from 0 to 100'
  example: 50.0
  predicate(v) {
    return v >= 0 && v <= 100
  }
}

function discounted(price: 80.0, off: Percent): 40.0 {
  return price * (1 - off / 100)
}

console.log(discounted(80, 25)) // 60
console.log(discounted(80, 250))
// MonadicError: Expected Percent for '…discounted.off', got number
console.log(discounted(80, '25'))
// MonadicError: Expected Percent for '…discounted.off', got string
```

`: 40.0` is a worked example: TJS calls `discounted(80.0, 50.0)` at build time, using the
parameter examples, and expects `40`. The `.0` marks a float, as above. `example: 50.0`
also makes `Percent` a number, so `discounted(80, '25')` is refused before the predicate
runs. Inside a `Type` block the predicate can also use the type's name for the value being
tested (`predicate { return Percent >= 0 && Percent <= 100 }`); the two spellings mean the
same thing.

### JSON at the boundary is unchecked

The previous three are one problem seen from three sides. Every TypeScript program has a
boundary where untyped data becomes typed data, and at that boundary the type system has
nothing to say. Teams solve it by adding a second type system: Zod, io-ts, Ajv, a
hand-written validator. Now each type is written twice, in two languages, and the two copies
drift.

In TJS the type is the validator, so there is nothing to write twice. The `User` in the
`as` example above was an ordinary TypeScript interface, and it checked the parsed JSON
with no second schema. [Replacing Zod, io-ts and Ajv](ts-from-zod.md) works through the
migration from each of those libraries.

The quietest form of the problem is equality. `==` between a string and a number is a
compile error in TypeScript, when it can see both types. When the string came from
`JSON.parse`, it cannot, and JavaScript's coercion decides:

```ts:inline
/* @tjs TjsStrict */

const fromTheWire = JSON.parse('"5"')
console.log('JSON "5" == 5?', fromTheWire == 5) // JSON "5" == 5? false
```

Under `tsc` that prints `true`. This page prints `false`: in TJS `==` never converts one
type to another, so a string is never equal to a number, whether or not anyone knew the
types in advance. [TJS vs TypeScript](../../docs/tjs-vs-typescript.md) runs this
comparison, and many like it, through `tsc --strict` and TJS on every test run.
[Validating JSON at the Boundary](ts-json-boundary.md) is the practical chapter.

## The Ugly

TypeScript's types grew into a second programming language. It has conditionals, loops
(by recursion), pattern matching (`infer`), string manipulation (template literal types)
and it is Turing-complete. People write parsers in it.

```typescript
type DeepReadonly<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => any
  ? T
  : T extends object
    ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }
    : T

type RouteParams<S extends string> =
  S extends `${string}:${infer P}/${infer Rest}`
    ? { [K in P | keyof RouteParams<Rest>]: string }
    : S extends `${string}:${infer P}`
      ? { [K in P]: string }
      : {}
```

This language has no debugger, no tests, error messages that print the whole expansion,
and a runtime of zero: everything it computes is deleted before the program runs. Its
results cannot be checked against a value, because there are no values in it. It is often
harder to read than the code it describes.

TJS has no type-level language. A type is an example, and when an example cannot say
enough, a predicate says the rest, in the same JavaScript as the rest of the program. Here
is a rule TypeScript cannot state, because it relates two values rather than describing
each one: _a range's `min` is not above its `max`._

```tjs:inline
Type Range {
  description: 'a range whose min is not above its max'
  example: { min: 0, max: 10 }
  predicate(r) {
    return r.min <= r.max
  }
}

function width(r: Range): 10 {
  return r.max - r.min
}

console.log(width({ min: 2, max: 5 })) // 3
console.log(width({ min: 5, max: 2 }))
// MonadicError: Expected Range for '…width.r', got object
console.log(width(JSON.parse('{"min": 0, "max": "9"}')))
// MonadicError: Expected Range for '…width.r', got object
```

The example makes `Range` an object with integer `min` and `max`, which is why the last
call, where `max` arrived as a string, is refused. The predicate says the rest. Where
TypeScript can state a rule, a predicate still differs in when it runs. Since TypeScript
4.4, ``type Flags = { [k: `is${string}`]: boolean }`` says that every key starting
with `is` holds a boolean, but only for values the compiler can see:
`JSON.parse('{"isOpen": "yes"}') as Flags` gets through. A TJS predicate checks the value
that actually arrives.

The cost is real: a predicate is checked when the program runs, not when it compiles.
TypeScript would reject some of these mistakes before you ran anything. The argument of
this book is that the mistakes that matter most are in values you cannot see at compile
time, and that a check which runs is worth more than a proof about a value that never
arrives.

### What you keep at compile time

Migrating does not mean giving up build-time checks. At build time TJS checks that every
file parses and that every signature's worked example holds (`add(2, 3)` really is `5`);
`tjs check` runs both, and fails the build when an example does not hold. What it does not do is static type
inference across calls: nothing at build time proves that `total(form.price, 5)` passes a
number.

In a mixed project you keep `tsc` for the `.ts` files, and TypeScript code that imports a
`.tjs` file is typed through the `.d.ts` that TJS emits for it. Once a file is graduated,
`tsc` no longer reads it, so inside that file you trade `tsc`'s checking for TJS's runtime
checks and worked examples. [Build, CI and Editors](ts-build-and-tooling.md) shows the
commands for both halves.

## What TJS does not fix

- **Checks cost something.** Validating inputs at every call is not free. It is cheap
  next to the work most functions do, and you can turn validation off for one function by
  putting `!` first in its parameter list (`function hot(! x: 0)`) when the data is
  already trusted.
- **Converted code keeps JavaScript's behaviour until you opt in.** A converted file is a
  faithful translation: it behaves exactly as the TypeScript compiler's output would,
  including `==` coercion and unchecked parameters. Checking starts when you graduate the
  file to native TJS, or mark it `TjsStrict`. See
  [Converting a TypeScript Project](ts-converting-a-project.md).
- **Generic relationships are not checked.** `function first<T>(xs: T[]): T` says the
  result has the type of the elements. TJS checks the values a function receives, not
  relationships between type parameters, so an unconstrained `T` becomes `any`.
- **Some type-level types have no runtime meaning, and generics lose detail in `.d.ts`.**
  A conditional or mapped type alias is kept verbatim in the `.d.ts` output, but nothing
  is checked at run time for it. A function signature that uses a type parameter is
  emitted with `any` in its place: `freeze<T>(x: T): DeepReadonly<T>` comes out as
  `freeze(x: any): DeepReadonly`. [Generic .d.ts Emission](../../docs/generic-dts-design.md)
  is the design work on closing that gap.

## How this book is organized

The chapters, in the order the navigation shows them:

- **This chapter**, with three pages beneath it:
  - [TJS vs TypeScript](../../docs/tjs-vs-typescript.md): the measured comparison, for
    anyone who wants each difference shown rather than claimed. Every row is executed
    against `tsc --strict` and TJS on every test run.
  - [Generic .d.ts Emission](../../docs/generic-dts-design.md): design notes on how
    generic types reach the `.d.ts` output, for library authors whose public API is
    generic.
  - [Post-mortem](../../docs/postmortem-ts-emitter.md): seven months spent testing
    TypeScript's compiler instead of ours, for anyone judging how far to trust the
    project's test evidence.
- [TJS for TypeScript Programmers](../../TJS-FOR-TS.md): Part 1, using TJS from a
  TypeScript codebase; Part 2, the syntax reference for migrating to it. Beneath it:
  - [TypeScript Examples](ts-examples.md): real TypeScript, converted and run on the page,
    in four groups (Introduction, Validation, Patterns, Advanced).
  - [Converting a TypeScript Project](ts-converting-a-project.md): `tjs convert`, the
    named escapes conversion writes, and graduation to native TJS.
  - [Validating JSON at the Boundary](ts-json-boundary.md): one type, written once,
    checked where the data comes in.
  - [Publishing a TJS Library to TypeScript](ts-publishing-a-library.md): shipping TJS
    code as an npm package that TypeScript consumers install and type-check as usual.
  - [Replacing Zod, io-ts and Ajv](ts-from-zod.md): moving a validation layer onto TJS
    types, library by library.
  - [Build, CI and Editors](ts-build-and-tooling.md): `.tjs` next to `.ts` in one project,
    what to run in CI, and editor support.

# TJS for TypeScript Programmers

_What if your types didn't disappear at runtime?_

---

TypeScript checks your code against its types when it compiles, and then erases them. At
run time a `User` parameter accepts whatever arrives: a `JSON.parse` result, a value cast
with `as any`, a field the API renamed last week.

TJS keeps the types. A TJS type is an **example value**, and the example survives to run
time, where it is a check, documentation and test data. This page is the reference for a
TypeScript developer:

- **[Part 1: Using TJS from TypeScript](#part-1-using-tjs-from-typescript)**. Keep your
  codebase. Import `.tjs` modules, turn on checks for one `.ts` file, run untrusted code
  and agents in a sandbox.
- **[Part 2: TypeScript to TJS, a syntax reference](#part-2-typescript-to-tjs-a-syntax-reference)**.
  What each TypeScript construct becomes in TJS, and the few places where TJS behaves
  differently.

[TypeScript: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly](guides/sections/typescript-good-bad-ugly.md)
makes the case for runtime types, and
[TJS vs TypeScript](docs/tjs-vs-typescript.md) is a comparison table in which every row is
executed against `tsc --strict` and TJS. The chapters below this page go deeper:
[TypeScript Examples](guides/sections/ts-examples.md) to run in the page,
