more instructions. Later chapters explain each of these properly.

Now change it. Replace `world` with your own name, then press ⌘S (Ctrl+S on Windows and
Linux) to run your new version. The greeting in the preview changes.

Nothing you do here can harm your computer or the page. A mistake in a program only produces
a message saying what went wrong, and you can fix it or undo it. Your changes last until you
reload the page; to keep them, choose **Save changes (local)** from the example's menu (the
⋮ button above the code).

## Reading code

Code in this book is written in a typewriter-style font, like `preview.append`. Type it
exactly as shown: every letter, comma, bracket and quote mark matters. Two details catch
almost everyone at first:

- **Capital letters matter.** `preview`, `Preview` and `PREVIEW` are three different names.
- **Quote marks must be plain.** Programs use the straight quotes on your keyboard: `'` and
  `"`. Word processors turn them into curly ones, ‘like these’, which a program does not
  understand. If you copy code from a document and it will not run, look at the quotes first.

Quote marks come in pairs: one opens a piece of text and the other closes it.

## One step after another

A program with more than one instruction runs them in order, from the top down:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
preview.append('First this, ')
preview.append('then this, ')
preview.append('and last of all, this.')
```

Each line is one instruction. Notice the space before each closing quote: without it the
pieces would run together, because `append` adds exactly what is between the quotes and
nothing more.

Before you touch anything, predict what the preview will say if the first and last lines
swap places. Then swap them, run it, and check. Being able to predict what a program will
do, before it does it, is the skill this book is building.

## Breaking things on purpose

Mistakes are not a disaster here; they are a lesson you can have whenever you like. Try
this in the example above:

1. On the second line, delete the `'` just before the closing parenthesis, so the line reads
   `preview.append('then this, )`. Run it. The program no longer makes sense, so it does not
   run. Instead you see a message saying what TJS could not understand, and on which line.
2. Put the quote back. Everything works again.
3. Now change `preview` to `Preview`, with a capital P. This time the program makes sense as
   a sentence, but there is no box called `Preview` (capital letters matter, as above). The
   message says that `Preview` is not defined: the computer has never heard of anything by
   that name. TJS programs run inside your web browser, and the browser picks the exact words:
   some say `Preview is not defined`, others `Can't find variable: Preview`. Both mean the
   same thing.

Mistakes come in two broad kinds. Either the program does not make sense, so it cannot run at
all, or it runs and goes wrong: it stops with a message, as `Preview` did, or it quietly gives
the wrong answer. TJS tells you about the first kind and about many of the second. For the
rest, you tell TJS what should happen, using tests, which you will meet below. A later
chapter, When Things Go Wrong, sorts mistakes more finely. This book shows you TJS's messages
as you go, so they are familiar by the time you need them.

If a change goes badly and you cannot see how to fix it, open the example's menu (the ⋮
button) and choose **Undo**, or press ⌘Z (Ctrl+Z on Windows and Linux). Once you have changed
an example, the same menu has **Revert to original**, which puts it back the way it was.

bottom of it is the prompt, a line starting with `›` where you can type. Type something there,


# React Todo (Comparison)

React todo app for comparison with the tosijs version. This would be easier with JSX, but we're not supporting JSX build magic (yet).

```javascript
import { useState, createElement as h } from 'react'
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'

// Without JSX, we use createElement (aliased as h for brevity)
// h(type, props, ...children)

function TodoApp() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState(['bathe the cat', 'buy milk'])
  const [newItem, setNewItem] = useState('')

  const addItem = () => {
    if (newItem !== '') {
      setItems([...items, newItem])
      setNewItem('')
    }
  }

  return h(
    'div',
    null,
    h('h1', null, 'To Do'),
    h(
      'ul',
      null,
      items.map((item, i) => h('li', { key: i }, item))
    ),
    h(
      'label',
      null,
      'New item',
      h('input', {
        placeholder: 'enter thing to do',
        value: newItem,
        onChange: (e) => setNewItem(e.target.value),
      }),
      h(
        'button',
        {
          disabled: !newItem,
          onClick: addItem,
        },
        'Add'
      )
    )
  )
}

const root = document.createElement('div')
root.setAttribute('id', 'root')
document.body.append(root)
createRoot(root).render(h(TodoApp))
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## Why this page exists

This is the yardstick for the next chapter, [tosijs Todo App](/tosijs-todo/). Both programs
do the same thing: show a list, let the user type a new item, add it on a button press, and
disable the button while the input is empty. Read them side by side and count what each one
asks you to manage.

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

- **State lives inside a function that runs again and again.** `useState` gives `TodoApp` a
  value and a setter, and every keystroke calls `setNewItem`, which re-runs the whole
  function and rebuilds the element tree for React to diff. Correctness depends on the
  rules of hooks: the calls must happen in the same order on every render.
- **Updates must be immutable.** `setItems([...items, newItem])` copies the array, because
  React decides what changed by comparing references. `items.push(newItem)` would mutate the
  state in place, React would see the same array, and nothing would re-render.
- **The input is "controlled".** Its `value` comes from state and every change goes through
  `onChange` back into state. That round trip is the price of keeping the DOM and the data
  in agreement.
- **Lists need keys.** `{ key: i }` tells React which `<li>` is which between renders. Using
  the index works here because items are only ever appended; it misbehaves once items can
  be removed or reordered.
- **No JSX means `createElement`.** JSX is a build-time syntax. In an unbundled page the
  calls have to be written out, which is what makes the nesting above hard to read.

The tosijs version replaces all five of these with bindings: state is an ordinary object,
`push` works, the input is bound to a path rather than controlled through a callback, and the
list is bound to an array.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Limits of the comparison

- **This page's code is plain JavaScript**, not TJS, and it is shown as a listing rather than
  run on this page: it needs React from a CDN and a DOM to render into. It runs in the
  [playground](https://tjs-platform.web.app).
- **It is a small app.** React's model pays for itself in large teams and large component
  trees; the point here is narrower. For a page you want to ship without a build step, the
  ceremony is real, and it is all visible in forty lines.

# Starfield

> New to WASM in TJS? Start with the **[WASM Quick Start](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/blob/main/docs/WASM-QUICKSTART.md)**.

Interactive space flythrough with parallax stars and nebula clouds. Uses `wasmBuffer()` for zero-copy WASM memory and SIMD-accelerated particle movement.

```tjs:inline
/#
# Space Flythrough Demo

A Star Trek-style starfield with parallax depth and nebula clouds.
Uses `wasmBuffer()` to allocate particle arrays directly in WASM memory —
no copy-in/copy-out overhead. SIMD processes 4 particles per instruction.

**Controls:**
- Move mouse **left/right** to steer laterally
- Move mouse **up/down** to steer vertically
- **Scroll wheel** to control speed
- **Click** to pause/resume
#/

// Configuration
const NUM_STARS = 50000
const NUM_NEBULA = 5000
const MAX_DEPTH = 1000
const BASE_SPEED = 8

// Particle arrays in WASM memory (zero-copy when passed to wasm blocks)
const starX = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, NUM_STARS)
const starY = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, NUM_STARS)
const starZ = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, NUM_STARS)

const nebulaX = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, NUM_NEBULA)
const nebulaY = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, NUM_NEBULA)
const nebulaZ = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, NUM_NEBULA)
const nebulaR = new Float32Array(NUM_NEBULA)
const nebulaG = new Float32Array(NUM_NEBULA)
const nebulaB = new Float32Array(NUM_NEBULA)

// Initialize stars
for (let i = 0; i < NUM_STARS; i++) {
  starX[i] = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 2000
  starY[i] = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 2000
  starZ[i] = Math.random() * MAX_DEPTH
}

// Initialize nebula with random positions and colors
for (let i = 0; i < NUM_NEBULA; i++) {
  nebulaX[i] = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 1500
  nebulaY[i] = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 1500
  nebulaZ[i] = Math.random() * MAX_DEPTH
  nebulaR[i] = 0.3 + Math.random() * 0.7
  nebulaG[i] = 0.2 + Math.random() * 0.6
  nebulaB[i] = 0.4 + Math.random() * 0.6
}

// Move particles — SIMD accelerated with wasmBuffer (zero-copy)
// Moves along Z (forward) and applies XY drift from steering
function moveParticles(! xs: Float32Array, ys: Float32Array, zs: Float32Array, len: 0, dx: 0.0, dy: 0.0, dz: 0.0) {
  wasm {
    let vdx = f32x4_splat(dx)
    let vdy = f32x4_splat(dy)
    let vdz = f32x4_splat(dz)
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4
      f32x4_store(xs, off, f32x4_add(f32x4_load(xs, off), vdx))
      f32x4_store(ys, off, f32x4_add(f32x4_load(ys, off), vdy))
      f32x4_store(zs, off, f32x4_sub(f32x4_load(zs, off), vdz))
    }
  } fallback {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
      xs[i] += dx
      ys[i] += dy
      zs[i] -= dz
    }
  }
}

// Respawn stars that passed camera or went too far
function respawnStars(xs, ys, zs, len, maxDepth) {
  for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
    if (zs[i] < 1 || zs[i] > maxDepth) {
      if (zs[i] < 1) {
        zs[i] = maxDepth * (0.7 + Math.random() * 0.3)
      } else {
        zs[i] = 10 + Math.random() * 50
      }
      xs[i] = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 2000
      ys[i] = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 2000
    }
  }
}

// Respawn nebula particles
function respawnNebula(xs, ys, zs, len, maxDepth) {
  for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
    if (zs[i] < 1 || zs[i] > maxDepth) {
      if (zs[i] < 1) {
        zs[i] = maxDepth * (0.5 + Math.random() * 0.5)
      } else {
        zs[i] = 50 + Math.random() * 100
      }
      xs[i] = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 1500
      ys[i] = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 1500
    }
  }
}

// Render into the example's own box: the doc site gives an example a `preview` element (its
// page IS the doc page); the old playground ran each example in a page of its own.
const stage = typeof preview === 'undefined' ? document.body : preview
if (stage !== document.body) stage.style.cssText += ';position:relative;height:480px'

// Create canvas
const canvas = document.createElement('canvas')
canvas.style.background = '#000'
canvas.style.display = 'block'
canvas.style.cursor = 'crosshair'
canvas.style.width = '100%'
canvas.style.height = '100%'
canvas.style.position = 'absolute'
canvas.style.top = '0'
canvas.style.left = '0'

const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d')

let width, height, halfW, halfH, fov

function resize() {
  width = canvas.width = canvas.offsetWidth || 800
  height = canvas.height = canvas.offsetHeight || 500
  halfW = width / 2
  halfH = height / 2
  fov = width * 0.7
}

stage.appendChild(canvas)
resize()
window.addEventListener('resize', resize)

// Mouse state — position controls steering, scroll controls speed
let mouseX = 0.5, mouseY = 0.5
let speedMultiplier = 1.0

canvas.addEventListener('mousemove', (e) => {
  const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect()
  mouseX = (e.clientX - rect.left) / width
  mouseY = (e.clientY - rect.top) / height
})

canvas.addEventListener('wheel', (e) => {
  e.preventDefault()
  speedMultiplier = Math.max(0.1, Math.min(4.0, speedMultiplier - e.deltaY * 0.002))
}, { passive: false })

canvas.addEventListener('click', () => {
  speedMultiplier = speedMultiplier > 0.5 ? 0.0 : 1.0
})

// FPS tracking
let frameCount = 0
let fps = 0
let lastFpsTime = performance.now()

function animate() {
  // Stop when the canvas leaves the page (a reader navigated away, or the example re-ran).
  if (!canvas.isConnected) return
  frameCount++
  const now = performance.now()
  if (now - lastFpsTime > 1000) {
    fps = frameCount
    frameCount = 0
    lastFpsTime = now
  }

  const speed = BASE_SPEED * speedMultiplier
  // Steering: mouse offset from center generates lateral drift
  const dx = (mouseX - 0.5) * speed * 3
  const dy = (mouseY - 0.5) * speed * 3

  // Clear
  ctx.fillStyle = '#08080f'
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, height)

  // Update particles
  moveParticles(starX, starY, starZ, NUM_STARS, dx, dy, speed)
  respawnStars(starX, starY, starZ, NUM_STARS, MAX_DEPTH)
  moveParticles(nebulaX, nebulaY, nebulaZ, NUM_NEBULA, dx * 0.25, dy * 0.25, speed * 0.25)
  respawnNebula(nebulaX, nebulaY, nebulaZ, NUM_NEBULA, MAX_DEPTH)

  // Draw nebula (behind stars)
  for (let i = 0; i < NUM_NEBULA; i++) {
    const z = nebulaZ[i]
    if (z < 1) continue

    const x = (nebulaX[i] / z) * fov + halfW
    const y = (nebulaY[i] / z) * fov + halfH

    if (x < -100 || x > width + 100 || y < -100 || y > height + 100) continue

    const depth = 1 - z / MAX_DEPTH
    const alpha = depth * depth * 0.08
    const size = depth * 60 + 30

    const r = Math.floor(nebulaR[i] * 255)
    const g = Math.floor(nebulaG[i] * 255)
    const b = Math.floor(nebulaB[i] * 255)

    const gradient = ctx.createRadialGradient(x, y, 0, x, y, size)
    gradient.addColorStop(0, `rgba(${r},${g},${b},${alpha})`)
    gradient.addColorStop(0.5, `rgba(${r},${g},${b},${alpha * 0.3})`)
    gradient.addColorStop(1, 'rgba(0,0,0,0)')
    ctx.fillStyle = gradient
    ctx.beginPath()
    ctx.arc(x, y, size, 0, Math.PI * 2)
    ctx.fill()
  }

  // Draw stars
  for (let i = 0; i < NUM_STARS; i++) {
    const z = starZ[i]
    if (z < 1) continue

    const x = (starX[i] / z) * fov + halfW
    const y = (starY[i] / z) * fov + halfH

    if (x < 0 || x > width || y < 0 || y > height) continue

    const depth = 1 - z / MAX_DEPTH
    const brightness = depth * depth
    const size = brightness * 2 + 0.5

    const c = Math.floor(180 + brightness * 75)
    ctx.fillStyle = `rgba(${c},${c},255,${0.6 + brightness * 0.4})`
    ctx.beginPath()
    ctx.arc(x, y, size, 0, Math.PI * 2)
    ctx.fill()

    if (brightness > 0.5) {
      ctx.fillStyle = `rgba(220,230,255,${(brightness - 0.5) * 0.4})`
      ctx.beginPath()
      ctx.arc(x, y, size * 2.5, 0, Math.PI * 2)
      ctx.fill()
    }
  }

  // Subtle vignette
  const vignette = ctx.createRadialGradient(halfW, halfH, height * 0.3, halfW, halfH, height * 0.8)
  vignette.addColorStop(0, 'rgba(0,0,0,0)')
  vignette.addColorStop(1, 'rgba(0,0,0,0.4)')
  ctx.fillStyle = vignette
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, height)

  // HUD
  ctx.fillStyle = '#fff'
  ctx.font = 'bold 16px monospace'
  const simdLabel = typeof WebAssembly === 'object' && globalThis.__tjs_wasm_enabled !== false ? 'SIMD' : 'JS'
  ctx.fillText(`FPS: ${fps} | ${simdLabel} | Stars: ${NUM_STARS.toLocaleString()} | Speed: ${speedMultiplier.toFixed(1)}x`, 10, 24)
  ctx.font = '14px monospace'
  ctx.fillText('Steer: mouse | Speed: scroll/click', 10, height - 12)

  requestAnimationFrame(animate)
}

animate()
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## How it works

Each frame moves 55,000 particles and draws them. The moving is the part that runs in WASM,
and it is the simplest possible SIMD kernel: `moveParticles` adds a steering offset to every
`x` and `y` and subtracts the forward speed from every `z`, four particles per instruction.

The design choices are the interesting part:

- **Positions live in WASM memory; colours do not.** `starX`, `starY` and `starZ` are
  `wasmBuffer`s because `moveParticles` reads and writes them every frame, and copying 50,000
  floats three times in and three times out per frame would cost more than the arithmetic.
  The nebula colours are plain `Float32Array`s because no WASM ever touches them.
- **Everything is allocated once.** `wasmBuffer` is a bump allocator with no free, so
  allocating inside `animate` would leak memory 60 times a second. The buffers are created
  when the example loads and reused for its lifetime.
- **Structure of arrays, not array of structures.** Keeping `x`, `y` and `z` in separate arrays
  is what lets one `f32x4_load` pick up four particles' `x` values at once. An array of
  `{ x, y, z }` objects cannot be loaded into a SIMD register at all.
- **Only the uniform work is in WASM.** Respawning a particle depends on its own `z` and calls
  `Math.random()`, which a WASM block cannot call, so `respawnStars` stays in JavaScript.
  Projection and drawing go through the canvas API, which is JavaScript too.
- **`NUM_STARS` and `NUM_NEBULA` are multiples of 4**, as every SIMD loop here requires.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Things to try

- Open the browser console and set `globalThis.__tjs_wasm_enabled = false`. Every block now
  runs its `fallback`, the HUD says `JS`, and the FPS counter shows what the SIMD path was
  buying you on your machine. Delete the flag to switch back.
- Raise `NUM_STARS` until the frame rate drops, then compare the two paths again. The gap
  grows with the particle count, because the per-call overhead is fixed and the per-particle
  work is not.
- Move the respawn test into the kernel with `f32x4_lt` and `f32x4_select` (see
  [WASM SIMD](/wasm-simd/)). The random new positions still have to come from JavaScript,
  which is a good lesson in where the WASM boundary belongs.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Limits

This example needs a page: it draws into a canvas and runs on `requestAnimationFrame`, so it
cannot run from the command line, and the test suite does not execute it. It stops itself
when the canvas leaves the page, so re-running the example does not leave old animation loops
behind.

The frame rate is a rough guide, not a benchmark: drawing 55,000 canvas circles usually
costs more than moving them, so the SIMD speed-up you see on screen understates the speed-up
of the kernel itself. For a measured comparison, see [Vector Search
Benchmark](/wasm-vector-search/).

# Start Here: Two AJS Examples

AJS is a JavaScript subset for agent code: it compiles to data (a JSON syntax tree) and runs in
a sandboxed VM that meters its work and has no IO except what the host grants. The host is the
program that embeds the VM and decides what an agent may reach. An agent is an AJS program the
host runs: it takes arguments, calls the operations it was given, and returns an object. See
[AJS](/ajs/) for the overview.

AJS exists to run code you did not write, such as agents submitted by users or written by an
LLM. These two examples show that such code always stops, and that it can still do real work
within the limits the host sets.

[Fuel Limits](/fuel-limits/) runs a loop that never ends, and the VM stops it. Every operation
costs fuel, the host sets the budget for the run, and when the budget is spent the run ends with
an `Out of Fuel` error value. The VM returns the error to the host rather than throwing it, so a
runaway agent cannot hang the page or crash the program that embeds it. The other limits, such
as quotas on model calls and the list of domains an agent may fetch from, build on this one: a
host can reason about what an agent will do only if the agent is certain to finish. This example
runs live in your browser, so start there.

[LLM + API Data](/llm-api-data/) is the shape of a real agent: fetch facts from an API, let a
model judge them, and return structured data. The VM has no model or network access of its own.
The host passes in an `llm` capability, and the built-in fetch reaches only the domains the host
lists, so the agent can do only what the host allows. Because it needs a model, the doc site does
not run it and shows a note saying so. The page includes the host code to run it yourself
against a local OpenAI-compatible model server, such as LM Studio or MLX (see
[MLX setup](/mlx-setup/) and [LM Studio setup](/lm-studio-setup/)).

After these, browse the rest of the [AJS examples](/ajs-examples/), or read
[Embedding the VM](/ajs-host/) to run agents from your own program.

# WASM Library: SIMD Linalg

A reusable WASM library exporting f32x4 SIMD vector kernels. Save this as `mylinalg`, then run the "Using a WASM Library" example.

```tjs:inline
/#
## A reusable WASM library

This file is the **library half** of a two-example demo. Save it in the
playground as a local module named `mylinalg`, then run the companion
example ("Using a WASM Library") which imports from it.

The exports below are real `wasm function` declarations — top-level
WebAssembly kernels with explicit parameters and SIMD f32x4 bodies.
Each is compiled to wasm bytecode at transpile time and exported as a
regular JS function that the consumer can call.

**Note:** TJS ships a fuller version of these (and more) in
`tjs-lang/linalg`. This example mirrors the source so you can read
exactly what a wasm library looks like.
#/

/**
 * Dot product of two f32 vectors of length `n`.
 * Returns the sum of element-wise products as f64.
 * `n` must be a multiple of 4 (the SIMD lane width).
 */
export wasm function dot(a: Float32Array, b: Float32Array, n: i32): f64 {
  let acc = f32x4_splat(0.0)
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i += 4) {
    let off = i * 4
    let av = f32x4_load(a, off)
    let bv = f32x4_load(b, off)
    acc = f32x4_add(acc, f32x4_mul(av, bv))
  }
  return f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 0)
    + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 1)
    + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 2)
    + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 3)
}

/**
 * Sum-of-squares of an f32 vector of length `n`.
 * For the L2 norm, take `Math.sqrt(norm_sq(a, n))` on the JS side.
 * Returning the squared value saves a sqrt; cosine similarity divides
 * by `sqrt(norm_sq(a) * norm_sq(b))`, which is one sqrt instead of two.
 */
export wasm function norm_sq(a: Float32Array, n: i32): f64 {
  let acc = f32x4_splat(0.0)
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i += 4) {
    let off = i * 4
    let av = f32x4_load(a, off)
    acc = f32x4_add(acc, f32x4_mul(av, av))
  }
  return f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 0)
    + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 1)
    + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 2)
    + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 3)
}

// Sanity check before saving as a module
const a = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, 8)
const b = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, 8)
for (let i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
  a[i] = i + 1 // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
  b[i] = i + 1
}

// dot([1..8], [1..8]) = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36 + 49 + 64 = 204
console.log('dot:', dot(a, b, 8))

// norm_sq([1..8]) = same as dot([1..8], [1..8]) = 204
console.log('norm_sq:', norm_sq(a, 8))

console.log('\nLooks good! Save this as `mylinalg` and run the consumer example next.')
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What makes this a library

Two words: `export wasm function`. Each declaration is a WebAssembly kernel compiled into
the file's one `WebAssembly.Module`, and `export` makes its JavaScript wrapper an ordinary
ES module export. Nothing else is needed: no build configuration, no `.wasm` file, no loader
code. The doc comments above each function are part of the API, and they say what a caller
must know that the types cannot: `n` must be a multiple of 4, and `norm_sq` returns the
**squared** norm.

The sanity check at the bottom is worth keeping in a real library too, or better, turning
into `test` blocks: a SIMD kernel with an off-by-four offset compiles perfectly and returns
plausible wrong numbers.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Design rule: the caller allocates

WASM code never allocates; JavaScript owns every byte. A library function that returns a
scalar, like `dot` or `norm_sq`, needs nothing more. A function that produces an **array**
takes an output parameter instead, so the caller can allocate it once with `wasmBuffer` and
reuse it. Here is that shape, a SIMD `axpy` (`out = a * x + y`, the classic linear-algebra
building block):

```tjs:inline
/**
 * out[i] = a * x[i] + y[i] for i < n.
 * `n` must be a multiple of 4. `out` may be `x` or `y` (an in-place update).
 */
export wasm function axpy(a: f64, x: Float32Array, y: Float32Array, out: Float32Array, n: i32) {
  let va = f32x4_splat(a)
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i += 4) {
    let off = i * 4
    let r = f32x4_add(f32x4_mul(va, f32x4_load(x, off)), f32x4_load(y, off))
    f32x4_store(out, off, r)
  }
}

const N = 8
const x = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, N)
const y = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, N)
const out = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, N)
for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
  x[i] = i
  y[i] = 100
}

axpy(2, x, y, out, N)
console.log('axpy(2, x, y):   ', Array.from(out).join(', '))

// The same output buffer, reused: no new allocation
axpy(-1, x, y, out, N)
console.log('axpy(-1, x, y):  ', Array.from(out).join(', '))
```

`axpy` has no return annotation, so it returns nothing; the result is in `out`. Returning
`f64` or nothing are the only choices today.

<!-- TODO review -->
## How a library is consumed

The same source serves two kinds of consumer:

- **Composed form.** A TJS consumer that transpiles with a `ModuleLoader` pulls the imported
  `wasm function`s into **its own** module at transpile time. Calls between the consumer's
  WASM and the library's are plain WASM calls, with no JavaScript in between.
- **Boundary form.** Everyone else imports the library's transpiled `.js`, which carries its
  own embedded WASM and JavaScript wrappers. Each call crosses from JavaScript into WASM;
  that costs a few nanoseconds, which matters only for very small kernels called in a tight
  JavaScript loop.

Both forms give identical results. A published library usually ships the TJS source for TJS
consumers and the transpiled `.js` for everyone else, selected by `package.json` `exports`:

```json
"exports": {
  ".": {
    "bun": "./src/index.tjs",
    "default": "./dist/index.js"
  }
}
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## Limits

- **Pure kernels only.** A `wasm function` cannot call JavaScript, so no `Math.sin`, no
  logging, no callbacks. Do that work in the JavaScript that calls the kernel.
- **Return `f64` or nothing.** Other return annotations are parsed but not yet honoured.
- **No tail loop.** SIMD kernels assume `n % 4 == 0`; document it, as these do, and let the
  caller pad.
- **Each `.js` dependency carries its own copy.** If two published libraries both embed the
  same kernels in their boundary form, the consumer ships both copies.

The next chapter, [Using a WASM Library](/wasm-library-consumer/), imports `dot` and
`norm_sq` from this file. The production versions live in `tjs-lang/linalg`, whose source,
`src/linalg/index.tjs`, reads much like this page.

# A First Agent

This chapter writes one agent, runs it in the page, looks at what it compiles to, and then runs
it from a host program in about ten lines. By the end you will have four words that the rest of
the book uses without stopping to explain them: **agent**, **atom**, **capability** and
**fuel**.

You need to know some JavaScript. You do not need to know anything about AJS.

## What an agent is

An **agent** is a function that takes one object of named inputs, destructured in its
parameter list, and returns one plain object. Here is the smallest useful one:

```ajs:inline
function greet({ name = 'World' }) {
  let message = `Hello, ${name}!`
  return { message }
}
```

It reads like JavaScript because it is a subset of JavaScript. It does not run the way
JavaScript does, though. Agents run in the **VM**, a virtual machine that is a sandbox: an
interpreter inside your program that can reach nothing outside the agent unless it is given
access. The program that owns the VM and runs agents in it is the **host**. On this site the
host is the page; in your app it is your server, page or worker. The VM does not read source
code either. A **transpiler** first turns the source into a tree of plain data, and that tree is
what the VM runs. You will see both steps below.

Three things about the agent's shape matter:

- **One object in.** The inputs are named fields of a single object, not positional arguments.
  `name = 'World'` makes `name` optional, with `'World'` used when the caller leaves it out. A
  default also declares the field's type, and only declared fields are accepted, so
  `{ name: 42 }` and `{ name: 'Ada', extra: 1 }` are both refused before the agent runs.
  [Contracts](/ajs-contracts/) explains.
- **One object out.** The agent returns `{ message }`, not the bare string. An object can grow
  a field later without breaking whoever reads it.
- **Objects all the way through.** Because every agent takes an object and returns an object,
  one agent's result can be passed as the next agent's input, when its fields match what the
  next agent declares. [Running it from a host](#running-it-from-a-host) shows a host doing
  that.

A source file may hold several functions. The **last** one is the agent, the entry point the
host calls; any before it are helpers it can call by name. AJS has no `export` (writing one is
an error) and no other way to name the entry point, so position is the rule. Get the order
wrong and the transpiler does not complain: the helper at the bottom becomes the agent, and the
run is usually refused because its inputs do not match. `greet` is alone, so it is the agent.

The site also has an example gallery, with one runnable agent per page; its
[Hello World](/hello-world/) is this agent with two variations. You do not need it to follow
this chapter.

## Running it in the page

The example above is live. Each `ajs` example in this book is a real run, with the page as
host: it transpiles the source, runs the agent with no arguments (so every default applies), and
shows the result, here `{ message: 'Hello, World!' }`, along with `fuelUsed`, a measure of how
much work the run did (more on fuel [below](#running-it-from-a-host)).

Try one edit. Change `'World'` to your own name in the example's code, then press the
**refresh** button in the code panel's tab bar (or ⌘S or ⌘R) to run it again. Editing alone
does not re-run an example. Then try `return message` instead of `return { message }`. The run
ends with an error, `Agent must return an object, got string`, shown where the result would be.
The page did not crash, and neither would a host: what an agent does wrong comes back as a
value.

## An agent that does some work

Here is an agent with more in it: a list of products, a price limit, and three steps over the
list.

```ajs:inline
function shortlist({ items = [
  { name: 'kettle', price: 40 },
  { name: 'toaster', price: 25 },
  { name: 'blender', price: 90 },
], maxPrice = 50 }) {
  let affordable = items.filter((item) => item.price <= maxPrice)
  let names = affordable.map((item) => item.name)
  let total = affordable.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0)
  return { names, total }
}
```

It returns `{ names: ['kettle', 'toaster'], total: 65 }`. `filter` keeps the items at or under
`maxPrice`, `map` takes their names, and `reduce` adds up their prices. A caller that passed
`{ maxPrice: 30 }` would get `{ names: ['toaster'], total: 25 }`. Change the default to `30` and
see.

The arrow functions passed to `filter`, `map` and `reduce` are callbacks. They can read any
variable of the function they are written in, as these read `maxPrice`. The rule that most
often catches people out is that a callback call stands alone as the value of its statement:
`items.filter(…).map(…)` on one line is refused, which is why this agent takes three lines.
[Decisions, Loops and Helpers](/ajs-control-flow/) has the rest.

## An agent that reaches outside

Neither agent so far touches the outside world. An agent that fetches a URL, asks a model or
reads a store does it by calling an **atom**, a built-in operation the VM provides. Atoms are
the only way an agent acts on anything outside itself, and they take named inputs:

```ajs:inline
function stars({}) {
  let repo = httpFetch({ url: 'https://api.github.com/repos/tonioloewald/tjs-lang' })
  return { stars: repo.stargazers_count }
}
```

It returns `{ stars: … }`, the repository's current star count. `httpFetch` made a request and
returned the response body, parsed from JSON. The agent did not write `await`: the VM waits for
every atom call itself.

This works here only because the page lets agents fetch from a few public APIs (GitHub is one).
Atoms that touch the world call something the host provides, and with nothing provided they
are refused. The next section shows the host's side. [Calling Atoms](/ajs-calling-atoms/) is the
chapter about atoms.

## What the transpiler produces

The transpiler turns the source into a JSON **AST** (an abstract syntax tree: the program as a
tree of plain objects), and the VM runs that. Here is `greet` as the transpiler writes it, with
the string concatenation in the third step trimmed:

```json
{
  "$ajs": 2,
  "op": "seq",
  "steps": [
    { "op": "varsImport", "keys": ["name"] },
    { "op": "if",
      "condition": { "$expr": "binary", "op": "==",
                     "left": { "$expr": "ident", "name": "name" },
                     "right": { "$expr": "literal", "value": null } },
      "then": [{ "op": "varAssign", "key": "name", "value": "World" }] },
    { "op": "varSet", "key": "message", "value": { "$expr": "binary", "op": "+", … } },
    { "op": "return", "value": { "message": { "$expr": "ident", "name": "message" } } }
  ],
  "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "name": { "type": "string" } }, "additionalProperties": false }
}
```

What to notice:

- **`"$ajs": 2`** is the format version. The VM reads it to know how to interpret the rest.
- **`seq`** is a sequence: its `steps` run in order. Each statement became a step, and the
  parameter list became two: `varsImport` copies `name` from the input into the agent's scope,
  and the `if` step applies the default when `name` is missing. The `if` keeps the steps it runs
  in a list under `then`.
- **Declaring and assigning are different steps.** `varSet` declares a new variable (it came
  from `let message`); `varAssign` writes one that already exists (here the default overwriting
  `name`).
- **A variable is an explicit node.** Wherever the agent reads `name` or `message`, the AST
  says `{ "$expr": "ident", "name": … }`. A bare string, like `"World"` in the `varAssign`, is
  always a literal value, never a variable lookup.
- **`inputSchema`** is the input contract, derived from the parameter list: `name` is a string,
  and no other key is accepted. The VM checks the arguments against it before the first step
  runs. A mismatch comes back as an error value like any other failure, with the message
  `Input validation failed: args do not match expected schema`, followed by the first argument
  that failed and why.

### Why code travels as data

An AST is plain JSON, and that changes where and when code can run. It can be stored in a
database and run later. It can be sent to the machine where the data lives, so the data does
not have to travel to the code. It can be read and audited before it runs: every atom call is a
named step, so you can see what an agent will try to do without running it. And it can be run
by a VM that contains no parser at all: a malicious source file cannot exploit a parser that is
not there. This is the idea in the title of the AJS guide,
[AJS: Code That Travels to Data](/ajs/).

The full format is documented in [JSON AST Format](/DOCS-AJS/#json-ast-format). You do not need
it to write agents.

## Running it from a host

In your own program, running an agent takes two calls: `transpile` turns source into an AST,
and `vm.run` runs it.

```typescript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang' // source -> AST (can run anywhere)
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast' // runs ASTs only; no parser

const source = `
function greet({ name = 'World' }) {
  let message = \`Hello, \${name}!\`
  return { message }
}
`
const { ast } = transpile(source) // throws a SyntaxError on source it cannot read
const vm = new AgentVM()
const { result, error, fuelUsed } = await vm.run(ast, { name: 'Ada' }, { fuel: 500 })
// result: { message: 'Hello, Ada!' }, error: undefined, fuelUsed: under 1
```

`tjs-lang/vm-ast` is the VM with no parser in it; it accepts only an AST, so transpiling and
running can happen in different places. `transpile` is the step that reads source, so it is the
one that throws: on source it cannot parse, or on a construct AJS leaves out. Once you have an
AST, the VM never throws for what the agent does.

Chaining agents is the host passing one run's `result` as the next run's arguments. With an
agent `summarize({ names = [''], total = 0 })` transpiled as `summarizeAst`:

```javascript
const first = await vm.run(shortlistAst, { maxPrice: 30 })
const second = await vm.run(summarizeAst, first.result)
```

Four facts about `vm.run` shape everything that follows:

- **It returns errors as values.** A failed run comes back with `error` set, and the host
  decides what to do. [When Things Fail](/ajs-errors/) covers errors.
- **Fuel stops every run.** **Fuel** is the run's budget for work: every step costs some (a
  single expression node such as a name or a `+` costs 0.01), and when the budget is spent the
  run ends with `Out of Fuel`, so even `while (true)` stops. `greet` used under 1; the
  `shortlist` agent above uses about 5. [Limits](/ajs-limits/) covers fuel, the default budget
  and the other budgets.
- **The VM has no IO unless the host grants it.** A **capability** is something the host hands
  the VM for one run, such as a `fetch`, a store or a model client. This is how a host gives the
  `stars` agent above its network access:

  ```javascript
  const { result } = await vm.run(starsAst, {}, {
    fuel: 500,
    capabilities: {
      fetch: async (url) => (await fetch(url)).json(), // what httpFetch returns is up to you
    },
  })
  ```

  With no capabilities, `stars` ends with
  `Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured. Set ctx.context.allowedFetchDomains or provide a custom fetch capability.`
  There are two built-in fallbacks. `httpFetch` uses the platform's own `fetch` for domains the
  host lists in its run options, which is how this page runs `stars` without passing a
  capability. The store atoms use an in-memory store that lasts one run and add a warning to the
  result. [Calling Atoms](/ajs-calling-atoms/) shows which atom needs which capability, and
  [Capabilities and Custom Atoms](/ajs-capabilities/) shows how to write one.

Everything else about the host side (run options, timeouts, memory ceilings, quotas, custom
atoms) is in Part II, [Embedding the AJS VM](/ajs-host/).

## What is different from JavaScript

AJS looks like JavaScript, and most of what you write will be ordinary JavaScript. A few things
are deliberately different, and each has a chapter:

- **No `await`.** The VM awaits every atom call for you, so writing `await` is a transpile
  error. The message comes from the parser and does not mention AJS:
  `Cannot use keyword 'await' outside an async function`. See
  [Calling Atoms](/ajs-calling-atoms/).
- **Atoms take named inputs.** `storeSet({ key, value })`, never `storeSet(key, value)`; the
  transpiler refuses the positional form. See [Calling Atoms](/ajs-calling-atoms/).
- **No `throw`.** An agent raises an error by calling `Error('message')` as a statement, without
  `new`. The steps after it do not run, unless a `try`/`catch` takes the error; an uncaught one
  ends the run, and the host receives it as the run's `error`. See
  [When Things Fail](/ajs-errors/).

  ```javascript
  if (name == '') {
    Error('name required')
  }
  ```

- **No C-style `for`, `break` or `continue`.** They are frequent sources of bugs in generated
  code, and `for...of`, `while` and `if` say the same things more plainly. Loop with `for...of`
  or `while`, or with `map`, `filter` and `reduce`; to stop early, put the stop condition in the
  `while`. See [Decisions, Loops and Helpers](/ajs-control-flow/).

## The four words

- An **agent** is a function that takes one object and returns one object; in a file of
  several functions, it is the last one.
- An **atom** is a built-in operation the VM provides, called with named inputs. It is the only
  way an agent acts on the outside world.
- A **capability** is what the host grants for one run (a fetch, a store, a model) so that an
  atom can work. Without one, an atom that needs it is refused, apart from the two fallbacks
  above, both of which the host controls.
- **Fuel** is the budget for work. Every step costs some, and a run that spends it all stops.

## The rest of Part I

1. **A First Agent** (this chapter).
2. [Values and Expressions](/ajs-values/): the values an agent works with, operators, methods
   and builtins, and where AJS refuses a JavaScript coercion.
3. [Calling Atoms](/ajs-calling-atoms/): named inputs, what each common atom returns, and the
   capability each one needs.
4. [Decisions, Loops and Helpers](/ajs-control-flow/): `if`, `for...of`, `while`, callbacks and
   helper functions.
5. [When Things Fail](/ajs-errors/): raising, catching, and errors that end a run.
6. [Contracts](/ajs-contracts/): what a parameter's default or example declares, and a declared
   result.
7. [Limits](/ajs-limits/): what a run costs, and the budgets every run is held to.

The language reference is [The AJS Language](/DOCS-AJS/), and every atom is listed in the
[Atom Reference](/ajs-atoms/).

# Arrays: Checking Every Element

A `number[]` that holds a string gives a wrong answer in TypeScript. With TjsStrict, the
same `number[]` checks every element and returns an error that names the bad one.

An array type in TypeScript says something about every element, and nothing checks any of
them at run time. Data that arrives as `any` (from `JSON.parse`, a fetch, a cast) is
accepted as `number[]` without a look inside. One string in the list turns `reduce` into
string concatenation, and the wrong answer comes out with no error anywhere.

The examples on this page run through the TS→TJS converter: `fromTS` from
`tjs-lang/lang/from-ts`, or `tjs convert` on the command line (see
[Converting a project](../../sections/ts-converting-a-project.md)). It turns `number[]`
into `[number]`, TJS's array type with a bare type name as its element.

By default the converter keeps JavaScript's behaviour: the types become metadata and
nothing is checked. That default is deliberate. TJS must run any JavaScript (or converted
TypeScript) unchanged, so checks are something a file opts into. The opt-in is the comment
`/* @tjs TjsStrict */` at the top of a `.ts` file. TypeScript reads it as an ordinary
comment; the converter reads it as "convert this file to full TJS", including input
validation. It applies to that one file only.

The first example below has no annotation and shows the bug. The second adds the comment.

## Without checks

```ts:inline
function sum(numbers: number[]): number {
  return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)
}

function average(numbers: number[]): number {
  if (numbers.length === 0) return 0
  return sum(numbers) / numbers.length
}

function filterPositive(numbers: number[]): number[] {
  return numbers.filter((n) => n > 0)
}

const data = [-1, 2, -3, 4, 5, -6, 7]
console.log('Sum:', sum(data))
console.log('Average:', average(data))
console.log('Positive only:', filterPositive(data))

// JSON.parse returns `any`, so TypeScript accepts this as number[].
// One element is a string.
const scores: number[] = JSON.parse('[1, "2", 3]')
// stringify so the quotes show: the result is a string
console.log('Sum of scores:', JSON.stringify(sum(scores)))
console.log('Average of scores:', average(scores))
```

The output:

```text
Sum: 8
Average: 1.1428571428571428
Positive only: [ 2, 4, 5, 7 ]
Sum of scores: "123"
Average of scores: 41
```

The first three lines are right. The last two are wrong, and nothing says so.
`sum(scores)` returns the string `"123"`: `0 + 1` is `1`, then `1 + '2'` is `'12'`, then
`'12' + 3` is `'123'`. `average` divides that string by 3, JavaScript converts it back to
a number, and the result is `41`. The real average is 2. A `NaN` would at least look
broken; `41` looks like an answer.

## With TjsStrict

The same three functions, with the annotation added at the top.

Under TjsStrict a bad call returns an error object instead of a number. That means the
TypeScript return type `number` no longer describes every outcome, so the code below types
each result `any` in order to read the error's fields: `path`, `expected`, `actual` and
`message`.

```ts:inline
/* @tjs TjsStrict */

function sum(numbers: number[]): number {
  return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)
}

function average(numbers: number[]): number {
  if (numbers.length === 0) return 0
  return sum(numbers) / numbers.length
}

function filterPositive(numbers: number[]): number[] {
  return numbers.filter((n) => n > 0)
}

const scores: number[] = JSON.parse('[1, "2", 3]')

const total: any = sum(scores)
console.log('is an error:', total instanceof Error)
console.log('path:', total.path)
console.log('expected:', total.expected, 'actual:', total.actual)
console.log('message:', total.message)

const mean: any = average(scores)
console.log('average path:', mean.path)

const positive: any = filterPositive(scores)
console.log('filterPositive path:', positive.path)

// Good data is unaffected
console.log('Sum:', sum([1, 2, 3]), 'Average:', average([1, 2, 3]))
console.log('Empty:', sum([]), average([]))
```

The output:

```text
is an error: true
path: <source>:3:sum.numbers[1]
expected: number actual: string
message: Expected number for '<source>:3:sum.numbers[1]', got string
average path: <source>:7:average.numbers[1]
filterPositive path: <source>:12:filterPositive.numbers[1]
Sum: 6 Average: 2
Empty: 0 0
```

- **The error names the element.** A path reads file, line, function, parameter and index.
  `<source>` stands for the file name; an inline snippet like this one has none, so it gets
  that label (from the CLI you would see the file's name). The line is the line in the
  TypeScript source where the function is declared, counted from the top of the block
  including the `@tjs` comment: `sum` is on line 3, `average` on 7, `filterPositive` on
  12. `[1]` is the `"2"`. `expected` is the element type, `actual` is what was there.
- **The bad call returns an error; it does not throw.** `total` is a `MonadicError`: a
  value TJS returns in place of throwing. It is an `Error`, so `instanceof Error` finds it,
  and `isMonadicError(x)` from `tjs-lang/runtime` tests for it specifically. Because nothing
  throws, the lines after it still run. See
  [Runtime Validation](./ts-runtime-validation.md) for what to do with one.
- **Each checked function checks its own input.** `average(scores)` fails at
  `average.numbers[1]`, before it ever calls `sum`. On good data, `average` checks the
  array and then `sum` checks it again.
- **An empty array is a valid `number[]`.** `sum([])` is `0`, as in TypeScript.

## What to notice

- **Array methods are untouched.** `reduce`, `filter` and the arrow functions convert as
  they are; only the signatures change. The bodies run exactly as they would after `tsc`.
- **The check covers the whole array, every call.** Checking an array costs time
  proportional to its length, and in the example above a good array is walked twice, once
  by `average` and once by `sum`. Next to the work most functions do with an array, that is
  usually noise; skip it only where profiling shows it matters. The
  [Performance Guide](../../performance.md) says how to measure.
- **The return type is not checked.** The converter writes the signature as
  `function sum(numbers: [number]):! number`. The `:!` marks a type-only return: TJS
  records it for documentation and does not test or validate what the function returns.
  The checks are on the way in. (In native TJS a plain `:` return is different; see below.)

## Skipping the check in a hot path

A converted `.ts` file has no per-function opt-out: TjsStrict turns checks on for the
whole file, and TypeScript has no syntax for TJS's `!` marker. If one function in a
TjsStrict file must not be checked, the choices are to leave that file without TjsStrict,
or to make it native TJS.

Native TJS means a `.tjs` file you write and maintain as TJS, not converted TypeScript.
[Converting a project](../../sections/ts-converting-a-project.md) describes how a
converted file graduates to one. Two pieces of TJS syntax appear in the example below,
and both read like TypeScript but are not:

- **A colon value is an example, not a literal type.** `numbers: [0.0]` means "an array
  whose elements are like `0.0`". `0.0` is a float, which accepts any number; `[0]` would
  mean an array of integers, and `1.5` would be refused. This is the same type the
  converter writes as `[number]`, spelled the native way.
- **A return example is a tested worked example.** `: 0.0` on `average` means TJS calls
  `average` with the parameter examples (`[0.0]`) when the file is checked and expects
  `0.0` back, which it gets. The converter writes `:!` precisely so that a TypeScript
  return type is not run as a test.

Put `!` before a parameter to turn off the check on that one function. The usual case is
an inner function whose callers have already checked the data:

```tjs:static
// Checked: called with data from outside
function average(numbers: [0.0]): 0.0 {
  if (numbers.length === 0) return 0
  return sum(numbers) / numbers.length
}

// Not checked: its callers are trusted to have checked the input
function sum(! numbers: [0.0]): 0.0 {
  return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)
}

console.log(average([1, 2, 3]))
console.log(sum([1, '2', 3]))
console.log(average([1, '2', 3]).message)
```

The output:

```text
2
123
Expected number for '<source>:2:average.numbers[1]', got string
```

`average` checks its input and catches the string. The direct `sum([1, '2', 3])` call
prints `123`: the original bug is back. `!` is a promise you make about every caller, and
nothing enforces it, so any caller that does not check its own input reintroduces the
silent wrong answer. (`! numbers` and `!numbers` are both accepted; the docs write it with
a space.)

See [Safety & Validation](../tjs/safety-validation.md) for the per-file and per-function
levels, and [Array Types](../tjs/array-types.md) for the TJS array syntax in full.

# Basics

AJS is a subset of JavaScript for agent code: programs written by people or by language models
that a host runs safely. An **agent** is one AJS function. The **host**, the program that embeds
the AJS VM, calls it with an object of inputs, runs it under a fuel budget with only the
capabilities it chooses to grant (such as `fetch`), and gets an object back.

These seven short pages are the tutorial for the language itself, one idea per page. They
assume you know basic JavaScript. For the full list of rules in one place, see [the language
guide](/DOCS-AJS/).

- [Hello World](/hello-world/): the shape of an agent, a function that takes one object of
  inputs with defaults and returns one object.
- [Math Operations](/math-operations/): arithmetic, `Math`, and turning text into numbers.
- [Conditional Logic](/conditional-logic/): `if`, the ternary, lookups instead of `switch`, and
  falsy values.
- [Loop & Filter](/loop-filter/): `for...of`, `while`, and the array methods that take a callback.
- [String Processing](/string-processing/): the string methods.
- [JSON Processing](/json-processing/): parsing text that may not be JSON, and checking its shape.
- [Error Handling](/ajs-error-handling/): errors are values, not thrown exceptions, and which
  ones a `catch` can take.

AJS looks like JavaScript, but a few things behave differently and some are refused. Reading a
member of `null` returns `undefined` instead of throwing, and `'total: ' + [1, 2]` is an error
instead of the string `total: 1,2`. Each page says where AJS differs from the JavaScript you
know for its topic, because those differences are what trip people up.

Every agent in these pages runs live: it is editable, and the page transpiles it and runs it on
the same sandboxed VM you would embed, with no arguments and a budget of 10,000 fuel. [AJS
Examples](/ajs-examples/) describes exactly how. None of these agents needs a network or a
model.

Read them in order. After the last one you can write an agent that takes input, computes, loops,
returns an error value instead of failing on bad input, and returns a result a host can use.

If you are embedding the VM, read these to learn what your agents will look like, then see
[Embedding the AJS VM](/ajs-host/) and [Capabilities and Custom Atoms](/ajs-capabilities/).
Calling the outside world from an agent comes next, in [APIs](/ajs-api/) and [LLMs](/ajs-llm/).

# Basics

The everyday language: how a TJS function says what it accepts and returns, and the
JavaScript behaviours a `.tjs` file changes. This section assumes you know JavaScript. If
you are new to programming, start with [Learn to Program](/learn-to-program/) instead.

Every chapter is a running example you can edit. Most end with `test` blocks: change the
code so a test fails and see what TJS reports.

Here is the idea the whole section builds on:

```tjs
function greet(name: 'Alice'): 'Hello, Alice!' {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`
}

console.log(greet('Bob')) // Hello, Bob!

const oops = greet(42)
console.log(isMonadicError(oops)) // true
console.log(oops.message) // Expected string for '…:1:greet.name', got number
console.log(oops.expected, oops.actual) // string number
```

The colon gives an example value: TJS reads `name: 'Alice'` as "a string, for instance
`'Alice'`". (It is not a TypeScript literal type; `greet('Bob')` is fine.) The colon also
makes the parameter required; `name = 'Alice'` would make it optional, as
[Required vs Optional](/required-vs-optional/) shows.

The return annotation `: 'Hello, Alice!'` is a worked example, and TJS tests it. Before your
code runs, TJS transpiles it to plain JavaScript (the live examples on this site do this
every time they run), and during that step it calls `greet('Alice')` and checks that the
result really is `'Hello, Alice!'`. Change the example to `'Hello, Alice?'` and TJS reports
a failed signature test: `Expected "Hello, Alice?" at 'greet', got "Hello, Alice!"`. The
return example is checked once, at that step. At run time every call checks its inputs;
checking return values too is opt-in (`:?`, see [Safety & Validation](/safety-validation/)).

When a caller passes a number, `greet` does not throw. It returns an error value, a
`MonadicError` (which is an `Error`), naming the parameter, the type it expected and what it
got. The start of the path in `message` is the source name and line, so it differs from page
to page. A returned error is an ordinary value you can inspect: nothing unwinds the stack, so
it arrives where the call was made instead of in whichever `catch` happens to be above. Check for it with `isMonadicError`, or pass it on: a
checked function that receives an error hands the same error straight back.

## The chapters, in order

1. [Hello TJS](/hello-tjs/), [Required vs Optional](/required-vs-optional/),
   [Object Types](/object-types/) and [Array Types](/array-types/) teach the central idea
   above: the value after a colon is an *example* that stands for a type, and a return
   example is a test. Hello TJS also shows everything an error carries: `message`, `path`,
   `expected` and `actual`.
2. [Control Flow: given](/given-dispatch/), [Dictionary Defaults](/dictionary-defaults-example/)
   and [const! and Bang Access](/const-and-bang/) cover the syntax TJS adds:
   - `given`, a replacement for `switch` whose cases cannot fall through into each other by
     accident;
   - object defaults that merge member by member;
   - `const!`, immutability checked at compile time;
   - `x!.foo` (bang access), which returns an error when `x` is null or undefined instead of
     throwing.
3. [Honest Equality](/honest-equality/) and [JS Footgun Fixes](/js-footgun-fixes/) cover what
   changes when you rename a `.js` file to `.tjs`. In Honest Equality, `==` and `!=` stop
   converting types (`'5' != 5`), and `Is` compares structure. JS Footgun Fixes lists
   everything else that changes, including:
   - `typeof null` is `'null'`;
   - `new Boolean(false)` (a boxed boolean) is falsy, like `false`;
   - a line starting with `(`, `[` or `` ` `` starts a new statement, so it can no longer
     join the line above by accident;
   - `MaxRetries = 3`, with no declaration, declares `const MaxRetries` instead of creating
     a global (or, in strict code, failing).
4. [Polymorphic Functions](/polymorphic-functions/), [Better Classes](/better-classes/),
   [Polymorphic Constructors](/polymorphic-constructors/) and
   [Local Class Extensions](/local-extensions/) show functions and classes doing more:
   several signatures under one name, classes you call without `new` whose constructors check
   their arguments, a class with one constructor per way of building it, and methods added to
   built-in types without touching their prototypes.
5. [Safety & Validation](/safety-validation/) shows where validation runs: on every call's
   inputs, on return values when you write `:?`, and on exceptions inside a `try` with no
   `catch` (TJS accepts `try { … }` on its own and turns a thrown exception into a returned
   error). It also shows how to turn the checks off for one function, with a `!` at the start
   of its parameter list (unrelated to bang access), or for a whole file with `safety none`,
   once you have measured that you need to.
   [What `.tjs` Refuses](/safer-code/) covers the four constructs that are errors in every
   `.tjs` file, and what to write instead: `var`, `eval(…)`, `new Date(…)` (use the
   `Timestamp` and `LegalDate` modules) and `new` on a class declared in the same file (call
   it as a function, as Better Classes shows).
6. [Built-in Types and Dates](/built-in-types/) shows built-in types as parameter types, the
   string and number types, types built from other types, and dates: the `Timestamp` and
   `LegalDate` modules that replace `new Date(…)`, used in a date pipeline.

After this section you should be able to write a TJS module whose signatures document,
test and validate themselves; read a `MonadicError` and know which argument caused it; and
know which JavaScript habits behave differently in a `.tjs` file.
[Patterns](/tjs-patterns/), the next section, puts these pieces to work in whole programs,
including how errors travel through one.
