# Why TJS

## Everyone has tried to fix JavaScript. This is what they left on the table.

> This chapter is for readers who already write JavaScript and know some of its history. New
> to programming? Start with [Learn to Program](/learn-to-program/) instead; you can come back
> here later.

JavaScript has been getting fixed for twenty years. The attempts were good, most of them
worked, and every one of them stopped somewhere short. TJS is an attempt to finish the job in
the space they left.

Two words carry the argument, so here is what they mean. A fix is **inside the language**
when it changes what the code actually does when it runs, and you choose it per file, the way
`'use strict'` changes how a file behaves. A fix is **outside the language** when it lives in
a separate tool (a linter, a type checker) and the running program never hears about it. A
fix is **rationed** when it is a fixed list that nobody can extend.

The short version: **the fixes that worked were the ones inside the language, and they were
rationed.** The fixes that could grow without limit were the ones outside it, and being
outside is what cost them.

---

## What each attempt got right, and where it stopped

### The doctrine: _JavaScript: The Good Parts_ (2008)

Douglas Crockford's book made the foundational point, and it still holds: **there is a good
language inside JavaScript, and you get to it by subtraction.** He named the parts that
produce bugs and said: use the rest. His list included:

- `==`, which converts its operands before comparing, so `'5' == 5` is true;
- `with`, which makes it impossible to tell which variable a name refers to;
- implied globals: assigning to a name you never declared silently creates a global variable;
- constructors called without `new`, which quietly write to the global object instead of
  building a new one;
- automatic semicolon insertion, which guesses where your statements end and sometimes
  guesses wrong;
- `typeof null`, which answers `'object'`.

That was a radical claim. Not "JavaScript is bad" and not "JavaScript is fine", but that the
language contains a smaller, coherent, better language, and that a disciplined programmer
can decline the rest. Every attempt since, including this one, is a variation on that
sentence.

**What it could not do is be anywhere except in your head.** A doctrine is enforced by memory
and code review, and it has to be taught again to every newcomer on every team, forever. The
book sold well, and the bad parts stayed in the language, stayed legal, and stayed what you
got by default.

### The enforcement: JSLint (2002)

Crockford had already made the doctrine executable, six years before the book explained it.
JSLint, his linter, checked code against rules that had not yet been written down in prose.
Its own warning label was "JSLint will hurt your feelings", and that sums up the whole
category: a tool that can object to your code but cannot explain the rule in your editor, and
cannot fix the language.

That is the structural limit: **a linter can only scold.** It cannot change what `==` does; it
can only object, every time, forever. So the rules became a config file, the config file
became a per-project argument, and the knowledge ended up in `.eslintrc` files and team
convention rather than in the language. Turn a rule off and the hazard (a *footgun*, a feature
that makes it easy to shoot yourself in the foot) is back.

**Left on the table:** the bad parts themselves. Being told `==` is wrong, in every project,
by a tool that cannot fix it, is worse than `==` being right.

### `use strict` (ES5, 2009)

The proof that **the language could fix itself.** Writing `'use strict'` at the top of a file
opts that file into stricter rules, and the rules are enforced by the JavaScript engine
itself, so it removed things JSLint could only complain about: assigning to an undeclared
name became an error instead of creating a global, `with` was gone, duplicate parameter names
were gone, and assignments that used to fail without a word (writing to a read-only property,
for example) started throwing errors.

It worked. It is the single most successful "fix JavaScript" project, and almost nobody
thinks about it any more, which is what success looks like.

And then it stopped. The list is short and it never grew. `==` survived. `typeof null`
survived. `NaN !== NaN` survived. There was no mechanism for "the next twenty things",
because each one would have needed its own standards-committee cycle and its own
compatibility argument.

**Left on the table:** everything after the first list. The mechanism was right and was used
once.

### TypeScript (2012) and Flow (2014)

Both understood that **types are the missing information**, and TypeScript in particular
understood what Flow did not: adoption has to be gradual, and tooling has to be excellent.
TypeScript won, deservedly, and it is better than what came before.

But look at what they are. Both are static checkers: they read your code before it runs,
report problems, and then **erase the types**, so the program that actually runs has never
heard of them. TypeScript describes a different language, a static one, and treats
JavaScript as the compile target it lowers to.

That makes TypeScript a checking layer, not a new runtime meaning. Its value is real, and it
is developer-experience value: editor intelligence, safe refactoring, errors caught before
you run. What it does not do is change anything about how the program behaves. Its escape
routes (`any`, `as`, `@ts-ignore`, `.d.ts` files that drift from the code they describe) are
places where the checking stops, and nothing at run time takes over.

That would be a reasonable trade if JavaScript had no types of its own at run time. It has,
and this is the part that gets missed.

JavaScript is often called weakly typed, because it **converts** values freely: `'5' * 2` is
`10`, and `'5' == 5` is true. That is a real problem, and TJS fixes it. But it is a different
property from **type safety** in the strict sense: a value can never be read as something it
is not. In that sense:

> **JavaScript is type-safe. TypeScript is not.**

Every JavaScript value carries its type at run time, and nothing lets you reinterpret a
string's bits as a number. The conversions are rules applied to values whose types are always
known. That is real, enforced, and always present. A TypeScript type is a _claim_, unsound by
design and erased before execution: `as` lets you assert something false, and nothing at
compile time or run time will contradict you. One of these systems can be lied to, and it is
not the one without a type checker.

So JavaScript already has the thing TypeScript is emulating. Its problem is not the absence
of runtime types; it is that **a few of them behave bizarrely**:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
typeof null           // 'object'  — a bug from 1995, never fixed
new Boolean(false)    // truthy!   — wraps false in an object, and objects are truthy
new String('')        // truthy!   — likewise
```

`new Boolean(false)` takes the primitive value `false` and wraps ("boxes") it in an object.
Every object is truthy, so `if (new Boolean(false))` takes the branch.

The set of types is also thin: `number` covers integers, floats and `NaN` (a value that
`typeof` reports as `'number'`) alike, and there is no way to say "a non-negative integer" or
"a valid CSS colour".

Which reframes the whole problem. The job is not to bolt a second, static, erasable type
system on top. It is to **fix the handful of broken runtime types and widen the vocabulary**,
staying in the system that actually enforces something. Run this in a `.tjs` file:

```tjs
console.log(typeof null)                     // null (the string 'null')
console.log(new Boolean(false) == false)     // true: the boxed value is unwrapped
console.log(new Boolean(false) ? 'yes' : 'no') // no: a boxed false is falsy
console.log('5' == 5)                        // false: no type conversion
console.log(null == undefined)               // true: both mean "nothing"
console.log(NaN == NaN)                      // true
console.log(typeof NaN)                      // number: unchanged
```

`==` in TJS is `===` with the traps removed (boxed primitives, `null` versus `undefined`, and
`NaN` never equalling itself), not JavaScript's converting `==`. `typeof NaN` is still
`'number'`: `NaN` is a number value, and TJS leaves that alone. The plain-JavaScript
behaviour of each fix is still there when you need it, under a name that says what it is;
see the third commitment below.

Widening the vocabulary looks like this. A parameter's example says what it accepts, and
`+0` means "a non-negative integer". A `Type` can carry a predicate for anything the examples
cannot say:

```tjs
function at(index: +0) { return ['a', 'b', 'c'][index] }

Type HexColor {
  example: '#ff8800'
  predicate(x) {
    return x.length === 7 && x.startsWith('#') &&
      x.slice(1).split('').every((c) => '0123456789abcdef'.includes(c))
  }
}

function paint(color: HexColor) { return `painting ${color}` }

console.log(at(1))                          // b
console.log(isMonadicError(at(-1)))         // true: -1 is not a non-negative integer
console.log(paint('#336699'))               // painting #336699
console.log(isMonadicError(paint('blue')))  // true: not a hex colour
```

Full CSS colours (names, `rgb()`, `hsl()` and the rest) are in `tjs-lang/css`; see
[Predicate types](/predicate-types/).

**Left on the table:** the runtime, and the recognition that the runtime already had a type
system worth repairing.

### ESM (ES6, 2015)

The other great inside-the-language success, and the closest precedent for what TJS is doing.
Modules had been a community problem with community answers (AMD, CommonJS, UMD, bundler
conventions), and the fix was not a better convention. It was **new syntax with different
semantics**, living beside the old one.

`import` is not `require` with nicer spelling. Imports are resolved before any code runs,
they always see the exporting module's current value of a binding rather than a copy, and a
module is strict by default. The old form still works; nobody's code broke; the new form is
better, and it won by being better.

**That is the model.** Not a lint rule, not a superset that erases, not a committee-sized
list of removals: a real alternative inside the language, chosen file by file.

#### And `.mjs` is the mechanism we borrowed outright

Node had to run two incompatible module systems in one toolchain, and the answer was not a
pragma. It was **the file extension**: `.mjs` means ESM, `.cjs` means CommonJS, and
`"type": "module"` in `package.json` flips what a bare `.js` means. The unit of choice is the
file, and the switch lives in its name.

That looks like a packaging detail and is actually a deep constraint. **You cannot put "this
is a module" inside the file, because you have to know it before you can parse the file.**
How imports resolve and whether the whole body is strict are all decided before the first
token is read. A directive like `'use strict'` can sit in the source because it changes so
little; module-ness changes too much to be announced from within.

TJS has the same constraint, for the same reason: the dialect changes what the parser does,
so it cannot be discovered inside the parse. Hence `.tjs`. (TJS once had in-file mode
directives; they were removed in favour of the extension, arriving later and the hard way at
the answer Node had already found.)

---

## Where that leaves the gap

The table below asks three questions of each attempt:

- **Inside JS?** Does it change what the running code does, rather than living in a separate
  tool?
- **Survives to runtime?** Is anything it knows still present while the program runs?
- **Unlimited scope?** Can it keep growing, or is it a fixed list?

|                  | inside JS?                         | survives to runtime? | unlimited scope?        |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------- | -------------------- | ----------------------- |
| _The Good Parts_ | no — a doctrine in your head       | no                   | yes, but unenforced     |
| JSLint           | no — a separate tool that scolds   | no                   | yes, but advisory       |
| `use strict`     | **yes**                            | **yes**              | no — one fixed list     |
| Flow             | no — a checker, types erased       | no                   | yes                     |
| TypeScript       | no — a checker, types erased       | no                   | yes                     |
| ESM              | **yes**                            | **yes**              | no — one problem        |
| **TJS**          | **yes** — repairs JS's own types   | **yes**              | **yes**                 |

The obvious objection: TJS is also a separate file type compiled by a transpiler, exactly like
TypeScript. The difference is what comes out. TypeScript's compiler deletes the types, so the
JavaScript it emits behaves as if they were never written. TJS's transpiler turns them into
code: the emitted JavaScript checks arguments, keeps the type information as data you can
inspect, and runs `==` and `typeof` with the fixed meanings. The fixes are in the program
that runs, not in a report that came before it.

Nobody has occupied the bottom row, and not because it is a bad idea. Each project had a good
reason to stop: a committee cannot ship twenty semantic changes, a type checker that runs
costs time on every call, and a linter that changes your program is frightening.

TJS's bet is that each of those reasons has weakened:

- **The committee.** TJS does not need one. The fixes ship in a transpiler, so the list can
  grow without waiting on the language standard, and the `.tjs` extension keeps every new rule
  away from code that did not ask for it.
- **Performance.** Validation runs on each call, checking the arguments and the result, and
  its cost is proportional to the shape being checked: about one and a half to two times the
  cost of the bare call for a trivial function, and invisible when the function does real
  work. A function that
  is trivial and hot can be marked `!` to skip validation. The numbers and the guidance are
  in the [performance guide](/performance/). Validation at a boundary is also something
  people already do anyway, by hand, and worse.
- **A linter that changes your program.** TJS is not one. It is a different file type you
  choose on purpose, its changes are documented rules rather than a tool's guesses, and every
  change has a named way back to JavaScript's behaviour (the third commitment below).

And the number of footguns that have been a lint rule for fifteen years (flagged, argued
about, never removed) is the size of the opportunity.

---

## What "inside JavaScript" actually means here

Three commitments, and they are testable rather than aspirational.

**1. TJS accepts all of JavaScript.** Every JavaScript program is accepted by the TJS
toolchain. As a `.js` file it keeps JavaScript's meaning exactly. Renamed to `.tjs`, it still
parses unchanged, but `==`, `typeof` and the other fixes take effect. **The extension is the
gate**, borrowed from `.mjs`, and nothing inside the file has to be remembered or configured.
This is guarded rather than promised:
[a test in the TJS repository](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/blob/main/src/lang/subset-invariant.test.ts)
fails if TJS ever rejects code that plain JavaScript accepts.

**2. Types are examples that survive.** Instead of a separate type language that is erased,
a type is a **value**:

```tjs
function greet(name: 'Alice'): 'Hello, Alice!' {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`
}

const result = greet(42)
console.log(greet('Bob'))           // Hello, Bob!
console.log(isMonadicError(result)) // true
console.log(result.message)         // Expected string for '…greet.name', got number
```

`'Alice'` is not a string-literal type. It is an example, and it widens to "a string", so
`greet('Bob')` is fine and `greet(42)` is refused at run time.

The refusal is **returned, not thrown**: `greet(42)` hands back an error value instead of
raising an exception. A bad argument then cannot unwind through code that was never written
to expect it; you check for it with `isMonadicError(x)` where you care, and the runtime also
keeps a log of recent type errors so an ignored one is not lost.

The return annotation is a worked example: when the file is transpiled, TJS calls
`greet('Alice')` and checks that the answer really is `'Hello, Alice!'`. Change the template
to `Hi, ${name}!` and the transpile (on this page, through `tjs()`, or with `tjs check`) stops
with "Function signature example is inconsistent": the file fails its own test before any of
it runs. (The `tjs run` command reports the failure but still runs the file; that gap is
known.) Because the example really is called, a function whose example call should not
happen at build time, one that writes files or calls a server, declares its return type with
`:!` instead, which states the type without running anything.

Because the example stays a real value, the one annotation serves as documentation, a
runtime contract, a test, and the source of a JSON Schema, the standard format that other
tools (API validators, form builders, LLM tool definitions) read to know what a function
accepts. One artifact rather than four that drift.

**3. The escape hatches are named and ugly.** Every fix can be opted out of, one place at a
time, through something greppable and deliberately unattractive:

- `LegacyTypeOf(x)`: JavaScript's `typeof`, where `null` is `'object'`.
- `DangerousLegacyEquals(a, b)`: JavaScript's converting `==`.
- `LegacyDate(x)`: a real `Date`. A `.tjs` file refuses `new Date(…)`, because a `Date` is a
  mutable object with a time zone hidden inside it; TJS offers `Timestamp` instead, and
  `LegacyDate` when you need the real thing.
- `LegacyDefault({ … })`: JavaScript's all-or-nothing parameter default. In a `.tjs` file an
  object-literal default fills in each missing member, so `f({ x: 5 })` with a default of
  `{ x: 0, y: 0 }` gets `{ x: 5, y: 0 }`; `LegacyDefault` gives you `{ x: 5 }` back.

A confession, not a suppression:

```tjs
console.log(typeof null)                     // null
console.log(LegacyTypeOf(null))              // object, JavaScript's answer
console.log(DangerousLegacyEquals('5', 5))   // true, JavaScript's converting ==
```

Search a codebase for `Legacy` and `Dangerous` and you have the complete list of places that
still depend on the old behaviour. You can adopt TJS one file at a time and opt out one
construct at a time, but there is deliberately no quiet project-wide switch that turns the
fixes off.

---

## Standing on their shoulders

The previous attempts are why this is possible, not competition for it. Crockford's list is
still the list. `use strict` and ESM proved the inside-the-language route works and is
survivable. TypeScript did the adoption research the hard way and established that a superset
with gradual typing is something working programmers will accept.

TJS is what you get by taking those lessons seriously at the same time: fix the bad parts
rather than flagging them, keep the fixes in the language rather than in a config file, and
let the types live long enough to be useful.

The rest of this book takes those fixes one at a time. Three pages elsewhere on the site
cover the same ground from other directions:

- **[TJS for JavaScript Programmers](/TJS-FOR-JS/)** (a standalone guide, outside this
  book) is the practical tour of what is fixed and how.
- **[TJS for TypeScript Programmers](/TJS-FOR-TS/)** (in the TypeScript book) covers
  migration and interop.
- **[The difference table](/tjs-vs-typescript/)** (in the TypeScript book) lists every
  divergence. It is generated from executable rows, so each claim on it is run against
  `tsc --strict` and TJS on every build rather than asserted here.

# Writing Agents

An AJS agent is a small JavaScript function that a host runs inside a sandbox, with a fuel
budget and only the capabilities the host gives it. This part teaches you to write one, a step
at a time: a first agent, then values and expressions, calling atoms, decisions and loops,
errors, the contract an agent declares, and the limits every run is held to. Every example runs

# Agents that call APIs

These example agents reach out to the world. Each one calls a public API (weather, music, code
repositories), reshapes the answer, and returns only what matters. The example pages below run
live: the doc site acts as the host and passes each `vm.run` an allowlist of three domains,
`api.open-meteo.com`, `itunes.apple.com` and `api.github.com`. Any other URL is refused.

## The network is something the host grants

AJS code cannot open a connection. An agent calls `httpFetch`, an atom (a built-in operation),
and `httpFetch` has no network access of its own: every request goes through what the host
grants for that run (one `vm.run` call). That grant is a capability, an I/O function or
permission the host passes in; an agent has none by default. The host can grant the network in
two ways, and both are options to `vm.run`:

```javascript
// The built-in client, limited to the domains you name
await vm.run(ast, args, {
  context: { allowedFetchDomains: ['api.open-meteo.com'] },
})

// Your own fetch function, which replaces the built-in client
await vm.run(ast, args, {
  capabilities: { fetch: myFetch },
})
```

When both are given, the allowlist still applies: the VM checks every URL against it before
your `fetch` sees the request. Given a `fetch` capability and no allowlist, your function
decides where requests may go.

With neither, nothing is allowed. A public URL is refused with an error beginning
`Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured`. A private or internal address (`localhost`,
`10.x` and so on) is refused with `Blocked URL: private/internal addresses not allowed in
default fetch`, and a scheme other than `http:` or `https:` is always refused.

Allowlist entries are exact. `example.com` admits `example.com` on the scheme's default port
and nothing else: write `*.example.com` to admit its subdomains (and `example.com` itself), and
`api.example.com:8443` to admit another port.

## The three examples

Read [Weather API](/weather-api/) first. It shows the call, the host code that grants the
domain, and why an HTTP error status is not an AJS error. A 404 or 500 does not stop the agent
or become an error it can [catch](/ajs-error-handling/): `httpFetch` returns the body the server
sent as ordinary data, so the agent has to check that body before using it. Redirects are not
followed either; one comes back as data, `{ redirect: true, status, location }`.

[iTunes Search](/itunes-search/) adds encoded queries and a server that labels its JSON
`text/javascript`. `httpFetch` parses a body on its own only when it is labeled
`application/json`, so this agent asks for `responseType: 'json'`. The agent also
trims a large response down to the few fields a caller needs. Size matters for the host, not
only for tidiness: every value crossing between host and agent is capped by `membraneMaxBytes`
(4 MB by default, and a response body over it is refused, not truncated), copying data costs
fuel, and a result passed to a model costs context.

[GitHub Repos](/github-repos/) adds rate limits and shows where an API token belongs: in the
host's `fetch` capability, never in agent source.

After these you can write an agent that calls an API safely, handles the answers that are not
the data you asked for, and returns a result small enough to hand to a model. The
[fetch policy](/ajs-host/#fetch-policy) section of the host chapter has the full rules for
domains, methods, headers and redirects.

# AJS Examples

Runnable AJS agents, from first steps to multi-agent pipelines.

AJS is a subset of JavaScript that compiles to data: a JSON program the VM runs in a sandbox,
under a budget, with no network or storage unless the host grants it. It is for hosts that need
to run code they did not write, such as an agent a user submitted or a model generated, without
trusting it.

Every `ajs` block on these pages is live: you can edit the code and run it again in place. Each
chapter is built around an agent you can run (the ones that call a model show their code and how
to run it locally), then what to notice about it, a variation, and the place where it differs
from JavaScript or where it can fail. Here is the smallest one. Change `'World'` and run it
again:

```ajs
function hello({ name = 'World' }) {
  return { message: `Hello, ${name}!` }
}
```

What to notice: an agent takes one object of named inputs and returns a value, here an object.
The page calls it with `{}`, so `name` takes its default.

## How the examples run

They run on the same sandboxed VM you would embed, under the same rules:

- **No arguments.** The page calls each agent with an empty object, so every input takes its
  default. That is why the examples declare defaults like `name = 'World'`.
- **A budget of 10,000 fuel.** Fuel is the VM's unit of work: every operation and expression
  costs some, so the budget bounds how long a run can take. `hello` uses under 1 fuel; a
  `while` loop that adds up 1,000 numbers uses about 500. A loop that never ends stops when the
  budget runs out and returns an `Out of Fuel` error; it does not hang the page.
- **Errors are results.** A run comes back as `{ result, error, fuelUsed }`. When the agent
  fails at run time (out of fuel, a blocked fetch), `error` is set, and the page shows it next to
  the fuel used. Nothing is thrown at the page. Code that does not transpile is a different
  case: the page reports it as a syntax error before anything runs, and no fuel is spent.
- **Three hosts on the network.** The VM has no network access of its own. `httpFetch` is the
  built-in operation (an atom) that makes a request, and only to domains the host lists in
  `allowedFetchDomains`. The page lists `api.open-meteo.com`, `itunes.apple.com` and
  `api.github.com`, and nothing else, so an edited example cannot reach an arbitrary site from
  your browser.
- **No language model.** A static page has none to call, so an example that calls one prints a
  message instead of running. [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/) shows how to run them locally.

To run an example on your own machine, transpile it and hand the AST (the JSON program the
transpiler produces) to the VM, with the page's budget and network allowlist. Save the agent as
`hello.ajs`, then:

```javascript
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
// `transpile` turns AJS source into the agent's AST (TJS uses `tjs()` instead).
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

const { ast } = transpile(readFileSync('hello.ajs', 'utf8'))
const vm = new AgentVM()
const run = await vm.run(
  ast,
  { name: 'Ada' },
  {
    fuel: 10_000,
    context: {
      allowedFetchDomains: [
        'api.open-meteo.com',
        'itunes.apple.com',
        'api.github.com',
      ],
    },
  }
)
console.log(run.result) // { message: 'Hello, Ada!' }
console.log(run.error) // undefined
console.log(run.fuelUsed) // about 0.6
```

Locally you can pass real arguments: here `name: 'Ada'` replaces the default. The allowlist is
enough for `httpFetch` to work, using the host's `fetch`; a host that wants to control requests
itself passes a `fetch` capability instead.

When a run fails, `error` holds the error value (and `result` holds the same value). With
`fuel: 100` and a loop that never ends, `run.error` is
`{ $error: true, message: 'Out of Fuel', op: 'seq' }`.

`tjs-lang/vm-ast` is the VM without a parser: it accepts an AST only, so the transpile step runs
outside the sandbox. That matters because parsing hostile source is the one step whose cost the
attacker controls before any budget applies. With the parser outside, a bad payload can only
stall your transpile step, which you can run in a worker or cap with `maxSourceBytes`, never the
VM. [Safe Eval](/safe-eval/) covers budgets and capabilities in full.

## Where to start

Read in order if AJS is new to you. Featured shows why AJS exists, Basics covers the language,
APIs the network, LLMs models, and Advanced agents that combine them. Afterwards you can write
an agent, run it with a budget and capabilities of your choosing, and let a model write one.

<!-- toc -->
- [Featured](/ajs-featured/)
- [Basics](/ajs-basics/)
- [APIs](/ajs-api/)
- [LLMs](/ajs-llm/)
- [Advanced](/ajs-advanced/)
<!-- /toc -->

# Async Functions

The converter keeps only what the promise resolves to. Under `TjsStrict`, a bad argument
makes the promise resolve to an error. It does not reject.

An async function always returns a `Promise`, so TypeScript annotates it
`Promise<string>`. Every async function returns a Promise, so the wrapper carries no
information; the `string` inside is what matters. `fromTS`, the converter from TypeScript
to TJS, unwraps it:

```text
async function fetchData(url: string): Promise<string>   // TypeScript
async function fetchData(url: string):! string           // TJS, after fromTS
```

`:!` declares the return type without checking it (more on that below). It is not a
non-null assertion. Everything else about `async` and `await` is plain JavaScript and
converts unchanged.

By default a converted file keeps JavaScript semantics and checks nothing at run time;
`/* @tjs TjsStrict */` turns its parameter types into runtime checks. That changes how a
bad argument shows up. This example opts in, then makes two good calls and three bad ones.

```ts:inline
// One line opts this converted file in to runtime checks
// on parameter types (see Runtime Validation):
/* @tjs TjsStrict */

async function fetchData(url: string): Promise<string> {
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 100)) // stands in for a real fetch
  return `Data from ${url}`
}

async function fetchMultiple(urls: string[]): Promise<string[]> {
  return Promise.all(urls.map(fetchData))
}

async function main() {
  console.log('single:', await fetchData('/api/users'))
  console.log('multiple:', await fetchMultiple(['/api/a', '/api/b', '/api/c']))

  // A bad argument. `as any` stands in for data from JSON or a form,
  // which tsc never sees. If the promise rejected, bad would be this string.
  const bad: any = await fetchData(42 as any).catch(() => 'caught (does not happen)')
  console.log('bad is an Error:', bad instanceof Error)
  console.log('message:', bad.message)

  // Through fetchMultiple, the whole batch fails up front.
  const batch: any = await fetchMultiple(['/api/a', 42 as any])
  console.log('batch:', batch.message)

  // Through a raw map, each element is checked on its own call, and
  // Promise.all does not short-circuit: the error is one of the values.
  const mixed: any[] = await Promise.all(['/api/a', 42 as any].map(fetchData))
  console.log('mixed:', mixed.map(r => (r instanceof Error ? 'error' : r)))
}

main()
```

The output:

```text
single: Data from /api/users
multiple: [ "Data from /api/a", "Data from /api/b", "Data from /api/c" ]
bad is an Error: true
message: Expected string for '<source>:5:fetchData.url', got number
batch: Expected string for '<source>:10:fetchMultiple.urls[1]', got number
mixed: [ "Data from /api/a", "error" ]
```

In each message, `<source>` stands for the file name (run the converted file with
`tjs run ex.tjs` and it reads `ex.tjs`), and the number is the line of the function in the
snippet.

## What to notice

- **Both return annotations are unwrapped.** `fetchMultiple` converts to
  `async function fetchMultiple(urls: [string]):! [string]`: "resolves to an array of
  strings". `[string]` is not a tuple: in TJS it means an array of strings, the same thing
  as `string[]`. A bare type name like `string` is allowed in TJS and stays as written.
- **The good calls behave exactly as they would after `tsc`.** Without the `TjsStrict`
  line they print the same thing, and so do the bad calls: `fetchData(42)` would resolve to
  `'Data from 42'`.
- **`fetchMultiple` checks every element.** The batch call fails on `urls[1]` before
  `fetchData` is called at all. The raw `map` in the last call goes straight to `fetchData`,
  so only the bad element fails and the good one still runs.

## The gotcha: a failed check resolves, it does not reject

TJS reports a type error by returning it as a value (a `MonadicError`, a subclass of
`Error`), not by throwing it. In an async function, that returned value becomes what the
promise resolves to. So `fetchData(42 as any)` returns a promise that _resolves_ to a
`MonadicError`. That is why the `.catch()` in the example never runs and `bad` is the error
itself, and why `Promise.all` in the last call resolves normally with the error as one of
its values.

If your TypeScript relies on `.catch()` or `try`/`catch` around `await` to handle bad
input, that handler will not see a TJS type error. Check the awaited value instead, as you
would the result of an ordinary function. `instanceof Error` works, because `MonadicError`
extends `Error`, but it is also true for any `Error` your own code returns. To ask only
"is this a TJS type error?", use `isMonadicError`:

```javascript
import { isMonadicError } from 'tjs-lang/runtime'

const result = await fetchData(input)
if (isMonadicError(result)) {
  // result.message names the parameter and what it got
}
```

Errors your own code throws, and rejections from things like a real `fetch`, still reject
as usual.

## Return types are declared, not checked

An async function that resolves to the wrong type is not caught, under `TjsStrict` or not.
TJS has three ways to write a return type:

- `:!` declares the type and checks nothing. This is what `fromTS` writes for every return
  type.
- `:?` checks the value at run time. On an async function, a wrong resolved value then
  becomes a `MonadicError`, like a bad argument.
- `:` is a worked example, run once at build time as a test. Build-time examples run
  synchronously, so on an async function it is not run.

To use `:?`, take the file on to native TJS: a `.tjs` file with the conversion annotation
removed. To test an async function from a `.ts` file, see Embedded Tests.

# Capabilities and Custom Atoms

An agent can only do what its host hands it. This chapter is for the host: how to give an agent
network, storage and a model, what those functions may return, and how to add operations of your
own without opening a hole in the sandbox.

Two words carry the whole chapter:

- An **atom** is an operation an agent calls by name, such as `httpFetch({ url })`. It declares
  the inputs it takes, what it returns, and what it costs in fuel. The VM ships about fifty core
  atoms, plus six battery atoms, and you can add more.
- A **capability** is a host function that an atom calls to reach the world: your `fetch`, your
  store, your model client. You pass capabilities to each run, in `capabilities`.

Three more terms recur:

- **Fuel** is the run's work budget. Every atom and every expression step spends some, and the
  run stops with `Out of Fuel` when it is gone. A run gets 1000 by default; a `storeGet` costs 5,
  an `httpFetch` 5 and an `llmPredict` 100. The full table is in
  [What a run costs](/DOCS-AJS/#what-a-run-costs).
- The **guest** is the agent: its code and every value it holds.
- The **boundary** is the copy that every value crossing between guest and capability goes
  through, in both directions. An atom tagged `'io'` (the default) puts its inputs and its return
  through it.

An agent never sees a capability. A call to an IO atom goes like this:

1. The agent calls the atom with named inputs: `httpFetch({ url })`.
2. The VM checks the call's quota and charges its fuel.
3. **Outbound copy.** The inputs are copied out of the guest and checked against the atom's
   input schema.
4. The atom's body runs and calls the capability you passed for this run.
5. **Inbound copy.** Whatever the capability returns is copied back in as plain data and checked
   against the atom's output schema.
6. The agent gets the copy.

When a capability is absent, the atom decides what happens. With no `fetch`, `httpFetch` uses
the built-in client, which fetches nothing unless the run names the domains it may reach. With no
`llm`, `llmPredict` fails with `Capability 'llm.predict' missing`.

```javascript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

const source = `function lookup({ id = 'u1' }) {
  let user = storeGet({ key: 'user:' + id })
  let summary = llmPredict({ prompt: 'Describe this user in one line: ' + JSON.stringify(user) })
  return { user, summary }
}`

const data = new Map([['user:u1', { name: 'Ada', role: 'admin' }]])

const vm = new AgentVM()
// atoms: vm.atoms lets the transpiler check every atom call (see Registering atoms)
const { ast } = transpile(source, { atoms: vm.atoms })
const run = await vm.run(ast, { id: 'u1' }, {
  fuel: 1000,
  capabilities: {
    store: {
      get: async (key) => data.get(key),
      set: async (key, value) => void data.set(key, value),
    },
    llm: { predict: async (prompt) => `(model reply to ${prompt.length} chars)` },
  },
  // request-scoped data for the VM: here, the only domains the built-in client may fetch
  context: { allowedFetchDomains: ['api.example.com'] },
})
console.log(run.result)
// → { user: { name: 'Ada', role: 'admin' }, summary: '(model reply to 61 chars)' }
```

`vm.run` resolves to `{ result, error, fuelUsed, … }` and does not throw for anything the agent
does; [What `vm.run` returns](/ajs-host/#what-vmrun-returns) has every field.

Capabilities are passed per run, not per VM. One `AgentVM` can serve many agents, each with a
different set. This chapter refers to several other run options (`context`, `quotas`,
`quotaUsed`, `timeoutOverrides`, `membraneMaxBytes`, `maxHeapBytes`); each is described in
[Run options](/ajs-host/#run-options).

---

## The Capabilities interface

These are the keys the built-in atoms look for. Any key you add is yours to read from your own
atoms. In the table, `data` means plain data, as defined in
[What a capability may return](#what-a-capability-may-return).

| Key          | Signature                                                   | Used by                                                                                                     | When absent                                                                              |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fetch`      | `(url, init) => Promise<data>`                              | `httpFetch`                                                                                                 | The built-in client, limited to `context.allowedFetchDomains`                            |
| `store`      | `{ get, set, query?, queryPredicate?, vectorSearch?, … }`   | `storeGet`, `storeSet`, `storeQuery`, `storeQueryWhere`, `storeVectorSearch`; battery atoms `storeSearch`, `storeCreateCollection`, `storeVectorAdd` | A fresh in-memory store for each run                                                     |
| `llm`        | `{ predict(prompt, options?) => Promise<string>, embed? }`  | `llmPredict`                                                                                                | `llmPredict` fails: `Capability 'llm.predict' missing`                                   |
| `agent`      | `{ run(agentId, input) => Promise<data> }`                  | `agentRun`, for an `agentId` that is neither an AST nor a stored procedure token                            | `agentRun` with such an id fails: `Capability 'agent.run' missing`                       |
| `code`       | `{ transpile(source) => ast }`                              | `runCode`, `transpileCode`                                                                                  | Both fail: `Capability 'code.transpile' missing. …`                                      |
| `xml`        | `{ parse(xml) => Promise<data> }`                           | `xmlParse`                                                                                                  | `xmlParse` fails: `Capability 'xml.parse' missing`                                       |
| `clock`      | `{ now() => number }`, synchronous                          | `Date.now()`, `Date()` with no argument                                                                     | Those calls fail: `Date.now() needs the 'clock' capability: …`                           |
| `random`     | `{ next() => number }`, synchronous, in [0, 1)              | `Math.random()`, `random`, `uuid`                                                                           | Those calls fail: `Math.random() needs the 'random' capability: …`                       |
| `llmBattery` | `{ predict(system, user, tools?, responseFormat?), embed }` | `llmPredictBattery`, `llmVision` (battery atoms)                                                            | Those atoms fail                                                                         |
| `vector`     | `{ embed(text) => Promise<number[]> }`                      | `storeVectorize` (battery atom)                                                                             | `storeVectorize` fails                                                                   |

Every failure in the last column is an ordinary error the agent can catch. What each atom sends
and returns is in the [Atom Reference](/ajs-atoms/). What follows is what your function
receives.

### fetch

`httpFetch({ url, method, headers, body, responseType })` admits the request, then calls your
function:

```javascript
fetch(url, {
  method, //       'GET', 'POST', … (upper case), or undefined when the agent gave none
  headers, //      the agent's headers, plus X-Agent-Depth (added by the VM)
  body, //         the agent's body AS DATA: an object stays an object; serialize it yourself
  signal, //       the run's AbortSignal: pass it on, so a timed-out run cancels the request
  responseType, // 'json' | 'text' | 'dataUrl' if the agent asked, else undefined
})
```

Whatever your function resolves to is what the agent's `httpFetch` returns. Return the body, or
a small object such as `{ ok, status, body }`; never the `Response` (see
[What a capability may return](#what-a-capability-may-return)). A throw becomes an ordinary error
the agent can catch, with your message.

**The VM checks these whatever `fetch` you pass:**

- The URL is `http:` or `https:`. A plain relative path (`/users/1`) is also handed to your
  function when no allowlist is set, so decide what it means or refuse it.
- The method is GET or HEAD, unless `context.allowedFetchMethods` adds more.
- Every header name is on a closed list: `accept`, `accept-language`, `authorization`,
  `cache-control`, `content-language`, `content-type`, the four `if-…` conditional headers,
  `range`, `user-agent`, `x-api-key`, `x-request-id`, `x-correlation-id` and
  `x-requested-with`. `context.allowedRequestHeaders` adds names.
- The request depth (`context.requestDepth`) is below 10.
- When `context.allowedFetchDomains` is set, the host is on it.

**Your `fetch` owns everything else:** which hosts it reaches when no allowlist is set,
redirects, cookies and other ambient credentials, how much of the body it reads, rate limits and
retries, and what `responseType` means. The boundary still refuses a return over
`membraneMaxBytes` (4MB by default), but only after your function has read it into memory.

The built-in client makes those decisions like this: it follows no redirects and returns one as
`{ redirect: true, status, location }` with `location` made absolute; it sends no cookies; it
reads at most `membraneMaxBytes` of the body; it returns parsed JSON for a JSON content type or
`responseType: 'json'`, a `data:` URL for `responseType: 'dataUrl'`, and text otherwise.
[Writing a safe fetch capability](#writing-a-safe-fetch-capability) builds one that makes the
same decisions. [Fetch policy](/ajs-host/#fetch-policy) has the run options in full.

### store

```javascript
const store = {
  get: async (key) => value, //       storeGet({ key })
  set: async (key, value) => {}, //   storeSet({ key, value })
  // optional:
  query: async (query) => [rows], //  storeQuery({ query }); what `query` means is yours
  queryPredicate: async ({ collection, predicate, limit }) => [rows], // storeQueryWhere
  vectorSearch: async (collection, vector, k, filter) => [docs], // storeVectorSearch passes no
  //                                     filter; only the battery atom storeSearch passes one
}
```

Only `get` and `set` are required. `storeQuery` returns `[]` when your store has no `query`, and
`storeVectorSearch` returns `[]` without `vectorSearch`. `storeQueryWhere` is the exception: the
agent calls `storeQueryWhere`, the VM calls your `queryPredicate`, and without one it fails
(`Capability 'store.queryPredicate' missing …`) rather than return unfiltered rows, because a
filter that silently does not filter is a data leak. Its `predicate` is a canonical verified
predicate, built with `canonicalizePredicate` from `tjs-lang/lang`: a pure function in a
normalized form, with a `key` that is the same for any two predicates that mean the same thing.
The store can evaluate it next to the data, and cache results on that `key`.

When you pass no `store`, each run gets its own in-memory store, discarded when the run ends. So
this agent, run without a store, always returns a count of 1, because every run starts empty:

```ajs
function visits({ page = '/home' }) {
  let before = storeGet({ key: page })
  let count = (before ?? 0) + 1
  storeSet({ key: page, value: count })
  return { page, count }
}
```

It returns `{ page: '/home', count: 1 }`. Pass a `store` and the count survives between runs.

### llm

`llmPredict({ prompt, options })` calls `llm.predict(prompt, options)` and must get a **string**
back. Anything else, including `null`, fails output validation, which the agent can catch.

`options` arrives as the agent wrote it, after the VM has checked it. Only these keys are
admitted: `model`, `temperature`, `maxTokens`, `max_tokens`, `topP`, `top_p`, `stop`, `seed`,
`responseFormat`, `tools`. Any other key fails the call (an agent cannot pass `apiKey` or
`baseUrl` to your client). `responseFormat` arrives in OpenAI's `response_format` shape, one of
`{ type: 'text' }`, `{ type: 'json_object' }` or `{ type: 'json_schema', json_schema: { name,
schema } }`, and its schema and any `tools` schemas have already been checked against the
restricted schema dialect agents may use. Map them to your provider's request yourself; nothing
is forwarded for you.

`predict` receives no `AbortSignal`. When the run times out, or `llmPredict`'s own 120-second
timeout passes, the agent stops waiting, but your request keeps going unless you bound it
yourself, as the example does with `AbortSignal.timeout`:

```javascript
const llm = {
  async predict(prompt, options = {}) {
    const res = await fetch('https://llm.internal/v1/chat/completions', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', authorization: `Bearer ${API_KEY}` },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        model: 'house-model', // the host picks the model; ignore options.model if you prefer
        messages: [{ role: 'user', content: prompt }],
        temperature: options.temperature,
        max_tokens: options.maxTokens ?? options.max_tokens,
        response_format: options.responseFormat,
      }),
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(120_000),
    })
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`model server: HTTP ${res.status}`)
    const json = await res.json()
    // content is null when the model answers with tool calls: turn that into a string
    return json.choices[0].message.content ?? ''
  },
}
```

The API key lives in the capability, where the agent cannot read it. `embed` is part of the
interface for your own atoms; no core atom calls it.

### agent

`agentRun({ agentId, input })` runs a sub-agent. When `agentId` is an AST, or a token returned
by `storeProcedure` (see [Stored procedures](/ajs-atoms/#stored-procedures)), the sub-agent runs
inside the current run on the same fuel and needs no capability. Any other `agentId` (a name, a
URL) goes to `agent.run(agentId, input)`, which receives copies of both. Return the sub-agent's
result. If you return the `RunResult` of your own `vm.run` (the `{ result, error, … }` object),
the atom unwraps it and turns its `error` into an error in the caller.

A new `vm.run` inside `agent.run` starts a fresh fuel budget and fresh quotas. To hold a quota
(a cap on calls per atom, such as `quotas: { llmPredict: 3 }`) across the nested run, pass the
same `quotaUsed` counter object to both runs; see
[Quotas across nested runs](/ajs-host/#quotas-across-nested-runs).

### code

`runCode({ code, args })` and `transpileCode({ code })` let an agent compile AJS it wrote itself.
Both need `code.transpile(source)`, which returns the AST. Pass the VM's atoms so calls in the
generated code are checked like any other:

```javascript
const code = { transpile: (source) => transpile(source, { atoms: vm.atoms }).ast }
```

This puts a parser back on the agent's path. `tjs-lang/vm-ast` has none, so that nothing an
agent sends can reach parser code, and this capability runs the parser on source the agent
chose. Source over 8KB is refused before it reaches you, because parsing runs before fuel can
stop it; a run's `maxSourceBytes` can lower that cap but not raise it. Where a slow parse would
hurt, run `transpile` in a worker. [Transpile where parsing is safe](/ajs-host/#transpile-where-parsing-is-safe)
explains the trade-off.

`runCode`'s program shares the run's fuel, its heap budget (`maxHeapBytes`, the bytes the agent
may hold at once) and its capabilities, but sees only the `args` it is given.

### xml

`xmlParse({ str })` calls `xml.parse(str)` with the agent's string and returns what it resolves
to, under the same rules as every other capability: plain data only, through the boundary.

### clock and random

An agent has no clock and no random number generator of its own: time and randomness are
granted, like everything else. `clock.now()` returns milliseconds since the epoch and
`random.next()` a number from 0 up to 1. Both are called synchronously, from inside an
expression, so they must return a number, not a Promise; what they return is checked, and a
string, `NaN`, a Promise or a value out of range is refused.

```javascript
import { AgentVM, systemClock, systemRandom } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

// the real ones
await vm.run(ast, args, { capabilities: { clock: systemClock, random: systemRandom } })

// a simulation clock that the host advances, and a seeded random source
let tick = 0
const clock = { now: () => tick * 16 } // 16 ms per frame
let seed = 42
const random = { next: () => ((seed = (seed * 16807) % 2147483647) - 1) / 2147483646 }
await vm.run(ast, args, { capabilities: { clock, random } })
```

Withholding them is the default: a run with neither cannot read the time or draw a random
number, so it cannot time anything and its result depends only on its inputs. `Eval`,
`SafeFunction` and the batteries grant `systemClock` and `systemRandom` unless you pass your own
(or `clock: undefined` to withhold one). A `cache` entry's expiry uses the granted clock when
there is one, so a replay sees the same hits and misses. Why this is a capability, and what it
protects against, is in [The Sandbox](/ajs-sandbox/#time-and-randomness-are-capabilities).

### llmBattery and vector (the batteries)

The batteries are the zero-config local setup: an OpenAI-compatible model server (LM Studio, MLX)
for chat and embeddings, plus an in-memory key-value and vector store. The battery atoms are
registered on the VM; the capabilities come from `getBatteries()`:

```javascript
import { AgentVM, batteryAtoms } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast' // also exported by tjs-lang/vm
import { getBatteries } from 'tjs-lang/batteries'

const vm = new AgentVM(batteryAtoms)
const batteries = await getBatteries() // probes the local server once, then caches the audit

// batteries = {
//   llmBattery, // { predict(system, user, tools, responseFormat), embed }
//   vector, //     { embed }
//   store, //      key-value plus createCollection / vectorAdd / vectorSearch
//   models, //     what the audit found
// }
const run = await vm.run(ast, args, { fuel: 1000, capabilities: batteries })
```

`llmBattery` and `models` are `null`, and `vector` is `undefined`, only in a browser page served
over HTTPS, which cannot call a local `http:` endpoint. The battery atoms then fail with a
"missing" error the agent can catch. Anywhere else the capabilities are always present: when no
server answers, `getBatteries()` logs that it could not connect and still returns them, and each
call then fails at the connection, again as an error the agent can catch. `TJS_LLM_BASE_URL`
picks the server; the setup guides are [MLX](/mlx-setup/) and [LM Studio](/lm-studio-setup/).

`llmPredictBattery` returns the model's message object (`{ role, content, tool_calls }`), not a
string; `llmPredict` returns a string. To use the battery atoms with your own backends, supply
the same keys: `llmBattery.predict(system, user, tools, responseFormat)`, `vector.embed(text)`,
and a `store` with `createCollection(name, schema, dimension)` (`storeCreateCollection` always
passes `undefined` for `schema`), `vectorAdd(collection, doc)` and
`vectorSearch(collection, vector, k, filter)`.

## What a capability may return

Everything a capability returns is copied into the run before the agent sees it. The copy is
built from what the VM reads, one value at a time, and only these values cross:

- plain objects (prototype `Object.prototype` or `null`) and arrays, from the VM's own realm;
- strings, numbers, booleans, `null` and `undefined`;
- `Date`, copied by its time value.

Shared references and cycles are kept. Everything else is refused: functions, `Map`, `Set`, typed
arrays, `ArrayBuffer`, `RegExp`, `Error`, class instances (including a `Response`), subclasses of
`Array` or `Date`, and objects from another realm (an iframe, a `node:vm` context).

Convert such a value yourself, field by field: a `Map` to an object or to an array of
`[key, value]` pairs, an instance to the fields the agent needs. A
`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value))` round-trip is not a fix. It loses data silently: a `Map` or
`Set` becomes `{}`, a `Date` becomes a string, and functions vanish.

A refused return is a bug in the host, so it **ends the run**, even inside the agent's `try`. A
return that is merely too large (over `membraneMaxBytes`, 4MB by default) or too deeply nested is
the world's doing, and the agent can catch it.

The common mistake is returning the `Response`:

```javascript
// Wrong: a Response is a class instance. The run ends with
// "capability return contains an instance of Response; only plain data (and Date) crosses".
const fetchCap = async (url, init) => fetch(url, init)
```

Spreading it is worse, because it fails silently. A `Response` keeps `ok`, `status` and
`headers` on its prototype, so the spread copies nothing:

```javascript
// Wrong, silently: the agent receives {}
const fetchCap = async (url, init) => ({ ...(await fetch(url, init)) })
```

A getter is refused too. It is host code, and the copy never runs host code to find out what a
value is:

```javascript
// Wrong: "capability return has an accessor property 'status'"
const fetchCap = async (url, init) => {
  const res = await fetch(url, init)
  return { ok: res.ok, get status() { return res.status }, body: await res.json() }
}
```

Read each field once and name it:

```javascript
// Right: plain data, built field by field
const fetchCap = async (url, init) => {
  const res = await fetch(url, init)
  return { ok: res.ok, status: res.status, body: await res.json() }
}
```

The same rule covers what a capability **receives**. An atom's inputs are copied out of the run
before your function is called, so a capability never holds a live object the agent can still
change.

## Which failures an agent can catch

A failure is either catchable, so the agent's `try`/`catch` sees it as a string, or it **ends the
run**: nothing after it runs, not even a `catch` block, and the host gets it as `run.error`. The
rule is who caused it. The world's failures are catchable; bugs, in the agent or in the host, end
the run, because a program that could catch a bug could loop on it.

| Failure                                                       | Whose fault | Result         | Message, for an atom `forecast`                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| The capability throws                                         | the world   | catchable      | your message, such as `HTTP 503`                                   |
| The atom's body throws (a missing capability, a bad value)    | the world   | catchable      | the body's message, such as `Capability 'weather' missing`         |
| The return is too large or too deeply nested                  | the world   | catchable      | `… the value exceeds the 4194304-byte membrane budget`             |
| The return does not match the output schema                   | the world   | catchable      | `Output validation failed for 'forecast'`                          |
| The atom's own timeout passes                                 | the world   | catchable      | `Atom 'forecast' timed out`                                        |
| A quota is used up                                            | the world   | catchable      | `Quota exceeded for 'forecast': 0 calls allowed`                   |
| An IO atom's input does not match its input schema            | the agent   | ends the run   | `'forecast': its input does not have the shape the atom declares`  |
| The capability returns a value that is not plain data         | the host    | ends the run   | `… capability return contains a Map; only plain data (and Date) crosses …` |
| Fuel runs out, or the run's timeout passes                    | the budget  | ends the run   | `Out of Fuel`, `Execution timeout after …`                         |

In AJS, a caught error is a string, the error's message. This agent asks for a page its host does
not allow and catches the refusal:

```ajs
function tryFetch({ url = 'https://not-on-the-list.example/' }) {
  try {
    let page = httpFetch({ url })
    return { page }
  } catch (err) {
    return { failed: err }
  }
}
```

It returns `{ failed: 'Fetch blocked: …' }`, with a message that says why: no allowlist was
configured, or the domain is not on it. [Catchable failures and run-ending refusals](/ajs-host/#catchable-failures-and-run-ending-refusals)
covers the host's side, and [Catchable, and run-ending](/DOCS-AJS/#catchable-and-run-ending) the
agent's.
