# Nested Objects

Real data is objects inside objects: a person with an address, an order with line items, a
response with a payload. In TypeScript each level is an `interface` that refers to the
others by name, and `tsc` checks every level. But those checks exist only at compile time,
and only for values `tsc` can see. `JSON.parse`, a `fetch` response, a message from another
service and an `as any` cast all hand you data that nobody checked.

The TS→TJS converter (`fromTS`, which runs when the page or your build converts a `.ts`
file) turns each interface into a TJS `Type`: a type that can be checked at run time. It
keeps the references between them, so once you opt in with the `/* @tjs TjsStrict */`
comment at the top of the example, checking the outer type checks every level inside it.

This example runs in the page: edit it and the output below it updates.

```ts:inline
// Converted TypeScript keeps JavaScript's behaviour until you opt in. This one
// line opts in to full TJS, which turns the types into runtime checks:
/* @tjs TjsStrict */

interface Address {
  street: string
  city: string
  zip: string
}

interface Person {
  name: string
  address: Address
}

function formatAddress(person: Person): string {
  console.log('formatting', person.name)
  const { name, address } = person
  return `${name}\n${address.street}\n${address.city}, ${address.zip}`
}

const john: Person = {
  name: 'John Doe',
  address: { street: '123 Main St', city: 'Springfield', zip: '12345' },
}
console.log(formatAddress(john))

// Data tsc never sees: JSON.parse returns `any`, so this compiles.
// The outer object is fine; the mistake is one level down.
const jane = formatAddress(JSON.parse('{"name":"Jane","address":{"street":1}}'))
console.log('Bad address:', jane)

// Arrays of objects are checked element by element.
interface LineItem {
  sku: string
  qty: number
}

interface Order {
  id: string
  items: LineItem[]
}

function totalQty(order: Order): number {
  return order.items.reduce((n, item) => n + item.qty, 0)
}

const good = '{"id":"A1","items":[{"sku":"pen","qty":2},{"sku":"ink","qty":3}]}'
const bad = '{"id":"A2","items":[{"sku":"pen","qty":2},{"sku":"ink","qty":"3"}]}'
console.log('qty:', totalQty(JSON.parse(good)))
console.log('Bad order:', totalQty(JSON.parse(bad)))

// A type may refer to itself, and the check follows the chain.
interface ListNode {
  value: number
  next: ListNode | null
}

function sum(node: ListNode): number {
  return node.value + (node.next ? sum(node.next) : 0)
}

const list = { value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: { value: 3, next: null } } }
console.log('sum:', sum(list))
const badList = '{"value":1,"next":{"value":2,"next":{"value":"three","next":null}}}'
console.log('Bad list:', sum(JSON.parse(badList)))
```

It prints:

```text
formatting John Doe
John Doe
123 Main St
Springfield, 12345
Bad address: MonadicError: Expected Person for '…formatAddress.person', got object
qty: 5
Bad order: MonadicError: Expected Order for '…totalQty.order', got object
sum: 6
Bad list: MonadicError: Expected ListNode for '…sum.node', got object
```

There is no `formatting Jane`: the bad call is stopped at `formatAddress`'s parameter, and
the body never runs. Each rejected call returns a `MonadicError`, an error value the
function returns in place of its result rather than throwing. `tsc` still believes
`formatAddress` returns a `string`; at run time the caller gets the error instead, and tests
for it with `isMonadicError(result)` from `tjs-lang/runtime`. The
[runtime validation](ts-runtime-validation.md) chapter covers the error object, and
[Validating JSON at the Boundary](../../sections/ts-json-boundary.md) shows a caller
handling one.

## What to notice

- **Each interface becomes a `Type` with an example.** The converter writes:

  ```text
  Type Address {
    example: { street: '', city: '', zip: '' }
  }

  Type Person {
    example: { name: '', address: Address }
  }
  ```

  A TJS type is described by an example value: `''` means "a string", `0.0` means "a
  number". The converter picks the example from your TypeScript type, so you never write
  one yourself.
- **`address: Address` is a reference, not a copy of `Address`'s shape.** That is what lets a
  type name itself, as `ListNode` does in `next: ListNode | null`, or name a type declared
  later in the file, just as TypeScript interfaces can.
- **`| null` is checked, not ignored.** It becomes a runtime union, so the last node's
  `null` passes and anything else in `next` must be a `ListNode`. The bad list is rejected
  because of the `"three"` in its third node.
- **`LineItem[]` checks every element.** The second order fails because one item's `qty` is
  the string `"3"`.
- **Destructuring is unchanged.** `const { name, address } = person` runs exactly as it
  would in JavaScript.

Delete the `/* @tjs TjsStrict */` line and run it again to see what the checks are buying
you. Without it the converted code keeps JavaScript's behaviour: the bad call prints
`formatting Jane`, then `Jane`, `1` and `undefined, undefined`; the bad order's quantity is
the string `'23'`; and the bad list sums to the string `'12three0'`.

## The check is deep, the message is not

The error names the outer type that failed (`Expected Person`), not the member that was
wrong. `{ street: 1 }` has two faults, a number where a string belongs and no `city` or
`zip`, and either one alone is enough to reject it, but the message cannot tell you which.
The same holds for `Expected Order` and `Expected ListNode`. Its `path` field
(`formatAddress.person`) tells you which parameter to look at; finding the bad member inside
it is up to you. See [Object Validation](ts-object-validation.md) for the flat case.

## What it costs

Every call checks its whole argument, every level of it. That is cheap for one call on an
ordinary payload, but it adds up when a function calls itself: each `sum(node.next)`
re-checks the rest of the list, so summing a list of _n_ nodes does work proportional to
_n_². On a 2,000-node list that is a few hundred milliseconds.

The fix is to check once at the entry and recurse through a helper whose parameter is
`any`, which the converter leaves unchecked:

```typescript
function sum(list: ListNode): number {
  return sumUnchecked(list) // the whole list is checked once, here
}

function sumUnchecked(node: any): number {
  return node.value + (node.next ? sumUnchecked(node.next) : 0)
}
```

The same advice holds for large payloads in general: check at the boundary where the data
arrives, not in every helper it passes through. The [performance guide](../../performance.md)
has measurements.

## The gotcha: `?` does not mean `null`

An optional member, `address?: Address`, may be missing. It may not be `null`, exactly as
under `strict` in TypeScript. The difference is that `tsc` catches a literal `null` in your
code, while JSON from an API often sends `"address": null` for "no address", and nothing
looked at it until now.

```ts:inline
/* @tjs TjsStrict */

interface Address {
  street: string
  city: string
  zip: string
}

interface Contact {
  name: string
  address?: Address // may be missing, may not be null
}

interface NullableContact {
  name: string
  address?: Address | null // may be missing or null
}

function label(c: Contact): string {
  return c.name
}

function nullableLabel(c: NullableContact): string {
  return c.name
}

// Many APIs send an explicit null for "no address".
const noAddress = '{"name":"Sam","address":null}'
console.log(label(JSON.parse('{"name":"Ann"}')))
console.log(label(JSON.parse(noAddress)))
console.log(nullableLabel(JSON.parse(noAddress)))
```

The first call prints `Ann`. The second is rejected
(`Expected Contact for '…label.c', got object`), because `null` is not an `Address`. The
third prints `Sam`. If the data can send `null`, say so in the interface:
`address?: Address | null`.

# Patterns

Basics shows the language one feature at a time. Patterns shows it doing the work of a real
module: running from files, handling failures as values, checking data at the edges,
importing other code, and moving a hot loop into WebAssembly.

This section assumes you write JavaScript. If you are new to programming, finish
[Learn to Program](/learn-to-program/) first. It also assumes you have read
[Basics](/tjs-basics/), or at least [Hello TJS](/hello-tjs/),
[Required vs Optional](/required-vs-optional/) and
[Safety & Validation](/safety-validation/).

The chapters come in six groups, in this order:

- **Running code.** [Running TJS: Files, the CLI and Bundlers](/running-tjs/) comes first,
  because a real module lives in a file, not in a page. It covers `tjs check` and `tjs run`
  on the command line, importing `.tjs` files directly under Bun, and adding TJS to a
  bundled build.
- **Functions.** Higher-Order Functions and Async Functions show that typed signatures
  survive what JavaScript programs do all the time: pass functions around, and await them.
- **Errors.** Safety & Validation showed that a typed function returns an error instead of
  throwing it, and that a typed function handed that error returns it unchanged without
  running its body. Error Handling shows how that plays out across a program and where to
  check. Flight Recorder covers the runtime's error history: a log of every error it saw,
  including the ones your code ignored.
- **Types at runtime.** TypeScript's types vanish when it compiles; TJS keeps every
  function's signature at runtime. Types at Runtime shows how to inspect a signature,
  validate data against it, and turn it into a JSON Schema (a description of what valid
  data looks like).
- **Imports.** Date Formatting, Local Module Imports and Lodash Utilities show TJS using
  other code: npm packages and your own modules. On these pages a bare import such as
  `'date-fns'` resolves from a CDN, so there is no bundler and no install step; in your own
  project it resolves through `node_modules`, and Running TJS covers the build.
- **WebAssembly.** WebAssembly (WASM) is a low-level format that browsers run at close to
  native speed. Inline WASM, WASM SIMD, WASM Memory and WASM Functions are a short course in
  using it from a TJS file: a hot loop in a `wasm { }` block, then SIMD (one instruction
  working on four numbers at once), then buffers shared with WASM without copying, then
  reusable kernels. When WASM is not available, a block runs as JavaScript instead. Skip
  these until you have measured a loop worth speeding up.

# Required vs Optional

In JavaScript every parameter is optional. Leave one out and the function quietly gets
`undefined`, and the bug surfaces somewhere else, later. TJS makes the choice part of the
signature, and one character carries it:

| Syntax            | Meaning                                         |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `param: 'value'`  | **Required.** The caller must pass it.          |
| `param = 'value'` | **Optional.** Leave it out and it is `'value'`. |

In both cases the value after the punctuation is an example, and the parameter accepts
anything of the example's type: `'value'` means any string, `false` any boolean. Numbers are
more precise than in JavaScript. An integer example such as `0` accepts only integers, while
a decimal example such as `0.0` accepts any number. You can also write a type name instead
of an example (`string`, `number`, `boolean`). [TJS Syntax](/TJS-SYNTAX/) has the full list.

A colon after the closing parenthesis means something else. The return annotation is not a
type but a worked example, and TJS tests it: it calls the function with the parameter
examples and checks that the result is exactly the annotation. The first example below uses
one.

```tjs:inline
/#
## Required vs Optional Parameters

`name` and `email` are required (`:`); `age` and `admin` are optional (`=`).
#/
// A /# … #/ block is documentation: the page shows it above the code.
function createUser(
  name: 'anonymous',
  email: 'user@example.com',
  age = 0,
  admin = false
): { name: 'anonymous', email: 'user@example.com', age: 0, admin: false } {
  return { name, email, age, admin }
}

// Optional parameters left out take their defaults
console.log(createUser('Alice', 'alice@example.com'))
// { name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com', age: 0, admin: false }
console.log(createUser('Bob', 'bob@example.com', 42, true))
// { name: 'Bob', email: 'bob@example.com', age: 42, admin: true }

// A missing required parameter is an error, and the body never runs
const missing = createUser('Carol')
console.log(isMonadicError(missing), missing.message)
// true Expected string for '…createUser.email', got undefined

// An optional parameter is still checked when you pass it
const wrongAge = createUser('Dan', 'dan@example.com', 'old')
console.log(isMonadicError(wrongAge), wrongAge.message)
// true Expected integer for '…createUser.age', got string

// A test block runs when the file is transpiled, like the return example
test 'optional parameters default' {
  const user = createUser('Alice', 'alice@test.com')
  expect(user.age).toBe(0)
  expect(user.admin).toBe(false)
}
```

The `…` in each message stands for the file name and line, which depend on where the code
runs.

## What to notice

- `email: 'user@example.com'` is **required**. `createUser('Carol')` does not run the body
  with `email` set to `undefined`. It returns a `MonadicError`, an `Error` subclass whose
  message names `createUser.email`. The error is returned, not thrown, so nothing unwinds:
  the caller decides what to do with it. `isMonadicError(x)`, which TJS provides, tells you
  whether you got one; [Error Handling](/error-handling/) says more.
- `age = 0` is **optional**. Leave it out and it is `0`. Pass a value and it is checked
  against the type of the default. `0` is an integer example, so `'old'` is rejected rather
  than stored as an age, and so is `1.5`.
- The return annotation is checked when the file is transpiled, which happens before any of
  it runs (in the page, when the example loads; at the command line, under `tjs check`). TJS
  calls `createUser('anonymous', 'user@example.com')` and compares the result with
  `{ name: 'anonymous', email: 'user@example.com', age: 0, admin: false }`. If the body
  returned a different `age`, transpiling would fail. The optional parameters are left out
  of that call, so the example also shows their defaults.

TJS attaches a record of each function's signature to the function, as `__tjs`. Its
`params` entry describes every parameter:

```tjs:inline
function createUser(name: 'anonymous', age = 0) {
  return { name, age }
}

for (const [param, info] of Object.entries(createUser.__tjs.params)) {
  console.log(param, info.type.kind, info.required ? 'required' : 'optional', info.default)
}
// name string required null
// age integer optional 0
```

A required parameter has no default, so its `default` is `null`. The record keeps the
type of an example, not the example itself, which is why `'anonymous'` does not appear.
Tools such as the documentation generator and the JSON Schema exporter read this record;
you can too.

## Skipping an optional parameter

Arguments are positional, as in JavaScript. To reach a later parameter while leaving an
earlier optional one at its default, pass `undefined` for it. `null` does not mean "use the
default": it is a value, and it is checked like any other.

```tjs:inline
function pad(text: 'x', width = 4, fill = ' ') {
  return text.padStart(width, fill)
}

console.log(pad('7'))                              // "   7"
console.log(pad('7', undefined, '0'))              // "0007": width keeps its default
console.log(isMonadicError(pad('7', null)))        // true: null is not an integer
console.log(isMonadicError(pad(undefined)))        // true: undefined counts as missing
console.log(pad('7', 4, '0', 'extra'))             // "0007": extra arguments are ignored
```

Passing `undefined` to a required parameter is the same as leaving it out, so it is an
error. Extra arguments are ignored, as in JavaScript.

For the same reason, put required parameters first. TJS allows a required parameter after
an optional one, and does not warn, but then every call has to fill the optional slot,
usually with `undefined`, just to reach the required one. With
`function late(a = 1, b: 'x')` you must write `late(undefined, 'y')`, and `late('y')` is an
error, because `'y'` lands in `a` and `b` is missing.

## A type and a separate default

Sometimes the default is not a good example of the type. A mode that is either `'grant'` or
`'deny'` should default to `'grant'`, but `mode = 'grant'` would accept any string. Write the
type, then the default, the way TypeScript does.

Here the type is `'grant' | 'deny'`. A lone string example widens to "any string", but
string literals joined by `|` are a closed set: the parameter accepts exactly those values
(see [Literal unions](/TJS-SYNTAX/#literal-unions)).

```tjs:inline
// Optional, checked against the type, defaulting to the default
function setMode(mode: 'grant' | 'deny' = 'grant') {
  return mode
}

function repeat(text: 'ab', times: number = 2): 'abab' {
  return text.repeat(times)
}

console.log(setMode())                                // grant
console.log(setMode('deny'))                          // deny
console.log(isMonadicError(setMode('maybe')))         // true: not in the set

console.log(repeat('xy'))                             // xyxy
console.log(repeat('xy', 3))                          // xyxyxy
console.log(isMonadicError(repeat('xy', 'many')))     // true
```

A default that fails its own type, such as `n: 0 = 'x'`, stops the file from transpiling.
The message is:

```text
The default of 'n: 0 = 'x'' does not satisfy its own type. Change the default, or the type.
```

## Things that trip people up

**`= null` accepts any value.** A bare `null` (or `undefined`) default tells TJS nothing
about the type, so it does not invent one:

```tjs:inline
// A bare null default means "anything, defaulting to null"
function describe(thing = null) {
  return thing == null ? 'nothing' : typeof thing
}
console.log(describe(), describe(42), describe({ a: 1 })) // nothing number object
```

If you mean "only `null`", write `thing: null`, which is required and rejects everything
else.

- **`name?: ''` is the TypeScript spelling of `name = ''`.** TJS accepts it as written,
  so you may use either. Both are optional, default to the
  empty string, and reject a non-string.
- **An object default is not atomic.** `opts = { x: 0, y: 0 }` merges a partial argument
  with the default member by member (`f({ x: 5 })` gets `{ x: 5, y: 0 }`). That is the
  subject of [Dictionary Defaults](/dictionary-defaults-example/). To get JavaScript's
  all-or-nothing default back for one parameter, write `opts = LegacyDefault({ x: 0, y: 0 })`.
  A type plus a default is atomic too: with `Type Point { example: { x: 0, y: 0 } }`
  declared, `p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2 }` checks a passed value as a whole `Point`, so
  `{ x: 5 }` is rejected rather than filled in. Merging is what an untyped object default
  means; once you name a type, the argument has to be one.

<!--{"section": "tjs-for-js", "group": "docs", "order": 2, "navTitle": "TJS for JS Devs", "parent": "tjs.md", "placement": {"language": {"parent": "for-programmers.md", "order": 20}}}-->

# TJS for JavaScript Programmers

_Everything you already know, plus the things you always wished JavaScript had._

---

## The One-Sentence Pitch

TJS is JavaScript with types that actually exist at runtime, equality that actually works, and errors that don't crash your program.

---

## What Stays the Same

TJS is a superset of JavaScript. All of this works exactly as you expect:

```javascript
const x = 42
let name = 'Alice'
const items = [1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2)
const user = { name: 'Bob', age: 30 }
const { name: userName, age } = user
const merged = { ...defaults, ...overrides }
const greeting = `Hello, ${name}!`

for (const item of items) {
  console.log(item)
}
while (condition) {
  /* ... */
}
if (x > 0) {
  /* ... */
} else {
  /* ... */
}

try {
  riskyThing()
} catch (e) {
  handleError(e)
}

class Dog {
  #name
  constructor(name) {
    this.#name = name
  }
  get name() {
    return this.#name
  }
}

import { something } from './module.js'
export function myFunction() {
  /* ... */
}
```

The _syntax_ above is all valid TJS. But note the next section: when you transpile **native TJS**, TJS also _improves_ some runtime behaviour (footgun-free `==`, honest truthiness, …). Those improvements are exactly the point of writing TJS — but they would change the meaning of existing JavaScript.

So TJS gates them on a **dialect**:

```javascript
import { tjs } from 'tjs-lang/lang'

tjs(jsSource) //                    → native TJS (improvements ON — the default)
tjs(jsSource, { dialect: 'js' }) // → plain JS  (semantics preserved, untouched)
```

For file-based tools, the extension is the dialect — `.js`/`.mjs` ⇒ `dialect: 'js'`, `.tjs` ⇒ native. Use the canonical helper so every tool agrees:

```javascript
import { tjs, dialectForFilename } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
tjs(source, { dialect: dialectForFilename(filename) })
```

Handling `.ts` too (a doc system, a bundler plugin)? Route the TS path through `fromTS`, imported from its own entry so the TypeScript compiler only loads when you actually transpile TS — `tjs-lang/lang` itself stays TS-free:

```javascript
import { tjs, sourceKindForFilename } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { fromTS } from 'tjs-lang/lang/from-ts' // TS compiler — only on the ts path

const kind = sourceKindForFilename(filename) // 'js' | 'ts' | 'tjs'
const code =
  kind === 'ts'
    ? tjs(fromTS(source, { emitTJS: true }).code).code
    : tjs(source, { dialect: kind }).code
```

With `dialect: 'js'` (or a `.js` file), if you don't use any TJS features your code is just JavaScript — same behaviour, no lock-in.

This extends to advanced patterns too: **Proxies**, **WeakMap/WeakSet**, **Symbols**, **generators**, **async iterators**, **`Object.defineProperty`** — all work identically. TJS adds type checks at function boundaries; it doesn't wrap or intercept any JS runtime behavior.

---

## What's Different

### 1. Types Are Example Values

In JavaScript, there are no types. In TJS, you annotate parameters with
an example of a valid value:

```javascript
// JavaScript
function greet(name) {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`
}

// TJS - name is required and must be a string (like 'World')
function greet(name: 'World'): 'Hello, World!' {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`
}
```

The `: 'World'` means "required, must be a string, here's an example." The `: 'Hello, World!'` means "returns a string, and here is what it returns for that example": TJS calls `greet('World')` at transpile time and checks the answer. These aren't abstract type annotations -- they're concrete values the system can use for testing, documentation, and validation.

| You Write         | TJS Infers                    |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------- |
| `name: 'Alice'`   | Required string               |
| `count: 42`       | Required integer              |
| `rate: 3.14`      | Required number (float)       |
| `age: +20`        | Required non-negative integer |
| `flag: true`      | Required boolean              |
| `items: [0]`      | Required integer[]            |
| `values: [0.0]`   | Required number[]             |
| `user: { n: '' }` | Required object               |
| `id: 0 \| null`  | integer or null               |

All of these are valid JavaScript expressions. `42` vs `42.0` vs `+42` are
all legal JS -- TJS leverages this to distinguish integer, float, and
non-negative integer types at the syntax level.

Note: `| null` means the value accepts the base type _or_ `null`, but not
`undefined`. TJS treats `null` and `undefined` as distinct types
(`typeOf(null) === 'null'`, `typeOf(undefined) === 'undefined'`).

**Optional** parameters use `=` (just like JS default values):

```javascript
function greet(name = 'World') {
  /* ... */
} // optional, defaults to 'World'
function retry(count = 3) {
  /* ... */
} // optional, defaults to 3 (integer)
```

**The difference:** `: value` means required. `= value` means optional with a default. In plain JS, both would be written as `= value`.

### 2. Numeric Type Narrowing

TJS distinguishes three numeric types using valid JavaScript syntax:

```javascript
function process(
  rate: 3.14,    // number (float) -- has a decimal point
  count: 42,     // integer -- whole number, no decimal
  index: +0      // non-negative integer -- prefixed with +
) { /* ... */ }
```

| You Write | Type Inferred          | Validates                       |
| --------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `3.14`    | `number` (float)       | Any number                      |
| `0.0`     | `number` (float)       | Any number                      |
| `42`      | `integer`              | `Number.isInteger(x)`           |
| `0`       | `integer`              | `Number.isInteger(x)`           |
| `+20`     | `non-negative integer` | `Number.isInteger(x) && x >= 0` |
| `+0`      | `non-negative integer` | `Number.isInteger(x) && x >= 0` |
| `-5`      | `integer`              | `Number.isInteger(x)`           |
| `-3.5`    | `number` (float)       | Any number                      |

These are all valid JavaScript expressions -- TJS just reads the syntax more
carefully than JS does. At runtime, passing `3.14` to a parameter typed as
integer returns a monadic error.

### 3. Return Type Annotations

TJS uses `:` for return types (same as TypeScript):

```javascript
// Returns an integer
function add(a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  return a + b
}

// Returns an object with this shape. `:!` means the example is the TYPE only.
function getUser(id: 0):! { name: '', age: 0 } {
  return { name: 'Alice', age: 30 }
}
```

The return example doubles as an automatic test. When you write `: 0`, TJS calls `add(0, 0)` at transpile time and checks that the result **equals** `0` (deep equality: it is a worked example, not just a type). When you only mean the shape of the result, as for `getUser`, write `:!` and no test runs.

### 4. Equality That Works

JavaScript's `==` is notoriously broken (type coercion). TJS fixes `==` to be a
**footgun-free `===`** — and adds `Is` for deep structural comparison:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```javascript
// JavaScript
'5' == 5                    // true  (coercion — footgun!)
0 == false                  // true  (coercion — footgun!)
new Boolean(false) == false // false (boxed primitive — footgun!)

// TJS (footgun-free == is on by default)
'5' == 5                    // false (no coercion)
0 == false                  // false (no coercion)
new Boolean(false) == false // true  (unwraps boxed primitives)
null == undefined           // true  (nullish equality)
NaN == NaN                  // true  (JS gets this wrong)

// TJS == is NOT structural — distinct objects are distinct:
[1, 2] == [1, 2]            // false (different references)
{ a: 1 } == { a: 1 }        // false (different references)

// For deep structural comparison, use Is:
[1, 2] Is [1, 2]            // true (same structure)
{ a: 1 } Is { a: 1 }        // true (same structure)
```

TJS redefines the operators:

| Operator | JavaScript          | TJS                                                                                           |
| -------- | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `==`     | Coercive equality   | Footgun-free `===` (no coercion, unwraps boxed, `null==undefined`); NOT structural — use `Is` |
| `!=`     | Coercive inequality | Negation of the above                                                                         |
| `===`    | Strict equality     | Identity (same ref) — unchanged from JS                                                       |
| `!==`    | Strict inequality   | Not same reference — unchanged from JS                                                        |

For deep structural comparison, use the explicit forms `Is` and `IsNot`:

```javascript
user Is expectedUser       // structural deep equality
result IsNot errorValue    // structural deep inequality
```

Classes can define custom equality:

```javascript
class Point {
  constructor(x: 0, y: 0) { this.x = x; this.y = y }
  Equals(other) { return this.x === other.x && this.y === other.y }
}

Point(1, 2) Is Point(1, 2)  // true, uses .Equals
```

Note: `Is` (structural comparison) does not handle circular references. Use `==`
or `===` for objects that might be circular, or define an `.Equals` method.

### 5. Errors Are Values, Not Exceptions

In JavaScript, type errors crash your program. In TJS, they're values:

```javascript
function double(x: 0): 0 {
  return x * 2
}

double(5) // 10
double('oops') // MonadicError: "Expected integer for 'double.x', got string"
```

No `try`/`catch`. No crashes. The caller gets a clear error value they can inspect:

```javascript
const result = double(input)
if (isMonadicError(result)) {
  console.log(result.message) // handle gracefully
} else {
  useResult(result)
}
```

Errors propagate automatically through function calls. If you pass a monadic error to another TJS function where it does not fit the parameter's type, it passes through without executing:

```javascript
const a = step1(badInput) // MonadicError
const b = step2(a) // skips execution, returns the same error
const c = step3(b) // skips again -- error flows to the surface
```

This is sometimes called "railway-oriented programming." A function that declares it takes
anything (`x: any`, `x: unknown`) receives the error and runs; that is how a handler works. A
plain `Error` passed where something else is expected is an ordinary type error.

### 6. Classes Without `new`

TJS classes are callable as functions:

```javascript
// JavaScript
const p = new Point(10, 20)

// TJS - both work, but the clean form is preferred
const p1 = Point(10, 20) // works
const p2 = new Point(10, 20) // also works (linter warns)
```

This is cleaner and more consistent with functional style. Under the hood, TJS uses a Proxy to auto-construct when you call a class as a function.

### 7. `const` for Free

Uppercase identifiers automatically get `const`:

```javascript
// TJS
Config = { debug: true, version: '1.0' }
MaxRetries = 3

// Transpiles to
const Config = { debug: true, version: '1.0' }
const MaxRetries = 3
```

Lowercase identifiers behave normally. This is a **native-TJS** feature — it's
off when you transpile a plain-JS file (`dialect: 'js'`), so JS keeps its own
semantics. It also only applies to the **first** assignment of an
otherwise-undeclared uppercase name: `let B = null; … B = 2` (a reassignment) is
left alone. Since the first assignment becomes a `const`, use `let Foo = …` up
front if `Foo` needs to change later — otherwise a later `Foo = …` throws.

---

## The Type System

JavaScript has no type system. Libraries like Zod and Ajv bolt one on,
but they're separate from your function signatures -- a second source of
truth that drifts. TJS's `Type()` built-in gives you as much narrowing
and specificity as you want, in one place, using plain functions you
already know how to write.

### From Simple to Sophisticated

```javascript
// Simple -- infer type from an example value
Type Name 'Alice'                            // any string

// Descriptive -- add documentation
Type User {
  description: 'a registered user'
  example: { name: '', age: 0, email: '' }
}

// Constrained -- add a predicate for narrowing
Type PositiveNumber {
  description: 'a number greater than zero'
  example: 1
  predicate(x) { return typeof x === 'number' && x > 0 }
}

// Domain-specific -- real business rules
Type USZipCode {
  description: '5-digit US zip code'
  example: '90210'
  predicate(v) { return typeof v === 'string' && /^\d{5}$/.test(v) }
}

Type Email {
  description: 'email address'
  example: 'user@example.com'
  predicate(v) { return typeof v === 'string' && /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(v) }
}
```

The key insight: a `predicate` is just a function that returns `true` or
`false`. If you can express a constraint as a boolean check, you can make
it a type. No schema DSL to learn, no special syntax -- it's JavaScript
all the way down.

Types work in function signatures:

```javascript
function sendWelcome(email: Email, name: Name): '' {
  return `Welcome, ${name}! Confirmation sent to ${email}.`
}

sendWelcome('alice@example.com', 'Alice') // works
sendWelcome('not-an-email', 'Alice') // MonadicError
```

TJS also ships common types out of the box: `TString`, `TNumber`,
`TBoolean`, `TInteger`, `TPositiveInt`, `TNonEmptyString`, `TEmail`,
`TUrl`, `TUuid`, `Timestamp`, `LegalDate`. No imports from a validation
library needed.

### Combinators

Compose types from other types:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```javascript
Type OptionalEmail Nullable(Email)         // Email | null
Type UserIds TArray(TPositiveInt)           // array of positive integers
```

### Unions and Enums

```javascript
// Union of string literals
Union Status 'task status' 'pending' | 'active' | 'done'

// Enum with named members
Enum Color 'CSS color' {
  Red = 'red'
  Green = 'green'
  Blue = 'blue'
}

// Discriminated union -- like tagged unions or sum types
const Shape = Union('kind', {
  circle: { radius: 0 },
  rectangle: { width: 0, height: 0 }
})
```

### Generics

Runtime-checkable generic types:

```javascript
Generic Box<T> {
  description: 'a boxed value'
  predicate(x, T) {
    return typeof x === 'object' && x !== null && 'value' in x && T(x.value)
  }
}

// Instantiate with a concrete type
const NumberBox = Box(TNumber)
NumberBox.check({ value: 42 })     // true
NumberBox.check({ value: 'nope' }) // false
```

---

## Runtime Metadata

Every TJS function carries its type information at runtime via `__tjs`:

```javascript
function createUser(input: { name: '', age: 0 }):! { id: 0 } {
  return { id: 123 }
}

createUser.__tjs
// {
//   params: { input: { type: { kind: 'object', shape: {...} }, required: true } },
//   returns: { type: { kind: 'object', shape: { id: { kind: 'integer' } } } }
// }
```

This metadata enables autocomplete from live objects, automatic documentation
generation, and runtime reflection -- things that require build tools and
external libraries in vanilla JavaScript.

---

## Safety Levels

You control how much validation TJS applies:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```javascript
// Per-module (top of file)
safety none     // Metadata only -- no runtime checks (fastest)
safety inputs   // Validate inputs only (default)
safety all      // accepted; same as safety inputs

// Per-function
function fastPath(! x: 0) { /* ... */ }   // Skip validation
```

Use `!` (skip validation) only in hot loops where every microsecond counts
and the data source is already trusted. In all other cases, the ~1.5x
overhead of `safety inputs` is negligible compared to the bugs it catches.

### There Is No `unsafe { }` Block

There is no `unsafe` block, and the old `unsafe <expr>` prefix is deprecated. To skip
validation for a hot path, mark the FUNCTION with `!`:

```javascript
function hotLoop(! data: [0]) {
  let total = 0
  for (let i = 0; i < data.length; i++) total += data[i]
  return total
}
```

---

## Inline Tests

Tests live next to the code they test and run at transpile time:

```javascript
function isPrime(n: 2): true {
  if (n < 2) return false
  for (let i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) {
    if (n % i === 0) return false
  }
  return true
}

test 'prime detection' {
  expect(isPrime(2)).toBe(true)
  expect(isPrime(4)).toBe(false)
  expect(isPrime(17)).toBe(true)
}
```

Tests are stripped from production output. They're also generated
automatically from return type annotations -- `: true` means TJS will call
`isPrime(2)` and verify it returns a boolean.

---

## WASM Blocks

For compute-heavy code, drop into WebAssembly:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```javascript
const add = wasm (a: i32, b: i32): i32 {
  local.get $a
  local.get $b
  i32.add
}

add(1, 2)  // 3, runs as native WASM
```

WASM is compiled at transpile time and embedded as base64 in the output.
No separate `.wasm` files.

### Reusable WASM Functions

For a kernel that other files can import, use a top-level `wasm function`
declaration:

```javascript
export wasm function dot(a: Float32Array, b: Float32Array, n: i32): f64 {
  // ... SIMD f32x4 implementation ...
}
```

Other files can import it directly:

```javascript
import { dot } from './my-lib.tjs'
// `dot` is composed into your file's wasm module at transpile time
// — no JS↔WASM boundary on intra-library calls
```

The first stdlib built on this is `tjs-lang/linalg` — SIMD vector kernels
ready to use:

```javascript
import { dot, norm_sq } from 'tjs-lang/linalg'
const cos = dot(a, b, n) / Math.sqrt(norm_sq(a, n) * norm_sq(b, n))
```

See [`DOCS-WASM.md`](DOCS-WASM.md) for the full story — declaration syntax,
the JS-owns-memory model, cross-file composition, and the two distribution
forms (composed vs. boundary).

---

## Safe Eval

The killer feature for many use cases. Run untrusted code safely:

```javascript
import { Eval, SafeFunction } from 'tjs-lang/eval'

// One-shot evaluation
const { result } = await Eval({
  code: 'return items.filter(x => x > threshold)',
  context: { items: [1, 5, 10, 15], threshold: 7 },
  fuel: 1000,
})
// result: [10, 15]

// Reusable safe function
const transform = await SafeFunction({
  body: 'return x * multiplier',
  params: ['x'],
  fuel: 500,
})

await transform(21) // { result: 42, fuelUsed: 8 }
```

- Gas-limited (fuel runs out = execution stops, no infinite loops)
- Capability-based (no I/O unless you grant it)
- No `eval()`, no CSP violations, no containers

---

## What You Give Up

TJS is opinionated. Here's what changes:

| JavaScript                 | TJS                           | Why                             |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `==` (type coercion)       | `==` (footgun-free `===`)     | Coercion is a bug factory       |
| Exceptions for type bugs   | Monadic error values          | Exceptions escape, values don't |
| `new ClassName()`          | `ClassName()` preferred       | Cleaner, more functional        |
| No runtime types           | `__tjs` metadata on functions | Types should exist at runtime   |
| `typeof null === 'object'` | `typeOf(null) === 'null'`     | JS got this wrong in 1995       |

Nothing is taken away. `new` still works. `===` still works. You can write
plain JavaScript in a `.tjs` file and it works. The type-related additions
use explicit syntax (`:` annotations, `:` return types, `Type` declarations).
Behavioral modes like footgun-free `==`, callable classes, and honest
`typeof` are enabled by default in native TJS files. Use `TjsCompat` at the
top of a file to disable all modes for gradual migration or JS interop.

---

## Getting Started

```bash
npm install tjs-lang
```

### Try It in the Browser

The playground runs the full TJS compiler in your browser -- no backend needed:

**[tjs-platform.web.app](https://tjs-platform.web.app)**

### CLI

```bash
bun src/cli/tjs.ts check file.tjs   # Parse and type check
bun src/cli/tjs.ts run file.tjs     # Transpile and execute
bun src/cli/tjs.ts emit file.tjs    # Output transpiled JS
bun src/cli/tjs.ts test file.tjs    # Run inline tests
```

### From Code

```javascript
import { tjs } from 'tjs-lang'

const output = tjs`
  function add(a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
    return a + b
  }
`
```

---

## Runtime Traceability

Every TJS function carries its source identity in `__tjs` metadata.
When validation fails, the error tells you exactly which function and
parameter failed, in which source file:

```javascript
function add(a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  return a + b
}

add.__tjs.source // "mymodule.tjs:3"
add('oops', 1) // MonadicError { path: "mymodule.tjs:3:add.a", expected: "integer", actual: "string" }
```

No source maps. No build artifacts. The function _knows where it came from_.

---

## Learn More

- [TJS Language Reference](DOCS-TJS.md) -- Full syntax and features
- [AJS Agent Language](DOCS-AJS.md) -- The sandboxed agent VM
- [TJS for TypeScript Programmers](TJS-FOR-TS.md) -- Coming from TypeScript?
- [Playground](https://tjs-platform.web.app) -- Try it live

# Validation

TJS converts a `.ts` file (with `fromTS`) into JavaScript that can keep its types as checks
that run when the code does. Your source stays TypeScript; the conversion is a build step
([Converting a Project](/ts-converting-a-project/) shows the pipeline). Those runtime checks
are the reason to put TypeScript through TJS at all.

They are off by default. Converted TypeScript keeps JavaScript's behaviour and validates
nothing, so it runs exactly as `tsc` output would. A `/* @tjs TjsStrict */` comment at the
top of a file opts that file in to full TJS, and from then on every parameter type is a check
that runs on every call, including calls with data the compiler never saw: JSON, form input,
anything cast with `as any`. ([`@tjs` annotations](/TJS-FOR-TS/) lists the others.)

```ts:inline
/* @tjs TjsStrict */

function half(n: number): number {
  console.log('half ran') // never printed below
  return n / 2
}

const order = JSON.parse('{"count": "10"}') // a string where a number belongs

const result: any = half(half(order.count)) // the outer call receives an error
if (result instanceof Error) console.log('rejected:', result.message)
else console.log('result:', result)
```

This prints one line, `rejected: Expected number for '…half.n', got string`, and `half ran`
never appears: the inner call refused the string, and the outer call refused the error it
was handed. Delete the `TjsStrict` line and it prints `half ran` twice, then `result: 2.5`:
JavaScript coerced `'10'` to a number and nothing noticed. (`result` is typed `any` because
`tsc` believes `half` always returns a number; see below.)

## What a failed check returns

A failed check does not throw. The function returns a `MonadicError`, a subclass of `Error`
that names the parameter, the type it expected and what it got. Test for it with
`isMonadicError(value)`, imported from `tjs-lang/runtime`, or with `instanceof Error`.

This means a function declared `: string` can return an error object, and the TypeScript
signature does not say so. `tsc` still believes the result is a `string`. The checks are for
data that arrives at run time, where `tsc` was never going to see it; test the result with
`isMonadicError` at the places where such data comes in.

Inside TJS code, an error passed on does not cause new ones. A checked function that receives
a `MonadicError` where it expects a typed value returns that error unchanged without running
its body. A parameter typed `any` or `unknown` is not checked, so a function with one runs
its body with the error as an ordinary value. Outside TJS (plain JavaScript, a library,
string concatenation) a `MonadicError` is an ordinary `Error` object, and nothing stops it
from being treated as data. That boundary is where you test for it.

## What it checks, and what it costs

Parameters are checked; return types are not. `fromTS` writes a TypeScript return type as a
type-only annotation, so a function that returns the wrong type returns it unchecked.

Primitive types, interfaces and object types (each member is checked; extra keys pass
through), and unions of those are checked. Types with no runtime form degrade to `any` and
check nothing: unconstrained generics (`<T>`), unions of literal values (`'a' | 'b'`),
utility types such as `Partial<T>`, and enum-typed parameters. The converter marks each one
with a `TODO: TS types degraded` comment, so you can find every check it could not make.
[TJS for TypeScript Programmers](/TJS-FOR-TS/) has the full table.

A check is cheap, and its cost is paid by the function being called, on every call. The
[Performance Guide](/performance/) shows the shape of that cost and how to skip the checks in
a function where you have measured a problem.

## The examples

<!-- prettier-ignore-start -->

<!-- toc -->
- [Runtime Validation](/ts-runtime-validation/)
- [Object Validation](/ts-object-validation/)
- [Optional Parameters](/ts-optional-parameters/)
- [Embedded Tests](/ts-embedded-tests/)
<!-- /toc -->

<!-- prettier-ignore-end -->

- **Runtime Validation**: primitive parameters checked on every call, and an error passed on
  without running the next function.
- **Object Validation**: an interface checked as a whole shape.
- **Optional Parameters**: `?` and `= default` survive conversion, and `undefined` is not
  `null`.
- **Embedded Tests**: the other way TJS checks a TypeScript file. Tests are written inside
  `/*test … */` comments, which `tsc` ignores; TJS runs them when it compiles the file, not
  when your code is called.

# Values and Expressions

AJS is a JavaScript subset. At the level of a single expression it reads like the JavaScript you
know: `let` and `const`, arithmetic, comparisons, template strings, `trim` and `slice` and
`push`. This chapter covers what a value can be, how variables and assignment work, and which
operators, methods and builtins exist.

Three differences from JavaScript matter most, and each has its own section:

- **An object or array is never converted to a primitive behind your back.** `'tags: ' + tags`
  is an error, not `'tags: a,b'`. See [No hidden conversions](#no-hidden-conversions).
- **You cannot write into an object or array.** `o.a = 1` and `xs[0] = v` are refused; you
  build a new value instead. See [Assignment](#assignment-writes-a-variable-never-a-member).
- **Reading a member never throws.** `user.address.city` with no address gives `undefined`. See
  [Member access is null-safe](#member-access-is-null-safe).

Smaller differences (no `new`, a closed list of methods, a 1-based month) are flagged where they
come up, and the [last table](#refused-and-what-to-write-instead) collects them.

Every runnable example is a small agent. It takes no input (or uses the defaults it declares)
and returns an object, so running it shows you the values. Snippets in a plain `javascript`
block are fragments, usually code AJS refuses; they are there to read, not to run.

**Refused** in this chapter always says when: **at transpile time** means the agent never
starts and the error points at the line; **when the line runs** means the agent starts and fails
at that line, as an ordinary error a `try` can catch ([When Things Fail](/ajs-errors/)).

## Values are data

A value in AJS is data: a number, a string, a boolean, `null` or `undefined`, an array, or a
plain object. Sets and dates are data too.

```ajs:inline
function values() {
  const count = 3
  const price = 2.5
  const name = 'Ada'
  const active = true
  const nothing = null
  const tags = ['new', 'sale']
  const item = { name, price, tags }
  const unique = Set(['a', 'b', 'a'])
  const when = Date('2024-01-15T10:00:00Z')
  return { count, price, name, active, nothing, tags, item, unique, when }
}
```

`unique` comes back as `['a', 'b']`: a set **is** an array of its items. `when` comes back as a
plain object of UTC fields, starting `{ value: '2024-01-15T10:00:00.000Z', timestamp:
1705312800000, year: 2024, month: 1, … }`. While the agent runs, the VM remembers that these
values are a set and a date and gives them methods; see [Set](#set) and [Date](#date) below.

Two details about the empty values:

- A `let x` with no value starts as `null`, not `undefined` as in JavaScript.
- A result field whose value is `undefined` is **left out** of what the host receives, as
  `JSON.stringify` would leave it out; an `undefined` inside an array becomes `null`.

A function or a namespace is never a value. You call it; you cannot hold it. Each of these is
refused at transpile time:

```javascript
const m = Math              // a builtin namespace is not a value
const f = text.trim         // 'trim' is a method: call it, text.trim()
items.map(parseInt)         // pass an arrow: items.map((x) => parseInt(x))
```

The last one fails with `Method 'map' is not available in AsyncJS`, which reads as if `map` did
not exist. It does; the message means "pass an arrow, not a function name".

The reason for the rule: everything an agent holds can be copied, printed and counted against
the run's budgets, and a function can be none of those. (Every run has a budget for work,
called fuel, and one for memory; the VM charges each operation against them before doing it.
[Your First Agent](/ajs-first-agent/#running-it-from-a-host) introduced fuel, and
[Limits](/ajs-limits/) covers the budgets.)

## No hidden conversions

This is the main difference from JavaScript. In JavaScript, `'tags: ' + tags` with an array
quietly calls the array's `toString` and gives `'tags: a,b'`. In AJS the same line is an error.
So are these:

```javascript
'tags: ' + tags      // '+' needs a string, number, boolean or null, not an array
`tags: ${tags}`      // the same error, also naming '+'
tags < 5             // '<' needs a string, number, boolean or null, not an array
obj[tags]            // a computed key needs a string, number, boolean or null, not an array
Math.max(tags)       // max()'s argument 1 must be a number
```

Operators, template interpolation, computed keys and most method arguments take primitives. An
object or array where a primitive belongs is an error, not a silent conversion.

Primitives still mix as they do in JavaScript: `'item ' + 7` is `'item 7'`, `'5' + 1` is `'51'`,
`'5' < 6` is true and `true + 1` is 2. So does `undefined`: `'Hi ' + user.nmae`, where the
field is missing, gives `'Hi undefined'`, in a template too. The rule is narrow on purpose: AJS
never turns an object or array into a primitive.

The reason: turning an array or object into a string is an allocation whose size depends on the
data, and an implicit one happens where the VM cannot charge for it before it is made. Rather
than guess, AJS refuses, and you write the conversion yourself, where it is visible and paid for.

The fix is to say which string you mean:

```ajs:inline
function explicit({ tags = ['a', 'b'], scores = [3, 9, 4], order = { id: 7, total: 12 } }) {
  return {
    joined: 'tags: ' + tags.join(','), // 'tags: a,b'
    listed: `tags: ${tags.join(', ')}`, // 'tags: a, b'
    json: 'order ' + JSON.stringify(order), // 'order {"id":7,"total":12}'
    count: 'tags: ' + tags.length, // 'tags: 2'
    biggest: Math.max(scores[0], scores[1], scores[2]), // 9
  }
}
```

`Math.max` takes numbers, so pass it numbers. For the largest item of an array of any length,
`reduce` does the job; it is covered in [Decisions, Loops and Helpers](/ajs-control-flow/).

Two things to know about the error when you hit it:

- **It is refused when the line runs, not at transpile time.** The transpiler does not know
  that `tags` holds an array. If nothing catches the error, the run ends and the host receives
  it as the run's `error`.
- **The message names `'+'` even for a template string.** `` `tags: ${tags}` `` fails with
  `'+' needs a string, number, boolean or null, not an array`, because a template is built by
  concatenation. If you see a `'+'` error on a line with no plus sign, look for an interpolated
  array or object.

## Variables

Declare a variable with `let` (it may be reassigned) or `const` (it may not). A name must be
declared before it is read, and variables are block-scoped, as in modern JavaScript:

```ajs:inline
function counters() {
  let total = 10
  total += 5
  total *= 2
  total -= 6
  let visits = 0
  visits++
  visits++
  let note = 'outer'
  if (total > 20) {
    let note = 'inner' // a different variable, alive only inside these braces
    total = total + 1
  }
  return { total, visits, note }
}
```

This returns `{ total: 25, visits: 2, note: 'outer' }`. The `total = total + 1` inside the `if`
writes the outer `total`; the inner `let note` is a new variable that disappears at the closing
brace.

Reading a name that was never declared is refused at transpile time, and the error names it, so
a misspelled name you **read** is caught before anything runs:

```javascript
let count = 0
return { n: cuont }
// 'cuont' is not defined. Declare it with let or const, or take it as a parameter.
```

A misspelled name you **assign to** is refused the same way. `totl = 5`, meant for `total`, would
otherwise create a new variable `totl` and leave `total` unchanged:

```javascript
let total = 0
totl = 5
// 'totl' is not declared, so assigning to it would create a new variable silently.
// Declare it with let (let totl = …), or check the spelling.
```

Reassigning a `const` is refused when the line runs, with `Cannot reassign const variable 'c'`,
and a `try` can catch it. The transpiler could see this one too; today it leaves it to the VM.

Give a variable one kind of value for its whole life: a count stays a number, a label stays a
string. Nothing enforces this; it is advice, because a variable that changes kind is hard to
read. When you need a value of another kind, declare another variable.

### Assignment writes a variable, never a member

> **Works differently, silently: `Object.assign`.** In JavaScript, `Object.assign(user, extra)`
> changes `user`. In AJS it **returns a new object and leaves `user` alone**, and nothing warns
> you. When you mean to change `user`, assign the result: `user = Object.assign(user, extra)`
> (with `let user`), or `user = { ...user, ...extra }`.

Every compound operator works (`+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `**=`, `??=`, `||=`, `&&=`), and so
do `++` and `--` as statements of their own. `++` used as a value, as in `let y = x++`, is
refused at transpile time. Split it into two lines in the order you mean: `let y = x` then
`x++` for `y = x++` (y gets the old value), or `x++` then `let y = x` for `y = ++x` (y gets the
new one).

What you cannot do is write into an object or array. `o.a = 1` and `xs[0] = v` are refused at
transpile time with `Only simple variable assignment is supported`. Build a new value instead:
spread for an object, `with` to replace one item of an array, or a method that changes the array
in place, such as `push`:

```ajs:inline
function update() {
  let user = { name: 'Ada', role: 'user' }
  const promoted = { ...user, role: 'admin' }
  let scores = [3, 5, 8]
  scores = scores.with(0, 4) // replace item 0
  const tags = ['a']
  tags.push('b') // in place
  const more = [...tags, 'c']
  const merged = Object.assign(user, { team: 'core' })
  return { user, promoted, scores, tags, more, merged }
}
```

This returns `user: { name: 'Ada', role: 'user' }`, `promoted: { name: 'Ada', role: 'admin' }`,
`scores: [4, 5, 8]`, `tags: ['a', 'b']`, `more: ['a', 'b', 'c']` and `merged: { name: 'Ada',
role: 'user', team: 'core' }`. Note that `user` is unchanged: that is the `Object.assign`
difference above.

**Which methods change their array?** The same ones as in JavaScript: `push`, `pop`, `shift`,
`unshift`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse`, `fill` and `copyWithin` change the array they are called
on, even through a `const`. `const` stops you assigning the name, not changing the array, as in
JavaScript. The others, including `with`, `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced`, `slice` and
`concat`, return a new array and leave the original alone. The one exception to "as in
JavaScript" is `Object.assign`.

## Operators

Arithmetic and comparison work as in JavaScript on numbers, strings and booleans:

```ajs:inline
function arithmetic({ a = 7, b = 2 }) {
  return {
    sum: a + b, // 9
    quotient: a / b, // 3.5
    remainder: a % b, // 1
    power: a ** b, // 49
    bigger: a > b, // true
    joined: 'item ' + a, // 'item 7'
    alphabetical: 'apple' < 'banana', // true
  }
}
```

### Equality

`==` is `===`, with two exceptions: `null == undefined` is true, and `NaN == NaN` is true. `===`
and `!==` are JavaScript's own, with no exceptions: `null === undefined` and `NaN === NaN` are
both false. Neither operator ever coerces (`'1' == 1` is false), and objects and arrays compare
by identity, not by contents:

```ajs:inline
function equality() {
  const a = { id: 1 }
  const b = a
  return {
    noCoercion: '1' == 1, // false
    nullish: null == undefined, // true
    nan: NaN == NaN, // true
    sameObject: a == b, // true: the same object
    notStructural: [1, 2] == [1, 2], // false: two distinct arrays
    sameContents: JSON.stringify(a) == JSON.stringify({ id: 1 }), // true
  }
}
```

To compare contents, compare the fields you care about (`a.id == c.id`), or compare
`JSON.stringify` of both sides when their keys are in the same order. Use `==` unless you need to
tell `null` from `undefined`.

### Logical operators and the ternary

`&&`, `||`, `??` and `cond ? x : y` behave as in JavaScript. Notice the difference between `||`
and `??` on an empty string:

```ajs:inline
function logic({ name = '', count = 0 }) {
  return {
    orFallback: name || 'anonymous', // 'anonymous': '' is falsy
    nullishFallback: name ?? 'anonymous', // '': only null and undefined fall through
    zeroKept: count ?? 10, // 0
    status: count > 0 ? 'some' : 'none', // 'none'
    both: count > 0 && name != '', // false
  }
}
```

Use `??` for "a default when missing" and `||` only when every falsy value (`''`, `0`, `false`)
should be replaced.

## Member access is null-safe

Agents work on data from outside: API responses, model output, stored records. A field is often
missing, and a crash on the first absent one would turn every agent into a pile of checks. So
every member read behaves like optional chaining: reading a property of `null` or `undefined`
gives `undefined` instead of throwing.

```ajs:inline
function lookup({ user = { name: 'Ada', address: null }, key = 'name' }) {
  const city = user.address.city // user.address is null: city is undefined
  const value = user[key] // computed access with a variable
  const initial = user.name[0] // an index into a string
  return { city, value, initial }
}
```

This returns `{ value: 'Ada', initial: 'A' }`. There is no `city` in the result: it was
`undefined`, and an `undefined` field is left out.

The cost is real: a typo such as `user.nmae` also reads as `undefined` instead of failing, and
`'Hi ' + user.nmae` quietly gives `'Hi undefined'`. Use names carefully, and let the agent's
declared inputs and result catch some of these at the edges; see [Contracts](/ajs-contracts/).

Computed access, `items[i]` or `user[key]`, works with literals and variables alike. The key must
be a primitive; an `undefined` key is read as the key `'undefined'`, as in JavaScript. `?.` is
accepted, but adds nothing: every read is already null-safe.

## Template strings

Template strings work as in JavaScript, as long as every interpolated value is a primitive:

```ajs:inline
function templates({ name = 'Ada', count = 3, done = false }) {
  const line = `${name} has ${count} items`
  const flag = `done: ${done}`
  const asText = `${count}` // the way to turn a number into a string
  return { line, flag, asText }
}
```

This returns `{ line: 'Ada has 3 items', flag: 'done: false', asText: '3' }`.

## Methods

Strings, numbers, arrays and objects have a **closed** list of methods: the ones in the
[Methods table](/DOCS-AJS/#methods). Anything not on the list is refused, and the error names the
method. `text.matchAll(/a/g)` is refused because `matchAll` is not on the list.

```ajs:inline
function methods({ text = '  Hello World  ', nums = [3, 1, 2] }) {
  const clean = text.trim()
  const words = clean.split(' ')
  const shout = clean.toUpperCase()
  const padded = '7'.padStart(3, '0')
  const sorted = nums.toSorted() // a new array; nums is unchanged
  const has = nums.includes(2)
  const firstTwo = nums.slice(0, 2)
  const labels = ['b', 'a', 'c']
  labels.sort() // in place
  const backwards = labels.toReversed()
  return { clean, words, shout, padded, nums, sorted, has, firstTwo, labels, backwards }
}
```

This returns `clean: 'Hello World'`, `words: ['Hello', 'World']`, `shout: 'HELLO WORLD'`,
`padded: '007'`, `nums: [3, 1, 2]`, `sorted: [1, 2, 3]`, `has: true`, `firstTwo: [3, 1]`,
`labels: ['a', 'b', 'c']` and `backwards: ['c', 'b', 'a']`.

**Sorting has two traps.** First, `sort()` and `toSorted()` compare items **as text**, exactly
as JavaScript's default sort does, so `[10, 9, 1]` sorts to `[1, 10, 9]`. The `[3, 1, 2]` above
only looks numeric because every item has one digit. Second, there is no comparator:
`xs.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)` is refused at transpile time with the unhelpful
`Unsupported expression type in condition: ArrowFunctionExpression`. So sorting strings, and
reversing with `toReversed()` for descending order, works. Sorting numbers by value, or objects
by a field (an array of objects is refused when the line runs), has no built-in way today; it
takes a loop, written with the tools in [Decisions, Loops and Helpers](/ajs-control-flow/).

Two rules apply to every call. Both are checked when the line runs:

- **Exactly the arguments the method takes, with exactly the types it reads.**
  `'x'.repeat('3')` is an error (`repeat()'s argument 1 must be a number`), and so is
  `text.slice(0, 1, 2)` (`slice() takes at most 2 argument(s)`). JavaScript would have
  converted the `'3'` or ignored the extra argument.
- **Arguments are primitives, unless the method stores, searches for or copies the argument
  itself.** `xs.includes(item)`, `xs.indexOf(item)`, `xs.push(item)`, `xs.with(0, item)`,
  `xs.concat(other)` and `Object.keys(obj)` take objects and arrays, because the object is the
  thing they work with. `'abc'.includes(['a'])` is an error: a string search needs a string.

Why the list is closed: every method on it has a declared bound on what one call may allocate,
so the VM can charge the run's budget for the call before it runs. A method with no such bound
is not on the list.

`map`, `filter`, `find` and `reduce` take a callback, and they have rules of their own. They
belong to [Decisions, Loops and Helpers](/ajs-control-flow/).

[String Processing](/string-processing/) has more string examples.

## Builtins

Expressions have a fixed set of builtins. Like methods, they are called, never held.

### Math, JSON and the statics

```ajs:inline
function builtins() {
  return {
    floor: Math.floor(3.7), // 3
    biggest: Math.max(4, 9, 2), // 9
    root: Math.sqrt(16), // 4
    parsed: JSON.parse('{"a": 1}'), // { a: 1 }
    text: JSON.stringify({ a: [1, 2] }), // '{"a":[1,2]}'
    isList: Array.isArray([1, 2]), // true
    keys: Object.keys({ a: 1, b: 2 }), // ['a', 'b']
    pairs: Object.fromEntries([['x', 1]]), // { x: 1 }
    letter: String.fromCharCode(65), // 'A'
    int: parseInt('42px'), // 42
    float: parseFloat('3.5'), // 3.5
    query: encodeURIComponent('a b&c'), // 'a%20b%26c'
  }
}
```

All of JavaScript's `Math` is there, including `Math.random()`, which reads a random source the
host grants; see [time and randomness](#time-and-randomness) below. `parseInt`, `parseFloat` and
`encodeURIComponent` are plain functions, and `Number.parseInt` and `Number.parseFloat` work
too. `JSON.parse` on text that is not JSON is refused when the line runs, as an ordinary
catchable error. The full list of statics on `Array`, `Object`, `String` and `Number` is under
[Expression Builtins](/DOCS-AJS/#expression-builtins); [Math Operations](/math-operations/) and
[JSON Processing](/json-processing/) are worked examples.

**`String(n)` and `Number(s)` do not exist.** To turn a number into a string, write
`` `${n}` ``; to read a number from a string, write `parseFloat(s)` or `parseInt(s)`. `Set` and
`Date` can be called like this because AJS defines them as its own builtins; `String` and
`Number` are only namespaces for their statics (`String.fromCharCode`, `Number.isInteger`).

`let s = String(n)` is refused at transpile time with a confusing message:
`'String' takes named arguments`. The transpiler treats a call to a name it does not know as a
call to an **atom**, an operation the host provides (the [next chapter](/ajs-calling-atoms/)
covers them), and atoms take named arguments. Read it as "`String` is not available".

### Set

`Set(items)` makes a set of unique items. Write it without `new`; AJS has no `new`, and
`new Set(xs)` is refused at transpile time.

```ajs:inline
function sets() {
  const tags = Set(['a', 'b', 'b']) // ['a', 'b']
  tags.add('c') // in place
  tags.remove('a') // remove, not delete
  const stored = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(tags)) // back to a plain array
  const again = Set(stored)
  return {
    tags, // ['b', 'c']
    has: tags.has('b'), // true
    size: tags.size, // 2
    first: tags[0], // 'b'
    diff: tags.diff(['b']), // ['c']: diff, not difference
    union: tags.union(['d']), // ['b', 'c', 'd']
    asArray: tags.toArray().join('+'), // 'b+c'
    againHas: again.has('c'), // true
  }
}
```

A set is not JavaScript's `Set`. It is an array of its items that the VM marks as a set for the
rest of the run, and the marked array gets set methods instead of array methods:

- **What still works as on an array:** `length`, reading by index (`tags[0]`), `map`, `filter`,
  `find` and `reduce`, and `Array.isArray` (true).
- **Set methods:** `add`, `remove`, `clear`, `has`, `size`, `union`, `intersection`, `diff` and
  `toArray`. The names are AJS's own, so `remove` and `diff`, not JavaScript's `delete` and
  `difference`. The rest are under [Set](/DOCS-AJS/#set).
- **Array methods are not there.** `push`, `slice`, `join` and the rest fail when the line runs,
  with `'push' is not a function`. Call `toArray()` to get a plain array when you need one.

The JavaScript names fail in different ways, so the messages are worth recognising.
`tags.delete('a')` is refused at transpile time with `Method 'delete' is not available in
AsyncJS`. `tags.difference(['b'])` is refused when the line runs with `Security Error: method
'difference' is not callable in AsyncJS`; despite the wording, that only means the method is not
on the list.

`JSON.stringify`, a store or a capability sees a set as a plain array. After a round trip through
any of them it is a plain array again, without set methods; call `Set(x)` on it to get them back.

### Date

A date is made by calling `Date` without `new` (`new Date(s)` is refused at transpile time):

- `Date(text)` from an ISO string. Text that does not parse is refused when the line runs, with
  `Invalid date: 'nope' does not parse`, and a `try` can catch it.
- `Date(ms)` from a number of milliseconds since 1970.
- `Date(stored)` from a date that went through JSON, a store or a capability (see below).
- `Date()` with no argument: now, read from the clock the host grants. `Date.now()` is now as a
  number of milliseconds. See [time and randomness](#time-and-randomness).

```ajs:inline
function dates() {
  const d = Date('2024-01-15T10:00:00Z')
  const later = d.add({ days: 10 }) // a new date; d is unchanged
  const stored = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ d })).d // what a store would give back
  const restored = Date(stored)
  return {
    year: d.year, // 2024
    month: d.month, // 1: January is 1, not 0
    day: d.day, // 15, the day of the month
    weekday: d.dayOfWeek, // 1: Monday (Sunday is 0)
    hours: d.hours, // 10, in UTC
    iso: later.value, // '2024-01-25T10:00:00.000Z'
    days: later.diff(d, 'days'), // 10
    formatted: later.format('YYYY-MM-DD'), // '2024-01-25'
    sameMoment: restored.timestamp == d.timestamp, // true
  }
}
```

What to know about a date:

- **It is a data object** with the fields `value` (the ISO string), `timestamp` (milliseconds),
  `year`, `month`, `day`, `hours`, `minutes`, `seconds` and `dayOfWeek`.
- **Every field is in UTC**, so an agent gives the same answer on every host.
- **`month` runs from 1 to 12**, unlike JavaScript's 0 to 11. `dayOfWeek` runs from 0 (Sunday)
  to 6, as in JavaScript. `day` is the day of the month.
- **You cannot change a field.** `add` makes a new date.
- **After JSON, a store or a capability, a date is a plain object.** `Date(stored)` turns it
  back into one with methods.

The rest of the API (`isBefore`, `format` keywords) is under [Date](/DOCS-AJS/#date).

### Time and randomness

An agent has no clock and no random number generator of its own. `Date()` with no argument,
`Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, and the `random()` and `uuid()` atoms read a clock and a random
source the host grants, as it grants `fetch`, and without them those calls are refused. The
examples on this site run with the real ones. A host can also grant a fixed clock or a seeded
random source, so the same run gives the same answer every time; see
[The Sandbox](/ajs-sandbox/#time-and-randomness-are-capabilities).

In logic you want to check or replay, you often do not need them at all: use fixed dates like the
ones above, and when the answer depends on the time, take "now" as an argument from the caller.

### Regular expressions

A regex literal is a value: you can write it inline or keep it in a variable
(`const dash = /-/`). It works as a search pattern in `replace`, `replaceAll`, `split`, `match`
and `search`, with the flags `g`, `i`, `m`, `s`, `u` and `y`:

- `'a-b c'.split(/[- ]/)` gives `['a', 'b', 'c']`.
- `'aba'.replace(/a/g, 'x')` gives `'xbx'`.

A regex has no methods of its own: `re.test(text)` is refused when the line runs. Write
`text.search(re) != -1` instead. The VM's regex engine supports no backreferences and no
lookaround; a pattern using them is refused at transpile time. The details are under
[Regular expressions](/DOCS-AJS/#regular-expressions).

Use regex today where a plain string method will not do. It is deprecated in AJS in favour of
[Pattern](/pattern/), which will replace it but is not in the VM yet.

### Schema

`Schema` builds JSON schemas, and like everything else in an agent, a schema is data. It belongs
to [Contracts](/ajs-contracts/).

## Refused, and what to write instead

The constructs from this chapter that AJS refuses, and the one that silently differs:

| Instead of                                      | Write                                                       |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `const m = Math`, `const f = text.trim`         | call it: `Math.max(a, b)`, `text.trim()`                    |
| `items.map(parseInt)`                           | `items.map((x) => parseInt(x))`                             |
| `let y = x++`                                   | `let y = x`, then `x++`                                     |
| `let y = ++x`                                   | `x++`, then `let y = x`                                     |
| `o.a = 1`                                       | `o = { ...o, a: 1 }`                                        |
| `xs[0] = v`                                     | `xs = xs.with(0, v)`                                        |
| `Object.assign(o, extra)` to change `o` (runs, but leaves `o` alone) | `o = Object.assign(o, extra)` or `o = { ...o, ...extra }` |
| `'tags: ' + tags`, `` `${tags}` ``              | `tags.join(',')`                                            |
| `'order ' + order`                              | `JSON.stringify(order)`                                     |
| `arr < 5`, `obj[arr]`                           | compare or index with a primitive (`arr.length < 5`)        |
| `Math.max(arr)`                                 | `Math.max(a, b)` with numbers, or `reduce` over the array   |
| `xs.sort((a, b) => a - b)`                      | `sort()` for text; a loop for numbers or fields             |
| `'x'.repeat('3')`, `text.slice(0, 1, 2)`        | the exact arguments: `'x'.repeat(3)`, `text.slice(0, 1)`    |
| `String(n)`, `Number(s)`                        | `` `${n}` ``, `parseFloat(s)`                               |
| `new Set(xs)`, `new Date(s)`                    | `Set(xs)`, `Date(s)`                                        |
| `tags.delete(x)`, `tags.difference(ys)`, `tags.push(x)` on a set | `tags.remove(x)`, `tags.diff(ys)`, `tags.add(x)` |
| `re.test(text)`                                 | `text.search(re) != -1`                                     |
| `[1, 2] == [1, 2]` to compare contents          | compare fields, or `JSON.stringify` both sides              |

The full list for the language is the [What's Forbidden](/DOCS-AJS/#whats-forbidden) table, and
[What to Write Instead](/patterns/#what-to-write-instead) collects the rewrites. The next chapter
calls atoms: the operations, such as fetching a URL or asking a model, that reach outside the
agent.
