# Array Types

Typed array parameters, rest parameters and array returns

An array type in TJS is written the way every other TJS type is: as an example. `[0]` is an
example of an array of integers, `['']` of an array of strings, `[{ x: 0, y: 0 }]` of an
array of points. TJS reads the example for its **element type** and checks every element on
every call.

A call that fails its check does not throw. The function returns an error value (a
`MonadicError`) instead of running, and that value has a `.message` saying what went wrong.
That is why the last two lines below read `.message` off a function's result.

```tjs:inline
function sum(numbers: [3, 7]): 10 {
  return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)
}

function average(numbers: [10, 30]): 20.0 {
  if (numbers.length === 0) return 0
  return sum(numbers) / numbers.length
}

function stats(data: [10, 20, 30]): { min: 10, max: 30, avg: 20.0 } {
  if (data.length === 0) {
    return { min: 0, max: 0, avg: 0 }
  }
  return {
    min: Math.min(...data),
    max: Math.max(...data),
    avg: average(data),
  }
}

test 'sum adds numbers' {
  expect(sum([1, 2, 3, 4])).toBe(10)
}

test 'stats calculates correctly' {
  const s = stats([10, 20, 30])
  expect(s.min).toBe(10)
  expect(s.max).toBe(30)
  expect(s.avg).toBe(20)
}

console.log(sum([1, 2, 3, 4]))           // 10
console.log(average([1, 2]))             // 1.5
console.log(stats([4, 8, 15, 16, 23]))   // { min: 4, max: 23, avg: 13.2 }
console.log(stats([]))                   // { min: 0, max: 0, avg: 0 }
console.log(sum([1, 2.5]).message)       // ...sum.numbers[1]', got number
console.log(sum('1,2').message)          // ...sum.numbers', got string
```

The `test '…' { }` blocks are extra tests you write yourself. They run alongside the
signature test described next; see [Test blocks](/TJS-SYNTAX/#test-blocks).

## What to notice

**The signature is a worked example, and it is run.** This is the *signature test*: when
TJS compiles the file (in the playground, on this page, or with `tjs check`), it calls
`sum([3, 7])` and checks that the answer is `10`, and it calls `average([10, 30])` and
checks for `20.0`. Pick array examples that make a meaningful test, not just the right
type.

The return example does a second job: it declares the return type, which is what the
generated docs and `.d.ts` report. A plain `:` return is not checked on every call; write
`:?` if you want each result checked as well. If you want the type without the test,
write `:!` instead of `:`:

```javascript
function sum(numbers: [3, 7]):! 0 {   // declares "returns an integer", runs no test
  return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)
}
```

See [Return annotations](/TJS-SYNTAX/#return-annotations) for all three.

**The example says "array of integers", not "these numbers".** `[3, 7]` and `[10, 20, 30]`
describe the same type: an array whose elements are integers, of any length. The element
*values* matter only to the signature test. The element *kinds* (integer, number,
string, …) set the type, and mixing kinds makes a union; see the table below.

**`average` returns `20.0`, not `20`, and so does `stats`'s `avg` field.** To the signature
test the two are the same value (in JavaScript `20 === 20.0`), so the test passes either
way. What differs is the type the example declares: `20` says "returns an integer", `20.0`
says "returns any number". The example inputs happen to average to a whole number, but
averages in general do not, so `20` would put the wrong type in the docs, and under `:?`,
which checks every result, `average([1, 2])` would come back as a type error because it
returns `1.5`. Write the return example for the general case. Returning `0` on the empty
path is fine: an integer is also a number.

**An empty array is a valid argument.** `stats([])` passes the check, because there are no
elements to get wrong. The type cannot promise you a non-empty array, so `average` and
`stats` test for `length === 0` in the body.

## Every element is checked, and errors name the index

The check visits each element, so a bad value deep in a long list is reported where it is,
including the field inside an object element:

```tjs:inline
function total(prices: [0.0]): 0.0 {
  return prices.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0)
}

function centroid(points: [{ x: 0.0, y: 0.0 }]): { x: 0.0, y: 0.0 } {
  const n = points.length
  if (n === 0) return { x: 0, y: 0 }
  return {
    x: points.reduce((s, p) => s + p.x, 0) / n,
    y: points.reduce((s, p) => s + p.y, 0) / n,
  }
}

console.log(total([9.99, 5, 0.01]))       // 15
console.log(total([1, '2', 3]).message)
// Expected number for '<source>:1:total.prices[1]', got string

console.log(centroid([{ x: 0, y: 0 }, { x: 2, y: 4 }]))   // { x: 1, y: 2 }
console.log(centroid([]))                                 // { x: 0, y: 0 }
console.log(centroid([{ x: 0, y: 0 }, { x: 2 }]).message) // ...points[1].y', got undefined
```

A full message says what was expected, where (the file and line, then the path such as
`total.prices[1]`), and what arrived. The comments elsewhere on this page show only the
end of the message, from the `...`. [Safety & Validation](/safety-validation/) covers what
you can do with the error value.

## Ways to write an array type

| Example | Means |
| ------- | ----- |
| `[0]` | array of integers |
| `[0.0]` | array of numbers (any number, including `1.5`) |
| `[+0]` | array of non-negative integers (`+0` is the example for "zero or more") |
| `['']` | array of strings |
| `[{ x: 0, y: 0 }]` | array of objects with integer `x` and `y` |
| `[[0]]` | array of arrays of integers |
| `['', 0]` | array whose elements are each a string or an integer |
| `[3, 7.5]` | integers and numbers mixed: in effect any number, like `[0.0]` |
| `[]` | array of anything |
| `number[]` | array of numbers, the TypeScript spelling (same as `[0.0]`) |
| `int[]` | array of integers (same as `[0]`) |
| `string[][]` | arrays nest in the suffix spelling too |

The suffix spelling exists so that TypeScript you paste in keeps working. `number[]` means
any number, not integers, because `number` has to keep meaning what it means in
TypeScript. `int` is not TypeScript: it is one of TJS's own type names, alongside `float`
and `unsigned` (see [Type names](/TJS-SYNTAX/#type-names)). The generic spelling
`Array<number>` is not accepted: it is a syntax error (`Unexpected token`) at the `<`, so
write `number[]`.

## Rest parameters

A rest parameter collects the remaining arguments into an array, and you type it with an
array example, exactly like an array parameter. The difference is only in how it is
called: with separate arguments, not one array.

```tjs:inline
function count(...ids: [1, 2, 3]): 3 {
  return ids.length
}

function label(prefix: 'item', ...parts: ['a', 'b']): 'item:a-b' {
  return prefix + ':' + parts.join('-')
}

console.log(count(10, 20, 30, 40))       // 4
console.log(count())                     // 0: no arguments gives an empty array
console.log(count(1, 2.5).message)       // Expected integer for '...count.ids[1]', got number
console.log(label('row', 'x', 'y'))      // row:x-y
console.log(label('row'))                // row:
console.log(label('row', 'x', 7).message) // ...label.parts[1]', got number
```

`count(1, 2.5)` fails because `[1, 2, 3]` is an array of integers, and `2.5` is a number
but not an integer.

The signature test spreads the example too: `count(...ids: [1, 2, 3]): 3` is tested by
calling `count(1, 2, 3)` and checking for `3`.

## Arrays as return values

A return example that is an array is compared with the actual result element by element,
like any other worked example:

```tjs:inline
function doubled(xs: [1, 2]): [2, 4] {
  return xs.map((x) => x * 2)
}

console.log(doubled([5, 6, 7]))   // [ 10, 12, 14 ]
```

At compile time TJS calls `doubled([1, 2])` and requires exactly `[2, 4]`. A function whose
real output for that input differs fails the check, even if the result is "an array of
integers". To declare only the type, write `:! [0]`.

## Things that trip people up

- **`[0]` is an array of integers.** `total([1.5])` would fail if `total` took `[0]`. Use
  `[0.0]`, or `number[]`, for any number.
- **A mixed example is a union, not a tuple.** `['', 0, true]` means "every element is a
  string, an integer or a boolean", in any order and any length. It does not mean "three
  elements: a string, then an integer, then a boolean".
- **An empty array passes any array type.** If your function cannot cope with `[]`, check
  for it in the body.
- **A rest parameter cannot have a default.** An ordinary parameter takes a default with
  `=`, but `...xs: [0] = [1]` is a compile error. A rest parameter is always bound (to `[]`
  when nothing is passed), so the default could never apply.
- **Checking costs a pass over the array.** The check visits every element on every call,
  so its cost grows with the length of the array. For a hot function that takes large
  arrays, measure first; if it matters, check once in an outer function and do the work in
  an inner function whose parameter list starts with `!`, which skips the checks:

  ```javascript
  function sumFast(! xs: [0]) { /* no checks here */ }
  function sum(xs: [0]) { return sumFast(xs) }   // checked once, here
  ```

  See [Safety & Validation](/safety-validation/) and
  [Safety markers](/TJS-SYNTAX/#safety-markers).

# Checking Your Work

Many examples so far have ended with a test, and you have watched them turn green and red. Now
that you can write functions, you can write tests of your own. They are how you find out that
a program does what you meant, and keep finding out every time you change it.

Why not look at the answer instead? Because looking does not last. Take `tip` from Functions,
which works out 15% of a bill. You run `tip(40)`, see 6, and are satisfied. A week later you
change `tip` to round to the nearest penny, and you look at `tip(40)` again. It is still 6.
You do not look at `tip(20.5)`, which now comes out a penny wrong. A test is a look you only
have to take once: written down, it is taken again, automatically, every time the program
runs.

## A test is a small program about another program

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function double(n: 0) {
  return n * 2
}

test 'double doubles' {
  expect(double(21)).toBe(42)
}
```

- `test 'double doubles' { … }` names a test and holds its checks. The name says what should
  be true, so a failure reads like a sentence: "double doubles" failed.
- `double(21)` runs the code you are checking, and `expect(…)` takes its answer so you can
  check it.
- `.toBe(42)`, joined on with a dot, says what the answer should be.

A test does not change what the program does. It runs beside it, and reports. The line under
the code shows the report: how many tests passed, or, in red, which one failed, what it
expected and what it got.

## Several checks in one test

A test can check several things. All of them must pass for the test to pass, and the test
stops at the first check that fails:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function initials(first: 'Ada', last: 'Lovelace') {
  return first[0] + last[0]
}

preview.append(initials('Grace', 'Hopper'))

test 'initials take the first letter of each name' {
  expect(initials('Ada', 'Lovelace')).toBe('AL')
  expect(initials('Grace', 'Hopper')).toBe('GH')
  expect(initials('Alan', 'Turing').length).toBe(2)
}
```

`first[0]` is the first letter. The letters of a string are numbered from 0, not 1, so
`first[1]` is the second letter. (Lists, later in this book, are numbered the same way.)
`.length` is how many letters a string has.

## The checks you will use most

- `toBe(value)` for one number, string or true/false: `expect(2 + 2).toBe(4)`.
- `toEqual(value)` for something with parts, such as the lists and objects you will meet
  later, compared by what is inside them. (In TJS, `toBe` compares those by their insides
  too, but `toEqual` says so in its name.)
- `toContain(part)` for a string or list that should include something.
- `toBeGreaterThan(n)` and `toBeLessThan(n)` when only a range matters.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
const greeting = 'Hello, world!'

function percent(part: 1.0, whole: 4.0) {
  return part / whole * 100
}

preview.append(`1 out of 3 is ${percent(1, 3)}%`)

test 'a few kinds of check' {
  expect(greeting).toContain('world')
  expect(greeting.startsWith('Hello')).toBe(true)
  expect(percent(1, 3)).toBeGreaterThan(33)
  expect(percent(1, 3)).toBeLessThan(34)
}
```

`greeting.startsWith('Hello')` is a question you can ask a string. Its answer is `true` or
`false`, and `toBe(true)` checks it. Any question with a yes-or-no answer can be tested this
way. One out of three is a third, which has no exact decimal, so the last two checks only ask
that it lands between 33 and 34. You will see why that matters below.

## A signature example is a test

You met this in Functions, and it deserves a closer look, because it is the cheapest test you
will ever write. Put an example of the **answer** after the parentheses:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function fahrenheit(celsius: 100.0): 212.0 {
  return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
}

preview.append(`Water boils at ${fahrenheit(100)}°F.`)
```

The first line says: "`fahrenheit(100)` is 212".

The examples are written `100.0` and `212.0` for the reason you saw in Functions: `100` would
allow only whole numbers, and `100.0` allows any number, including temperatures like 36.6. On
the answer side the decimal point changes nothing about the check: `212.0` still has to equal
the real answer, 212.

TJS reads that line as a test. It takes the example on the parameter (`100`), calls the
function with it, and compares the answer with the example after the parentheses (`212`). It
does this every time the program runs, and reports the result alongside your `test` blocks.

Try it. Change `9 / 5` to `5 / 9`, the classic slip in this formula. The line under the code turns red:
`fahrenheit(100)` should have been 212, and was 87.55555555555556. You did not write a `test`
block, and the mistake was still caught.

Three things are worth knowing about signature examples:

1. **The answer must be exactly right.** `212` means 212, not "some number". A function
   `add(a: 2, b: 3): 0` fails, because `add(2, 3)` is 5, not 0. The answer example is a
   worked example, not a description of the kind of answer.
2. **They check one call, with the examples you chose.** One example cannot try the edges.
   That is what `test` blocks are for.
3. **They are documentation that cannot go stale.** Anyone reading the first line of
   `fahrenheit` learns what it does from an example. If someone changes the function so the
   example is no longer true, the example says so the next time the program runs.

Give every function whose answer you can predict a good signature example, one where a wrong
function would give a different answer. Add `test` blocks for everything else: the edges, the
mistakes it should refuse (more on those below), and answers too long to fit on the first
line.

## Test the edges

Most mistakes happen at the edges: zero, one, the empty string `''`, the exact boundary. A good set of
tests always tries them.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function canVote(age: 0) {
  return age >= 18
}

test 'the edges of voting age' {
  expect(canVote(17)).toBe(false)
  expect(canVote(18)).toBe(true)
  expect(canVote(19)).toBe(true)
  expect(canVote(0)).toBe(false)
}
```

`>=` means "at least", and `>` means "more than". Change `>=` to `>` in `canVote`. The test
goes red: the check at exactly 18 fails, and it is the one that matters. The other checks
would have passed, because 17, 19 and 0 get the same answer either way.

## Does your test catch anything?

A test that only checks easy cases misses the mistakes you are likely to make. Here is a test
that looks fine:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function canVote(age: 0) {
  return age >= 18
}

test 'voting' {
  expect(canVote(40)).toBe(true)
  expect(canVote(5)).toBe(false)
}
```

It passes. Now change `18` to `16`, or to `21`, or `>=` to `>`. It still passes: every one of
those wrong programs still lets a 40-year-old vote and stops a 5-year-old. The test checks
easy cases that any reasonable version gets right.

The way to find out whether a test is any good is to **break the program on purpose** and see
whether the test notices. If you can make a mistake and the tests stay green, you have found a
check that is missing. This is called **mutation testing**, and programmers do it so often
that there are tools that do it automatically. You can do it by hand, in the page, right now.

## Numbers with fractions are not exact

Here is a surprise that catches every programmer once. Type `0.1 + 0.2` at the console's prompt (the line where you type, under the
console's messages) and press Enter:

```tjs:inline {"view": "console"}
console.log('Type 0.1 + 0.2 at the prompt below.')
```

The answer is `0.30000000000000004`. Computers store numbers in binary, as ones and zeros, and most decimal
fractions (like 0.1) cannot be written exactly in binary, just as 1/3 cannot be written exactly
in decimals. The error is tiny, but `toBe(0.3)` asks for **exactly** 0.3, and fails.

When an answer may have a fraction in it, test it to the precision you care about. Rounding
to the nearest penny is one way. `Math.round` rounds a number to a whole number, so
multiplying by 100 first, rounding, and dividing by 100 again rounds to whole pennies:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function priceWithTax(price: 0.0) {
  return price * 1.1
}

function toPennies(amount: 0.0) {
  return Math.round(amount * 100) / 100
}

preview.append(`1.10 with tax is ${priceWithTax(1.1)}`)

test 'tax, to the nearest penny' {
  expect(toPennies(priceWithTax(1.1))).toBe(1.21)
  expect(priceWithTax(1.1)).toBeGreaterThan(1.2)
  expect(priceWithTax(1.1)).toBeLessThan(1.22)
}
```

Look at what the page shows: not 1.21, but 1.2100000000000002. The checks say the same thing
in two ways: rounded to pennies it is 1.21, and it is between 1.2 and 1.22. Whole numbers have
no such problem: `6 * 7` is exactly 42, always.

`priceWithTax` itself does not round. The tiny error does no harm until someone sees the
number, so the rounding goes where the number is shown or checked.

Signature examples are compared exactly too. Choose ones whose answers come out exact, like
212 for `fahrenheit`, and use `test` blocks with rounding or a range for the rest.

## Mistakes are values, and you can test for them

When a function is called with the wrong kind of value, TJS does not crash: the call gives
back an **error**. That error is a value like any other, so a test can check for it:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function double(n: 0) {
  return n * 2
}

test 'the wrong kind of value gives back an error' {
  expect(double('ten') instanceof Error).toBe(true)
  expect(isMonadicError(double('ten'))).toBe(true)
  expect(double(5)).toBe(10)
}
```

`instanceof Error` asks "is this an error?". `isMonadicError(x)` asks a narrower question: is
this one of the errors TJS gives back when a call has the wrong kind of value? Later chapters
meet other errors, and later chapters for working programmers use `isMonadicError` to tell
them apart. (The odd name is a programmer's word; you do not need to know what it means.)
Both checks pass here. Testing the mistakes your function refuses
is as useful as testing the answers it gives.

## Reading a failure

When a check fails, the line under the code turns red. It names the test and the line where
the test starts, and says what was expected and what came back. Go back to `initials` and
change `first[0]` to `first[1]`. The failure reads something like this:

```text
Test 'initials take the first letter of each name' (line 5) failed:
  Expected "AL" but got "dL"
```

The second line is the useful part. The test expected `"AL"` and got `"dL"`: the second letter
of `'Ada'` instead of the first. It does not say which check failed, but the expected answer
tells you, and since a test stops at its first failed check, the checks after it have not run
yet. The failure tells you where to look.

Read a failure before you change anything. There are always two possibilities: the program is
wrong, or the test is. A test is a program too, and it can have a typo in it. Ask which of the
two answers, the expected one or the one you got, is actually right. Then fix that side, and
only that side. Changing the test until it agrees with the program is easy, and it turns a test
into a record of whatever the program happens to do.

## Write the test first

Here is a good habit: before writing a function, write the test that says what it should do.
Then write the function until the test passes. The test is your description of the job, and it
tells you when you are finished. A test may sit above the function it calls: TJS reads the
whole program before it runs the tests.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
// First the tests: what should shout do?
test 'shout makes it loud' {
  expect(shout('hello')).toBe('HELLO!')
  expect(shout('')).toBe('!')
}

// Then the function that makes them pass.
function shout(words: 'hello') {
  return words.toUpperCase() + '!'
}
```

Writing the test first does three things for you. It makes you decide what the function
should do before you decide how (what should `shout('')` give? You have to choose, and the
test records the choice). It lets you see the test fail before it passes, which proves it can.
Try that here: change the function's last line to `return words`, a first version that is
wrong on purpose. The test goes red, expecting `"HELLO!"` and getting `"hello"`. Put
`.toUpperCase() + '!'` back and it turns green. (A test that calls a function you have not
written at all is reported as "inconclusive" (it could not run), not as a failure, so start with a wrong version
rather than none.) And it tells you when to stop: when the tests pass, the job is done.

## Try it

Write the tests first, then the function: `average(a: 0.0, b: 0.0, c: 0.0)` gives back the
average of three numbers (add them up, divide by 3). Test `average(1, 2, 3)`, three numbers
that are all the same, and some negative numbers. Then try `average(1, 2, 2)`: the answer is
5/3, which has no exact decimal. Decide how to test it, using what you learned about
fractions.

More to try:

- Give `average` a signature example: `average(a: 1.0, b: 2.0, c: 3.0): 2.0`. Then break the
  function by dividing by 2 instead of 3, and see which checks notice: the example, the tests,
  or both.
- Take `canVote` and its tests from "Test the edges". Make three different mistakes in the
  function, one at a time. Did the tests catch every one? If one got through, write the check
  that would have caught it.
- Come back to this one after the next chapter, Decisions, which introduces `&&` ("and": both
  sides must be true). Write `isTeenager(age: 0)`, true from 13 to 19, as
  `age >= 13 && age <= 19`. Write the tests first, and test both edges from both sides: 12,
  13, 19 and 20.

Work them here:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
// Your code here. Show results with preview.append(…), check them with a
// test block, then press the refresh button (or ⌘S / Ctrl+S) to run it.
```

# Decisions, Loops and Helpers

An agent rarely runs straight through. It routes a request one way or another, walks a list of
results, keeps the items worth keeping, and names a piece of logic it needs twice. This chapter
covers the statements that do that: `if` and its relatives, the two loops AJS has, the four
methods that take a callback, and helper functions in the same source. It ends with what AJS
leaves out, and why.

Most of it is JavaScript you already know. The differences are deliberate, and each one comes
with what to write instead.

## Decisions

Here is an agent that quotes a shipping price. It uses an `if`/`else if`/`else` chain, the
ternary, and the three logical operators:

```ajs:inline
function quote({ weightKg = 3.5, country = 'DE', member = false, coupon = '' }) {
  let rate = 0
  if (country == 'DE') {
    rate = 4.9
  } else if (country == 'FR' || country == 'NL') {
    rate = 7.5
  } else {
    rate = 15
  }

  const heavy = weightKg > 5
  const surcharge = heavy ? 6 : 0
  const freeShipping = member && !heavy
  const code = coupon || 'none'
  const total = freeShipping ? 0 : rate + surcharge
  return { rate, surcharge, freeShipping, code, total }
}
```

With no arguments it returns
`{ rate: 4.9, surcharge: 0, freeShipping: false, code: 'none', total: 4.9 }`. With
`{ member: true }` the total is `0`; with `{ country: 'US', weightKg: 8 }` it is `21`.

All of this behaves as it does in JavaScript:

- **`let` is block-scoped, and assignment reaches out.** `rate` is declared above the `if`, so
  `rate = 7.5` inside a branch changes it. A `let` declared inside a branch stays there.
- **Truthiness is JavaScript's.** The falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `''`, `null`,
  `undefined` and `NaN`, so `if (coupon)` is false for an empty string.
- **`&&`, `||` and `??` work as in JavaScript.** `coupon || 'none'` above relies on that; the
  difference between `||` and `??` is in
  [Values and Expressions](/ajs-values/#logical-operators-and-the-ternary).

What is different is `==`, which never coerces (`'5' == 5` is `false`); that is covered in
[Values and Expressions](/ajs-values/#equality). The DOCS-AJS
[rule engine](/DOCS-AJS/#rule-engines) is a slightly larger agent of the same shape, and
[Conditional Logic](/conditional-logic/) has more variations.

### No `switch`

`switch` is a transpile error, and the message shows the `if`/`else if` chain to write instead.
When each case only picks a value, a lookup object is shorter and reads as a table.

One care is needed when the key comes from outside. Reading a method name such as `toString`
off an object fails, because a method is not a value in AJS. So check that the key is one of the
table's own before reading it:

```ajs:inline
function rateFor({ country = 'FR' }) {
  const rates = { DE: 4.9, FR: 7.5, NL: 7.5 }
  let rate = 15
  if (Object.keys(rates).includes(country)) {
    rate = rates[country]
  }
  return { rate }
}
```

It returns `{ rate: 7.5 }`; `{ country: 'US' }` gets the fallback, `{ rate: 15 }`, and so does
`{ country: 'toString' }`.

The shorter `rates[country] ?? 15` is not safe. It works for `'US'`, but for `'toString'` the
read itself fails, with `'toString' is a method: call it — a method is not a value in AsyncJS`,
before `??` gets to supply the fallback. That is an ordinary error: it skips the rest of the
agent unless a `try` catches it, as [When Things Fail](/ajs-errors/) explains. (Some refusals
are different and end the run even inside a `try`; that chapter lists them under
[Refusals that end the run](/ajs-errors/#refusals-that-end-the-run-a-bugs).)

When each case does different work, call a helper per case; there is an example under
[Helper functions](#helper-functions) below, and another in
[Switch Statements](/patterns/#switch-statements).

## Loops

AJS has two loops: `for...of` over an array, and `while`.

```ajs:inline
function cartTotal({ prices = [4, 10, 6] }) {
  let total = 0
  for (const price of prices) {
    total = total + price
  }
  return { total }
}
```

It returns `{ total: 20 }`. The loop body updates `total`, which was declared outside it; any
variable in an enclosing scope can be assigned this way, and `total += price` works too.

To walk an object, loop over its keys (`for...in` is refused; see the table below):

```ajs:inline
function stockValue({ stock = { apple: 3, pear: 0, plum: 5 }, price = 2 }) {
  let value = 0
  const empty = []
  for (const name of Object.keys(stock)) {
    value = value + stock[name] * price
    if (stock[name] == 0) {
      empty.push(name)
    }
  }
  return { value, empty }
}
```

It returns `{ value: 16, empty: ['pear'] }`. `empty` is a `const` because the variable is never
reassigned; `push` changes the array it holds, as in JavaScript. `Object.entries(stock)` gives
`[name, count]` pairs if you want both; read them as `pair[0]` and `pair[1]`, because a
destructured loop variable (`for (const [k, v] of …)`) is refused.

`while` takes a condition, as in JavaScript. Use it when you need the position, not only the
item:

```ajs:inline
function numbered({ lines = ['buy milk', 'call Ada', 'ship it'] }) {
  let i = 0
  const out = []
  while (i < lines.length) {
    out.push(`${i + 1}. ${lines[i]}`)
    i = i + 1
  }
  return { out }
}
```

It returns `{ out: ['1. buy milk', '2. call Ada', '3. ship it'] }`.

**Always change the counter.** A `while` whose condition never becomes false does not hang the
host: it spends the run's fuel and stops with `Out of Fuel`, having done nothing useful. Fuel is
the subject of [Limits](/ajs-limits/).

### The loops AJS does not have

Each of these is a transpile error. The messages for the first three rows go on to show a
corrected loop in code:

| You write               | The message begins                                     | Write instead                                  |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `for (let i = 0; …; …)` | ``AJS has no `for` loops. Use `while` with a counter`` | `while` with a counter, as in `numbered` above |
| `for (const k in obj)`  | ``AJS has no `for...in`. Get the keys and walk them``  | `for (const k of Object.keys(obj))`            |
| `do { … } while (c)`    | ``AJS has no `do...while`. Use `while` ``              | `while`, with the condition checked first      |
| `break`                 | `Unsupported statement type: BreakStatement`           | a stop condition, below                        |
| `continue`              | `Unsupported statement type: ContinueStatement`        | an `if` around the work, below                 |

The `for...in` message's code gets the keys with the `keys` atom, which returns the same array as
`Object.keys`, and walks them with a `while`. The `for...of` in the last column is shorter.

### Without `break` or `continue`

Four shapes cover what `break` and `continue` did.

**Stop early: put the stop condition in the `while`.** This finds the first order over a limit
and looks no further:

```ajs:inline
function firstLarge({ orders = [12, 40, 7, 95], limit = 30 }) {
  let at = -1
  let i = 0
  while (at == -1 && i < orders.length) {
    if (orders[i] > limit) {
      at = i
    }
    i = i + 1
  }
  return { at, examined: i }
}
```

It returns `{ at: 1, examined: 2 }`: the loop ended as soon as `at` was set, without looking at
the last two orders.

**Skip an item: wrap the work in an `if`.** Where JavaScript would `continue`, the body only acts
when the condition holds:

```ajs:inline
function paidTotal({
  invoices = [
    { amount: 50, paid: true },
    { amount: 20, paid: false },
    { amount: 30, paid: true },
  ],
}) {
  let total = 0
  for (const inv of invoices) {
    if (inv.paid) {
      total = total + inv.amount
    }
  }
  return { total }
}
```

It returns `{ total: 80 }`. Filtering first, then looping over what is left, says the same thing;
`filter` is in the next section.

**Walk indices: `while` with a counter**, as `numbered` does above.

**Leave the loop and the function: `return`.** A `return` inside a loop ends both, which is
often exactly what a search wants:

```ajs:inline
function routeRequest({
  path = '/api/users/42',
  rules = [
    { prefix: '/api/', backend: 'api-pool' },
    { prefix: '/static/', backend: 'cdn' },
  ],
}) {
  for (const rule of rules) {
    if (path.startsWith(rule.prefix)) {
      return { backend: rule.backend }
    }
  }
  return { backend: 'web-pool' }
}
```

It returns `{ backend: 'api-pool' }`; `{ path: '/about' }` falls through to `'web-pool'`.

## Callbacks: map, filter, find and reduce

Four array methods take a function: `map`, `filter` and `find` take `(item) => …`, and `reduce`
takes `(acc, item) => …` and an initial value. They do most of the work of shaping a list:

```ajs:inline
function invoice({
  lines = [
    { sku: 'pen', qty: 3, unit: 2 },
    { sku: 'pad', qty: 0, unit: 5 },
    { sku: 'ink', qty: 1, unit: 12 },
  ],
  taxRate = 0.25,
}) {
  const billed = lines.filter((line) => line.qty > 0)
  const amounts = billed.map((line) => line.qty * line.unit * (1 + taxRate))
  const total = amounts.reduce((sum, a) => sum + a, 0)
  const ink = lines.find((line) => line.sku == 'ink')
  const missing = lines.find((line) => line.sku == 'tape')
  return { count: billed.length, amounts, total, inkQty: ink.qty, missing }
}
```

It returns `{ count: 2, amounts: [7.5, 15], total: 22.5, inkQty: 1, missing: null }`.

**`find` gives `null` when nothing matches**, unlike JavaScript, which gives `undefined`. A test
written `x == null` works either way, because AJS `==` treats `null` and `undefined` as equal
(see [Equality](/ajs-values/#equality)); `x === undefined` would be false here.

The callback in the `map` reads `taxRate`, a parameter of the agent. A callback is part of the
function it is written in, so it can read any variable that function can.

### The rules

**A callback method call stands on its own.** It must be one of:

- the whole value of a declaration or assignment: `const billed = lines.filter(…)`, or
  `billed = lines.filter(…)`;
- a statement by itself: `lines.map(…)` alone on a line (legal, though the result is lost);
- the whole value of a helper's `return`: `return lines.map(…)`.

These are the same positions a helper call or an atom call may take
([Helper functions](#helper-functions) below). Anywhere inside a larger expression it is refused,
and so is a call inside an object literal, even in a `return`:

```javascript
const amounts = lines.filter((l) => l.qty > 0).map((l) => l.unit) // chained
const count = lines.filter((l) => l.qty > 0).length               // used in an expression
const first = lines.find((l) => l.qty > 0) ?? null                // used in an expression
if (lines.find((l) => l.sku == 'ink') == null) { }                // in a condition
return { amounts: lines.map((l) => l.unit) }                      // inside an object
```

The message for each is `Unsupported expression type in condition: ArrowFunctionExpression`,
even where there is no condition. It means "this callback call is not standing on its own":
split the line into two statements, assigning the call first and using the variable after.

**`filter` and `find` take an expression body.** `(x) => { return x > 1 }` is refused with
`find callback must be an expression, not a block` (or `filter callback …`). `map` and `reduce`
accept a block body with `const` lines and a `return`, but one expression is the habit that works
everywhere.

**There is no index argument.** `xs.map((x, i) => i)` fails to transpile with
`'i' is not defined`, because only the first parameter is bound. When you need the position, use
a `while` with a counter, or a `for...of` that counts.

**Callback parameters are plain names.** `({ qty }) => qty` fails with
`'qty' is not defined. Declare it with let or const, or take it as a parameter.`: the pattern is
not bound, so the name inside it is unknown. Write `(line) => line.qty`.

**An arrow function exists only as a callback.** `const isPaid = (inv) => inv.paid` is refused
with `Unsupported expression in AsyncJS: ArrowFunctionExpression`. A function is not a value in
AJS: it cannot be stored, put in an object, passed to an atom or returned. For logic you want to
name and reuse, write a helper function (next section).

**A callback may call an atom.** The callback's body counts as a statement of its own, so it may
make one atom call per item, and each call costs fuel like any other. The core
[`hash`](/ajs-atoms/#utilities) atom takes its text as the named input `value`:

```ajs:inline
function nameDigests({ names = ['report.pdf', 'notes.txt'] }) {
  const digests = names.map((name) => hash({ value: name }))
  return { digests }
}
```

It returns one SHA-256 hex string per name (of the name, not of any file). The same shape fetches
one URL per item; see [Callbacks](/patterns/#callbacks) in Patterns.

**Only these four take a callback.** `some`, `every`, `findIndex` and `flatMap` are refused with
a message pointing at `for...of` and these four. `find` and `filter` cover the first two:

```ajs:inline
function checks({ scores = [72, 88, 95] }) {
  const high = scores.find((s) => s > 90)
  const anyHigh = high != null
  const failing = scores.filter((s) => s < 50)
  const allPass = failing.length == 0
  return { anyHigh, allPass }
}
```

It returns `{ anyHigh: true, allPass: true }`. For `findIndex`, use the stop-early loop above.

**`sort` takes no comparator.** `xs.sort((a, b) => a - b)` fails with the same
`Unsupported expression type in condition: ArrowFunctionExpression` as a chained call, so the
message will not point you here. `sort()` and `toSorted()` with no argument work, and order
items as JavaScript's do: as strings, so `[3, 10, 1]` becomes `[1, 10, 3]`. AJS has no way to
sort numbers numerically or objects by a field. Pass the list in already sorted, or have the
host provide an atom that sorts. The array methods that take no callback are listed under
[Methods](/ajs-values/#methods) in Values and Expressions.

## Helper functions

A source file holds only function declarations. As [A First Agent](/ajs-first-agent/#what-an-agent-is)
said, the **last** one is the agent's entry: it takes the object of named inputs and returns the
result object. The ones before it are helpers, which the entry and other helpers call by name.
Put a helper after the entry and that helper becomes the agent; the transpiler does not
complain, and the run is usually refused because its inputs do not match.

```ajs:inline
function applyTransform(item, transform) {
  if (transform == 'double') {
    return item * 2
  }
  if (transform == 'negate') {
    return -item
  }
  return item
}

function summarize(values) {
  const total = values.reduce((sum, v) => sum + v, 0)
  return [total, values.length]
}

function processBatch({ items = [1, 2, 3], transform = 'double' }) {
  const results = []
  for (const item of items) {
    const processed = applyTransform(item, transform)
    results.push(processed)
  }
  const stats = summarize(results)
  return { results, total: stats[0], count: stats[1] }
}
```

It returns `{ results: [2, 4, 6], total: 12, count: 3 }`; with `{ transform: 'negate' }` the
results are `[-1, -2, -3]`.

Helpers are ordinary functions, with a few rules:

- **Positional arguments, any return value.** `applyTransform(item, transform)` takes two
  arguments; `summarize` returns an array. Only the entry must return an object (a helper's
  return value is not the run's result).
- **The argument count must match.** Calling `summarize(a, b)` is a transpile error:
  `Helper 'summarize' expects 1 argument(s), got 2`.
- **Helpers are siblings, not closures.** A helper sees only its own parameters. If
  `applyTransform` read `results`, which is declared in `processBatch`, the transpiler would
  refuse it with `'results' is not defined`. Pass what a helper needs as an argument. (A callback
  is the exception: it is part of its caller's body.)
- **Nothing else at the top level.** A top-level `const` is not visible inside the functions, so
  reading it is the same `is not defined` error; put constants inside the entry, or pass them in.
  A function declared inside another function is a transpile error too.
- **A helper call stands on its own**, under the same rule as an atom call or a callback method
  call: the whole value of a declaration or assignment, a statement by itself, or a `return`
  value. A helper call may also be the body of a callback
  (`items.map((x) => applyTransform(x, 'double'))`). In a condition or a larger expression it is
  refused, with a message that says to assign the result first.
  [Calling Atoms](/ajs-calling-atoms/#a-call-stands-on-its-own) explains why.

When each case of a decision does different work, a helper per case keeps the entry readable:

```ajs:inline
function refund(order) {
  return { action: 'refund', amount: order.total }
}

function reship(order) {
  return { action: 'reship', items: order.items.length }
}

function handleComplaint({ kind = 'damaged', order = { total: 30, items: ['mug', 'plate'] } }) {
  let outcome = { action: 'escalate' }
  if (kind == 'lost') {
    outcome = refund(order)
  } else if (kind == 'damaged') {
    outcome = reship(order)
  }
  return outcome
}
```

It returns `{ action: 'reship', items: 2 }`; `{ kind: 'lost' }` returns
`{ action: 'refund', amount: 30 }`, and any other kind `{ action: 'escalate' }`.

### Recursion

A helper may call itself:

```ajs:inline
function fact(n) {
  if (n <= 1) {
    return 1
  }
  const rest = fact(n - 1)
  return n * rest
}

function factorial({ n = 5 }) {
  const value = fact(n)
  return { value }
}
```

It returns `{ value: 120 }`. Note `const rest = fact(n - 1)` on its own line: `return n * fact(n - 1)`
would put a helper call inside an expression.

Runaway recursion cannot take the host down. Every call costs fuel, and helper calls nest at most
256 deep; one level more fails with an ordinary error:

```text
Maximum helper call depth (256) exceeded — likely infinite recursion in 'fact'
```

Like other ordinary errors, it skips the rest of the agent unless a `try` catches it; `try` is
covered in [When Things Fail](/ajs-errors/).

A compiled agent is JSON that a host stores, sends and checks before running, so its size
matters. A helper's body appears once in that JSON and is called by name, so calling a helper
from a loop, or from many places, does not make the agent any larger.

## What AJS leaves out, and why

Every construct missing from AJS is missing for one of a few reasons.

**Routes out of the sandbox.** `eval`, `Function`, `import`, `class`, `this` and `new` would each
give an agent a way to reach the host or run text as code. An agent gets the outside world only
through the atoms its host provides.

**Syntax that is easy to get wrong.** `switch` fall-through, early exits (`break`, `continue`)
scattered through a loop body, and the three clauses of a C-style `for` are frequent sources of
bugs in generated code, and AJS is written by models as often as by people. With `if`,
`for...of` and `while`, the conditions that decide what runs are in one place, where a reader can
see them.

**Code that is hard to audit.** Because a function is not a value, every call in a compiled agent
names exactly what it calls: an atom, a helper, a builtin, or one of four callback methods. A
reviewer, or a host checking an agent before running it, never has to work out which function a
variable might hold at run time.

**Every construct is a promise.** Today's VM is written in JavaScript; a second one, written in
Rust and compiled to WebAssembly, is planned. Each construct the language accepts is behaviour
both VMs must reproduce exactly, so the language refuses constructs that would cost the VM
complexity for little gain. See the [native VM plan](/ajs-native-vm/).

**Waiting belongs to the host.** An agent's steps run one at a time, in order. There is no
parallelism, no `sleep` and no backoff in AJS, because time and concurrency are the host's to
spend, and a run that is waiting is not doing work fuel can measure. A host that wants many
requests in flight exposes an atom that fans them out; one that wants backoff puts it in its
`fetch` capability. The agent sees one call that succeeds or fails. See
[Parallel Execution](/patterns/#parallel-execution) and [Retry](/patterns/#retry) in Patterns.

Reading the time is something the host grants: `Date()` with no argument and `Date.now()` read
the clock the host injects, as it injects `fetch`, and are refused without one. When a result
should not depend on when it ran, pass "now" in as an argument instead.
[Date](/ajs-values/#date) in Values and Expressions has the details, and
[The Sandbox](/ajs-sandbox/#time-and-randomness-are-capabilities) explains why.

The full list of refused constructs, with what to write for each, is in
[What's Forbidden](/DOCS-AJS/#whats-forbidden) and
[What to Write Instead](/patterns/#what-to-write-instead).

# JS Footguns That TJS Quietly Fixes

JavaScript has a small set of legendary, well-documented gotchas that no one
defends but that the spec will never change. Native TJS fixes them at the
language level so you don't have to remember which version of an idiom to
use in which context.

A runnable demo lives at [`examples/js-footguns-fixed.tjs`](../examples/js-footguns-fixed.tjs):

```bash
bun src/cli/tjs.ts run examples/js-footguns-fixed.tjs
```

All the fixes below are **always on in `.tjs`** (the default for
native TJS files). They are **off** under `TjsCompat`, in `fromTS`-emitted
code, and in AJS/VM targets — so existing JS/TS semantics are preserved
when you opt out.

---

## 1. `Boolean(new Boolean(false))` is `true` (and friends)

A boxed primitive is an `Object`, and the spec's `ToBoolean` operation
declares any `Object` truthy. The result:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```js
Boolean(new Boolean(false))   // true   — wrong!
if (new Boolean(false)) { ... }   // enters branch — wrong!
!new Boolean(false)           // false  — wrong!
new Boolean(false) || 'x'     // Boolean { false } — wrong!
new Boolean(false) ? 'y' : 'n'  // 'y' — wrong!
```

`Symbol.toPrimitive` doesn't fire for boolean coercion, so there is no
hook to fix this in plain JS. **TJS rewrites every truthiness context**
(including `if`, `while`, `for`, `do`, `!`, `&&`, `||`, ternary, and
top-level `Boolean(x)` calls) to call `__tjs.toBool(x)`, which unwraps
boxed primitives before applying `ToBoolean`:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```tjs
const b = Object(false)
Boolean(b)                     // false  ✓
if (b) ...                     // does not enter  ✓
!b                             // true   ✓
b || 'x'                       // 'x'    ✓
```

The `&&` / `||` rewrites preserve JS's value-returning semantics: `a && b`
still returns `a` when `a` is falsy (after unwrapping) and `b` otherwise.
Side effects fire exactly as they would in raw JS — `inc() && inc()` calls
`inc` twice. No double-evaluation.

`??` (nullish coalescing) is intentionally **not** rewritten. Its semantics
are about `null`/`undefined` specifically, not truthiness, so boxed
primitives behave correctly already (`new Boolean(false) ?? 'fallback'`
returns the wrapper, which is what you'd want).

`===` / `!==` (identity) are also not touched — that's a different
footgun, handled by the `Is` operator (see below).

> **Why fix, and ban only the constructors?** Boxed primitives have legitimate
> uses (passing primitives by reference, attaching properties for tagging), so
> TJS lets you use them and makes them work the way the name implies. What it
> refuses is `new Boolean(x)`, `new String(x)` and `new Number(x)`: almost
> always a slip for `Boolean(x)` and friends. A deliberate wrapper has a
> spelling that says so, `Object(x)`.

## 2. `==` is a coercion lottery; `NaN !== NaN`

Raw JS `==` coerces wildly across types:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```js
'5' == 5     // true
'' == false  // true
0 == ''      // true
[1] == 1     // true
```

…and `NaN` is famously unequal to itself, which makes "is this a real
number?" checks awkward.

Native TJS rewrites `==` and `!=` to **honest equality** (the `Eq` /
`NotEq` runtime functions):

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```tjs
'5' == 5          // false  ✓ (different types, no coercion)
NaN == NaN        // true   ✓
null == undefined // true   (preserved — this one is actually useful)
```

Boxed primitives are unwrapped before comparison: `new Boolean(false) == false`
is `true`.

For **deep structural equality** of objects, arrays, Maps, and Sets, use
the explicit `Is` / `IsNot` operators:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```tjs
Is({a: 1}, {a: 1})    // true   ✓
Is([1, 2], [1, 2])    // true   ✓
{a: 1} Is {a: 1}      // true   ✓ (infix form)
```

Identity comparison stays available as `===` / `!==` when you really
mean "same reference."

## 3. `typeof null === 'object'`

The original JS bug, preserved forever for backward compatibility.
In `.tjs`, `typeof` is rewritten to a runtime helper that returns
`'null'` for `null`:

```tjs
typeof null   // 'null'  ✓
typeof undefined   // 'undefined'
typeof 42     // 'number'
```

## 4. `let x` (uninitialized) silently leaves a hole

Raw JS: `let x` declares a variable bound to `undefined`. There's no
indication whether you forgot to initialize it, intend to assign it
later, or intend it to actually be undefined.

The linter's `safe-assign-let-needs-type` rule warns:

```tjs
let x                     // ⚠ let needs initializer or type annotation
let y = undefined         // ⚠ same
let z = null              // ⚠ same
let result: ''            // ✓ type annotation, no init
let count = 0             // ✓ inferable from init
```

Once a `let` is "typed" (annotated or inferable), assigning literal
`undefined` / `null` / `void 0` to it is also flagged:

```tjs
let name = 'world'
name = undefined          // ⚠ Cannot assign undefined to typed let 'name'
```

These are lint warnings: `tjs check` reports them, and under `TjsStrict` they are errors that
fail the check. From code, call `lint()` from `tjs-lang/lang`.

## 5. Classes that require `new`

Calling a class without `new` throws a `TypeError`. (The sloppy-mode leak to
the global object is the older `function` constructor's footgun.) TJS wraps user classes (always, in
`.tjs`) so they are CALLED — and because the two forms then produce identical
objects, `new` on a class declared in the file is an error rather than a synonym:

<!-- tjs-doc: expect-error -->

```tjs
class Point {
  constructor(x: 0, y: 0) { this.x = x; this.y = y }
}

Point(1, 2)              // ✓ the TJS way
new Point(1, 2)          // ✗ ERROR — the two forms are identical, so `new` said nothing
```

Scoped to classes declared in the file. For a built-in, `new` is **mandatory**:
`new Float32Array(4)` throws without it, so those are untouched.

## 6. `var` hoisting and the temporal dead zone

`var` declarations are a parse error in `.tjs`. Use
`let` and `const` exclusively, get block scoping, and avoid the entire
class of "wait, that's hoisted?" bugs.

---

## Opting out

If you have a specific file where you need raw JS semantics:

```tjs
TjsCompat // read this file as JavaScript: the .tjs rules are off
```

Code converted from TypeScript (`fromTS`) is read as JavaScript by default;
add `TjsStrict` to opt it into the `.tjs` rules, including input validation.

# Optional Parameters

`?` and `= default` both survive conversion, `undefined` is not `null`, and every function
can tell you at runtime which of its parameters are required.

TypeScript has two ways to make a parameter optional: `greeting?: string`, which may be
`undefined`, and `punctuation: string = '!'`, which has a default. Both convert to TJS, and
both keep their meaning.

By default, converted TypeScript validates nothing: it behaves exactly like the JavaScript
`tsc` would emit. That is deliberate. Conversion should not change what your program does,
and full TJS changes more than validation (for example, `==` stops coercing, and object
defaults merge, as described at the end of this page). The first line of the example,
`/* @tjs TjsStrict */`, opts this one file in to full TJS, and the types become checks that
run on every call.

Whether or not you opt in, each function also carries a description of its parameters at
runtime: which are required, and what the defaults are. The example shows both.

```ts:inline
/* @tjs TjsStrict */

function createGreeting(
  name: string,
  greeting?: string,
  punctuation: string = '!'
): string {
  const g = greeting ?? 'Hello'
  return `${g}, ${name}${punctuation}`
}

// Every way TypeScript allows you to call it still works
console.log(createGreeting('World'))
console.log(createGreeting('World', 'Hi'))
console.log(createGreeting('World', undefined, '?'))
console.log(createGreeting('World', 'Hey', '...'))

// In real code, bad values arrive from parsed JSON, from JavaScript callers, or through
// `any`; `as any` stands in for that here. Calls that bypass TypeScript's checks now fail
// when they run. The error is returned, not thrown.
function show(result: unknown) {
  // `unknown` accepts anything, including the returned error
  console.log(result instanceof Error ? `error: ${result.message}` : result)
}
show(createGreeting('World', null as any)) // optional means "may be undefined", not "may be null"
show(createGreeting('World', 42 as any))
show(createGreeting('World', 'Hi', 3 as any))

// The function carries its own parameter metadata at runtime
console.log('\nFunction metadata:')
for (const [param, info] of Object.entries((createGreeting as any).__tjs.params)) {
  const { required, default: fallback } = info as any
  console.log(
    `  ${param}: ${required ? 'required' : 'optional'}` +
      (!required && 'default' in (info as any) ? `, default ${JSON.stringify(fallback)}` : '')
  )
}
```

It prints:

```text
Hello, World!
Hi, World!
Hello, World?
Hey, World...
error: Expected string | undefined for '<source>:3:createGreeting.greeting', got null
error: Expected string | undefined for '<source>:3:createGreeting.greeting', got number
error: Expected string for '<source>:3:createGreeting.punctuation', got number

Function metadata:
  name: required
  greeting: optional
  punctuation: optional, default "!"
```

The start of each error message names the source, the line of the function and the
parameter that failed.

## What the converter writes

Here is the signature before and after conversion:

```javascript
// TypeScript
function createGreeting(name: string, greeting?: string, punctuation: string = '!'): string

// TJS, as the converter writes it
function createGreeting(name: string, greeting: string | undefined, punctuation = '!'):! string
```

TJS describes types with example values: `name: 'Alice'` means "a string, like this one".
A bare type name such as `string` is also accepted and means the same thing, which is why
the converter can leave `name: string` as it is. The `:!` before the return type means "this
is the type of the result, not a worked example to test".

## What to notice

- **`greeting?: string` becomes `greeting: string | undefined`.** The parameter is
  optional, and when it is present it must be a string. The metadata records it as
  `required: false`.
- **`punctuation: string = '!'` becomes `punctuation = '!'`.** A default does two jobs in
  TJS: it is the value you get when the argument is omitted, and it is the example that sets
  the type. So the parameter is optional, defaults to `'!'`, and a value that is passed must
  be a string. That is why `3` is refused.
- **Errors are returned, not thrown.** A failed check makes the call return an error
  value instead of running the body, so the next line still runs. The value is a
  `MonadicError`, which extends `Error`: it has a `message`, plus `path` (where the check
  failed), `expected` and `actual`. Test for it with `instanceof Error`, as the example does,
  or with `isMonadicError` from `tjs-lang/runtime`.
- **The declared return type does not mention the error.** `createGreeting` is still typed
  as returning `string`, so TypeScript will let a caller call `.toUpperCase()` on an error.
  Check where untrusted data enters your program, a parsed response or a form, rather than
  after every call: an error passed into another checked TJS function comes straight back
  out, so a chain of calls can be checked once at the end.
- **Remove the `/* @tjs TjsStrict */` line** (you can edit the example above) and the three
  bad calls print `Hello, World!`, `42, World!` and `Hi, World3`: plain JavaScript
  behaviour. The metadata is there either way.

## The metadata

Every TJS function has a `__tjs` property. Its `params` entry maps each parameter name to a
description. For `punctuation` it is:

```javascript
{ type: { kind: 'string' }, required: false, default: '!' }
```

`greeting` has `required: false` and no `default` key; `name` has `required: true`. A
required parameter also carries `default: null`, which is why the example prints a default
only for optional parameters. Next to `params`, `__tjs` holds `returns` (the return type)
and `source` (the file and line).

`__tjs` is added by the transpiler, so TypeScript does not know about it; that is what the
`as any` casts are for. To turn it into something standard, `functionMetaToJSONSchema(fn.__tjs)`
from `tjs-lang/lang` gives a JSON Schema for the function's input and output, built from the
code that is actually running. [From Zod to TJS](../../sections/ts-from-zod.md) uses it.

## The gotcha: `null` that used to work

With `strictNullChecks`, TypeScript already refuses `null` for `greeting?: string`. What
changes under `TjsStrict` is that the rule is now enforced at runtime. The body uses `??`,
which treats `null` like `undefined`, so in the plain JavaScript output
`createGreeting('World', null)` quietly printed `Hello, World!`. Under `TjsStrict` the same
call returns an error, as the example shows.

An optional parameter accepts `undefined`, because that is what an omitted argument is, but
not `null`. If a caller may pass `null` on purpose, say so in the type:
`greeting?: string | null`.

## `TjsStrict` also changes object defaults

Under `TjsStrict` an _object_ default becomes a dictionary default: each member is
defaulted separately, and a partial argument is merged with the defaults. In
`function f(opts = { x: 0, y: 0 })`, calling `f({ x: 5 })` gives `{ x: 5, y: 0 }`. Without
`TjsStrict`, converted TypeScript keeps JavaScript's all-or-nothing default and gives
`{ x: 5 }`. This is a behaviour change, so check your object defaults when you opt a file
in. See [Converting a TypeScript Project](../../sections/ts-converting-a-project.md).
title: Optional Parameters
description: `?` and `= default` both survive conversion, `undefined` is not `null`, and every function can tell you at runtime which of its parameters are required. TypeScript has two ways to make a parameter optional: `greeting?: string`, which may be `undefined`, and `punctuation: string = '!'`, which has a default. Both convert to TJS, and both keep their meaning. By default, converted TypeScript validates nothing: it behaves exactly like the JavaScript `tsc` would emit. That is deliberate. Conversion should not change what your program does, and full TJS changes more than validation (for example, `==` stops coercing, and object defaults merge, as described at the end of this page). The first line of the example, `/* @tjs TjsStrict */`, opts this one file in to full TJS, and the types become checks that run on every call. Whether or not you opt in, each function also carries a description of its parameters at runtime: which are required, and what the defaults are. The example shows both.

# Publishing a TJS Library to TypeScript

The other chapters in this book go one way: TypeScript in, TJS out. This one goes the
other way. You have a module in TJS, and the people who will import it write TypeScript.
What do they see, and what do they have to do differently?

Two things, mostly:

1. They see a `.d.ts` file the toolchain generated from your source, so their editor
   autocompletes your functions and `tsc` checks their calls as usual.
2. A call can fail at runtime in a way the `.d.ts` does not mention. A **checked
   function** is any TJS function whose parameters are given as examples (`x: 0`,
   `name: ''`), unless it is marked unsafe with `!`; it checks every argument when it is
   called. Given a bad argument, it does not throw. It returns a `MonadicError`, a
   subclass of `Error`, as its result. Consumer code should check for one where data comes
   from outside: see [Handling a rejected call](#handling-a-rejected-call-from-typescript).

Which parts of this chapter apply depends on where your source lives:

- **Written in `.tjs`.** All of it.
- **Converted from `.ts` with `tjs convert`, and now maintained and published as `.tjs`.**
  All of it, plus [`@tjs` annotations](#types-with-no-runtime-meaning-tjs-annotations),
  which steer that conversion. [Converting a TypeScript
  Project](/ts-converting-a-project/) covers the conversion itself.
- **Still `.ts`, published as `.ts`.** None of it. `tsc --declaration` already gives
  TypeScript consumers your real types.

## Building: `tjs emit --dts`

```bash
tjs emit --dts src/ -o dist/
```

For each `.tjs` file under `src/` this writes three files to `dist/`, keeping the
directory layout:

- `name.js`: the JavaScript, with the runtime checks and a small inline runtime. It is
  an ES module and runs in Node, Bun or a browser with nothing else installed.
- `name.d.ts`: the TypeScript declarations.
- `name.md`: documentation generated from the source. `--no-docs` turns it off;
  `--docs-dir docs/` writes it somewhere else.

Things to know about it:

- `--dts` only works with `-o`. Emitting to stdout (`tjs emit --dts file.tjs > file.js`)
  silently writes just the JavaScript and exits 0.
- Relative imports of `./x.tjs` become `./x.js` in both the `.js` and the `.d.ts`, so the
  output loads with no `.tjs` loader.
- The tests run first: every `test` block, and every **signature example**, which is a
  function's parameter examples run against its return example (`add(a: 2, b: 3): 5` is a
  test that `add(2, 3)` returns `5`). If one fails, that file is not written and the
  command exits 1. `--jfdi` ("just do it") writes the file anyway. Do not use it for a
  build you publish: the failure is telling you the code and its examples disagree.
- A return example that calls a function **imported from another module** cannot run
  during `emit`, so the file fails with `✗ Signature: one is not defined`, although
  `tjs check` passes the same file. Until that is fixed, give such a function a type-only
  return (`:!`, below).
- The `tjs` command is a Bun script, so the machine that builds needs Bun. The output does
  not.

From a build script, the same declarations come from `generateDTS` in `tjs-lang/lang`:

```typescript
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
import { tjs, generateDTS } from 'tjs-lang/lang'

const source = readFileSync('src/geometry.tjs', 'utf8')
const result = tjs(source, { filename: 'geometry.tjs' })
const js = result.code
const dts = generateDTS(result, source)
```

<!-- TODO review -->

## A module and its declarations

Here is a small TJS module with one of each common declaration. The comments say what
each one is; [TJS Syntax](../../TJS-SYNTAX.md) introduces `Type`, `Enum`, `Generic` and
`FunctionPredicate` properly.

```tjs
// A Type: a named runtime check, here built from an example value.
export Type Point {
  description: 'a point on the plane'
  example: { x: 0.0, y: 0.0 }
}

// An Enum: the string after the name is its description.
export Enum Direction 'compass direction' {
  North = 'N'
  South = 'S'
}

// A FunctionPredicate: a function signature, written as examples.
export FunctionPredicate Format {
  params: { value: 0.0, digits: 0 }
  returns: ''
}

// A Generic: T arrives in the predicate as a check function, so T(x.value)
// asks "is x.value a T?". The declaration block is what TypeScript sees.
export Generic Tagged<T> {
  description: 'a value with a label'
  predicate(x, T) {
    return typeof x === 'object' && x !== null && 'value' in x && T(x.value)
  }
  declaration {
    value: T
    label: string
  }
}

// :! declares the return type without a tested value.
export function distance(a: Point, b: Point):! 0.0 {
  return Math.hypot(b.x - a.x, b.y - a.y)
}

// A plain : return example is a test: scale({ x: 3, y: 4 }) must give { x: 6, y: 8 }.
export function scale(p: { x: 3.0, y: 4.0 }, by = 2.0): { x: 6.0, y: 8.0 } {
  return { x: p.x * by, y: p.y * by }
}

// A dictionary default: pass any subset of opts; missing members are filled in.
export function label(p: { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 }, opts = { digits: 1, unit: 'px' }): '1.0px, 2.0px' {
  return `${p.x.toFixed(opts.digits)}${opts.unit}, ${p.y.toFixed(opts.digits)}${opts.unit}`
}

export class Counter {
  #n = 0
  constructor(start: 0) {
    this.#n = start
  }
  increment(): 1 {
    this.#n += 1
    return this.#n
  }
}
```

And here is the `geometry.d.ts` that `tjs emit --dts` writes for it, unedited:

```typescript
export declare function distance(a: Point, b: Point): number;
export declare function scale(p: { x: number; y: number }, by?: number): { x: number; y: number };
export declare function label(p: { x: number; y: number }, opts?: { digits?: number; unit?: string }): string;
export declare function Counter(start: number): any;
export declare class Counter {
  constructor(start: number);
  increment(): number;
}
export type Point = { x: number; y: number };
export declare const Point: { check(value: any): boolean; default: { x: number; y: number }; (value: any): boolean; };
export type Direction = "N" | "S";
export declare const Direction: { check(value: any): boolean; values: Direction[]; members: Record<string, Direction>; names: Record<string, string>; keys: string[]; };
export interface Tagged<T> {
  value: T
  label: string
}
export type Format = (value: number, digits: number) => string;
```

This file compiles under `tsc --strict` (checked with TypeScript 5.8), together with a
consumer that calls `new Counter(3)`, `distance` and `label`. The `function Counter` and
`class Counter` pair is legal: TypeScript merges a function declaration with an ambient
class of the same name.

Two details in the source matter for the output. `distance` uses `:!`, a type-only return
example. Its parameters are declared Types, so the signature has no literal arguments to
call it with: a plain `: 0.0` would be skipped as untestable, and `:!` says so outright.
`scale` uses a plain `:`, so `scale({ x: 3, y: 4 })` must return `{ x: 6, y: 8 }` or the
build fails. Both become `number` in the declaration either way: the `.d.ts` keeps the
type of an example, never its value.

The descriptions (`'a point on the plane'`, `'compass direction'`) are kept at runtime, as
`Point.description` and `Direction.description`, but they do not reach the `.d.ts` as
JSDoc, nor the generated `.md`. That is a gap, listed at the end.

<!-- TODO review -->

## What each construct becomes

| TJS                                  | In the `.d.ts`                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `function f(a: 0, b: '')`            | `declare function f(a: number, b: string)`. A parameter with a default is optional (`by?: number`). With no return example, the declared return type is `any`; `:! 0` gives `number` without a tested value. |
| Object example `{ x: 0.0 }`          | An object type, `{ x: number }`.                                                                                                       |
| Dictionary default `opts = { digits: 1 }` | The parameter and every member are optional (`opts?: { digits?: number }`), at every depth, because a caller may pass any subset.  |
| Literal union in a parameter         | The same union: `m: 'on' \| 'off'` stays `"on" \| "off"`.                                                                              |
| `Type Point`                         | A type alias **and** a value of the same name, so `Point` works as a type and `Point.check(x)` compiles.                               |
| `Enum Direction`                     | The union of its member values (`"N" \| "S"`), plus a value with `check`, `values`, `members`, `names` and `keys`.                     |
| `Generic X<T>` with `declaration {}` | `interface X<T> { … }` with the block's contents, or `type X<T> = …` for the `// TS:` form (next section).                             |
| `Generic X<T>` without one           | `declare function X(...args: any[]): { check(value: any): boolean; (value: any): boolean; }`: a checker factory, with nothing about `T`. |
| `FunctionPredicate F`                | A function type, `type F = (value: number, digits: number) => string`. Used as a parameter type, it becomes `any` (a gap).             |
| `Union U 'u' 'a' \| 'b'`             | Nothing: `U` is missing, so a function that takes a `U` fails to compile (a gap).                                                      |
| `Union U 'u' { 'a' \| 'b' }`         | `type U = string`, not the literal union (a gap).                                                                                      |
| `class C`                            | Two declarations: a callable `C(...)` that returns `any`, and a `declare class C` with the constructor and methods.                   |
| `./other.tjs` import or re-export    | The same statement naming `./other.js`.                                                                                                |

A single literal in an example position widens to its type: `m: 'on'` means "a string,
for example `'on'`". A union of literals does not widen. `'on' | 'off'` reads as an
enumeration of the allowed values, so it is checked and declared exactly.

If a file has no `export` at all, every top-level declaration is exported in the `.d.ts`.

The class row needs a word. TJS drops JavaScript's requirement that a class be
constructed with `new`: `Counter(3)` builds the same instance as `new Counter(3)`. The
callable declaration records that, but returns `any`, which is a known gap. From
TypeScript, write `new Counter(3)`: that form is fully typed.

## Generics: the `declaration` block

A `Generic`'s predicate is code, and the emitter cannot turn code into a TypeScript type.
Without help, `Generic Box<T>` is declared as the checker factory in the table above, and
a TypeScript consumer learns nothing about what is inside a `Box<T>`.

A `declaration` block supplies the TypeScript-visible shape. It has no effect at runtime;
its contents are TypeScript, copied into the `.d.ts`. The `Tagged<T>` example above uses
the interface form: each line is a member, and the output is `interface Tagged<T> { … }`.

For a type an interface cannot express, start the block with `// TS:` and the rest is
emitted as a type alias. This is the reactive-proxy case, where every property of a wrapped
value is itself wrapped:

```tjs
export Generic Watched<T> {
  description: 'a watched value'
  predicate(x, T) {
    return typeof x === 'object' && x !== null && 'path' in x
  }
  declaration {
    // TS: { [K in keyof T]: Watched<T[K]> } & { path: string; observe(cb: (path: string) => void): void }
  }
}
```

which becomes

```typescript
export type Watched<T> = { [K in keyof T]: Watched<T[K]> } & { path: string; observe(cb: (path: string) => void): void };
```

The predicate here never calls `T`. It checks only the outer shape, that the value is a
watched proxy, and leaves the wrapped value unchecked on purpose: checking it would mean
walking the whole proxied object on every call. The declaration still carries `T`, so a
consumer gets the full type:

```typescript
declare const app: Watched<{ user: { name: string } }>
app.user.name.path // autocompletes, and is a string
```

What you cannot yet do is declare a TJS **function** generic over `T`. A function returning
a `Watched<T>` for whatever it was given, `watch<T>(value: T): Watched<T>` in TypeScript,
has no TJS spelling. The closest is an empty object example, `watch(value: {}): {}`, and an
empty object example is declared as `Record<string, any>`, so the declaration comes out as
`(value: Record<string, any>) => Record<string, any>`.

For such a function, write its declaration by hand and put it over the generated one after
the build. `tjs emit` overwrites `dist/watch.d.ts` every time, so keep the hand-written
file outside `dist/`, for example `types/watch.d.ts`, and copy it in as the last build step:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "tjs emit --dts src/ -o dist/ && cp types/watch.d.ts dist/watch.d.ts"
  }
}
```

Put the generic function in a module of its own, so that file replaces nothing else.

## The declarations are wider than the contract

TypeScript has one `number`. TJS tells integers from floats, and non-negative integers
from both, because the example says which one you meant: `3` is an integer, `3.0` is a
float, and `+3` is a non-negative integer. The `.d.ts` can only say `number`, so a call
that `tsc` accepts can still be refused when it runs:

```tjs:inline
function repeat(text: 'ab', times: +3): 'ababab' {
  return text.repeat(times)
}

console.log(repeat('xy', 2))          // xyxy
console.log(repeat('xy', 2.5).message) // Expected non-negative-integer for '…repeat.times', got number
console.log(repeat('xy', -1).message)  // the same message
```

The declaration for `repeat` is `(text: string, times: number): string`. `2.5` and `-1`
both type-check, and both come back as errors, because `+3` asks for a non-negative
integer.

The same holds for a `Type` with a `predicate`, for an `Enum` given a string that is not a
member, and for any value whose shape is wrong at runtime because it came from
`JSON.parse` or a cast, where `tsc` believed the static type. The `.d.ts` is what
TypeScript can check. The runtime check is the contract, with one exception: a parameter
typed as a `FunctionPredicate` is not checked at runtime at all (`tjs check` warns about
it), and its declaration is `any`. See [Current gaps](#current-gaps).

## Handling a rejected call from TypeScript

A checked TJS function does not throw on a bad argument. It returns a `MonadicError`, a
subclass of `Error` carrying where the check failed (`path`), what it wanted
(`expected`), and what it got (`actual`). `path` starts with the file and line of the
function, then the function and parameter: `geometry.tjs:33:distance.b`.

The declared return type does not include the error. `distance` is declared as returning
`number`, and on bad input it returns a `MonadicError`. Declaring `number | MonadicError`
would be honest, but it would make the compiler demand a check after every call, including
the calls inside a chain of TJS functions where an error is passed along without harm
(below). The emitter has no option to declare the union today.

A TypeScript consumer checks with `isMonadicError` from `tjs-lang/runtime`, which is a
type guard:

```typescript
import { isMonadicError } from 'tjs-lang/runtime'
import { distance, type Point } from 'geometry'

export function report(from: Point, to: Point): string {
  const d = distance(from, to)
  if (isMonadicError(d)) {
    // e.g. "rejected geometry.tjs:33:distance.b: expected Point, got object"
    return `rejected ${d.path}: expected ${d.expected}, got ${d.actual}`
  }
  return d.toFixed(1) // d is a number here
}
```

Use `isMonadicError` rather than `instanceof`. It checks the error's shape
(`e instanceof Error && e.name === 'MonadicError' && 'path' in e`), so it recognizes an
error from any TJS module. `instanceof MonadicError` also works across TJS modules in one
program, because they share one class through a global (see Packaging), but not across a
realm boundary such as an iframe or a worker, which has its own globals. If you would
rather not depend on `tjs-lang` for one function, write the shape test out as above.

You do not need a check after every TJS call. An error passed into another checked TJS
function comes straight back out unchanged, so a chain of TJS calls can be checked once,
at the end. That holds only between TJS functions. Your own TypeScript code in between
sees the error typed as the success type: `distance(a, b) * 2` compiles, and gives `NaN`
when `distance` returned an error. Check before TypeScript code uses the value, and check
where data enters your program: a parsed response, a form, a message from a worker.

Here is the whole exchange in one file you can run. To run both sides in one box, this
example writes the library half in TypeScript and converts it with the `TjsStrict`
annotation, which makes converted TypeScript check its parameters the way a TJS module
does. In a real project the library half is a `.tjs` file, and the consumer needs no
annotation. On this page `isMonadicError` is supplied for you; in your project it is the
import above.

```ts:inline
/* @tjs TjsStrict */

// Library side: a function whose parameters are checked at runtime.
export function area(width: number, height: number): number {
  return width * height
}

// Consumer side: the cast tells the compiler what it wants to hear.
const rows = JSON.parse('[[2, 3], [2, "three"]]') as [number, number][]

for (const [width, height] of rows) {
  const result = area(width, height)
  if (isMonadicError(result)) {
    console.log(`rejected ${result.path}: expected ${result.expected}, got ${result.actual}`)
  } else {
    console.log(`area ${result}`)
  }
}
```

It prints:

```text
area 6
rejected <source>:4:area.height: expected number, got string
```

The cast compiled because the compiler cannot see JSON.
