## Types with no runtime meaning: `@tjs` annotations

This section is for a library that started as TypeScript and was converted with
`tjs convert`. The converter carries the TypeScript types across, and some of them have no
runtime check in TJS today: conditional types and mapped types, which compute a type from
another type, and intersections (`A & B`), which TJS does not check yet. The converter
keeps those as a `Generic` (or, for a non-generic type such as an intersection, a `Type`)
whose body holds the original TypeScript in a `// TS:` comment, so they reach the `.d.ts`
unchanged.

Where the default is not what you want, a `/* @tjs … */` comment in the `.ts` file steers
the conversion of the declaration right after it. The TypeScript compiler ignores it. The
grammar is `@tjs` followed by a keyword and that keyword's argument: a value after
`example:`, a block after `declaration` or `predicate(x, T)`. `@tjs-skip` is the one
exception, a single word with nothing after it.

```typescript
/* @tjs-skip */
type Unboxed<T> = T extends { value: infer U } ? U : T

/* @tjs example: { name: 'Alice', age: 30 } */
export interface User {
  name: string
  age: number
}

/* @tjs declaration { value: T; path: string } */
export interface Boxed<T> {
  value: T
}

/* @tjs predicate(x, T) { return typeof x === 'object' && T(x.value) } */
export interface Box<T> {
  value: T
}
```

- `@tjs-skip` drops the next declaration from the conversion entirely. It is then absent
  from the TJS **and** from the `.d.ts`. A conditional type like `Unboxed<T>` converts and
  round-trips without it; skip one when it is a compile-time helper used only inside the
  file and you want no runtime value for it. Nothing outside the file can name it
  afterwards.
- `@tjs example:` replaces the example the converter would infer. Here it also tightens the
  runtime check: `age: 30` is an integer, so `User.check({ name: 'a', age: 30.5 })` is
  false, though TypeScript's `age: number` would allow it. The declared type stays
  `{ name: string; age: number }`.
- `@tjs declaration { … }` replaces the generated interface body. Use it when the runtime
  value has members the TypeScript interface does not list. If the library's `box()`
  attaches a `path` to every box it returns, the annotation above declares `Boxed<T>` with
  `value: T; path: string`, so consumers can read `b.path`.
- `@tjs predicate(x, T) { … }` supplies the runtime check for a generic interface: here,
  that a `Box<T>` is an object whose `value` is a `T`.

The full list of `@tjs` annotations is in [TJS for TypeScript
Programmers](../../TJS-FOR-TS.md).

<!-- TODO review -->

## Packaging

A TJS library ships the emitted `dist/`, not the `.tjs` source, and points `exports` at it
with the `types` condition first. The package entry is `src/index.tjs`, a module that
re-exports the others (`export * from './geometry.tjs'`), so it is emitted as
`dist/index.js` and `dist/index.d.ts`:

```json
{
  "name": "geometry",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
      "default": "./dist/index.js"
    }
  },
  "files": ["dist"],
  "scripts": {
    "build": "tjs emit --dts src/ -o dist/"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "tjs-lang": "…"
  }
}
```

The `build` script runs `tjs`, which needs Bun on the build machine, as noted above. In
`devDependencies`, pin the `tjs-lang` version you built and tested with.

`tjs-lang` is a **dev** dependency. Each emitted file carries the part of the runtime it
uses, so your consumers install nothing extra to run your code. They add `tjs-lang`
themselves only if they want `isMonadicError` from `tjs-lang/runtime`.

Several TJS modules in one program still agree with each other: they share one
`MonadicError` class through a global, so `instanceof` works across module boundaries and
across copies of your package within one realm. (The design is in [Runtime
Fusion](../../docs/runtime-fusion.md).)

Before you publish:

- The output is ES modules only. There is no CommonJS build; a CommonJS consumer loads
  the package with `import()`.
- No source maps are written. A stack trace points into `dist/*.js`.
- Run `tsc --noEmit --strict` over `dist/*.d.ts` with a small consumer file that imports
  your entry point. The emitter does not check that its output compiles, and the gaps
  below include cases where it does not.

## One runtime per bundle

This section is for applications, not for a published library. Do not use it for
`dist/` files you put on npm; the reason is at the end.

Each emitted file carries its own copy of the inline runtime, the **prelude**: the small
set of helpers the checks call. An application that bundles many TJS modules therefore
parses that code once per module. When you build the bundle yourself with Bun,
`tjsPlugin({ sharedPrelude: true })` makes every module import a single copy from
`tjs-lang/prelude` instead:

```typescript
import { tjsPlugin } from 'tjs-lang/bun-build-plugin'

await Bun.build({
  entrypoints: ['src/index.tjs'],
  outdir: 'dist',
  plugins: [tjsPlugin({ sharedPrelude: true })],
})
```

The programmatic spelling is `tjs(source, { prelude: 'import' })`. The shared copy is the
full runtime, so it pays off only with many modules; for a handful, the default output is
smaller.

Why not for a library: a module emitted this way imports `tjs-lang/prelude` and refuses to
load against any prelude whose code differs from the one it was compiled against. The
check is a content hash of the prelude, and the prelude can change in any `tjs-lang`
release, a patch included. A package that published such files would break for any
consumer whose installed `tjs-lang` shipped a different prelude. Publish the default,
self-contained output. See the [module system notes](../../DOCS-TJS.md#module-system) for
more.

<!-- TODO review -->

## Current gaps

The emitter is newer than the rest of the toolchain, and these are known not to work yet.
Each is a defect, not a design decision.

- **An inline `Union` is not declared.** `export Union Unit 'unit' 'px' | 'em'` produces no
  `Unit` in the `.d.ts`, so a function that takes a `Unit` makes the declaration file fail
  to compile. The block form, `Union Size 'size' { 'sm' | 'lg' }`, is declared, but as
  `string` rather than `"sm" | "lg"`. Until this is fixed, use an `Enum`, or write the
  literal union in the parameter (`unit: 'px' | 'em'`), which is declared exactly.
- **Enum members are not declared as properties.** `Direction.North` works at runtime, but
  the `.d.ts` declares only `members`, `values` and friends, so TypeScript rejects it.
  Write `'N'`, or `Direction.members.North`.
- **A `Generic` with a `declaration` block is declared only as a type.** The runtime
  factory (`Tagged(isNumber)`) is not declared as a value, so calling it from TypeScript
  does not compile.
- **A class called without `new` is declared as returning `any`.** Use `new` from
  TypeScript.
- **A `FunctionPredicate` used as a parameter type is declared `any`.** It is also not
  checked at runtime; `tjs check` warns about this.
- **Descriptions do not reach the `.d.ts`.** A `Type`'s or `Enum`'s description is
  available at runtime but is not emitted as JSDoc, so editor hovers do not show it.
- **A return example that calls an import fails `tjs emit`**, though `tjs check` passes it.
  Use `:!` on such a function.

# String Processing

Text is what agents mostly move around: a user's question, a page they fetched, a model's
answer. AJS (short for AsyncJS) has JavaScript's everyday string methods, but only those whose
cost the VM can bound, and it checks their argument types strictly.

```ajs:inline
function processText({ text = '  Hello World  ' }) {
  let clean = text.trim()
  let upper = clean.toUpperCase()
  let lower = clean.toLowerCase()
  let words = clean.split(' ')
  let initials = words[0].slice(0, 1) + words[1].slice(0, 1)
  return { clean, upper, lower, words, wordCount: words.length, initials }
}
```

An agent takes one object of named inputs. The host supplies it when it runs the agent; the
`= '  Hello World  '` default is used when the caller passes no `text`, and is what the live
example on this page runs with. With it, the agent returns `clean: 'Hello World'`,
`upper: 'HELLO WORLD'`, `lower: 'hello world'`, `words: ['Hello', 'World']`, `wordCount: 2`
and `initials: 'HW'`.

## What to notice

- **A method may be called only if the VM knows its cost.** Every operation costs fuel, the
  run's work budget; when it runs out, the run stops (see [Fuel Limits](/fuel-limits/)). Each
  callable method has an entry in the VM's method table that bounds what one call can allocate,
  so the call is paid for before it runs. `trim`, `slice`, `split`, `replace`, `padStart`,
  `includes`, `startsWith` and most other string methods are in the table. A method that is
  not is refused when the source is compiled, before anything runs: `text.matchAll(/a/g)` fails
  with `Method 'matchAll' is not available in AsyncJS`. The rules per receiver type are in
  [Methods](/DOCS-AJS/#methods).
- **Arguments must already have the type the method takes.** AJS refuses where JavaScript would
  quietly convert: `'ab'.repeat('3')` returns `'ababab'` in JavaScript, but in AJS it is an error,
  `repeat()'s argument 1 must be a number`. The error happens when the call runs. It is an
  ordinary AJS error: a `try`/`catch` in the agent can catch it, and otherwise the run ends and
  the host receives it as the run's `error`. See [Error Handling](/ajs-error-handling/).

## A variation

Regex in AJS is deprecated as of 0.14 and planned to leave the core VM in 0.15. It works today;
prefer plain string methods (`split`, `includes`, `startsWith`, `slice`) where they do the job.
Where they don't, regular expressions work as search patterns in `match`, `replace`, `split`,
`replaceAll` and `search`:

```ajs:inline
function textStats({
  text = 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. The dog sleeps.',
}) {
  let words = text.toLowerCase().match(/[a-z]+/g) ?? []
  let longest = words.reduce((best, w) => (w.length > best.length ? w : best), '')
  let unique = Set(words)
  let slug = text.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-').replace(/^-+|-+$/g, '')
  return { wordCount: words.length, uniqueWords: unique.size, longest, slug }
}
```

With the default text this returns `wordCount: 12`, `uniqueWords: 9`, `longest: 'sleeps'` and
`slug: 'the-quick-brown-fox-jumps-over-the-lazy-dog-the-dog-sleeps'`.

- **`match` returns `null` when nothing matches,** as in JavaScript. Without the `?? []`, text
  with no letters (`'123 456'`) would end the run at the next line with
  `reduce: items is not an array`. With it, that text returns `wordCount: 0` and `longest: ''`.
- **Chaining string methods is fine.** AJS allows at most one callback-taking call (`map`,
  `filter`, `find`, `reduce`) per statement, and it must be the whole right-hand side, so
  `words.map(…).filter(…)` has to be split in two (see [Loop & Filter](/loop-filter/)). The
  `reduce` line follows that rule. `toLowerCase().match(…)` and the two `replace` calls take no
  callback, so they chain freely.
- **`Set(words)` makes a set of the unique words.** AJS has no `new`; builtins such as `Set`
  and `Date` are called as functions, and `new Set(words)` is refused at compile time. A set in
  AJS is an array of its unique items that also has a `size` (equal to its `length`) and set
  methods such as `has` and `union`. See [Set](/DOCS-AJS/#set).

## The gotcha

AJS regexes run on the VM's own engine, not on the regex engine of the JavaScript program that
embeds the VM (the host). A carefully built pattern can make the host's engine run for a very
long time on a short input (ReDoS); the VM's engine never backtracks, so its time is linear in
the input times the pattern's size, no pattern can hang a run, and its work is charged as fuel.

The price is that it has no backreferences (`\1`) and no lookahead or lookbehind (`(?=…)`). A
regex that uses them is rejected when the source is compiled, before anything runs, with an
error pointing at the pattern (`Lookahead and lookbehind are not supported in AsyncJS regexes`).
Most such patterns can be rewritten as two steps: match more than you need, then trim the rest.
Instead of `text.match(/\d+(?=usd)/)`, which is refused:

```ajs:inline
function price({ text = 'total: 120usd' }) {
  let found = text.match(/\d+usd/)
  let amount = found ? found[0].slice(0, -3) : null
  return { amount }
}
```

This returns `amount: '120'`, and `amount: null` for text with no price. The full list of what
the engine supports is in [Regular expressions](/DOCS-AJS/#regular-expressions).

What replaces regex is Pattern, a grammar built as data. It is not available in AJS yet, so
until it is, use string methods, or regex within the limits above. The plan is in the
[Pattern design note](/pattern/); the engine is the separate
[tosijs-pattern](https://pattern.tosijs.net) library, which is not yet on npm.

# The Full Picture: an order handler end to end

_A small order handler, written in TypeScript, with its types checked at run time._

This is a small but complete piece of business logic: two interfaces, a validator and a
function that ties them together, the way a request handler is usually written. The
validator checks business rules (an order needs products and a customer). It assumes the
_types_ are already right, because TypeScript said so. The last call breaks that
assumption, the way real data does, and then hands the result to `JSON.stringify`, standing
in for code that knows nothing about TJS.

The code below is ordinary TypeScript. The TJS converter (`fromTS` in
`tjs-lang/lang/from-ts`, or `tjs convert` on the command line) turns it into TJS, and the
page runs the result. [Converting a TypeScript Project](ts-converting-a-project.md) covers
doing the same to your own files.

```ts:inline
// Converted TypeScript keeps JavaScript's behaviour until you opt in. This one
// line opts in to full TJS, which turns the types into runtime checks:
/* @tjs TjsStrict */

interface Product {
  id: number
  name: string
  price: number
}

interface Order {
  products: Product[]
  customer: string
}

function calculateTotal(order: Order): number {
  return order.products.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.price, 0)
}

function validateOrder(order: Order): string | null {
  if (order.products.length === 0) {
    return 'Order must have at least one product'
  }
  if (!order.customer) {
    return 'Customer name is required'
  }
  return null
}

function processOrder(order: Order): { success: boolean; total?: number; error?: string } {
  const error = validateOrder(order)
  if (error) {
    return { success: false, error }
  }
  return { success: true, total: calculateTotal(order) }
}

const validOrder: Order = {
  customer: 'Alice',
  products: [
    { id: 1, name: 'Widget', price: 9.99 },
    { id: 2, name: 'Gadget', price: 19.99 }
  ]
}
console.log('Valid order:', JSON.stringify(processOrder(validOrder)))

const emptyOrder: Order = { customer: 'Carol', products: [] }
console.log('Empty order:', JSON.stringify(processOrder(emptyOrder)))

// `as any` stands in for JSON.parse or a request body: data the compiler
// never saw. This product's price is a string.
const stringPrice = {
  customer: 'Dee',
  products: [{ id: 3, name: 'Gizmo', price: '9.99' }]
} as any
console.log('String price:', JSON.stringify(processOrder(stringPrice)))

// This order has no products array at all.
const badOrder = { customer: 'Bob' } as any
const result = processOrder(badOrder)

// What a caller that knows nothing about TJS receives:
console.log('Bad order:', result)
console.log('result.success:', result.success)
```

It prints (`…` stands for a prefix naming the source and line, which varies by where the
code runs):

```text
Valid order: {"success":true,"total":29.979999999999997}
Empty order: {"success":false,"error":"Order must have at least one product"}
String price: {"path":"…:processOrder.order","expected":"Order","actual":"object","name":"MonadicError"}
Bad order: MonadicError: Expected Order for '…:processOrder.order', got object
result.success: undefined
```

The long total is ordinary floating point, not TJS; the gotchas section below comes back
to it.

## What to notice

- **The bad order never reaches `validateOrder`.** `processOrder` declares an `Order`
  parameter, so the missing `products` array is caught at its door. The function returns
  a `MonadicError` (an error object that TJS returns instead of throwing) in place of a
  result. Delete the `/* @tjs TjsStrict */` line and the same call reaches
  `order.products.length` and throws, in the middle of a function that was supposedly
  validating its input:

  ```text
  TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'order.products.length')
  ```

  (That is Bun's wording; Node and Chrome say
  `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'length')`.)

- **Two kinds of validation, in two places.** The type check answers "is this an order at
  all?" automatically, from the interface. `validateOrder` answers "is this order
  acceptable?", which only you can write. The empty order passes the first and fails the
  second. TypeScript leaves you to write both, or to skip the first; TJS writes the first
  from the declaration you already have.
- **Nested types are checked all the way down.** `Order` contains `Product[]`, so each
  product's `id`, `name` and `price` are checked too, and the string price is rejected at
  the same door as the missing array. Checking a parameter walks the whole value, so its
  cost grows with the size of the data; the [performance guide](performance.md) covers
  where that cost lands and when to turn it off.
- **The error says where, not what.** Both rejections report the same thing: the `order`
  parameter of `processOrder` is not an `Order`. Neither names the field that failed
  (`products` missing, `price` a string). For an array parameter the path does name the
  element, as `products[0]` in the last example shows, but not the field inside it.

`TjsStrict` does more than turn on these checks: it gives the whole file TJS's rules,
including an `==` that does not coerce types. Read
[Converting a TypeScript Project](ts-converting-a-project.md) before putting it on a file
you are migrating.

## At the boundary

The error is returned, not thrown, so nothing stops the program; the last two lines show
what that means for a caller outside TJS, such as the code that serializes a response.

`JSON.stringify` keeps the error's `path`, `expected`, `actual` and `name`. It drops
`message` (`Expected Order for '…processOrder.order', got object`), which is not an
enumerable property, so log it explicitly if you want it. And the caller's own
`result.success` is `undefined`: the declared return type says `boolean`, but the value is
not the declared shape at all. A caller that tests `if (!result.success)` treats it as a
failure by accident, then finds no `error` string to report.

So check at the boundary. TJS code uses `isMonadicError(result)` (from `tjs-lang/runtime`)
before trusting a result; a plain-JavaScript caller can test
`result.name === 'MonadicError'`. The [runtime validation](ts-runtime-validation.md)
chapter covers the error object itself.

## The gotchas

Converted return types are never checked; parameter types are. Here is what the converter
writes for the three signatures:

```text
function calculateTotal(order: Order):! number
function validateOrder(order: Order):! string | null
function processOrder(order: Order):! { success: boolean, total: number | undefined, error: string | undefined }
```

`:!` marks a return type as documentation only: the returned value is not checked against
it. (A plain `:` return annotation in TJS is a worked example the function is tested
against, which a TypeScript return type is not; that is why the converter writes `:!`.)
Optional members become `T | undefined`. So the result's
shape is only verified when it is passed to the next function that declares it as a
parameter. Checking parameters is the design: that is where outside data enters a
function, and each value is checked once on the way in rather than again on every return.

The converter also drops ordinary comments, so the converted file starts with a bare
`TjsStrict` line where the `/* @tjs TjsStrict */` directive was.

The total is the other thing worth a look: `9.99 + 19.99` prints `29.979999999999997`.
That is floating point, and it is why money is usually counted in integer cents. TypeScript
cannot say "integer", and the converter reads every `number` as "any number", so `9.99` is
accepted.

Native TJS (a hand-written `.tjs` file, as opposed to converted TypeScript) can say it. In
TJS a type is written as an example value, and TJS tells integers from other numbers: `999`
is an integer example, so a `price` must be an integer, while `9.99` would mean any number.
The [syntax reference](TJS-SYNTAX.md) has the full rules.

```tjs:static
Type Product {
  example: { id: 1, name: 'Widget', price: 999 }
}

function totalCents(products: [Product]):! 0 {
  return products.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.price, 0)
}

const cart = [
  { id: 1, name: 'Widget', price: 999 },
  { id: 2, name: 'Gadget', price: 1999 },
]
console.log('total:', totalCents(cart))

const dollars = [{ id: 1, name: 'Widget', price: 9.99 }]
console.log('dollars:', JSON.stringify(totalCents(dollars)))
```

Three pieces of syntax are new here. `Type Product { example: … }` declares a type by its
example. `[Product]` means an array of `Product` (TypeScript's `Product[]`). `:! 0` says
the function returns an integer, as documentation only. Without the `!`, `0` would be a
worked example (this input gives exactly `0`), which is not what `totalCents` returns.

It prints:

```text
total: 2998
dollars: {"path":"…:totalCents.products[0]","expected":"Product","actual":"object","name":"MonadicError"}
```

The cart totals `2998` cents, exactly. The dollar cart is rejected: its first product is
not a `Product`, because its price is not an integer.

The validator checks business rules (an order needs products and a customer). It assumes the _types_ are already right, because TypeScript said so. The last call breaks that assumption, the way real data does, and then hands the result to `JSON.stringify`, standing in for code that knows nothing about TJS. The code below is ordinary TypeScript. The TJS converter (`fromTS` in `tjs-lang/lang/from-ts`, or `tjs convert` on the command line) turns it into TJS, and the page runs the result. [Converting a TypeScript Project](ts-converting-a-project.md) covers doing the same to your own files.

# CDN Hints (overriding the default)

By default the playground resolves bare imports through JSDelivr's `/+esm`
bundles. When you need a specific CDN — to test an unreleased build, work
around a transform issue, or load a module straight from GitHub — prefix
the spec with a CDN hint.

```tjs:inline
TjsCompat
/#
## Per-import CDN hints

The first path segment of the import spec selects the CDN:

| Hint | Resolves to |
|------|-------------|
| `jsdelivr/<spec>` | JSDelivr `/+esm` (the default) |
| `esmsh/<spec>` | esm.sh (peer-dep dedup, e.g. React) |
| `unpkg/<spec>` | UNPKG with `?module` |
| `github/<user>/<repo>/<path>` | esm.sh's `/gh/` route |

No hint = default routing (JSDelivr, with esm.sh allowlist for React).

For full URLs (your own host, raw.githubusercontent.com, etc.) just
write the URL — it's left untouched.
#/

// Default routing: JSDelivr
import { tosi, elements } from 'tosijs'

// Force a specific CDN
import { html, render } from 'unpkg/lit'
import _ from 'jsdelivr/lodash-es'

// Pin a version
import { format } from 'jsdelivr/date-fns@3.0.0'

// Load straight from a GitHub repo (esm.sh handles fetching/transform)
// Format: github/<user>/<repo>[@ref]/<path>
// (Comment out — the example repo is illustrative)
// import { thing } from 'github/preactjs/preact@10.22.0/dist/preact.module.js'

// Or, for the truly DIY case, paste the full URL
// import { x } from 'https://my.com/dist/index.js'

const { div, h1, button } = elements

const state = tosi({
  count: 0,
  inc() { state.count++ },
})

// Render into the example's own box: the doc site gives an example a `preview` element (its
// page IS the doc page); the old playground ran each example in a page of its own.
const stage = typeof preview === 'undefined' ? document.body : preview
stage.append(
  div(
    h1({ bindText: state.count }),
    button({ onClick: state.inc }, '+1')
  )
)

// date-fns (loaded via JSDelivr hint) used directly
console.log('Today:', format(new Date(), 'yyyy-MM-dd'))
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

- **The hint is part of the import string, and nothing else changes.** `import { format }
  from 'jsdelivr/date-fns@3.0.0'` is still an ordinary ES import. The playground rewrites the
  specifier to a same-origin path, and its service worker maps the first path segment
  (`jsdelivr/`, `esmsh/`, `unpkg/`, `github/`) to a CDN, fetches the module and caches it.
  The browser's own module loader does the rest.
- **Versions go where npm puts them.** `date-fns@3.0.0` pins a release; `tosijs@^1.6` takes a
  range. Without a version you get the latest, which is convenient for a sketch and a hazard
  for anything you mean to keep.
- **Full URLs are left alone.** If you already know where the module lives, write the URL;
  no hint is needed or applied.

<!-- TODO review -->
## When to reach for a hint

The default (JSDelivr's `/+esm` bundles) works for most packages, ESM or CommonJS. Use a hint
when it does not:

| symptom | try |
|---------|-----|
| a library with peer dependencies loads its own copy of them (React itself is already routed to esm.sh; a React-like package is not) | `esmsh/<spec>`, so peers are shared rather than bundled inline |
| an unreleased fix that only exists on a branch | `github/<user>/<repo>@<ref>/<path>` |
| a package JSDelivr transforms badly | `unpkg/<spec>` or `esmsh/<spec>` |

Pin a version whenever you use a hint. The point of a hint is to control exactly what loads,
and an unpinned spec gives that control back to whatever was published last.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Limits

- **This is the playground's resolver, not a language feature.** TJS itself does not know
  about CDNs: the rewrite is done by the playground and the local dev server
  (`bun run dev`). In your own pages, `tjs-lang/import-resolver` provides the same
  bundler-free bare imports, with the worker copied to your site root. A bundler or a
  `node_modules` install resolves imports its own way and ignores these prefixes.
- **Everything is fetched at run time.** A CDN outage, a rate limit or a removed version
  breaks the page. For production, pin versions, or vendor the modules you depend on.
- **This example needs a browser and the network**, so it is not run by the command-line
  harness. The full routing rules are in [Playground Imports](/playground-imports/).

# Control Flow: `given`

`given` picks one block of code to run, based on a value. You write the value, then a list
of **arms**: each arm is one or more values to match, followed by the block to run when the
value matches one of them. `else` runs when no arm matches.

```tjs:inline
function describe(kind: '') {
  given kind {
    'cat', 'dog' { return 'pet' }
    'lion', 'tiger' { return 'wild' }
  } else {
    return 'unknown'
  }
}

console.log('cat   ->', describe('cat'))   // pet
console.log('dog   ->', describe('dog'))   // pet
console.log('tiger ->', describe('tiger')) // wild
console.log('emu   ->', describe('emu'))   // unknown

test 'several values share one arm' {
  expect(describe('cat')).toBe('pet')
  expect(describe('dog')).toBe('pet')
}

test 'else catches every value no arm matches' {
  expect(describe('emu')).toBe('unknown')
}
```

Two pieces of TJS syntax appear here and in every example below:

- **`kind: ''`** declares a parameter whose value is a string. The value after the colon is
  an _example_, not a TypeScript literal type: `''` means "a string", `0` means "an integer",
  `[0]` means "an array of integers". See [TJS syntax](/tjs-syntax/).
- **`test '…' { … }`** is an inline test that runs alongside the example.
  `expect(x).toBe(y)` checks that `x` equals `y`.

The arms are tried from top to bottom and the first match wins. An arm's values are only
evaluated until one matches, so a later arm's values may never be evaluated.

## What `given` replaces

JavaScript already has a construct for this, `switch`, and `given` exists because `switch`
has four defects. Here is the `switch` version of the first arms above, with the bug most
people write at least once:

```tjs:inline
function withSwitch(kind: '') {
  let label = 'unknown'
  switch (kind) {
    case 'cat':
    case 'dog':
      label = 'pet'      // no break: runs on into the next case
    case 'lion':
      label = 'wild'
  }
  return label
}

console.log('switch, cat ->', withSwitch('cat')) // wild: wrong

function withGiven(kind: '') {
  let label = 'unknown'
  given kind {
    'cat', 'dog' { label = 'pet' }
    'lion' { label = 'wild' }
  }
  return label
}

console.log('given,  cat ->', withGiven('cat'))  // pet

test 'no fallthrough: the next arm does not run' {
  expect(withGiven('cat')).toBe('pet')
  expect(withGiven('lion')).toBe('wild')
}
```

TJS compiles `withSwitch` with a warning that points at `given`. The four defects:

1. **Fallthrough is the default.** When a `case` has no `break`, the next case runs too.
   That is why `'cat'` ends up `'wild'` above. In `given`, an arm's block runs and then
   control continues after the whole `given`.
2. **Several values on one arm can only be written as fallthrough.** The two stacked `case`
   labels share a block only because the first one falls into the second. In `given`, you
   list the values with commas: `'cat', 'dog'`.
3. **One shared scope.** All the cases of a `switch` declare into one block, so this is an
   error, because `label` is declared twice:

   ```javascript
   switch (lang) {
     case 'en': let label = 'Hello'; break
     case 'fr': let label = 'Bonjour'; break // SyntaxError: redeclaration
   }
   ```

   In `given`, each arm's body is its own `{ }` block, so each `let` is a separate variable.
4. **It compares with `===`.** TJS's `==` is different from JavaScript's (see below), so a
   `switch` in a `.tjs` file would compare values differently from `==` in the same file.
   `given` matches with TJS's `==`.

## How arms match

An arm matches when the value `==` the arm's value, using TJS's
[honest equality](/honest-equality/). Three rules follow from that:

- **A boxed primitive matches its plain value.** A boxed string is an object wrapped around
  a string, made with `Object('cat')`. `===` says it is not `'cat'`; TJS's `==` unwraps
  it and compares the string inside.
- **Nothing is coerced.** Coercion is JavaScript converting one type to another before
  comparing. TJS does not do that, so the number `200` does not match the string `'200'`.
- **`null` and `undefined` match each other.**

```tjs:inline
function greet(lang: '') {
  given lang {
    'en' {
      let label = 'Hello'
      return label + '!'
    }
    'fr' {
      let label = 'Bonjour'
      return label + ' !'
    }
  } else {
    return '...'
  }
}

console.log('en ->', greet('en')) // Hello!
console.log('fr ->', greet('fr')) // Bonjour !

// Local values, because `describe(kind: '')` above only accepts plain strings.
function boxedStillMatches() {
  const kind = Object('cat')
  given kind {
    'cat', 'dog' { return 'pet' }
  } else {
    return 'unknown'
  }
}

function numberVsString() {
  const code = 200
  given code {
    '200' { return 'matched' }
  } else {
    return 'no match'
  }
}

function nullVsUndefined() {
  const missing = undefined
  given missing {
    null { return 'matched null' }
  } else {
    return 'no match'
  }
}

console.log('Object("cat")     ->', boxedStillMatches()) // pet
console.log('200 vs "200"      ->', numberVsString())    // no match
console.log('undefined vs null ->', nullVsUndefined())   // matched null

test 'each arm has its own scope' {
  expect(greet('en')).toBe('Hello!')
  expect(greet('fr')).toBe('Bonjour !')
}

test 'matching uses TJS ==' {
  expect(boxedStillMatches()).toBe('pet') // a switch, using ===, gives 'unknown'
  expect(numberVsString()).toBe('no match')
  expect(nullVsUndefined()).toBe('matched null')
}
```

The `else` arm is optional. Without one, a value that matches no arm does nothing, like a
`switch` with no `default`.

## Arms that do work instead of returning

An arm does not have to end with `return`. It is a block; when it finishes, control
continues after the `given`. Arm values can be any expression, including named constants,
and a `given` can sit inside an arm:

```tjs:inline
const LOW = 1
const HIGH = 3

function priority(level: 0) {
  let label = 'normal'
  given level {
    LOW { label = 'low' }
    HIGH, 4 { label = 'high' }
  }
  // no `else`: level 2 matches nothing and label stays 'normal'
  return label
}

function httpText(code: 200) {
  given code {
    200, 204 { return 'ok' }
    404 { return 'not found' }
  } else {
    given Math.floor(code / 100) {
      5 { return 'server error' }
    } else {
      return 'other'
    }
  }
}

console.log(priority(1), priority(2), priority(3), priority(4))
// low normal high high
console.log(httpText(204), httpText(404), httpText(503), httpText(302))
// ok not found server error other
```

If two arms list the same value (say `LOW` and `1`), the first one wins and the second never
runs.

## `given` inside a loop

An arm never needs `break`. If you write one anyway, it does what it does in a `switch`: it
ends the `given`, and the loop carries on. `continue` goes to the next iteration of the
loop. To leave the loop from inside an arm, give the loop a label (`scan:` below names the
`for` loop) and write `break scan`.

```tjs:inline
function collect(items: [0]) {
  const kept = []
  scan: for (const n of items) {
    given n {
      0 { continue }       // skip zeros
      -1 { break scan }    // stop the loop at the first -1
      99 { break }         // here only to show that `break` ends the given, not the loop
    }
    kept.push(n)
  }
  return kept
}

console.log(collect([1, 0, 99, 2, -1, 3])) // [1, 99, 2]
```

`99` is still kept: its `break` ends the `given`, and the loop goes on to `kept.push(n)`.

## Things that trip people up

- **`switch` still works, unchanged.** TJS accepts every JavaScript program, so a `switch`
  in a `.tjs` file keeps JavaScript's semantics exactly, fallthrough and all. It compiles,
  with a warning that points at `given`. No rule silently changes what a `switch` means,
  because that would break code pasted from JavaScript.
- **Converting a `switch` is not always a rename.** If an arm deliberately falls into the
  next one, `given` cannot express that directly. When you convert JavaScript or TypeScript
  to TJS and then make the file native TJS (this step is called graduation; see
  [Converting a project](/ts-converting-a-project/)), TJS rewrites a `switch` to `given` only
  if no arm can run into the next one: every non-empty arm except the last must leave
  (`break`, `return`, `throw` or `continue`). Where an arm genuinely falls through, it leaves
  the `switch` alone and adds a note.
- **`break` inside an arm leaves the `given`, not the loop around it.** To leave the loop,
  use a labelled `break` or `return`, as in `collect` above.
- **Arms compare values; they are not patterns.** `given` has no ranges, guards or
  destructuring. For "any 5xx code", compute the thing you want to compare, as `httpText`
  does with `Math.floor(code / 100)`, or use `if`.
- **`given` is TJS syntax.** It is not valid JavaScript, so it cannot appear in a `.js`
  file. It is also not part of [AJS](/ajs/), the sandboxed language for agent code.

## Why a new word instead of fixing `switch`

Because a silent change of meaning is the worst outcome. TJS first tried keeping the word
`switch` and changing its rules. It then measured the result by showing AI language models
the code and asking what it returned: a model reads the code the way a person skimming it
does, from its shape and from what that shape usually means.

Shown a C-style `switch` (`case` labels and colons) in a `.tjs` file, the models gave a
confident wrong answer, assuming fallthrough, in every run, on both models tested. Every new
shape that was tried produced no wrong answers at all, whatever keyword it used.

A confident wrong answer is the failure that ships bugs, so the shape had to change, and the
keyword with it. `switch` still means exactly what it means in C and JavaScript. The
measurements, including the ones that turned out to be noise, are in the
[case study on fixing `switch`](/case-study-switch/).

# Decisions

Every program so far has done the same thing every time. Real programs decide: if the user
is new, say welcome; if the number is too big, say so. This chapter is about making a program
choose what to do.

## Questions with yes-or-no answers

A decision starts with a question whose answer is `true` or `false`. You met the first of these
in Values and Names: `7 > 3` is `true`. Here is the whole family:

| question | means                                   | example          |
| -------- | --------------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| `a < b`  | is `a` less than `b`?                   | `3 < 5` is true  |
| `a > b`  | is `a` greater than `b`?                | `3 > 5` is false |
| `a <= b` | is `a` less than or equal to `b`?       | `5 <= 5` is true |
| `a >= b` | is `a` greater than or equal to `b`?    | `4 >= 5` is false |
| `a == b` | is `a` the same value as `b`?           | `5 == 5` is true |
| `a != b` | is `a` a different value from `b`?      | `5 != 5` is false |

`==` is strict about kinds of value: `5 == '5'` is `false`, because one is a number and the
other is a string, and `'Sunday' == 'sunday'` is `false`, because a capital letter is a
different letter.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
const age = 17

preview.append(`At ${age}, old enough to vote: ${age >= 18}`)

test 'comparisons answer true or false' {
  expect(age >= 18).toBe(false)
  expect(age < 18).toBe(true)
  expect(age != 18).toBe(true)
}
```

Change `age` to `18` and then to `19`, and before each change, predict the sentence. The test
will turn red when you do. It was written for an age of 17, and it is telling you the answers
have changed. That is a test doing its job, not something you broke; change `age` back to 17
and it passes again.

The difference between `>` and `>=` is exactly one value: the edge. Decisions go wrong at their
edges more than anywhere else.

## `if`: only sometimes

`if` runs a block of code only when a condition is true. The condition goes in parentheses,
and the code to run goes in braces:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function advice(temperature: 0) {
  let message = 'Have a nice day.'
  if (temperature < 10) {
    message = 'Take a coat.'
  }
  return message
}

preview.append(advice(5))

test 'a coat when it is cold, not when it is warm' {
  expect(advice(5)).toBe('Take a coat.')
  expect(advice(20)).toBe('Have a nice day.')
}
```

`message` starts out holding one sentence, and the line inside the braces replaces it with
another. That is why it is made with `let`, not `const`: a `let` name can be given a new value
(see Values and Names). `temperature < 10` is a comparison, so its value is `true` or `false`.
When it is true, the block runs and `message` changes; when it is false, the block is skipped.
Change `advice(5)` to `advice(25)` and watch the advice change.

## A decision is only as good as its input

What happens if `advice` is asked about something that is not a temperature at all? In the
`advice` example above, change `advice(5)` to `advice('cold')`. Without a check, the comparison
`'cold' < 10` would quietly answer `false`, and the program would cheerfully tell you to have a
nice day. TJS does not let that happen. The example value in `temperature: 0` says `advice`
takes a whole number, so the call never reaches the `if`. It gives back an error instead, and
that error is what appears on the page. Its message says `Expected integer` (integer is the
programmer's word for a whole number) and ends `got string`.

Now change it to `advice(9.5)`. That is refused too, with a message ending `got number`, and
this time TJS is right and the program is wrong. Temperatures have fractions, but the example
value `0` says "whole number". As you saw in Functions, an example value is a sample of the
kind of value you expect, and writing `0.0`, with a decimal point, says fractions are welcome.
Here is the same function with `0.0` as the example value:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function advice(temperature: 0.0) {
  let message = 'Have a nice day.'
  if (temperature < 10) {
    message = 'Take a coat.'
  }
  return message
}

preview.append(advice(9.5))

test 'any number is a temperature; a word is not' {
  expect(advice(9.5)).toBe('Take a coat.')
  expect(advice(10)).toBe('Have a nice day.')
  expect(advice('cold') instanceof Error).toBe(true)
}
```

Now `advice(9.5)` works. The example value in a function's parentheses is a statement about
what the function accepts, and it is worth getting right.

The last check is the one from Checking Your Work: `x instanceof Error` asks "is `x` an error?".
A wrong kind of value gives back an error, and a test can say so.

## `else`: one or the other

`else` gives the other choice: what to do when the condition is false.

The example below uses `%`, which gives the **remainder** after dividing: `7 % 2` is 1, because
7 is three 2s and 1 over. An even number leaves no remainder when divided by 2, so "`n` is
even" is written `n % 2 == 0`.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function describe(n: 0) {
  if (n % 2 == 0) {
    return `${n} is even`
  } else {
    return `${n} is odd`
  }
}

preview.append(describe(7))

test 'even and odd' {
  expect(describe(4)).toBe('4 is even')
  expect(describe(7)).toBe('7 is odd')
}
```

Notice that each branch can `return` straight away: once a function returns, nothing after it
runs.

## One equals sign, or two?

`=` stores a value; `==` asks a question. Typing one when you meant the other is perhaps the
most famous mistake in programming. Try it: in `describe`, change `n % 2 == 0` to `n % 2 = 0`.
The example stops with an error before anything runs, because "store 0 in `n % 2`" makes no
sense: `n % 2` is a calculation, not a name.

The mistake is sneakier when the left side **is** a name. First, one new fact: when `if` is
given something other than `true` or `false`, it decides for itself. `0`, `''` (empty text),
`null` and `undefined` count as false; every other value counts as true.

Now, `if (n = 0)` is legal. It stores 0 in `n`, then treats that 0 as the answer to the
question, and 0 counts as false, so the block never runs, whatever `n` was. TJS does not warn
about this one:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function isZero(n: 0) {
  if (n = 0) {
    return 'zero'
  }
  return 'not zero'
}

preview.append(`isZero(0) says: ${isZero(0)}`)

test 'isZero' {
  expect(isZero(5)).toBe('not zero')
}
```

It says `not zero` for 0, and its one test passes, because that test only asks about the
"not zero" branch. Add a test for the other branch, `expect(isZero(0)).toBe('zero')`, and it
turns red. Put the second `=` back, `if (n == 0)`, and both pass.

Your tests are what catch this mistake, which is why the tests in this book check both
branches of every decision: a decision that always goes the same way passes half its tests,
and the other half tell you something is wrong.

## `else if`: more than two choices

Chain `else if` to test one condition after another. The first one that is true wins, and the
rest are skipped:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function grade(score: 0) {
  if (score >= 90) {
    return 'A'
  } else if (score >= 80) {
    return 'B'
  } else if (score >= 70) {
    return 'C'
  } else {
    return 'keep practising'
  }
}

preview.append(`85 earns ${grade(85)}`)

test 'grades' {
  expect(grade(95)).toBe('A')
  expect(grade(85)).toBe('B')
  expect(grade(70)).toBe('C')
  expect(grade(10)).toBe('keep practising')
}
```

The order matters. 95 is also at least 80, but the `score >= 90` test comes first, so it wins.
Try swapping the numbers in the first two questions, so the first reads `if (score >= 80)` and
the second `else if (score >= 90)`, and see which expectation fails, and why.

Read the chain as a series of narrowing questions. By the time the program asks
`score >= 80`, it already knows the score is **not** 90 or more, so that branch means "80 to
89". Each `else if` only has to rule out what is left. And the final `else` catches
everything nothing else did, so `grade` always gives back an answer.

## Combining conditions

Three symbols build bigger conditions out of smaller ones. Read them aloud as words:

- `&&` means **and**: both must be true.
- `||` means **or**: at least one must be true.
- `!` means **not**: it turns true into false and false into true.

You have already met `!` in `!=`, "not equal". On most keyboards `|` is Shift plus the
backslash key, `\`.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function canRide(age: 0, height: 0) {
  return age >= 8 && height >= 120
}

preview.append(`An 8-year-old who is 130cm tall can ride: ${canRide(8, 130)}`)

test 'old enough AND tall enough' {
  expect(canRide(8, 130)).toBe(true)
  expect(canRide(8, 100)).toBe(false)
  expect(canRide(6, 130)).toBe(false)
}
```

Notice that `canRide` has no `if` at all. `age >= 8 && height >= 120` already **is** `true` or
`false`, so the function can return it directly. Writing
`if (condition) { return true } else { return false }` is a long way to say `return condition`.

`||` and `!` work the same way:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function isWeekend(day: 'monday') {
  return day == 'saturday' || day == 'sunday'
}

function isWorkday(day: 'monday') {
  return !isWeekend(day)
}

preview.append(`Is Sunday a workday? ${isWorkday('sunday')}`)

test 'or, and not' {
  expect(isWeekend('saturday')).toBe(true)
  expect(isWeekend('sunday')).toBe(true)
  expect(isWeekend('tuesday')).toBe(false)
  expect(isWorkday('tuesday')).toBe(true)
}
```

A common slip is to write `day == 'saturday' || 'sunday'`, the way you would say it aloud.
It does not do what it says. For `'tuesday'` the answer is not `false` but the text `'sunday'`,
and text that is not empty counts as true, so `if (isWeekend(day))` would treat every day as a
weekend. Each side of `||` has to be a whole question, so the comparison must be written out
twice. Try the slip in `isWeekend` and watch the test go red: even `isWeekend('sunday')` now
gives back the text `'sunday'` rather than `true`.

## Choosing between two values

When a decision only picks one of two values, there is a shorter form:
`condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`. It reads "if the condition is true, this, otherwise
that". Before the `?` is the question; between `?` and `:` is the value to use when the answer
is true; after the `:` is the value to use when it is false.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function fruit(count: 0) {
  return `${count} ${count == 1 ? 'apple' : 'apples'}`
}

const apples = 1

preview.append(`You have ${fruit(apples)}.`)

test 'one apple, many apples' {
  expect(fruit(1)).toBe('1 apple')
  expect(fruit(3)).toBe('3 apples')
  expect(fruit(0)).toBe('0 apples')
}
```

Change `apples` to `0`, then `3`. The whole `count == 1 ? 'apple' : 'apples'` is a value, which
is why it can sit inside `${ }` in a template string, where an `if` cannot. Written with `if`,
the same function needs a name to store the word in first:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function fruitWithIf(count: 0) {
  let word = 'apples'
  if (count == 1) {
    word = 'apple'
  }
  return `${count} ${word}`
}

preview.append(`You have ${fruitWithIf(3)}.`)

test 'the same answers as fruit' {
  expect(fruitWithIf(1)).toBe('1 apple')
  expect(fruitWithIf(3)).toBe('3 apples')
}
```

Use `? :` for small choices like a label or a word. When either choice takes more than a line,
or when the choice is to do something rather than to pick a value, `if` and `else` are easier
to read. Programmers call `? :` the **conditional operator**, or the **ternary** operator
because it has three parts.

## `given`: choosing by value

When the decision is "which of these values is it?", a chain of `else if`s gets long. `given`
lists the values instead. Each **arm** names one or more values, then the block to run:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function kindOfDay(day: 'monday') {
  given day {
    'saturday', 'sunday' {
      return 'weekend'
    }
    'friday' {
      return 'almost the weekend'
    }
  } else {
    return 'a working day'
  }
}

preview.append(`Friday is ${kindOfDay('friday')}.`)

test 'days of the week' {
  expect(kindOfDay('sunday')).toBe('weekend')
  expect(kindOfDay('friday')).toBe('almost the weekend')
  expect(kindOfDay('tuesday')).toBe('a working day')
}
```

Exactly one block runs: the one whose value matches, or the `else` block when none does. The
`else` comes after the closing brace of the whole `given`, the same way it follows the closing
brace of an `if`. It is optional; without it, a value that matches nothing runs no block at all.

Values are compared the way `==` compares them, so `'Friday'` with a capital F does not match
`'friday'`, and `given` works on numbers as well as words:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function howMany(n: 0) {
  given n {
    1, 2, 3 {
      return 'a few'
    }
  } else {
    return 'more than a few'
  }
}

preview.append(`2 is ${howMany(2)}.`)

test 'numbers work too' {
  expect(howMany(2)).toBe('a few')
  expect(howMany(7)).toBe('more than a few')
}
```

`given` is how TJS does what JavaScript and TypeScript do with `switch` and `case`, and it
does what you almost always want. In a `switch`, forgetting one word, `break`, makes the next
choice run as well; a `given` arm cannot run into the next one.

> **If you already know JavaScript:** `switch` still works in a `.tjs` file, with exactly
> JavaScript's semantics. Cases fall through unless you write `break`, they share one scope,
> and they compare with `===`. TJS leaves it alone so that JavaScript you paste in still means
> what it meant, and warns at each `switch`, pointing at `given`. A `given` arm never falls
> through, each arm has its own scope, and one arm can list several values, which is the
> legitimate use of fallthrough in a `switch`.

Why TJS added a new word rather than quietly changing what `switch` does is a story of its
own: testing showed that a new keyword, carefully explained, surprised people less. See
[Case study: fixing switch](/case-study-switch/).

## Try it

A cinema charges children (under 12) 5, seniors (65 and over) 6, and everyone else 10. Write
`ticketPrice(age: 0)` and test all three prices, plus the edges: an 11-year-old, a
12-year-old, a 64-year-old and a 65-year-old. Edges are where decisions go wrong, so they are
where tests earn their keep.

Then:

1. Add a rule: on Tuesdays everyone pays 4. Give `ticketPrice` a second parameter,
   `day: 'monday'` (`'monday'` is only the example value: any day's name will do), and decide
   which check should come first. Test a Tuesday child and a Tuesday senior.
2. Write `bigger(a: 0.0, b: 0.0)` that gives back whichever number is larger, using `? :`.
   What should it give back when they are equal? Test that case too.
3. Use `given` to write `vowel(letter: 'a')` that is `true` for `'a'`, `'e'`, `'i'`, `'o'` and
   `'u'`, and `false` for anything else. Each arm, and the `else`, needs its own `return`.

Work them here:


# Dictionary Defaults

In a `.tjs` file, an object literal used as a parameter default is a **dictionary**: each
member is its own default, and a caller who passes part of the object gets the rest filled
in.

```tjs:inline
function place(args = { x: 0, y: 0 }) {
  return args
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(place()))             // {"x":0,"y":0}
console.log(JSON.stringify(place({ x: 5 })))     // {"x":5,"y":0}
console.log(JSON.stringify(place({ y: 7 })))     // {"y":7,"x":0}
console.log(place({ x: 'five' }).message)
// Expected integer for '…place.args.x', got string
```

The result keeps the caller's keys in the caller's order and appends the filled-in
defaults after them, which is why `{ y: 7 }` comes back as `{"y":7,"x":0}`. Order carries
no meaning. The last call shows a failed check: `x: 0` declares an integer, so `'five'` is
refused, and the call returns an error object instead of running the body. (The `…` stands
for the file and line, which the real message starts with.)

In JavaScript the same signature is all or nothing: `place({ x: 5 })` returns `{ x: 5 }`
and `y` is `undefined`. This chapter is the reference for the TJS rule. For a guided tour
with tests, see the [Dictionary Defaults example](/dictionary-defaults-example/).

## Why

Options objects are everywhere in JavaScript, and nobody who passes `{ x: 5 }` means "and
throw away every other default". So every options function merges by hand, and the
hand-written merges are where the bugs are:

- `Object.assign(defaults, payload)` writes into the shared defaults object, so one call
  changes the defaults for every later call.
- `{ ...defaults, ...payload }` merges one level. A nested default disappears as soon as
  the caller passes part of the nested object.
- Destructuring with defaults works, but moves the shape, the types and the defaults out of
  the signature and into the body.

The web platform already does it the other way. `addEventListener(type, fn, { once: true })`
keeps the defaults for `capture` and `passive`; `fetch(url, { method: 'POST' })` keeps every
other option. Those options objects are WebIDL _dictionaries_, and their members default
individually. TJS gives your own functions the same behaviour, with no new syntax: the
declaration `args = { x: 0, y: 0 }` already says which members exist, what type each has,
and what each defaults to.

## The rule

A parameter declared `name = { … }` with an object literal:

1. **Fills absent members** from the default, recursively through nested objects.
2. **Checks present members** against the default, which is also an example of the
   member's type. `x: 0` means "an integer, defaulting to 0"; write `ratio: 1.0` for a
   member that takes any number. The default is read the way any
   [parameter example](/TJS-SYNTAX/#parameters) is.
3. **Keeps keys the default does not mention.**
4. **Rejects `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype`** as keys.
5. **The merge never writes into the caller's object.** A complete argument is passed to
   the function as is; a partial one produces a new object. Your function body can still
   change a complete argument, as in JavaScript (see
   [A complete argument is passed as is](#a-complete-argument-is-passed-as-is)).

A failed check is not thrown. The function body does not run, and the call returns a
`MonadicError` whose message names the member (`place.args.x`). Test for one with
`isMonadicError(result)`, which every `.tjs` file can call without an import; see
[Errors](/TJS-SYNTAX/#errors). The rest of this chapter covers each rule and its edge
cases.

It works on any function form: declarations, arrow functions and class methods.

## When a default is used

| The caller passes                  | The member gets                                  |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| nothing, or `undefined`, for the whole argument | a fresh copy of the whole default   |
| an object without the key          | the member's default                             |
| the key with the value `undefined` | the member's default                             |
| the key with the value `null`      | an error, unless the member's default is `null` or `undefined` |
| the key with any other value       | that value, checked against the default's type   |
| `null`, or any non-object (a number, a string, an array), for the whole argument | an error at the parameter: `null` is a value, not an absence |

Falsy values count as values: `0`, `''` and `false` win over the default. `null` is never
quietly replaced by a default, because doing so would hide a caller's bug.

A member whose default is `null` or `undefined` accepts **any** value. That is how you
declare an option with no natural default:

```tjs:inline
function open(opts = { parent: null, storage: undefined, retries: 3 }) {
  return opts
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(open()))                    // {"parent":null,"retries":3}
console.log(JSON.stringify(open({ parent: 'root' })))  // {"parent":"root","retries":3}
console.log(open({ storage: new Map() }).storage.size) // 0: any value is accepted
console.log(JSON.stringify(open({ retries: 0 })))      // {"retries":0,"parent":null}
console.log(open(null).message)
// Expected object for '…open.opts', got null
```

(`storage` is missing from the `JSON.stringify` output only because `JSON.stringify` omits
`undefined` members.)

## Nested objects merge too

A nested object literal in the default is a dictionary in its own right. A caller who
passes part of it gets the rest of it filled in, and its members are checked:

```tjs:inline
function move(args = { pos: { x: 0, y: 0 }, label: '' }) {
  return args
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(move({ pos: { x: 5 } })))
// {"pos":{"x":5,"y":0},"label":""}

console.log(move({ pos: { x: 'five' } }).message)
// Expected integer for '…move.args.pos.x', got string
console.log(move({ pos: null }).message)
// Expected object for '…move.args.pos', got null

// Filled-in defaults are fresh on every call: changing one cannot change the next.
const first = move({ label: 'a' })
first.pos.x = 999
console.log(move({ label: 'b' }).pos.x)             // 0
```

## Arrays are values

An array in the default is replaced wholesale, never merged index by index. Its elements
are checked against the default's first element, the same way an [array example](/TJS-SYNTAX/)
is checked anywhere else:

```tjs:inline
function tag(args = { tags: [''], n: 0 }) {
  return args
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(tag({ n: 1 })))                // {"n":1,"tags":[""]}
console.log(JSON.stringify(tag({ tags: ['a', 'b'] })))    // {"tags":["a","b"],"n":0}
console.log(isMonadicError(tag({ tags: ['ok', 42] })))    // true: 42 is not a string
```

An empty array default (`tags: []`) has no element to check against, so it accepts an
array of anything. Give it an example element, as `['']` above, to check the elements.

Because arrays are not merged, an object inside an array is not filled in either. With a
default of `{ points: [{ x: 0, y: 0 }] }`, every point a caller passes must have both `x`
and `y`. The error for a point that lacks one names only the array, and currently reads
`Expected array of object for '…points', got array of object`.

## Excess keys pass through

A key the default does not declare is kept, unchecked, in the result:

```tjs:inline
function sized(opts = { w: 100, h: 100 }) {
  return opts
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(sized({ w: 5, color: 'red' })))
// {"w":5,"color":"red","h":100}
```

That has one cost: a misspelled option is accepted silently. `sized({ widht: 5 })` keeps
`w: 100` and carries `widht` along, and nothing fails at runtime. The linter's
`dict-default-excess-key` rule catches it when the misspelled key is in an object literal
written at a call to a function declared in the same file:

```javascript
import { lint } from 'tjs-lang/lang'

const source = `
function sized(opts = { w: 100, h: 100 }) { return opts }
sized({ widht: 5 })
`
for (const d of lint(source).diagnostics) console.log(d.rule, d.message)
// dict-default-excess-key 'widht' is not a member of sized's dictionary parameter — check
// the spelling (it is passed through, so it will have no effect)
```

A payload built elsewhere and passed in a variable, or one containing a spread, is not
checked. `tjs check` runs the rule (a warning, an error under `TjsStrict`); from code, call
`lint` from `tjs-lang/lang`.

> **Where TJS diverges from WebIDL**
>
> | | WebIDL dictionary | TJS dictionary default |
> | --- | --- | --- |
> | Excess keys in the payload | **stripped** | **passed through** |
> | Missing members | filled from the default | filled from the default |
> | Wrong member type | rejected | rejected |
> | `__proto__` / `constructor` / `prototype` | n/a | rejected |
>
> **Why WebIDL strips, and TJS does not.** A WebIDL dictionary is a wire format: its job is
> to turn an untrusted bag into exactly the declared shape before it crosses into browser
> internals, so anything undeclared is noise. A TJS `= { … }` parameter is an options
> object inside one program, and those routinely carry more than the callee declares: a
> caller forwards its own options, one object goes to two functions, a component spreads
> its props. Deleting the caller's data there is not normalisation, it is loss.
>
> Two more reasons. **Nothing else in TJS removes or rejects an excess key**: shape checks
> on `:` parameters and `Type` checks both accept them (see [Type identity](/type-identity/)).
> And **TypeScript cannot express a closed type**: its excess-property check applies only
> to a fresh object literal, and there is no `Exact<T>`, so a stricter runtime rule would
> be one TypeScript users could not reason about. (TJS 0.12 did strip excess keys; the
> [CHANGELOG](/CHANGELOG/) entry for 0.13.0 records the reversal.)
>
> A dictionary default is therefore not a sanitiser. If you need exactly the declared
> keys, strip them yourself: `const clean = ({ x, y }) => ({ x, y })`. Untrusted data
> belongs in an [AJS](/DOCS-AJS/) sandbox, not behind a parameter default.

## Prototype keys are rejected

`__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` are refused as keys at every level, because a
merge is exactly where prototype pollution happens. The payload below is what an attacker
gets from `JSON.parse`, which creates `__proto__` as an ordinary own key:

```tjs:inline
function place(args = { x: 0, y: 0 }) {
  return args
}

const hostile = JSON.parse('{"x":1,"__proto__":{"polluted":true}}')
console.log(isMonadicError(place(hostile)))   // true
console.log({}.polluted)                      // undefined
```

## Defaults must be literals

Every member of the default must be a literal: a number literal (a negative one such as
`-1` is fine), a quoted string, `true`, `false`, `null`, `undefined`, or an array or object
literal made of those. A function call, a variable, `new`, a template literal or a getter
is a compile error. So are `NaN` and `Infinity`, which are variables in JavaScript, not
literals:

```text
function stamp(opts = { at: Date.now(), by: '' }) { … }

Dictionary default for '…stamp.opts.at' must be a pure literal — member 'at' is not a
clonable literal value. Compute impure values inside the function body, or use a
colon-form (required) parameter. For JavaScript's atomic default, wrap it in
LegacyDefault(…).
```

(The colon form is described below, under "`=`, `:` and a typed default".)

The reason is how the merge is built. The transpiler writes the merge code for each
signature when it compiles the file, with the default's values copied into that code as
literals. There is nowhere in that code for a value that has to be computed on each call,
so the compiler refuses one rather than computing it at the wrong time.

Two cases are not caught yet, and give a wrong default instead of an error: a computed key
(`{ [k]: 1 }` uses the name `k` as the key) and a call inside an array member
(`{ at: [tick()] }` fills `[null]`). Do not write either.

To compute a value on each call, give the member the default `undefined`, which accepts
any value, and fill it in the body:

```tjs:inline
let counter = 0

function nextId(opts = { id: undefined, prefix: 'id' }) {
  const id = opts.id ?? ++counter    // computed in the body, on each call
  return `${opts.prefix}-${id}`
}

console.log(nextId(), nextId(), nextId({ id: 0 }))   // id-1 id-2 id-0
```

## A complete argument is passed as is

When the caller's object already has every declared member, and every member checks, the
function receives **that object**: no copy is made, so supplying everything costs nothing
beyond the check. Extra keys do not change this. The same goes for a nested object: in
`move({ pos: { x: 1, y: 2 } })` the result's `pos` is the caller's `pos` object, even
though the outer object is new. When members are missing, the function receives a new object, and the
caller's object is left alone:

```tjs:inline
function sized(opts = { w: 100, h: 100 }) {
  return opts
}

const full = { w: 1, h: 2 }
console.log(sized(full) === full)    // true: the same object

const part = Object.freeze({ w: 1 })
const merged = sized(part)
console.log(merged === part)         // false: a new object
console.log(JSON.stringify(part))    // {"w":1}: the caller's object is unchanged
```

The frozen object shows the merge never writes into what it was given. One consequence of
the identity rule: if your function changes `opts`, it changes the caller's object when the
caller passed a complete one, as in plain JavaScript. Copy first if you need to modify it.

## `=`, `:` and a typed default

Three signatures put an object in a parameter, and only the first is a dictionary. The
third gives a parameter both a type and a default (`name: Type = value`); here `Point` is
declared as `Type Point { example: { x: 0, y: 0 } }`.

| Declaration                   | The argument  | Its members                                       |
| ----------------------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `opts = { retries: 3 }`       | optional      | each optional, filled from the default, checked   |
| `opts: { retries: 3 }`        | required      | each required and checked                         |
| `p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2 }`   | optional      | if passed, must be a whole `Point`; not merged    |

"Each required and checked" means the object must have every listed member, each of the
listed type.

The [example chapter](/dictionary-defaults-example/) runs all three side by side.

There is no marker for "a required member inside a dictionary": if the caller must supply
it, it is not a default. Put required values in their own parameters, before the options,
the way `addEventListener(type, listener, options)` does:

```tjs:inline
function connect(url: 'https://example.com', opts = { retries: 3, timeout: 1000.0 }) {
  return `${url} retries=${opts.retries} timeout=${opts.timeout}`
}

console.log(connect('https://a.dev', { timeout: 250.5 }))
// https://a.dev retries=3 timeout=250.5
console.log(isMonadicError(connect()))   // true: url is required
```

## Only object-literal defaults

The rule applies only when the default is an object literal written in the signature.
Every other default keeps JavaScript's meaning:

```tjs:inline
function f(x = 0, list = []) {
  return JSON.stringify({ x, list })
}

console.log(f())          // {"x":0,"list":[]}
console.log(f(5, [1]))    // {"x":5,"list":[1]}
```

A default that names a variable (`opts = shared`) is not an object literal either, so it is
not a dictionary: a caller's object replaces it whole.

Nor is a destructured parameter. `function d({ a, b } = { a: 1, b: 2 })` keeps
JavaScript's all-or-nothing default, so `d({ a: 5 })` sees `b` as `undefined`. For
per-member defaults, declare `opts = { a: 1, b: 2 }` and destructure in the body.

## Opting out: `LegacyDefault` and `!`

To keep JavaScript's all-or-nothing default for one parameter, wrap the literal in
`LegacyDefault`. A `!` at the start of the parameter list turns validation off for the
whole function (see [Safety markers](/TJS-SYNTAX/#safety-markers)); such a function also
keeps JavaScript's default, along with skipping every other check:

```tjs:inline
function legacy(opts = LegacyDefault({ x: 0, y: 0 })) {
  return JSON.stringify(opts)
}

function fast(! opts = { x: 0, y: 0 }) {
  return JSON.stringify(opts)
}

console.log(legacy({ x: 5 }))     // {"x":5}: replaced, not merged
console.log(fast({ x: 5 }))       // {"x":5}
console.log(fast({ x: 'five' }))  // {"x":"five"}: nothing is checked
```

`LegacyDefault` is one of TJS's [named escapes](/TJS-SYNTAX/#named-escapes): each brings
back one JavaScript behaviour at one site, under a long name that is easy to find in
review.

## Which files get dictionary defaults

Dictionary defaults are a rule of native TJS. They are on in every `.tjs` file, and off
wherever the same source must keep its JavaScript meaning:

| Source                                         | Object-literal default        |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| a `.tjs` file                                  | dictionary                    |
| a `.js` file, or `tjs(src, { dialect: 'js' })` | JavaScript's atomic default   |
| a `.tjs` file whose first line is the `TjsCompat` directive | JavaScript's atomic default |
| TypeScript converted with `fromTS` (or `tjs convert`) | JavaScript's atomic default, written as `LegacyDefault({ … })` |
| converted TypeScript marked with the comment `/* @tjs TjsStrict */` | dictionary  |

`TjsCompat` and `TjsStrict` are described under [TJS syntax](/TJS-SYNTAX/). Where the rule
is off, the literal-only restriction is off too: `args = { at: Date.now() }` is legal
JavaScript and stays legal. Converting TypeScript writes `LegacyDefault` explicitly,
so a converted file keeps its behaviour when it later becomes native `.tjs`.

The same characters mean something different in JavaScript and in TJS here, as they do for
`==` (which in TJS does not coerce types). That is allowed because choosing a `.tjs` file
is the opt-in; see [Principles](/PRINCIPLES/).

## What TypeScript callers see

The generated `.d.ts` describes what a caller may pass, so a dictionary-default parameter
is **deep-partial**: the parameter and every member are optional, recursively. Arrays are
not made partial, since they are replaced whole.

```tjs:static
export function place(args = { pos: { x: 0, y: 0 }, label: '' }, tags = { list: [''] }) {
  return args
}
```

generates:

```ts
export declare function place(
  args?: { pos?: { x?: number; y?: number }; label?: string },
  tags?: { list?: string[] }
): any
```

Inside the function every member is present, because the merge has filled them.

## Implementation notes

The transpiler emits merge-and-check code specialised to each signature, with the
default's members inlined as fresh literals, so no shared template object exists to be
corrupted. Three invariants hold, and
[`src/lang/dict-defaults.test.ts`](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/blob/main/src/lang/dict-defaults.test.ts)
tests them: the merge never writes into the caller's object; no result shares a mutable
part with another call's result; a complete argument is returned by identity, with no
allocation. Measured when it shipped, a complete argument took about 91 ns and a partial
one about 73 ns, against about 276 ns for a careful hand-written merge that does no
type checking.

The design history (the spikes, the benchmarks against hand-written merges, the staged
rollout and the resolved open questions) is in the
[previous version of this page](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/blob/47303274/docs/dictionary-defaults.md).
