# Playground Imports

The playground (https://tjs-platform.web.app) and the local dev server
both let you `import` external packages without a bundler or
`node_modules`. There's no setup — just write the import. This page
documents how it works and the CDN-hint syntax for power users.

## Quick reference

```javascript
// Plain bare import — JSDelivr `/+esm` by default (works for ESM-native
// and CJS packages alike; deps bundled inline)
import { tosi, elements } from 'tosijs'
import { debounce } from 'lodash-es'
import { marked } from 'marked'

// Versioned: pin a specific release (or range)
import { tosi } from 'tosijs@1.6.1'
import { tosi } from 'tosijs@^1.6'

// Subpath into a package
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'
import { getAuth } from 'firebase/auth'

// Full URL — passes through unchanged. Useful for arbitrary hosts:
// your GitHub repo, a CodePen-style snippet, anything that serves ESM.
import { thing } from 'https://example.com/my-module.js'
import { x } from 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/user/repo/main/file.js'

// CDN hints (escape hatch when default routing picks the wrong CDN)
import { useState } from 'esmsh/react@18'
import { tosi } from 'jsdelivr/tosijs'
import { preact } from 'unpkg/preact'
import { whatever } from 'github/user/repo@v1.2/dist/index.js'
```

## How it works

1. **Source rewrite at transpile time** (`demo/src/imports.ts`): bare
   specifiers like `'tosijs'` get rewritten to `'/tfs/tosijs'`. Relative
   paths (`'./foo'`), absolute paths (`'/foo'`), and full URLs
   (`'https://...'`) are left alone.
2. **Service worker intercept** (`demo/src/tfs-worker.js`): the playground
   iframe is loaded from a same-origin `/iframe/<sessionId>` URL, so the
   TFS service worker controls all its fetches. When the iframe imports
   from `/tfs/<spec>`, the SW resolves it to a CDN URL, fetches the
   module, optionally rewrites the response body, and serves it back.
3. **Browser ESM loader** does the rest — follows imports, dedupes by
   URL, evaluates modules.

## Default CDN routing

By default, `/tfs/<spec>` resolves to JSDelivr's `/+esm` endpoint:

```
import 'tosijs'
  → /tfs/tosijs
  → https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/tosijs@latest/+esm
```

JSDelivr's `/+esm` returns a self-contained Rollup-bundled ESM module.
It works cleanly for ESM-native packages (tosijs, lodash-es) AND CJS
packages (most things), inlines `process` polyfills, and bundles
dependencies inline.

The bundle-inline behavior breaks one specific case: packages with peer
dependencies that need to be the SAME instance across modules. React is
the canonical example — react-dom and your code both need to use the
same React, or hooks crash (`Cannot read properties of null (reading
'useState')`). For these, the SW has a small allowlist that routes
through esm.sh instead, which dedupes by URL.

Current allowlist: `react`, `react-dom`. Easy to extend in the SW source.

## CDN hints

When you want to override the default routing, prefix the spec with a
CDN name. The first path segment is treated as the hint:

| Hint                                | Resolves to                                    | Use when                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `jsdelivr/<spec>`                   | `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/<spec>/+esm`     | Force JSDelivr (e.g. for a peer-dep package not on the allowlist)             |
| `esmsh/<spec>`                      | `https://esm.sh/<spec>`                        | Force esm.sh (e.g. for a different React-like package needing peer-dep dedup) |
| `unpkg/<spec>`                      | `https://unpkg.com/<spec>?module`              | UNPKG, returns ESM via `?module`                                              |
| `github/<user>/<repo>[@ref]/<path>` | `https://esm.sh/gh/<user>/<repo>[@ref]/<path>` | Load directly from a GitHub repo (esm.sh handles fetching + transformation)   |

The hint name occupies what would normally be the package name slot, so
named imports work normally:

```javascript
import { tosi, elements } from 'jsdelivr/tosijs@1.6.1'
import { useState } from 'esmsh/react'
```

Why `esmsh` and not `esm`: `esm` is a popular npm package (the legacy
ESM loader for Node), and we don't want to clash with `import 'esm'`.
`jsdelivr`, `unpkg`, and `github` aren't taken as bare top-level npm
packages.

## Full URLs

Anything starting with `http://` or `https://` passes through the
rewriter unchanged. Use this for one-off cases:

```javascript
// Your own deployed module
import { thing } from 'https://my.com/module.js'

// A GitHub raw URL (only works if the file is already valid ESM —
// raw GitHub doesn't transform CJS or resolve bare specifiers; for
// that use the `github/` hint, which routes through esm.sh)
import { x } from 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/me/repo/main/dist/index.mjs'

// Any other CDN
import { y } from 'https://cdn.example.com/foo@1.0.0/+esm'
```

## What lives where

- **`demo/src/imports.ts`** — `rewriteImports()` (rewrites at transpile
  time) and `registerIframeContent()` (postMessage handshake)
- **`demo/src/tfs-worker.js`** — the service worker: serves the iframe
  HTML at `/iframe/<id>`, proxies `/tfs/<spec>` to the appropriate CDN,
  rewrites response bodies for esm.sh dedup
- **`demo/src/tjs-playground.ts`** / **`demo/src/ts-playground.ts`** —
  generate `iframeDoc`, register it with the SW, set `iframe.src`

## Future: virtual modules

The SW architecture is set up to also serve user-saved modules at
`/vmod/<path>` (or similar). This will let you "save" a snippet to a
virtual endpoint and `import` from it elsewhere — the b8rjs pattern.
Tracked in `TODO.md` under playground IDE features.

## Cache and debugging

- **Status**: GET `/tfs/__status` (in a new tab) — returns JSON with the
  SW version, the CDN routing config, the cached URLs, and the active
  iframe sessions
- **Clear**: GET `/tfs/__clear` — drops the cached responses

The SW caches CDN responses in a named `Cache` (`tfs-v4-mixed-cdn`).
Bumping `SW_VERSION` in `tfs-worker.js` automatically clears old caches
on activate.

# The universal endpoint: isomorphic atoms, one security model

The AJS VM was built to run untrusted agent code safely: fuel-metered, capability-sandboxed,
with errors as values instead of exceptions. Running the same program in a browser and on a
server was never a goal. It falls out of the design anyway, and it gives an application
something that is hard to get any other way: one agent program, one set of tools, and one set
of authorization rules, running unchanged on both sides.

This chapter assumes you know how to define an atom and inject a capability. Both are covered
in [Hosting the VM](/ajs-host/) and [Capabilities and Custom Atoms](/ajs-capabilities/).

## The pattern

An **agent endpoint** is an `AgentVM` plus the atoms agents run against. A **universal**
endpoint is a pair of them, one in the web client and one in the data center, whose atoms have
the same names and the same input and output schemas: **isomorphic atoms**. Because the
contracts match, the same agent AST runs against either side.

The example below has one such pair, `getRecords`:

- **The client `getRecords`** looks in the records the page has already loaded. If they are
  all there, it returns them with no network request. If some are missing, it sends the server
  a small, fixed read agent for just those ids, and merges the reply.
- **The server `getRecords`** queries the datastore.

The agent calls `getRecords({ ids })` and does not know which implementation answered. The
local-first lookup and the fallback live in the atom, not in the program. Only the read crosses
the wire: the agent that called `getRecords` keeps running in the browser, and nothing it did
before or after the call runs again on the server. So any agent that reads records gets the
local-first behaviour, whatever else it does and whatever it returns.

What this buys:

1. **One security model.** The same capability, fuel and authorization rules run in the browser
   and on the server, because they are the same code. The server's copy is what enforces; the
   client's copy keeps the page consistent with it (see [One rule set, two
   places](#one-rule-set-two-places)).
2. **Data locality.** Reads that hit data the client already holds never leave the browser;
   only real misses reach the server.
3. **The same toolset on both sides.** An orchestration can run partly local and partly remote
   without being rewritten per environment.

## A working pair

Both sides are below in one file, so you can run it with Bun. The client's `fetch` capability
calls the server's handler in-process; in a browser it would be a wrapper around `window.fetch`
and the handler would sit behind a real route.

```javascript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM, defineAtom } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'
import { s } from 'tjs-lang/schema'
import { buildRuleContext, evaluateAccessShortcut } from 'tjs-lang/rbac'

// ---- Shared by both sides ----------------------------------------------
const In = s.object({ ids: s.array(s.string) })
const Out = s.array(s.object({ id: s.string, title: s.string }))

// One authorization rule, imported by the client and the server alike.
function canRead(user, doc) {
  const context = buildRuleContext({
    uid: user.uid,
    roles: user.roles,
    method: 'read',
    collection: 'notes',
    docId: doc.id,
    doc,
  })
  // 'owner:ownerId' allows when doc.ownerId equals the user's uid.
  return evaluateAccessShortcut('owner:ownerId', context).allowed
}

// Records as the agent sees them: no ownerId.
const view = ({ id, title }) => ({ id, title })

// ---- Server --------------------------------------------------------------
const datastore = new Map([
  ['n1', { id: 'n1', title: 'Shopping', ownerId: 'ada' }],
  ['n2', { id: 'n2', title: 'Talk notes', ownerId: 'ada' }],
  ['n3', { id: 'n3', title: 'Diary', ownerId: 'grace' }],
])

const serverVM = new AgentVM({
  getRecords: defineAtom('getRecords', In, Out, async ({ ids }, ctx) => {
    const { user } = ctx.capabilities // set by the host, invisible to the agent
    return ids
      .map((id) => datastore.get(id))
      .filter((doc) => doc && canRead(user, doc))
      .map(view)
  }),
})

// The read agent the client sends on a miss. It does one thing, so a miss
// re-runs only the read on the server, never the agent that asked for it.
const readAgent = transpile(
  `function read({ ids = ['n1'] }) {
    let records = getRecords({ ids })
    return { records }
  }`,
  { atoms: serverVM.atoms }
).ast

// POST /agent. `user` comes from the request's session, never from the body.
async function agentEndpoint(request, user) {
  const { ast, args } = await request.json()
  const run = await serverVM.run(ast, args, {
    fuel: 100,
    timeoutMs: 1000,
    capabilities: { user },
  })
  return Response.json(run.error ? { error: run.error.message } : run.result)
}

// ---- Client --------------------------------------------------------------
const user = { uid: 'ada', roles: ['user'] } // the signed-in user
const loaded = new Map([['n1', datastore.get('n1')]]) // already in the page

const clientVM = new AgentVM({
  getRecords: defineAtom('getRecords', In, Out, async ({ ids }, ctx) => {
    const found = new Map()
    for (const id of ids) {
      const doc = loaded.get(id)
      // Loaded but not readable: dropped, as the server would drop it.
      if (doc && canRead(user, doc)) found.set(id, view(doc))
    }
    const missing = ids.filter((id) => !loaded.has(id))

    if (missing.length > 0) {
      const reply = await ctx.capabilities
        .fetch('/agent', {
          method: 'POST',
          body: JSON.stringify({ ast: readAgent, args: { ids: missing } }),
        })
        .then((response) => response.json()) // plain data, not the Response
      if (reply.error) throw new Error(reply.error)
      for (const record of reply.records) found.set(record.id, record)
    }

    // In the order asked for.
    return ids.filter((id) => found.has(id)).map((id) => found.get(id))
  }),
})

// Any agent that calls getRecords. This one does more than read.
const { ast } = transpile(
  `function summary({ ids = ['n1'] }) {
    let records = getRecords({ ids })
    return { count: records.length, records }
  }`,
  { atoms: clientVM.atoms }
)

// In the browser this is a wrapper around window.fetch. Here it calls the
// server in-process.
let requests = 0
const fetch = (url, init) => {
  requests++
  const request = new Request(new URL(url, 'https://app.example'), init)
  return agentEndpoint(request, user)
}

const run = (ids) =>
  clientVM.run(ast, { ids }, { fuel: 100, capabilities: { fetch } })

console.log((await run(['n1'])).result)
// { count: 1, records: [ { id: 'n1', title: 'Shopping' } ] }
console.log(requests) // 0: n1 was already in the page

console.log((await run(['n3', 'n2', 'n1'])).result)
// { count: 2, records: [ { id: 'n2', title: 'Talk notes' }, { id: 'n1', title: 'Shopping' } ] }
console.log(requests) // 1: n2 and n3 in one request; n3 is grace's, so it never comes back
```

If the server refuses (here, if its run ran out of fuel), the client atom throws. A thrown
error in an atom is an ordinary failure, not the end of the run: the agent can catch it with
`try`/`catch` (the catch binding is the error's message), and if it does not, the run stops
with `run.error`, an `AgentError` whose `message` is the thrown one (`'Out of Fuel'` in that
case) and whose `op` is `'getRecords'`.

### What carries the safety

**The server treats the agent as untrusted.** It sets its own fuel and timeout, it decides which
atoms exist, and it takes the user from the request's session, not from anything in the body.
The client sends the read agent, but nothing stops a hostile client sending any AST it likes, so
the server cannot rely on that. A hostile AST can ask for any ids; the server atom answers only
for records the user may read, which is why `n3` never comes back. Besides `getRecords`, the
server VM has the built-in core atoms, and the ones that touch the world need a capability the
server does not pass: with no `fetch` capability and no `allowedFetchDomains`, `httpFetch`
fetches nothing, there is no `llm`, and the store atoms see only an in-memory store that belongs
to that one run. What remains is pure computation, bounded by fuel and the timeout. For a public
route, also cap atom calls with `quotas` and the size of what crosses the boundary with
`argsMaxBytes` and `membraneMaxBytes` ([Hosting the VM](/ajs-host/)).

**The AST is the wire format.** The client never sends source; the server receives an AST and
runs it on `tjs-lang/vm-ast`, which contains no parser. A server that accepts agents from clients
should never parse their source, for the reasons in [Hosting the VM](/ajs-host/). The read agent
is transpiled against `serverVM.atoms`, and the calling agent against `clientVM.atoms`; either
check is valid on the other side because the two `getRecords` atoms declare the same schemas.

**The user reaches the atom through capabilities.** `ctx.capabilities` is the host's object as
passed to `run()`; the agent cannot read it. Putting per-request identity there keeps it out of
the agent's reach while letting every server atom see it.

**Both atoms are behind the membrane.** Neither `defineAtom` call passes `effects`, and for an
atom you define the default is `'io'`. That puts every call through the capability boundary: the
input reaches the atom as a copy checked against `In`, and the atom's return is copied back as
plain data, checked against `Out`. The agent cannot hand the atom anything but `{ ids: [...] }`,
and the atom cannot hand the agent a live host object. `Out` is also why `view` is there and not
cosmetic: it admits only `id` and `title`, so an atom that returned the raw record would fail
with `Output validation failed for 'getRecords'` rather than leak `ownerId` to the agent. Do not
mark either atom `'pure'`; they read host state.

**The client atom returns data, not a `Response`.** The membrane admits JSON data plus `Date`.
An atom that returned `ctx.capabilities.fetch(...)` directly would hand back a `Response`, which
is a class instance: the boundary refuses it, and because JSON could not have produced that
value, the refusal ends the run rather than becoming a catchable error. Read the body
(`.then((response) => response.json())`) and return that.

**The client atom calls `fetch` itself, so `httpFetch`'s checks do not apply.** The allowlist,
method and header checks and the `X-Agent-Depth` header belong to the built-in `httpFetch`
atom; an atom you write that calls the `fetch` capability directly gets none of them. Give the
client atom a `fetch` capability scoped to the endpoint. This pair cannot loop, because the
server passes no `fetch` capability at all; a server whose atoms make further agent calls should
read the incoming `X-Agent-Depth` header and pass it back in as `context.requestDepth` (see [AJS
Patterns](/patterns/)).

## Why it falls out of the architecture

Three properties make this work, and none was added for it. They are there for sandboxed
execution.

**Code is data.** An agent compiles to a JSON AST (`transpile()`), not to JavaScript. The same
AST runs anywhere an `AgentVM` exists: a Node or Bun server, a cloud function, a browser tab.
AJS's motto, "code travels to data", becomes a deployment option.

**All IO is injected.** An `AgentVM` has no IO of its own. Every effect on the world arrives
through `ctx.capabilities` (`fetch`, `store`, `llm`, and whatever else the host passes to
`run()`). The client passes browser capabilities, the server passes data-center capabilities,
and the program cannot tell the difference.

**Atoms are the seam.** `new AgentVM(customAtoms)` adds your atoms to the built-in ones every VM
has. The contract an agent compiles against is the atom's name and input schema
(`transpile(source, { atoms: vm.atoms })` checks every call against it); the implementation is
whatever the VM it runs on supplies. Give each side its own implementation of the same contract,
and the same AST runs on both.

## One rule set, two places

Usually the client and the server each implement data access and authorization, kept in step by
hand. The client cannot safely share the server's rules, so the server re-checks everything and
there are two security surfaces to maintain.

Here the rules are one piece of code. The example imports `buildRuleContext` and
`evaluateAccessShortcut` from `tjs-lang/rbac`, the published rule layer: pure functions with no
IO, so the same import works in the browser bundle and in the server. `buildRuleContext` turns
the user, the operation and the document into the context a rule reads (`_uid`, `_roles`,
`_method`, `_collection`, `doc`, …). `evaluateAccessShortcut` evaluates a rule written as a
string: `'owner:ownerId'` allows when the document's `ownerId` field equals the user's uid. The
other shortcuts are `'all'`, `'none'`, `'authenticated'`, `'admin'`, `'author'` and
`'role:<name>'`; they are documented in `src/rbac/rules.tjs`. A request denied in the page is
denied for the same reason it would be denied on the server, because it is the same rule running.

A rule that a shortcut cannot express can be an agent itself. Run it in the VM and pass its
result through `interpretRuleResult`, which turns the rule's `{ allow, reason }` into
`{ allowed, reason }` (an empty reason becomes `null`). It grants only a real boolean `true` or
`{ allow: true }`. Anything else denies, including a rule that ran out of fuel or returned a
truthy string:

```javascript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'
import { interpretRuleResult } from 'tjs-lang/rbac'

const { ast: rule } = transpile(`function published({ doc = { published: false } }) {
  if (doc.published) return { allow: true, reason: '' }
  return { allow: false, reason: 'not published' }
}`)

async function check(doc, fuel = 10) {
  const run = await new AgentVM().run(rule, { doc }, { fuel })
  return interpretRuleResult(run.result)
}

console.log(await check({ published: true })) // { allowed: true, reason: null }
console.log(await check({ published: false })) // { allowed: false, reason: 'not published' }
console.log(await check({ published: true }, 0.01)) // out of fuel:
// { allowed: false, reason: 'rule returned an object whose `allow` is not a boolean — denying' }
```

To use such a rule in the pair, have `canRead` call `check(doc)` and both `getRecords` atoms
await it. Ship the rule's AST to the client as data, in the bundle or from the server, rather
than its source, so both sides run the same AST. Running a rule inside an atom is a nested
`vm.run`: it has its own fuel and its own quota counter, separate from the agent's. To hold a
quota across both, pass the same `quotaUsed` object to each run ([Hosting the
VM](/ajs-host/)).

Be precise about what "one security model" means. The client's copy of a rule is not what
protects the data: a hostile client can skip it, or run without the page at all. What protects
the data is the server applying the same rule to every request it receives, as `getRecords`
does above. The client's copy means the page never shows or offers what the server would
refuse, and that the two can never disagree, because there is only one definition. Fuel
metering, the membrane and errors-as-values apply the same way in both runtimes.

## When to reach for it

- A rich client that already holds a working set of data, where most reads can be served
  locally and only misses need the server.
- A system where you want one authorization story, rather than a client SDK's rules and a
  server API's rules drifting apart.
- Agent or tool orchestration that should run wherever the data is cheapest to reach, without
  rewriting the program per environment.

It is not worth it when the client holds little of the data, so nearly every read is a miss
and the local lookup only adds work; or when the authorization a read needs is something only
the server can decide (it depends on data the client must not see), so the client's copy of the
rule cannot answer and the page cannot stay consistent with it.

## See also

- [Capabilities and Custom Atoms](/ajs-capabilities/): defining atoms, `effects`, and what may
  cross the capability boundary.
- [Hosting the VM](/ajs-host/): fuel, timeouts, the heap ceiling, quotas, and why the VM should
  receive ASTs rather than source.
- [AJS Patterns](/patterns/): why defences such as fetch allowlists and request depth belong in
  capabilities rather than agent code.
- [VM budgets](/vm-budgets/): how fuel and the heap ceiling stay true.
title: The universal endpoint: isomorphic atoms, one security model

# Things with Parts

A list keeps values in order. Often what you want instead is one thing with several named
parts: a person has a name and a birth year, a rectangle has a width and a height. In TJS that
is an **object**.

Why not just use lists? You could keep names in one list and birth years in another, and match
them up by position: the first name goes with the first year. It works until someone adds a
name and forgets the year, or sorts one list and not the other. Then every person after the
mistake has someone else's birthday, and nothing complains. An object keeps the parts of one
thing together, so they cannot drift apart.

## Making an object

An object is written in braces, as `name: value` pairs separated by commas. Each part is
called a **property**, and you read one with a dot:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
const ada = { name: 'Ada Lovelace', born: 1815 }

preview.append(`${ada.name} was born in ${ada.born}.`)

test 'reading properties' {
  expect(ada.name).toBe('Ada Lovelace')
  expect(ada.born).toBe(1815)
}
```

Ask the console for `ada.born + 36`, then for `ada.died` (type each at its prompt and press
Enter, as in the Lists chapter): an object with no `died` property
answers `undefined`, just as a list does past its end.

That `undefined` is worth a second look, because it is also what you get from a **typo**.
Write `ada.nmae` instead of `ada.name` and there is no error: the object has no part
called `nmae`, so the answer is `undefined`, and the page says "undefined was born in 1815".
Try it. Later in this chapter you will see how to make TJS check that the parts you need are
really there.

## Changing and adding parts

Assign to a property to change it: `counter.count = 5`. Assign to a property the object does
not have yet, and the object gains it.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
const counter = { label: 'clicks', count: 0 }
counter.count = counter.count + 1
counter.count = counter.count + 1
counter.colour = 'green'

preview.append(`${counter.label}: ${counter.count} (${counter.colour})`)

test 'parts can change, and new parts can be added' {
  expect(counter.count).toBe(2)
  expect(counter.colour).toBe('green')
}
```

`counter.colour = 'green'` adds a part that was not there before.

But isn't `counter` a `const`? It is, and `const` means the name `counter` always points at
the same object. Changing the object's parts is fine. Pointing the name at a different object
is not: add the line `counter = { label: 'taps' }` and the program stops with an error saying
`counter` is a constant. The section Same parts, different objects, below, comes back to what
"points at" means.

## Parts inside parts

A property can hold any value, including a list or another object. Chain the dots to reach
inside:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
const book = {
  title: 'Frankenstein',
  year: 1818,
  author: { name: 'Mary Shelley', born: 1797 },
  chapters: ['Letter 1', 'Letter 2', 'Letter 3'],
}

preview.append(
  `${book.title} was written by ${book.author.name}, ` +
    `aged ${book.year - book.author.born}. It opens with "${book.chapters[0]}".`
)

test 'reaching inside' {
  expect(book.author.name).toBe('Mary Shelley')
  expect(book.chapters.length).toBe(3)
}
```

Read `book.author.name` from left to right: take `book`, then its `author`, then that
author's `name`. Most real data is shaped like this: a thing, with parts, some of which have
parts of their own.

## Parts named by a value

The dot needs the property's name written out in the program. When the name is in a value
instead, use square brackets, as you would for a list:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function countWords(words: ['']) {
  const counts = {}
  for (const word of words) {
    if (counts[word] == undefined) {
      counts[word] = 0
    }
    counts[word] = counts[word] + 1
  }
  return counts
}

const tally = countWords(['the', 'cat', 'saw', 'the', 'other', 'cat'])

preview.append(`"the" appears ${tally.the} times, "cat" ${tally['cat']} times.`)

test 'counting words' {
  expect(tally['the']).toBe(2)
  expect(tally.saw).toBe(1)
  expect(tally.dog).toBe(undefined)
}
```

An empty pair of braces, `{}`, is an object with no parts yet. `counts[word]` means "the
part of `counts` whose name is whatever `word` is". The first time a word turns up there is
no such part yet (`undefined`), so it is set to 0 before adding one.
`tally.the` and `tally['the']` mean the same thing; the brackets are for when you do not
know the name until the program runs.

## Going through the parts

`Object.keys` gives you a list of an object's property names, which you can go through with
`for … of`, like any list:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
const stock = { apples: 12, pears: 0, plums: 30 }

const lines = []
for (const fruit of Object.keys(stock)) {
  lines.push(`${fruit}: ${stock[fruit]}`)
}

preview.append(lines.join(', '))

test 'every fruit gets a line' {
  expect(Object.keys(stock)).toEqual(['apples', 'pears', 'plums'])
  expect(lines[1]).toBe('pears: 0')
}
```

The names come out in the order the parts were added. (One exception: names that are whole
numbers come first, smallest first, so `Object.keys({ b: 1, 2: 1, a: 1 })` gives
`['2', 'b', 'a']`.)

## Lists of objects

Real data usually comes many at a time: a list of objects. Rows in a table, people in a
class, items in a basket.
Everything from Lists works on them. `map` turns each row into a line of text, and `for … of`
adds up the bill:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
const basket = [
  { item: 'bread', price: 2.5, quantity: 1 },
  { item: 'apples', price: 0.5, quantity: 6 },
  { item: 'cheese', price: 4, quantity: 1 },
]

const lines = basket.map((row) => `${row.quantity} x ${row.item}`)

let total = 0
for (const row of basket) {
  total = total + row.price * row.quantity
}

preview.append(`${lines.join(', ')}: ${total}`)

test 'adding up a basket' {
  expect(lines[1]).toBe('6 x apples')
  expect(total).toBe(9.5)
}
```

Inside the loop, `row` is one whole object, so `row.price` and `row.quantity` are that row's
parts. Follow `total` through the three rounds:

| round | `row.item` | `row.price * row.quantity` | `total` afterwards |
| ----- | ---------- | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
| 1     | bread      | 2.5 × 1 = 2.5              | 0 + 2.5 = 2.5      |
| 2     | apples     | 0.5 × 6 = 3                | 2.5 + 3 = 5.5      |
| 3     | cheese     | 4 × 1 = 4                  | 5.5 + 4 = 9.5      |

## Functions that make objects

A function can give back an object, which is how you return several answers at once. Here
`numbers: [0.0]` means a list of numbers, decimals allowed, as in Functions:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function stats(numbers: [0.0]) {
  let smallest = numbers[0]
  let largest = numbers[0]
  for (const n of numbers) {
    if (n < smallest) {
      smallest = n
    }
    if (n > largest) {
      largest = n
    }
  }
  return { smallest, largest }
}

const result = stats([4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42])

preview.append(`From ${result.smallest} to ${result.largest}.`)

test 'one call, two answers' {
  expect(stats([4, 8, 15]).smallest).toBe(4)
  expect(stats([4, 8, 15])).toEqual({ smallest: 4, largest: 15 })
}
```

`{ smallest, largest }` is short for `{ smallest: smallest, largest: largest }`: when a part
has the same name as the value you are putting in it, you can write the name once. (Given an
empty list, both answers are `undefined`: there is no first number to start from.)

## Same parts, different objects

Look at the last test again. It uses `toEqual`, not `toBe`. That matters:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
const a = { x: 1, y: 2 }
const b = { x: 1, y: 2 }
const c = a

preview.append(`a == b is ${a == b}, a == c is ${a == c}, Is(a, b) is ${Is(a, b)}`)

test 'equal parts are not the same object' {
  expect(a == b).toBe(false)
  expect(a == c).toBe(true)
  expect(Is(a, b)).toBe(true)
  expect(a).toEqual(b)
}
```

`a` and `b` have the same parts, but they are two separate objects, made by two separate
pairs of braces. For numbers and strings, `==` compares values, as it always has. For
objects and lists it asks "is this the very same object?", and they are not. `c` is not a
copy: `const c = a` gives the same object a second name, so `a == c` is true. Add the lines
`c.x = 5` and `preview.append(a.x)` at the end to see it.

To ask "do these have the same parts?", use `Is(a, b)`, which looks inside. `Is` is built into
TJS; there is nothing to import or write. Tests make the same split: `toBe` asks the `==`
question and `toEqual` asks the `Is` question, which is why the tests on this page use
`toEqual` for objects and lists. (TJS keeps `==` as a quick "same thing?" question on
purpose: comparing every part of two large objects can take a long time, and you should be
able to see when a program does that.)

## An object as a parameter

A parameter's example can be an object. Then the example says which parts the object must
have, and what kind each part is. Here both parts are `0.0`, any number, so a rectangle
can be 2.5 wide:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function area(rect: { width: 0.0, height: 0.0 }) {
  return rect.width * rect.height
}

preview.append(`A 3 by 4 rectangle has an area of ${area({ width: 3, height: 4 })}. `)
preview.append(`Without a height: ${area({ width: 3 }).message}`)

test 'area needs both parts' {
  expect(area({ width: 3, height: 4 })).toBe(12)
  expect(area({ width: 2.5, height: 4 })).toBe(10)
  expect(area({ width: 3, height: 4, colour: 'red' })).toBe(12)
  expect(area({ width: 3 }) instanceof Error).toBe(true)
}
```

Extra parts are fine (the rectangle can have a colour). A missing part is refused: the
function does not run, and its answer is an error value instead, which `instanceof Error`
recognises, as in Checking Your Work. The error names the part. The preview shows its
`message`: a number was expected for `rect.height`, and it got `undefined`. (The message
also says where in the program the call was checked.) Had the example been
`{ width: 0, height: 0 }`, only whole numbers would be accepted, and
`area({ width: 2.5, height: 4 })` would be refused.

This is the answer to the typo problem from the start of the chapter. Call
`area({ width: 3, hieght: 4 })` and TJS does not quietly multiply by `undefined`: at the
moment the mistake happens, it says a number was expected for `rect.height` and it got
`undefined`. Try it. The example in the parameter is a promise about the parts, and TJS checks the promise on every call.

## Naming a shape: `Type`

When the same shape turns up in several places, give it a name. A `Type` describes a shape
with a sentence and an example. `Type` is its own kind of declaration, not an object, so its
lines need no commas.

The example below works out the straight-line distance between two points, by Pythagoras:
3 across and 4 up is 5 away. Two new pieces of arithmetic do it: `**` raises to a power, so
`3 ** 2` is 9, and `Math.sqrt` is the square root.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
Type Point {
  description: 'a position on a grid'
  example: { x: 0, y: 0 }
}

function distance(a: Point, b: Point) {
  return Math.sqrt((a.x - b.x) ** 2 + (a.y - b.y) ** 2)
}

preview.append(`From (0, 0) to (3, 4) is ${distance({ x: 0, y: 0 }, { x: 3, y: 4 })}.`)

test 'a Point is anything shaped like one' {
  expect(distance({ x: 0, y: 0 }, { x: 3, y: 4 })).toBe(5)
  expect(Point.check({ x: 1, y: 2 })).toBe(true)
  expect(Point.check({ x: 'one', y: 2 })).toBe(false)
}
```

- `a: Point` reads "a must be a Point". It works like writing the example `{ x: 0, y: 0 }`
  there yourself, with a name and a description attached, and it is checked on every call.
- A `Type` has parts of its own. `check` is one of them, and it is a function you call:
  `Point.check(value)` asks the question yourself: is this shaped like a Point?
- The example uses whole numbers, so a `Point` has whole-number parts: positions on a grid.
  Try `Point.check({ x: 1.5, y: 2 })`. For any position, the example would be
  `{ x: 0.0, y: 0.0 }`.

The description is for people. It says what the example alone cannot, and a program can read
it back as `Point.description`.

## A shape with a rule

Some things are not described by their shape alone. A percentage is a number, but not any
number: it is between 0 and 100. A `Type` can carry a **predicate**, a small function that
answers "is this value acceptable?" with `true` or `false`:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
Type Percent {
  description: 'a whole number from 0 to 100'
  example: 50
  predicate(value) {
    return value >= 0 && value <= 100
  }
}

function progressBar(done: Percent) {
  const filled = Math.round(done / 10)
  return '#'.repeat(filled) + '.'.repeat(10 - filled) + ` ${done}%`
}

preview.append(progressBar(70))

test 'a Percent must be from 0 to 100' {
  expect(progressBar(70)).toBe('#######... 70%')
  expect(Percent.check(100)).toBe(true)
  expect(Percent.check(101)).toBe(false)
  expect(progressBar(150) instanceof Error).toBe(true)
}
```

`predicate(value) { … }` is a function written inside the `Type`, without the word
`function`; TJS calls it for you. It does not need to check "whole number": the example `50`
already says that, so `50.5` is refused before the predicate is asked.

`progressBar(150)` never runs: 150 is a whole number, but the predicate says no, so the call
gives back an error value that says a `Percent` was expected. Without the check, the body would
ask for `-5` dots, and `repeat` would give a different kind of error: one that stops the whole
program, and says nothing about percentages. The rule is written once, in the `Type`, and
every function that takes a `Percent` gets it for free.

Keep a predicate a plain check: comparisons on the value, combined with `&&` and `||`. No
loops (a loop might never finish, and a check that never answers is no check), nothing
fetched from the internet, nothing changed. A predicate like that is one TJS can prove safe:
whatever value it is handed, it answers yes or no, quickly, and touches nothing else. The
[Predicate Types](/predicate-types/) page shows what that proof makes possible; it is written
for working programmers, so save it for after this book.

## Try it

Make a `Type Book` with a `title` and a number of `pages`. Write `longBooks(books: [Book])` that
gives back the titles of the books with more than 300 pages, and test it with a list of three
books (one short, two long), and with an empty list. `[Book]` means "a list of Books", just
as `['']` meant a list of strings, and every book in it is checked. Test that a list with a
book missing its `pages` is refused:
`expect(longBooks([{ title: 'Short' }]) instanceof Error).toBe(true)`. This error points at
the book (`books[0]`) rather than at the missing part.

More to try:

- Use `countWords` to find which letter is most common in a sentence. (A string can be split
  into a list of its letters with `sentence.split('')`.) Then go through `Object.keys` of the
  result, as in the stock example, keeping the letter with the biggest count, the way `stats`
  keeps the largest number. Spaces count too: what does that do to your answer?
- Write `Type Temperature` for a number of degrees Celsius that cannot be below -273.15
  (absolute zero; nothing is colder). Give it a description, an example with a decimal point
  such as `20.5` (with a whole-number example, `20.5` itself would be refused, as with `area`),
  and a predicate. Test that -273.15 is accepted and -273.16 is refused.
- Write `swap(point: { x: 0, y: 0 })` that gives back a **new** point with `x` and `y`
  exchanged. Test it with `toEqual`, and test that the point you passed in has not changed.

Work them here:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
// Your code here. Show results with preview.append(…), check them with a
// test block, then press the refresh button (or ⌘S / Ctrl+S) to run it.
```

# Context: Working with `tosijs-schema`

You are an expert in `tosijs-schema`, a lightweight, schema-first, LLM-native replacement for Zod. Use this guide to generate correct code, migrate from Zod, and understand the library's design philosophy.

## 1. Core Philosophy & Design

- **Schema-First:** The primary artifact is a standard JSON Schema object. `tosijs-schema` is a fluent API to generate these schemas.
- **LLM-Native:** The generated schemas are optimized for LLM consumption (cleaner, flatter, fewer tokens than Zod-to-JSON-Schema adapters).
- **Strict by Default:** Objects automatically set `additionalProperties: false` and mark all keys as `required` to satisfy OpenAI Structured Output requirements out-of-the-box.
- **Performance:** Uses "Ghost Constraints" for expensive checks (like `maxProperties` on large objects) and a "prime-jump" strategy for validating large arrays in O(1) time.
- **Validation Separation:** Separates "Is this valid?" (fast, boolean return) from "Why is it invalid?" (detailed debugging).

## 2. Basic Setup & Syntax

### Imports

```typescript
import { s, type Infer } from 'tosijs-schema'
```

### Defining Schemas

Use the `s` proxy to define schemas. The syntax is property-based and chainable.

```typescript
const UserSchema = s.object({
  id: s.string.uuid, // Format shorthand
  username: s.string.min(3).max(20), // Chainable constraints
  email: s.email, // First-class email type (no .string wrapper needed)
  age: s.integer.min(0).optional, // Optional integer
  tags: s.array(s.string).min(1), // Array with constraints
  role: s.enum(['admin', 'user']), // Enums
  meta: s.record(s.string), // Record/Dictionary
})
```

### Type Inference

Inference works similarly to Zod but exports `Infer` directly.

```typescript
type User = Infer<typeof UserSchema>
```

### Accessing the JSON Schema

You can access the raw JSON schema object via the `.schema` property.

```typescript
console.log(UserSchema.schema)
// Outputs standard JSON Schema object: { type: "object", properties: { ... } }
```

## 3. Validation API

**Crucial Difference from Zod:**

- `tosijs-schema` validation is optimized for speed and returns a **boolean** by default.
- It does **not** throw errors or return a parsed object like Zod's `.parse()`.

```typescript
const data = { ... };

// Fast validation (returns true/false)
if (UserSchema.validate(data)) {
  // logic here
} else {
  // Handle invalid data
}
```

## 4. Migration Guide (Zod vs. tosijs-schema)

| Feature         | Zod (`z`)                  | tosijs-schema (`s`)                      |
| --------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| **String**      | `z.string()`               | `s.string`                               |
| **Email**       | `z.string().email()`       | `s.email` (First-class citizen)          |
| **UUID**        | `z.string().uuid()`        | `s.string.uuid` or `s.uuid`              |
| **Optional**    | `schema.optional()`        | `schema.optional` (Property, not method) |
| **Objects**     | `z.object({...})`          | `s.object({...})`                        |
| **Strict Mode** | `z.object({...}).strict()` | **Default** (No method needed)           |
| **Arrays**      | `z.array(schema)`          | `s.array(schema)`                        |
| **Enums**       | `z.enum(['a', 'b'])`       | `s.enum(['a', 'b'])`                     |
| **Unions**      | `z.union([a, b])`          | `s.union([a, b])`                        |
| **Inference**   | `z.infer<typeof T>`        | `Infer<typeof T>`                        |
| **Metadata**    | `.describe("...")`         | `.describe("...")` / `.title("...")`     |

## 5. Monadic Pipelines (`M`)

`tosijs-schema` includes a "Railway Oriented Programming" module for building type-safe tool chains. This is especially useful for **AI Agents**, ensuring that hallucinations or bad data are caught immediately at the source (Input vs Output) rather than cascading.

### 1. Guarded Functions (`M.func`)

Create functions that enforce schemas on both input and output.

```typescript
import { M, s } from 'tosijs-schema'

// M.func(InputSchema, OutputSchema, Implementation)
const getSize = M.func(s.string, s.number, (str) => {
  return str.length
})

// Usage:
const len = getSize('hello') // Returns 5
// getSize(123) // Throws SchemaError (Input mismatch)
```

### 2. Execution Contexts (`new M`)

Chain multiple functions together. The execution context handles error propagation automatically.

```typescript
const pipeline = new M({
  getSize,
  isEven: M.func(s.number, s.boolean, (n) => n % 2 === 0),
})

const result = pipeline
  .getSize('hello') // Output: 5
  .isEven() // Input: 5 -> Output: false
  .result() // Returns false | Error

// If any step fails schema validation, .result() returns the specific error.
```

## 6. Advanced Features

### Ghost Constraints

Constraints that are computationally expensive (O(N)) are documented in the schema but skipped by the runtime validator for performance (O(1)).

- **Example:** `.max(n)` on Objects/Records.
- `minProperties` is strictly validated.
- `maxProperties` is a "Ghost" constraint (documentation only).

### Metadata & LLM Optimization

Use metadata methods to enrich schemas for LLMs or OpenAPI docs without affecting runtime validation.

```typescript
const ApiKey = s.string
  .min(32)
  .describe("The user's secret API key") // standard JSON schema "description"
  .title('API Key')
  .default('sk-...')
```

### Date Handling

`tosijs-schema` treats dates as strings with format validation, aligning with JSON transport.

```typescript
const Timestamp = s.string.datetime // Validates ISO string format
```

## 6. Common Patterns & Gotchas

1. **Chaining Order:** Primitives (like `s.string`) start the chain. Constraints (`.min()`) and metadata (`.describe()`) follow. The `.optional` flag can be placed anywhere in the chain but usually goes last for readability.
2. **No Transformers:** Unlike Zod, `tosijs` is a pure validation/schema library. It does not "transform" data (e.g., string to number coercion) during validation.
3. **Strict Objects:** Remember that `s.object()` disallows unknown keys by default. If you need a flexible object, use `s.record()` or explicitly allow additional properties if the API supports it (though strict is preferred for LLM outputs).
4. **Tuples:** Use `s.tuple([s.string, s.number])` for fixed-length arrays.

## 7. Example: LLM Structured Output

When defining a response format for an LLM:

```typescript
const ResponseSchema = s.object({
  reasoning: s.string.describe('Step-by-step thinking process'),
  final_answer: s.string.describe('The concise final answer'),
  confidence: s.number
    .min(0)
    .max(1)
    .describe('Confidence score between 0 and 1'),
})

// Pass to LLM
const jsonSchema = ResponseSchema.schema
```

# FunctionPredicate: Design Notes

_How TJS describes the type of a function: what was proposed, what shipped, and what did
not._

> **In brief**
>
> - To type a callback parameter, give it a function example:
>   `function greet(format: (s: '') => '')`. A typed function passed in is checked against
>   that shape.
> - `FunctionPredicate` declares a named function type. Its runtime check is only "can this
>   value be called?"; its parameters and return example are metadata for docs, `.d.ts`
>   output and introspection.
> - `function run(fn: Formatter)`, with `Formatter` a `FunctionPredicate`, checks **nothing**,
>   not even callability. See [What did not ship](#what-did-not-ship).

This began as a proposal; most of it shipped in a smaller form. For day-to-day use, see
[Declarations](/declarations/) and [Higher-order functions](/higher-order-functions/); this
note records why it works the way it does.

A few terms used below. In TJS a parameter's annotation is an **example value**, not a type:
`0` means integer, `0.0` any number, `''` a string (see [TJS syntax](/TJS-SYNTAX/)). The
**kind** of an example is the type inferred from it: `integer`, `number`, `string`, and so on.
`Type` is a named runtime type built from an example, and `Generic` is a `Type` with type
parameters. A `MonadicError` is an error value a function returns instead of throwing; test
for one with `isMonadicError`. `fromTS` is the TypeScript-to-TJS converter, and `__tjs` is the
metadata TJS attaches to every function it transpiles.

---

## The problem

A callback parameter needs a type. Before `FunctionPredicate`, TJS had no way to say "this
parameter is a function taking a string and returning a string", and `fromTS` dropped
TypeScript function types such as `() => void` entirely. Callbacks, event handlers and
higher-order functions lost their type at exactly the boundary where a type helps most.

## Design principles

1. **A function is a value, so it can be an example.** `0` means "integer" and `''` means
   "string"; a function with typed parameters should mean "a function shaped like this".
2. **A function type works like `Type` and `Generic`.** It is a value you call to check a
   candidate, and it carries metadata that tools can read.
3. **The return contract is part of the signature.** The three return markers (`:`, `:?`,
   `:!`) say how much the author promises about the result, so a function type records which
   one it expects.

## The three return contracts

The markers on a function's return annotation (see
[Return annotations](/TJS-SYNTAX/#return-annotations)):

| Marker | Contract name    | What happens                                                                      |
| ------ | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `:`    | `returns`        | A worked example: the function is called with its parameter examples when the file is transpiled, and the result must equal the annotation. |
| `:?`   | `checkedReturns` | The same worked example, plus a check of every result at runtime. A wrong result is returned as a `MonadicError`, not thrown. |
| `:!`   | `assertReturns`  | The return type only. Nothing runs and the result is never checked.                |

`assertReturns` is named the way a TypeScript `as` assertion is: the author asserts the
return type and nothing verifies it.

A `FunctionPredicate` stores one of these names in its `returnContract` property. That
property is **metadata**: a `FunctionPredicate` never calls a function, so nothing is tested,
thrown or wrapped because of it, and the contract is never compared with a callback's.

## What shipped

### The `FunctionPredicate` declaration

A block declares a function type by its parameters and its return example:

```tjs
FunctionPredicate Formatter {
  description: 'formats a string for a locale'
  params: { input: '', locale: 'en' }
  returns: ''
}

console.log(Formatter((s) => s.trim()))      // true
console.log(Formatter('not a function'))     // false
console.log(Formatter((a, b, c, d) => a))    // true: arity is not compared
console.log(Formatter.description)           // formats a string for a locale
console.log(Object.keys(Formatter.params).join(', '))  // input, locale
console.log(Formatter.returns === '')        // true
console.log(Formatter.returnContract)        // assertReturns
```

**The runtime check is callability only.** `Formatter(x)` is `true` for any function and
`false` for anything else. Whether a function honours a signature is something you learn by
calling it, and a type check must not call the value it checks.

The parameters and return example are used elsewhere: the generated `.d.ts` (see
[Declaration files](#declaration-files)), documentation, and introspection through
`.params`, `.returns` and `.returnContract`. Where a callback's shape is actually checked is
a parameter whose example is a function; see
[A function as a parameter example](#a-function-as-a-parameter-example).

The block accepts four members:

- `params`: the parameter examples.
- `returns`: the return example. This key holds only the example value; it does not select
  the `returns` contract.
- `returnContract`: one of the three contract names above. The default is
  `'assertReturns'`, whatever `returns` holds.
- `description`: the default is the declaration's name.

Any other key is silently ignored. Writing `checkedReturns: ''` in place of `returns: ''`
gives a type with no return example and the default contract; write
`returnContract: 'checkedReturns'` instead.

### Generic function types

A `FunctionPredicate` can take type parameters, as `Generic` does. `T = 0` declares a type
parameter whose default example is an integer. Calling the declaration with an example value
substitutes it for `T`, so `Mapper('')` is a mapper from strings to strings.
`typeParamNames` lists the declared parameters. The concrete type still checks callability
only:

```tjs
FunctionPredicate Mapper<T = 0> {
  params: { value: T }
  returns: T
}

const StringMapper = Mapper('')
console.log(Mapper.typeParamNames.join(', '))    // T
console.log(StringMapper.returns === '')          // true
console.log(StringMapper((s) => s), StringMapper(3)) // true false
```

### The function form

`FunctionPredicate Name(fn, 'description')` was meant to take a type from an existing
function's metadata. It takes only the description; the parameters, return example and
contract are not copied, in any TJS program. Use the block form instead.

```tjs
function next(n: 1): 2 { return n + 1 }

FunctionPredicate Step(next, 'one step forward')

console.log(Step.description)                 // one step forward
console.log(Object.keys(Step.params).length)  // 0: the parameters were not copied
console.log(Step(next), Step(null))           // true false
```

### A function as a parameter example

The idea from the first principle did ship, through parameter examples rather than through
`FunctionPredicate`. When a parameter's example is a function with typed parameters, the
check on a passed value has two parts: it must be a function, and if it carries TJS
metadata, its declared parameter kinds and return kind must match the example's.

```tjs
function shout(s: 'hi'): 'HI!' { return s.toUpperCase() + '!' }
function next(n: 1): 2 { return n + 1 }
function zero(s: ''): 0 { return 0 }

// `format`'s example is a function, so its shape is the expected shape
function greet(format: (s: '') => '') { return format('hello') }

console.log(greet(shout))                  // HELLO!
console.log(greet((s) => s + '?'))         // hello?  (untyped: not compared)
console.log(isMonadicError(greet(next)))   // true: next declares an integer parameter
console.log(isMonadicError(greet(zero)))   // true: zero returns an integer
console.log(isMonadicError(greet(42)))     // true: not a function
```

Three decisions are visible here:

- **Untyped functions pass.** A plain arrow such as `(s) => s + '?'` has no metadata to
  compare, so only callability is checked. Rejecting untyped functions was considered and
  turned down, because it would make every plain JavaScript callback an error.
- **The check runs at the call that passes the function**, not on each invocation of it. A
  callback with the wrong shape is one error at the boundary, not one error per invocation.
- **Kinds must match exactly** where both sides declare one: an `integer` parameter does not
  match a `number` (`0.0`) one. A side whose kind is `any` matches anything. Parameter count
  is not compared: a callback may declare fewer or more parameters than the example, and
  only the positions both declare are checked.

A `!` at the start of the parameter list turns off every check on that function's
parameters, this one included. `function greet(! format: (s: '') => '') { … }` accepts
`42` for `format` without complaint. See [Safety markers](/TJS-SYNTAX/#safety-markers).

The same check applies when the parameter's default is a previously declared TJS function
(`function greet(format = shout)`): the default's signature becomes the expected shape.
Naming such a function as the example (`function greet(format: shout)`) also performs the
check, but `tjs check` warns that `shout` "could not be resolved to a runtime type" and is
unchecked. The warning is wrong here: the parameter is checked. Until that is fixed, use the
arrow example or the default.

### Conversion from TypeScript

`fromTS` now converts function types instead of dropping them:

| TypeScript                                       | Converted TJS                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `type Formatter = (input: string) => string`     | a `FunctionPredicate Formatter { params: { input: '' } returns: '' }` block |
| a member `onChange: (v: number) => void`         | `onChange: FunctionPredicate('function', { params: { v: 0.0 } })` in the `Type` example |
| a parameter `fn: (x: number) => string`          | `fn: FunctionPredicate('function', { params: { x: 0.0 }, returns: '' })` |

The last two rows use a call form: `FunctionPredicate(name, { params, returns })` builds an
unnamed function type inline, with `'function'` as its name. A `void` return becomes no
`returns` key, so the result is unconstrained.

A member converted this way is checked for callability when the enclosing `Type` is checked.
A parameter converted this way is not checked. Converted code defaults to `safety none`,
which turns off parameter checks for the whole file; and even with checks turned on, the
inline `FunctionPredicate(…)` call is not read as a runtime type, so the parameter is treated
as `any`. For a parameter, the conversion keeps the information for docs and `.d.ts` output
only.

### Declaration files

A `FunctionPredicate` block becomes a TypeScript function type in the generated `.d.ts`:

```text
FunctionPredicate Formatter {        →   export type Formatter = (input: string, locale: string) => string;
  params: { input: '', locale: 'en' }
  returns: ''
}
```

## What did not ship

- **A `FunctionPredicate` name as a parameter annotation.** `function run(fn: Formatter)`
  transpiles, but `tjs check` warns that `Formatter` "could not be resolved to a runtime
  type", and the parameter is not checked at all, not even for callability. Use a function
  example for the parameter, and call `Formatter(fn)` yourself where you want the named check.
- **Shape matching inside `FunctionPredicate`.** The proposal had it compare arity, parameter
  types, return type and return contract against the candidate's `__tjs` metadata. TJS
  programs check callability only. (A separate runtime implementation compares arity and
  parameter kinds, but TJS programs never use it; see [Type identity](/type-identity/).)
- **Return-contract strictness.** The proposal ranked the contracts (`checkedReturns`
  satisfies any requirement, `assertReturns` only itself) and would have refused a callback
  whose contract was too weak. `returnContract` is recorded and never compared.
- **Copying metadata in the function form**, as shown above.

A `FunctionPredicate` in a TJS program has no `toJSONSchema()`. That is not a gap: JSON
Schema cannot describe a function.

# GitHub Repos

A research agent's first step: find the candidates and keep only what you need from each. This
one searches GitHub for repositories and returns names, stars and descriptions, most-starred
first.

```ajs:inline
function searchRepos({ query = 'tosijs', perPage = 5 }) {
  let url =
    'https://api.github.com/search/repositories?q=' +
    encodeURIComponent(query) +
    '&per_page=' +
    perPage +
    '&sort=stars'
  let response = httpFetch({ url })
  if (response.items == null) {
    return {
      total: 0,
      repos: [],
      error: response.message ?? 'unexpected response',
    }
  }
  let repos = response.items.map((x) => ({
    name: x.full_name,
    stars: x.stargazers_count,
    description: x.description,
  }))
  return { total: response.total_count, repos }
}
```

`httpFetch` is the built-in fetch atom. It returns the response body, parsed as JSON when the
server sends JSON. It does not return the HTTP status or a `Response` object. Besides `url` it
accepts `method`, `headers` and `body`; `httpFetch({ url, headers: { Accept: 'text/plain' } })`
is a valid call.

The agent's parameters are the run's arguments: the host passes an object such as
`{ query: 'language:rust', perPage: 10 }`, and the defaults apply to whatever it leaves out.

## What to notice

- **The query is encoded.** GitHub's search syntax uses spaces, `:` and `>`, so a query like
  `language:typescript stars:>1000` must go through `encodeURIComponent` to arrive intact.
- **The shape is checked before the `map`.** When GitHub refuses a search, it still answers
  with JSON, but with a `message` instead of `items`. For an empty query GitHub answers
  `{ "message": "Validation Failed", … }`, and the agent turns that into
  `{ total: 0, repos: [], error: 'Validation Failed' }`. Without the `if`, the agent would call
  `map` on `undefined` and the run would fail with `map: items is not an array`.
- **Both outcomes have the same shape.** Success and failure each return `total` and `repos`,
  and only a failure has `error`. A caller, or a model reading the result, checks for `error`.
- **The result is small on purpose.** GitHub returns dozens of fields per repository; the agent
  keeps three, plus the total match count. Everything passing between the agent and the host is
  copied as plain JSON data, so a smaller result is a smaller copy, and whatever the agent hands
  a model costs tokens.
- **The domain is allowed by the host.** The live examples on this site run with
  `context: { allowedFetchDomains: ['api.github.com', …] }`. In your own host you pass that
  yourself; the host code at the end of this page shows where.

## A variation

One repository's vital signs:

```ajs:inline
function repoInfo({ owner = 'tonioloewald', repo = 'tjs-lang' }) {
  let r = httpFetch({
    url:
      'https://api.github.com/repos/' +
      encodeURIComponent(owner) +
      '/' +
      encodeURIComponent(repo),
  })
  if (r.full_name == null) {
    return { error: r.message ?? 'not found' }
  }
  return {
    name: r.full_name,
    stars: r.stargazers_count,
    language: r.language,
    openIssues: r.open_issues_count,
  }
}
```

The owner and repository names are encoded too. A real GitHub name never needs it, but the
arguments come from whoever runs the agent, and a `repo` of `'x/../../users/someone'` would
otherwise point the request at a different endpoint.

A missing repository does not make `httpFetch` fail. GitHub answers 404 with a JSON body
(`{ "message": "Not Found", … }`), and, as above, `httpFetch` hands the agent that body, not the
status. With `repo: 'no-such-repo'` this agent returns `{ error: 'Not Found' }`. The `if` is how
you tell.

## The gotchas

- **Rate limits.** Without a token, GitHub allows about 60 requests an hour from one address,
  and search has its own, tighter limit of about 10 requests a minute. Past either limit it
  answers with `{ "message": "API rate limit exceeded for …" }` instead of data, which both
  examples above return as their `error`. If they stop returning results, that is why.
- **`openIssues` is not a bug count.** GitHub's `open_issues_count` counts open pull requests as
  well as open issues, so it is a rough measure of activity.
- **Never put a token in agent source.** Source is data: it is stored, logged, sent to models
  and passed around. A token written into an agent is a token published to everyone who handles
  that agent.

### Where the token goes instead

A host that needs authenticated requests puts the credential in its own `fetch` capability, a
function the host passes to `vm.run`. The agent calls `httpFetch` exactly as above. The VM checks
the request (the scheme, the method, the agent's headers against a fixed list, and the domain
against the allowlist) and then calls the capability with it, including any headers the agent
set. The capability adds the token on the way out, so the agent can use the token without ever
holding it. This sample is Node or Bun code (it reads `process.env`):

```javascript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

const token = process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN
if (!token) throw new Error('GITHUB_TOKEN is not set')

// Called with the request after the VM's checks. Returns plain JSON data.
const githubFetch = async (url, { method, headers, body, signal }) => {
  const h = new Headers(headers)
  h.set('Accept', 'application/vnd.github+json')
  // set() replaces an Authorization header the agent sent, in any spelling
  h.set('Authorization', `Bearer ${token}`)
  const res = await fetch(url, {
    method,
    signal,
    headers: h,
    body: body === undefined ? undefined : JSON.stringify(body),
  })
  return res.json()
}

// agentSource: the repoInfo agent above, as a string
const agentSource = `function repoInfo({ owner = 'tonioloewald', repo = 'tjs-lang' }) { … }`

// Transpile on your side: vm-ast runs ASTs only. Passing the VM's atoms lets the
// transpiler check every atom call against the atom's declared inputs.
const vm = new AgentVM()
const { ast } = transpile(agentSource, { atoms: vm.atoms })
const run = await vm.run(
  ast,
  { owner: 'tonioloewald', repo: 'tjs-lang' }, // the agent's arguments
  {
    fuel: 1000, // the run's work budget; this agent uses about 7
    capabilities: { fetch: githubFetch }, // the IO functions the agent may reach
    context: { allowedFetchDomains: ['api.github.com'] }, // policy the VM enforces
  }
)

if (run.error) console.error(run.error.message)
else console.log(run.result) // { name: 'tonioloewald/tjs-lang', stars: …, … }
```

The two option bags do different jobs. `capabilities` holds the functions that do the IO.
`context` holds the run's policy, which the VM applies before any capability is called, so the
allowlist goes there and not inside your function. Fuel is the run's budget for work: each step
costs a little and a fetch costs 5, so 1000 is generous for one request. A 100-result search uses
about 26, because mapping more items is more work. See [Fuel Limits](/fuel-limits/).

What the allowlist does depends on which fetch the run uses:

- **The built-in fetch, no allowlist:** every request is refused with
  `Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured`.
- **Your own `fetch`, no allowlist:** the VM does not check the destination. Your capability
  owns it, and this one would attach your token to whatever URL the agent chose.
- **Either fetch, with an allowlist:** a request to any other host fails with
  `Fetch blocked: domain not in allowlist` before your capability runs. Keep it.

If the capability throws, the agent sees an ordinary error: `try`/`catch` in the agent catches
it, and the caught value is the error's message as a string. Do not put anything secret in that
message. Without a `try`, the run ends with that message as its `error`. This sample does not
check `res.ok`, because GitHub's error responses are JSON bodies the agents above already handle;
a capability for an API that answers errors with HTML should check the status and return or
throw something the agent can read.

Return data, not the `Response`. A live host object cannot cross into the agent: a capability
that returns one ends the run. [Capabilities and Custom Atoms](/ajs-capabilities/) covers what
a capability may return and has a fuller safe fetch.

# Responding to the Reader

Until now your programs have run once and stopped. An interactive program waits: it shows
something, and when the reader clicks or types, it changes. This chapter adds buttons and text
boxes, and a way to make the page update by itself whenever a fact in your program changes.

Every app you have used works this way. A to-do list waits for you to type, a game waits for
you to press a key, a shop waits for you to click "add to basket". The program sets things up,
then hands control to the reader, and runs a little piece of code each time they do something.
Those pieces of code are called **event handlers**: an **event** is something that happened (a
click, a key press), and the handler is the function that responds.

## A button that does something

The examples use tosijs, the library from Hello, Screen, and pick their building blocks out of
`elements` the same way: `button` makes a button. As before, everything a program shows goes
into `preview`, the box under the code.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements } from 'tosijs'

const { button } = elements

preview.append(
  button({ onClick: () => preview.append(' 👋') }, 'Wave')
)
```

`onClick` is a function the button runs every time it is clicked. Click **Wave** a few times.
The function runs on each click, not once when the program starts: that is what makes a page
interactive.

The `{ onClick: … }` in front of the label is an object (see Things with Parts) of settings
for the button. `() => preview.append(' 👋')` is a function written with an arrow as in
Lists, but with empty brackets because it needs no input. It is not called here: it is handed
to the button, which calls it later, once per click.

### A common mistake: calling the handler too early

What happens if you write the handler without the `() =>`?

```tjs:static
button({ onClick: preview.append(' 👋') }, 'Wave') // wrong
```

Then `preview.append(' 👋')` runs **immediately**, once, while the button is being made, and
what is handed to the button is its answer, not a function. You see one wave as soon as the
page loads, and clicking does nothing. If a button seems to have fired before anyone touched
it, look for a missing `() =>`.

## A model the page follows

Most interactive programs keep their facts in one place, the **model**, and show them on the
page. Then the page cannot fall out of step with the program: change a fact, and every place
that shows it changes too. tosijs makes that almost free: wrap your facts in `tosi`, put parts of the model on the
page, and from then on changing the model changes the page. You never redraw anything yourself.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

const { counter } = tosi({ counter: { count: 0 } })

const { div, button, span } = elements

preview.append(
  div(
    'Clicked ',
    span(counter.count),
    ' times. ',
    button({ onClick: () => { counter.count = counter.count + 1 } }, 'Click me'),
    button({ onClick: () => { counter.count = 0 } }, 'Reset')
  )
)
```

- `tosi({ counter: { count: 0 } })` makes the model. The outer object is the whole model, and
  it has one named part, `counter`, which holds `{ count: 0 }`. A model can have many parts,
  which is why each one gets a name.
- `const { counter } = …` takes that part back out by its name, the same way
  `const { button } = elements` takes out `button`, so the name on the left must match the
  name inside. What comes out is a watched version of `{ count: 0 }`: tosijs notices whenever it changes.
- `span(counter.count)` puts a part of the model on the page. Handed to an element like this,
  `counter.count` stays linked: the span keeps showing whatever `counter.count` is now.
- `counter.count = counter.count + 1` changes the model, and the span follows on its own. In
  arithmetic like `counter.count + 1`, the part counts as the value it holds right now.

The handlers here have curly braces after the `=>`, and the Wave handler did not. Without
braces, the arrow gives back the answer of one expression. With braces, it holds statements,
like the body of any function. A handler that changes something, such as
`counter.count = 0`, is written with braces.

Notice what the buttons do *not* do: they never touch the span. They change the model, and
everything showing it updates. Add a second `span(counter.count)` anywhere and it keeps up
too.

Why is this better than changing the span directly? Because as a program grows, the same fact
turns up in many places: a score in the corner, in the title, on the "game over" screen. If
every button had to remember every place the score is shown, sooner or later one would be
forgotten, and the page would contradict itself. With a model, a button only has to get the
**fact** right. Showing it is the job of the line that put it on the page, written once;
tosijs keeps it up to date.

## Many buttons, one function

Buttons that do similar things can share a function, each passing its own value:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

const { tally } = tosi({ tally: { total: 0 } })

function add(amount: 1) {
  tally.total = tally.total + amount
}

const { div, button, strong } = elements

preview.append(
  div('Total: ', strong(tally.total)),
  div(...[1, 5, 10, 50].map((amount) => button({ onClick: () => add(amount) }, `+${amount}`)))
)
```

`amount: 1` is an example, as always in TJS: `amount` can be any whole number, and the buttons
pass 1, 5, 10 and 50.

The row of buttons is made with `map`, from a list of amounts, the way the planets were in
Lists. `map` gives back a list of buttons, and `...` spreads it out so that `div` receives each
button as a separate item. Add `100` to the list and a new button appears.

## Typing

Buttons are one way to respond; text boxes are the other. An `input` element makes a box the
reader can type in, and a `label` is text that belongs to a box. `bindValue` ties the box to a
part of the model: what the reader types goes into the model, and anything showing that part
follows as they type.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

const { visitor } = tosi({ visitor: { name: 'Ada' } })

const { h2, input, label } = elements

preview.append(
  label('Your name: ', input({ bindValue: visitor.name })),
  h2('Hello, ', visitor.name, '!')
)
```

Type in the box. The heading changes with every key, and you did not write an event handler:
`bindValue` is a two-way link. The box shows the model, and typing in the box changes the
model, which changes the heading.

## Numbers from a text box

Everything typed into a box arrives as **text**, even when it looks like a number: the
reader types `37`, and the program receives the string `'37'`. Values and Names showed what
goes wrong when text is treated as a number. So before building a temperature converter,
write the rule that turns what the reader typed into an answer, and test it on its own:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function fahrenheit(celsius: 100.0): 212.0 {
  return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
}

function convert(text: '100'): 212.0 {
  return fahrenheit(Number(text))
}

preview.append(`'37' typed in a box is ${convert('37')} °F`)

test 'convert turns typed text into degrees Fahrenheit' {
  expect(convert('0')).toBe(32)
  expect(convert('-40')).toBe(-40)
}
```

- `Number(text)` turns the text `'100'` into the number `100`.
- `convert` takes text (its example is `'100'`, a string) and gives back a number. The
  arithmetic is in `fahrenheit`, which has its own signature example, as in Checking Your
  Work.

Now make the classic mistake. In `convert`, change `fahrenheit(Number(text))` to
`fahrenheit(text)`, handing over the text without turning it into a number. `convert`'s own
example fails as soon as you run the program (⌘S), because `convert('100')` no longer gives
212. The line under the code turns red, as in Checking Your Work: the error comes from
`fahrenheit`, and says it expected a number and got a string. The mistake is caught where it
was made.

(In plain JavaScript the slip is harder to spot: `*` quietly turns text into a number, so
`'100' * 9` is 900, while `+` joins, so `'100' + 32` is `'10032'`. A formula can work for months
and then give nonsense when someone rearranges it.)

Now the converter itself. `bindValue` would copy the text into the model exactly as typed, but
here the text has to be converted first. So an `onInput` handler reads the box, converts it,
and puts the answer into the model:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

function fahrenheit(celsius: 100.0): 212.0 {
  return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
}

function convert(text: '100'): 212.0 {
  return fahrenheit(Number(text))
}

const { weather } = tosi({ weather: { fahrenheit: convert('20') } })

const { div, input, strong } = elements

preview.append(
  div(
    input({
      value: '20',
      onInput: (event) => { weather.fahrenheit = convert(event.target.value) },
    }),
    ' °C is ',
    strong(weather.fahrenheit),
    ' °F'
  )
)
```

`onInput` runs on every change to the box. The browser hands every handler an **event**
object describing what happened; the earlier handlers ignored it, and this one names it
`event`. `event.target` is the box itself, so `event.target.value` is the text in it.

The box starts with `'20'` in it, and the model starts from `convert('20')`, not from 68 worked
out by hand. Writing 68 would put the same fact in two places, and change one without the other
and the page would contradict itself before anyone typed.

Type `abc` into the box and you meet the other kind of bad input. `Number('abc')` is `NaN`
("not a number", from Values and Names). Any arithmetic on NaN gives NaN, so the page shows
`NaN °F`. Deciding what to
show for input that makes no sense is part of writing an interactive program. Decisions has
the tools; one of the exercises below asks you to use them.

## Keep the rules out of the buttons

Look at how the converter was built: the handler is one short line that calls `convert`, and
`convert` calls `fahrenheit`. Neither function knows about boxes or typing, so both were
tested before there was a box at all, with exactly the text a reader would type.

That is the habit to build. Put the rules of your program in functions with examples and
tests; keep the handlers so short that there is nothing in them to get wrong. Here is the rule
for a traffic light, written with `given` from Decisions:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function nextLight(colour: 'red'): 'green' {
  given colour {
    'red' {
      return 'green'
    }
    'green' {
      return 'amber'
    }
  } else {
    return 'red'
  }
}

preview.append(`red, then ${nextLight('red')}, then ${nextLight('green')}, then ${nextLight('amber')}`)

test 'the lights go round' {
  expect(nextLight('green')).toBe('amber')
  expect(nextLight('amber')).toBe('red')
}
```

`nextLight` is the whole rule: red goes to green, green to amber, and anything else, including
amber, goes back to red. Its signature example and test check every step of the cycle. In the
next example the button only asks for the next colour and stores it:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

function nextLight(colour: 'red'): 'green' {
  given colour {
    'red' {
      return 'green'
    }
    'green' {
      return 'amber'
    }
  } else {
    return 'red'
  }
}

const { light } = tosi({ light: { colour: 'red' } })

const { div, button, strong } = elements

preview.append(
  div('The light is ', strong(light.colour), '. '),
  button({ onClick: () => { light.colour = nextLight(light.colour) } }, 'Next')
)
```

`nextLight(light.colour)` hands the function the model's part itself, not a copy of the text.
TJS checks it, and `given` and `==` compare it, by the value it holds, so `nextLight` treats it
as `'red'`. (`===` is stricter and does not look inside: `light.colour === 'red'` is `false`.
Use `==` with parts of a model.)

## Try it

Make a model with a `score`. Give it buttons for **+1**, **-1** and **double**, and show the
score on the page. Then add a line that shows `'You win!'` when the score reaches 100.
(Hint: give the model a second part, `message: ''`, and show it on the page. In each button's
handler, after changing the score, use an `if` to set `message` to `'You win!'` or back to
`''`.)

More to try:

- Make the converter go the other way too: a second box for °F that updates the °C. Write
  `celsius(degrees: 212.0): 100.0` first, with its example.
- Make the page say `'please type a number'` instead of showing `NaN` when the box holds
  something that is not a number. `Number.isNaN(value)` asks whether a value is NaN. First
  write a test that `Number.isNaN(convert('abc'))` is true, then give the model a second part,
  a `message`, set in the handler.
- Real traffic lights in some countries show red and amber together before green. Add that
  step to `nextLight`, and to its test, before you touch the button.

Not every event is a click or a key press. A timer going off is an event, and so is an answer
arriving from the network; a later chapter, Things That Take Time, shows how to wait for them.
Work them here:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
// Your code here. Show results with preview.append(…), check them with a
// test block, then press the refresh button (or ⌘S / Ctrl+S) to run it.
```
