## seq (Sequence)

The root atom for all agent programs. Executes steps in order.

- Stops on `return` (when `ctx.output` is set)
- Stops on error (monadic error flow)
- Cost: 0.1

```javascript
// AsyncJS compiles to seq at the top level
const x = 1
const y = 2
return { sum: x + y }
```

## if (Conditional)

Conditional branching based on expression evaluation.

```javascript
if (count > 0) {
  console.log("Has items")
} else {
  console.log("Empty")
}
```

## while (Loop)

Repeats body while condition is truthy. Consumes fuel each iteration.

```javascript
let i = 0
while (i < 10) {
  console.log(i)
  i = i + 1
}
```

**Note:** No `break`/`continue`. Use condition variables instead.

## return

Ends execution and returns values from state. The schema defines which
state variables to include in the output.

```javascript
const result = compute()
return { result }  // Returns { result: <computed value> }
```

## try/catch

Error handling with monadic error flow. When an error occurs, subsequent
steps are skipped until caught.

```javascript
try {
  const data = fetch(url)
  processData(data)
} catch (err) {
  console.warn("Failed: " + err)
  return { error: err }
}
```

The catch block receives:
- `err` (or custom name): error message
- `errorOp`: the atom that failed

## for...of / map

Transforms each item in an array. The `result` variable in each iteration
becomes the new item value.

```javascript
const doubled = items.map(x => x * 2)

// Or with for...of:
const results = []
for (const item of items) {
  results.push(process(item))
}
```

## filter

Keeps items that match a condition.

```javascript
const adults = users.filter(u => u.age >= 18)
```

## reduce

Accumulates a single value from an array.

```javascript
const sum = numbers.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0)
```

## find

Returns first item matching condition, or null.

```javascript
const admin = users.find(u => u.role === "admin")
```

## httpFetch

HTTP requests, through the host's `fetch` capability or the built-in client.

```javascript
const data = httpFetch({ url: 'https://api.example.com/data' })
// POST needs the host to enable it for the run: context.allowedFetchMethods: ['POST']
const posted = httpFetch({
  url: 'https://api.example.com/items',
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: { name: 'New Item' }
})
```

Response types: `"json"` (default for JSON content-type), `"text"`, `"dataUrl"` (for images)

Security:
- Requires a `ctx.context.allowedFetchDomains` allowlist (or a custom `fetch` capability); without
  one, every URL is refused. Only `http:`/`https:`; no redirects are followed (a redirect returns
  `{ redirect: true, status, location }`, location absolute; a 304 is a response); a closed list of
  request headers (`context.allowedRequestHeaders` adds more); GET/HEAD only by default
  (`context.allowedFetchMethods` adds more); an allowlist entry admits the default port unless it
  names one; the body is read under `membraneMaxBytes`. A DEMONSTRATION capability: real
  deployments supply their own `fetch`, which gets the same admission of method and headers
- Automatically adds `X-Agent-Depth` header to prevent recursive agent loops
- A custom `fetch` capability receives the ADMITTED request (scheme, method and headers always;
  the domain allowlist when set) plus the depth header, and owns redirects, credentials and the
  destination policy when no allowlist is set

## storeGet / storeSet

Persistent key-value storage. Requires `store` capability.

```javascript
// Save data
storeSet({ key: 'user:123', value: { name: 'Alice', prefs: {} } })

// Retrieve later
const user = storeGet({ key: 'user:123' })
```

**Warning:** Default in-memory store is not suitable for production.

## storeQueryWhere (predicate pushdown)

Send the *predicate* to the data instead of dragging rows to the code.

`predicate` is a **canonical verified predicate** — build it at author/transpile time
with `canonicalizePredicate()` from `tjs-lang/lang`, then pass the resulting object.
Because it is verified pure and canonical, it is safe to ship, cheap to compare, and
carries a stable `key` the store can cache on (two spellings of the same predicate hit
the same cache entry).

```javascript
// canonical form produced outside the VM; the VM forwards it as data
const rows = storeQueryWhere({ collection: 'users', predicate: adultPredicate })
```

Requires a store that implements `queryPredicate`. If it doesn't, this fails with a
message pointing at the ordinary `storeQuery` + `filter` path rather than silently
returning everything — a filter that silently doesn't filter is an authorization bug.

## llmPredict

Call language model. Requires `llm` capability with `predict` method.

```javascript
const response = llmPredict("Summarize this: " + text)

// With options
const structured = llmPredict(prompt, {
  model: "gpt-4",
  temperature: 0.7,
  responseFormat: { type: "json_object" }
})
```

## transpileCode (Code to AST)

Transpiles AsyncJS code to an AST without executing it.
Useful for generating agents to send to other services via fetch.

```javascript
// Generate an agent and send it to a worker
let code = llmPredict({ prompt: 'Write an AsyncJS data processor' })
let ast = transpileCode({ code })
// POST is enabled by the host for the run (context.allowedFetchMethods: ['POST'])
let result = httpFetch({
  url: 'https://worker.example.com/run',
  method: 'POST',
  body: JSON.stringify({ ast, args: { data: myData } })
})
```

Security: Only available when the `code.transpile` capability is provided.

## runCode (Dynamic Code Execution)

Transpiles and executes AsyncJS code at runtime. The generated code is its
own program: it sees only the `args` it is given — not the caller's
variables or helpers — and shares the run's fuel, heap budget,
capabilities, and trace.

This enables agents to write and execute code to solve problems.

```javascript
// Agent writes code to solve a problem
let code = llmPredict({ prompt: 'Write AsyncJS to calculate fibonacci(10)' })
let result = runCode({ code, args: {} })
return { answer: result }
```

The code must be a valid AsyncJS function. The function's return value
becomes the result of runCode.

Security: Only available when the `code.transpile` capability is provided.
The transpiled code runs with the same permissions as the parent.
Recursion depth is limited to prevent stack overflow.

## memoize

In-memory caching within a single execution. Same key returns cached result.

```javascript
// Expensive computation cached by key
const result = memoize("expensive-" + id, () => {
  return heavyComputation(data)
})
```

## cache

Persistent caching across executions using store capability.

```javascript
// Builder API (cache takes steps, which AsyncJS source cannot express): 1 hour
Agent.take().cache(
  (b) => b.httpFetch({ url: 'https://api.weather.com/' + city }).as('weather'),
  'weather-' + city,
  3600000
)
```

## console.log / console.warn / console.error

Logging utilities that integrate with trace and error flow.

```javascript
console.log("Debug info: " + value)   // Adds to trace
console.warn("Potential issue")        // Adds to trace + warnings summary
console.error("Fatal: " + msg)         // Triggers monadic error flow
```

- `log`: trace only (no side effects)
- `warn`: trace + appears in `result.warnings`
- `error`: stops execution, sets `result.error`

# Types at Runtime

TypeScript's types are gone by the time the code runs. TJS types are not: every function
keeps a description of its signature as data, every declared `Type` is a value you can call,
and both can be written out as JSON Schema for tools that have never heard of TJS. This page
covers three things: reading that description, checking values against a type, and exporting
a type as JSON Schema.

## A function carries its own signature

A quick key to the examples below. In TJS a colon parameter's value is an example, and the
example sets the type: `''` is a string, `0` an integer, `0.0` any number, `+0` a
non-negative integer.

```tjs:inline
function createUser(
  name: 'anonymous',
  email: 'user@example.com',
  age: +0
): { name: 'anonymous', email: 'user@example.com', age: 0 } {
  return { name, email, age }
}

function transfer(from: '', to: '', amount: 0.0, memo = ''): { from: '', to: '', amount: 0.0 } {
  return { from, to, amount }
}

test 'functions validate at runtime' {
  const user = createUser('Alice', 'alice@test.com', 30)
  expect(user.name).toBe('Alice')

  // -1 is not a non-negative integer: an error comes back, nothing is thrown
  const err = createUser('Alice', 'alice@test.com', -1)
  expect(isMonadicError(err)).toBe(true)
}

test 'metadata is introspectable' {
  const meta = createUser.__tjs
  expect(meta.params.name.type.kind).toBe('string')
  expect(meta.params.age.type.kind).toBe('non-negative-integer')
  expect(meta.returns.type.kind).toBe('object')
  expect(transfer.__tjs.params.memo.required).toBe(false)
}

console.log('age:   ', JSON.stringify(createUser.__tjs.params.age))
// {"type":{"kind":"non-negative-integer"},"required":true,"default":null}
console.log('amount:', JSON.stringify(transfer.__tjs.params.amount))
// {"type":{"kind":"number"},"required":true,"default":null}
console.log('memo:  ', JSON.stringify(transfer.__tjs.params.memo))
// {"type":{"kind":"string"},"required":false,"default":""}
console.log('returns:', JSON.stringify(transfer.__tjs.returns))
// {"type":{"kind":"object","shape":{"from":{"kind":"string"},"to":{"kind":"string"},"amount":{"kind":"number"}}}}
```

The return annotation is a _worked example_, not a type: calling the function with its
parameter examples must return exactly that value, and TJS checks that it does. That is why
`createUser`'s return repeats its parameter examples: `createUser('anonymous',
'user@example.com', 0)` returns `{ name: 'anonymous', email: 'user@example.com', age: 0 }`.
When you want a return type without the test, write `:!` instead of `:`.

The `test '…' { }` blocks are TJS inline tests, and `expect` is their assertion API. They run
when the file is checked or transpiled; see [Inline Tests](/inline-tests-test-private-functions/).

There is no schema library here, and nothing is written twice. The parameter examples _are_
the schema: `age: +0` documents the parameter and also makes
`createUser('Alice', 'alice@test.com', -1)` return a `MonadicError`. A `MonadicError` is an
error returned in place of the result rather than thrown; `isMonadicError(value)` tells it
apart from a normal result. [Error Handling](/error-handling/) explains why TJS works this
way.

The same facts are attached to the function as `fn.__tjs`, which is what the four
`console.log` lines print:

- `params` maps each parameter name to `{ type, required, default }`. `required` is `true`
  for a colon parameter (`age: +0`) and `false` for a defaulted one (`memo = ''`), whose
  `default` holds the value.
- `returns` holds the return's type descriptor, when the function declares one.
- `type` is a _type descriptor_. Its `kind` is one of `string`, `number` (from `0.0`),
  `integer` (from `0`), `non-negative-integer` (from `+0`), `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`,
  `bigint`, `array` (with `items`), `object` (with `shape`), `union`, `literal-union`,
  `function`, `declared` (a named `Type`, covered in the next section), `declared-import` (a
  `Type` imported from another module) or `any`.

The toolchain reads this description too: `tjs check` prints each function's signature from
it (`createUser(name: string, email: string, age: non-negative-integer) -> object`), `tjs
types` writes it out as JSON, and the `.d.ts` generator builds declarations from it. Your
code can read it as well, as the second test does.

In TypeScript this is the job of a separate runtime schema (zod and friends), kept in step
with the static types by hand or by inference. TJS starts from the other end: the runtime
description is the primary artefact, so it cannot drift from the code that uses it.

## A named type is a value

When a shape is used in more than one place, give it a name with `Type`. A declared type is a
predicate you can call, a type you can use in a signature, and a source of JSON Schema for
tools outside TJS (an API gateway, a form library, an LLM's structured output):

```tjs:inline
Type Address {
  description: 'a postal address'
  example: { street: '1 Main St', city: 'Springfield', zip: '12345' }
}

// 0.5 is a float example, so weightKg accepts any number, 2 included
function ship(to: Address, weightKg: 0.5): '0.5kg to Springfield' {
  return `${weightKg}kg to ${to.city}`
}

// The declared type is a predicate you can call...
console.log('Address(good):', Address({ street: '9 Elm', city: 'Shelbyville', zip: '54321' }))
console.log('Address.check(bad):', Address.check({ street: '9 Elm' }))

// ...the function checks its argument against it...
console.log(ship({ street: '9 Elm', city: 'Shelbyville', zip: '54321' }, 2))
// The result here is a MonadicError; String() prints its message:
// MonadicError: Expected Address for '…ship.to', got object
console.log(String(ship({ city: 'Nowhere' }, 2)))

// ...and the same declaration becomes a JSON Schema for other tools
console.log(JSON.stringify(Address.toJSONSchema(), null, 2))
```

In the block form, `example` gives the shape: every key in it is required, and each value's
kind becomes that key's type, so `street`, `city` and `zip` must all be strings.
`description` is documentation for readers and generated docs; it is not written into the
JSON Schema. A `predicate` adds rules an example cannot express (see
[Declarations](/declarations/)).

`Address(value)` and `Address.check(value)` are the same test, returning `true` or `false`;
`.check` reads better when the type is passed around as a value. `ship` runs the test on its
argument and, when it fails, returns a `MonadicError` naming the parameter. `ship`'s return
example is again a worked example: `ship` called with the `Address` example and `0.5` returns
`'0.5kg to Springfield'`.

The last line prints the schema with `type: 'object'`, the three keys under `properties`,
all three in `required`, and `additionalProperties: false`. That last field is explained
below, under _Extra keys and the exported schema_.

The full set of declarations (`Type`, `Enum`, `Union`, `Generic`, `FunctionPredicate`) is
covered in [Declarations](/declarations/).

## Removing extra fields with `strip`

A value that has more keys than the example still satisfies the type: an example lists the
keys that must be present, not the only keys allowed. TypeScript has no exact object types,
and TJS does not invent one. When you do want only the declared keys, for example before
storing a request body or sending a record to a client, ask for it with `strip`:

```tjs:inline
Type Address {
  example: { street: '1 Main St', city: 'Springfield', zip: '12345' }
}

const body = { street: '9 Elm', city: 'Shelbyville', zip: '54321', isAdmin: true }

console.log('passes check:', Address(body))
console.log('stripped:', JSON.stringify(Address.strip(body)))

// strip removes keys; it does not validate
const partial = Address.strip({ city: 'Nowhere', isAdmin: true })
console.log('stripped partial:', JSON.stringify(partial), Address(partial))
```

`strip` returns a new object holding only the example's keys; the input is not changed. A
value that is not an object is returned as it is. `strip` does not check anything, so a value
missing `street` comes out still missing `street`. Check first (or check the stripped result)
when the shape matters.

## A whole function as JSON Schema

`functionMetaToJSONSchema` turns a function's `__tjs` into an `input` schema (the parameters
as one object) and an `output` schema (the return type). It is part of the toolchain
(`tjs-lang/lang`), not of the language, so this example is code for a module of your own that
imports it, not a live example:

```javascript
import { functionMetaToJSONSchema } from 'tjs-lang/lang'

// transfer as defined at the top of this page
const { input, output } = functionMetaToJSONSchema(transfer.__tjs)
// input:
//   { type: 'object',
//     properties: {
//       from: { type: 'string' },
//       to: { type: 'string' },
//       amount: { type: 'number' },
//       memo: { type: 'string' } },
//     required: ['from', 'to', 'amount'] }
// output:
//   { type: 'object',
//     properties: {
//       from: { type: 'string' },
//       to: { type: 'string' },
//       amount: { type: 'number' } },
//     required: ['from', 'to', 'amount'],
//     additionalProperties: false }
```

The defaulted `memo` is in `properties` but not in `required`. This is the shape a
tool-calling LLM or an RPC layer wants: one object describing what the function accepts.

The `input` schema says nothing about extra keys, so JSON Schema's default applies and they
are allowed. The `output` schema closes the return shape with `additionalProperties: false`,
the same way `toJSONSchema()` does.

## Extra keys and the exported schema

The exported schema is stricter than the type. `Address(...)` accepts a value with keys the
example does not name, but in a `.tjs` file `Address.toJSONSchema()` writes
`additionalProperties: false`, on the top-level object and on every object nested inside it,
array items included. A JSON Schema validator fed that schema rejects extras the TJS check
accepts.

This is a known inconsistency, not a rule of the language. Emitted `.tjs` code uses TJS's
small inline runtime, whose `toJSONSchema()` still closes object shapes; the library's
`Type(...)` (imported from `tjs-lang`) re-opens them and writes `additionalProperties: true`.
See [Type Identity](/type-identity/) for the details.

Until the two agree, open the schema yourself when the tool receiving it should accept extra
keys. Setting the flag at the top level is not enough, because nested objects are closed
too, so walk the whole tree:

```tjs:inline
Type Order {
  example: { id: 'A1', customer: { name: 'Ada' }, items: [{ sku: 'X' }] }
}

// Set additionalProperties: true on every object schema in the tree.
// The parameter is untyped because a schema node can be any JSON value.
function openSchema(schema) {
  if (Array.isArray(schema)) return schema.map(openSchema)
  if (!schema || typeof schema !== 'object') return schema
  const out = {}
  for (const key of Object.keys(schema)) out[key] = openSchema(schema[key])
  if (out.type === 'object') out.additionalProperties = true
  return out
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(Order.toJSONSchema()))
console.log(JSON.stringify(openSchema(Order.toJSONSchema())))
```

The first line shows `additionalProperties: false` three times (the order, `customer`, and
each item); the second shows `true` in the same three places.

## Gotchas

- **An example is a value, so pick a representative one.** `'user@example.com'` makes the
  parameter a string; it does not make it an email. When the rule matters, declare a `Type`
  with a `predicate`, such as `predicate(x) { return x.includes('@') }`. The `Email` type in
  [Declarations](/declarations/) is a fuller version, and
  [Predicate Types](/predicate-types/) covers predicates in depth.
- **The exported schema rejects extra keys the type accepts.** See _Extra keys
  and the exported schema_ above.
- **`strip` is shallow.** It removes extra keys at the top level only. An extra key inside a
  nested object (`{ customer: { name, password } }`) or inside array items is kept.
title: Types at Runtime
description: TypeScript's types are gone by the time the code runs. TJS types are not: every function keeps a description of its signature as data, every declared `Type` is a value you can call, and both can be written out as JSON Schema for tools that have never heard of TJS. This page covers three things: reading that description, checking values against a type, and exporting a type as JSON Schema. ## A function carries its own signature A quick key to the examples below. In TJS a colon parameter's value is an example, and the example sets the type: `''` is a string, `0` an integer, `0.0` any number, `+0` a non-negative integer.

# AJS LLM System Prompt

An AJS agent is a function that runs inside the AgentVM sandbox. It can reach the outside world
only by calling **atoms**: functions the **host** (your application, the code that runs the VM)
registers with the VM and backs with capabilities such as a model client or an HTTP client. The
VM meters the work an agent does in **fuel** and stops it when the budget runs out. The
[AJS overview](/ajs/) has the rest.

This page holds the system prompt we maintain for models that write AJS. Paste the block under
[System Prompt](#system-prompt) into your model's system message, add the list of atoms your
host provides, then ask for an agent. The prompt is measured against a small model, so it is
kept deliberately narrow: it teaches one way to do each thing.

## How to use it

1. Put the System Prompt block in the system message.
2. Below it, list the atoms the model may call, each with its named inputs and what it returns.
   The model cannot know your atoms otherwise, and a call to an atom it invents fails with
   `Unknown Atom: <name>` when the agent runs. See [The atom list](#the-atom-list).
3. Take the code out of the reply. Models usually wrap it in a ` ```javascript ` fence and add
   prose around it; transpile only what is inside the fence.
4. Transpile it with your atoms, so calls to them are checked too, and then **run** it. Some
   mistakes pass the transpiler and fail only when the agent runs (see
   [Self-correction loop](#self-correction-loop)), so a reply that only transpiles has not been
   checked.
5. If either step fails, send the error message back to the model verbatim.

Steps 3 to 5 in code:

```javascript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM, defineAtom } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'
import { s } from 'tjs-lang/schema'

// One host atom. Core atoms (template, llmPredict, …) are already on every VM.
const getWeather = defineAtom(
  'getWeather',
  s.object({ city: s.string }),
  s.object({ temp: s.number, condition: s.string }),
  async ({ city }) => ({ temp: 80, condition: 'humid' })
)
const vm = new AgentVM({ getWeather })

function extractCode(reply) {
  const fenced = reply.match(/```(?:javascript|js|ajs)?\s*\n([\s\S]*?)```/)
  return (fenced ? fenced[1] : reply).trim()
}

async function runReply(reply, args) {
  let ast
  try {
    ast = transpile(extractCode(reply), { atoms: vm.atoms }).ast
  } catch (e) {
    return { problem: e.message } // send this back to the model
  }
  const { result, error } = await vm.run(ast, args, {
    fuel: 1000,
    capabilities: { llm: { predict: async (prompt) => 'It is humid.' } },
  })
  return error ? { problem: error.message } : { result }
}
```

For a reply that calls `getWeather` and then `llmPredict`, `runReply(reply, { city: 'Tokyo' })`
gives `{ result: { city: 'Tokyo', temp: 80, summary: 'It is humid.' } }`; for one with a C-style
`for` loop it gives `{ problem: 'Unsupported statement type: ForStatement. …' }`.
[Hosting the VM](/ajs-host/) covers the other `vm.run` options (timeouts, fetch domains, call
quotas) and why the transpile step belongs outside the VM host.

### The atom list

Every VM has the core atoms, listed in the [Atom Reference](/ajs-atoms/). `template` and the
other pure ones always work. The ones that reach outside need a capability from you:
`llmPredict` fails with `Capability 'llm.predict' missing` unless the run has an `llm`
capability, and `httpFetch` fetches nothing unless the run sets `allowedFetchDomains`. The
prompt's examples use `llmPredict`, `httpFetch` and `storeGet` and tell the model to use them
only if they are listed, so list every atom that will work in this run, core or your own, and
leave the rest out.

Put the list straight after the block, in the same plain style the prompt uses, with a
realistic example value for each input:

```text
### Atoms available to you

- getWeather({ city: 'Tokyo' }) returns { temp: 80, condition: 'humid' }
  The current weather for a city, temperature in Fahrenheit.
- convertTemp({ fahrenheit: 72 }) returns a number
  Fahrenheit to Celsius, rounded.
- llmPredict({ prompt: 'Summarize: ...' }) returns the model's reply as a string
- template({ tmpl: 'Hi {{name}}', vars: { name } }) returns a string

### Task

Write an agent called weatherReport that takes a city and returns { city, tempC, condition }.
```

---

## System Prompt

````
You write AJS, a small subset of JavaScript for AI agents. AJS looks like JavaScript but has
strict rules. Follow every rule below.

### 1. INPUT AND OUTPUT
- An agent is one function with ONE destructured object parameter. Give each input an EXAMPLE
  value after a colon:
  - `function greet({ name: 'World' })` — `name` is a required string
  - `function factorial({ n: 5 })` — `n` is a required integer (write `5.0` for any number)
  - `function search({ query: 'cats', limit = 10 })` — `limit` is optional, default 10
- The example value sets the type. Use the real value, never a type written as a string:
  - WRONG: `{ count: 'number' }` or `{ count: '5' }` — those are STRINGS
  - RIGHT: `{ count: 5 }` — a bare number (integer; `5.0` allows decimals)
- The agent MUST return a plain object:
  - WRONG: `return 42`, `return 'hello'`, `return [1, 2]`
  - RIGHT: `return { result: 42 }`, `return { message: 'hello' }`, `return { items: [1, 2] }`
- Do NOT write a return type after the parameters.
  - WRONG: `function foo({ x: 0 }): number { ... }`
  - RIGHT: `function foo({ x: 0 }) { ... }`
- No `async`, no `await`. Every atom call already waits for its result.
  - WRONG: `let page = await fetch(url)`
  - RIGHT: `let page = httpFetch({ url })`

### 2. STATEMENTS
- Variables: `let` and `const`. Destructuring a variable is not allowed:
  - WRONG: `let { a } = obj`
  - RIGHT: `let a = obj.a`
- Loops: `for (const x of list)` and `while`. Nothing else.
  - WRONG: `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)`, `for (const k in obj)`
  - RIGHT: `for (const item of items) { ... }`
  - RIGHT: `let i = 1` then `while (i <= n) { total = total + i; i = i + 1 }`
  - Always change the counter inside a `while`, or the agent is stopped for running too long.
  - For an object's keys: `for (const k of Object.keys(obj)) { ... }`
- NO `break`, NO `continue`, NO `switch`.
  - Instead of `switch`, use `if` / `else if` / `else`.
  - Instead of `break`, `return` from inside the loop, or use a flag in the `while` condition:
    `while (i < items.length && found == null) { ... }`
  - Instead of `continue`, wrap the rest of the loop body in an `if`.
- Assign only to plain variables. You cannot assign to a property or an index:
  - WRONG: `obj.count = 5`
  - RIGHT: `obj = { ...obj, count: 5 }`
  - WRONG: `arr[0] = 'x'`
  - RIGHT: build a new list with a loop and `push`, then assign it: `arr = changed`
  - `push` changes a list in place and is allowed: `results.push(item)`
- Errors: no `throw`. `Error('message')` fails like `throw`: inside `try` it jumps to `catch`;
  outside `try` it stops the agent with that error.
  - WRONG: `throw new Error('bad input')`
  - RIGHT: `if (n < 0) { Error('n must not be negative') }`
- `try { ... } catch (err) { ... }` recovers from a failed atom call or `Error()`. `err` is the
  error MESSAGE, a string: use `err`, not `err.message`. Without `try`, a failure stops the agent.
- No `class`, `new`, `this`, `import`, `require`.

### 3. CALLS
- Atoms are the tools the host gives you. Call ONLY the atoms listed for you. `template` is
  always available. The examples below also use `llmPredict`, `httpFetch` and `storeGet`: use
  those only if they are listed. An atom takes ONE object of named inputs:
  - RIGHT: `llmPredict({ prompt: question })`, `httpFetch({ url })`, `storeGet({ key })`
  - WRONG: `llmPredict(question)` (refused): a positional call
- An atom call must be the WHOLE right-hand side of `let`, `const` or an assignment, or a
  statement on its own. Store the result, then use it:
  - WRONG: `return { reply: llmPredict({ prompt }) }`
  - RIGHT: `let reply = llmPredict({ prompt })` then `return { reply }`
- `template` fills in text:
  `let message = template({ tmpl: 'Hello, {{name}}!', vars: { name } })`
  Template literals also work:
  ``let message = `Hello, ${name}!` ``
- You may write helper functions above the agent. The LAST function is the agent. A helper
  cannot read the agent's variables: pass in what it needs as arguments. A helper takes
  positional arguments, may call atoms and earlier helpers, and may return any value. Like an
  atom, a helper call must be the whole right-hand side: `const d = double(n)`, not
  `double(n) + 1`.
- Builtins use normal JavaScript syntax: `Math.max(a, b)`, `JSON.parse(text)`,
  `JSON.stringify(obj)`, `Object.keys(obj)`, `text.split(',')`, `text.trim().toLowerCase()`.

### 4. ARRAYS
- Use `map`, `filter`, `find` and `reduce` with an arrow function: `items.map(x => x * 2)`
- ONE arrow-function method per statement. Do not chain them:
  - WRONG: `let r = items.filter(x => x > 1).map(x => x * 2)`
  - RIGHT: `let big = items.filter(x => x > 1)` then `let r = big.map(x => x * 2)`
- `some` and `every` are NOT available. Use `filter` and check the length:
  `let bad = items.filter(x => x < 0)` then `if (bad.length > 0) { ... }`
- `sort()` takes no comparator:
  - WRONG: `items.sort((a, b) => a - b)`
  - RIGHT: `items.sort()`

### 5. VALUES AND OPERATORS
- Operators (`+`, `<`, ...) need strings, numbers or booleans, never arrays or objects:
  - WRONG: `'items: ' + items`
  - RIGHT: `'items: ' + items.join(', ')`
- Method arguments must have the right type: a count is a number, not a string.
  `'ab'.repeat(3)`, not `'ab'.repeat('3')`.
- `==` never converts types: `'1' == 1` is false. `null == undefined` is true.
- Reading a property of null gives undefined, not an error: `user.address.city` is safe.
- A method is not a value. Call it (`s.trim()`), never store it (`const f = s.trim`).
- Regexes work in `replace`, `split`, `match` and `search`: `s.replace(/\s+/g, ' ')`.
  - `re.test(s)` is NOT available. Use `s.search(re) !== -1`.
  - No backreferences (`\1`), no lookahead or lookbehind (`(?=`, `(?<=`), no `\p{...}`.

### 6. DATES, SETS, SCHEMAS
- No `new`. `Date()` is now; `Date('2024-01-15')` parses an ISO string.
  - A Date is immutable and UTC. Months are 1 to 12 (1 = January).
  - Fields: `.year`, `.month`, `.day`, `.hours`, `.minutes`, `.seconds`, `.timestamp`,
    and `.value` (the ISO string).
  - `d.add({ days: 5 })` returns a NEW Date. `d.format('YYYY-MM-DD')` returns a string.
- `Set([1, 2, 2])` is a list of unique items: `.add(x)`, `.remove(x)`, `.has(x)`, `.size`,
  `.toArray()`, and `.union(other)`, `.intersection(other)`, `.diff(other)`, which return NEW sets.
- `filter(data, { a: 0, b: '' })` with TWO arguments is a builtin, not the array method
  `items.filter(x => ...)`. It returns a copy of `data` with only the keys `a` and `b`. The
  example values are checked like an agent's inputs: here `a` must be a whole number and `b` a
  string, and both must be present, or the step fails. Use it to clean up an API or model response.
- Schemas are plain data. `Schema.string`, `Schema.number`, `Schema.email` are ready-made
  schemas (values, not functions). `Schema.object({ ... })` builds an object schema. Write
  limits as keywords, not chained calls like `.min()`:
  `let ok = Schema.isValid(x, Schema.object({ name: Schema.string, age: { type: 'integer', minimum: 0 } }))`

### 7. REPORTING
- Put everything the caller needs in the returned object. Do not use `console.log`: its output
  goes only to a debug trace, so the caller never sees it.

### EXAMPLES

**Example 1: Calling atoms**
```javascript
function summarizeTopic({ topic: 'quantum computing', maxWords = 50 }) {
  if (topic.trim() == '') {
    return { error: 'No topic given' }
  }
  let prompt = template({
    tmpl: 'Explain {{topic}} in at most {{maxWords}} words.',
    vars: { topic, maxWords },
  })
  let summary = llmPredict({ prompt })
  return { topic, summary }
}
```

**Example 2: Factorial with a while loop (number parameter)**
```javascript
function factorial({ n: 5 }) {
  let result = 1
  let i = n
  while (i > 1) {
    result = result * i
    i = i - 1
  }
  return { result }
}
```

**Example 3: Several number parameters**
```javascript
function calculateVolume({ width: 2, height: 3, depth: 4 }) {
  let volume = width * height * depth
  return { volume }
}
```
Note: width, height and depth have BARE NUMBER examples (2, 3, 4), not strings like '2' or 'number'.

**Example 4: Greeting with the template atom (optional parameter)**
```javascript
function greet({ name: 'World', greeting = 'Hello' }) {
  let message = template({ tmpl: '{{greeting}}, {{name}}!', vars: { greeting, name } })
  return { message }
}
```

**Example 5: Looping, filtering, recovering from an error**
```javascript
function priceReport({ items: [{ name: 'pen', price: 2 }], limit = 10 }) {
  let cheap = items.filter(item => item.price <= limit)
  let names = cheap.map(item => item.name)
  let total = 0
  for (const item of cheap) {
    total = total + item.price
  }
  let average = 0
  try {
    if (cheap.length == 0) {
      Error('no items under the limit')
    }
    average = total / cheap.length
  } catch (err) {
    return { names, total, average, note: err }
  }
  return { names, total, average }
}
```
````

---

## Why the prompt is shaped this way

**One signature shape.** The prompt teaches a single destructured parameter with example values,
and a returned object. AJS also accepts positional parameters (`function f(n: 5)`), and both run
the same way. A destructured signature matches how agents are called (with one arguments
object) and how they compose (one agent's result object is the next one's arguments). Teaching
two shapes gives a small model two chances to mix them up.

**No declared result.** AJS lets a signature declare the object an agent returns, after the
parameters:

```ajs
function double({ x = 3 }): { y: 0 } {
  return { y: x * 2 }
}
```

The VM enforces it exactly: every declared member present with the declared type, and no extra
members (see
[Both sides of a typed signature are enforced](../DOCS-AJS.md#both-sides-of-a-typed-signature-are-enforced)).
Returning `{ y: x * 2, z: 1 }` from `double` fails the run with
`Result does not match the declared result type`. That strictness is the problem for a small
model: it is likely to write TypeScript's `): number`, which is refused at transpile time, or to
declare a result and then return one extra key. So the prompt says not to write one.

If you want an output contract, keep it on your side: state the result shape in the task ("return
an object with `city`, `tempC` and `condition`"), and add the declared result to the signature
yourself before you transpile the reply.

---

## Self-correction loop

The transpiler's error messages name the construct and, mostly, the fix, so the cheapest repair
loop is to send the message straight back:

1. Ask the model for an agent, using the prompt above.
2. Take the code out of the fence, transpile it with your atoms
   (`transpile(source, { atoms: vm.atoms })`), and run it.
3. If either step fails, reply with the error message: "That failed with: `<message>`. Fix it
   and send only the code." If the message is one that names the symptom rather than the fix
   (see the hints below), append the hint to that reply.
4. Cap the loop at a few attempts. A model that repeats the same mistake needs a better hint,
   not another try.

**Hints worth adding**, because the message does not say what to do:

- A chained `filter(…).map(…)` or a `sort` comparator both give
  `Unsupported expression type in condition: ArrowFunctionExpression`. Say "put each array
  method in its own `let`", or "`sort()` takes no comparator; call `sort()` alone or build the
  order in a loop".
- `re.test(s)`: say "use `s.search(re) !== -1`".
- An atom call inside an expression: say "store the atom's result in a variable first".
- `await` in a plain function gives `Cannot use keyword 'await' outside an async function`,
  which points the model at adding `async`, the wrong fix. Say "remove `await`; atom calls
  already wait".
- A string example like `'number'`: say "use a bare example value, such as `0`".

The messages below are what the transpiler and VM give for the mistakes models make most
often. AJS is called AsyncJS in some of them; it is the same language. A message may continue on
further lines (often with a code sample) and ends with the source position, which is left out
here.

**Caught when transpiling:**

| The model wrote                          | Start of the error                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)`            | ``Unsupported statement type: ForStatement. AJS has no `for` loops. Use `while` with a counter:``                                      |
| `for (const k in obj)`                   | ``Unsupported statement type: ForInStatement. AJS has no `for...in`. Get the keys and walk them with `while`:``                        |
| `switch (x) { … }`                       | ``Unsupported statement type: SwitchStatement. AJS has no `switch`. Use `if`/`else if`:``                                              |
| `break` / `continue`                     | `Unsupported statement type: BreakStatement` (or `ContinueStatement`)                                                                  |
| `throw new Error('…')`                   | `'throw' is not supported in AsyncJS. Use Error('message') to trigger error flow`                                                      |
| `new Date()`                             | `The 'new' keyword is not supported in AsyncJS. Use Date() or Date('2024-01-15') instead - no 'new' needed.`                           |
| `await` in a plain function              | `Cannot use keyword 'await' outside an async function`                                                                                 |
| `await` in an `async` function           | `Unsupported expression in AsyncJS: AwaitExpression`                                                                                   |
| `obj.x = 5` or `arr[0] = 5`              | `Only simple variable assignment is supported`                                                                                         |
| `let { a } = obj`                        | `Only simple variable names are supported`                                                                                             |
| `items.some(…)`                          | `Method 'some' is not available in AsyncJS — use for...of, or map/filter/find/reduce with an arrow function`                           |
| `a.filter(…).map(…)`                     | `Unsupported expression type in condition: ArrowFunctionExpression`                                                                    |
| `a.sort((x, y) => x - y)`                | `Unsupported expression type in condition: ArrowFunctionExpression`                                                                    |
| `/^\d+$/.test(s)`                        | `Method 'test' is not available in AsyncJS`                                                                                            |
| `llmPredict(question)` (refused)         | `'llmPredict' takes named arguments: write llmPredict({ name: value, … }), not llmPredict(a, b). Positional arguments are for local functions.` |
| `llmPredict({ system, user })`           | `'llmPredict' has no input 'system'. It takes llmPredict({ prompt, options }).`                                                        |
| `function f({ x: 0 }): number`           | `Declared result: an agent returns an object, so a declared number result can never be met. Declare the object it returns, e.g. ): { value: 0 }` |

**Caught only when the agent runs:**

| The model wrote                   | Start of the error                                           |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `return { v: llmPredict({ … }) }` | `Atom 'llmPredict' cannot be called inside an expression`    |
| `search({ query })` (not an atom) | `Unknown Atom: search`                                       |
| `return { total }` (never declared) | `'total' is not defined`                                   |
| `return total`                    | `Agent must return an object, got number`                    |
| `function f({ n: 'number' })`     | `Input validation failed: args do not match expected schema` |

The last row needs care. `{ n: 'number' }` declares `n` as a string, so the run fails only when
the caller passes a number. If the caller happens to pass a string, nothing fails, and the
mistake can go unnoticed. Check the signature yourself.

---

## Compact version (for context-limited models)

Use this when the full prompt does not fit. It keeps the rules small models break most often,
and drops: helper functions, `try`/`catch`, `Object.keys` for walking an object's keys,
`filter(data, shape)`, `Schema`, the Set methods, the `console.log` rule, and every example.
Expect more of the mistakes in the tables above. Only the full prompt is measured against a
model; this one is not.

````
You write AJS, a subset of JavaScript for agents. Rules:

1. One destructured parameter with EXAMPLE values; return a plain object:
   `function add({ a: 0, b: 0 }) { return { sum: a + b } }`
   - Numbers are bare: `{ n: 5 }`, never `{ n: '5' }` or `{ n: 'number' }`.
   - Optional input: `{ limit = 10 }`. No return type after the parameters.
   - WRONG: `return 42`. RIGHT: `return { result: 42 }`.
2. NO: async, await, new, class, this, import, throw, switch, break, continue,
   C-style `for (;;)`, `for...in`. Loops are `for (const x of list)` and `while`.
3. Assign only to variables: not `obj.x = 1` but `obj = { ...obj, x: 1 }`. `list.push(x)` is fine.
4. Call ONLY the atoms listed for you. Atoms take one object of named inputs:
   `llmPredict({ prompt })`, `httpFetch({ url })`.
   An atom call is the whole right-hand side: `let r = llmPredict({ prompt })`, then use `r`.
5. One arrow-function array method per statement (no `.filter().map()` chains).
   No `some`, `every`, or `sort` comparator.
6. Errors: `Error('message')` fails like `throw`; outside `try` it stops the agent.
   In `catch (err)`, `err` is a string.
7. Create dates and sets without `new`: `Date()`, `Date('2024-01-15')`, `Set([1, 2])`.
   Dates are immutable, UTC, months 1 to 12.
8. Regex: `s.search(re) !== -1`, never `re.test(s)`. No backreferences or lookaround.
9. Operators take primitives: `'n=' + list.join(',')`, never `'n=' + list`.
````

---

## Maintaining this prompt

This prompt must change when [DOCS-AJS.md](../DOCS-AJS.md) changes (signatures, loops, forbidden
constructs, builtins, atoms). It is also a test input: `src/use-cases/ajs-grokkability.test.ts`
reads the System Prompt block from this exact file (the first four-backtick block after the
`## System Prompt` heading) and measures how often a small pinned model (gemma-4-e2b) writes AJS
that runs. Run `bun run test:grok` before and after any edit to the block, record both rates in
the commit message, and treat a drop as a regression in the prompt. The compact version is not
measured.

# Case study: fixing `switch`

A record of one language decision, start to unfinished, including the measurements that
misled us and the ones that held. Written down because the *process* turned out to be more
interesting than the conclusion, and because several of the wrong turns are the kind nobody
writes up.

Outcome: **`given` shipped, `switch` reverted to C semantics with a warning, and existing
code is upgraded automatically where that is provably safe.** The keyword was chosen on
structural argument, because the measurement that appeared to rank the candidates turned out
to be noise — which is the most useful thing in this document.

`given` is TJS's replacement for `switch`. Each arm can list several values, no arm runs into
the next, and values compare the way TJS's `==` does:

```tjs
function shape(kind: 'circle'): 'round' {
  given kind {
    'circle', 'ellipse' { return 'round' }
    'square' { return 'square' }
  } else {
    return 'unknown'
  }
}

console.log(shape('ellipse'), shape('square'), shape('blob'))
// round square unknown
```

This page is a design record: why the construct exists and why it looks the way it does. For
how to use it, see [Control Flow: given](/given-dispatch/).

Much of the evidence below comes from asking an AI language model what a program returns.
Models now read and write a large share of code, and they are a cheap stand-in for a reader
meeting TJS for the first time, so "can a model read this correctly?" was the test. The
model-reading test turned out not to separate the keyword candidates, so the keyword was
chosen on design grounds (collision risk and meaning) instead.

---

## 1. The defect

`switch` in JavaScript is C's, and it carries four problems that have nothing to do with each
other except a common origin:

1. `case` compares with `===`. In TJS, `==` is a comparison without the footguns (no type
   coercion, `null` equals `undefined`; see [Honest Equality](/honest-equality/)), so
   `switch` silently disagrees with the rest of the file: `case null:` does not match
   `undefined`, though `undefined == null` is true.
2. Multiple values sharing one block is only expressible **as** fallthrough.
3. Fallthrough is the **default**, so correctness requires `break` on every arm.
4. All arms share **one scope**, so `let` leaks and `const` collides.

```javascript
switch (x) {
  case 'a':            // problem 2: 'a' reaches the shared block only by falling through
  case 'b':
    const n = 1
    log(n)             // problem 3: no break, so 'a' and 'b' also run the next arm
  case 'c':
    const n = 2        // problem 4: SyntaxError, `n` is already declared in this scope
    break
}
```

Two of these ship as errors in `eslint:recommended` (`no-fallthrough`, `no-case-declarations`).
The ecosystem decided the defaults were wrong long ago and has been hand-patching ever since,
because the language cannot change. That is the observation the whole project rests on: *a
pattern that needs a heavy-handed lint rule is a language defect, not a user error.*

## 2. What we built first — and later reversed

Swift's answer is to end every arm on its own (an implicit `break`). That one decision fixes
problems 2, 3 and 4 together: arms can list several values, fallthrough becomes something you
ask for, and each arm gets its own scope. For problem 1, compare with `Eq`, the function
behind TJS's `==`.

That shipped ([#43]) — multi-value `case 'a', 'b':`, opt-in `fallthrough`, per-arm scope, and
the switched-on value compared the same way `==` compares. It also needed `Exactly(…)`
underneath. In TJS a colon value is an example that widens to its type, so a field written
`kind: 'circle'` means "any string", and two types that differ only in that field (a
`Circle` and a `Rect`) looked identical when the switch dispatched on them. `Exactly('circle')`
keeps the literal.

Three implementation traps, each worth remembering:

- **Rewriting to an if-chain is wrong.** `break` inside a `switch` breaks the switch; inside
  an `if` it breaks the enclosing *loop*. That rewrite silently changes control flow.
- **Per-arm scope cannot be added after parsing.** A switch body is one block scope in JS,
  so two `const`s with the same name are a syntax error, and the parser (acorn) is right to
  reject them. Each arm has to be wrapped in braces in the source text before it is parsed.
- **Fixing the runtime changed nothing that ships.** Each compiled file carries its own small
  copy of the runtime, so a fix to the main runtime's `Type()` did not reach compiled code
  until the copy (its `__match` helper) learned the same rule.

All of this made `switch` mean something different in a `.tjs` file than in a `.js` one.
Section 3 shows why that was a problem; section 4 is where it was reversed.

## 3. The measurement that changed the plan

We showed a model a short `switch`, varied only the file extension, and asked what `f('a')`
returned. Without `break`, JavaScript's arms fall through and the answer is `1,2`; under the
reworked TJS `switch` they did not, and the answer is `1`. "Correct" means the answer the
file's own rules give: `1,2` for the `.js` file without `break`, `1` for the `.tjs` one. Each
condition was asked five times. The probe is `experiments/agent-legibility/switch-probe.ts`;
the numbers below are from qwen3.8-27b, a 27-billion-parameter model (the full series is in
`switch-probe-results.md` beside it):

| condition | correct | **wrong** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| explicit `break`, as `.js` | 5/5 | 0 |
| no `break`, as `.js` | 5/5 | 0 |
| no `break`, as **`.tjs`** | **0/5** | **5** |

Not "poorly" — the **worst possible result**, and not from uncertainty: both controls are
100%. Shown identical text as `.tjs`, it applied C fallthrough five times out of five,
confidently.

Its own reasoning, verbatim: *"…maybe has 'case' with comma to group multiple cases? There is
a language 'TJS'…"* The model has no prior knowledge of the extension. The `.tjs` extension
is the only thing that tells a reader this file follows TJS rules: it is an *out-of-band* marker, outside the
code itself. It is what lets TJS change `==` for a whole file, which an in-code directive
like `"use strict"` never could, and it carries **nothing** to a reader.

A one-line comment in the file stating the rule (that arms do not fall through) took the 27B
model to 5/5. A much smaller model (gemma-4-e4b, about 4 billion parameters) was unmoved by
anything in the file: it scored 0/5 on every TJS condition, comment or not. So the
affordance has to be in the code, and even there it only reaches a reader capable of acting
on it.

## 4. The reframe: if it behaves differently, it should look different

The comment fixes the file that carries it. It does not reach the places where only a few lines
of the file are visible: a snippet in chat, a diff, a stack trace, a search result. [#48]
proposed the alternative: **stop changing what `switch` means, and give the fixed construct a
different name.**

Then a stronger form of the idea — change the *shape* too, not just the word:

```text
given x {
  'a', 'b' { … }
} else { … }
```

No `case`. No colons. No implicit blocks. `else` for the remaining arm. Every difference
visible.

Measured on qwen3.8-27b, five samples each. The keyword was not yet decided, and in this run
it was `match`; sections 7 and 8 are how it became `given`. "NEW syntax" is the brace-and-comma
form above, every condition is a `.tjs` file, and "no-answer" means the model did not commit
to a return value:

| condition | correct | **wrong** | no-answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `switch`, C syntax | 0/5 | **5** | 0 |
| `switch`, NEW syntax | 0/5 | 0 | **5** |
| new keyword, NEW syntax | 4/5 | 0 | 1 |

**Two findings, and the second was a surprise.** Changing the shape eliminated every
confident wrong answer — 5 to 0 — which is the failure mode that ships bugs. But keeping the
*name* while changing the shape produced five **no-answers**: the model cannot reconcile "this
is `switch`" with "this does not look like `switch`", and stalls. The keyword and the shape
have to move together.

## 5. Syntax details that earned themselves

These were worked out while the keyword was `match`; they apply unchanged to `given`.

**No parentheses.** This is already valid JavaScript:

```javascript
match (x)
{ … }
```

JavaScript inserts a semicolon at the line break, so it reads as a call, `match(x);`,
followed by an ordinary block. Without parentheses, `match x {` is never valid JavaScript, so
the transpiler can tell the construct apart from ordinary code. The choice that looked like
taste is what makes detection possible.

**Detection is the hard part.** Detection means the transpiler finding the construct in source
text, and it is hard because no candidate keyword is reserved: any of them can also be a
variable, a property or a word in a string. A first prototype mangled
`const match = 1; if (y) { … }` into `switch (= 1; if (y))`. It was fixed by requiring the
value after the keyword to look like an expression (no `;`, no leading operator) and by
skipping declarations (`const given = …`) and property access (`obj.given`). The
false-positive shapes we found, including the keyword inside a string literal, are now left
untouched.

The fallback block is `else`; section 9 says why.

## 6. Rewriting existing code, which is the actual job

Adding a better alternative is not fixing the language. `switchToGiven` rewrites a C `switch`
**only where it provably means the same thing**: every non-empty arm leaves
(`return`/`throw`/`break`/`continue`), so implicit-versus-explicit break is unobservable.
Stacked empty arms become multi-value; trailing `break` is dropped as dead code; `default`
becomes `else`. Where an arm genuinely runs into the next, the switch is **not** rewritten,
and a note naming its line says why. A converter that is occasionally wrong is worse than one
that is honest.

Two terms matter here. **Conversion** (`fromTS`) turns a TypeScript file into TJS that still
behaves like JavaScript; its output carries a `/* tjs <- source */` comment, which means "JS
semantics". **Graduation** removes that comment, which turns on every TJS rule. The rewrite
runs at graduation, not conversion, and the distinction is load-bearing: `given` is lowered
only for native TJS, so emitting it at conversion time would produce files that do not parse.
That is exactly the shape of [#37], where dropping `new` at conversion time shipped modules
that could not be imported. Graduation strips the annotation, applies both rewrites, then
checks that the result still compiles as native TJS, returning the input unchanged (and
saying why) if it does not. It is one function, `graduate.ts`.

On our own source: **44 switches upgraded across 19 files, 0 declined**, which is consistent
with `no-fallthrough` being an error in our lint. The dogfood check, which converts and then
graduates each of our own source files, went from 104 of 105 files to all **105**.

### Three defects the rewrite found, none of them in the rewrite

Worth recording because all three were **silent**, and two predate this work entirely:

1. **It deleted every comment.** Arm text is sliced from the first statement to the last, so
   anything sitting *between* arms simply vanished — including a twenty-line rationale block in
   our own converter. Every test stayed green, because no test asserted that comments survive.
   The comments are usually the part of a file you cannot reconstruct; a converter that drops
   them is worse than one that declines.
2. **`given` did not nest.** Lowering slices an arm's body as *text* rather than re-scanning
   it, so one pass reached only the outermost construct and the inner one arrived at the parser
   as `given b {`, which is not JavaScript. The transform now runs to a fixpoint. This shipped
   with `given` and no test had nested one.
3. **The JS-semantics check was blind to string literals.** The annotation that means "JS
   semantics" was detected by scanning **raw** source text, so any file that merely *mentioned* `/* tjs <- … */` in a string was
   read as TS-originated and silently lost the entire language — `==` stopped being `Eq`,
   dictionary defaults went atomic, `given` never lowered. `from-ts.ts` emits that annotation
   from a template, so **the converter's own source was the first casualty**, and had been for
   as long as the check existed.

The pattern is the same one this whole document keeps running into: the failures that matter
here do not throw. They produce plausible output. The third is the most common defect in this
codebase, a pass that misreads code merely *mentioning* what it scans for, appearing in the one
place nobody had thought to look: the check that decides *which language the file is written
in*.

## 7. The keyword, and how the data failed us

Candidates measured cold (no explanation or cheat sheet), same program, only the word
varying. The `match` row is the same run as section 4's last row. These tables, and the
re-run below, are in `experiments/agent-legibility/FINDINGS.md` (the "`match` vs `switch`" and
"Keyword candidates" sections, 2026-08-29):

| keyword | correct | **wrong** | no-answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `match` | 4/5 | 0 | 1 |
| `when` | 3/5 | 0 | 2 |
| `given` | 1/5 | 0 | 4 |

That looked like a ranking, and it was written up as one. **Then the identical `given`
condition was re-run and scored 4/5.** A swing of three in a sample of five, same model, same prompt.

So the ranking was noise. What the re-run establishes is a property of the *instrument*:

> **Correctness is stable; willingness to commit is not.** Every new keyword produced zero
> wrong answers in every run. The thing that varied wildly was whether the model answered at
> all.

This matters beyond the keyword, because it means a probe scored on "correct out of N"
silently mixes a stable signal with a noisy one. The two should be read separately, and the
no-answer column is the one that needs a much larger N.

**What survives.** The bare `.tjs` `switch` scored 0/5 in every run, on both models, and on
the 27B model every condition that used the new shape gave zero wrong answers, whatever the
keyword. Only the first finding below was also checked on the 4B model:

- the C shape in `.tjs` produces **confident wrong answers**, reliably;
- **any** new shape produces **zero** wrong answers, reliably;
- an inline comment stating the rule takes comprehension to 5/5, on a model large enough to
  use it.

**What does not survive:** any ranking among `match` / `when` / `given`.

## 8. Where that leaves the decision

The measurement does not choose the keyword, so the structural arguments do. Both favour
`given`:

**Collision risk**, counted in our own source on 2026-08-29:

| keyword | occurrences | as a **method call** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `match` | 417 | **33** (`.match(…)`) |
| `when` | 423 | 0 |
| `given` | 21 | 0 |

None are reserved, so detection must exclude every one of those other uses, which is why
`when`'s 423 still count against it. `match` is worst, in the dangerous way: a method call is
the shape most easily mistaken for the construct.

**Semantics.** This construct compares **values** with `Eq`. It does not destructure, bind, or
guard. `match` names what Rust, Python and Scala do — *pattern matching* — so it over-promises
to precisely the reader whose prior it was meant to recruit. `given x` reads in English as
"given this value, these are the cases", which is what the code does.

There are also advantages a comprehension probe structurally cannot see: a rarer word is
easier to search for, and documentation about `given` is not competing with a decade of
`String.prototype.match` results. A cold-reading probe measures recognition, not
findability — and recognition is the one thing a novel keyword is guaranteed to lose at.

That is worth stating carefully rather than as a rationalisation. The risk of reasoning this
way is obvious: it can excuse any result. The check is that the argument was made *before*
the re-run collapsed the ranking (in `FINDINGS.md` the collision and semantics arguments
precede the retraction), and that the ranking collapsed on its own evidence rather than
being argued away.

## 9. The fallback block: a measurement that legitimately abstains

Three spellings, same program, asking what an unmatched value returns. This was a one-off
run, recorded only in the message of commit `1906d626`:

| spelling | correct | wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `given x { … } else { … }` | 5/5 | 0 |
| `given x { … default { … } }` | 5/5 | 0 |
| `given x { … } otherwise { … }` | 5/5 | 0 |

**All three, perfectly.** Unlike the keyword ranking this is not noise — it is a real
negative result, and the reason is structural: the fallback block's meaning is carried by its
POSITION, not its name. A reader who has understood the arms understands the leftover block
whatever it is called.

So the choice is design, and the argument that decides it is the same one that drove the
rename:

- **`default` re-imports the prior we just escaped.** A reader who sees `default` inside
  `given` has been handed a piece of `switch`, and may reasonably reach for the rest of it —
  `case`, `break`, fallthrough. Renaming to shed a prior and then keeping one of its keywords
  gives back part of what the rename bought.
- **`otherwise` is not a reserved word**, so it carries the same collision problem `given`
  does, for no gain over a word that is.
- **`else` is reserved, and already means exactly this.** It parallels `if`/`else`, which
  every JavaScript reader knows, and it sits outside the arm list where it visually separates
  "the cases" from "everything else".

`else` it is. Worth recording that this was decided on argument with the measurement
explicitly abstaining, rather than the measurement being ignored.

## 10. Where it landed, and what is still open

**Decided and shipped.** `given` is the construct; `else` is the fallback; `switch` keeps C
semantics exactly and gets a warning pointing at the replacement, so nothing silently changes
meaning. Existing code is upgraded at graduation where that is provably safe.

**Still open** (as of 2026-11-06):

- **Re-measure with a cheat sheet.** The no-answer mode is exactly what guidance fixes: in an
  earlier experiment, a small model writing AJS succeeded 0% of the time with no guidance and
  67% with a short cheat sheet (`FINDINGS.md`, "Guidance A/B"). and cold reading is the worst case for a
  novel word and the best case for a familiar one. The keyword ranking should be re-taken under
  those conditions, with a much larger N on the no-answer column specifically.
- **`else if (cond) { }`, considered and not taken.** If `else` reads as `if`/`else`, that is
  the obvious next step. It would mix value dispatch with condition dispatch in one construct,
  which is a bigger change than it looks, and nothing needs it today.

## 11. What generalises

Three things, none of them about `switch`:

1. **A pattern that needs a heavy-handed lint rule is a language defect.** That is what
   started this, and it held up.
2. **Correctness is stable; willingness to commit is not.** A probe scored "correct out of N"
   silently mixes a stable signal with a noisy one. Read the columns separately, and treat a
   ranking built on the noisy one as unmeasured until it replicates. We wrote one up as a
   finding before it did.
3. **If it behaves differently, it should look different.** The out-of-band signal — the file
   extension — carries nothing to a reader. This is the single most transferable result here,
   and it applies to every remaining place TJS changes a JavaScript meaning in place.

[#43]: https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/issues/43
[#48]: https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/issues/48
[#37]: https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/issues/37

# Date Formatting (with import)

This chapter uses [date-fns](https://date-fns.org), an ordinary npm package, from a native
`.tjs` file (one with no `TjsCompat` line at the top, so every TJS rule applies). The
library knows nothing about TJS. The functions you write around it have TJS signatures,
and those signatures are where bad input is stopped.

It covers, in order: checking input at the signature, why you do not write `new Date()`,
importing an npm package with no install step, return examples that cannot be run, time
zones, and `TjsCompat` for converting a whole file.

One rule to read the code by: in a TJS signature, the value after a colon is an
**example**, not a type. `date: '2024-01-15'` accepts any string, and `days: 5` any integer.
The value after the closing parenthesis is a **return example**: calling the function with
the parameter examples should give exactly that result. [TJS Syntax](/tjs-syntax/) has the
full rules.

```tjs:inline
import { format, formatDistance, addBusinessDays, parseISO } from 'date-fns'
import { Timestamp } from 'tjs-lang'

// Reformat a 'YYYY-MM-DD' date with a date-fns pattern
function formatDate(date: '2024-01-15', pattern: 'yyyy-MM-dd'): '2024-01-15' {
  return format(parseISO(date), pattern)
}

// Five working days after Monday 15 January is Monday 22 January
function addWorkdays(date: '2024-01-15', days: 5): '2024-01-22' {
  return format(addBusinessDays(parseISO(date), days), 'yyyy-MM-dd')
}

// "How long ago", measured from `now` rather than from the clock,
// so the same arguments always give the same answer
function timeAgo(date: '2024-01-15', now: '2024-01-22'): '7 days ago' {
  return formatDistance(parseISO(date), parseISO(now), { addSuffix: true })
}

// The end date is `workdays` working days after the start, skipping weekends
function describeEvent(
  event: { title: 'Meeting', startDate: '2024-01-15', workdays: 1 }
): 'Meeting: Jan 15 - Jan 16, 2024' {
  const start = parseISO(event.startDate)
  const end = addBusinessDays(start, event.workdays)
  return `${event.title}: ${format(start, 'MMM d')} - ${format(end, 'MMM d, yyyy')}`
}

console.log(formatDate('2024-01-15', 'MMMM d, yyyy'))
console.log(addWorkdays('2024-01-19', 1)) // Friday + 1 working day = Monday
console.log(timeAgo('2024-01-15', '2024-03-15'))
console.log(timeAgo('2024-01-15', Timestamp.iso(Timestamp.now())))
console.log(describeEvent({ title: 'Launch', startDate: '2024-03-01', workdays: 2 }))

// Bad calls are refused by the signature, before date-fns sees them
console.log(String(formatDate(20240115, 'yyyy')))
console.log(String(describeEvent({ title: 'Launch', startDate: '2024-03-01' })))
```

It prints (the fourth line depends on today's date):

```text
January 15, 2024
2024-01-22
2 months ago
almost 3 years ago
Launch: Mar 1 - Mar 5, 2024
MonadicError: Expected string for 'formatDate.date', got number
MonadicError: Expected integer for 'describeEvent.event.workdays', got undefined
```

(The error messages also name the file and line, which differ between the page and your
machine.) The launch runs from Mar 1 to Mar 5 because 1 March 2024 is a Friday: two working
days later is the following Tuesday.

## What to notice

**The signature checks the input.** `formatDate(date: '2024-01-15', pattern: 'yyyy-MM-dd')`
says both parameters are required strings. Called with a number, it does not throw: it
**returns** a `MonadicError`, an error value naming the parameter, and the program carries
on with the next line. That is better than handing `20240115` to date-fns and getting back
a `RangeError: Invalid time value` from somewhere inside the library. (`String(…)` is there
to print the error as one line of text; logged directly, it prints as an object with all
its fields. [Error Handling](/error-handling/) covers what to do with one.)

The object parameter of `describeEvent` is checked member by member, and because it is
declared with a colon, every member is required. A missing `workdays` is reported by its
path. The message says `integer` because `1` is an integer example; `1.0` would accept any
number.

**Only one line needs the clock.** `timeAgo` takes `now` as an argument, so the function
is pure: same inputs, same output, no reading of the clock. That is what makes its return
example true for good: `timeAgo('2024-01-15', '2024-01-22')` is `'7 days ago'` today and
next year. (Whether TJS can _run_ that example is a separate question, answered in the next
section.) The current time enters at the one call that wants it, `Timestamp.now()`, which
is milliseconds since 1970 UTC (the number `Date.now()` returns). `Timestamp.iso` turns it
into a string `parseISO` reads. `Timestamp` is imported from `'tjs-lang'`; it and its
companion `LegalDate` are documented in [Built-in Types and Dates](/built-in-types/).

**No raw `Date` is constructed.** In a native `.tjs` file, `new Date(…)` is a compile
error: the file does not transpile, and the message suggests what to write instead. The
reason is that a `Date` is mutable and most of its methods answer in the time zone of
whatever machine runs the code ([What `.tjs` Refuses](/safer-code/) has the details).
date-fns creates `Date` objects internally, and `parseISO` returns one; that is allowed.
The rule is about the syntax you write, not about values a library hands you. When you do
want a real `Date` yourself, write `LegacyDate(x)`. It needs no import, because it is the
compiler's spelling of `new Date(x)`, named so a reviewer can find it.
`LegacyDate().toISOString()` would have worked as the `now` argument above.

**The import is a bare specifier.** On this page there is no bundler and no install step:
the bare name `'date-fns'` is resolved to a CDN and cached (see
[CDN Hints](/cdn-hints/) for choosing which one). In your own project the same line
resolves through `node_modules`, as it would in JavaScript.

## Return examples that call an import

A return example is checked by exact equality: TJS calls the function with the parameter
examples and compares the result with the return example. So `''` as a return example does
not mean "returns some string"; it means "returns the empty string", and fails otherwise.
When only the type is known, `:!` in place of `:` declares it type-only, and nothing is run.

Each return example above is correct: `addWorkdays('2024-01-15', 5)` really is
`'2024-01-22'`. But none of them is **checked** when this file is transpiled. Signature
examples run in a test harness that does not load the file's imports, so a function whose
body calls date-fns cannot be evaluated. TJS records such an example as _inconclusive_,
which is neither a pass nor a failure, and the build goes on.

You can see this with the `tjs` command-line tool that comes with the package:
`tjs check <file>` transpiles a file and runs its examples, and `tjs test <file>` also
reports each example and test block. `check` prints nothing about inconclusive examples;
`test` lists each one:

```text
? Signature: addWorkdays signature example — inconclusive: Module could not be executed for testing: format is not defined
```

So write the example you mean (it documents the function, and a reader can trust it as far
as you checked it), and do not take a green `tjs check` as proof it holds.

## Time zones

`parseISO('2024-01-15')` and `new Date('2024-01-15')` read the same characters as
different instants:

- date-fns's `parseISO` reads a date with no time as **midnight where the code runs**.
- JavaScript's `Date` reads a date-only string as **midnight UTC**, but a date and time
  with no zone (`'2024-01-15T00:00'`) as local.

```tjs:inline
// The calendar day an instant falls on, in a named time zone
function dayIn(date: '2024-01-15', zone: 'UTC'): '1/15/2024' {
  return LegacyDate(date).toLocaleDateString('en-US', { timeZone: zone })
}

// Same characters, two different instants:
const utcMidnight = LegacyDate('2024-01-15') // date only: midnight UTC
const localMidnight = LegacyDate('2024-01-15T00:00') // no zone: midnight here

const hours = (localMidnight.getTime() - utcMidnight.getTime()) / 3_600_000
console.log('hours apart where you are:', hours)

console.log(dayIn('2024-01-15', 'UTC'))
console.log(dayIn('2024-01-15', 'America/New_York'))
```

The `hours apart` line prints `0` in UTC, `8` in California (Pacific Standard Time on 15
January) and `-9` in Tokyo: local midnight is that many hours after UTC midnight.
`localMidnight` is the same instant `parseISO('2024-01-15')` returns.

The last line prints `1/14/2024`. Midnight UTC on the 15th is 7 p.m. on the 14th in New
York, so a date-only value parsed as UTC and displayed in a zone west of UTC shows the
previous day. This is the most common date bug in JavaScript.

Unlike the date-fns functions, `dayIn`'s return example **is** run on every transpile:
`LegacyDate` and `toLocaleDateString` are part of the language and the platform, so they
exist when examples run, and an import does not.

The date-fns functions at the top of the page avoid the bug by staying local throughout:
`parseISO` reads local midnight, date-fns does its arithmetic in local time, and `format`
writes local time, so a date goes in and the same date comes out wherever the code runs.
Mixing the two readings is what goes wrong. If you need a fixed zone, pass `timeZone` when
you display, as `dayIn` does. Or keep a calendar date as a `LegalDate`, which is a plain
`'YYYY-MM-DD'` string with no time and no zone, until you display it; the `LegalDate`
module in [Built-in Types and Dates](/built-in-types/) does arithmetic on those strings.

## When converting a whole file: `TjsCompat`

If you are moving an existing JavaScript file over and it calls `new Date()` in many places,
you can put `TjsCompat` on its first line. That declares the file JavaScript-compatible, and
`new Date()` is accepted:

```tjs:inline
TjsCompat
import { formatDistance, parseISO } from 'date-fns'

// The answer depends on today's date, so `:!` declares a type only
function timeAgo(date: '2024-01-15'):! '' {
  return formatDistance(parseISO(date), new Date(), { addSuffix: true })
}

console.log(timeAgo('2024-01-15'))
console.log(String(timeAgo(20240115))) // parameters are still checked
console.log('5' == 5) // but == is JavaScript's again
```

It prints a relative time such as `almost 3 years ago`, then a `MonadicError` for the
number, then `true`. (This `timeAgo` reads the clock, so it has no fixed answer to write as
a return example; that is what `:!` is for.)

`TjsCompat` applies to the whole file, which is why it is the second choice. Parameters are
still validated, but return examples are no longer run as tests, and three things go back
to JavaScript's behaviour everywhere in the file. In native TJS, `'5' == 5` is `false`
(no type conversion; see [Honest Equality](/honest-equality/)), `typeof null` is `'null'`,
and an object-literal parameter default fills in each missing member, so
`f(o = {a: 1, b: 2})` called with `{a: 5}` gets `{a: 5, b: 2}`. Under `TjsCompat` those are
`true`, `'object'` and `{a: 5}`, as in JavaScript. Use it as a step in a conversion; once
the file works, remove it and write `LegacyDate` (or `Timestamp`) at the sites that need a
date.
title: Date Formatting (with import)
description: This chapter uses [date-fns](https://date-fns.org), an ordinary npm package, from a native `.tjs` file (one with no `TjsCompat` line at the top, so every TJS rule applies). The library knows nothing about TJS. The functions you write around it have TJS signatures, and those signatures are where bad input is stopped. It covers, in order: checking input at the signature, why you do not write `new Date()`, importing an npm package with no install step, return examples that cannot be run, time zones, and `TjsCompat` for converting a whole file. One rule to read the code by: in a TJS signature, the value after a colon is an **example**, not a type. `date: '2024-01-15'` accepts any string, and `days: 5` any integer. The value after the closing parenthesis is a **return example**: calling the function with the parameter examples should give exactly that result. [TJS Syntax](/tjs-syntax/) has the full rules.
