# Small parsers for the TJS preprocessor

> **Design note for maintainers of the TJS parser.** It does not teach the language, and you
> do not need it to write TJS. The question was whether to rewrite the `preprocess` stage of
> the parser (`src/lang/parser.ts`, `src/lang/parser-transforms.ts`,
> `src/lang/parser-params.ts`). This note says no: give it a small layer of shared syntactic
> helpers instead, and explains why.
>
> **Status (checked 2026-11-06): partly done.** See [Status](#status) at the end.

## The pipeline

TJS turns into JavaScript in three steps:

```text
TJS source  →  preprocess  →  acorn  →  emit
```

acorn is a standard JavaScript parser. It cannot read TJS syntax: in `function f(x: 0)`
the `: 0` is an example value, which is not JavaScript. So `preprocess` first rewrites
TJS-specific syntax into plain JavaScript (here `function f(x)`, with the example kept as
metadata), and only then does acorn parse it. `preprocess` is a long sequence of transforms,
each a regex or a hand-written character scan over the source text.

Converting TypeScript to TJS (`fromTS`) already works on the TypeScript compiler's syntax
tree, and everything after `preprocess` works on acorn's. Only `preprocess` is hand-rolled,
so only `preprocess` is in question.

## The diagnosis

The transforms worked while the rewrites were local. They stopped working, and the evidence
was not a hunch: it was the bug list from a single day (2026-09-02).

| bug | the mechanism that failed |
| --- | --- |
| `new E({x:1})` in a class field read as a method head | regex plus a **single-character** look-back |
| a destructuring rename rewritten as a dictionary member | `^(\w+)\s*:\s*(.+)$` — cannot tell a rename from an example |
| the polymorphic merge grouping across scopes | a regex sweep over the whole file with **no notion of scope** |
| a generic type-param list split inside its own braces | `.split(',')`, not depth-aware |
| a generic default containing `=>` silently dropped | `.split('=')`, not depth-aware |
| `<T = () => 0>` unparseable | the `<…>` scan reads `=>`'s `>` as the closing bracket |
| a ternary's `:` consumed as an annotation | no way to know which kind of `:` this is |
| `:!` return example runs into the body | no way to know where an expression ends |

Glosses: a *dictionary member* is a parameter default written as an object
(`opts = { x: 0 }`, see [dictionary defaults](/dictionary-defaults/)); the *polymorphic merge*
combines same-named function declarations into one dispatcher; `:!` marks a return example
that is a type only, not a tested value. In the second row, `const { a: b } = o` (rename `a`
to `b`) looks to a regex exactly like a member with example `b`.

Most rows have since been fixed by targeted repairs; one has not (see [Status](#status)). The
table stays because it is the argument.

Every one is the same shape: **a scanner that knows characters but not grammar.** They reduce
to two questions that masking (blanking out strings and comments so a scan cannot misread
them) cannot answer, because both are about grammar, not about which characters are code:

1. **Where does this expression end?**
2. **What does this `:` mean here?**

## The layer that is missing

The repo already has a **lexical** layer, and it works. `src/strip-comments.ts` owns literals,
comments, balanced braces (`matchingBrace`) and depth-aware splitting (`splitTopLevel`).
Consolidating on it closed the whole *literal-blindness* family (a pass misreading code that
merely mentions the syntax it scans for, such as a `:` inside a string): six live bugs across
eight files at `0.13.0-beta.1`. `src/lang/literal-blindness.test.ts` keeps it closed.

What is missing is the layer above: **syntactic primitives**, built on the lexical ones and
used by the transforms.

```text
  transforms           — the preprocess rewrites
  syntactic primitives — expression extent, colon disambiguation   (src/lang/expression-context.ts)
  lexical primitives   — literals, comments, braces, splitting      (src/strip-comments.ts)
```

## Two primitives cover most of it

### 1. Expression extent

> Given a start offset, where does this expression end?

Respecting literals, nesting and, the case that kept biting, `=>`.

The reason that still holds is duplication. Two hand-written scanners answer a special case
of this question ("where is the top-level `=`?"): `topLevelDefaultEq` in
`parser-transforms.ts`, and `topLevelDefaultEquals` in `parser-params.ts` (added for typed
defaults, `name: Type = default`). Both should be deleted when the primitive lands.

Native `Generic` headers are the other open case. `Generic Box<T = () => 0> { … }` is still a
syntax error, parenthesised or not, because the `<…>` scan still stops at `=>`'s `>`.

Historical motivation, now fixed by other means:

- `<T = () => 0>` in converted TypeScript. `fromTS` rewrites the default to a
  `FunctionPredicate(…)` before the TJS parser sees it, and `parseGenericTypeParams` splits
  the parameter list with `splitTopLevelTrimmed` and finds the first top-level `=` that is not
  part of `=>`, `==`, `<=`, `>=` or `!=`.
- `function Array$(value):! { value: null } {`: where the return example ends and the body
  begins. This parses now.

**Not built.** Nothing in `src/` exports an expression-extent scanner.

### 2. Colon disambiguation

> Is this `:` a ternary's, a type annotation's, or an object key's?

One line can hold all three:

```text
function sign(x: 0) { return x < 0 ? { sign: -1 } : { sign: 1 } }
               ^                           ^      ^       ^
```

From left: an example value, an object key, the ternary's colon, another object key.

It needs little more than "have I seen an unmatched `?` at this depth". It resolved the
ternary/arrow mangling in two files of the compat corpus (real TypeScript projects such as
zod and effect that the repo converts as a test; `RpcServer.ts` and `commandExecutor.ts` are
from effect). It is also the question behind the destructuring-rename bug, which was fixed by
*guessing from the shape of the value* because nothing could answer it directly.

**Shipped 2026-09-02** as `src/lang/expression-context.ts`: `isTernaryColon(source, index)`
for one colon, `ternaryColons(source)`, which finds every ternary-alternative colon in one
forward pass so a caller asking about many colons pays O(n) once, and the reference
implementation `isTernaryColonScan`. `parser-params.ts` uses it. The first version walked
backwards per query and went quadratic on many colons in one expression; a process-wide memo
added to fix that was thrashed by nested sources and was removed. Its tests are
`src/lang/expression-context.test.ts`.

Each primitive is small and independently testable, and **not throwaway**. An
expression-extent scanner is a fragment of a Pratt parser (the standard operator-precedence
technique for parsing expressions), and a CST (concrete syntax tree: a parse tree that keeps
every character, so source can be rewritten losslessly) needs exactly that to parse
expressions. So the incremental work is a down payment on a rewrite, not scaffolding for one.

## The discipline that decides whether this works

The failure mode is proliferation: several half-parsers that disagree. This is not
hypothetical. It is how the current situation arose, recorded in
`literal-blindness.test.ts`: *"each pass had hand-rolled its own partial tracking."*

It nearly recurred twice on the day this note was written:

- `topLevelDefaultEq` is a private depth scanner, written instead of extending the shared one.
  This is still open, and has gained a sibling, `topLevelDefaultEquals`.
- Outside the parser, the same copy-drift: a `messageText` fix landed in `batteries/` and left
  six copies untouched in `demo/src/capabilities.ts`, which broke four LLM examples. That one
  is resolved; the demo now imports the shared `messageText`.

`splitTopLevel`'s own docstring records the subtler version: it was extracted to stop a fourth
copy of a scan, and then two callers immediately wrote byte-identical wrappers around it — *"a
consolidation that goes three-to-one and grows two wrappers has gone three-to-three."*

So the rule is not "write small parsers". It is:

> **One implementation per concept, in a shared leaf, in the shape callers actually reach for,
> with a guardrail test that fails when a second copy appears.**

That is what made the lexical layer succeed, and it is the only thing that will make this
layer succeed.

## The measurable payoff

`preprocess` is quadratic in file size on some inputs: doubling the input quadruples the
time. The input is prefixes of effect's 1.96MB generated `httpApiSwagger.ts`, which is one
long string literal.

| size | 2026-09-02 | 2026-11-06 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 16KB | 182ms | 105ms |
| 32KB | 642ms | 397ms |
| 64KB | 2.5s | 1.6s |
| 128KB | 10.2s | 6.3s |
| 256KB | 39.4s | — |

The 2026-09-02 series extrapolated to about 37 minutes for the whole file. Ordinary code of
the same size is linear: about 64ms for 128KB of small functions. `scripts/compat-scan.ts`
skips corpus files over 400KB for this reason, and prints each skip.

Where the time goes is **not known**. Timing the individual `source = transform(source)`
steps on 2026-09-02 accounted for only about 15ms of it, so no single transform is to blame.
The hypothesis is that the cost lies in many transforms each re-scanning the source, and that
shared primitives which compute positions once would collapse it. That is a hypothesis to
measure, not a result: a slowdown triggered by one long string literal may well sit in the
lexical layer instead. Either way, this is the first parser work in this repo with a
benchmark attached rather than only a cleaner design.

## Sequencing

As proposed on 2026-09-02, with what has happened since:

1. **Done.** **`convert` validates its own output.** Orthogonal (reporting, not parsing), and
   it turns every remaining parse failure from a silent bad artifact into a named error.
   Before this, `tjs convert --emit-tjs` exited 0 and wrote a `.tjs` that `tjs check` then
   rejected. The converter owns both halves, so it can check itself; it now does
   (`src/cli/convert-self-check.test.ts`).
2. **Not started.** **Expression extent.** Proposed to fix `<T = () => 0>` and effect's
   `Schema.ts`, two of the seven corpus failures then remaining. Both were fixed by other
   means the same day. What it would deliver now: one scanner in place of the two top-level-`=`
   copies, native `Generic` headers with arrow defaults, and possibly the quadratic.
3. **Done.** **Colon disambiguation**, which fixed `RpcServer.ts` and `commandExecutor.ts`.
4. **Due.** Reassess. If the remaining failures still reduce to grammar questions, the
   primitives have earned a CST; if they do not, they were cheap and the transforms are
   cleaner anyway.

## Status

**Checked 2026-11-06: partly done.**

- The trigger was met on 2026-09-02: `PLAN.md`'s parser reassessment said revisit *if edge
  cases increase*, and the seven compat-corpus failures then remaining reduced to roughly six
  bugs, essentially all of this class.
- The same day the corpus reached 1973/1973 files converting and parsing, and the ratchet's
  known-failure list (`KNOWN` in `scripts/compat-scan.ts`) has been empty since. The corpus no
  longer argues for the work.
- Shipped: the convert self-check, and colon disambiguation (`src/lang/expression-context.ts`).
- Not shipped: expression extent. What remains of the case for it, none of it a corpus
  failure:
  - two top-level-`=` scanners where there should be one;
  - native `Generic` headers with an arrow default (`<T = () => 0>`) are still a syntax error;
  - two sites in `parser-transforms.ts` (the `FunctionPredicate` and `Generic` generic forms)
    still derive type-parameter names with a plain `.split(',')` then `.split('=')`, the
    mechanism in the table, instead of `parseGenericTypeParams(...).names`;
  - the quadratic on long string literals, whose cause is unmeasured.
- No decision has been taken on step 4. Until one is, nothing is scheduled.

# Store Interface

Abstract storage interface that can be backed by Firestore, IndexedDB,
Postgres, filesystem, or any other storage backend.

This enables:
1. Testing RBAC logic without Firebase
2. Running locally with IndexedDB
3. Self-hosted deployments with Postgres/SQLite
4. "Directory full of crap" development mode

# Things That Take Time

So far, every line of your programs has run as soon as the line before it finished. Even the
buttons in Responding to the Reader worked that way: a click ran a handler, and the handler
ran straight through. Real programs also have to wait. A kitchen timer waits for minutes to
pass. A weather app waits for another computer, somewhere else in the world, to send it the
forecast.

This chapter is about programs that wait: timers, a way of writing "do this, wait, then do
that" in order, and asking another computer for information.

## Later, not now

`setTimeout` asks for a function to be run later. You give it the function and how long to
wait, in **milliseconds** (thousandths of a second, so 2000 is two seconds):

```tjs:inline {"view": "console"}
console.log('Putting the kettle on.')

setTimeout(() => console.log('The kettle has boiled.'), 2000)

console.log('Getting out a cup.')
```

`() => console.log(…)` is a function with no name, written with an arrow, as in Responding
to the Reader. It is handed to `setTimeout`, not called.

Look at the order the lines appear in. The program does not stop at `setTimeout` and wait
two seconds. It hands the function over to be run later, carries on at once, and gets out
the cup. Two seconds after that, the kettle boils.

This is the same idea as an event handler. A button's `onClick` is a function that runs when
the reader clicks; the function you give `setTimeout` is one that runs when the time is up.
In both cases you are writing code now that will run later, and the program does not wait
for it.

Here is a timer on the page. It shows its message with a model: as in Responding to the
Reader, a model is an object made with `tosi`, and when one of its parts changes, the page
changes to match.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

const { reminder } = tosi({ reminder: { message: 'No reminder set.', count: 0 } })

function remindLater() {
  reminder.message = 'Waiting…'
  setTimeout(() => {
    reminder.count = reminder.count + 1
    reminder.message = `Reminder ${reminder.count}: time to stand up and stretch!`
  }, 3000)
}

const { div, button } = elements

preview.append(
  div(reminder.message),
  button({ onClick: remindLater }, 'Remind me in 3 seconds')
)
```

The button is given `remindLater` itself, with no `( )` after it: as in Responding to the
Reader, the button needs a function to call later, not the answer of calling it now. Each
click sets a new reminder. Click three times quickly and you get three reminders, each
arriving three seconds after its own click: the count goes 1, 2, 3. Nothing stops a second
reminder being set while the first is still waiting. Sometimes that is what you want; the
next example shows how to prevent it when it is not.

## A countdown

`setInterval` is the repeating version: it runs a function again and again, with a pause
between each run, until you tell it to stop. A countdown needs that, and it needs a rule for
what happens on each tick. As in Responding to the Reader, write the rule as a function with
an example and a test, before there is any timer:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

function tick(seconds: 10): 9 {
  if (seconds > 0) {
    return seconds - 1
  }
  return 0
}

const { countdown } = tosi({ countdown: { seconds: 10, running: false } })

let timer = null

function start() {
  if (countdown.running) {
    return
  }
  countdown.seconds = 10
  countdown.running = true
  timer = setInterval(() => {
    countdown.seconds = tick(countdown.seconds)
    if (countdown.seconds == 0) {
      clearInterval(timer)
      countdown.running = false
    }
  }, 1000)
}

const { div, button, strong } = elements

preview.append(
  div({ style: { fontSize: '3em' } }, strong(countdown.seconds)),
  button({ onClick: start }, 'Start')
)

test 'tick counts down, and stops at zero' {
  expect(tick(3)).toBe(2)
  expect(tick(1)).toBe(0)
  expect(tick(0)).toBe(0)
}
```

- `let timer = null` makes the name before there is a timer to put in it. `null` means
  "nothing yet". It is `let`, not `const`, because a timer is put into it later. It is
  outside `start`, so the function inside `setInterval` can still find it, every second,
  long after `start` has finished.
- `setInterval(…, 1000)` runs its function once a second. It gives back a **timer id**, a
  value that stands for this particular timer. The program keeps it in `timer`.
- `clearInterval(timer)` stops the timer that id stands for. Without it, the function would
  go on running every second, for as long as the page is open.
- `running` remembers whether a countdown is already going. Without that check, a second
  click on **Start** would start a second timer, and the number would fall twice a second.
  Try it: delete the three lines starting `if (countdown.running)`, and click **Start** twice.

That experiment shows something else too. At zero, only one of the two timers stops. The
second click put the second timer's id into `timer`, so the first id was lost, and
`clearInterval(timer)` stops only the second timer. The first goes on running `tick(0)` every
second, and nothing can stop it, because a timer whose id is lost can never be stopped.
Reload the page to clear it.

The timer's function is two lines: it asks `tick` for the next number, and stops at zero.
The rule itself is in `tick`, where a test can check it without waiting ten seconds.

One thing to know about timers in these examples: if you change an example while one of its
timers is running, the old timer does not stop. It goes on changing the model, and the page
can look as if two countdowns are fighting. Let the countdown finish, or reload the page.

## Waiting in order

Timers are enough for one thing happening later. They get awkward for a sequence: boil an
egg for three minutes, then make toast for two, then serve. With only `setTimeout`, each
step goes inside the function of the step before, and the code drifts further to the right
with every step:

```javascript
breakfast.step = 'Boiling an egg…'
setTimeout(() => {
  breakfast.step = 'Making toast…'
  setTimeout(() => {
    breakfast.step = 'Breakfast is ready.'
  }, 2000)
}, 3000)
```

Two steps are already hard to read: the 2000 belongs to the toast, but it sits far below it,
and the 3000 for the egg comes last of all. Every new step adds another level.

TJS, like JavaScript, has a better way to write it: an **async function**, in which you can
**await** a wait. First, a small function that waits:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->
```tjs:static
function wait(ms: 1000) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms))
}
```

`wait(3000)` gives back a **promise**: a value that stands for something that has not
happened yet. It is like the ticket you get at a busy counter. The ticket is not your
sandwich, but it is a promise that a sandwich is coming, and you can wait for it. This
promise is kept when the timer goes off, three seconds later. You do not need to follow
every part of that line yet; it is a recipe, and you can copy it as it is.

Now the breakfast:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

function wait(ms: 1000) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms))
}

const { breakfast } = tosi({ breakfast: { step: 'Press the button to start.' } })

async function makeBreakfast() {
  breakfast.step = 'Boiling an egg…'
  await wait(3000)
  breakfast.step = 'Making toast…'
  await wait(2000)
  breakfast.step = 'Breakfast is ready.'
}

const { div, button } = elements

preview.append(
  div(breakfast.step),
  button({ onClick: makeBreakfast }, 'Make breakfast')
)
```

- `async` in front of `function` says that this function can wait.
- `await wait(3000)` pauses `makeBreakfast` until the promise is kept, then carries on with
  the next line. The steps read from top to bottom, in the order they happen.

Compare it with the `setTimeout` version above: the same steps, the same waits, and each wait
sits next to the step it belongs to.

While `makeBreakfast` is paused, the rest of the page is not. The browser goes on responding
to the reader, and other examples on this page go on working. Only `makeBreakfast` waits.
`await` is what makes that possible: it hands control back to the page while it waits. A
program that waited without it, by going round a loop until the time was up, would keep the
page busy the whole time, and the page would freeze.

You can see that the page keeps working: press **Make breakfast**, and press it again while
the egg is boiling. Now two breakfasts are being made at once, and their messages tangle:
the first says "Breakfast is ready." while the second is still making toast. This is the
same problem as clicking **Start** twice on the countdown, and the same `running` check would
fix it.

`await` can only be used inside an `async` function, or at the top level of an example,
outside every function, as the next examples do.

## An answer that takes time

An async function can give back an answer, with `return`, like any function. The answer
arrives when the function finishes, so you `await` it:

```tjs:inline {"view": "console"}
function wait(ms: 1000) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms))
}

async function slowDouble(n: 0) {
  await wait(1000)
  return n * 2
}

console.log('Asking…')
const answer = await slowDouble(21)
console.log('The answer is', answer)

test 'slowDouble doubles, eventually' {
  expect(await slowDouble(21)).toBe(42)
  expect(await slowDouble(0)).toBe(0)
}
```

The test uses `await` too. A test can wait for an answer in the same way as the rest of the
program, and it is checked when the answer arrives.

Notice that `slowDouble` has no worked example of its answer, no `: 42` after the
parentheses. TJS checks a worked example by calling the function and comparing the answer
straight away, and at that moment an async function's answer has not arrived, so the example
cannot be checked. If you write one anyway, TJS does not complain, even when it is wrong, so
leave it off and write a test that awaits the answer. `wait` has no worked example for the
same reason: what it gives back is a promise.

### A common mistake: using the ticket as if it were the sandwich

What if you forget the `await`?

```tjs:inline {"view": "console"}
function wait(ms: 1000) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms))
}

async function slowDouble(n: 0) {
  await wait(1000)
  return n * 2
}

const ticket = slowDouble(21)
console.log(`Without await: ${ticket}`)
console.log('Without await, plus one:', ticket + 1)
console.log('With await:', await ticket)
```

Calling an async function always gives back a promise, at once, before the answer exists.
Without `await`, that promise is what you get: shown as text it is `[object Promise]`, and
"adding one" to it glues `1` onto that text. If a page ever shows `[object Promise]`, or
something that should be a number is nonsense, look for a missing `await`.

The last line shows that the ticket was good all along. `await ticket` waits for the promise
and gives back the answer, 42.

### Mistakes arrive later too

A typed async function checks what it is given, as every TJS function does, and when the
value is wrong it gives back an error instead of an answer (When Things Go Wrong). The check
happens as soon as the function is called, before any waiting, so a wrong value is refused
at once, without the one-second wait. But like everything an async function gives back, the error comes wrapped in a
promise. You only see it once you `await`: without the `await`, `slowDouble('ten')` is a
promise, and asking whether a promise is an error says no.

```tjs:inline {"view": "console"}
function wait(ms: 1000) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms))
}

async function slowDouble(n: 0) {
  await wait(1000)
  return n * 2
}

const result = await slowDouble('ten')

if (result instanceof Error) {
  console.log('Something went wrong:', result.message)
} else {
  console.log('The answer is', result)
}

test 'a wrong value arrives as an error' {
  const wrong = await slowDouble('ten')
  expect(wrong instanceof Error).toBe(true)
  expect(wrong.received).toBe('ten')
}
```

`received`, as in When Things Go Wrong, is the value that was refused.

So the habit from When Things Go Wrong carries over unchanged: await the result, then check
it with `instanceof Error` before you use it.

## Asking another computer

A web page can ask another computer for information with `fetch`. You give it an address,
and it gives back a promise of the reply. The reply takes time to arrive, from a few
hundredths of a second to many seconds, which is why everything in this chapter so far has
been leading here.

Many services answer in **JSON**, a way of writing data that looks almost exactly like the
objects in Things with Parts. This example asks [Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com), a free
weather service, for the temperature in Berlin right now. Many services only answer pages
on their own website, or ask for a key first; Open-Meteo answers any web page, which is why
this book uses it. (Asking a service that does not answer your page looks like the "could
not be reached" failure described below.)

Its reply looks like this, with a few parts left out:

```json
{
  "latitude": 52.52,
  "longitude": 13.42,
  "current_units": { "time": "iso8601", "temperature_2m": "°C" },
  "current": { "time": "2026-11-10T15:45", "temperature_2m": 4.0 }
}
```

The reply is an object with parts, and the part called `current` is an object too. Inside
it, `temperature_2m` is the temperature 2 metres above the ground, in °C. So once the reply is
turned into an object called `data`, the temperature is at `data.current.temperature_2m`.

One more new thing before the example: `fetch` can fail by **throwing** an error, as the
mistakes that stop the program do (When Things Go Wrong), but this time something can be done
about it. `try { … } catch { … }` is the part that deals with it, and it is explained just
after the example, under "Throwing, and catching".

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

async function currentTemperature(latitude: 52.52, longitude: 13.41) {
  const address =
    'https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast' +
    `?latitude=${latitude}&longitude=${longitude}&current=temperature_2m`
  try {
    const response = await fetch(address)
    if (!response.ok) {
      return Error(`the weather service answered ${response.status}`)
    }
    const data = await response.json()
    return data.current.temperature_2m
  } catch {
    return Error('the weather service could not be reached')
  }
}

function weatherReport(celsius: 21.5): 'It is 21.5 °C in Berlin right now.' {
  return `It is ${celsius} °C in Berlin right now.`
}

const { berlin } = tosi({ berlin: { report: 'Press the button to ask.' } })

async function ask() {
  berlin.report = 'Asking…'
  const celsius = await currentTemperature(52.52, 13.41)
  if (celsius instanceof Error) {
    berlin.report = `Sorry, ${celsius.message}. Try again in a minute.`
  } else {
    berlin.report = weatherReport(celsius)
  }
}

const { div, button } = elements

preview.append(
  div(berlin.report),
  button({ onClick: ask }, 'How warm is Berlin?')
)

test 'the report reads well' {
  expect(weatherReport(-3)).toBe('It is -3 °C in Berlin right now.')
}
```

There are two waits in `currentTemperature`. `await fetch(address)` waits for the reply to
start arriving; `await response.json()` waits for the rest of it, and turns the JSON into an
object: the one shown above.

The address carries the question. After the `?`, an address can hold named values, each
written `name=value`, with `&` between them. Here there are three: the latitude, the
longitude, and `current=temperature_2m`, which says what we want to know. The address is
built from the latitude and longitude, so it works for anywhere: Paris is
48.85 and 2.35. One of the exercises below asks you to add a second city.

### When the other computer does not answer

Asking another computer can fail in ways your own program never does. The network can be
down, the service can be busy, the address can be wrong. A program that talks to the network
has to expect that, and `currentTemperature` turns every such failure into an error value,
so that `ask` only has to check for one thing:

- `response.ok` is true when the service answered and was happy with the question. When it
  is false, `response.status` is a number saying why (404 means "no such address"). The
  function gives back an `Error` with that number in it.
- When there is no reply at all, `fetch` does not give back an error value: it throws one.
  The `catch` block turns that into an `Error` value, like the rest of the function.

### Throwing, and catching

A thrown error stops the function right there: the lines after it do not run. It keeps going
up through every function that called it, stopping each one, until something catches it.
`try { … } catch { … }` is what catches it: if anything inside the `try` block throws, the
program jumps to the `catch` block and carries on from there.

`JSON.parse`, which turns JSON text into an object, throws when the text is not JSON, so it
makes a small example:

```tjs:inline {"view": "console"}
console.log('Before.')

try {
  JSON.parse('{ this is not JSON')
  console.log('This line never runs.')
} catch {
  console.log('Caught it: that was not JSON.')
}

console.log('After.')
```

The line after `JSON.parse` never runs, because the throw jumps straight to `catch`. Then the
program carries on after the whole `try … catch`. To see the difference, delete everything
from `try {` to the last `}` except the `JSON.parse` line: now the example stops at
`JSON.parse` and shows its message, and "After." never appears.

Try the failures on purpose, in the weather example. Change `api.open-meteo.com` to
`api.open-meteo.co` (a computer that does not exist) and press the button: after a moment,
which can be a few seconds, the page says "Sorry, the weather service could not be reached.
Try again in a minute." Then put it back, and change `forecast` to `forcast` (an address the
service does not have): now it says "Sorry, the weather service answered 404. Try again in a minute."

You have met thrown errors before. The mistakes that stop the program, in When Things Go
Wrong, such as `… is not defined`, are thrown errors too. Until now there was nothing to do
about them but fix the typo. `fetch` is different: it throws because of the world, not
because of a mistake in your code, so it is worth catching. A good place for `try` is
exactly here, around the code that talks to the network, turning a throw into an error value
that the rest of your program already knows how to check.

### Testing the parts that wait

The test above checks `weatherReport`, not `currentTemperature`. A test that called the real
service would fail whenever the network did, and it would ask Berlin for the weather every
time the page is opened. The temperature changes, too, so there is no answer it could expect.
Instead, keep the network call small, and put everything that can be worked out without the
network into a function like `weatherReport`, with examples and tests.

The test gives `weatherReport` a whole number, -3, although its example is 21.5. That is
fine: a number with a decimal point as the example accepts any number, whole or not
(Functions), and temperatures can be either.

## Try it

**A stopwatch.** Make a model with `seconds` and `running`, and three buttons:

- **Start** starts a timer that adds one to `seconds` every second. Starting a stopwatch that
  is already running should do nothing (remember the countdown).
- **Stop** stops the timer, with `clearInterval`, and leaves the time showing.
- **Reset** sets `seconds` back to 0. Decide what it should do while the stopwatch is
  running, and make it do that.

Write the rule for the display first, with an example and a test: a function `showTime` that
turns seconds into minutes and seconds, so that `showTime(75)` is `'1:15'` and `showTime(5)`
is `'0:05'`. `Math.floor(75 / 60)` is the whole minutes, and `75 % 60` is the seconds left
over. The `0` in `'0:05'` is a decision (Decisions): add it when the seconds are less than 10.

**A random saying.** `https://api.github.com/zen` answers with a short, random saying about
programming, a different one each time. It answers in plain text, not JSON, so read it with
`await response.text()` instead of `response.json()`. Make a button that fetches one and
shows it. GitHub allows only about sixty of these requests an hour from each computer; when
you go over, `response.ok` is false and `response.status` is 403 (sometimes 429). Make the page show a
friendly message instead of the saying when that happens, or when the network is down, and
try it by changing the address.

More to try:

- Add Paris (48.85, 2.35) to the weather example, as a second button. Give `weatherReport` a
  second parameter for the city's name, and update its example and test first.
- Make the countdown start from a number the reader types (Numbers from a text box, in
  Responding to the Reader, shows how). What should happen if they type `abc`?
- Use `await wait(…)` to make a traffic light (Responding to the Reader) that changes by
  itself: red for three seconds, green for three, amber for one, and round again, until a
  **Stop** button is pressed. A `while` loop from Repetition can do the going round, as long
  as it awaits inside: `while (lights.running)` with an `await` in it pauses on each turn,
  and the page keeps working while it waits. Without the `await`, the loop would never let
  the page do anything else, and the page would freeze.

Work them here:

title: Things That Take Time

text:
<!--{"parent": "learn-to-program.md", "order": 12}-->
<!-- TODO review -->

# A Calculator

Time to build something real: a pocket calculator, with buttons you press and a display that
answers. It uses nearly everything in the book so far: names, functions, tests, decisions,
loops, things with parts, a model on the page, and errors. It is small enough to understand
completely, and once it works you will think of keys to add.

## How a calculator thinks

A simple calculator keeps four facts:

- **X**, the number on the display: what you are typing, or the latest answer.
- **Y**, the number it is holding on to while you type the next one.
- **op**, the operation waiting to happen: `+`, `-`, `×` or `÷`, or nothing.
- **fresh**, true or false: does the next digit start a new number, or go on the end of the
  one on the display? It is the fact people forget, and without it the calculator cannot work.

Press `1`, `2`: X is 12. Press `+`: the calculator moves 12 into Y, remembers `+`, sets fresh
to true, and waits. Press `3`: because fresh is true, the 3 starts a new number, so X is 3, not
123, and fresh becomes false. Press `=`: it works out Y + X, and X becomes 15.

Notice that this section has no code in it. Deciding what a program has to **remember** is
the most important step in writing it, and it is easier to get right in sentences than in
code. Try it with a real calculator, or the one on your phone: press keys, and after each one
say what X, Y, op and fresh are. If you can always say, the plan is complete. Everything below
is that plan, written out for the computer.

## The brain

The calculator's brain is `press`, which takes the calculator and a key, and updates it. It
has a helper, `calculate`, that does the arithmetic, and the tests use a third function, `run`,
that presses a whole row of keys. None of them knows anything about buttons or screens, so they
are easy to test.

The keys `×`, `÷` and, later, `√` and `±` are not on most keyboards. When you write a test that
uses one, copy it from this page and paste it in.

As in every chapter, you can change the code and press ⌘S (Ctrl+S on Windows and Linux) to run
it again. Test results turn green or red, as in Checking Your Work.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function calculate(op: '+', y: 0.0, x: 0.0) {
  given op {
    '+' { return y + x }
    '-' { return y - x }
    '×' { return y * x }
    '÷' { return y / x }
  } else {
    return x
  }
}

function press(calculator: { x: 0.0, y: 0.0, op: '', fresh: true }, key: '7') {
  given key {
    'C' {
      calculator.x = 0
      calculator.y = 0
      calculator.op = ''
      calculator.fresh = true
    }
    '+', '-', '×', '÷' {
      if (calculator.op && !calculator.fresh) {
        calculator.x = calculate(calculator.op, calculator.y, calculator.x)
      }
      calculator.y = calculator.x
      calculator.op = key
      calculator.fresh = true
    }
    '=' {
      if (calculator.op) {
        calculator.x = calculate(calculator.op, calculator.y, calculator.x)
        calculator.op = ''
        calculator.fresh = true
      }
    }
  } else {
    const digit = Number(key)
    if (calculator.fresh) {
      calculator.x = digit
      calculator.fresh = false
    } else {
      calculator.x = calculator.x * 10 + digit
    }
  }
}

function run(keys: '12+3=') {
  const calculator = { x: 0, y: 0, op: '', fresh: true }
  for (const key of keys) {
    press(calculator, key)
  }
  return calculator.x
}

preview.append(`12 + 3 = ${run('12+3=')}`)

test 'typing a number' {
  expect(run('123')).toBe(123)
}

test 'one operation' {
  expect(run('12+3=')).toBe(15)
  expect(run('7×6=')).toBe(42)
  expect(run('1÷4=')).toBe(0.25)
  expect(run('3-5=')).toBe(-2)
}

test 'each operator finishes the one before' {
  expect(run('2+3×4=')).toBe(20)
}

test 'clear starts over' {
  expect(run('12+3C5=')).toBe(5)
}

test 'press changes the calculator it is given' {
  const mine = { x: 0, y: 0, op: '', fresh: true }
  press(mine, '5')
  press(mine, '2')
  expect(mine.x).toBe(52)
}

test 'a calculator with the wrong parts is refused' {
  const wrong = press({ x: '12', y: 0, op: '', fresh: true }, '3')
  expect(wrong instanceof Error).toBe(true)
  expect(wrong.message).toContain('press.calculator.x')
  const missing = press({ x: 12, y: 0, op: '' }, '3')
  expect(missing instanceof Error).toBe(true)
  expect(missing.message).toContain('press.calculator.fresh')
}
```

- `calculate` does the arithmetic for an operation, with `given` (from Decisions). An `op` it
  does not know gives back X unchanged.
- `press` changes the calculator for one key: `C` clears, an operator moves X into Y (first
  finishing any operation already waiting), `=` finishes the waiting one, and anything else is a
  digit. One arm of `given` can list several keys, separated by commas, as in Decisions: the
  `'+', '-', '×', '÷'` arm handles all four operators.
- `if (calculator.op)` asks whether an operation is waiting. An empty string `''` counts as
  no, and any other string counts as yes. `calculator.op && !calculator.fresh` uses `&&` (and)
  and `!` (not) from Decisions: an operation is waiting, and a number has been typed since.
- `Number(key)` turns the text `'7'` into the number 7. A digit either starts a new number or,
  as `x * 10 + digit`, adds a digit to the end: 12 becomes 123.
- `run` presses a whole row of keys, which is what the tests use. `for … of` on a string goes
  through its characters one at a time.

`press` gives nothing back. It changes the object it is given. When `run` calls
`press(calculator, key)`, `press` does not get a copy: `run` and `press` are looking at the
same object. So after the loop, `run` reads `calculator.x` and finds the answer `press` put
there. The test 'press changes the calculator it is given' shows the same thing with an object
called `mine`: after pressing `5` and `2`, `mine.x` is 52.

`2+3×4=` gives 20, not 14: like a pocket calculator, it works each operation out when the next
one is pressed. The test says so, so nobody "fixes" it by accident.

## The example on `press`

Look at the first line of `press` again:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->
```tjs:static
function press(calculator: { x: 0.0, y: 0.0, op: '', fresh: true }, key: '7') {
```

The example for `calculator` is a list of the calculator's facts: two numbers, a string and a
true-or-false. It is the plan from the top of this chapter, written where TJS can check it.
`0.0` means "any number, decimals allowed", so the whole number 0 that `run` starts with fits
it, and so does 0.25.

Hand `press` an object that is missing `fresh`, or one where `x` is the text `'12'` instead of
the number 12, and the call is refused: `press` gives back an error, as in When Things Go
Wrong, whose message includes the part that was wrong (`press.calculator.x`,
`press.calculator.fresh`). The last test in the brain example does exactly that.

When you add a fact (the decimal-point exercise needs one), add it to the example too. From
then on, every call to `press` with a calculator that lacks the new fact is refused. TJS does
not list the places that build one; you find them when they are used. In `run`, the tests go
red. On the finished calculator below, a refused press simply does nothing, because the button
ignores what `press` gives back, so a button that has stopped working is the sign to look for.

## Adding a key, test first

New keys are easy, because each is one more case in `press`. Here is what one looks like. A
square root works on X straight away, without waiting for `=`:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->
```tjs:static
// in press, beside the other cases:
'√' {
  calculator.x = Math.sqrt(calculator.x)
  calculator.fresh = true
}
```

It sets `fresh`, because after `√` the display shows an answer, and the next digit should
start a new number. You don't need to type this one in: the finished calculator below has it.

Here is the whole method, worked through for one more key: **±**, which changes the sign of
X, so that `5` becomes `-5`.

**1. Write the test.** Before touching `press`, say what the new key should do. In the brain
example above, add a check to the tests:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->
```tjs:static
test 'plus-minus' {
  expect(run('5±')).toBe(-5)
}
```

**2. Watch it fail, and read why.** Run it, and the new test turns red. You might expect a
message saying `±` is an unknown key. Instead it reads something like:

```text
'plus-minus' — Expected -5 but got NaN
```

NaN means "not a number". `press` has no case for `±`, so the key
falls through to the `else` branch, which treats every key it does not recognise as a digit.
`Number('±')` is NaN, and `5 * 10 + NaN` is NaN. The failing test has already taught you
something about the program: unknown keys are not refused, they quietly turn the display into
nonsense. (One of the exercises fixes that.) The example on `press` does not catch the NaN
either, because JavaScript counts NaN as a number; more on that below.

**3. Make it pass.** Add the smallest case that does the job:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->
```tjs:static
'±' {
  calculator.x = -calculator.x
}
```

Unlike `√`, it does not set `fresh`: on a pocket calculator you can press ± halfway through
typing a number.

**4. Run every test, not just the new one.** A new case can break an old one. Press ⌘S and
check that every test is green, not only 'plus-minus'. If they are, the key is done, and the
brain example now has one new case, `±`, and one new test.

## The finished calculator

Now give it a face. The calculator becomes a tosijs model, as in Responding to the Reader: an
object the page watches, so whatever shows it updates when it changes. The display shows
`calculator.x`, and every button calls `press`.

Compared with the brain above, what is new is:

- the `√` and `±` cases in `press` (marked `// new`),
- `: 15` on the first line of `run`,
- everything after `run`: the model, the keys and the face.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

function calculate(op: '+', y: 0.0, x: 0.0) {
  given op {
    '+' { return y + x }
    '-' { return y - x }
    '×' { return y * x }
    '÷' { return y / x }
  } else {
    return x
  }
}

function press(calculator: { x: 0.0, y: 0.0, op: '', fresh: true }, key: '7') {
  given key {
    'C' {
      calculator.x = 0
      calculator.y = 0
      calculator.op = ''
      calculator.fresh = true
    }
    '+', '-', '×', '÷' {
      if (calculator.op && !calculator.fresh) {
        calculator.x = calculate(calculator.op, calculator.y, calculator.x)
      }
      calculator.y = calculator.x
      calculator.op = key
      calculator.fresh = true
    }
    '=' {
      if (calculator.op) {
        calculator.x = calculate(calculator.op, calculator.y, calculator.x)
        calculator.op = ''
        calculator.fresh = true
      }
    }
    '√' { // new
      calculator.x = Math.sqrt(calculator.x)
      calculator.fresh = true
    }
    '±' { // new
      calculator.x = -calculator.x
    }
  } else {
    const digit = Number(key)
    if (calculator.fresh) {
      calculator.x = digit
      calculator.fresh = false
    } else {
      calculator.x = calculator.x * 10 + digit
    }
  }
}

function run(keys: '12+3='): 15 {
  const calculator = { x: 0, y: 0, op: '', fresh: true }
  for (const key of keys) {
    press(calculator, key)
  }
  return calculator.x
}

const { calculator } = tosi({
  calculator: { x: 0, y: 0, op: '', fresh: true },
})

const { div, button } = elements

const keys = [
  'C', '±', '√', '÷',
  '7', '8', '9', '×',
  '4', '5', '6', '-',
  '1', '2', '3', '+',
  '0', '=',
]

preview.append(
  div(
    { style: { fontSize: '2em', textAlign: 'right', padding: '0.25em', background: '#eee' } },
    calculator.x
  ),
  div(
    { style: { fontSize: '0.8em', color: 'gray' } },
    'Y: ',
    calculator.y,
    '   op: ',
    calculator.op
  ),
  div(
    { style: { display: 'grid', gridTemplateColumns: 'repeat(4, 3em)', gap: '4px' } },
    ...keys.map((key) => button({ onClick: () => press(calculator, key) }, key))
  )
)

test 'the old keys still work' {
  expect(run('123')).toBe(123)
  expect(run('1÷4=')).toBe(0.25)
  expect(run('2+3×4=')).toBe(20)
  expect(run('12+3C5=')).toBe(5)
}

test 'square root' {
  expect(run('16√')).toBe(4)
  expect(run('9√+1=')).toBe(4)
}

test 'plus-minus' {
  expect(run('5±')).toBe(-5)
  expect(run('5±±')).toBe(5)
  expect(run('3±+8=')).toBe(5)
}
```

The face uses only things from Responding to the Reader: `import` brings in `elements` and
`tosi`, `const { … } =` takes named parts out of an object, `keys.map((key) => button(…))`
makes one button per key, `...` spreads that list of buttons into the `div`, and
`onClick: () => press(calculator, key)` is the function each button runs when clicked. The
`style` objects set how things look, as CSS does.

Press `1`, `2`, `+`, `3`, `=` and watch the small line under the display: Y takes the 12 when
you press `+`, op shows the `+` that is waiting, and op clears when `=` finishes the sum (Y
keeps the last number it held until something replaces it). That is the calculator's whole
mind, on screen.

The buttons never touch the display. `press` changes the model, and everything showing it
follows. And this is the same `press` the tests check: it does not care whether it is given a
plain object from `run` or a model on a page.

`run` now has a signature example, `run(keys: '12+3='): 15`. The brain's first version did
not have one yet. The `: 15` after the parentheses is a worked example of the answer (Checking
Your Work): TJS calls `run('12+3=')` and checks that it really gives 15. That check runs along
with the tests every time the example runs, and turns red like a test if the answer is wrong,
so the most basic sum stays checked even if you delete every test.

## When the answer makes no sense

Press `1 ÷ 0 =` on the face. The display says `Infinity`. That is JavaScript's answer for
dividing by zero, and it is not wrong, exactly, but it is not what a pocket calculator says
either, and pressing `+ 1 =` afterwards gives Infinity again. Now press `C`, then
`0 ÷ 0 =`: the display says `NaN`, the same "not a number" the unknown `±` key produced
before it had a case. Most calculators show `Error` for both, and wait for `C`.

Notice that the example on `press` did not stop either of them. Infinity and NaN are,
strangely, numbers as far as JavaScript is concerned, so they pass the `0.0` check. The
example checks what **kind** of value X is; whether that value makes sense is up to you.

So should `1 ÷ 0` show Infinity, NaN or `Error`? None of them is right until you decide. That is a large part of programming: the
computer does exactly what the program says, and the program has to say something about every
case, including the ones nobody thought of. When you find one, write down what should happen
as a test, then make the program agree. The last exercise below does that for `1 ÷ 0`.

## Try it

The workbench at the end of this section is the calculator again, cut down to digits, the four
operations, `=` and `C`. Add keys to it, test first each time, and add a button for each to
`keys`. Make each key a single character, because `run` types its keys one character at a time.

Start with the two keys it is missing:

- **√** (square root): `run('16√')` is 4. Write the test, add the case to `press`, add the
  button. Then compare yours with the `√` case in "The finished calculator" above. Did you
  remember `fresh`? (What happens if you type a digit straight after `√` without it?)
- **±** (change sign): `run('5±')` is -5, and `run('5±±')` is 5. Again, compare when it works.

Then try these:

- **n!** (factorial) multiplies X by every whole number below it: `run('5!')` is 120. You wrote
  this kind of loop in Repetition. There is another way to write it, a function that calls
  itself, and it is where the next chapter, [Recursion](/recursion/), begins: it might be
  interesting to read before you write the loop, or after.
- **Power**: the key is `'^'`, and `run('2^10=')` is 1024, the first number raised to the
  power of the second (calculators often label it xʸ). It is an operator like `+`, so it
  belongs in `calculate` (`**` is the power operator) and in the operator arm of `press`.
- **.** (decimal point), the hardest: typing `1`, `.`, `5` should give 1.5. Hint: remember how
  many digits have come after the point, as a new fact in the calculator. Add it in the example
  on `press`, in `run`, in the `tosi({ calculator: … })` line, and in the `C` case, which has to
  put it back to its starting value. Nothing checks that last one for you: forget it, and the
  next number after `C` still counts digits after the point.

And some bugs to find, each starting with a test:

- What should `5±3` give? On a pocket calculator, typing 3 after -5 makes -53. Write that
  test. It fails: what does it give, and why? (Work out `x * 10 + digit` by hand for x = -5.)
- Make `press` ignore keys it does not know, instead of turning them into NaN. Test that
  `run('12?3')` is 123.

And a larger one: make `1 ÷ 0 =` show an error, in steps.

1. **The test.** Write down what should happen: `run('1÷0=')` gives back an error.
   `expect(run('1÷0=') instanceof Error).toBe(true)` says so.
2. **The error.** In `calculate`, when the operation is `÷` and X is 0, give back
   `Error('cannot divide by zero')`, as `divide` did in When Things Go Wrong. The new test
   passes.
3. **The refusal.** The `=` that made the error works: it stores the error in X. The next key
   is the problem. X is now an error, not a number, and the example on `press` says X must be a
   number, so that press is refused. On the face the button does nothing, because it ignores
   what `press` gives back. A test shows it: make a calculator, press `1`, `÷`, `0`, `=` on it,
   then check that `press(it, '+') instanceof Error` is true. That refusal is TJS keeping your
   plan.
4. **The fix.** In `press`, check the answer with `instanceof Error` before storing it. Keep
   the message as a new fact, `error: ''` (added everywhere a calculator is built, as with the
   decimal point), show it on the display when it is set, and let only `C` clear it.
5. **The decisions.** Decide what every other key should do while the error is showing, and
   test those decisions too.

Work them here. This is the workbench: the finished calculator without `√` and `±`.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

function calculate(op: '+', y: 0.0, x: 0.0) {
  given op {
    '+' { return y + x }
    '-' { return y - x }
    '×' { return y * x }
    '÷' { return y / x }
  } else {
    return x
  }
}

function press(calculator: { x: 0.0, y: 0.0, op: '', fresh: true }, key: '7') {
  given key {
    'C' {
      calculator.x = 0
      calculator.y = 0
      calculator.op = ''
      calculator.fresh = true
    }
    '+', '-', '×', '÷' {
      if (calculator.op && !calculator.fresh) {
        calculator.x = calculate(calculator.op, calculator.y, calculator.x)
      }
      calculator.y = calculator.x
      calculator.op = key
      calculator.fresh = true
    }
    '=' {
      if (calculator.op) {
        calculator.x = calculate(calculator.op, calculator.y, calculator.x)
        calculator.op = ''
        calculator.fresh = true
      }
    }
  } else {
    const digit = Number(key)
    if (calculator.fresh) {
      calculator.x = digit
      calculator.fresh = false
    } else {
      calculator.x = calculator.x * 10 + digit
    }
  }
}

function run(keys: '12+3='): 15 {
  const calculator = { x: 0, y: 0, op: '', fresh: true }
  for (const key of keys) {
    press(calculator, key)
  }
  return calculator.x
}

const { calculator } = tosi({
  calculator: { x: 0, y: 0, op: '', fresh: true },
})

const { div, button } = elements

const keys = [
  '7', '8', '9', '÷',
  '4', '5', '6', '×',
  '1', '2', '3', '-',
  '0', 'C', '=', '+',
]

preview.append(
  div(
    { style: { fontSize: '2em', textAlign: 'right', padding: '0.25em', background: '#eee' } },
    calculator.x
  ),
  div(
    { style: { display: 'grid', gridTemplateColumns: 'repeat(4, 3em)', gap: '4px' } },
    ...keys.map((key) => button({ onClick: () => press(calculator, key) }, key))
  )
)

test 'the four operations' {
  expect(run('123')).toBe(123)
  expect(run('1÷4=')).toBe(0.25)
  expect(run('2+3×4=')).toBe(20)
  expect(run('12+3C5=')).toBe(5)
}
```

# Ambient Contracts — probe reality, derive verified predicate contracts

> **Status: exploratory design note (written 2026-07-03, checked 2026-11-06).**
> This describes a direction, not a feature you can use today. The contract
> tooling is not built: there is no probe, derive or conform step in the package,
> only an experimental spike (see the contributor note at the end). What you can
> use today is the pieces it builds on: verified predicates (`verifyPredicate` in
> `tjs-lang/lang`) and the CSS validators in `tjs-lang/css`, which shipped after
> this note was written (0.9.0, 2026-07-06).

Terms used throughout. An **ambient** object is one the environment hands your
code rather than one you created: the browser's `document`, an event, Node's
`process`. A **predicate** is a function that answers true or false about a
value. A **verified** predicate is one TJS has checked is pure: it only reads,
never changes anything and never throws. A **contract** is a predicate that
describes what an object must look like.

## The itch

Static types are pessimistic about ambient runtime environments (the DOM, Node
globals, `window`, host objects) in ways that create ceremony without safety.
The canonical example:

```ts
element.addEventListener('input', (e) => {
  const value = e.target.value // ❌ TS: Property 'value' does not exist on 'EventTarget'
})
```

In TypeScript, `e.target` is declared as a generic `EventTarget | null`, and
`EventTarget` has no `.value`, so the compiler rejects this until you assert the
type with `(e.target as HTMLInputElement).value` or narrow it with
`if (e.target instanceof HTMLInputElement)`. But the honest situation is: **at
runtime the value is either there or it isn't, and a one-line runtime check can
tell you which; the cast tells you nothing.** It silences a compiler that can't
see the real object. A runtime predicate is the truthful tool here, and it is
plain JavaScript, which is the point:

```tjs
// Pure and total: it only reads properties, and it never throws.
function hasValueTarget(e) {
  return e != null && e.target != null && typeof e.target.value === 'string'
}

// Event-shaped objects, like the ones a browser hands a listener.
const inputEvent = { type: 'input', target: { tagName: 'INPUT', value: 'hi' } }
const clickOnDiv = { type: 'click', target: { tagName: 'DIV' } }

console.log(hasValueTarget(inputEvent)) // true
console.log(hasValueTarget(clickOnDiv)) // false: a <div> has no value
console.log(hasValueTarget(null)) // false, not a crash

// The usage: no cast, and no crash when the value is missing.
const e = inputEvent
console.log(hasValueTarget(e) ? e.target.value : undefined) // hi
```

"Pure" means it changes nothing; "total" means it gives an answer for every
input. That predicate is exactly what the verifier accepts: `verifyPredicate`
(from `tjs-lang/lang`) reports it safe, because member access and `typeof` are
pure. It compiles to native JavaScript, and it is **serializable**: it is source
text, so it can be captured in one place and used in another (see the next
section).

Hand-writing a predicate for every host object you touch is tedious, and the
result drifts from what the browser really does. So the thought: could tooling
**probe a real ambient environment and derive the predicate contracts
automatically?**

## The payoff: author against an environment you're not running in

The headline use: **type-checking and autocompletion against a
non-ambient runtime — editing in a Node-based toolchain while _targeting_ the
browser** (or the reverse, or Electron, or a specific Bun). Normally you have no
target environment to introspect, so you fall back to a hand-maintained
`.d.ts` (`lib.dom`: TypeScript's hand-written description of the browser APIs)
that drifts from what the engine actually does.

Because a probed contract is a **serializable predicate**, it decouples _capture_
from _consumption_ in time and space: probe the real target once (locally or in
CI), bottle the contract, and a Node-side editor/typechecker consumes it with **no
target present**. It beats a `.d.ts` on three axes:

- **Grounded in reality, not a drifting spec** — it's what the target _actually_
  exposes. happy-dom, a simulated browser used for testing in Node, reported
  about 1 own key on an element's `style` where real Chrome reports 678 (see
  the real-browser findings below); a captured contract records the real one.
- **Target-specific and versioned** — capture from the _actual_ target (this
  browser, this Electron, this Bun), selectable/pinned, not a lowest-common-
  denominator lib.
- **The same artifact validates at runtime** — a `.d.ts` evaporates; a predicate
  contract can stay as a runtime check, and it can feed autocomplete:
  `suggest()` (from `tjs-lang/lang`) reads a predicate and lists the concrete
  values it accepts, so a check for `x === 'red' || x === 'blue'` yields the
  completions `red` and `blue`.

Why it's plausible _here_ and not a research project: TJS can already embed a
predicate inside a JSON Schema (the `$predicate` keyword, via `tjs-lang/schema`),
so the contract format exists. The playground's autocomplete already asks a live
object for its members; it could ask a captured contract instead. And a planned
feature, argument-type-driven completion (for example, knowing that
`createElement('input')` returns an input element), needs exactly this metadata,
taken from reality instead of written by hand.

## Contract vs. shim — the distinction that decides feasibility

"A predicate that stands in for the DOM" can mean two very different things:

1. **A contract / validator** — "does this value behave enough like an
   `HTMLElement` / an input event / a `CSSStyleDeclaration`?" Predicates are
   _pure validators_, so this is squarely in scope: shape, property presence,
   method arity, pure invariants.
2. **A behavioral substitute** — something that, when code calls
   `document.createElement('div')`, actually _does_ it. Predicates **cannot** be
   this (they're pure, stateless, effect-free). That's a shim — happy-dom/jsdom
   territory.

The valuable, on-thesis move is **#1 as the bridge to #2**: probe the real
environment, emit a serializable predicate _contract_, and use it to **certify a
stand-in** in whatever setting. The predicate isn't the DOM — it's the portable,
verifiable spec a substitute must satisfy, auto-derived from reality and from the
surface a given program actually touches.

## Why it fits this project

- **The introspection probe already exists.** The autocomplete work runs code in
  a real iframe and reads live scope (`introspect-value.ts`,
  `introspection-bridge.ts`), and any automated real browser (a headless Chrome,
  say) can do the same against the real target. That's the "kick the tires"
  mechanism.
- **Predicates are the serializable contract form** — verified, compile to
  native, and travel as data (the `$predicate` keyword already embeds them in JSON
  Schema, evaluated by `tosijs-schema` via `tjs-lang/schema`). See the trust
  constraint below.
- **The AJS VM already models this as capabilities.** AJS, TJS's sister
  language, runs code in a sandbox (the VM) that gets outside powers such as
  `fetch` or a store only when the host passes them in explicitly. "The DOM as a
  capability, checked by a predicate where it is passed in" is the same pattern:
  a headless setting passes in a stub, and the predicate catches where it
  differs from the real thing.
- **"Types are examples" already.** In TJS, `function greet(name: 'Alice')`
  means "name is a string like `'Alice'`": the type comes from an example. A
  probed contract does the same, with the example taken from the real
  environment instead of written in the source.

## The honest constraints

- **Most of the DOM's contract is _behavioral_** (layout, events, mutation),
  which a pure predicate can't capture — only shape + pure invariants. So:
  - **Scope to the used surface.** Trace which ambient APIs the code actually
    touches (in the real iframe) and derive a contract for _that slice_, not all
    of `lib.dom.d.ts`.
  - **Behavioral conformance is a separate, impure harness** — run the same probe
    battery against the real env and a candidate stub, diff the outputs. The
    predicate is the pure shape-gate; the harness is the behavior-gate.
- **A contract is code, so trust matters.** TJS's `$predicate` paths run a
  predicate's source only if you have marked it trusted (registered with
  `trustPredicate`, or the `trustAllPredicates` option). Verification is a
  promise to the author about their own code, not a sandbox for hostile source.
  So share contracts only from probes you ran yourself; accepting untrusted
  ones would need predicates to run on the AJS VM, which is planned, not built.
- **Snapshots drift.** Browsers evolve; a captured contract is a dated snapshot.
  Fine — it's re-derivable, and versioning it is a feature (conformance over
  time).
- **Non-determinism / side effects** must stay outside predicates (the `effects`
  tag already enforces this): a predicate validates the _data_ crossing the
  boundary, never performs the effect.

## Shape of the tooling (sketch)

1. **Probe** — in a real environment (an automated real browser, or the
   introspection iframe), walk an ambient object / a program's used surface and
   record: property names + `typeof`, method names + `.length` (arity), and a few
   sampled input→output pairs for getters whose value depends only on the
   object.
2. **Derive** — turn the probe record into a predicate cluster (shape checks +
   `typeof` guards + membership sets), run it through `verifyPredicate` (so the
   emitted contract is itself certified safe), and `suggest()`-mine it for the
   enumerable leaves.
3. **Emit** — a `$predicate` schema (naive validators see structure, aware ones
   run the contract) + optionally a `.d.ts`-ish view for editors.
4. **Conform** — a harness that validates a stand-in (happy-dom, a hand stub, a
   VM capability) against the contract, failing loud where it diverges. This is
   what lets you test code that expects `HTMLElement` to exist from Node, where
   it doesn't.

## First spike — CSS + DOM (the convergence point)

Both parts of this spike were built; the results are under Findings below.

`element.style` (`CSSStyleDeclaration`) is the ideal first target: it's an
object the browser provides, its contents change as styles are set, and we
_already have a full CSS value grammar as predicates_ (`tjs-lang/css`). So the
loop is concrete and small:

- **`event.target` demo** — show the `hasValueTarget` predicate compiles, is
  verified pure, is total, and validates a real input event while rejecting a
  click on a `<div>`. The predicate TypeScript won't let you write cleanly is a
  perfectly ordinary verified predicate. (This needs no browser: synthetic
  event-shaped objects suffice for the unit; a real browser confirms on live
  events.)
- **`CSSStyleDeclaration` probe** — introspect real `element.style` in a browser,
  derive a shape contract, and diff a happy-dom `style` against it: where does the
  stub lie? Leaf _values_ ride the existing CSS predicates (`isColorValue`,
  `isDimension`, …), so this exercises probe → contract → conformance end-to-end
  while reusing the colour, dimension, shorthand and style-object validators
  `tjs-lang/css` already ships.

## Asking the browser directly: `CSS.supports`

`CSS.supports(property, value)` is a standard browser function that tells you
whether the browser accepts a CSS declaration. It is the strongest form of
"probe reality" for CSS: exact, always current with the engine's real support
(vendor prefixes, new features, the full `calc()`/`var()` grammar), and
zero-maintenance. It closes the gap the hand-written grammar has (checked
2026-11-06):

```javascript
import { isCssProperty } from 'tjs-lang/css'

isCssProperty('align-kontent') // true: it only checks the name looks like a property
CSS.supports('align-kontent', 'center') // false in a real browser
```

Property names for autocomplete come from the same place (a throwaway element's
`.style` keys / `CSSStyleDeclaration.prototype`). The tosijs 2.0 port reached
the same idea independently; its notes live in the `tosijs` repository.

This sharpens the contract-vs-fallback split by **when** validation runs:

- **Runtime, in a browser** → `CSS.supports` is ground truth (exact, free). A
  `CSS.supports`-based check is harmless to run, but it can't be _verified_: the
  verifier only certifies code whose behaviour it can see, and `CSS.supports` is
  a call into the browser it cannot inspect, so it counts as outside the
  verified world.
- **Transpile-time / SSR / Node** → no `CSS`, so the hand-authored grammar
  predicates (`isColor`/`isLength`/`isStyleValueFor`) are the portable fallback.

So the ideal CSS-value check (not built; `tjs-lang/css` has only the grammar
half) prefers `CSS.supports` when `typeof CSS !== 'undefined'`
and falls back to the grammar predicate otherwise — which is exactly the
probe-reality / portable-fallback pairing this whole note is about, one leaf down.
**Caveat (verified, and it's the same "the stand-in lies" finding): happy-dom
stubs `CSS.supports` to return `true` for everything** (even `width: banana`) — so
tests can't rely on it; ground truth needs a real browser or a real CSS engine.

## Findings from the first spike (2026-07-03)

Built in `experiments/ambient/` (`probe.ts` plus two demo tests, 7 tests, still
green on 2026-11-06). Nothing below has moved out of `experiments/` since:

- **The `event.target` predicate is ordinary.** `hasValueTarget(e)` (reads
  `e.target.value`, the thing TS rejects) verifies pure/safe, compiles native, and
  is total — no throw on a missing target. The cast TS demands buys nothing a
  predicate doesn't.
- **Host objects hide their surface on the prototype.** Probed a real
  `CSSStyleDeclaration` via happy-dom: `Object.keys(style)` is nearly empty, yet
  `typeof style.color === 'string'` and `typeof style.setProperty === 'function'`.
  So a naive own-enumerable probe derives an empty contract — **the probe must
  walk the prototype chain** (`getOwnPropertyNames` per proto) or check a scoped
  key list. `probeShape`, a helper in the spike (not part of the package), now
  does both.
- **Scope to the used surface — the full proto chain is huge.** An `HTMLElement`'s
  chain is hundreds of props; a whole-shape contract would be enormous and
  over-specified. A `keys: [...]` scope (the surface a program actually touches,
  traced from the real env) is the right input. Demonstrated: a 4-key contract for
  `style` verifies safe, accepts a real happy-dom `style` and a conforming hand
  stub, rejects a plain object missing the methods.
- **Reading accessors during a probe can have side effects** (`offsetWidth` forces
  layout). A scoped key list bounds this; a stricter probe would read property
  _descriptors_ rather than the values. Getters that throw are skipped.
- **CSS convergence holds.** Leaf values off the real object ride the existing
  `tjs-lang/css` predicates (`isColorValue(style.color)`), so shape-gate (contract)
  plus value-grammar (css) compose. The recursive style-object structure in
  `tjs-lang/css` is the same shape a DOM-derived contract would target.

Net: the probe→derive→verify→conform loop works end-to-end on a real host object;
the open work is sourcing the used-surface scope (trace) and the behavioral half.

### Real-browser findings (live Chrome, 2026-07-03)

Confirmed against a real browser (not happy-dom), by evaluating code in a live
Chrome tab. This sharpened three points:

- **Builtins don't honor `new`.** `new HTMLDivElement()` → `TypeError: Failed to
  construct 'HTMLDivElement': Illegal constructor`. You **don't need `new`** — the
  shape is on the constructor's `.prototype` chain
  (`HTMLDivElement → HTMLElement → Element → Node → EventTarget`), readable
  statically, no instance, no side effects. Cleaner than instantiating.
- **A factory tells you the type.** `document.createElement('div').constructor ===
  HTMLDivElement` (and `'a' → HTMLAnchorElement`, `'input' → HTMLInputElement`).
  So a factory's output gives you _both_ a live example (real default values — the
  "types are examples" leaf) _and_ the type identity (`.constructor` → name +
  `.constructor.prototype` → the surface). Two complementary probe sources that
  cross-check: the factory's result, and the class its `.constructor` names.
- **Structural contracts are realm-portable; `instanceof` is not — proved.** Each
  window or iframe gets its own copy of the built-in classes (its own "realm"),
  so an input created inside an iframe is an instance of the iframe's
  `HTMLInputElement`, not the parent page's. An `<iframe>`'s input: `instanceof HTMLInputElement` (top realm) = **false**, but
  the structural predicate (`typeof x.value === 'string' && x.tagName === 'INPUT'`)
  = **true**. This is the whole argument in one line: nominal DOM types are
  realm-bound (the stand-in problem _is_ a realm problem), a derived structural
  predicate crosses realms. (happy-dom couldn't show this — it shares one
  `HTMLInputElement` across `Window`s; the real browser does.)
- **Bonus — the stand-in already diverges from reality.** Real Chrome's `style`
  has **678 own keys** (CSS properties as own props); happy-dom's had ~1 (on the
  proto). Same object, wildly different probe result — exactly the conformance gap
  the harness exists to catch, and proof that you must probe _reality_, not a
  stand-in, to derive the contract.

### Generalizes beyond the DOM — Node/Bun internals

The probe is environment-agnostic: `process`, `Buffer`, `node:fs`, `Bun.*`,
`globalThis` are ambient objects with the same shape. Derive a used-surface
contract from the _real_ runtime and certify a stand-in — e.g. "does my `process`
usage survive in the browser polyfill?" or "does Bun's `process` satisfy the
contract my code derived from Node's?". It's the realm/stand-in problem one level
up: cross-_runtime_ portability instead of cross-_frame_. Same tool.

## Open questions

- Where's the line between "derive automatically" and "author, then verify
  against reality"? The probe likely _proposes_ a contract a human trims.
- Method behaviour: can a probe derive useful facts about what methods do (that
  calling one twice gives the same result, say, or the shape of what
  `getComputedStyle(el)` returns), or only their signatures?
- Editor story: a derived `$predicate` contract as the source of both validation
  _and_ autocomplete for host objects that ship no good `.d.ts`.

## For contributors

The spike is `experiments/ambient/`: `probe.ts` (`probeShape`,
`deriveShapeContract`), `event-target.demo.test.ts` and
`css-style-probe.demo.test.ts`. Related code: the predicate engine
(`src/lang/predicate.ts`), the autocomplete introspection bridge
(`demo/src/introspection-bridge.ts`, `editors/introspect-value.ts`; the
playground's `getMembers` hook), and the VM capability model (`src/vm/`).
title: Ambient Contracts — probe reality, derive verified predicate contracts
