# Full-Stack Demo: User Service

A complete backend service with typed endpoints - save this first!

<!-- TODO review -->
```tjs:inline
/#
## User Service

A complete backend service running in the browser.
Save this module as "user-service", then run the client example.

Features:
- Type-safe endpoints with validation
- In-memory data store
- Full CRUD operations
#/

// In-memory store (would be a real DB in production)
const users = new Map()
let nextId = 1

// Create a new user
export function createUser(input: {
  name: 'Alice',
  email: 'alice@example.com'
}):! { id: 0, name: '', email: '', createdAt: '' } {
  const user = {
    id: nextId++,
    name: input.name,
    email: input.email,
    // Raw `Date` is not allowed in .tjs; LegacyDate is the named escape.
    createdAt: LegacyDate().toISOString()
  }
  users.set(user.id, user)
  return user
}

// Get user by ID (null if there is no such user)
export function getUser(input: { id: 1 }):! { id: 0, name: '', email: '', createdAt: '' } | null {
  return users.get(input.id) ?? null
}

// Update a user (null if there is no such user)
export function updateUser(input: {
  id: 1,
  name: 'Alice',
  email: 'alice@example.com'
}):! { id: 0, name: '', email: '', createdAt: '' } | null {
  const existing = users.get(input.id)
  if (!existing) return null

  const updated = { ...existing, name: input.name, email: input.email }
  users.set(input.id, updated)
  return updated
}

// Delete a user
export function deleteUser(input: { id: 1 }):! { success: true, deleted: 0 } {
  const existed = users.has(input.id)
  users.delete(input.id)
  return { success: existed, deleted: existed ? input.id : 0 }
}

// List all users
export function listUsers(input: { limit: 10, offset: 0 }):! { users: [{ id: 0, name: '', email: '', createdAt: '' }], total: 0 } {
  const all = [...users.values()]
  const slice = all.slice(input.offset, input.offset + input.limit)
  return { users: slice, total: all.length }
}

// Search users by name
export function searchUsers(input: { query: '' }):! { users: [{ id: 0, name: '', email: '', createdAt: '' }] } {
  const query = input.query.toLowerCase()
  const matches = [...users.values()].filter(u =>
    u.name.toLowerCase().includes(query)
  )
  return { users: matches }
}

// Test the service
test 'createUser creates user with ID' {
  const user = createUser({ name: 'Test', email: 'test@test.com' })
  expect(user.id).toBeGreaterThan(0)
  expect(user.name).toBe('Test')
}

test 'getUser returns created user' {
  const created = createUser({ name: 'Bob', email: 'bob@test.com' })
  const fetched = getUser({ id: created.id })
  expect(fetched.name).toBe('Bob')
}

test 'updateUser modifies user' {
  const user = createUser({ name: 'Original', email: 'orig@test.com' })
  const updated = updateUser({ id: user.id, name: 'Updated', email: 'new@test.com' })
  expect(updated.name).toBe('Updated')
}

test 'deleteUser removes user' {
  const user = createUser({ name: 'ToDelete', email: 'del@test.com' })
  const result = deleteUser({ id: user.id })
  expect(result.success).toBe(true)
  expect(getUser({ id: user.id })).toBe(null)
}

test 'a wrong input type is an error value, not a crash' {
  const bad = createUser({ name: 123, email: 'x@example.com' })
  expect(bad instanceof Error).toBe(true)
}

// Demo
console.log('=== User Service Demo ===\n')

const alice = createUser({ name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@company.com' })
console.log('Created:', alice)

const bob = createUser({ name: 'Bob', email: 'bob@company.com' })
console.log('Created:', bob)

const carol = createUser({ name: 'Carol', email: 'carol@company.com' })
console.log('Created:', carol)

console.log('\nAll users:', listUsers({ limit: 10, offset: 0 }))
console.log('\nSearch "ob":', searchUsers({ query: 'ob' }))

// Type validation in action: the call returns an error VALUE
console.log('\nType validation test:')
const bad = createUser({ name: 123, email: 'x@example.com' })
console.log('createUser({ name: 123 }) ->', bad.message)
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

- **Each endpoint's input is a typed object, given by example.** `createUser(input: { name:
  'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com' })` says the input must be an object with string `name`
  and `email`. The example values double as documentation of what a real request looks like.
- **A bad request is a value, not an exception.** The last line calls `createUser` with a
  number for `name`. The function body never runs; the call returns a `MonadicError` naming
  the path that failed (`createUser.input.name`), which the caller can inspect, log or pass
  back over the wire. Nothing throws, so one bad request cannot take a handler down.
- **The returns are `:!`, type-only.** A plain `:` return is a worked example: TJS would call
  `createUser` with the example input at build time and require the result to deep-equal the
  annotation. These endpoints mutate a store and stamp the time, so no fixed result could
  match; `:!` keeps the return shape as documentation without running it.
- **"Not found" is `null`.** `getUser` returns the record or `null`, and the return annotation
  says so with `| null`.
- **Tests travel with the module.** The `test` blocks run when the file is transpiled and
  are stripped from the output, so the service carries its own checks without shipping them.

<!-- TODO review -->
## A typed endpoint with defaults

Optional query parameters are the other half of most endpoints. An object-literal default
in TJS is a *dictionary*: each member has its own default, and a partial argument is merged
with them, so a caller can send only what it cares about:

```tjs:inline
const items = Array.from({ length: 25 }, (_, i) => `item ${i + 1}`)

function page(query = { limit: 10, offset: 0 }):! { items: [''], total: 0 } {
  const { limit, offset } = query
  return { items: items.slice(offset, offset + limit), total: items.length }
}

console.log('page()                ->', page().items.join(', '))
console.log('page({ offset: 20 })  ->', page({ offset: 20 }).items.join(', '))
console.log('page({ limit: 2 })    ->', page({ limit: 2 }).items.join(', '))

// Members are type-checked, so a string offset is refused before the body runs.
const bad = page({ offset: 'ten' })
console.log('page({ offset: "ten" }) ->', bad instanceof Error ? bad.message : bad)
```

`page({ offset: 20 })` gets `limit: 10` from the default; JavaScript would have replaced the
whole default object and left `limit` undefined. See [Dictionary
Defaults](/dictionary-defaults-example/) for the full rules.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Limits

- **The store is a `Map` in memory.** It lives as long as the page. In production the same
  functions would wrap a database; the signatures, validation and tests would not change.
- **Validation checks inputs, not return values.** By default TJS validates what comes *in*
  to a function (`safety inputs`). The `:!` returns here are not checked at runtime.
- **Running in the browser is not the same as being a server.** This module has no network
  boundary of its own. To expose it to other machines you still need a transport (an HTTP
  handler, or the AJS VM as in [The Universal Endpoint](/the-universal-endpoint/)).

Save this module as `user-service` in the playground, then run
[Full-Stack Demo: Client App](/full-stack-demo-client-app/), which imports it.

# LLM Structured Output

Free text is hard for a program to use. Ask the model for JSON in a declared shape instead, and
an agent can pull fields out of prose, classify a message, or fill in a form.

The VM has no model of its own. The **host**, the JavaScript program that runs the VM, passes in
an `llm` capability with a `predict` function, and every `llmPredict` call goes to it. This site's
host provides no model, so the examples that call one show "This example needs an LLM, which the
static site does not provide. Run it locally with tjs-lang and LM Studio (see the AJS guide)."
instead of a result. [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/) has a ready-made host to run them locally.

The examples use three AJS built-ins: `llmPredict({ prompt, options })` sends a prompt to the
model and returns its reply as a string; `Schema` builds and checks JSON schemas; `JSON.parse`
works as in JavaScript. `llmPredict`'s `options` may contain `responseFormat` (below),
`temperature`, `maxTokens`, `topP`, `stop`, `seed`, `model` and `tools` (`max_tokens` and `top_p` are accepted as spellings too); any
other key is refused. `temperature: 0` asks the model for its most likely answer every time, which suits
extraction.

```ajs:inline
function extractInfo({
  text = 'John Smith is a 35-year-old software engineer from San Francisco who loves hiking and photography.',
}) {
  let schema = Schema.response('person_info', {
    name: '',
    age: 0,
    occupation: '',
    location: '',
    hobbies: [''],
  })
  let prompt = 'Extract the person described in this text: ' + text
  let reply = llmPredict({ prompt, options: { responseFormat: schema } })
  let person = JSON.parse(reply)
  return { person }
}
```

With a model that follows the schema, the result is:

```javascript
{
  person: {
    name: 'John Smith',
    age: 35,
    occupation: 'software engineer',
    location: 'San Francisco',
    hobbies: ['hiking', 'photography'],
  },
}
```

## What to notice

- **The schema is built from an example.** `Schema.response(name, example)` returns plain JSON,
  the OpenAI-style response format:
  `{ type: 'json_schema', json_schema: { name, strict: true, schema } }`. From the example above,
  `schema` says `name` is a string, `age` an integer, `hobbies` an array of strings, and every
  field is required.
- **`responseFormat` is passed through to the host.** `llmPredict` hands `options` to the host's
  `predict` unchanged; the host from [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/) sends it to the server as
  `response_format`. The VM checks its shape first: only the `json_schema` form above,
  `{ type: 'json_object' }` and `{ type: 'text' }` are accepted. Anything else fails the call
  with `responseFormat is not available in AsyncJS: use { type: 'json_schema', json_schema: { name, schema } } (Schema.response builds it)`
  (AsyncJS is AJS's full name). The refusal is an ordinary error: a `try` around the call
  catches it.
- **The reply is still a string.** `llmPredict` returns text, and `JSON.parse` turns it into data.
  If the reply is not JSON, `JSON.parse` fails, and with no `try` around it the agent stops
  there. `vm.run` does not throw: it resolves with `run.error` set to the parse error (for
  example `JSON Parse error: Unexpected identifier "Sure"`) and no `person`. See
  [Error Handling](/ajs-error-handling/).

## Checking the reply

The schema is a request, not a guarantee. A server that supports structured output constrains
the model to it; another may treat it as a hint or ignore it, and the model can still answer
with prose. So an agent that other code depends on parses inside `try` and validates what
it got.

`Schema.response` wraps the JSON Schema in the response format, so the schema itself is at
`schema.json_schema.schema`. `Schema.isValid(value, schema)` takes that inner schema, not the
wrapper. And unlike JavaScript, a caught error in AJS is a string (its message), which is why the
`catch` can write `'reply is not JSON: ' + e`.

```ajs:inline
function extractChecked({ text = 'Ada Lovelace, 36, mathematician, London.' }) {
  let schema = Schema.response('person', { name: '', age: 0, occupation: '' })
  let reply = llmPredict({
    prompt: 'Extract the person described in this text: ' + text,
    options: { responseFormat: schema, temperature: 0 },
  })
  try {
    let person = JSON.parse(reply)
    // the inner JSON Schema, not the response-format wrapper
    if (!Schema.isValid(person, schema.json_schema.schema)) {
      return { error: 'reply does not match the schema', person }
    }
    return { person }
  } catch (e) {
    return { error: 'reply is not JSON: ' + e, reply }
  }
}
```

The three outcomes, for three replies:

| The model replies                                                  | The agent returns                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `{"name":"Ada Lovelace","age":36,"occupation":"mathematician"}`    | `{ person: { … } }`                                   |
| `{"name":"Ada Lovelace","age":"36","occupation":"mathematician"}` | `{ error: 'reply does not match the schema', person }` |
| `Sure! Here is the JSON`                                           | `{ error: 'reply is not JSON: …', reply }`            |

The second reply differs from the first only in `"36"`: the age is a string, and the schema says
integer.

Validation costs **fuel**, the VM's work budget: the host sets it for each run, every step
spends some, and the run stops with `Out of Fuel` when it is gone. Validation costs in proportion
to the size of the schema times the size of the data, which is small next to the `llmPredict`
call itself (about 100 fuel). [Fuel Limits](/fuel-limits/) shows a run hitting its budget.

A schema built from an example lists every field as required but does not forbid extra ones: a
reply with an added `notes` field passes `isValid`. To refuse extra fields, build the object with
`Schema.object`, which takes the same kind of example and adds `additionalProperties: false`,
and pass the result to `Schema.response`:

```ajs:inline
function strictPerson({}) {
  let schema = Schema.response(
    'person',
    Schema.object({ name: '', age: 0, occupation: '' })
  )
  let reply = { name: 'Ada Lovelace', age: 36, occupation: 'mathematician', notes: 'x' }
  return { ok: Schema.isValid(reply, schema.json_schema.schema) }
}
```

This returns `{ ok: false }`; without the `notes` field it would be `{ ok: true }`.

## Classifying

A fixed set of answers is an `enum`. An example value cannot say "one of these four strings", so
put a schema value in the example at that spot, and fall back to a safe default when the reply
does not fit:

```ajs:inline
function classify({ ticket = 'The app crashes every time I open the settings page.' }) {
  let schema = Schema.response('triage', {
    category: Schema.enum(['bug', 'billing', 'feature', 'other']),
    urgent: false,
    summary: '',
  })
  let reply = llmPredict({
    prompt:
      'Triage this support ticket. Summarize it in one sentence.\n\n' + ticket,
    options: { responseFormat: schema, temperature: 0 },
  })
  try {
    let triage = JSON.parse(reply)
    if (Schema.isValid(triage, schema.json_schema.schema)) {
      return { triage }
    }
  } catch (e) {}
  return { triage: { category: 'other', urgent: false, summary: ticket } }
}
```

`Schema.enum([...])` becomes `{ type: 'string', enum: [...] }`, so a reply with
`"category": "crash"` fails validation and the agent returns the fallback instead of an
unexpected category. The fallback puts the whole ticket in `summary` on purpose: when the model's
answer is unusable, the raw text is kept for a person to read, so nothing is lost.

### Schema values you can put in an example

Anywhere an example takes a value, a schema value can stand in for it:

- **Ready-made schemas, used without a call:** `Schema.string`, `Schema.number`,
  `Schema.integer`, `Schema.boolean`, `Schema.email` and the other named formats. Each is
  already a plain JSON schema: `Schema.number` is `{ type: 'number' }`, `Schema.email` is
  `{ type: 'string', format: 'email' }`.
- **Builders, called with arguments:** `Schema.enum([...])`, `Schema.const(value)`,
  `Schema.object({ ... })`, `Schema.array(item)` and a few more.
- **A plain JSON Schema object**, for constraints no builder covers:
  `{ type: 'integer', minimum: 0, maximum: 150 }`.

The full list is under Schema in the [AJS guide](/DOCS-AJS/).

## Fractional numbers: use `Schema.number`

`price: 0.0` in a `Schema.response` example gives an **integer** schema, so a model held to it
cannot answer `19.99`. For a field that may hold a fraction (a price, a score, a confidence),
write `Schema.number`.

The reason: in an agent's own parameters, `0.0` means "a number that may be fractional" and `0`
means "an integer", because the transpiler reads the example from the source text, where the two
are written differently. `Schema.response` runs inside the VM and receives a value, not source
text, and `0.0` and `0` are the same number, so both mean integer there.

```ajs:inline
// An agent always takes one object of named inputs; this one needs none.
function priceSchemas({}) {
  let fromExample = Schema.response('item', { name: '', price: 0.0 })
  let explicit = Schema.response('item', { name: '', price: Schema.number })
  return {
    fromExample: fromExample.json_schema.schema.properties.price,
    explicit: explicit.json_schema.schema.properties.price,
  }
}
```

This returns `{ fromExample: { type: 'integer' }, explicit: { type: 'number' } }`. A
non-integer example, such as `0.5`, also gives `{ type: 'number' }`.

With the integer schema, a server that enforces it will not let the model write `19.99`, and
`Schema.isValid` refuses a `19.99` that gets through anyway.

## Which schema keywords are allowed

A schema the agent builds is **guest** data: it comes from the agent, which may be untrusted, so
the VM checks it before using it. It admits only keywords it can check while metering the work:
`type`, `properties`, `required`, `items`, `additionalProperties`, `enum`, `const`, `anyOf`,
`oneOf`, the numeric and length bounds (`minimum`, `maxLength`, and so on), `format` with one of
`email`, `uuid`, `uri`, `ipv4`, `date`, `date-time` or `emoji`, and the annotation keywords
`title`, `description`, `default` and `examples`. The full list is under Schema in the
[AJS guide](/DOCS-AJS/).

`pattern` is refused. Checking it would run the host's regex engine, which the VM does not meter,
so a hostile pattern could hang the host. The message says so and names the replacement:

```text
This schema is not available in AsyncJS (.properties.z.pattern: a 'pattern' is compiled by the host's regex engine). Guest schemas may use only the validation keywords the VM admits; for a pattern, use regexMatch (it runs on the VM's regex engine).
```

Like the `responseFormat` refusal, this is an ordinary error, and a `try` around the call that
used the schema (`Schema.isValid` here) catches it.

To check a field against a pattern, parse the reply and test the field with
`regexMatch({ pattern, value })`, which runs on the VM's own regex engine and returns `true` or
`false`:

```javascript
let order = JSON.parse(reply)
let codeOk = regexMatch({ pattern: /^[A-Z]{2}-\d{4}$/, value: order.code }) // true for 'AB-1234'
```

## Testing an agent without a model

Capabilities are the only way an agent reaches the outside world, and the VM calls
`capabilities.llm.predict(prompt, options)` for every `llmPredict({ prompt, options })`: the
agent's one object becomes two positional arguments. So a host can stand in for the model with a
`predict` that returns a canned reply. That makes the checking code above testable without a
server, and shows exactly what the agent sent:

```javascript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

const sent = []
const llm = {
  async predict(prompt, options) {
    sent.push({ prompt, options })
    return '{"name":"Ada Lovelace","age":"36","occupation":"mathematician"}'
  },
}

const source = `
function extractChecked({ text = 'Ada Lovelace, 36, mathematician, London.' }) {
  let schema = Schema.response('person', { name: '', age: 0, occupation: '' })
  let reply = llmPredict({
    prompt: 'Extract the person described in this text: ' + text,
    options: { responseFormat: schema, temperature: 0 },
  })
  try {
    let person = JSON.parse(reply)
    if (!Schema.isValid(person, schema.json_schema.schema)) {
      return { error: 'reply does not match the schema', person }
    }
    return { person }
  } catch (e) {
    return { error: 'reply is not JSON: ' + e, reply }
  }
}
`

const { ast } = transpile(source)
// {} passes no inputs, so the agent uses its default `text`
const run = await new AgentVM().run(ast, {}, { fuel: 1000, capabilities: { llm } })
console.log(run.result) // { error: 'reply does not match the schema', person: { … } }
console.log(sent[0].options.responseFormat.json_schema.schema.properties.age) // { type: 'integer' }
```

If the run itself fails (out of fuel, a missing capability, an error nothing caught), `run.error`
holds the failure. Each `llmPredict` call costs about 100 fuel and this run uses about 101, so
1000 is generous for one call; budget for the number of model calls an agent makes, or a run
with 50 fuel stops with `Out of Fuel` at its first `llmPredict`.
title: LLM Structured Output
description: Free text is hard for a program to use. Ask the model for JSON in a declared shape instead, and an agent can pull fields out of prose, classify a message, or fill in a form. The VM has no model of its own. The **host**, the JavaScript program that runs the VM, passes in an `llm` capability with a `predict` function, and every `llmPredict` call goes to it. This site's host provides no model, so the examples that call one show "This example needs an LLM, which the static site does not provide. Run it locally with tjs-lang and LM Studio (see the AJS guide)." instead of a result. [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/) has a ready-made host to run them locally. The examples use three AJS built-ins: `llmPredict({ prompt, options })` sends a prompt to the model and returns its reply as a string; `Schema` builds and checks JSON schemas; `JSON.parse` works as in JavaScript. `llmPredict`'s `options` may contain `responseFormat` (below), `temperature`, `maxTokens`, `topP`, `stop`, `seed`, `model` and `tools` (`max_tokens` and `top_p` are accepted as spellings too); any other key is refused. `temperature: 0` asks the model for its most likely answer every time, which suits extraction.

# Lodash Utilities (with import)

[lodash](https://lodash.com/docs/) is a popular library of untyped JavaScript helpers. This
example wraps four of them: `sortBy` (sort a list by a field), `uniqBy` (drop records that
repeat a field), `chunk` (split a list into pages) and `groupBy` (bucket records by a
field). It adds a fifth function, a small pipeline that combines them. Each wrapper's
signature says, by example, what goes in and what comes out, so calls are checked at the
wrapper and the worked examples test lodash itself.

## Reading the signatures

Two rules from [TJS syntax](/TJS-SYNTAX/) make the code below readable:

- **A parameter's value after `:` is an example, not a default and not a literal type.**
  TJS infers a type from it and checks every call against that type. `users: [{ name:
  'Ann', age: 40 }, { name: 'Bo', age: 25 }]` means "an array of `{ name, age }`
  records", of any length. `name` is a string and `age` is an integer: a whole number
  means integer, so `age: 25.5` is refused (write `40.0` to allow fractions). The same
  reading makes `id: 0` and `count: 0` integers. The second record in the example does
  not make the array a pair; it is there to feed the worked example.
- **A return value after `:` is a worked example.** TJS calls the function with the
  parameter examples and compares the result to the return example by deep equality.

There are three ways to write a return:

| Form | Runs the worked example | Checks real calls' results |
| ---- | ----------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `): example` | yes | no |
| `):! example` | no | no |
| `):? example` | yes | yes |

`:!` is a declaration only. It still feeds the function's type metadata (what `tjs types`,
generated `.d.ts` files and editors show), so `processUserData`'s detailed `:!` shape
documents the result without checking it.

The code opens with a `/# … #/` block: a TJS doc comment, rendered as markdown above the
code (see [Doc comments](/TJS-SYNTAX/#doc-comments-)).

```tjs:inline
/#
## Typed wrappers around lodash

lodash is plain JavaScript with no types. Each wrapper below states, by example, what it
accepts and what it returns. The library stays untyped; the boundary does not.
#/

import { groupBy, sortBy, uniqBy, chunk } from 'lodash-es'

// A worked example: called with the two users shown, it must return them youngest first.
// `age: 40` is an integer example, so fractional ages are refused.
function sortByAge(
  users: [{ name: 'Ann', age: 40 }, { name: 'Bo', age: 25 }]
): [{ name: 'Bo', age: 25 }, { name: 'Ann', age: 40 }] {
  return sortBy(users, ['age'])
}

// The first record with each email wins
function uniqueByEmail(
  users: [{ email: 'a@x.com', name: 'Ann' }, { email: 'a@x.com', name: 'Annie' }]
): [{ email: 'a@x.com', name: 'Ann' }] {
  return uniqBy(users, 'email')
}

// Array examples nest: the result is an array of arrays of strings
function paginate(items: ['a', 'b', 'c'], pageSize: 2): [['a', 'b'], ['c']] {
  return chunk(items, pageSize)
}

// The keys of a grouped result are data, so the return is type-only (`:!`):
// "an object", with no worked example to check
function groupUsers(users: [{ name: '', dept: '' }], key: 'dept'):! {} {
  return groupBy(users, key)
}

// A pipeline built from the same pieces
function processUserData(input: {
  users: [{ id: 0, name: '', email: '', dept: '' }]
}):! {
  byDept: {},
  unique: [{ id: 0, name: '', email: '', dept: '' }],
  count: 0
} {
  const unique = uniqBy(input.users, 'email')
  return {
    byDept: groupBy(unique, 'dept'),
    unique: sortBy(unique, ['name']),
    count: unique.length
  }
}

test 'groupUsers groups by department' {
  const grouped = groupUsers([
    { name: 'Alice', dept: 'eng' },
    { name: 'Bob', dept: 'sales' },
    { name: 'Carol', dept: 'eng' }
  ], 'dept')
  expect(grouped.eng.length).toBe(2)
  expect(grouped.sales.length).toBe(1)
}

test 'paginate leaves the remainder on the last page' {
  const pages = paginate(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'], 2)
  expect(pages.length).toBe(3)
  expect(pages[2]).toEqual(['e'])
}

test 'the wrapper refuses what lodash would accept' {
  // lodash would sort the string's characters; the wrapper refuses it
  expect(isMonadicError(sortByAge('not an array'))).toBe(true)
  expect(isMonadicError(sortByAge([{ name: 'Cy', age: 'old' }]))).toBe(true)
}

// Try it
const users = [
  { id: 1, name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@co.com', dept: 'Engineering' },
  { id: 2, name: 'Bob', email: 'bob@co.com', dept: 'Sales' },
  { id: 3, name: 'Carol', email: 'carol@co.com', dept: 'Engineering' },
  { id: 4, name: 'Dave', email: 'alice@co.com', dept: 'Marketing' }, // reuses Alice's email
]

const result = processUserData({ users })
console.log('Unique users:', result.count)
console.log('Departments:', Object.keys(result.byDept))
console.log('Engineering team:', result.byDept['Engineering'].map(u => u.name))
console.log(sortByAge('not an array').message)
```

It prints:

```text
Unique users: 3
Departments: [ "Engineering", "Sales" ]
Engineering team: [ "Alice", "Carol" ]
Expected array of object for '<file>:12:sortByAge.users', got string
```

Dave reuses Alice's email, so `uniqBy` drops him and `Marketing` never appears among the
departments. The last line is the wrapper's refusal. An error message names the file and
line where the function is declared, then the parameter; the file name depends on where
the code runs, so it is shown here as `<file>`.

## The boundary is the signature

lodash accepts almost anything. `sortBy('not an array', ['age'])` does not complain: it
treats the string as a collection and hands back its characters as an array. Code that
passed the wrong value would carry on with nonsense.

`sortByAge` cannot be called that way. Its parameter example is an array of
`{ name, age }` records, so a string, or a record whose `age` is `'old'`, is refused before
lodash runs. The call does not throw. It returns a `MonadicError`, an `Error` object that
TJS hands back as the result, naming the parameter (`sortByAge.users`, or
`sortByAge.users[0].age`). `isMonadicError(x)` tells you whether you got one; see
[Error Handling](/error-handling/). The library is unchanged; what changed is the edge
your own code touches.

The check is on shape, not on the length of the example: `sortByAge` accepts one record or
a hundred.

## Choosing worked examples

The three worked examples in the code are:

- `sortByAge` is called with Ann (40) and Bo (25) and must return Bo first.
- `uniqueByEmail` is called with two records sharing an email and must keep the first.
- `paginate(['a', 'b', 'c'], 2)` must return `[['a', 'b'], ['c']]`.

Because the bodies call lodash, each of these is a test of lodash too: if `sortBy` sorted
the other way, or `chunk` dropped the remainder, the example would fail. Choose examples
that would catch a mistake. A one-element array would "sort" correctly whatever the body
did.

`groupUsers` and `processUserData` use `:!`. A grouped result's keys are data (`'eng'`,
`'sales'`), so no single result is worth asserting. The `test` blocks cover what the
examples cannot.

## Checking every result with `:?`

A plain `:` return is a test, not a runtime check: a real call's result is not validated.
If you do not trust a library to return what you declared, use `:?`. Here is a wrapper
with a bug, mapping `age` where it meant `name`:

```javascript
import { map } from 'lodash-es'

function names(users: [{ name: 'Ann', age: 40 }]):? ['Ann'] {
  return map(users, 'age') // the bug: should be 'name'
}

names([{ name: 'Bo', age: 25 }]).message
// Expected array of string for '<file>:3:names:return', got array of number
```

Both halves of `:?` catch it. The worked example fails, because `[40]` is not `['Ann']`.
And every real call returns the `MonadicError` shown instead of a list of numbers. With a
plain `:` return, only the worked example would catch it; with `:!`, nothing would.

## Where the tests run, and where they cannot

The tests and worked examples need lodash, so where they run decides what they report.

- **On this page**, the example runs in the browser. A service worker fetches the bare
  import `'lodash-es'` from a CDN (see [Date Formatting (with
  import)](/date-formatting-with-import/) and [CDN Hints](/cdn-hints/)). The tests and
  worked examples run in the page after the import has loaded, against the real library,
  and pass.
- **With the `tjs` CLI**, the tests run at transpile time. TJS executes the module's own
  code with its `import` statements left out, so lodash is never loaded there, even when
  `lodash-es` is installed. `tjs test` lists every test and worked example that reaches
  lodash as `?` (inconclusive: neither passed nor failed) and exits 0. `tjs check` runs the
  same tests but does not report inconclusive ones: it prints a tick and the signatures and
  exits 0. A green `check` on this file means the tests did not run, not that they passed.
- **`tjs run`** loads `lodash-es` the way Bun resolves any import (from your
  `node_modules`, or by Bun's auto-install when there is none), so its console output is
  real.
- **If the CDN is unreachable**, the import fails, so the example stops at its first line
  with an error instead of printing, and its tests cannot run. You see a failure to load,
  never a wrong answer. (A copy the service worker cached on an earlier visit may still
  load.)

Two separate things make a CLI test inconclusive:

1. A test or worked example that calls lodash is always inconclusive on the CLI.
2. The module's top level runs before any test, so top-level code that calls lodash stops
   the whole module. Here `processUserData({ users })` at the bottom does that, so even
   `the wrapper refuses what lodash would accept`, which never reaches lodash, comes out
   inconclusive.

Keeping demo calls out of the module you test fixes the second, not the first: the tests
that do not touch lodash then run and pass, and the ones that do stay inconclusive.

## Gotchas

- **A wrapper's types are only as good as its example.** `[{ name: '', dept: '' }]` checks
  that every element has a string `name` and `dept`; it does not check that `key` names a
  field that exists. `groupUsers(users, 'nope')` is well typed and groups everything under
  the key `'undefined'`. A rule like that belongs in the function body, or in a `Type` with
  a predicate (see [Predicate Types](/predicate-types/)).
- **Excess keys pass.** A record with extra fields still matches `{ name: '', dept: '' }`,
  so `groupUsers` accepts full user records, `id` and `email` included, though its example
  names only `name` and `dept`.
- **`age: 40` is an integer.** See [Reading the signatures](#reading-the-signatures):
  `age: 25.5` is refused unless the example is `40.0`.

# Full-Stack Demo: Client App

Frontend that calls the User Service - run after saving user-service!

> **Needs a second module.** This example imports the `user-service` module from the "User Service" example, which a single example on this
> page cannot load. Run it in the [playground](https://tjs-platform.web.app) after saving that
> module, or locally with `tjs run` beside it.

```tjs:static
/#
## Client Application

A frontend that calls the User Service.

**First:** Run the "User Service" example and save it as "user-service"
**Then:** Run this client to see full-stack in action

This demonstrates:
- Importing local TJS modules
- Type-safe service calls
- Error handling
#/

// Import from local module (saved in playground)
import { createUser, getUser, listUsers, searchUsers } from 'user-service'

// Helper to display results
function display(label: '', data: {}) {
  console.log(`\n${label}:`)
  console.log(JSON.stringify(data, null, 2))
}

// Main app
async function main() {
  console.log('=== Client App ===')
  console.log('Connecting to user-service...\n')

  // Create some users
  const user1 = createUser({ name: 'Dave', email: 'dave@startup.io' })
  display('Created user', user1)

  const user2 = createUser({ name: 'Eve', email: 'eve@startup.io' })
  display('Created user', user2)

  // Fetch a user
  const fetched = getUser({ id: user1.id })
  display('Fetched user', fetched)

  // List all
  const all = listUsers({ limit: 100, offset: 0 })
  display('All users', all)

  // Search
  const results = searchUsers({ query: 'eve' })
  display('Search results for "eve"', results)

  // Type error handling: the error comes back as a value; nothing is thrown
  console.log('\n--- Type Validation Demo ---')
  const badResult = createUser({ name: 999 })
  if (badResult instanceof Error) {
    console.log('Got a type error back:', badResult.message)
  }

  console.log('\n=== Full-Stack Demo Complete ===')
  console.log('Everything ran in the browser. No server. No build step.')
}

main()
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

- **The import is the whole integration.** `import { createUser, … } from 'user-service'`
  pulls in the module you saved from the User Service example. There is no client SDK, no
  generated stubs and no schema file: the service's function signatures *are* its contract,
  and they are enforced on every call because the validation lives in the service's own
  emitted code.
- **Errors arrive as values.** `createUser({ name: 999 })` does not throw into `main`. It
  returns a `MonadicError` (which is an `Error`, so `instanceof Error` works), and the client
  decides what to do with it.
- **`display(label: '', data: {})` is typed too.** The client is TJS as well, so its own
  helpers get the same checks as the service.

<!-- TODO review -->
## The same pattern, on one page

A client of a typed service has three outcomes to handle: the data, "not found", and "you
sent the wrong thing". This version inlines a stand-in for the service so it runs here:

```tjs:inline
// A stand-in for the user-service module, so this example runs on its own.
const users = new Map([[1, { id: 1, name: 'Dave' }]])

function getUser(input: { id: 1 }):! { id: 0, name: '' } | null {
  return users.get(input.id) ?? null
}

// The client: three outcomes, three branches.
function show(input) {
  const user = getUser(input)
  if (user instanceof Error) return `bad request: ${user.message}`
  if (user === null) return `no user ${input.id}`
  return `found ${user.name}`
}

console.log(show({ id: 1 }))
console.log(show({ id: 7 }))
console.log(show({ id: 'one' }))
```

Check for the error first. A `MonadicError` is an object, so a client that tested only for
`null` would treat it as a user and read `undefined` fields off it.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Limits

- **`'user-service'` is a playground module name**, not an npm package. The playground
  resolves it to the module you saved. In a project, import the file by path (for example
  `./user-service.tjs`) with the Bun plugin or a build step that handles `.tjs`.
- **This is not a network call.** Client and service run in the same JavaScript context. The
  point of the demo is that the *contract* (typed inputs, error values) is the same one you
  would put behind HTTP; the transport is still yours to add.

# LLM + API Data

The shape of a real agent: fetch facts from an API, let a model reason over them, and return a
structured answer. Here the facts are iTunes search results and the question is which of them are
cover versions. It needs an LLM, so on this site it prints a message instead of running; run it
locally with the host (the JavaScript program that runs the VM) shown below.

```ajs:inline
function findCovers({ song = 'Yesterday', artist = 'Beatles' }) {
  // Search iTunes for the song
  let term = encodeURIComponent(song + ' ' + artist)
  let url = `https://itunes.apple.com/search?term=${term}&limit=25&media=music`
  // iTunes serves JSON as `text/javascript`, so ask for JSON explicitly.
  let response = httpFetch({ url, responseType: 'json' })
  let results = response.results || []

  // Nothing found (or the body was not read as JSON): say so, and skip the model.
  if (results.length == 0) {
    return { originalArtist: artist, song, covers: [], note: 'no search results' }
  }

  // One line per track: all the model needs to see
  let tracks = results.map(
    (x) => `"${x.trackName}" by ${x.artistName} (${x.collectionName || 'single'})`
  )
  let trackList = tracks.join('\n')

  // The shape the answer must come back in, written as an example
  let schema = Schema.response('cover_versions', {
    covers: [{ track: '', artist: '', album: '' }],
  })

  let prompt = `Search results for "${song}" by ${artist}:\n\n${trackList}\n\nList cover versions (tracks NOT by ${artist}).`

  let reply = llmPredict({ prompt, options: { responseFormat: schema } })
  let parsed = JSON.parse(reply)
  if (!Array.isArray(parsed.covers)) {
    return { originalArtist: artist, song, covers: [], note: 'the model did not list covers' }
  }
  return { originalArtist: artist, song, covers: parsed.covers }
}
```

`httpFetch`, `llmPredict` and `Schema` need no import: they are built into AJS. `httpFetch` and
`llmPredict` are atoms, the VM's operations, and an atom takes its inputs by name in a single
object (`httpFetch({ url })`, never `httpFetch(url)` (refused)).

## What to notice

- **The agent does the boring part itself.** Fetching, trimming 25 results to one line each, and
  joining them is plain code: cheap, deterministic, and paid for in fuel, the VM's budget for
  work (see below). The model is asked only the question that needs judgment.
- **It checks for data before it asks.** If the search found nothing, the agent returns at once
  and no model call is made. Without that check the model would be asked about an empty list,
  and it would answer anyway (see the gotcha below).
- **The model sees text, the program gets data.** The prompt is a string the agent built. The
  answer comes back in a declared shape: `Schema.response(name, example)` turns an example
  object into an OpenAI-style `response_format` (a strict JSON Schema), the host hands it to the
  model server, and `JSON.parse` turns the reply into an object the agent (and whoever receives
  its result) can use without reading prose.
- **`llmPredict` returns a string**, even with a response format. That is why the agent parses
  it. If the reply is not JSON at all, `JSON.parse` fails and the run ends with that error. If it
  is JSON without a `covers` list, the `Array.isArray` check returns an empty answer with a note
  rather than `covers: undefined`.
- **Two grants, and nothing else.** The `llm` capability, and network access limited to the
  domains in `allowedFetchDomains`. The agent cannot reach anything the host did not grant.

## Running it locally

The host supplies an `llm` capability: an object whose `predict(prompt, options)` returns the
model's reply as a string. This one talks to any OpenAI-compatible server (LM Studio's default
port here); [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/) explains it and a fuller version.

The network is not passed as a capability. `httpFetch` uses the VM's built-in fetch client,
which fetches only from the domains in `context.allowedFetchDomains`. Without that list (or a
`fetch` capability of the host's own, which then replaces the built-in client) every request is
refused: `Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured`.

```javascript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

const llm = {
  async predict(prompt, options = {}) {
    const res = await fetch('http://localhost:1234/v1/chat/completions', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        model: 'local-model',
        messages: [{ role: 'user', content: prompt }],
        response_format: options.responseFormat,
      }),
    })
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`model server answered ${res.status}`)
    const data = await res.json()
    return data.choices[0].message.content ?? ''
  },
}

const { ast } = transpile(source) // source: the agent above, as a string
const run = await new AgentVM().run(
  ast,
  { song: 'Yesterday', artist: 'Beatles' },
  {
    fuel: 1000,
    capabilities: { llm },
    context: { allowedFetchDomains: ['itunes.apple.com'] },
    quotas: { llmPredict: 1 },
  }
)
console.log(run.result ?? run.error?.message)
console.log(run.fuelUsed) // about 123
```

**Fuel** is the VM's budget for work. Every operation costs some, and when the budget is used up
the run stops with an error. `run.fuelUsed` reports what was spent: a little over 120 units
here, 100 for the model call, 5 for the fetch, and the rest for building the prompt. The budget
of 1000 leaves room for a longer result list without letting a runaway agent go on for long.

**`quotas`** caps how many times an atom may run. Fuel counts the VM's work, so it cannot say "at
most one model call", and model calls are what cost money. With `quotas: { llmPredict: 1 }` a
second call would fail with `Quota exceeded for 'llmPredict': 1 call allowed`.

## A variation

This version searches for the song alone, drops tracks by the original artist in code, and asks
the model only if anything is left:

```ajs:inline
function findCoversCheaply({ song = 'Yesterday', artist = 'Beatles' }) {
  let term = encodeURIComponent(song)
  let url = `https://itunes.apple.com/search?term=${term}&limit=25&media=music`
  let response = httpFetch({ url, responseType: 'json' })
  let results = response.results || []
  let others = results.filter((x) => !x.artistName.includes(artist))
  if (others.length == 0) {
    return { song, covers: [], note: 'no other artists found; model not asked' }
  }
  let lines = others.map((x) => `${x.trackName} by ${x.artistName}`)
  let schema = Schema.response('cover_versions', {
    covers: [{ track: '', artist: '' }],
  })
  let prompt = `Which of these are covers of "${song}" by ${artist}?\n${lines.join('\n')}`
  let reply = llmPredict({ prompt, options: { responseFormat: schema } })
  let parsed = JSON.parse(reply)
  if (!Array.isArray(parsed.covers)) {
    return { song, covers: [], note: 'the model did not list covers' }
  }
  return { song, covers: parsed.covers }
}
```

When nobody else recorded the title, the filter answers on its own: the model is never asked
and the run costs about 8 units of fuel instead of 123. For a popular title that rarely happens.
A search for "Yesterday" returns 22 tracks by other artists, so the model is asked anyway. Note
too that `includes` is case-sensitive and literal: it removes "The Beatles" but keeps "Paul
McCartney", and the search also returns unrelated songs with the same title. Telling those apart
is the judgment left to the model.

## The gotcha: forget `responseType` and the model answers anyway

Remove `responseType: 'json'` from the fetch and nothing fails. iTunes labels its JSON
`text/javascript`, so the built-in client returns the body as a string. A string has no
`.results` property, so `response.results` is `undefined`, `response.results || []` is an empty
list, and without the `results.length == 0` check the prompt the model receives is:

```text
Search results for "Yesterday" by Beatles:



List cover versions (tracks NOT by Beatles).
```

The model is asked to find covers in an empty list, and it answers anyway. Models fill gaps.
That is why the agent checks that the data is really there before it asks: with the check, the
same mistake returns `{ covers: [], note: 'no search results' }` and costs no model call.

# Native Engine Integration: TJS in V8 or JavaScriptCore

_Status: speculative design exploration (no engine work exists). Nothing on this page
describes shipped behaviour except the "Today" paragraphs, which describe what the
transpiler does now. It is written for readers curious about JavaScript engine internals;
you do not need any of it to use TJS._

---

## Why Native?

TJS transpiles to standard JavaScript. This works, but it means:

- Type checks are ordinary user code the JIT can't reason about
- Every validated function calls into a call-stack ring buffer (`__tjs.pushStack`, and `__tjs.popStack`)
- Structural comparison (`Is()`) is a recursive JS function call
- Inline `test` blocks run via `new Function()` at transpile time
- The source is parsed twice (TJS parse → emit JS → engine's JS parse)

Native engine support would turn TJS's type examples into **information the JIT can use
directly**, the same way it already uses hidden classes (the engine's internal record of
an object's property layout) and speculative type profiling, but with declared types
instead of observed ones.

---

## The Big Wins

### 1. Function Boundary Validation

**Today:** TJS emits `typeof` checks, `Number.isInteger()` calls and object shape
validation as inline JS. The JIT treats these as generic user code.

For this source, where `a: 0` is an example value (not a TypeScript literal type): it makes
`a` a required integer. The return `: 0` is an example result too, and it is tested (see
section 4):

```tjs
function add(a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  return a + b
}
```

`tjs emit` produces this function (captured 2026-11-06; the full output also carries a
per-file inline runtime above it and an `add.__tjs` metadata object below it):

```javascript
function add(a,b) {
  __tjs.pushStack('add.tjs:1:add');
  const __cv_a = __tjs_rt.__tv(a);
  if ((typeof __cv_a !== 'number' || !Number.isInteger(__cv_a))) { return __tjs.typeError('add.tjs:1:add.a', 'integer', __cv_a); }
  const __cv_b = __tjs_rt.__tv(b);
  if ((typeof __cv_b !== 'number' || !Number.isInteger(__cv_b))) { return __tjs.typeError('add.tjs:1:add.b', 'integer', __cv_b); }

  return a + b

  __tjs.popStack();
}
```

`__tjs` and `__tjs_rt` are the TJS runtime (shared and per-file); `__tjs_rt.__tv` unwraps a
tosijs reactive proxy to its value before the check. The trailing `popStack()` sits after
the `return`, so it is never reached: with the per-file inline runtime each call leaves
its name in the 64-slot ring, and a later error's call stack lists frames that already
returned. (The shared runtime records only with `configure({ callStacks: true })`.) That
is an emitter defect, not intended behaviour; native stack tracking would not have it.

The cost of these checks is measured in [benchmarks.md](../benchmarks.md) (generated
2026-08-19): on the simple-arithmetic benchmark the validated ("safe") version took about
1.5x as long as the unvalidated baseline, and the unsafe version (`function add(! a: 0,
b: 0)`, where the leading `!` turns the function's checks off) about 1.0x. A
three-function chain took 2.0x, because each function re-validates.

**Native:** Type checks become bytecode-level guards, the mechanism the JIT already uses
for speculative optimization:

- The guard still runs, because plain JS callers can pass anything. But everything after it can be compiled for integers from the first call, from the declaration rather than from observing 1000 calls. **No warmup period.**
- Integer checks use the engine's internal small-integer (Smi) representation directly, not `typeof` plus `Number.isInteger()`.
- Stack tracking disappears: the engine has its own call stack.
- The monadic error return path could be a deopt trap (a bail-out from optimized code to a slower path) rather than a function call, or the engine could build the `MonadicError` directly without the `typeError()` indirection.

### 2. Cross-Function Type Propagation

**Today:** Each function validates its own inputs. A leading `!` turns off all of a
function's checks, but that is a manual decision about which checks are redundant.

**Native:** The engine can **propagate types across call boundaries**:

```tjs
function add(a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  return a + b
}

function calc(a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  return add(a, b) // a and b already passed calc's integer guards
}
```

`calc` passes its own already-checked parameters straight to `add`, so the engine can prove
that `add`'s guards are satisfied on this call and **skip them**.

A source-level transpiler cannot do this in general, because any caller (including plain
JS) may call `add`. The engine can keep two entry points: a guarded one for unknown callers
and an unguarded one it calls directly when it has proved the arguments' types. That turns
per-function overhead into per-call-chain overhead: the outermost typed function pays, and
calls whose argument types are proven skip their guards.

The call counts in this table are illustrative, not measured. The transpiled checks cannot
be eliminated by today's JIT because a failed check returns a value, which is observable
control flow:

| Scenario | Current (transpiled) | Native engine |
|---|---|---|
| First call | Interpreted, runs typeof checks | JIT with declared types, no warmup |
| Warmup (100-1000 calls) | JIT profiles, still runs typeof checks | Already optimized |
| Hot (10000+ calls) | JIT may inline typeof but can't eliminate | Guards are internal, may be elided |
| Cross-function calls | Each function re-validates independently | Types propagate, redundant guards skipped |

### 3. Structural Equality as Engine Primitive

**Today:** Deep comparison is the `Is()` / `IsNot()` function, which recursively walks both
values. (`==` in native TJS is not structural: it is `===` with boxed primitives such as
`new Boolean(false)` unwrapped, and `null == undefined`.) Every `Is()` call pays function
call overhead plus property enumeration.

**Native:** The engine has internal knowledge that source-level code doesn't:

- **Hidden class comparison:** If two objects have the same hidden class (same properties in the same order, all primitive values), the engine can compare the stored values directly, close to a byte comparison (`memcmp`) of the value slots. The comparison stays O(n) in the number of slots, but loses the per-property lookup and call overhead.
- **Reference equality fast path:** `Is()` returns early on identical references, but only after probing both sides for a custom-equality hook and unwrapping boxed primitives. Natively the identity check could come first and skip the call.
- **Immutable value interning:** For small objects and arrays that are structurally identical and that the engine can prove are never mutated (frozen, for example), it could intern them (as it does for short strings), making the comparison a pointer check.
- **The custom-equality hook as engine trap:** an object can define its own equality with a `[Symbol.for('tjs.equals')](other) { … }` method, which `Is()` consults before comparing structurally. The engine could recognize it the way it recognizes `Symbol.toPrimitive`, without the generic property lookup.

### 4. Inline Tests as Compilation Assertions

**Today:** TJS runs `test` blocks and signature examples at transpile time, executing the
compiled code via `new Function()`. The results are reported separately from the emitted
code.

**Native:** Tests become part of the compilation contract:

- **Fail before bytecode:** If a function's test fails, the engine can refuse to compile it, catching the bug before any user code runs. Running tests on every load would work against the performance case, so this belongs in development or at build/install time, with production loading cached results (next bullet).
- **Cached test results:** The engine can key results to source hashes and skip re-running tests for unchanged functions across page loads and process restarts.
- **Test results as type hints:** A return example is both the declared result type and a test: `function add(a: 2, b: 3): 5` runs `add(2, 3)` and expects exactly `5`. One passing example proves nothing about other inputs, but it is a hint the JIT could speculate on in callers.
- **Assertion-based narrowing:** Tests that assert properties of return values (`expect(typeof result.name).toBe('string')`) give the JIT shape information about the returned object.

### 5. WASM Blocks

**Today:** a TJS function can contain an inline WebAssembly body, a `wasm {}` block, with
its ordinary JS body as the fallback ([DOCS-WASM.md](../DOCS-WASM.md)). The blocks are
compiled at transpile time into one module per file,
embedded as base64 in the JS output. At load the output decodes it and instantiates it
synchronously (`new WebAssembly.Module`), falling back to async
`WebAssembly.instantiate` where synchronous compilation is refused (a browser main
thread with a module over 4KB). Each block keeps its JS fallback if WebAssembly is
unavailable.

**Native:** The engine could compile WASM blocks in the same pipeline as the JS: no
base64 encoding and decoding, and no async path. It could also inline across the JS/WASM
boundary for small functions.

---

## Which Engine?

### JavaScriptCore (WebKit/Bun): more practical

- **Bun is built on JavaScriptCore**, and Bun's team maintains patches against it
- **JSC's B3/Air backend** (its lowest optimizing tiers) looks, in our judgment, easier than V8's optimizing compiler to extend with new type guard primitives
- **Slower release cadence** than V8, so a fork is easier to maintain

In either engine, TJS syntax could be implemented as **desugaring in the parser**
(rewriting it into equivalent standard AST nodes), keeping changes out of the rest of the
engine.

### V8 (Chrome/Node/Deno): more impact

- **Most deployed engine** (Chrome, Node, Deno, Electron)
- Its parser is heavily optimized (lazy parsing, preparsing, parallel compilation), so changes are higher risk
- V8 releases about every four weeks, so maintaining a fork is more work

**Suggested starting point:** JSC via Bun. tjs-lang is developed on Bun and already ships
a Bun plugin for importing `.tjs` files (the plugin runs the transpiler; it is not engine
work), so Bun is the natural first host.

A native engine would be an accelerator, not a replacement. Browsers, Node and any
unpatched Bun would still run transpiled output, so the transpiler stays the portable path,
and native behaviour would have to match it exactly (checked by differential tests against
transpiled output).

---

## Scope of JSC Changes

These lists cover the main constructs, not every one; [TJS-SYNTAX.md](../TJS-SYNTAX.md)
is the full reference.

### Lexer / contextual keywords
TJS syntax would be enabled only for `.tjs` modules; plain `.js` parses exactly as today,
so `test`, `given` and the rest stay ordinary identifiers there.

- `:` in parameter and return position (already a valid token; needs context-sensitive handling), plus the `:!` / `:?` return markers and `!` / `?` parameter markers
- `Type`, `Generic`, `FunctionPredicate`, `Union`, `Enum` as contextual keywords
- `extend`, `given`, `test`, `wasm` as contextual keywords
- `const!` (compile-time immutability)
- `TjsStrict` / `TjsCompat` dialect directives (which language a file is)

### Parser
- Desugar `:` params to validated parameters (as the transpiler does today)
- Record `:` return examples as metadata and signature tests
- Desugar `Type`/`Generic`/`Union`/`Enum` declarations to `const` plus runtime calls
- Desugar `extend` blocks (local methods on existing classes, no prototype changes) to `.call()` rewriting
- Desugar `given` to `switch` with explicit breaks
- Desugar `wasm {}` blocks (or hand them to a WASM compiler)
- Desugar polymorphic functions (several same-name declarations) to a dispatcher plus variants

### Bytecode Compiler
- Emit type guard bytecodes at function entry instead of `typeof` check sequences
- Attach type metadata to function objects (replacing the `.__tjs` property assignment)
- Emit TJS equality bytecodes for `==` / `!=` (every `.tjs` file uses TJS equality)

### JIT (DFG/FTL, JSC's optimizing tiers)
- Use declared types as initial type assumptions (skip profiling warmup)
- Propagate types across call boundaries
- Speed up `Is()` using hidden class information

### What Stays Untouched
- Garbage collector
- Object model / hidden classes
- Module loader (TJS keeps ES module semantics)
- Most built-in functions
- Debugger protocol

---

## A Possible Rollout

Each phase would be useful on its own:

1. **Parser only.** Extend JSC's parser to understand TJS syntax, desugaring to the same JS the transpiler produces today. No runtime changes. Benefit: one parse, and errors that point at the `.tjs` source directly, where transpiled output needs source maps to do that.
2. **Type guards.** Replace the emitted `typeof` checks with bytecode-level guards. Benefit: warmup-free optimization and cross-function type propagation.
3. **Structural equality.** Implement `Is()` / `IsNot()` as engine primitives using hidden class information.
4. **Inline tests.** Run tests inside the compilation pipeline. Benefit: compile-time verification, and test results as type hints for the JIT.

WASM blocks are left out: they already compile at transpile time, so folding them into the
engine pipeline only saves the base64 step and can wait until the phases above exist.

Nothing here is scheduled.
title: Native Engine Integration: TJS in V8 or JavaScriptCore

# Recursion

A function can call other functions; Functions showed `bill` calling `cost` and `withTax`. A
function can also call **itself**. That sounds like a way to go round in circles forever, and
done carelessly it is. Done properly, it is one of the most useful ideas in programming: to
solve a problem, solve a **smaller copy of the same problem**, and use that answer to finish
the job. This is called **recursion**.

Some problems are shaped like that already. A tree is a trunk with smaller trees growing from
it. A box can hold things, and some of those things are boxes. For problems like these,
recursion is not a trick: it is the plainest way to say what you mean.

## Factorial, two ways

The factorial of a number, written with an exclamation mark, multiplies together every whole
number from 1 up to it: 5! is 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 × 5, which is 120. Repetition asked you to write
it with a loop, and the calculator's n! key needs it. Here is the loop version beside a
recursive one:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function factorialLoop(n: 0) {
  let answer = 1
  for (let i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
    answer = answer * i
  }
  return answer
}

function factorial(n: 0) {
  if (n == 0) {
    return 1
  }
  return n * factorial(n - 1)
}

preview.append(`5! is ${factorialLoop(5)} with a loop, and ${factorial(5)} without one.`)

test 'both ways give the same answers' {
  expect(factorial(5)).toBe(120)
  expect(factorial(0)).toBe(1)
  for (let n = 0; n <= 10; n++) {
    expect(factorial(n)).toBe(factorialLoop(n))
  }
}
```

The loop version builds the answer up, one multiplication per round. The recursive version
has no loop at all. It says two things:

- The factorial of 0 is 1. (Mathematicians agree, and it makes the rest work.)
- The factorial of any other number is that number times the factorial of the number below
  it. 5! is 5 × 4!, because 4! is already 1 × 2 × 3 × 4.

Both of those are true, and together they are the whole definition. `factorial(5)` does not
know what 4! is, so it asks: it calls `factorial(4)`, which asks `factorial(3)`, and so on
down to `factorial(0)`, which knows the answer without asking anyone.

The test does more than check two answers: its `for` loop checks that the two versions agree
for every number from 0 to 10. A loop is allowed inside a test, and when you rewrite a
function a new way, checking it against the old one is a good test to write.

## What each call is waiting for

When `factorial(5)` calls `factorial(4)`, it does not stop and forget what it was doing. It
**waits**, holding on to its own `n`, which is 5, until `factorial(4)` gives back an answer.
Then it multiplies and gives back its own. Each call has its own `n`, just as Functions said
names inside a function stay inside: the `n` of `factorial(5)` and the `n` of `factorial(4)`
are different names that happen to be spelled the same.

Here is `factorial(4)` worked out by hand. Each line replaces one call with what that call
works out:

```text
factorial(4)
= 4 × factorial(3)
= 4 × 3 × factorial(2)
= 4 × 3 × 2 × factorial(1)
= 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 × factorial(0)
= 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 × 1
= 24
```

Going down, every call is waiting. Only when `factorial(0)` answers can the multiplications
happen, on the way back up. This version says out loud what each call is doing:

```tjs:inline {"view": "console"}
function factorial(n: 0) {
  if (n == 0) {
    console.log('factorial(0) is 1, without asking anyone')
    return 1
  }
  console.log(`factorial(${n}) waits for factorial(${n - 1})`)
  const answer = n * factorial(n - 1)
  console.log(`factorial(${n}) is ${answer}`)
  return answer
}

factorial(4)

test 'talking does not change the answer' {
  expect(factorial(4)).toBe(24)
}
```

The console shows four calls waiting, one after another, then the answers coming back in the
opposite order: the last call to start is the first to finish. Type `factorial(6)` at the
prompt to watch a longer one.

## The base case

The `if (n == 0)` is called the **base case**: the copy of the problem small enough to answer
straight away. Every recursion needs one. Without it, each call asks the next, which asks the
next, and nothing ever answers.

Try it. In the first example of this chapter, delete the three lines of the `if` in
`factorial`, so it reads:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->
```tjs:static
function factorial(n: 0) {
  return n * factorial(n - 1)
}
```

and run it. The example stops, and instead of a result it shows an error:
**Maximum call stack size exceeded**. (Firefox says **too much recursion**.) It is not
running forever, as a `while` loop with the wrong condition would. Every call that is waiting
takes up a little memory, to remember its own `n` and where to carry on. The list of waiting
calls is called the **call stack**, and it has a limit. `factorial(5)` called `factorial(4)`,
then `factorial(0)`, then `factorial(-1)`, then `factorial(-2)`, and so on, thousands of
calls deep, until there was no room for one more. Then the program stopped.

That message is one of the mistakes that stop the program, like `is not defined` in When
Things Go Wrong: there is no sensible value to give back. When you see it, look for a
function that calls itself, and ask two questions. Does it have a base case? Does every call
get closer to it?

### A base case that is stepped over

Put the `if` back, so the tests pass again. The base case is there now, but it can still be
missed. `factorial(-1)` calls `factorial(-2)`, which calls `factorial(-3)`: counting down from
a negative number never reaches 0. The example `n: 0` means any whole number, and -1 is one.

The factorial of a negative number has no meaning, so the honest fix is to refuse one, and
you already know how: the example `+0` means a whole number that is zero or more.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function factorial(n: +0) {
  if (n == 0) {
    return 1
  }
  return n * factorial(n - 1)
}

const answer = factorial(-1)
if (answer instanceof Error) {
  preview.append(answer.message)
} else {
  preview.append(`The answer is ${answer}.`)
}

test 'factorial of a negative number is refused' {
  expect(factorial(6)).toBe(720)
  expect(factorial(-1) instanceof Error).toBe(true)
}
```

Now `factorial(-1)` never runs at all: it gives back an error saying it expected a
non-negative integer. Change `n: +0` back to `n: 0` and run it again to see the call stack
overflow instead. The example on the parameter is what keeps every call on the road to the
base case.

## A tree

Factorial can be written either way. A tree is different: it is made of smaller copies of
itself. A tree is a trunk with two smaller trees growing from its tip, each a little shorter
and leaning a little to one side. Each of those is a trunk with two smaller trees on it, and
so on, until the trees are too small to bother with. That sentence is the program:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { svgElements } from 'tosijs'

const { svg, line } = svgElements

// Every line in a tree: its trunk, then the lines of two smaller trees on top.
function tree(x: 50.0, y: 100.0, length: 30.0, angle: 0.0, depth: 0) {
  if (depth == 0) {
    return []
  }
  const tipX = x + length * Math.cos(angle)
  const tipY = y + length * Math.sin(angle)
  const trunk = { x1: x, y1: y, x2: tipX, y2: tipY }
  const left = tree(tipX, tipY, length * 0.7, angle - 0.5, depth - 1)
  const right = tree(tipX, tipY, length * 0.7, angle + 0.5, depth - 1)
  return [trunk, ...left, ...right]
}

const up = -Math.PI / 2 // a quarter turn: on screen, y counts down, so up is negative

const picture = svg({ viewBox: '0 0 100 100', width: 240, height: 240 })
for (const l of tree(50, 100, 30, up, 8)) {
  picture.append(line({ x1: l.x1, y1: l.y1, x2: l.x2, y2: l.y2, stroke: 'sienna' }))
}
preview.append(picture)

test 'a tree is a trunk with two smaller trees on it' {
  expect(tree(50, 100, 30, up, 0)).toEqual([])
  expect(tree(50, 100, 30, up, 1).length).toBe(1)
  expect(tree(50, 100, 30, up, 2).length).toBe(3)
  expect(tree(50, 100, 30, up, 8).length).toBe(255)
}

test 'the trunk grows straight up from the bottom' {
  const trunk = tree(50, 100, 30, up, 1)[0]
  expect(trunk.x2).toBe(50)
  expect(trunk.y2).toBe(70)
}
```

`tree` does not draw anything itself. It gives back a list of lines, each an object with a
start (`x1`, `y1`) and an end (`x2`, `y2`), and the loop after it draws them. Keeping the
drawing apart from the working-out is what lets the tests check the tree: they count its
lines, and look at where the trunk ends.

Read `tree` from the top:

- The base case: a tree with a `depth` of 0 has no lines at all, so it gives back an empty
  list.
- Otherwise it works out where the trunk's tip is, with `Math.cos` and `Math.sin` turning an
  angle into how far across and how far down, as in Repetition's polygons. (Angles here are
  measured the same way, in fractions of `2 * Math.PI`: 0.5 is about a twelfth of a turn.)
- It asks for two smaller trees, starting at the tip: each 0.7 times as long, one leaning
  left (`angle - 0.5`) and one right (`angle + 0.5`), and each one level less deep. Each
  `depth - 1` is the problem getting smaller, so the calls are sure to reach 0.
- It gives back its trunk followed by the lines of both smaller trees. `...left` spreads one
  list's items into another, as in Lists.

A tree of depth 1 is one line. Depth 2 is that line and two more: 3. Each level doubles the
number of branches at the top, so depth 8 is 255 lines, from a function of a dozen lines.
Change the 8 to 4 to see the shape clearly, or to 11 for a full tree (2,047 lines). Change
`0.5` to `0.3` for a tall, thin tree, or `0.7` to `0.8` for a bushy one.

Try writing this with loops alone. It can be done, but you have to keep your own list of
branches still to draw, which is the call stack's job here. Recursion keeps that list for you.

## Lists inside lists

A list can hold other lists, which can hold more lists. How many things are in this box?

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function countItems(list: []) {
  let count = 0
  for (const item of list) {
    if (Array.isArray(item)) {
      count = count + countItems(item)
    } else {
      count = count + 1
    }
  }
  return count
}

const box = ['spoon', ['fork', 'knife'], [['cup', 'saucer'], 'plate']]

preview.append(`There are ${countItems(box)} things in the box.`)

test 'counting every item, however deep' {
  expect(countItems(box)).toBe(6)
  expect(countItems(['a', 'b'])).toBe(2)
  expect(countItems([])).toBe(0)
  expect(countItems([[[]]])).toBe(0)
}
```

The example `[]` is an empty list, which says "a list of anything": the items can be words,
numbers or other lists. (`[0.0]` in Lists meant a list of numbers; with nothing in the
example, nothing is said about the items.) `Array.isArray(item)` asks "is this item a list?",
and is true for `['fork', 'knife']` and false for `'spoon'`.

So `countItems` goes through the list, as `for … of` always does, and counts each item as
one, except that an item which is itself a list is counted by asking `countItems` about it.
The inner list is part of the outer one, so it is a smaller copy of the problem.

Where is the base case? There are two, and neither is an `if` at the top. An item that is not
a list is answered straight away: it counts as 1. And an empty list is answered without
calling anything, because the loop runs zero times and `count` stays 0. That is why
`countItems([[[]]])`, three lists one inside another with nothing in the middle, is 0.

A loop alone cannot do this, because you do not know how deep the lists go. Two levels would
need a loop inside a loop; three levels, three loops. `countItems` handles any depth, because
each call only has to handle one level and pass the rest on.

## A shopping list with sections

Real data is often nested the same way. This shopping list has sections, and one section has
a section of its own. Each entry has a `name`; an entry with `items` is a section, and an
entry with a `price` is a thing to buy.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements } from 'tosijs'

const { pre } = elements

const shopping = {
  name: 'Shopping',
  items: [
    { name: 'bread', price: 2.5 },
    {
      name: 'fruit',
      items: [
        { name: 'apples', price: 3 },
        { name: 'pears', price: 1.75 },
      ],
    },
    {
      name: 'party',
      items: [
        { name: 'balloons', price: 4 },
        {
          name: 'cake',
          items: [
            { name: 'flour', price: 1.25 },
            { name: 'eggs', price: 2.5 },
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}

function cost(entry: { name: '' }) {
  if (entry.items == undefined) {
    return entry.price
  }
  let sum = 0
  for (const part of entry.items) {
    sum = sum + cost(part)
  }
  return sum
}

function outline(entry: { name: '' }, indent = '') {
  let text = `${indent}${entry.name}\n`
  if (entry.items != undefined) {
    for (const part of entry.items) {
      text = text + outline(part, indent + '  ')
    }
  }
  return text
}

preview.append(pre(outline(shopping)), `It all comes to ${cost(shopping)}.`)

test 'a section costs what its parts cost' {
  expect(cost({ name: 'eggs', price: 2.5 })).toBe(2.5)
  expect(cost(shopping.items[1])).toBe(4.75)
  expect(cost(shopping)).toBe(15)
}

test 'the outline indents each section' {
  expect(outline(shopping.items[1])).toBe('fruit\n  apples\n  pears\n')
}
```

`cost` has the same shape as `countItems`. Its base case is a thing to buy, which costs its
`price`. A section costs the total of its parts, and each part is either a thing (answered
straight away) or a smaller section (asked about). The `{ name: '' }` example says every
entry must have a name; `items` and `price` are allowed as extra parts. Change `name` to
`title` on the pears and run it: `cost` refuses the pears with an error naming
`cost.entry.name`, and because `sum + …` sticks that error onto the total as text, the page
shows a jumble with the message in it. The tests go red too.

`outline` walks the same shape to make the text on the page. The `indent` parameter has a
default, `''`, so the first call needs only the list. Each call passes its own indent plus two
spaces to the parts inside it, so the deeper an entry is, the further in it sits. Nobody had
to say how deep the list goes. Add a section inside `cake` and both functions handle it.

## Forgetting to make it smaller

A recursion has two jobs: a base case, and a step that brings every call closer to it. The
first mistake in the base case section left out the base case. The other common mistake keeps
the base case, and forgets to make the problem smaller.

Here is a list of prices added up recursively. The total of an empty list is 0; the total of
any other list is its first price plus the total of the rest:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
function total(prices: [0.0]) {
  if (prices.length == 0) {
    return 0
  }
  return prices[0] + total(prices.slice(1))
}

preview.append(`The bill comes to ${total([2.5, 4, 1.25])}.`)

test 'adding up a list, one price at a time' {
  expect(total([2.5, 4, 1.25])).toBe(7.75)
  expect(total([9])).toBe(9)
  expect(total([])).toBe(0)
}
```

`prices.slice(1)` is the list without its first item: `slice` from Lists, from position 1 to
the end. So each call hands on a list one shorter than its own, and after as many calls as
there are prices, the list is empty and the base case answers.

Now make the mistake. Change `slice(1)` to `slice(0)`. It looks almost the same, and it is
an easy slip, but `slice(0)` copies the **whole** list. Each call hands on a list exactly as
long as its own, so the problem never shrinks, and the base case is never reached. Run it:
the example stops with Maximum call stack size exceeded.

Change it back, and try a quieter mistake. Change the base case to stop at one price instead
of none:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->
```tjs:static
  if (prices.length == 1) {
    return prices[0]
  }
```

Run it. The page still says the bill comes to 7.75, because a list of three prices shrinks to
one and stops. But the test goes red, on `total([])`: an empty list is not one price long, so
it is handed on, still empty, forever. Only the test noticed. The page used a list of three,
and nothing on it was wrong.

That is why the tests for a recursive function should always try the smallest cases: the
empty list, 0, the tree of depth 0. Those are where the base case lives, and a mistake there
does not show up in a big example that happens to step past it. Put the base case back to
`prices.length == 0`, and every test passes.

## Loop or recursion?

Anything a recursion does, a loop can do too, and the other way round, but one of them is
usually much easier to read.

Use a loop when you are going through things one after another: the numbers from 1 to 100, or
the items in a flat list. The loop says so directly, and it has no limit on how many rounds it
runs. A recursive `total` of a list with a hundred thousand prices would run out of call stack;
the loop in Lists would not notice.

Use recursion when the thing you are working on is made of smaller things of the same kind: a
tree of branches, lists inside lists, sections inside sections. Then the recursive function is
a description of the shape, and it works however deep the shape goes.

Either way, ask the two questions before you run it: what is the base case, and does every
call get closer to it?

## Try it

1. Write `power(base: 2.0, exponent: +0)` recursively: any number to the power of 0 is 1, and
   `base` to the power of `exponent` is `base` times `base` to the power of one less. Test that
   `power(2, 10)` is 1024 and `power(5, 0)` is 1. Then use it, or your recursive `factorial`, to
   add a key to the calculator from the last chapter.
2. Write `reverse(text: '')`, which gives back a string backwards: `reverse('stressed')` is
   `'desserts'`. Strings have a `slice` too: `'hello'.slice(1)` is `'ello'`, and `'hello'[0]` is
   `'h'`. Hint: the reverse of a word is the reverse of everything after its first letter, then
   its first letter. What is the base case? Test the empty string as well as a word.
3. Write `countdown(n: +0)`, which gives back `'3 2 1 lift off!'` for 3, without a loop.
   Then change the step from `n - 1` to `n - 2`, and test `countdown(3)`. What happens, and why?
   Which test would you write to catch it?
4. Write `deepest(list: [])`, which says how many lists deep the deepest item is:
   `deepest(['a'])` is 1, and `deepest(['a', ['b', ['c']]])` is 3. (`Math.max(a, b)` is the
   bigger of two numbers.)
5. Change the tree. Give it three branches at each tip instead of two (what happens to the
   number of lines?), or make the left and right branches lean by different amounts. Add a test
   that counts the lines.
6. Draw a Koch snowflake edge. At depth 0, it is one straight line. At any other depth, it is
   four edges, each a third as long, one level less deep, drawn one after another: the first
   at the same angle, the second turned by `-Math.PI / 3` (a sixth of a turn), the third by
   `Math.PI / 3` from the original angle, and the fourth at the original angle again. Each one
   starts where the one before ended. Start from `tree`: it already works out where a line
   ends. Three edges, turned a third of a turn each, make the whole snowflake.

Work them here:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
// Your code here. Show results with preview.append(…), check them with a
// test block, then press the refresh button (or ⌘S / Ctrl+S) to run it.
```
