# A Lean 4 specification of the AJS VM

> **Status (2026-11-01): PROPOSED.** Nothing in this chapter changes how you use AJS today. It is
> a research proposal for how the VM's safety promises could be proved rather than only tested.
> If you are embedding the VM or writing agents now, the promises below already hold, by testing;
> this page is about proving them later.

The plan is a short, time-boxed experiment (a spike) after 0.14 ships and after Pattern, the
proposed replacement for regex described under "What it costs", lands. That timing lets it shape
the 1.0 VM ([`ajs-native-vm.md`](ajs-native-vm.md)) rather than arrive after it.

The AJS VM makes promises: a program can do nothing except call the capabilities it was given,
every run halts, and nothing is allocated before it is paid for. Today those promises are held by
tests and review. Most of the 0.14 release candidates were spent finding places where untrusted
code could reach host behaviour or allocate memory it had not paid for, places the tests had
missed. This proposal is to state the promises as theorems about a formal model of the VM (a
precise definition of how it behaves), prove them in [Lean 4](https://lean-lang.org), and test
the shipping VM against that model.

Lean 4 is a programming language and proof assistant: you write a definition of how the VM
behaves, state properties of it as theorems, and the Lean kernel checks the proofs mechanically.

**The shipping VM itself will not be proved.** It will be tested against a proved model.

## The shape: Lean is the specification, not the VM

Lean is the reference semantics and the proofs. A separate implementation ships: the planned
Rust → wasm VM, and the JavaScript VM until then. The two are kept in agreement by
**differential testing**. Lean definitions are executable, so the specification is also an
interpreter: the same programs run on it and on the shipping VM, and any difference is a bug in
one of them.

AWS's Cedar authorization language is built this way. Its semantics and proofs are in Lean, and
its Rust implementation is tested against the Lean model by differential random testing. AJS is
unusually well placed to do the same, because the program is already DATA: the AST is versioned
JSON (`src/vm/ast-version.ts`, frozen by `src/vm/ast-fixtures/`). Both sides can read the same
programs with no parser in between, so a disagreement can only come from the two interpreters,
never from two parsers reading the source differently.

Writing the shipping VM in Lean (Lean compiles to C, and C can reach wasm) is possible. It is not
proposed: Lean's runtime and its compiled output are not what a small, embeddable sandbox wants,
and keeping the specification readable matters more than making it fast.

## What can be proved, and what each theorem needs defined first

| Property | What has to be defined | Difficulty |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **No ambient authority.** Every effect a run has is a call to an injected capability, with arguments the program computed. | A small-step semantics (a definition of what one execution step does) whose effects are a TRACE of capability calls, and nothing else. | Low. It follows from the definition, which is the point: the design is what makes it true. The hard part is showing the shipping VM matches the model (see "Where the gap is"). |
| **Termination.** Every run halts. | Fuel as a natural number that every step decreases (the VM's fractional costs scaled to integer units, which differential testing also needs in order to compare fuel exactly). | Low. |
| **Charge before allocation.** Nothing is allocated before it is charged; live memory stays under the ceiling. | A rule for how many bytes each value costs, and a way to measure how much memory a run holds at once. | Medium. This is the invariant the 0.14 reviews kept returning to (`docs/vm-budgets.md`). In Lean it is a step invariant, a property every execution step preserves, so proving it once for each kind of step covers every program, instead of checking each allocation site by hand. |
| **No data leakage** (noninterference): labelled inputs cannot influence chosen outputs, such as one capability's data reaching another capability's arguments: an agent given `store` (private) and `fetch` (public) cannot put store contents into a fetch URL. | Labels, and a policy saying which flows are allowed. AJS has neither today. | High, and the definition is the real work. |
| **Minimality** (asked for) of the instruction set: no instruction is expressible by the others. | The instruction set as a closed inductive type. | Medium. Provable, of limited value. |
| **Optimality** (asked for), for example fuel costs that track real work as closely as possible. | A cost model and an objective. | Not a theorem until both exist. Left out rather than claimed weakly. |

Two cautions about the leakage theorem:

- **Fuel is a channel.** What a run costs can depend on secret data, and the host can see the
  cost (a loop that runs once per character of a secret reveals its length in fuel used). A
  noninterference theorem must either treat cost as observable (and then prove that cost
  does not depend on secrets, which is rarely true) or explicitly exclude it. That choice is
  stated in the theorem, or the theorem promises more than it delivers.
- **Errors are a channel.** Which refusal ended a run, and its message, are outputs. The
  semantics has to model them, not just successful results.

## Where the gap is

A proof is about the model. Nearly every 0.14 blocker lived in the JavaScript the current VM
calls: string methods, the host regex engine, the JS object model (`docs/vm-budgets.md`). A Lean
model has none of that, so its proofs would not transfer to today's VM: they would be about a VM
we do not ship. Differential testing against today's VM is still useful for finding bugs, which
is what the spike does.

That is why this pairs with the Rust → wasm VM, whose point is that the AST executes with no
JavaScript invoked. Once the shipping VM calls no host builtins, the model and the implementation
can actually correspond, and differential testing covers what the proofs cannot reach.

What then remains trusted:

- the Lean kernel;
- the definitions, meaning that the theorems state what we actually care about (reviewed by
  people, which is where the effort belongs);
- **the agreement between the Lean model and the Rust VM, established by testing, not proof;**
- wasm's own sandbox;
- the host's capabilities, which are out of scope by design: a capability can do anything the
  host lets it.

## What it costs

The core is small: the expression nodes, the control-flow atoms (`seq`, `if`, `while`,
`try`), capability calls, fuel. Most of the work is the **method table** (the string, array and
other methods a guest program may call) and the string builtins, and above all the **regex
engine** (`src/vm/regex.ts`). No effort estimate exists yet; producing one is part of what the
spike is for. Pattern (`docs/pattern.md`, also proposed) would replace regex with a small grammar
run as data, which removes the hardest part to model. That is the argument for doing Pattern
first.

The same approach is proposed for Pattern itself, in tosijs-pattern (`docs-src/formal.md`): it is
smaller and pure, every claim it makes is precise, and it becomes this VM's matching builtin, so
its proofs would be a component of these. Prior art for the regex side of both: Warblre, an
executable mechanization (a formalization a machine can check) of ECMAScript 2023 regexes in
Rocq, the proof assistant formerly called Coq (De Santo, Barrière and Pit-Claudel, ICFP 2024).

## The spike

Small enough to stop cheaply if it goes badly. It has no timebox or owner yet.

1. **Model** the expression evaluator, `seq`, `if`, `while`, one capability call and fuel, over
   the v2 AST.
2. **Prove** termination and no ambient authority.
3. **Run** the golden fixtures (`src/vm/ast-fixtures/`) and the guest fuzzer's programs
   (`src/vm/guest-fuzz.test.ts`, a generator of random AJS programs used in the test suite) on
   both the Lean interpreter and the current VM, and compare
   results, refusals and fuel.

What would end it: the definitions turn out too awkward to state the properties we care about,
or the two interpreters disagree in ways that show the model cannot follow the real semantics
without modelling the JavaScript underneath. Either finding is worth having before the 1.0 VM's
design is fixed.

What would make it worth continuing: the two theorems go through, and differential testing
finds a real disagreement in the current VM. That is the evidence the approach finds defects the
existing tests do not.

## Constraints this puts on 1.0 now

None beyond those in [`ajs-native-vm.md`](ajs-native-vm.md): the AST format is versioned and
frozen by fixtures, which is what lets a second interpreter read the same programs. Keeping the
semantics free of host-dependent behaviour (no host regex, no host string methods in the trust
path) is already the direction; it is also what keeps a formal model honest.
title: A Lean 4 specification of the AJS VM

# Full-Stack Demo: Todo API

Complete REST-style Todo API over an in-memory store

<!-- TODO review -->
```tjs:inline
/#
## Todo API Service

A REST-style API for todo management.
Demonstrates a more complete service pattern.
#/

// Simulated persistence layer
const todos = new Map()
let nextId = 1

// Types are inferred from function signatures below
// Todo: { id: 0, title: '', completed: false, createdAt: '' }
// CreateInput: { title: 'Buy milk' }
// UpdateInput: { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', completed: false }

// POST /todos - Create
export function createTodo(input: { title: 'New todo' }):! { id: 0, title: '', completed: false, createdAt: '' } {
  const todo = {
    id: nextId++,
    title: input.title,
    completed: false,
    // Raw `Date` is not allowed in .tjs; LegacyDate is the named escape.
    createdAt: LegacyDate().toISOString()
  }
  todos.set(todo.id, todo)
  return todo
}

// GET /todos/:id - Read one (null if not found)
export function getTodo(input: { id: 1 }):! { id: 0, title: '', completed: false, createdAt: '' } | null {
  return todos.get(input.id) ?? null
}

// GET /todos - Read all, or filter with { completed: true | false }.
// A bare `null` default accepts any value, so the filter is optional AND free-form.
export function listTodos(filter = null):! { todos: [{ id: 0, title: '', completed: false, createdAt: '' }] } {
  let items = [...todos.values()]

  if (filter?.completed !== undefined) {
    items = items.filter(t => t.completed === filter.completed)
  }

  return { todos: items }
}

// PUT /todos/:id - Update (null if not found)
export function updateTodo(input: { id: 1, title: '', completed: false }):! { id: 0, title: '', completed: false, createdAt: '' } | null {
  const existing = todos.get(input.id)
  if (!existing) return null

  const updated = {
    ...existing,
    title: input.title ?? existing.title,
    completed: input.completed ?? existing.completed
  }
  todos.set(input.id, updated)
  return updated
}

// DELETE /todos/:id - Delete
export function deleteTodo(input: { id: 1 }):! { deleted: true } {
  const existed = todos.has(input.id)
  todos.delete(input.id)
  return { deleted: existed }
}

// PATCH /todos/:id/toggle - Toggle completion (null if not found)
export function toggleTodo(input: { id: 1 }):! { id: 0, title: '', completed: false, createdAt: '' } | null {
  const todo = todos.get(input.id)
  if (!todo) return null

  todo.completed = !todo.completed
  return todo
}

// DELETE /todos/completed - Clear completed
export function clearCompleted():! { cleared: 0 } {
  let cleared = 0
  for (const [id, todo] of todos) {
    if (todo.completed) {
      todos.delete(id)
      cleared++
    }
  }
  return { cleared }
}

// Tests
test 'CRUD operations work' {
  const todo = createTodo({ title: 'Test todo' })
  expect(todo.id).toBeGreaterThan(0)
  expect(todo.completed).toBe(false)

  const fetched = getTodo({ id: todo.id })
  expect(fetched.title).toBe('Test todo')

  const toggled = toggleTodo({ id: todo.id })
  expect(toggled.completed).toBe(true)

  const deleted = deleteTodo({ id: todo.id })
  expect(deleted.deleted).toBe(true)
  expect(getTodo({ id: todo.id })).toBe(null)
}

// Demo
console.log('=== Todo API Demo ===\n')

// Create todos
createTodo({ title: 'Learn TJS' })
createTodo({ title: 'Build something cool' })
createTodo({ title: 'Ship it' })

const titles = (list) => list.todos.map(t => t.title).join(', ')

console.log('Created 3 todos')
console.log('All:', titles(listTodos()))

// Complete first one
const first = listTodos().todos[0]
toggleTodo({ id: first.id })
console.log('\nToggled first todo')
console.log('Completed:', titles(listTodos({ completed: true })))
console.log('Pending:', titles(listTodos({ completed: false })))

// Clear completed
console.log('\nClearing completed...')
console.log(clearCompleted())
console.log('Remaining:', titles(listTodos()))

// A request with the wrong shape is refused before the handler runs
const bad = createTodo({ title: 42 })
console.log('\ncreateTodo({ title: 42 }) ->', bad instanceof Error ? bad.message : bad)
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

- **One function per route, one typed input per function.** The comments name the HTTP
  route each function would sit behind. The functions themselves know nothing about HTTP:
  they take a plain object and return a plain object, which is what makes them easy to test
  and easy to move behind any transport.
- **Required and optional are punctuation.** `createTodo(input: { title: 'New todo' })` uses
  a colon, so the input is required and must have a string `title`. `listTodos(filter =
  null)` uses `=`, so the argument is optional. A bare `null` default is the one default that
  says nothing about the type: it accepts any value, which suits a free-form filter.
- **Missing records are `null`, said in the signature.** `getTodo`, `updateTodo` and
  `toggleTodo` declare `{ … } | null` and return `null` for an unknown id, rather than an
  empty placeholder object a caller could mistake for a real todo.
- **The wrong shape is refused at the door.** `createTodo({ title: 42 })` returns a
  `MonadicError` naming `createTodo.input.title`; the body never runs, so no half-built todo
  reaches the store.

<!-- TODO review -->
## A gotcha: object defaults merge

Why `filter = null` and not `filter = { completed: false }`? In TJS an object-literal default
is a **dictionary**: members are defaulted one by one and merged into whatever the caller
passes. That is usually what you want, but it would turn "no filter" into "only pending":

```tjs:inline
function withDictionary(filter = { completed: false }) {
  return filter
}

function withNull(filter = null) {
  return filter
}

console.log('dictionary, called with {}:', JSON.stringify(withDictionary({})))
console.log('null default, called with {}:', JSON.stringify(withNull({})))
```

The dictionary filled in `completed: false` for the caller who asked for everything. When a
default should mean "absent" rather than "these values", use `null`, or keep JavaScript's
all-or-nothing default for one parameter with `LegacyDefault({ … })`.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Limits

- **"Persistence" here is a `Map`.** It resets when the page reloads. Swapping in a real
  database changes the function bodies, not their signatures or tests.
- **`:!` returns are not checked.** They document the shape. The store mutates and the
  timestamps change, so no fixed worked example could pass; inputs are what TJS validates by
  default.
- **Shared mutable state.** `toggleTodo` mutates the stored object in place and returns it,
  so a caller holding the object sees later changes. A real API would return a copy.

description: Complete REST-style Todo API over an in-memory store

# LLM with Tool

Models are bad at arithmetic and good at reading. So let the model read the question and write
down the calculation as data, let ordinary code (the "tool") do the arithmetic exactly, and let the
model phrase the answer. This is not OpenAI-style tool calling, where the model picks which tool
runs; here the program decides. [Why not native tool calling?](#why-not-native-tool-calling)
explains the trade.

The agent runs inside a host: the JavaScript program that transpiles it, supplies the `llm`
capability (the function that actually talks to a model) and calls
`vm.run(ast, args, { capabilities, fuel })`. Every operation costs fuel, and the run stops when
the fuel runs out. [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/#running-it-locally) has a complete host for a local
model server; [Embedding the AJS VM](/ajs-host/) covers the host side in full.

On this page the first example shows a "requires an LLM" message instead of running, because a
static page has no model to call. The `try` example further down needs no model and runs here.

```ajs:inline
// The tool: exact arithmetic, in code the host can read and the VM meters.
function applyOp(acc, op, value) {
  if (op == '+') {
    return acc + value
  }
  if (op == '-') {
    return acc - value
  }
  if (op == '*') {
    return acc * value
  }
  if (op == '/') {
    if (value == 0) {
      Error('division by zero') // ends the run, like a throw; see "When the tool refuses"
    }
    return acc / value
  }
  Error('unknown operator')
}

function mathAssistant({ question = 'What is 23 * 47 + 156?' }) {
  // 1. The model turns the question into a plan, as data.
  let calculation = Schema.object({
    start: Schema.number,
    steps: Schema.array(
      Schema.object({
        op: Schema.enum(['+', '-', '*', '/']),
        value: Schema.number,
      })
    ),
  })
  let planPrompt =
    'Turn this question into a calculation: the first number as start, then each ' +
    'operation in the order it must be applied (respect precedence).\nQuestion: ' +
    question
  let planText = llmPredict({
    prompt: planPrompt,
    options: { responseFormat: Schema.response('calculation', calculation) },
  })
  let plan = JSON.parse(planText)
  if (!Schema.isValid(plan, calculation)) {
    Error('the model returned a plan in the wrong shape')
  }

  // 2. The tool does the arithmetic.
  let result = plan.start
  for (const step of plan.steps) {
    result = applyOp(result, step.op, step.value)
  }

  // 3. The model phrases the answer around a number it did not compute.
  let answerPrompt =
    'The user asked: "' +
    question +
    '"\nThe exact result is: ' +
    result +
    '\nWrite a brief, friendly answer that states this result.'
  let answer = llmPredict({ prompt: answerPrompt })

  return { question, plan, result, answer }
}
```

The plan is a chain of operations applied left to right. That is a deliberate simplification:
it keeps the schema small, and it fits questions like this one. [The gotcha](#the-gotcha) shows
where it stops fitting.

## What to notice

- **The tool is a helper function.** A source file may declare several functions; the last one
  is the entry function, which the host calls with the run's arguments (here `mathAssistant`,
  and in the `try` example below, `tryStep`). The functions before it are helpers, called by
  name. A helper sees only its own parameters, never the caller's variables, so pass it
  everything it needs. It may return any value, and it runs under the same fuel budget.
- **A helper call stands alone.** It must be a statement of its own, as in
  `result = applyOp(...)`. Writing it inside a larger expression, such as
  `return { r: applyOp(...) }` or `1 + applyOp(...)`, fails at transpile time; assign the
  result to a variable first, then use the variable.
- **The model never does arithmetic.** It produces a plan in a declared shape, with
  `Schema.enum` limiting the operators. `23 * 47 + 156` becomes `start: 23`, then `* 47`, then
  `+ 156`, and the code computes 1237.
- **The response format asks the server for that shape.** `Schema.response(name, schema)` builds
  an OpenAI-style structured-output request, `{ type: 'json_schema', json_schema: { name,
  strict, schema } }`; the name is a label the server requires. The agent passes it as
  `responseFormat`, and the host turns that into the wire format's `response_format`.
- **The plan is checked before it runs.** A response format is a request to the model server, not
  a guarantee, so the agent checks the parsed plan with `Schema.isValid` against the same schema.
  A plan with `"%"` as an operator, or `"2"` (a string) as a value, stops the run there, after
  one model call. If the model's text is not JSON at all, `JSON.parse` ends the run with a parse
  error before the check is reached; wrap it in `try` to handle that case yourself.
- **`Schema.number`, not an example value.** `Schema.object` also accepts example values in place
  of schemas, as in `Schema.object({ value: 0 })`, but an example `0` means an integer, so that
  schema rejects `2.5`. A plan may contain `2.5`, so the field is written as `Schema.number`.
- **The model calls are the cost.** `llmPredict` costs 100 fuel per call by default (a host can
  change that with `costOverrides: { llmPredict: … }`), and everything else here costs about 6,
  so a run takes about 206 fuel. A budget of 500 leaves room. To cap model calls, which is what
  costs money, the host sets `quotas: { llmPredict: 2 }`.

The host side of a run looks like this, with `llm` as in [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/#running-it-locally):

```javascript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

const { ast } = transpile(source) // source: the agent above, as a string
const run = await new AgentVM().run(
  ast,
  { question: 'What is 12.5 * 4 - 7?' },
  { fuel: 500, quotas: { llmPredict: 2 }, capabilities: { llm } }
)
if (run.error) console.log('failed:', run.error.message, 'fuel used:', run.fuelUsed)
else console.log(run.result.answer, run.result.plan)
```

## When the tool refuses

`applyOp` ends in `Error('unknown operator')`, and `/` by zero raises `Error('division by zero')`.

Why not let the guard divide anyway? Dividing by zero in JavaScript gives `Infinity`, which JSON
cannot express: it would reach the host as `null` in the result.

`Error(...)` does not return: like a `throw`, it puts the program into its error state. Nothing
in the loop or the entry function catches it, so the rest of the program is skipped (the
remaining loop iterations, the second model call and the `return`), and the run ends with that
error. The host sees no `answer`. It reads `run.error.message`, which is `'unknown operator'` or
`'division by zero'`, and `run.fuelUsed`, the fuel spent so far. `run.result` is not empty: it
holds the same error as `{ $error: true, message, op: 'Error' }`, so check `run.error` before
using the result.

With the schema check in place a well-formed plan never reaches the unknown-operator branch. It
stays because the tool should not trust its caller either: a helper that guards its own input is
still correct when someone reuses it.

To recover instead of failing, wrap the call in `try`. The error from the helper propagates to
the caller's `catch`. Unlike JavaScript, the caught value is the message string itself, not an
Error object, so use `err`, not `err.message` (which is `undefined`):

```ajs:inline
function applyOp(acc, op, value) {
  if (op == '+') {
    return acc + value
  }
  Error('unknown operator')
}

function tryStep({ op = '%' }) {
  let result = 0
  try {
    result = applyOp(1, op, 2)
  } catch (err) {
    return { error: err }
  }
  return { result }
}
```

This returns `{ error: 'unknown operator' }`; with `op: '+'` it returns `{ result: 3 }`.

## Why not native tool calling?

In OpenAI-style tool calling the model answers with `tool_calls`, naming which tool to run and
with what arguments, and the program runs it. That needs the model's whole chat message back,
and `llmPredict` returns only its text.

The batteries can do it. They are optional atoms a host registers for a local model server, and
their `llmPredictBattery` returns the whole message, `tool_calls` included (see the
[AJS guide](/DOCS-AJS/)). The difference is who decides: with native calling the model chooses
which tool runs and when; in the pattern here the program fixes the steps, and the model only
fills in data that a schema checks. It also works with any model that can follow a schema,
including ones with no tool-calling support.

## The gotcha

The plan comes from a model, so it can be wrong in ways a schema cannot catch: the right
operators in the wrong order, a number misread from the question. The program is exact about
the plan it was given, not about the question. For anything that matters, show the plan
alongside the answer, as this agent does.

The question is also untrusted text, and it goes straight into both prompts. The schema check
and the exact arithmetic limit what a hostile question can make the code do: it can only produce
a plan of four operators and numbers, run under the host's fuel and quotas. They do nothing for
the phrased `answer`, which is still model output and can say anything.

The plan's shape also limits what it can say. It is a chain applied left to right, so
`23 * 47 + 156` fits directly but `10 - 2 * 3` does not: the product has to come first, so the
chain must be reordered (`start: 2`, then `* 3`, `* -1`, `+ 10`), and a model will not find that
reliably. When it misses, the plan computes something else, exactly. A tree-shaped plan would
lift the limit, but a guest schema cannot refer to itself (there is no `$ref`), so it could
describe only a fixed depth. Keep the questions to ones a chain can express, or show the plan.

# The AJS VM: Technical Context

AJS lets a program run code it did not write, from a user, another service or a language model,
without trusting it. The code runs inside a VM (a virtual machine: a program that executes other
programs). It cannot touch anything you did not hand it, and it always stops. AJS is a subset of
TJS: JavaScript with typed signatures. You do not need this chapter to write TJS or AJS programs.

This chapter is advanced material: the map of how the AJS VM is built, for people embedding the
VM in their own program or reviewing it. If you only want to write agents, read
[AJS: The Agent Language](/DOCS-AJS/) first, and you can skip this page. The day-to-day host API
(every run option, capabilities, quotas, tracing) is in [Embedding the AJS VM](/ajs-host/), and
writing atoms is in [Capabilities and Custom Atoms](/ajs-capabilities/).

## Terms

- **Host**: your program. It creates the VM, decides what the agent may do, and calls `vm.run`.
- **Agent**: the untrusted program the VM runs. (VM source code and some error messages call it
  the *guest*.)
- **Front end**: anything that produces an agent's AST: the transpiler, the builder, or a
  compiler of your own.
- **Atom**: one operation an agent can call, such as `httpFetch` or `storeGet`. The VM's core
  atoms are built in; the host can register more.
- **Capability**: a piece of the host's IO (a `fetch` function, a key-value store, a model client)
  that the host passes to a run. Atoms reach the outside world only through capabilities.
- **Fuel**: the work budget. Every step spends some, and the run stops when it reaches zero. An
  expression node costs 0.01, setting a variable 0.1, `storeSet` 5 and `llmPredict` 100; the
  default budget is 1000. The full table is in [What a run costs](/DOCS-AJS/#what-a-run-costs).
- **Membrane**: the copy-and-check layer every value passes through when it enters or leaves the
  VM. A value that crosses is a fresh copy of plain JSON data (plus `Date`), so the agent never
  holds a live host object, and the host never receives a live agent one.
- **Heap ceiling**: the cap on how much memory the agent may hold at once (`maxHeapBytes`).

## 1. The pieces

An agent travels as a **JSON AST**: its program written out as plain JSON data. A front end
produces the AST, and the VM runs it:

| Piece        | Where it lives                              | What it does                                                                                        |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Transpiler   | `transpile` from `tjs-lang/lang`            | AJS source to AST. Checks atom calls, parameters and syntax, and explains what to write instead.    |
| Builder      | `Agent` from `tjs-lang`, or `vm.Agent`      | Builds the same AST in code with a fluent API. It does not check atom calls or parameters.          |
| AST          | plain JSON, `"$ajs": 2` from the transpiler | The wire format. It can be stored, sent over a network and run elsewhere.                           |
| VM           | `AgentVM` from `tjs-lang/vm-ast`            | Runs an AST: the atoms, fuel, timeouts, the heap ceiling and the membrane.                          |
| Atoms        | core atoms, plus any the host registers     | The operations an agent can call (`httpFetch`, `storeGet`, `llmPredict`, your own).                 |
| Capabilities | the `capabilities` run option               | The host's IO: `fetch`, `store`, `llm`, `agent`, and whatever your own atoms read. Empty by default. |

The split between the front ends and the VM is deliberate. The builder and the transpiler
contain no execution logic, and the VM's core contains no parser; `tjs-lang/vm-ast` ships it
without one. That is why `vm-ast` is the recommended VM.

Parsing is the risky step. How long it takes and how much memory it uses is decided by the
source text, and it happens before fuel, timeouts or any other budget apply, so crafted source
can make it slow or memory-hungry. A VM with no parser cannot be attacked that way. So transpile
on the side that owns the source (your build, a worker, a separate process), and send the AST:

```typescript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

// Where the source is handled: source in, JSON AST out.
// Parameter values are examples, as in TJS: 0.0 means "a number".
const { ast } = transpile(`
  function total({ price: 0.0, taxRate: 0.0 }) {
    return { total: price * (1 + taxRate) }
  }
`)

// Where the agent runs: AST in, result out.
const vm = new AgentVM()
const run = await vm.run(ast, { price: 100, taxRate: 0.2 }, { fuel: 100 })
console.log(run.result, run.error) // { total: 120 } undefined
console.log(run.fuelUsed < 1) // true: this agent spends under 1 of its 100 fuel
```

`tjs-lang/vm` is the same `AgentVM` with the transpiler wired in, so it also accepts source.
Passing source to `vm.run` is deprecated as of 0.14.0; `tjs-lang/vm-ast` refuses it and says
where to transpile instead. On `tjs-lang/vm`, `vm.run(source)` refuses source over
`maxSourceBytes` (8 KB by default). If you call `transpile` yourself on source you did not write,
cap it the same way: `transpile(source, { maxSourceBytes: 64 * 1024 })`.

### The builder

The builder is for generating agents in code. Start with `Agent.take(schema)` (the input
schema), chain atom calls, and finish with `.toJSON()`. `vm.Agent` is the same builder with the
VM's custom atoms added.

```typescript
import { Agent, AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang'
import { s } from 'tjs-lang/schema'

const ast = Agent.take(s.object({ n: s.number })) // the input schema
  .varsImport(['n']) // copy the input field n into the agent's state
  .if(
    'n > 10', // the condition, as a string
    { n: 'n' }, // condition name -> state variable
    (then) => then.varSet({ key: 'size', value: 'big' }),
    (otherwise) => otherwise.varSet({ key: 'size', value: 'small' })
  )
  .return(s.object({ size: s.string })) // the output schema
  .toJSON()

const vm = new AgentVM()
console.log((await vm.run(ast, { n: 42 })).result) // { size: 'big' }
console.log((await vm.run(ast, { n: 1 })).result) // { size: 'small' }
```

An `if` or `while` condition in the builder is a string, parsed when the AST is built:

- **Supported:** comparisons, `&&`, `||`, `!`, arithmetic, parentheses, member access
  (`obj.foo.bar`) and literals.
- **Refused:** a ternary, an index (`a[0]`) or a call (`f(x)`). Building the AST throws
  `Unsupported condition syntax`.
- **The name map:** the second argument maps each name the condition uses to a variable (or a
  dotted path) in the agent's state. A name the condition reads that the map leaves out gets a
  `console.warn` from the builder, at build time.

To test something the condition grammar refuses, compute it first with a `varSet` whose value is
an expression node (see the next section), then test that variable:

```typescript
import { Agent, AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang'
import { s } from 'tjs-lang/schema'

const ast = Agent.take(s.object({ items: s.array(s.number) }))
  .varsImport(['items'])
  .varSet({
    key: 'first', // items[0], as an expression node
    value: {
      $expr: 'member',
      object: { $expr: 'ident', name: 'items' },
      property: { $expr: 'literal', value: 0 },
      computed: true,
    },
  })
  .if(
    'first > 10',
    { first: 'first' },
    (then) => then.varSet({ key: 'size', value: 'big' }),
    (otherwise) => otherwise.varSet({ key: 'size', value: 'small' })
  )
  .return(s.object({ size: s.string }))
  .toJSON()

const vm = new AgentVM()
console.log((await vm.run(ast, { items: [42] })).result) // { size: 'big' }
```

The builder writes a version-1 AST (`"$ajs": 1`), the older format, in which a bare string that
names a variable in scope is read as that variable. In the first builder example, `'big'` stays
a string only because the agent has no variable called `big`; if it had one, `size` would get
that variable's value. To write a string that is always a string, use a literal node:
`value: { $expr: 'literal', value: 'big' }`. The transpiler writes version 2, in which a bare
string is always a string, so for anything written by hand the transpiler is the safer front
end. Both formats run; they are described under [JSON AST Format](/DOCS-AJS/#json-ast-format).

### Expressions are nodes

There is no `eval` anywhere in the VM. Arithmetic and logic are AST nodes, evaluated by the VM:

| `$expr`           | Shape                                                                       |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `literal`         | `{ $expr: 'literal', value: 5 }`                                            |
| `ident`           | `{ $expr: 'ident', name: 'x' }`                                             |
| `member`          | `{ $expr: 'member', object, property, computed? }`; `computed` is `obj[key]` |
| `binary`          | `+ - * / % **`, comparisons, `==` `!=` `===` `!==`                          |
| `unary`           | `!`, `-`, `+`, `typeof`                                                     |
| `logical`         | `&&`, `\|\|`, `??`                                                           |
| `conditional`     | `test ? consequent : alternate`                                             |
| `array`, `object` | literals                                                                    |
| `call`            | a builtin (`Math.max`) or one of the agent's own [helper functions](/DOCS-AJS/#local-helper-functions) |
| `methodCall`      | a method the VM's method table lists (`name.trim()`)                        |
| `regex`           | a regex literal, run on the VM's own engine, whose running time cannot blow up on crafted input |

Each node costs 0.01 fuel. `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` are refused as property
names, read or written. `new` and `this` do not exist. A method can be called only if the
method table (`METHOD_TABLE` in `src/vm/runtime.ts`) has an entry for it, and every entry bounds
what the call can allocate; see [VM budgets](/vm-budgets/).

## 2. What happens in a run

`vm.run(ast, args, options)` does these things in order. The agent's code runs only in step 7.

```text
1. Admit the options      read each option once, check it, freeze the result
2. Resolve the AST        a stored-procedure token (proc_…) is looked up here (section 5)
3. Gate the format        an AST version this build cannot read is refused
4. Check the root         the AST's root must be a seq (its top-level list of steps)
5. Admit the arguments    copied through the membrane, budgeted by fuel and argsMaxBytes
6. Check the input        the arguments against the AST's inputSchema
7. Execute                the root seq, step by step, charging fuel; the run timeout,
                          the heap ceiling and per-atom quotas apply throughout
8. Check the output       the result against the AST's outputSchema, if it declares one
9. Return                 { result, error, fuelUsed, trace?, warnings? }
```

The schemas come from the front end. The transpiler derives `inputSchema` from the function's
parameter examples and `outputSchema` from a declared result; the builder takes them from
`.take()` and `.return()`.

Some failures come back as the run's `error`, and some throw into the host:

| Comes back as `error`                                        | Throws into the host                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Anything the agent does: a failed atom, `Error(...)`, out of fuel, a timeout | A token that is missing (`Procedure not found`) or expired (`Procedure expired`) |
| A bad run option (`fuel: -1`)                                | An AST format version this build cannot read              |
| Arguments the membrane refuses                               | A root that is not a `seq`                                |
| Arguments that do not match `inputSchema`                    | Source passed to `tjs-lang/vm-ast`                        |
| A result that does not match `outputSchema`                  | Source that fails to transpile, on `tjs-lang/vm`          |

The rule: what the agent does, and whether its options, arguments and result are admitted,
comes back as a value. A host mistake about *what* is being run throws.

`error` is an `AgentError` with the step that failed (`error.op`) and why (`error.message`).
Test for one with `isAgentError(value)`, exported from `tjs-lang/vm-ast`.

## 3. The security model

The sandbox protects the host from the **agent**: the AST is untrusted. It does not protect the
host from its own **atoms** and **capabilities**: you register those, and they are trusted to be
non-blocking, to stop when the run's abort signal (`ctx.signal`, an `AbortSignal`) fires, and to
return plain data.

**No ambient authority.** The VM has no IO of its own. Every network call, store read or model
call goes through a capability the host passed. See [Capabilities](/ajs-capabilities/).

**Bounded work.** Every step costs fuel; at zero the run ends with `Out of Fuel`. Work that grows
with its input (copying, string building, a regex) is charged in proportion. See
[VM budgets](/vm-budgets/).

**Bounded time.** Each run has a timeout. The default is the larger of 60 seconds and twice the
longest timeout of any registered atom; `timeoutMs` sets it. Each atom call also has its own
timeout, and the host can cancel a run with the `signal` option. See
[Run options](/ajs-host/#run-options).

**Bounded memory.** `maxHeapBytes` (64 MB by default) caps what the agent holds live;
`membraneMaxBytes` (4 MB) caps one value crossing to or from a capability. See
[VM budgets](/vm-budgets/).

**Bounded external calls.** `quotas: { llmPredict: 3 }` caps how many times an atom may be called
in a run, which fuel cannot express. See [Quotas](/ajs-host/#quotas-across-nested-runs).

**A closed boundary.** Values crossing to or from a capability are copies of JSON data plus
`Date`, built by the VM. Getters never run; functions and class instances are refused. See
[What a capability may return](/ajs-capabilities/#what-a-capability-may-return).

**No host code from the agent.** No `eval`, no function values, no prototype keys; only listed
methods; regexes on the VM's own engine. See [AJS: The Agent Language](/DOCS-AJS/).

**Errors are values.** Failures are returned as `AgentError`, never thrown into the host. Inside
the agent, AJS's `try`/`catch` can catch a failure of the outside world: a fetch that returns an
error or is blocked, a capability answer that is too large. A bug at the capability boundary
ends the run even inside a `try`: an atom called with input that does not match its declared
schema, or a capability that returns a class instance. See
[Catchable, and run-ending](/DOCS-AJS/#catchable-and-run-ending).

Each run starts with fresh state, and the host's `capabilities` object is used exactly as passed:
the VM never copies it or writes to it. When there is no `store` capability, the run gets a
private in-memory store, and a warning in the run's `warnings` if the agent uses it.

## 4. Request context

The `context` option carries request-scoped data, such as who is asking, to your atoms. The
agent cannot read it: it is not in the agent's scope, and `context` inside an agent is an
ordinary undefined name. So an atom can make authorization decisions that the agent cannot
influence.

`defineAtom` takes the atom's name, its input schema, its output schema and its implementation.
The implementation receives the input and `ctx`, the per-call context the VM passes to every
atom; `ctx.context` is the run's `context` option. An atom may throw: the VM turns that into a
failed step, which the agent can catch, and which otherwise becomes the run's `error`.

```typescript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM, defineAtom } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'
import { s } from 'tjs-lang/schema'

const readRecord = defineAtom(
  'readRecord', // name
  s.object({ id: s.string }), // input schema
  s.object({ id: s.string, owner: s.string }), // output schema
  async ({ id }, ctx) => {
    const user = ctx.context?.user
    if (!user?.permissions.includes('records:read'))
      throw new Error('not allowed to read records')
    return { id, owner: user.id }
  }
)

const vm = new AgentVM({ readRecord })
const { ast } = transpile(
  `function report({ id: 'r1' }) {
    const row = readRecord({ id })
    return { row }
  }`,
  { atoms: vm.atoms }
)

const allowed = await vm.run(ast, { id: 'r1' }, {
  context: { user: { id: 'u-123', permissions: ['records:read'] } },
})
console.log(allowed.result) // { row: { id: 'r1', owner: 'u-123' } }

const denied = await vm.run(ast, { id: 'r1' }, {
  context: { user: { id: 'u-456', permissions: [] } },
})
console.log(denied.error.message) // not allowed to read records
```

Passing `{ atoms: vm.atoms }` to `transpile` lets it check calls to `readRecord` the way it
checks core atoms. The VM itself reads a few `context` keys, all for `httpFetch`'s policy; they
are listed in [Fetch policy](/ajs-host/#fetch-policy).

### Streaming partial results

`vm.run` returns once, when the agent finishes. To send results while it runs, give it an atom
that calls a callback from `context`:

```typescript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM, defineAtom } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'
import { s } from 'tjs-lang/schema'

const emit = defineAtom(
  'emit',
  s.object({ data: s.any }),
  s.null,
  async ({ data }, ctx) => {
    await ctx.context?.onChunk?.(data)
    return null
  }
)

const vm = new AgentVM({ emit })
const { ast } = transpile(
  `function countdown({ from: 3 }) {
    let n = from
    while (n > 0) {
      emit({ data: { n } })
      n -= 1
    }
    return { done: true }
  }`,
  { atoms: vm.atoms }
)

const chunks = []
const run = await vm.run(ast, { from: 3 }, {
  context: { onChunk: (data) => chunks.push(data) },
})
console.log(chunks, run.result) // [{ n: 3 }, { n: 2 }, { n: 1 }] { done: true }
```

The agent writes `emit(...)` without `await`, but the VM waits for every atom call to finish
before the next step, so chunks arrive in order. In a server, `onChunk` would write to the
response (`res.write(JSON.stringify(data) + '\n')`). The atom's input has crossed the membrane,
so the callback receives a plain copy, never a live object from inside the agent.

## 5. Stored procedures

The `storeProcedure` atom stores an AST and returns a token, a string like
`proc_6f1c…` (`proc_` plus a random UUID). A token can be run anywhere an AST can: by the host
with `vm.run(token, args)`, or by an agent with `agentRun({ agentId: token, input })`. That lets
behaviour be passed around as a string, the way a function pointer would be.

```typescript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

const vm = new AgentVM()
const double = transpile(`function double({ n: 0 }) { return { n: n * 2 } }`).ast

// An agent that registers a handler and hands back its token.
// handler has no example value: it accepts anything, here an AST passed as plain JSON.
const register = transpile(`
  function register({ handler }) {
    const token = storeProcedure({ ast: handler, ttl: 300000 })
    return { token }
  }`).ast

// An agent that runs whichever handler it is given.
// 'proc_' is only an example value: it says "a string".
const dispatch = transpile(`
  function dispatch({ handler: 'proc_', value: 0 }) {
    const out = agentRun({ agentId: handler, input: { n: value } })
    return { answer: out.n }
  }`).ast

const { token } = (await vm.run(register, { handler: double })).result

console.log((await vm.run(token, { n: 21 })).result) // { n: 42 }
console.log((await vm.run(dispatch, { handler: token, value: 5 })).result) // { answer: 10 }
```

An AST is plain JSON, so it is a legal run argument: it crosses the membrane like any other
data.

How the store behaves:

- **It is in memory, per process.** Tokens do not survive a restart and are not shared between
  processes or machines. The store is `procedureStore`, a `Map` exported from the VM, so a host
  can inspect it or clear it.
- **Entries expire.** The default `ttl` is one hour (3,600,000 ms). Running an expired token
  fails with `Procedure expired`. `releaseProcedure({ token })` deletes one early and returns
  whether it existed; `clearExpiredProcedures()` sweeps expired entries and returns how many it
  removed.
- **Size is capped.** An AST over `maxSize` bytes of JSON is refused; the default is 100 KB, and
  `storeProcedure({ ast, maxSize })` sets another. The AST's root must have an `op` field (every
  AST from the transpiler or the builder has one); anything else is refused as `Invalid AST`.
- **The format is checked twice:** when the AST is stored and again when the token is run, so an
  AST this build cannot read fails at the door, not later in someone else's run.
- **A token is a capability to run code, not to gain privileges.** The stored AST runs with the
  capabilities, fuel and quotas of whoever runs the token, never of whoever stored it. Tokens are
  random, so they cannot be enumerated, but anyone holding one can run it in the same process.

| Atom                     | Base fuel | Notes                                                        |
| ------------------------ | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `storeProcedure`         | 1         | plus copying the AST, charged by its size ([VM budgets](/vm-budgets/)) |
| `releaseProcedure`       | 0.1       |                                                              |
| `clearExpiredProcedures` | 0.5       |                                                              |

## 6. Sub-agents and whose budget they spend

`agentRun({ agentId, input })` runs another agent, which sees only `input`. What `agentId` is
decides where it runs:

- **An AST, or a string starting with `proc_`** (a stored-procedure token) runs inside the
  caller's run. It spends the caller's fuel, counts against the caller's quotas, and uses the
  caller's capabilities. A sub-agent that loops forever runs the caller out of fuel; it cannot
  escape the budget.
- **Any other string** (usually a name) goes to the host's `agent` capability, whose minimal shape
  is `{ agent: { run: async (agentId, input) => result } }`. That is typically a new `vm.run`,
  with a fresh fuel budget and fresh quotas that the host chooses. Without an `agent` capability,
  the call fails with `Capability 'agent.run' missing`.

An inline sub-agent's declared parameters and result are **not** checked: steps 6 and 8 of a run
happen only in `vm.run`. A stored `function double({ n: 0 }): { n: 0 }` run through `agentRun`
with `{ n: 'x' }` runs and returns whatever it computes. If a sub-agent's contract matters, check
its result in the caller, or serve it through the `agent` capability with its own `vm.run`.

So the host decides how much a named sub-agent may spend. The worked example of holding one quota
across a whole call tree is in [Quotas across nested runs](/ajs-host/#quotas-across-nested-runs);
composition patterns (fan-out, pipelines, workers) are in
[Composing Agents](/patterns/#composing-agents).

## 7. Runs are not transactions

If an agent fails part way through, what it already did through a capability stays done. The VM
has no rollback, because it cannot undo a write it does not own:

```typescript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

const vm = new AgentVM()
const { ast } = transpile(`
  function transfer({ amount: 0 }) {
    storeSet({ key: 'debited', value: amount })
    if (amount > 100) {
      Error('limit exceeded') // AJS has no throw: calling Error(...) fails the run
    }
    storeSet({ key: 'credited', value: amount })
    return { ok: true }
  }`)

// The smallest store capability: async get and set.
const data = new Map()
const store = {
  get: async (key) => data.get(key),
  set: async (key, value) => {
    data.set(key, value)
  },
}

const run = await vm.run(ast, { amount: 500 }, { capabilities: { store } })
console.log(run.error.message, Object.fromEntries(data))
// limit exceeded { debited: 500 }
```

When several writes must succeed or fail together, make that one capability call that the host
performs atomically (a `transfer` atom that runs a database transaction), rather than a sequence
the agent drives. How `Error(...)` and `try`/`catch` work is in [Errors](/DOCS-AJS/#errors).

## 8. Dependencies and size

`tjs-lang/vm-ast` needs one package at runtime, `tosijs-schema` (`^1.12.0`), for schema
validation. 1.12 is the floor because it marks its schema builders, so tjs-lang can tell a
builder from a plain object that happens to have a `schema` key. The transpiler adds `acorn`,
the JavaScript parser. The package as a whole also ships `acorn-walk` (for the linter and the
predicate verifier) and `acorn-loose` (so editor tooling can read half-typed code). Between them
they pull in nothing else: `acorn-walk` and `acorn-loose` depend only on `acorn`, and `acorn` and
`tosijs-schema` have no dependencies.

Sizes, measured on the 2026-11-05 build with `tosijs-schema` left external: `tjs-lang/vm-ast`
is about 137 KB minified (43 KB gzipped); `tjs-lang/vm`, which adds the transpiler and acorn,
is about 324 KB (98 KB gzipped).

## Further reading

- [Embedding the AJS VM](/ajs-host/): run options, capabilities, quotas, tracing.
- [VM budgets](/vm-budgets/): how fuel and the heap ceiling are measured.
- [The universal endpoint](/universal-endpoint/): the same agent and atoms running in a browser and on a server, under one security model.

# Time and Events

Responding to the Reader made pages that wait for a click or a key. Things That Take Time made
programs that wait for a timer. Each kind of program sits still until something happens.

A game does not sit still. The ball keeps moving whether or not you touch anything, and when
you press a key, it moves the way you steer it, while it is still moving. This chapter puts
the two together: a program that changes over time **and** responds to the keyboard while it
does. By the end you will have a dot that falls down a board while you steer it left and
right, with buttons to start, pause and stop it. The next chapter turns that into a game of
Tetris.

## A clock that ticks

A countdown in Things That Take Time used `setInterval` to run a function once a second, and
`clearInterval` to stop it. A program that lives works the same way: on every **tick** of the
clock, it changes something, then shows the change. Here a dot moves along a line, one step
per tick, and comes back round to the start when it reaches the end:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

function step(position: 0, length: 12) {
  return (position + 1) % length
}

function track(position: 0, length: 12) {
  let text = ''
  for (let i = 0; i < length; i++) {
    if (i == position) {
      text = text + 'O'
    } else {
      text = text + '·'
    }
  }
  return text
}

let position = 0
let timer = null

const { page } = tosi({ page: { picture: track(0, 12) } })

function tick() {
  position = step(position, 12)
  page.picture = track(position, 12)
}

function start() {
  if (timer != null) {
    return
  }
  timer = setInterval(tick, 250)
}

function stop() {
  clearInterval(timer)
  timer = null
}

const { pre, button } = elements

preview.append(
  pre({ style: { fontSize: '2em', margin: '0' } }, page.picture),
  button({ onClick: start }, 'Start'),
  button({ onClick: stop }, 'Stop')
)

test 'the dot steps along, and comes back round' {
  expect(step(0, 12)).toBe(1)
  expect(step(11, 12)).toBe(0)
  expect(track(2, 5)).toBe('··O··')
}
```

Press **Start**. Four times a second, `tick` moves the dot one place and draws the line again.

- `step` is the rule for one tick: the next position. `%` is the remainder from Decisions:
  `(11 + 1) % 12` is 0, which is what brings the dot back to the start.
- `track` draws a position as text: a loop, as in Repetition, that puts an `O` where the dot
  is and a `·` everywhere else.
- `tick` is the only thing the clock runs, and it does two things: it changes the fact
  (`position`), then puts a fresh picture of it on the page.

`timer` does two jobs. It holds the timer id that `clearInterval` needs, as in the countdown,
and it says whether the clock is running: `null` means stopped. So `start` does nothing if
`timer` is not `null`, and a second click on **Start** cannot start a second clock. `stop`
puts `null` back, so that **Start** works again. One name for both jobs means they cannot
disagree: the countdown's `running` and its `timer` could, if you forgot to change one.

Notice that nothing happens until you press **Start**. A program on a page should not start a
clock as soon as it is loaded: the reader may not be looking, and a clock that starts by
itself is one nobody asked to stop.

Change the `250` to `50`, or to `1000`, and press **Start** again. The rule does not change,
only how often it runs.

## Keys that steer

A button hears clicks. To hear the keyboard, a program listens for the **keydown** event,
which happens every time a key goes down. It reaches whichever part of the page has the
**focus**: the part that the keyboard is talking to, the way a text box has the focus while
you type in it. Click a box and it has the focus; press Tab and the focus moves to the next
thing that can have it.

Most parts of a page cannot have the focus. `tabindex: 0` lets one take it. Click the line of
dots below, then press the left and right arrow keys. Press other keys too, to see their
names. If nothing happens, the line of dots does not have the focus: click it again.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

function steer(column: 3, key: 'ArrowLeft', columns: 7) {
  given key {
    'ArrowLeft' {
      return Math.max(0, column - 1)
    }
    'ArrowRight' {
      return Math.min(columns - 1, column + 1)
    }
  } else {
    return column
  }
}

function track(position: 0, length: 12) {
  let text = ''
  for (let i = 0; i < length; i++) {
    if (i == position) {
      text = text + 'O'
    } else {
      text = text + '·'
    }
  }
  return text
}

let column = 3

const { page } = tosi({ page: { picture: track(3, 7), key: 'none yet' } })

function onKey(event) {
  page.key = event.key
  if (['ArrowLeft', 'ArrowRight'].includes(event.key)) {
    event.preventDefault()
    column = steer(column, event.key, 7)
    page.picture = track(column, 7)
  }
}

const { div, pre } = elements

preview.append(
  pre(
    { tabindex: 0, onKeydown: onKey, style: { fontSize: '2em', margin: '0' } },
    page.picture
  ),
  div('The last key pressed was: ', page.key)
)

test 'the arrows steer, and the edges stop the dot' {
  expect(steer(3, 'ArrowLeft', 7)).toBe(2)
  expect(steer(3, 'ArrowRight', 7)).toBe(4)
  expect(steer(0, 'ArrowLeft', 7)).toBe(0)
  expect(steer(6, 'ArrowRight', 7)).toBe(6)
  expect(steer(3, 'x', 7)).toBe(3)
}
```

- `onKeydown: onKey` is like `onClick`: it hands `onKey` to the line of dots, to run each time
  a key goes down while it has the focus.
- `event.key` is the name of the key: `'a'` for the A key, `'ArrowLeft'` for the left arrow,
  `' '` (a space) for the space bar, `'Enter'`, `'Shift'`. The line under the dots shows the
  last one, so you can find the name of any key by pressing it.
- `steer` is the rule. `Math.max(0, column - 1)` is the larger of the two numbers, so the
  column never goes below 0, and `Math.min` keeps it below the right-hand edge. Any key that
  is not an arrow leaves the column where it is.

### Keeping the page still

The browser has its own uses for some keys. The arrow keys and the space bar scroll the page,
so without help, steering the dot would also move the whole page under you. Every event has
`preventDefault()`, which says "I have dealt with this; do not do what you normally do". Find
`event.preventDefault()` in `onKey`, delete it, and press the arrows: the page scrolls as the
dot moves.

`onKey` only prevents the keys it uses. Tab still moves the focus on, and every other key
still does whatever it usually does. A program that prevented every key would trap the
reader: they could not even Tab out of it.

## One state, two sources of change

Now put the clock and the keys together. The dot falls one row on every tick, the arrow keys
move it left and right while it falls, and when it reaches the bottom, it starts again at the
top.

There are now two things that can change the dot, at any moment, in any order. That sounds
complicated, and the way to keep it simple is the one from "A model the page follows", in
Responding to the Reader: keep the facts in one place, and let the page follow them. Here the
facts are a single object, the dot, with a row and a column. The clock and the keys each
change that object, and then call the same function, `show`, which draws the whole board
from the dot and nothing else.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

const rows = 8
const columns = 7

function fall(dot: { row: 0, column: 3 }, rows: 8) {
  if (dot.row < rows - 1) {
    return { row: dot.row + 1, column: dot.column }
  }
  return { row: 0, column: dot.column }
}

function steer(dot: { row: 0, column: 3 }, key: 'ArrowLeft', columns: 7) {
  given key {
    'ArrowLeft' {
      return { row: dot.row, column: Math.max(0, dot.column - 1) }
    }
    'ArrowRight' {
      return { row: dot.row, column: Math.min(columns - 1, dot.column + 1) }
    }
  } else {
    return dot
  }
}

function picture(dot: { row: 0, column: 3 }, rows: 8, columns: 7) {
  let text = ''
  for (let row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    for (let column = 0; column < columns; column++) {
      if (row == dot.row && column == dot.column) {
        text = text + 'O'
      } else {
        text = text + '·'
      }
    }
    text = text + '\n'
  }
  return text
}

let dot = { row: 0, column: 3 }
let timer = null

const { page } = tosi({ page: { picture: picture(dot, rows, columns) } })

function show() {
  page.picture = picture(dot, rows, columns)
}

function onTick() {
  dot = fall(dot, rows)
  show()
}

function onKey(event) {
  if (['ArrowLeft', 'ArrowRight'].includes(event.key)) {
    event.preventDefault()
    dot = steer(dot, event.key, columns)
    show()
  }
}

const { pre, button } = elements

const board = pre(
  { tabindex: 0, onKeydown: onKey, style: { fontSize: '2em', lineHeight: '1', margin: '0' } },
  page.picture
)

function start() {
  if (timer != null) {
    return
  }
  timer = setInterval(onTick, 500)
  board.focus()
}

function stop() {
  clearInterval(timer)
  timer = null
}

preview.append(
  board,
  button({ onClick: start }, 'Start'),
  button({ onClick: stop }, 'Stop')
)

test 'the dot falls, and starts again at the top' {
  expect(fall({ row: 0, column: 3 }, 8).row).toBe(1)
  expect(fall({ row: 7, column: 3 }, 8).row).toBe(0)
  expect(fall({ row: 7, column: 3 }, 8).column).toBe(3)
}

test 'steering keeps the row, and stops at the edges' {
  expect(steer({ row: 5, column: 3 }, 'ArrowLeft', 7).row).toBe(5)
  expect(steer({ row: 5, column: 3 }, 'ArrowLeft', 7).column).toBe(2)
  expect(steer({ row: 5, column: 6 }, 'ArrowRight', 7).column).toBe(6)
}

test 'the picture shows the dot where it is' {
  expect(picture({ row: 1, column: 0 }, 2, 3)).toBe('···\nO··\n')
}
```

Press **Start**, and steer the dot with the arrow keys as it falls. **Start** also gives the
board the focus with `board.focus()`, because clicking the button gave the focus to the
button, and the keys would have gone there.

Look at how little the clock and the keys do. `onTick` asks `fall` for the next dot and calls
`show`. `onKey` asks `steer` for the next dot and calls `show`. Neither knows the other
exists, and neither touches the board. Whatever order the ticks and key presses come in, each
one makes a new dot from the old one, and the board shows the latest.

That is why this program redraws the whole board itself, where the model in Responding to the
Reader updated the page for you. A model part on the page shows one fact, and the board is a
picture of two at once, the row and the column, so one function draws it from both. The idea
is the same: the facts live in one place, `dot`, and the page is made from them, every time,
by one function written once. Nothing is ever drawn by moving an `O` from one place to
another, so the picture cannot fall out of step with the dot.

The rules are plain functions over plain data. `fall`, `steer` and `picture` take a dot and
numbers and give back a new dot or some text; none of them knows about clocks, keys or pages.
So the tests can check them without pressing anything or waiting half a second, including
the cases that are hard to reach by hand, such as the bottom row and the right-hand edge.

`fall` and `steer` never change the dot they are given: each gives back a new one, and only
`onTick` and `onKey` put it into `dot`. A dot handed to `fall` is the same afterwards, which
makes the rules easier to test and harder to get wrong.

Now press **Stop**, and press the arrow keys again. The dot no longer falls, but it still
moves left and right: the clock has stopped, but the board is still listening. A stopped game
should not move. The next section fixes that.

## Starting, pausing and stopping

A game needs three buttons. **Start** sets it going, and if it was paused, carries on from
where it was. **Pause** stops it where it is. **Stop** ends the game and puts the dot back at
the top.

This version also listens to the keys in a different place. Rather than a board the reader
has to keep focused, it listens to the whole page, `document`, so the arrow keys steer the
dot wherever the focus is. But only while the game is running: **Start** adds the listener,
and **Pause** and **Stop** take it away again.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

const rows = 8
const columns = 7

function fall(dot: { row: 0, column: 3 }, rows: 8) {
  if (dot.row < rows - 1) {
    return { row: dot.row + 1, column: dot.column }
  }
  return { row: 0, column: dot.column }
}

function steer(dot: { row: 0, column: 3 }, key: 'ArrowLeft', columns: 7) {
  given key {
    'ArrowLeft' {
      return { row: dot.row, column: Math.max(0, dot.column - 1) }
    }
    'ArrowRight' {
      return { row: dot.row, column: Math.min(columns - 1, dot.column + 1) }
    }
  } else {
    return dot
  }
}

function picture(dot: { row: 0, column: 3 }, rows: 8, columns: 7) {
  let text = ''
  for (let row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    for (let column = 0; column < columns; column++) {
      if (row == dot.row && column == dot.column) {
        text = text + 'O'
      } else {
        text = text + '·'
      }
    }
    text = text + '\n'
  }
  return text
}

const startingDot = { row: 0, column: 3 }

let dot = startingDot
let timer = null

const { page } = tosi({
  page: { picture: picture(dot, rows, columns), status: 'Press Start.' },
})

function show() {
  page.picture = picture(dot, rows, columns)
}

function onTick() {
  dot = fall(dot, rows)
  show()
}

function onKey(event) {
  if (['ArrowLeft', 'ArrowRight'].includes(event.key)) {
    event.preventDefault()
    dot = steer(dot, event.key, columns)
    show()
  }
}

function start() {
  if (timer != null) {
    return
  }
  timer = setInterval(onTick, 500)
  document.addEventListener('keydown', onKey)
  page.status = 'Running: steer with the arrow keys.'
}

function pause() {
  clearInterval(timer)
  timer = null
  document.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey)
  page.status = 'Paused.'
}

function stop() {
  pause()
  dot = startingDot
  show()
  page.status = 'Stopped. Press Start for a new game.'
}

const { div, pre, button } = elements

preview.append(
  pre({ style: { fontSize: '2em', lineHeight: '1', margin: '0' } }, page.picture),
  div(page.status),
  button({ onClick: start }, 'Start'),
  button({ onClick: pause }, 'Pause'),
  button({ onClick: stop }, 'Stop')
)

test 'the rules have not changed' {
  expect(fall({ row: 7, column: 3 }, 8).row).toBe(0)
  expect(steer({ row: 0, column: 0 }, 'ArrowLeft', 7).column).toBe(0)
}

test 'a new game starts at the top' {
  expect(picture(startingDot, 2, 7)).toBe('···O···\n·······\n')
}
```

Press **Start**, steer, press **Pause**, and try the arrows: nothing moves, and the arrows
scroll the page again. **Start** carries on from where the dot was. **Stop** puts it back at
the top. `stop` begins by calling `pause`, because stopping is pausing and then starting
again from the beginning; writing those three lines twice would be two places to forget one.

`dot = startingDot` is safe because the rules never change a dot: `fall` and `steer` always
make a new one. If they changed the dot they were given, the first tick would move
`startingDot` itself, and the next new game would start wherever the last one stopped.

### Taking the listener away again

`document.addEventListener('keydown', onKey)` asks the page to call `onKey` on every key
press, from now on. `document.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey)` takes that request back.
Try it without: delete the `removeEventListener` line from `pause`, run the example, press
**Start** and then **Stop**. The dot stops falling, but the arrow keys still move it, and they
no longer scroll the page. The game looks stopped, and it is still eating your keys.

`removeEventListener` has to be given the **same function** that was added. That is why the
handler has a name, `onKey`, and is handed over by name both times. This looks right and does
nothing:

```tjs:static
document.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => onKey(event))
document.removeEventListener('keydown', (event) => onKey(event)) // removes nothing
```

Each `(event) => onKey(event)` makes a new function. The two do the same thing, but they are
two different functions, so the second line asks to remove one that was never added, and the
first stays.

`start` checks `timer` for the same reason as before, and here it matters twice over: a
second **Start** would add a second clock and a second listener, and each key press would
then move the dot two places.

### Cleaning up after yourself

A program that starts something is responsible for stopping it. A timer runs until it is
cleared, and a listener listens until it is removed, whether or not anything on the page
still needs it. Nothing tidies them up for you while the page is open.

Here a forgotten listener means that the arrow keys go on moving a game nobody is playing,
and the page will not scroll. In a bigger program the forgotten pieces pile up: every new game
adds another clock and another listener, the old ones never go away, and the program gets
slower and stranger the longer it runs. So whenever you write a line that starts something,
write the line that stops it, in the function that ends it, at the same time.

As in Things That Take Time, changing an example while it runs does not stop its old timers,
and here it does not remove its old listeners either. Press **Stop** before you edit, or reload
the page. While this game is running, the arrow keys steer the dot even while you are typing
in the code: one more reason a game listens to the whole page only while it runs.

## Smooth motion

The falling dot jumps a whole row at a time, twice a second, and for a game on a board, that
is right: the rule says one row per tick. But some things should glide. For those, the
browser offers `requestAnimationFrame`, which asks for a function to be run right before the
browser next draws the page. The browser draws a new **frame** about sixty times a second, so
a function that asks again every time it runs is called on every frame.

Here two balls move by the same rule, at the same speed. The top one is drawn on every frame;
the bottom one every 500 milliseconds, like the dot.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, tosi } from 'tosijs'

function across(elapsed: 1000.0, speed: 100.0, width: 260.0) {
  return ((elapsed / 1000) * speed) % width
}

const { motion } = tosi({ motion: { smooth: '0px', jumpy: '0px' } })

let startedAt = 0
let frame = null
let timer = null

function place() {
  return `${across(performance.now() - startedAt, 100, 260)}px`
}

function everyFrame() {
  motion.smooth = place()
  frame = requestAnimationFrame(everyFrame)
}

function start() {
  if (timer != null) {
    return
  }
  startedAt = performance.now()
  frame = requestAnimationFrame(everyFrame)
  timer = setInterval(() => {
    motion.jumpy = place()
  }, 500)
}

function stop() {
  cancelAnimationFrame(frame)
  frame = null
  clearInterval(timer)
  timer = null
}

const { div, button } = elements

function lane(left) {
  return div(
    { style: { position: 'relative', width: '280px', height: '24px', background: '#eee' } },
    div({
      style: {
        position: 'absolute',
        left: left,
        top: '2px',
        width: '20px',
        height: '20px',
        borderRadius: '50%',
        background: 'teal',
      },
    })
  )
}

preview.append(
  div('Every frame:'),
  lane(motion.smooth),
  div('Every 500 ms:'),
  lane(motion.jumpy),
  button({ onClick: start }, 'Start'),
  button({ onClick: stop }, 'Stop')
)

test 'the ball moves 100 pixels a second, and comes back round' {
  expect(across(0, 100, 260)).toBe(0)
  expect(across(500, 100, 260)).toBe(50)
  expect(across(3000, 100, 260)).toBe(40)
}
```

- `performance.now()` is the time in milliseconds, measured very precisely from when the page
  opened. `startedAt` remembers it at **Start**, so `performance.now() - startedAt` is how long
  the balls have been moving.
- `across` is the rule: where a ball is after so many milliseconds, at `speed` pixels a
  second. `%` brings it back to the left when it reaches the end, as `step` did for the dot.
- `everyFrame` places the smooth ball, then asks to be run again on the next frame. That
  request, every time, is what keeps it going. `requestAnimationFrame` gives back an id, as
  `setInterval` does, and `cancelAnimationFrame(frame)` cancels the request it stands for, so
  the next frame never comes.
- `left: left` puts a model part into the ball's style, so the ball moves whenever the model
  does. `lane` is handed `motion.smooth` for one ball and `motion.jumpy` for the other.

Notice that neither ball counts its steps. The position comes from the clock: how much time
has passed, times the speed. That matters, because frames do not come at an exact rate.
Sixty a second is usual, but a busy computer draws fewer, some screens draw more, and a page
in a tab you are not looking at draws none at all. A ball that moved two pixels per frame
would move at a different speed on every computer; a ball placed by the time arrives at the
same place on all of them.

So there are two kinds of time in a program that moves. **Rules** happen at the program's
pace: one row every 500 milliseconds, because that is how the game is played. **Drawing**
happens at the screen's pace: every frame, so that motion looks smooth. A game whose pieces
jump from square to square, such as the falling dot or the Tetris game in the next chapter,
needs only the first kind, because the picture only changes when a rule changes the state.
`show`, called after every change, already draws it exactly as often as it needs drawing.

## Try it

**A reaction-time tester.** A button says **Ready**. When it is pressed, the page waits a
random time between one and four seconds (`setTimeout`, and `Math.random()` from Functions),
then turns a box green and remembers `performance.now()`. The reader presses the space bar
as soon as they see green, and the page shows how many milliseconds it took. Pressing too
soon should say so, not report a time. Write the rule first, with tests: a function that
takes the time green appeared, the time of the key press (or `null` if it came before green)
and gives back the message to show. Listen for the space bar only from **Ready** until the
reader has pressed it, and remember `preventDefault`, or the space bar will scroll the page.

**Faster and faster.** In the game from "Starting, pausing and stopping", count the dots that
reach the bottom, and show the count. Every five, make the clock faster: write
`delay(landed: 0)` that gives back 500 for 0 to 4 landings, 450 for 5 to 9, and so on, but
never less than 100, and test it. To change how often a timer runs, clear it and start a new
one with the new delay.

More to try:

- Make the down arrow move the dot down a row at once, as a tick would. `fall` already knows
  how; `onKey` only has to call it.
- Make a dot that lands stay where it landed, and start a new dot at the top. The board now
  has to remember a list of landed dots (Lists), `picture` has to draw them too, and `fall`
  has to stop a dot that is above a landed one. This is most of what the next chapter does.
- **A snake.** The snake is a list of cells, each with a row and a column, head first. On each
  tick a new head goes on the front, one step in the snake's direction, and the last cell
  comes off the end, so the snake moves without growing. The arrow keys change the direction.
  When the head lands on a piece of food, leave the last cell on for that tick, and the snake
  grows by one. Write `move(snake, direction)` with tests before there is any clock or key.
- Give the gliding ball from "Smooth motion" a second rule, so that it bounces back from the
  right-hand edge instead of jumping back to the left.

Work them here:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
// Your code here. Show results with preview.append(…), check them with a
// test block, then press the refresh button (or ⌘S / Ctrl+S) to run it.
```
