# Honest Equality

This page is for readers who already know JavaScript. If you are learning to program, start
with [Decisions](/decisions/), which introduces `==` from scratch.

JavaScript's `==` converts between types before it compares, so `0 == ''` is `true`. Its
`===` doesn't convert, but it says a boxed string is not `'hi'` and that `NaN`
is not `NaN`. In a `.tjs` file, `==` and `!=` are fixed, `typeof null` is `'null'`, and
deep comparison has its own name, `Is`. This page covers all of it, including the escapes
back to JavaScript's behaviour.

All of this applies to `.tjs` files only. A `.js` file, and TypeScript run through the
converter, keep JavaScript's rules; the last section says why.

## `==` does not convert types

In JavaScript, `==` converts its operands to a common type first, with surprising results:

```text
0 == ''          // true in JavaScript
false == []      // true in JavaScript
'' == false      // true in JavaScript
1 == '1'         // true in JavaScript
```

In TJS, values of different types are never equal:

```tjs:inline
console.log(0 == '')         // false
console.log(false == [])     // false
console.log(false == '')     // false
console.log(1 == '1')        // false
console.log(1 != '1')        // true
```

## Boxed primitives unwrap

A _boxed primitive_ is an object wrapped around a plain value: `Object('hi')` is a box
holding the string `'hi'`. (JavaScript also makes one with `new String('hi')`; a `.tjs` file
refuses that spelling, because it is almost always a mistake for `String('hi')`, and keeps
`Object(x)` for the times you mean it.) Boxes still arrive from JavaScript libraries and
converted code. JavaScript's `===` compares the box, not what is in it, so
`Object('hi') === 'hi'` is `false`. TJS's `==` looks inside:

```tjs:inline
console.log(Object('hi') == 'hi')       // true
console.log(Object(false) == false)     // true
console.log(Object(42) == 42)           // true
```

## `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`

`null` still equals `undefined`, so the familiar `x == null` check catches both. Neither
equals anything else. And `NaN` equals `NaN`, which in JavaScript it does not, under either
operator:

```tjs:inline
console.log(null == undefined)   // true
console.log(null == 0)           // false
console.log(null == '')          // false
console.log(NaN == NaN)          // true (JavaScript: false)
```

## Objects compare by reference

For objects and arrays, `==` asks whether both sides are the very same object. It does not
look at what is inside them, so the answer takes the same tiny amount of time however large
the objects are:

```tjs:inline
const obj = { x: 1 }
console.log(obj == obj)              // true: same object
console.log({ x: 1 } == { x: 1 })    // false: two objects
console.log([1, 2] == [1, 2])        // false: two arrays
```

## `typeof null` is `'null'`

In JavaScript, `typeof null` is `'object'`, a bug kept for compatibility. So the obvious
check for "is this an object?" lets `null` through:

```text
if (typeof x === 'object') x.name   // throws in JavaScript when x is null
```

In TJS, `typeof null` is `'null'`, and every other answer is unchanged:

```tjs:inline
console.log(typeof null)        // null
console.log(typeof undefined)   // undefined
console.log(typeof {})          // object
console.log(typeof 42)          // number
```

## Three questions, three spellings

TJS gives each kind of comparison its own spelling, so the code says which question it is
asking:

| you want to know…                        | write                     | cost                 |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------- |
| are these the same value?                | `a == b`, `a != b`        | constant             |
| are these the very same object?          | `a === b`, `a !== b`      | constant             |
| do these have the same contents, deeply? | `Is(a, b)`, `IsNot(a, b)` | grows with the data  |

For objects, `==` and `===` agree (both check identity) unless the class defines
`asCompared()`, covered under "Your own types" below. They differ on boxed primitives, on
`null` against `undefined`, and on `NaN`.

`==` is the one you will use almost everywhere. It is JavaScript's `===` with these changes:

- a boxed primitive equals its plain value: `Object('hi') == 'hi'`
- `null` equals `undefined`, so `x == null` still checks for both
- `NaN` equals `NaN`
- an object with an `asCompared()` method compares as the value that method returns

It never converts between types, so `1 == '1'` is `false`. And it is deliberately **not**
structural (it does not compare contents): two separate arrays with the same items are two
different arrays, and finding that out costs nothing. If `==` compared contents, every
comparison of two large objects would quietly walk both of them.

`===` and `!==` keep exactly JavaScript's meaning. Reach for them when you mean identity,
"is this the same object?", and know that `NaN === NaN` is still `false` there:

```tjs:inline
const obj = { x: 1 }
console.log(obj === obj)                  // true
console.log(Object('a') === 'a')          // false: the box is not the string
console.log(NaN === NaN)                  // false, as in JavaScript
```

## What `Is` compares

`Is(a, b)` is **structural equality**: a deep comparison you ask for by name, so the cost
is visible. It walks both values. It compares plain objects key by key, arrays element by
element in order, `Set`s by membership regardless of order, `Map`s by entries, and dates
(`LegacyDate`) and regular expressions by value. It uses `==`'s rules at the leaves, so
`Is(5, '5')` is `false` and `Is([null], [undefined])` is `true`. A key that is present
with the value `undefined` still counts as a key: `Is({ a: 1, b: undefined }, { a: 1 })`
is `false`.

`IsNot(a, b)` is `!Is(a, b)`.

```tjs:inline
const people = [{ name: 'Ada' }, { name: 'Alan' }]
const wanted = { name: 'Ada' }

console.log(people.includes(wanted))               // false: no such object
console.log(people.some(p => Is(p, wanted)))       // true: same contents

console.log(Is([1, [2, 3]], [1, [2, 3]]))          // true: nested
console.log(Is([1, 2], [2, 1]))                    // false: order matters in arrays
console.log(Is(new Set([1, 2]), new Set([2, 1])))  // true: not in sets
console.log(Is(new Map([['a', 1]]), new Map([['a', 1]])))  // true
console.log(Is({ a: 1, b: undefined }, { a: 1 }))  // false: different keys
console.log(Is(5, '5'))                            // false: no conversion
console.log(IsNot([1, 2], [2, 1]))                 // true

test 'Is compares contents' {
  expect(Is({ a: 1, b: 2 }, { a: 1, b: 2 })).toBe(true)
  expect(Is([1, 2], [2, 1])).toBe(false)
}
```

The `test` block at the end runs as an inline check when the page loads; see
[Inline Tests](/inline-tests-test-private-functions/).

Three limits are worth knowing:

- **Prototypes are not compared.** Only own enumerable string keys are walked, so a class
  instance and a plain object with the same keys are `Is`-equal. Define `Equals` (below)
  if the class matters.
- **Set members and Map keys are matched the way JavaScript's `has` matches them**, which
  for objects means by identity. Only Map _values_ are compared with `Is`. So
  `Is(new Set([{ a: 1 }]), new Set([{ a: 1 }]))` is `false`.
- **In a `.tjs` file, dates are made with `LegacyDate` or `Timestamp`**, because
  `new Date()` is refused there.

```tjs:inline
class Point {
  constructor(x: 0) {
    this.x = x
  }
}
console.log(Is(Point(1), { x: 1 }))                      // true: prototype ignored
console.log(Is(new Set([{ a: 1 }]), new Set([{ a: 1 }])))  // false: two objects
console.log(Is(LegacyDate(5), LegacyDate(5)))            // true
console.log(Is(/a/g, /a/i))                              // false: different flags
```

(`Point(1)` without `new` is how TJS constructs a class; see
[Better Classes](/better-classes/). `x: 0` in the constructor declares an _example_ value,
not a type; see [Hello TJS](/hello-tjs/).)

You can also write `a Is b` and `a IsNot b`. The operands can be names, property paths,
calls, indexes or literals, and the form works inside an argument list, as in
`console.log(a Is b)`. When another operator touches an operand, as in `a + 1 Is b`, TJS
refuses with a syntax error that asks for `Is(a + 1, b)` rather than guessing the
precedence. The call form is never ambiguous.

## Your own types

A class has three ways to say what equality means for it. They answer different questions.

**`asCompared()` changes what `==` sees.** It returns a primitive (a number, string,
boolean, `null` or `undefined`) that stands for the object whenever it is compared. `==`,
`!=` and `Is` use it, and so does truthiness: an object whose `asCompared()` returns `0`
is falsy, so `if (price)` agrees with `price == 0`. A method that returns anything else,
or throws, is ignored, and the object compares by reference as usual.

**`Equals(other)` changes what `Is` decides.** `Is` calls it instead of walking the object.
Use it when two objects with different fields should still count as the same, for example
because one holds a cache. When a class defines both, `Is` uses `Equals`.

`==` never calls `Equals`. Apart from `asCompared()`, whose errors it ignores, `==` runs
none of your code, so it stays fast and cannot throw.

**`[tjsEquals](other)`** is the same hook as `Equals`, keyed by the symbol
`Symbol.for('tjs.equals')` instead of a name. Use it when an object might have a real
data property called `Equals`, such as a record whose fields come from outside your code.
When both are present, the symbol wins. `Is` checks both operands, so the hook works on
either side.

A `.tjs` file that calls `Is` or `IsNot` has `tjsEquals` in scope. A file that does not
must name the symbol itself, `const tjsEquals = Symbol.for('tjs.equals')`, and outside a
`.tjs` file you can import it: `import { tjsEquals } from 'tjs-lang/runtime'`.

```tjs:inline
class Cents {
  constructor(n: 0) {
    this.n = n
  }
  asCompared() {
    return this.n
  }
}

console.log(Cents(500) == Cents(500))       // true: both compare as 500
console.log(Cents(500) == 500)              // true
console.log(Cents(500) === Cents(500))      // false: still two objects
console.log(Cents(0) ? 'truthy' : 'falsy')  // falsy: compares as 0

class Money {
  constructor(cents: 0, currency: 'USD') {
    this.cents = cents
    this.currency = currency
    this.formatted = null
  }
  Equals(other) {
    return other instanceof Money &&
      other.cents == this.cents && other.currency == this.currency
  }
}

const a = Money(500, 'USD')
const b = Money(500, 'USD')
b.formatted = '$5.00'
console.log(Is(a, b))   // true: Equals ignores the cached string
console.log(a == b)     // false: == never calls Equals

// An object that compares as some other value
const canonical = { x: 1, y: 2 }
const view = {
  [tjsEquals](other) { return Is(canonical, other) }
}
console.log(Is(view, { x: 1, y: 2 }))   // true
console.log(Is({ x: 1, y: 2 }, view))   // true: the hook works on either side
console.log(IsNot(view, { x: 9 }))      // true
```

## The way back to JavaScript

When you genuinely need JavaScript's old operators, each has a long, deliberately awkward
name, so the exception is visible in review and easy to search for:

| JavaScript            | TJS escape                                                 |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `a == b` / `a != b`   | `DangerousLegacyEquals(a, b)` / `DangerousLegacyNot(a, b)` |
| `a === b` / `a !== b` | `LegacyExactly(a, b)` / `LegacyNotExactly(a, b)`           |
| `typeof x`            | `LegacyTypeOf(x)`                                          |

```tjs:inline
console.log(DangerousLegacyEquals(0, ''))       // true: conversion and all
console.log(DangerousLegacyEquals('5', 5))      // true
console.log(DangerousLegacyNot(0, ''))          // false
console.log(LegacyExactly(NaN, NaN))            // false
console.log(LegacyNotExactly(Object('a'), 'a'))  // true
console.log(LegacyTypeOf(null))                 // object
```

The `==` pair is called _Dangerous_ because JavaScript's conversion calls `valueOf()` or
`toString()` on any object operand, implicitly, so a comparison can run arbitrary code that
nobody wrote for that purpose. TJS's `asCompared()` is different: a class opts in by
defining it, and its errors are ignored. The `===` pair cannot run your code; its warts are
only wrong answers, so it is merely _Legacy_. There are no short aliases, on purpose.

You never need `LegacyExactly` or `LegacyNotExactly` in hand-written TJS: `===` and `!==`
already mean exactly that. They exist so the set of escapes is complete.

## Things that trip people up

### Library methods still use JavaScript's rules

`==` is rewritten in your code, but `includes`, `indexOf`, `Set`, `Map` and every other
built-in compare the way JavaScript does, and not even consistently with each other. When
it matters, compare with `==` or `Is` yourself.

```tjs:inline
const list = [1, 2, 3]
const boxed = Object(1)

console.log(boxed == 1)                    // true: your code, TJS rules
console.log(list.includes(boxed))          // false: JavaScript's method
console.log(list.some(x => x == boxed))    // true

console.log([NaN].includes(NaN))           // true
console.log([NaN].indexOf(NaN))            // -1: two methods, two rules
```

### `switch` compares with `===`

`switch` keeps JavaScript's semantics exactly, so `switch (Object('cat'))` never
reaches `case 'cat':`, and the transpiler warns when it sees a `switch` in a `.tjs` file.
Use [`given`](/given-dispatch/), which compares with `==` and has no fallthrough:

```tjs:inline
function label(kind) {
  given kind {
    'cat', 'dog' { return 'pet' }
  } else {
    return 'other'
  }
}
console.log(label(Object('cat')))          // pet
```

### `Is` is not free

It walks both values. Use it where you mean "same contents", such as in tests and change
detection, not as a habit in hot loops.

### Only `.tjs` files get this

A `.js` file keeps JavaScript's `==` and `typeof`, because TJS must run every JavaScript
program unchanged. So does TypeScript converted to TJS with `fromTS`: it is marked as
carrying JavaScript semantics until you graduate it to native TJS.

The rules belong to the file where the comparison is written, not to where the values came
from. A `.tjs` function that compares an object from a `.js` module uses TJS's `==`,
including that object's `asCompared()`. A `.js` module comparing objects from a `.tjs`
module uses JavaScript's `==`, and `asCompared()` means nothing there.

console.log(false == [])     // false
console.log(false == '')     // false
console.log(1 == '1')        // false
console.log(1 != '1')        // true

# Multi-Agent Pipeline

Split a job into roles (a researcher, a writer, an editor), each with its own instructions, and
pass each one's output to the next. Narrow prompts are easier for a model to follow and easier
for you to debug.

The agent needs a model, which the **host** supplies: the host is the JavaScript program that
runs the agent in an `AgentVM` and decides what it may touch. On this site there is no model, so
the example prints a message instead of running. To run it yourself, use the scripted model in
[Testing it without a model](#testing-it-without-a-model) below, or a real one as in
[LLM Chat](/llm-chat/).

```ajs:inline
function collaborativeWriting({ topic = 'the future of renewable energy' }) {
  // Role 1: researcher. A short, checkable list, not an essay.
  let researchPrompt =
    'You are a research agent. Generate 3 key facts or points about: ' +
    topic +
    '\nFormat as a numbered list. Be concise.'
  let research = llmPredict({ prompt: researchPrompt })

  // Role 2: writer. Works only from the researcher's points.
  let writerPrompt =
    'You are a writer agent. Using these research points:\n\n' +
    research +
    '\n\nWrite a short, engaging paragraph (2-3 sentences) about ' +
    topic +
    '.\nMake it informative and accessible.'
  let article = llmPredict({ prompt: writerPrompt })

  // Role 3: editor. Reviews the draft and rewrites it.
  let editorPrompt =
    'You are an editor agent. Review this draft:\n\n"' +
    article +
    '"\n\nSuggest one specific improvement. Then provide the improved version.\nFormat: "Suggestion: [your suggestion]\n\nImproved: [improved text]"'
  let edited = llmPredict({ prompt: editorPrompt })

  return {
    topic,
    researchPoints: research,
    firstDraft: article,
    editorReply: edited,
  }
}
```

`llmPredict({ prompt })` calls the host's `capabilities.llm.predict(prompt)` with the prompt
string and returns the model's reply as a string, which is why `research` can be concatenated
straight into the writer's prompt.

## What to notice

- **The roles are prompts, not separate programs.** This is one agent making three model calls in
  sequence; "agent" in the prompts means a role. That is usually what you want: one budget, one
  place to read the whole pipeline, and one trace if you run it with `trace: true`.
- **Each call finishes before the next starts.** AJS has no `await`: atom calls are awaited for
  you, so `research` is the reply, not a Promise, by the time the writer's prompt is built.
- **Every intermediate result is returned.** The host gets the research, the draft and the
  editor's reply, so a bad final answer can be traced to the step that went wrong. The editor's
  reply is returned as the model wrote it, suggestion and improved text together, because the
  model may not follow the requested format exactly; split it on `Improved:` in the host if you
  need the two parts.
- **Each `llmPredict` costs 100 fuel**, so three calls cost 300, plus a little for building the
  prompts. A run with less stops partway through with `Out of Fuel`; the calls before it were
  made (and, with a paid model, paid for), and the call that ran out is refused before it reaches
  the model.
- **Fuel is not money.** Fuel measures work the VM does, so a budget large enough for the string
  work also admits more model calls. To say "at most N model calls" whatever the fuel, set a
  quota: `quotas: { llmPredict: 3 }`.

## The gotcha

Each step feeds the next, so an early mistake compounds: a wrong "fact" from the researcher
becomes confident prose by the editor. Keep the early steps narrow and checkable (a list of
facts, not an essay), and if the result matters, check those facts against a source the agent
fetches with `httpFetch`. The network is a permission too: the host grants it with a `fetch`
capability or a domain allowlist, as in [Weather API](/weather-api/).

## Testing it without a model

The model is a capability the host injects, so a test can inject a scripted one. Each reply here
says which call it was, which is enough to check that every role ran and its output reached the
result. Paste the agent above into the template string:

```javascript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

const source = `function collaborativeWriting(...) { ... }` // the agent above

let calls = 0
const llm = {
  async predict(prompt) {
    calls++
    return `reply ${calls} (${prompt.length} chars in)`
  },
}

const { ast } = transpile(source)
const run = await new AgentVM().run(ast, {}, { fuel: 1000, capabilities: { llm } })
console.log(run.result.firstDraft) // "reply 2 (… chars in)": the writer's call
console.log(run.fuelUsed) // a little over 300: three calls plus the string work
```

`vm.run` resolves to `{ result, error, fuelUsed, … }`; it does not throw. When a run fails, the
error is all you get back: the earlier replies are not in `result`. Run with `trace: true` to see
each step, its result and the fuel it used, including the steps before the failure.

The failures, with the same scripted model:

- `fuel: 250`: `run.error.message` is `'Out of Fuel'` from the third `llmPredict`, after two
  calls to the model. `run.fuelUsed` reports about 301, more than the budget, because the refused
  call's cost is still counted.
- `quotas: { llmPredict: 2 }`: the third call fails with
  `Quota exceeded for 'llmPredict': 2 calls allowed`, whatever the fuel.
- No `llm` capability: the first call fails with `Capability 'llm.predict' missing`.

## Separate agents

When the roles really are separate programs (written by different people, stored, reused), one
agent can run another with `agentRun({ agentId, input })`. Passing the sub-agent's AST keeps it
on this run's fuel and quotas. Passing a name hands it to the host, which starts a separate run
with its own fuel and its own quota counter, unless the host passes the same `quotaUsed` object
to both. [Composing Agents](/patterns/#composing-agents) shows both routes.

AJS runs steps in sequence by design; there is no parallel fan-out inside an agent. A host that
wants roles to run at once does it behind an atom (see
[Parallel Execution](/patterns/#parallel-execution)) or starts separate runs itself.

# Tetris

The last project in this part is a game: Tetris. Shapes made of four squares fall into a well,
one at a time. You slide each one left or right and turn it as it falls. When it lands, it
stays where it is, and the next shape appears at the top. A row with no gaps in it disappears,
everything above it moves down, and you score points. The game ends when there is no room
for the next shape to appear.

It is a bigger program than [A Calculator](/a-calculator/), and it uses nearly every chapter
in this part: lists of lists for the well, objects for the shapes, loops inside loops to draw
them, decisions to say what may move where, tests for every rule, and, last of all, a clock
and the keyboard from [Time and Events](/time-and-events/).

## What the game remembers

Before any code, decide what the game has to remember, as the calculator chapter did. Tetris
needs five facts:

- **the board**: the well, as a grid of squares. Each square is empty or filled with a
  colour, left there by a shape that landed.
- **the piece**: the shape that is falling now.
- **its place**: which row and column of the board the piece is at.
- **the score**.
- **over**: true or false, has the game ended?

Notice that the falling piece is not part of the board. It moves on top of the board, and only
when it lands is it written into it. Keeping the two apart makes every rule simpler: "can the
piece go here?" means "are those squares of the board empty?", and the piece never gets in its
own way.

Everything below is built in steps, and every step is a live example that runs and tests what
it adds. A live example cannot use code from another example, so each one carries the
functions from the steps before it, unchanged, and adds its own after them. When an example
looks long, the new part is at the end, immediately above the tests.

The game rules are all plain functions that take plain data (a board, a piece, a place) and
give back an answer. None of them knows about the screen, the clock or the keyboard. That is
the lesson of Responding to the Reader's "Keep the rules out of the buttons", made bigger: the
tests can check every rule without a page, and the part that does touch the page stays so thin
there is little in it to get wrong.

## The board as data

A board is a grid: 20 rows, each 10 squares across. You already know how to keep a row, a list
of values (from [Lists](/lists/)). A board is a list of rows: a **list of lists**, which you
met in [Recursion](/recursion/) (Lists inside lists). Here every row is the same length, so
plain loops are enough, no recursion needed. Each square
holds a string, `''` for empty or a colour name, such as `'orange'`, for a square that is
filled.

To make an empty board, use loops inside loops, as `grid` did in [Repetition](/repetition/)
(Loops inside loops): the outer loop makes the rows, and for each row, the inner loop fills it
with empty squares.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements } from 'tosijs'

const { pre } = elements

function emptyBoard(rows: 20, columns: 10) {
  const board = []
  for (let row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    const cells = []
    for (let column = 0; column < columns; column++) {
      cells.push('')
    }
    board.push(cells)
  }
  return board
}

function boardText(board: [['']]) {
  let text = ''
  for (const row of board) {
    for (const cell of row) {
      text = text + (cell == '' ? '. ' : '# ')
    }
    text = text + '\n'
  }
  return text
}

const board = emptyBoard(20, 10)
board[19][0] = 'orange'
board[19][1] = 'orange'
board[18][0] = 'orange'

preview.append(pre(boardText(board)))

test 'an empty board' {
  expect(emptyBoard(2, 3)).toEqual([['', '', ''], ['', '', '']])
  expect(emptyBoard(20, 10).length).toBe(20)
  expect(emptyBoard(20, 10)[0].length).toBe(10)
  expect(emptyBoard(0, 10)).toEqual([])
}

test 'changing one square changes only that square' {
  const small = emptyBoard(2, 3)
  small[1][2] = 'red'
  expect(small).toEqual([['', '', ''], ['', '', 'red']])
}

test 'a board as text' {
  const small = emptyBoard(2, 3)
  small[1][0] = 'red'
  expect(boardText(small)).toBe('. . . \n# . . \n')
}
```

- Rows are counted from the top, starting at 0, and columns from the left, starting at 0, as
  lists always count. So the bottom row is row 19 and the right-hand column is column 9.
- `board[19][0]` reads from left to right, like `book.author.name` in Things with Parts:
  take the board, then its row 19, then square 0 of that row.
- `board: [['']]` is an example of a list of lists of strings. `['']` meant a list of strings,
  so `[['']]` means a list whose items are lists of strings. TJS checks every square: hand
  `boardText` a board with a number in it and the call is refused.
- `boardText` turns a board into text so it can be seen before there is any drawing: a dot for
  an empty square, a `#` for a filled one. It is the inner and outer loop again, going through
  a board that already exists rather than making one.

Change the three `orange` lines to put an L shape somewhere else on the board.

### A common mistake: one row, many names

Why does `emptyBoard` make `cells` **inside** the outer loop? Here is what happens if a board's
rows are all the same list:

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
const row = ['', '', '']
const shared = [row, row]

shared[0][1] = 'red'

preview.append(`row 0: [${shared[0]}], row 1: [${shared[1]}]`)

test 'two names for one row' {
  expect(shared[1][1]).toBe('red')
  expect(shared[0] == shared[1]).toBe(true)
}
```

Filling a square in row 0 fills the same square in row 1. `shared` is not two rows; it is one
row, listed twice. This is Same parts, different objects from Things with Parts: putting `row`
into a list does not copy it, it gives the same list another place to be found. In
`emptyBoard`, `const cells = []` runs again every round of the outer loop, so every row is a new
list of its own. Move that line above the outer loop, and the test 'changing one square changes
only that square' turns red: the `'red'` appears in both rows.

## Drawing the board

Text is enough to test with, but a game should look like one. Each square becomes a coloured
`rect` (a rectangle), drawn with `svg`, as the polygons were in Repetition (Shapes from a rule,
A honeycomb). A rectangle needs a position, `x` across and `y` down, and a `width` and
`height`.

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { svgElements } from 'tosijs'

const { svg, rect } = svgElements

function emptyBoard(rows: 20, columns: 10) {
  const board = []
  for (let row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    const cells = []
    for (let column = 0; column < columns; column++) {
      cells.push('')
    }
    board.push(cells)
  }
  return board
}

const squareSize = 16 // pixels across each square

function colourOf(cell: '') {
  return cell == '' ? 'gainsboro' : cell
}

function square(row: 0, column: 0, colour: 'red') {
  return rect({
    x: column * squareSize,
    y: row * squareSize,
    width: squareSize,
    height: squareSize,
    fill: colour,
    stroke: 'white',
  })
}

function drawBoard(board: [['']]) {
  const drawing = svg({
    width: board[0].length * squareSize,
    height: board.length * squareSize,
  })
  for (let row = 0; row < board.length; row++) {
    for (let column = 0; column < board[row].length; column++) {
      drawing.append(square(row, column, colourOf(board[row][column])))
    }
  }
  return drawing
}

const board = emptyBoard(20, 10)
board[19][0] = 'orange'
board[19][1] = 'orange'
board[18][0] = 'orange'
board[19][5] = 'cyan'
board[19][6] = 'cyan'
board[19][7] = 'cyan'
board[19][8] = 'cyan'

preview.append(drawBoard(board))

test 'the colour of a square' {
  expect(colourOf('')).toBe('gainsboro')
  expect(colourOf('orange')).toBe('orange')
}
```

- `square` puts a square at a row and column. Moving one column right moves it `squareSize`
  pixels across, so column 3 is at `x` 48. Row works the same way, downwards.
- `colourOf` decides the colour (with `? :` from [Decisions](/decisions/)): an empty square is
  pale grey (`gainsboro` is a colour name, like `teal`), and a filled one is the colour it
  holds.
- `drawBoard` is the honeycomb's two loops: down the rows, across the columns, one square
  each. The size of the drawing comes from the board itself, so a board of any size draws.

`drawBoard` depends on the board and nothing else. Give it the same board and you get the same
picture; change the board and draw it again, and the picture changes. The game will work
exactly that way: change the facts, then draw them.

Try `squareSize = 30`, or change `'gainsboro'` to `'black'` for a night-time well.

## A piece as data

There are seven pieces, named after the letters they look like: I, O, T, S, Z, J and L. Each
one is easiest to describe as a small picture, so the program writes it that way: a grid of
text in which `X` is a square of the piece and `.` is empty.

The rules need something else: a list of the piece's squares, each with a `row` and a
`column`, counted inside the little grid. `cellsOf` turns the picture into that list, with
loops inside loops once more. It reads each line of the picture one letter at a time:
`grid[row][column]` works on a list of strings as it does on a list of lists, because a string
can be read by position with square brackets, as a list can (`'.X.'[1]` is `'X'`).

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { svgElements } from 'tosijs'

const { svg, rect } = svgElements

function emptyBoard(rows: 20, columns: 10) {
  const board = []
  for (let row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    const cells = []
    for (let column = 0; column < columns; column++) {
      cells.push('')
    }
    board.push(cells)
  }
  return board
}

const squareSize = 16 // pixels across each square

function colourOf(cell: '') {
  return cell == '' ? 'gainsboro' : cell
}

function square(row: 0, column: 0, colour: 'red') {
  return rect({
    x: column * squareSize,
    y: row * squareSize,
    width: squareSize,
    height: squareSize,
    fill: colour,
    stroke: 'white',
  })
}

function drawBoard(board: [['']]) {
  const drawing = svg({
    width: board[0].length * squareSize,
    height: board.length * squareSize,
  })
  for (let row = 0; row < board.length; row++) {
    for (let column = 0; column < board[row].length; column++) {
      drawing.append(square(row, column, colourOf(board[row][column])))
    }
  }
  return drawing
}

// New in this step:

const shapes = {
  I: { colour: 'cyan', grid: ['....', 'XXXX', '....', '....'] },
  O: { colour: 'gold', grid: ['XX', 'XX'] },
  T: { colour: 'purple', grid: ['.X.', 'XXX', '...'] },
  S: { colour: 'green', grid: ['.XX', 'XX.', '...'] },
  Z: { colour: 'red', grid: ['XX.', '.XX', '...'] },
  J: { colour: 'blue', grid: ['X..', 'XXX', '...'] },
  L: { colour: 'orange', grid: ['..X', 'XXX', '...'] },
}

Type Piece {
  description: 'a shape: its colour, the size of its square grid, and its squares'
  example: { name: 'T', colour: 'purple', size: 3, cells: [{ row: 0, column: 0 }] }
}

Type Place {
  description: 'a row and a column on the board'
  example: { row: 0, column: 0 }
}

function cellsOf(grid: ['']) {
  const cells = []
  for (let row = 0; row < grid.length; row++) {
    for (let column = 0; column < grid[row].length; column++) {
      if (grid[row][column] == 'X') {
        cells.push({ row, column })
      }
    }
  }
  return cells
}

function makePiece(name: 'T') {
  const shape = shapes[name]
  return {
    name,
    colour: shape.colour,
    size: shape.grid.length,
    cells: cellsOf(shape.grid),
  }
}

function picture(piece: Piece) {
  const grid = emptyBoard(piece.size, piece.size)
  for (const cell of piece.cells) {
    grid[cell.row][cell.column] = 'X'
  }
  const lines = []
  for (const row of grid) {
    let line = ''
    for (const cell of row) {
      line = line + (cell == '' ? '.' : 'X')
    }
    lines.push(line)
  }
  return lines
}

function drawGame(board: [['']], piece: Piece, place: Place) {
  const drawing = drawBoard(board)
  for (const cell of piece.cells) {
    drawing.append(
      square(place.row + cell.row, place.column + cell.column, piece.colour)
    )
  }
  return drawing
}

for (const name of Object.keys(shapes)) {
  const piece = makePiece(name)
  const board = emptyBoard(piece.size, piece.size)
  preview.append(drawGame(board, piece, { row: 0, column: 0 }), ' ')
}

test 'a picture becomes a list of squares' {
  expect(cellsOf(['.X.', 'XXX', '...'])).toEqual([
    { row: 0, column: 1 },
    { row: 1, column: 0 },
    { row: 1, column: 1 },
    { row: 1, column: 2 },
  ])
}

test 'every piece has four squares, and draws back as its picture' {
  for (const name of Object.keys(shapes)) {
    const piece = makePiece(name)
    expect(piece.cells.length).toBe(4)
    expect(picture(piece)).toEqual(shapes[name].grid)
  }
}

test 'a piece knows its name, colour and size' {
  const t = makePiece('T')
  expect(t.name).toBe('T')
  expect(t.colour).toBe('purple')
  expect(t.size).toBe(3)
  expect(makePiece('I').size).toBe(4)
}

test 'a piece with a missing part is refused' {
  expect(picture({ name: 'T', colour: 'purple', cells: [] }) instanceof Error).toBe(true)
}
```

- `shapes` is an object whose parts are named by letter, and `shapes[name]` finds one by a
  name held in a value, as in Things with Parts (Parts named by a value). Each shape has a
  `colour` and its `grid`. Every grid is square (as many lines as letters across), which
  matters when turning a piece, two steps on.
- `makePiece('T')` builds the piece the rules use: its `name`, its `colour`, the `size` of its
  grid, and its `cells`. `{ row, column }` is short for `{ row: row, column: column }`, as in
  Things with Parts (Functions that make objects).
- `picture` goes the other way, from a piece to its picture. The tests use it: a list of
  strings such as `['.X.', 'XXX', '...']` is much easier to check by eye than a list of eight
  numbers. The second test checks all seven pieces with one loop.
- `Type Piece` and `Type Place` name the two shapes of data the rules pass around, as `Point`
  did in Things with Parts. Each function that takes a piece says `piece: Piece`, and TJS
  checks every call: the last test hands `picture` a piece with no `size`, and it is refused.
- `drawGame` draws the board, then the piece's squares on top of it, each moved by the place.
  The piece is drawn over the board, not written into it, as the plan said. Here each
  piece is drawn on a little board of its own, the size of its grid.

Change a grid in `shapes` (give the T a fifth square, say) and run it. The picture changes, and
the test 'every piece has four squares' says which piece broke the rule.

## Moving and colliding

The most important rule in the game is one question: can this piece be at this place? Every
move asks it. Sliding left asks it about the place one column to the left; falling asks it
about the place one row down; turning asks it about the turned piece. If the answer is no, the
move does not happen.

A piece fits if every one of its squares is on the board and empty. A loop goes through the
squares, and the first one that fails is enough to say no, so the function gives back `false`
at once, the way `break` stopped the search in Repetition (Stopping early with `break`):

```tjs:inline {"view": "code"}
import { elements, svgElements } from 'tosijs'

const { div } = elements
const { svg, rect } = svgElements

function emptyBoard(rows: 20, columns: 10) {
  const board = []
  for (let row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    const cells = []
    for (let column = 0; column < columns; column++) {
      cells.push('')
    }
    board.push(cells)
  }
  return board
}

const squareSize = 16 // pixels across each square

function colourOf(cell: '') {
  return cell == '' ? 'gainsboro' : cell
}

function square(row: 0, column: 0, colour: 'red') {
  return rect({
    x: column * squareSize,
    y: row * squareSize,
    width: squareSize,
    height: squareSize,
    fill: colour,
    stroke: 'white',

that is not `''` is already filled. Only a piece that gets past every check, for every square,
reaches `return true`.

column 8 it would need a column 10, and does not. Each pair of checks stands on either side of

## Turning a piece

Turning a piece a quarter turn clockwise changes where its squares are in its little grid.
Picture a sheet of squared paper turned to the right: the top row becomes the right-hand
column, and the left-hand column becomes the top row. For each square, that is:

- its new **row** is its old **column**, and
- its new **column** is `size - 1 - row`: row 0, the top, goes to the last column, and the
  bottom row goes to column 0.

Here is the T worked through, with `size` 3:

| square | old row, column | new row     | new column      |
| ------ | --------------- | ----------- | --------------- |
| top    | 0, 1            | 1           | 3 - 1 - 0 = 2   |
| left   | 1, 0            | 0           | 3 - 1 - 1 = 1   |
| middle | 1, 1            | 1           | 3 - 1 - 1 = 1   |
| right  | 1, 2            | 2           | 3 - 1 - 1 = 1   |

The T pointing up becomes a T pointing right: `['.X.', '.XX', '.X.']`. `rotate` does that to
every square, with one loop, and gives back a new piece; the piece it was given is left alone.

Turning can fail like any move. A long I standing upright against the right wall has no room
to lie down. `turn` asks `fits` about the turned piece, and gives back either the turned piece
or, when it does not fit, the piece unchanged:

cannot, which is Checking Your Work's question, Does your test catch anything?, again.

colour, and from then on they are part of the well. `land` gives back a new board with the

- `board.map((row) => [...row])` copies the board: `map` makes a new list of rows, and
  `[...row]` (from Lists, Putting a list in order) makes each row a new list of its own. Copying
  only the outer list would not be enough, for the reason in "One row, many names": the new
  board would share its rows with the old one, and writing a colour into one would write it
  into both. The first test checks the old board is still empty.
- `lowest` is the piece falling, all at once: while the row below still fits, go down one. It
  is a `while` loop, as in Repetition (`while`: until something changes), because nobody
  knows in advance how far a piece will fall. The loop always ends, because the floor stops it.
- `dropAndLand` puts the two together, so the example can build a board by dropping pieces into
  columns: a piece starts at row 0 of a column, falls as far as it can, and lands.

Why a copy, when the calculator's `press` changed the calculator it was given? Because a test
can then compare the board before and after, and because a board that is never changed in
place can be shared safely. `land` makes the new board; the program decides when to replace
the old one with it, in one assignment: `board = dropAndLand(…)`. That is why `board` is a
`let` here.

## Finished rows

A row with no empty square in it is finished. `isFull` asks a question of every square in a
row: the first empty one is enough to say no, and only a row that gets through the whole loop
is full. It is the same shape as `fits`, a loop that can stop at the first failure.

`clearRows` keeps the rows that are not full, with `filter` from Lists, and counts how many it
removed. The rows that are left are fewer than the board needs, so it puts that many new empty
rows on top. That is what makes everything above a cleared row move down: nothing moves at
all; there are fewer rows below it.

Points reward clearing several rows at once: 100 for one row, 300 for two, 500 for three, and
800 for four, which is called a Tetris.

- `!isFull(row)` uses `!` (not) from Decisions, so `filter` keeps the rows that are **not**
  full.
- `[...fresh, ...kept]` makes one new list from two: the `...` spreads out the items of each,
  as `[...numbers]` did in Lists, and the square brackets around them collect them, the empty
  rows first, then the kept ones.

  `cleared` of that list, so two rows score item 2, 300.
- `clearRows` gives back two answers, the new board and how many rows went, in one object, as
  `stats` did in Things with Parts (Functions that make objects).

The `mock` block (it holds setup for the tests, so the three sample rows are written once) makes

of ten, and a board of five three-square rows is one you can read in a test at a glance.

'two full rows, with a row between them' is the test most worth having. A first attempt at
`clearRows` often goes down the board removing rows one at a time, and gets confused when two
rows next to each other, or one apart, are both full. Keeping the rows that are not full, all
at once, cannot get confused that way.

## One turn of the game

The rules are all there. What is left is one more set of functions to say what happens on each
tick of the clock and each press of a key, and they put the five facts from the start of the
chapter into one object, the **game**. As with the calculator, these functions change the
object they are given rather than making a new one, because the game is the one thing that
lasts from the first piece to the last.

- `newGame(piece)` makes a game with an empty board and the first piece at the top.
- `move(game, down, across)` moves the piece if it fits there, and says whether it did.
- `fall(game, next)` is one tick of the clock: the piece moves down one row if it can. If it
  cannot, it lands, the full rows are cleared and scored, and `next` becomes the new piece at
  the top. If the new piece does not fit there, the game is over.
- `steer(game, key)` is one key press: left, right and down move the piece, and up turns it.

`fall` does not choose the next piece; whoever calls it does. On the clock, that will be a
random piece. In the tests it is whatever piece the test needs. A rule that picked its own
random piece could not be tested, because nobody could say what it should do.

import { elements, svgElements } from 'tosijs'

const { div } = elements
const { svg, rect } = svgElements

function emptyBoard(rows: 20, columns: 10) {
  const board = []
  for (let row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    const cells = []
    for (let column = 0; column < columns; column++) {
      cells.push('')
    }
    board.push(cells)
  }
  return board
}

const squareSize = 16 // pixels across each square

function colourOf(cell: '') {
  return cell == '' ? 'gainsboro' : cell
}

function square(row: 0, column: 0, colour: 'red') {
  return rect({
    x: column * squareSize,
    y: row * squareSize,
    width: squareSize,
    height: squareSize,
    fill: colour,
    stroke: 'white',
  })
}

function drawBoard(board: [['']]) {
  const drawing = svg({
    width: board[0].length * squareSize,
    height: board.length * squareSize,
  })
  for (let row = 0; row < board.length; row++) {
    for (let column = 0; column < board[row].length; column++) {
      drawing.append(square(row, column, colourOf(board[row][column])))
    }
  }
  return drawing
}

const shapes = {
  I: { colour: 'cyan', grid: ['....', 'XXXX', '....', '....'] },
  O: { colour: 'gold', grid: ['XX', 'XX'] },
  T: { colour: 'purple', grid: ['.X.', 'XXX', '...'] },
  S: { colour: 'green', grid: ['.XX', 'XX.', '...'] },
  Z: { colour: 'red', grid: ['XX.', '.XX', '...'] },
  J: { colour: 'blue', grid: ['X..', 'XXX', '...'] },
  L: { colour: 'orange', grid: ['..X', 'XXX', '...'] },
}

Type Piece {
  description: 'a shape: its colour, the size of its square grid, and its squares'
  example: { name: 'T', colour: 'purple', size: 3, cells: [{ row: 0, column: 0 }] }
}

Type Place {
  description: 'a row and a column on the board'
  example: { row: 0, column: 0 }
}

function cellsOf(grid: ['']) {
  const cells = []
  for (let row = 0; row < grid.length; row++) {
    for (let column = 0; column < grid[row].length; column++) {
      if (grid[row][column] == 'X') {
        cells.push({ row, column })
      }
    }
  }
  return cells
}

function makePiece(name: 'T') {
  const shape = shapes[name]
  return {
    name,
    colour: shape.colour,
    size: shape.grid.length,
    cells: cellsOf(shape.grid),
  }
}

function drawGame(board: [['']], piece: Piece, place: Place) {
  const drawing = drawBoard(board)
  for (const cell of piece.cells) {
    drawing.append(
      square(place.row + cell.row, place.column + cell.column, piece.colour)
    )
  }
  return drawing
}

  for (const cell of piece.cells) {
    const row = place.row + cell.row
    const column = place.column + cell.column
    if (row < 0 || row >= board.length) {
      return false // above the top, or below the floor
    }
    if (column < 0 || column >= board[0].length) {
      return false // through a wall
    }
    if (board[row][column] != '') {
      return false // the square is already filled
    }
  }
  return true
}

  const cells = []
  for (const cell of piece.cells) {
    cells.push({ row: cell.column, column: piece.size - 1 - cell.row })
  }
  return { name: piece.name, colour: piece.colour, size: piece.size, cells }
}

  const turned = rotate(piece)
  return fits(board, turned, place) ? turned : piece
}

  const landed = board.map((row) => [...row])
  for (const cell of piece.cells) {
    landed[place.row + cell.row][place.column + cell.column] = piece.colour
  }
  return landed
}

  for (const cell of row) {
    if (cell == '') {
      return false
    }
  }
  return true
}

  const kept = board.filter((row) => !isFull(row))
  const cleared = board.length - kept.length
  const fresh = emptyBoard(cleared, board[0].length)
  return { board: [...fresh, ...kept], cleared }
}

}

// New in this step:

Type Game {
  description: 'everything the game remembers'
  example: {
    board: [['']],
    piece: { name: 'T', colour: 'purple', size: 3, cells: [{ row: 0, column: 0 }] },
    place: { row: 0, column: 0 },
    score: 0,
    over: false,
  }
}

function startPlace(board: [['']], piece: Piece) {
  return { row: 0, column: Math.floor((board[0].length - piece.size) / 2) }
}

function newGame(piece: Piece) {
  const board = emptyBoard(20, 10)
  return { board, piece, place: startPlace(board, piece), score: 0, over: false }
}

function move(game: Game, down: 0, across: 0) {
  const place = { row: game.place.row + down, column: game.place.column + across }
  if (fits(game.board, game.piece, place)) {
    game.place = place
    return true
  }
  return false
}

function fall(game: Game, next: Piece) {
  if (game.over) {
    return
  }
  if (move(game, 1, 0)) {
    return // it fell one row, and that is all
  }
  const result = clearRows(land(game.board, game.piece, game.place))
  game.board = result.board
  game.score = game.score + points(result.cleared)
  game.piece = next
  game.place = startPlace(game.board, next)
  if (!fits(game.board, next, game.place)) {
    game.over = true
  }
}

function steer(game: Game, key: 'ArrowLeft') {
  if (game.over) {
    return
  }
  given key {
    'ArrowLeft' { move(game, 0, -1) }
    'ArrowRight' { move(game, 0, 1) }
    'ArrowDown' { move(game, 1, 0) }
    'ArrowUp' { game.piece = turn(game.board, game.piece, game.place) }
  }
}

- `startPlace` puts a piece in the middle of the top row. A 3-wide piece on a 10-wide board
  starts at column `Math.floor(7 / 2)`, which is 3, so it covers columns 3, 4 and 5.
  (`Math.floor` rounds down, as in Functions.)
- `move` builds the place the piece would go to, asks `fits`, and only then changes the game.
  A move that does not fit changes nothing, which is how a wall stops a piece: the test 'a wall
  stops the piece' presses left ten times, and the piece stops at column 0.
- `fall` has two `return`s near the top, each ending the turn early: a game that is over does
  nothing, and a piece that moved down has done all it needs to. Only a piece that could not
  move gets past them, to land.
- `steer` uses `given` from Decisions to choose by key. A key it does not list, such as
  `'Enter'`, matches no arm, so nothing happens.
- `Type Game` is the plan from the start of the chapter, written where TJS can check it, as
  the example on `press` was in A Calculator. The last test hands `fall` a game with no piece
  and no place, and it is refused.

The key names, `'ArrowLeft'` and the rest, are what the browser calls the arrow keys. They are
plain strings here, so the tests can press keys without a keyboard. The next step connects
them to a real one.

## The game loop

Now the game can be played. Everything new here is wiring, and each piece of it comes from
Time and Events:

- **The clock** (A clock that ticks). `setInterval` calls `onTick` every 500 milliseconds,
  twice a second, and `onTick` calls `fall` with a random next piece. `clearInterval` stops it.
- **The keys** (Keys that steer). A `keydown` listener on the whole page calls `steer` with
  `event.key`. `event.preventDefault()` stops the arrow keys doing what they normally do,
  scrolling the page (Keeping the page still), but only for the four keys the game uses, so
  every other key still works.
- **One state** (One state, two sources of change). The clock and the keys both change the same
  `game`, and after either one, `show` draws the whole game again from it, the way `drawBoard`
  was meant to be used. Neither the clock nor the keys draws anything itself.
- **Start, pause and game over** (Starting, pausing and stopping). Nothing runs until **Start**
  is pressed. Start does nothing if the game is already running, so pressing it twice cannot
  make two clocks. `stop` stops the clock and removes the key listener, and both **Pause** and
  game over use it. After game over, Start begins a new game.

  timer = null
  document.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey)
  status.message = message
}

function onTick() {
  fall(game, randomPiece())
  show()
  if (game.over) {
    stop('Game over. Press Start to play again.')
  }
}

function start() {
  if (timer != null) {
    return // already running
  }
  if (game.over) {
    game = newGame(randomPiece())
    show()
  }
  status.message = 'Left and right move, up turns, down drops faster.'
  timer = setInterval(onTick, 500)
  document.addEventListener('keydown', onKey)
}

function pause() {
  if (timer != null) {
    stop('Paused. Press Start to carry on.')
  }
}

preview.append(
  div('Score: ', strong(status.score), '. ', status.message),
  div(button({ onClick: start }, 'Start'), ' ', button({ onClick: pause }, 'Pause')),
  screen
)

test 'a random piece is one of the seven' {
  for (let tries = 0; tries < 20; tries++) {
    const piece = randomPiece()
    expect(Object.keys(shapes)).toContain(piece.name)
    expect(piece.cells.length).toBe(4)
  }
}

test 'the rules still hold' {
  const game = newGame(makePiece('I'))
  for (let column = 0; column < 6; column++) {
    game.board[19][column] = 'blue'
  }
  steer(game, 'ArrowRight')
  steer(game, 'ArrowRight')
  steer(game, 'ArrowRight')
  for (let tick = 0; tick < 19; tick++) {
    fall(game, makePiece('O'))
  }
  expect(game.score).toBe(100)
  expect(game.piece.name).toBe('O')
  expect(game.over).toBe(false)
}
```

Press **Start**, then use the arrow keys. Each piece falls, lands and is replaced; fill a row
and watch it go, and the score go up.

- `randomPiece` picks one of the seven names at random, the way `rollDie` rolled a die in
  Functions, and makes that piece. It is the only part of the game that is not the same every
  time, and it lives out here with the wiring, not in the rules.
- `status` is a tosijs model, as in Responding to the Reader, holding what the line above the
  board says: the score and a message. Changing `status.score` or `status.message` changes the
  page by itself.
- The board is not a model. `show` draws a new picture of the whole game and puts it in
  `screen` with `replaceChildren`, which empties an element and puts the new contents in, in one
  step. Drawing all 200 squares again on every tick and every key press sounds like a lot of
  work, but it is far less than a computer can do in the blink of an eye, and it means the
  picture can never disagree with the game.
- `let game`, `let timer` and `screen` are outside every function, so the clock, the keys and
  the buttons all find the same ones. `game` is a `let` because Start replaces it with a new
  game after game over.
- `timer` is `null` whenever the game is not running, which is how `start` and `pause` know
  whether it is: `stop` puts it back to `null` every time.

Every function in this step is a few lines, and none of them contains a rule of the game. The
test 'the rules still hold' plays the first piece of a game to the end with no clock and no
keys, so if the game ever misbehaves, start by asking whether the rules or the wiring are to
blame: a test can answer the first question in a moment.

Two things to know while you play. While the game runs, the arrow keys belong to it, all over
the page, even in the code editor; press **Pause** before you change the code. And if you change
the example while a game is running, the old game's clock and keys carry on, as the countdown's
timer did in Things That Take Time. Pause first, or reload the page.

## Try it

Work at the last example, the whole game. For each change, write the rule as a function with a
test first, as in A Calculator, then wire it in.

- **Hard drop.** Make the space bar drop the piece straight to the bottom. `event.key` is `' '`
  (a space) for the space bar. Bring `lowest` back from Landing a piece, add a `' '` arm to
  `steer` that moves the piece to `lowest(…)`, and add `' '` to `gameKeys`. Test that after a
  hard drop on an empty board, an O is at row 18.
- **Ghost piece.** Many versions show where the piece would land, as a pale outline at the
  bottom. In `drawGame`, before drawing the piece, draw its squares again at
  `lowest(board, piece, place)`, in `'silver'`.
- **Show the next piece.** Give the game a sixth fact, `next`, a piece. `fall` takes its new
  piece from `game.next` and puts the piece it is given into `game.next` instead. Draw the next
  piece beside the board on a little board of its own, as the seven pieces were drawn in A piece
  as data. Remember to add `next` to `Type Game` and to `newGame`.
- **Levels.** Count the rows cleared (another fact, `lines`), and every ten lines make the clock
  faster: 500 milliseconds at first, 450 after ten lines, and so on. Write
  `delay(lines: 0)` and test it first. A running interval cannot change its speed, so when the
  level changes, `clearInterval` the old timer and start a new one.
- **High score.** Keep the best score so far in `status`, beside the score, and update it at
  game over. It should survive Start, which makes a new game; why does it, when the score does
  not?
- **Turning the other way.** Make `z` turn the piece anticlockwise. Three quarter turns
  clockwise are one quarter turn the other way, so you need no new rule for squares: only a new
  arm in `steer`. Then test that `z` followed by up leaves a piece as it was.
- **A gentler wall.** When a turn does not fit, real Tetris tries the turned piece one column
  to the left, then one to the right, before refusing. Add that to `turn`, and change the test
  'a turn that does not fit is refused' to say what should happen now.
- **Recursion.** `lowest` is a loop. Write it again the way [Recursion](/recursion/) would: if
  the piece does not fit one row down, the lowest place is where it is; otherwise it is the
  lowest place from one row down. Do the tests from Landing a piece still pass?

# The Universal Endpoint

Most backends grow one route per operation: a URL, a request schema, a handler, a deploy.
This chapter builds the other kind, a single endpoint that accepts the client's *logic* as
data and runs it under limits the server sets. The handler is about thirty lines of TJS.

The client's logic is written in **AJS**, a sandboxed subset of JavaScript that compiles to
a JSON syntax tree (an AST) and runs on a metered virtual machine, `AgentVM`. Three words
come up throughout:

- **Fuel** is a run's work budget. Every step the VM takes costs some, and the run ends
  when it is gone.
- An **atom** is an operation an agent can call, such as `storeGet`, `httpFetch` or
  `llmPredict`. Atoms are AJS's built-in functions.
- A **capability** is an implementation the host hands in for the atoms that need one:
  a `store` for `storeGet`, a `fetch` for `httpFetch`, an `llm` for `llmPredict`. The VM
  has no IO of its own; what it can touch is exactly what the host passes in.

The agent source travels as a string inside this TJS file because, on a real server, it
arrives as a string in a request body. The [AJS book](/ajs/) covers the language itself.

The demo runs four requests. Three of them each show one property of the VM, and the
fourth shows where that property stops.

```tjs:inline
/#
## One endpoint that runs the client's logic

`post` is a complete request handler. The request carries AJS source, its
arguments and a fuel budget. The handler checks the caller's token,
transpiles the source to an AST, and runs it on `AgentVM` with a bounded
budget and only the capabilities this caller is allowed. Whatever the agent
does, `post` returns a value.

This page imports the full `tjs-lang` package because it transpiles in the
page. A production server would take an AST and use `tjs-lang/vm-ast`, which
has no parser in it (see "Making it real" below).
#/

import { AgentVM, transpile } from 'tjs-lang'

// One VM serves every request. It holds no per-request state.
const vm = new AgentVM()

// Per-caller data. A Map, not a plain object: a caller-supplied token such as
// 'constructor' must not find an inherited property and pass as valid.
const tenants = new Map([
  ['token_alice', new Map([['greeting', 'hello from alice']])],
  ['token_bob', new Map([['greeting', 'hello from bob']])],
])

// The store capability for one caller. The `storeGet` and `storeSet` atoms
// call its async `get(key)` and `set(key, value)`, so those are the names a
// store must have. It can reach only that caller's map.
function storeFor(token: '') {
  const data = tenants.get(token)
  if (!data) return undefined
  return {
    get: async (key) => data.get(key),
    set: async (key, value) => { data.set(key, value) },
  }
}

// The colon values are TJS examples, not defaults: `fuel: 1000` says
// `req.body.fuel` must be an integer. A request of the wrong shape gets a
// TJS type error (a MonadicError value) back and never reaches the VM.
async function post(req: {
  body: { agent: '', args: {}, fuel: 1000 },
  headers: { authorization: '' },
}) {
  // 1. Authorize first, before doing any work whose cost the caller controls.
  const store = storeFor(req.headers.authorization)
  if (!store) return { status: 'error', error: 'Unauthorized', fuelUsed: 0 }

  // 2. Parse. This runs before any fuel is charged, so untrusted source gets
  //    a size cap. `transpile` is ordinary host code and THROWS on bad source,
  //    so it needs a try/catch.
  let ast
  try {
    ast = transpile(req.body.agent, { maxSourceBytes: 16_000 }).ast
  } catch (e) {
    return { status: 'error', error: `Parse error: ${e.message}`, fuelUsed: 0 }
  }

  // 3. Run. The client asks for a budget; the server clamps it. `vm.run`
  //    never throws: a failed run comes back as `{ error }`, so no try/catch.
  const run = await vm.run(ast, req.body.args, {
    fuel: Math.min(req.body.fuel, 10_000),
    timeoutMs: 5000,
    capabilities: { store },
  })

  // Fuel is fractional (an expression node costs 0.01), so round for display.
  const fuelUsed = Math.round(run.fuelUsed * 100) / 100
  if (run.error) {
    return { status: 'error', error: run.error.message, fuelUsed }
  }
  return { status: 'ok', result: run.result, fuelUsed }
}

// An agent is a function taking one object of named arguments, and it
// returns an object. `{ }` means it takes no arguments.

// --- 1. A small computation ---
const sum = await post({
  body: {
    agent: `
      function compute({ x, y }) {
        return { sum: x + y, product: x * y }
      }`,
    args: { x: 7, y: 6 },
    fuel: 100,
  },
  headers: { authorization: 'token_alice' },
})
console.log('1. compute:', sum)

// --- 2. A loop that never ends ---
const loop = await post({
  body: {
    agent: `
      function spin({ }) {
        let i = 0
        while (true) {
          i = i + 1
        }
        return { i }
      }`,
    args: {},
    fuel: 50,
  },
  headers: { authorization: 'token_alice' },
})
console.log('2. while (true):', loop)

// --- 3. The same agent, three callers ---
const readGreeting = `
  function read({ }) {
    let greeting = storeGet({ key: 'greeting' })
    return { greeting }
  }`
for (const token of ['token_alice', 'token_bob', 'token_mallory']) {
  const reply = await post({
    body: { agent: readGreeting, args: {}, fuel: 100 },
    headers: { authorization: token },
  })
  console.log(`3. ${token}:`, reply)
}

// --- 4. Source that is not AJS ---
const bad = await post({
  body: { agent: 'function broken({ }) { return {', args: {}, fuel: 100 },
  headers: { authorization: 'token_alice' },
})
console.log('4. broken source:', bad)
```

The `/# … #/` block at the top of the example is a TJS doc comment: its markdown renders as
prose above the code.

## What the output shows

**1. A small computation** returns `{ status: 'ok', result: { sum: 13, product: 42 } }` and
reports about 0.5 fuel used, out of the 100 it asked for. Every operation the VM performs
costs fuel (an expression node costs 0.01, an atom call such as `storeGet` costs 5), so the
server knows what each request cost to run. The client chooses a budget, and `post` clamps
it to at most 10,000, so a client cannot buy unlimited work by asking for it.

**2. `while (true)`** is not detected as an infinite loop; it runs until its budget is
spent. The VM stops it at the first step that takes it past 50 fuel (that is why it reports
about 50.06) and `vm.run` returns `{ error }` with the message `Out of Fuel`. The endpoint
answers, and the next request is served as usual.

Fuel bounds computation. Waiting on a capability, such as a slow fetch, costs no fuel, so a
run also has a wall-clock limit. `post` sets it with `timeoutMs: 5000`. Without `timeoutMs`,
a run gets a default limit of at least 60 seconds, derived from the slowest registered atom.

**3. The same agent, sent by different callers,** reads different greetings. The agent
calls `storeGet({ key: 'greeting' })` with no `await`: atom calls are awaited implicitly.
The VM implements `storeGet` by calling `get(key)` on whatever `store` the host passed in
`capabilities`. `post` builds that store from the caller's token, so Alice's run can reach
Alice's data and nothing else. Mallory has no valid token and is turned away before the
source is even parsed, with zero fuel used. This is where authorization lives in this
design: not in the agent, and not in a check per route, but in which capabilities a run is
given.

**4. Source that does not parse** comes back as `Parse error: Unexpected token at
<source>:1:32`, with zero fuel used. This is the contrast case. `transpile` throws, like
any ordinary function, which is why `post` wraps it in `try`/`catch`. `vm.run` does not
throw, which is why the run in step 3 needs no `try` at all.

Three properties of the VM make this safe:

- **Fuel.** Work is metered, and the run ends when the budget is gone (test 2).
- **No ambient authority.** The VM has no IO of its own. It cannot read files, open sockets
  or make network requests unless the host grants it. Here the only capability is a
  per-caller store, so the agents can compute and read their own data, and nothing more
  (test 3).
- **Errors are values.** A failed run returns `{ error }` rather than throwing, so guest
  code never raises an exception in the endpoint's own control flow. That is why `post`
  reports "Out of Fuel" in the same shape as a success (test 2). The transpiler, which is
  host code, is not part of this promise (test 4).

Notice what the endpoint does *not* contain: no route per operation, no request schema per
operation, no deployment when the client wants a new query. The client's logic travels to
the data; the server decides what that logic may touch and how much it may spend.

## What you give up

The work does not disappear; it moves.

- **Discoverability.** Clients can only call atoms the VM has and read keys the store holds.
  You document that surface (the atoms you register, the capabilities you grant, the shape
  of the data) instead of documenting routes.
- **Cost inside the rules.** A tenant can do expensive but legal things to its own data.
  Fuel caps computation and quotas cap expensive atoms (below), but you choose the numbers.
- **Observability.** There is no route name to log. Log the agent (or a hash of its AST)
  and the run's `fuelUsed` and error, and use `vm.run(ast, args, { trace: true })` when you
  need to see what a run did step by step.

## Making it real

A production endpoint needs three more decisions. A sketch (host-side JavaScript, not
runnable on this page):

```javascript
// Client side: transpile before sending, and send the token.
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
const { ast } = transpile(agentSource)
await fetch('/agent', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { authorization: token, 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ ast, args }),
})

// Server side: the VM with no parser in it.
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

const vm = new AgentVM()

export async function post(req) {
  // storeFor as defined in the demo above. An absent `store` capability is
  // NOT refused: the VM falls back to a scratch in-memory store, and the
  // agent runs anyway. So check, and turn the caller away.
  const store = storeFor(req.headers.authorization)
  if (!store) return { status: 401, error: 'Unauthorized' }

  const { ast, args } = req.body
  const run = await vm.run(ast, args, {
    fuel: 1000,
    timeoutMs: 5000,
    maxHeapBytes: 16 * 1024 * 1024,
    // Only what this caller is entitled to. If you also grant `fetch` and
    // `llm` capabilities, the httpFetch and llmPredict atoms can use them.
    capabilities: { store },
    // Fuel is VM work; it cannot say "at most 3 model calls". Quotas can.
    quotas: { llmPredict: 3, httpFetch: 10 },
  })

  // Return a shaped reply, as the demo does, rather than the raw run object.
  if (run.error) return { status: 422, error: run.error.message }
  return { status: 200, result: run.result, fuelUsed: run.fuelUsed }
}
```

1. **Where parsing happens.** Parsing is the one step whose cost the *sender* controls and
   which runs before any fuel is charged. The live example authorizes first and then caps
   it with `transpile(source, { maxSourceBytes })`. Better: transpile on the client (or in
   a separate worker) and accept only an AST, served by `tjs-lang/vm-ast`, a VM bundle that
   contains no parser and so has no parser defect to reach. The demo above uses the full
   `tjs-lang` package only because it has to transpile in the page.
2. **Capabilities per caller.** Build them from the request's credentials, as `storeFor`
   does: a store scoped to the caller, a fetch limited to the hosts they may reach. Refuse
   the request when there are no credentials; do not run it without capabilities, because
   a missing store becomes a scratch store rather than an error.
3. **Quotas and space.** Fuel bounds work; `quotas` bounds how often an expensive atom may
   run; `maxHeapBytes` (default 64MB) bounds how much memory a run may hold at once.

## Limits

- **AJS is not all of JavaScript.** It is a subset with typed signatures: no classes, no
  `new`, no `this`, no prototype access, and a fixed table of callable methods. An agent
  that needs more asks the host to register an atom rather than reaching for the language.
- **Fuel is not money.** A fuel unit measures VM work. If an atom calls a paid API, cap it
  with a quota; do not try to price it in fuel.
- **A quota is per run.** It counts calls within one run. If a capability starts another
  `vm.run`, pass the same `quotaUsed` object (start it as `{}`) in the run options of both
  runs, or the nested run starts with a fresh allowance.

The [AJS book](/ajs/) covers the language, the atoms and the security model in full.

# Fuel Limits

This is the reason AJS exists. You can run an agent (an AJS program) you did not write, from a
user or a model, knowing it will stop.

**Fuel** is a work budget. The host, meaning your code that runs the agent, gives each run an
amount of fuel; every step the agent takes spends some, and when it reaches zero the run
stops. This page runs each example with 10,000 units. The VM's own default, if the host passes
none, is 1,000; the page gives more so the examples that should finish have room to.

The agent below counts to a million, far more work than 10,000 units pay for. The fuel runs
out first, and the run ends with an error value instead of hanging the page (or your server):

```ajs:inline
function countTo({ limit = 1000000 }) {
  let counter = 0
  let i = 0
  while (i < limit) {
    counter = counter + 1
    i = i + 1
  }
  return { counter }
}
```

## What to notice

- **The error is `Out of Fuel`, and it is a result, not a crash.** Nothing is thrown. The run
  hands the host its `error` and `fuelUsed`, and the host decides what to do.
- **The agent cannot catch it.** Running out of fuel ends the run whatever `try` blocks the
  agent has: wrap the loop in `try { … } catch (e) { return … }` and the `catch` branch never
  runs. An agent cannot swallow its budget and keep going.
- **The budget is the host's, not the program's.** A program cannot read or raise its own
  budget.
- **Fuel measures work.** Every expression, assignment and loop test costs a little. An
  **atom** (a built-in operation, such as an HTTP fetch or a model call) costs more:
  `httpFetch` costs 5 units, `llmPredict` 100. One trip round this loop costs about half a
  unit, so 10,000 units buy roughly 20,000 iterations.
- **`fuelUsed` can end a hair over the budget**, because the step that runs out is charged
  before it is refused. Read it as "the budget was spent", not as an exact count.

## Try different amounts

The same agent, unchanged, run with the argument `limit: 1000` (in your own host,
`vm.run(ast, { limit: 1000 })`; see below). A thousand iterations fit in the budget, so it
returns `{ counter: 1000 }`, and the page shows it used about 490 units:

```ajs:inline {"args": {"limit": 1000}}
function countTo({ limit = 1000000 }) {
  let counter = 0
  let i = 0
  while (i < limit) {
    counter = counter + 1
    i = i + 1
  }
  return { counter }
}
```

The same agent again, unchanged, with the same `limit: 1000` but a budget of 100 units. The
thousand iterations no longer fit: at about half a unit each, 100 units pay for about 200 of
them, and then the run ends with `Out of Fuel` and `fuelUsed` of about 100:

```ajs:inline {"fuel": 100, "args": {"limit": 1000}}
function countTo({ limit = 1000000 }) {
  let counter = 0
  let i = 0
  while (i < limit) {
    counter = counter + 1
    i = i + 1
  }
  return { counter }
}
```

## In your own host

The budget is an option on the run. Transpile the source in one step, run the AST in another.
The VM in `tjs-lang/vm-ast` contains no parser: it only ever sees an AST, so parsing source
you did not write happens outside the sandbox (or behind its own size cap, `transpile(source,
{ maxSourceBytes })`), and a parser bug cannot be reached from inside a run.

```javascript
import { transpile } from 'tjs-lang/lang'
import { AgentVM } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'

// the agent's source text, as a string
const source = `function countTo({ limit = 1000000 }) {
  let counter = 0
  let i = 0
  while (i < limit) {
    counter = counter + 1
    i = i + 1
  }
  return { counter }
}`

const vm = new AgentVM()
const { ast } = transpile(source)

// Enough fuel: the run succeeds
const ok = await vm.run(ast, { limit: 1000 }, { fuel: 1000 })
console.log(ok.result) // → { counter: 1000 }, the agent's return value
console.log(ok.error) // → undefined
console.log(ok.fuelUsed) // → about 493

// Too little fuel: the run fails
const run = await vm.run(ast, { limit: 1000 }, { fuel: 100 })
if (run.error) {
  console.log(run.error.message) // → Out of Fuel
  // the AST operation that was running when fuel ran out: here `varAssign`,
  // an assignment such as `counter = counter + 1`
  console.log(run.error.op)
  console.log(run.fuelUsed) // → about 100
}
```

A run returns `{ result, error, fuelUsed }`. On success `result` is the agent's return value
and `error` is undefined. On failure `error` is set, and `result` holds the same error value
rather than a partial result: whatever the agent had computed before it ran out is gone.

If you pass no `fuel`, a run gets 1,000 units. Pick the budget for the work you expect: enough
for a well-behaved agent to finish, small enough that a runaway one is cheap.

## The other limits

Fuel bounds **work**, so it is the time budget for computation. Three other limits cover what
it cannot:

- **`timeoutMs`**, wall-clock time. It is the backstop for waiting, not computing: an agent
  waiting on a slow fetch or model call spends time but no fuel, and the timeout ends that
  wait. Set `fuel` to bound a loop. Default: 240 seconds with the standard atoms (twice the
  longest atom timeout, a model call's 120 seconds, and never less than 60).
- **`maxHeapBytes`**, how much the program holds in memory at once (64 MB by default). Fuel
  bounds how much it allocates over the whole run, not how much it keeps.
- **`quotas`**, how many times an atom may be called, such as `{ llmPredict: 3 }`. A model
  call costs 100 units of fuel whatever it costs you in money, so only a quota can say "three
  calls, no more".

The VM has no network access of its own. The agent's `httpFetch` calls whatever `fetch`
function the host passes in `capabilities` (the IO the host grants the run), with the same
arguments as the standard `fetch(url, init)`, and that function's return value becomes the
agent's value: below, `a` is `{ ok: true }`. Return plain JSON data. `httpFetch` is a built-in
atom, so `new AgentVM()` needs nothing registered.

Here are `timeoutMs` and `quotas`, with a stand-in `fetch` (`maxHeapBytes` is not shown). This
continues from the snippet above, with the same `vm` and imports:

```javascript
const poller = transpile(`function poll({ url }) {
  let a = httpFetch({ url })
  let b = httpFetch({ url })
  let c = httpFetch({ url })
  return { a, b, c }
}`).ast
const args = { url: 'https://example.com' }

// A fetch that takes half a second, against a 50 ms deadline
const slowFetch = (url, init) =>
  new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(() => resolve({ ok: true }), 500))
const slow = await vm.run(poller, args, {
  timeoutMs: 50,
  capabilities: { fetch: slowFetch },
})
console.log(slow.error.message) // → Execution timeout after 50ms. …

// Three fetches against a quota of two
const capped = await vm.run(poller, args, {
  quotas: { httpFetch: 2 },
  capabilities: { fetch: async (url, init) => ({ ok: true }) },
})
console.log(capped.error.message) // → Quota exceeded for 'httpFetch': 2 calls allowed
```

The two failures behave differently, and the difference matters when the agent is untrusted:

- **A timeout ends the run**, like running out of fuel. No `try` in the agent can catch it,
  and nothing is returned: the fetches that finished before it are lost with the rest of the
  result.
- **A quota refusal is an ordinary error inside the agent.** The refused call does not
  happen. Here no `try` surrounds the third call, so the run ends with that error and `a` and
  `b` are not returned. Wrap the call in `try { … } catch (e) { … }` and the agent catches it
  and carries on, so it can fall back when its allowance is spent; it still cannot make the
  call.

See the [AJS guide](/DOCS-AJS/) for every run option.
title: Fuel Limits
description: This is the reason AJS exists. You can run an agent (an AJS program) you did not write, from a user or a model, knowing it will stop. **Fuel** is a work budget. The host, meaning your code that runs the agent, gives each run an amount of fuel; every step the agent takes spends some, and when it reaches zero the run stops. This page runs each example with 10,000 units. The VM's own default, if the host passes none, is 1,000; the page gives more so the examples that should finish have room to.
