# Built-in Types and Dates

The `tjs-lang` package ships ready-made types for values that come up in almost every
program: email addresses, URLs, UUIDs, positive integers, non-empty strings, and dates. It
also ships two modules of functions for working with dates without a `Date` object. This
chapter covers all of them, and ends with a small date pipeline you can copy.

None of them is part of the language. A `.tjs` file sees them only after it imports them,
and they all come from the package `'tjs-lang'`:

| Import                                                    | What it is                                                                 |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `TEmail`, `TUrl`, `TUuid`, `TNonEmptyString`              | types for strings                                                          |
| `TInteger`, `TPositiveInt`                                | types for numbers                                                          |
| `TimestampType`, `TimestampISO`, `LegalDateType`          | types for dates and times                                                  |
| `Nullable`, `Optional`, `TPair`, `TRecord`, `TArray`, `Union` | functions that build a new type from other types (`Union` is also a declaration form; see below) |
| `Timestamp`, `LegalDate`                                  | modules of date functions (`Timestamp.now()`, `LegalDate.addMonths(…)`, …) |

### Reading the examples

Three things hold for every example on this page.

- **A bad argument is answered, not thrown.** When an argument fails its parameter type,
  the function does not run; it returns an error value, a `MonadicError`, whose `.message`
  says what was expected. [Error Handling](/error-handling/) covers these values.
  `isMonadicError(x)` tells you whether `x` is one. It, `test` and `expect` are available
  in every `.tjs` file without an import.
- **The printed messages leave out the location.** A real message also names the file and
  line (`'invite.tjs:3:invite.email'`); the output shown here keeps only the function and
  parameter, because the location differs between this page and your machine.
- **The checks are in `test` blocks, not signature examples.** When TJS transpiles a file,
  it calls each function with the example values in its signature and compares the result
  with the return example. It does this before the file's imports are loaded, so it cannot
  run a function that uses an imported type or module; such a check is reported as
  _inconclusive_ (the [Date Formatting](/date-formatting-with-import/) chapter explains
  this). On this page the `test` blocks run with the imports loaded. From the command line,
  `tjs check` and `tjs test` cannot load them either: most of these tests come out
  inconclusive, and a test of a `Type` built from imported types can pass without checking
  anything, because the unloaded types accept every value.

## A built-in type as a parameter type

Import a type and write its name after the colon, where you would otherwise write an
example value:

```tjs:inline
import { TEmail, TPositiveInt } from 'tjs-lang'

function invite(email: TEmail, seats: TPositiveInt) {
  return `${seats} seat(s) for ${email}`
}

console.log(invite('ada@example.com', 3))
console.log(invite('ada.example.com', 3).message)
console.log(invite('ada@example.com', 0).message)

// A type is also a function you can call yourself
console.log(TEmail('ada@example.com'))
console.log(TPositiveInt(0))

test 'the parameter types are checked on every call' {
  expect(invite('ada@example.com', 3)).toBe('3 seat(s) for ada@example.com')
  expect(isMonadicError(invite('ada.example.com', 3))).toBe(true)
  expect(isMonadicError(invite('ada@example.com', 0))).toBe(true)
  expect(isMonadicError(invite('ada@example.com', 1.5))).toBe(true)
}

test 'a built-in type answers true, or the reason it failed' {
  expect(TEmail('ada@example.com')).toBe(true)
  expect(TPositiveInt(0)).toBe('0 is not positive')
}
```

It prints:

```text
3 seat(s) for ada@example.com
Expected TEmail for 'invite.email', got string
Expected TPositiveInt for 'invite.seats', got number
true
0 is not positive
```

### What to notice

- **The check happens at the call**, as for any TJS parameter. A bad argument does not
  reach the body: `invite` returns a `MonadicError` naming the parameter instead.
- **The error says what was expected, not why it failed.** `got string` names the kind of
  JavaScript value that arrived: `'ada.example.com'` is a string, just not an email. To
  find out why a value fails, call the type yourself, as the last two lines do.
- **There is no example value.** `email: TEmail` names a type, so TJS has nothing to call
  `invite` with when it transpiles the file. The `test` blocks do that job instead.
- **The string and number types answer `true` or a reason string**, never `false`.
  `TPositiveInt(0)` is `'0 is not positive'`. A non-empty string is truthy, so
  `if (TPositiveInt(n))` accepts everything; compare the result with `=== true`. (The date
  types, and every type the combinators below build, answer `true` or `false`. `=== true`
  is right for all of them.)

## The string and number types

Each of these is a function from a value to `true` or a reason string:

```tjs:inline
import { TEmail, TUrl, TUuid, TNonEmptyString, TInteger, TPositiveInt } from 'tjs-lang'

function subscribe(email: TEmail) { return `subscribed ${email}` }
function fetchFeed(url: TUrl) { return `fetching ${url}` }
function findOrder(id: TUuid) { return `order ${id}` }
function rename(title: TNonEmptyString) { return `renamed to ${title}` }
function moveBy(steps: TInteger) { return `moved ${steps}` }
function reserve(seats: TPositiveInt) { return `reserved ${seats}` }

console.log(subscribe('ada@example.com'))
console.log(fetchFeed('https://example.com/feed.xml'))
console.log(findOrder('123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000'))
console.log(rename('Q3 report'))
console.log(moveBy(-2))
console.log(reserve(4))

// Why a value fails: call the type directly
console.log(TEmail('ada@example'))
console.log(TUrl('example.com/feed.xml'))
console.log(TUuid('123e4567e89b12d3a456426614174000'))
console.log(TNonEmptyString(''))
console.log(TInteger(2.5))
console.log(TPositiveInt(0))

test 'each type accepts its values and refuses others' {
  expect(isMonadicError(subscribe('ada lovelace@example.com'))).toBe(true)
  expect(isMonadicError(fetchFeed('not a url'))).toBe(true)
  expect(isMonadicError(findOrder('order-17'))).toBe(true)
  expect(isMonadicError(rename(''))).toBe(true)
  expect(isMonadicError(moveBy(0.5))).toBe(true)
  expect(isMonadicError(reserve(-1))).toBe(true)
}

test 'the edges, as they really are' {
  expect(TUrl('mailto:ada@example.com')).toBe(true)
  expect(TUuid('123E4567-E89B-12D3-A456-426614174000')).toBe(true)
  expect(TNonEmptyString('   ')).toBe(true)
  expect(TInteger(0)).toBe(true)
  expect(TPositiveInt(0)).toBe('0 is not positive')
}
```

It prints:

```text
subscribed ada@example.com
fetching https://example.com/feed.xml
order 123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000
renamed to Q3 report
moved -2
reserved 4
"ada@example" is not a valid email
"example.com/feed.xml" is not a valid URL
"123e4567e89b12d3a456426614174000" is not a valid UUID
string is empty
2.5 is not an integer
0 is not positive
```

What each one accepts:

| Type              | Accepts                                                                                                   |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `TEmail`          | a string of the form `something@something.something` with no spaces. It checks the shape, not that the address exists. |
| `TUrl`            | any string the platform's `URL` parser accepts. That needs a scheme (`https:`, `mailto:`, …), so `example.com` fails. |
| `TUuid`           | 8-4-4-4-12 hexadecimal digits with hyphens, in either case and of any version                            |
| `TNonEmptyString` | any string with at least one character. `'   '` passes; trim first if blanks should not.                 |
| `TInteger`        | a number with no fractional part, negative and zero included                                             |
| `TPositiveInt`    | an integer greater than zero. `0` fails.                                                                  |

`TString`, `TNumber` and `TBoolean` are exported too, but in a `.tjs` signature an example
says the same thing more briefly: `name: ''`, `price: 0.0`, `active: false`. Likewise
`count: 0` is an integer and `count: +0` a non-negative integer (see
[the syntax reference](/TJS-SYNTAX/)). No example value means "greater than zero", though:
`+0` allows `0`, and `TPositiveInt` refuses it. Reach for `TPositiveInt` when zero is not
allowed, and for `TInteger` when you want the type to have a name or are checking a value
outside a signature.

## Building types from other types

`Nullable`, `Optional`, `TPair` and `TRecord` take types and return a new type. To use the
result as a parameter type, give it a name with a `Type` declaration (introduced in
[Declarations](/declarations/)), whose `example` can be the call. The declaration is not
optional: the compiler resolves a parameter type only when it is imported or declared with
`Type`, `Generic`, `Union` or `Enum` in the file, so `const MaybeEmail = Nullable(TEmail)`
makes a working type, but `p: MaybeEmail` is not checked. The compiler warns that the
annotation "could not be resolved to a runtime type".

```tjs:inline
import { TEmail, TString, TNumber, TInteger, TPair, TRecord, Nullable, Optional } from 'tjs-lang'

Type ManagerEmail { example: Nullable(TEmail) }     // an email, or null
Type ReplyTo { example: Optional(TEmail) }          // an email, null, or undefined
Type Entry { example: TPair(TString, TNumber) }     // ['apples', 3]
Type Scores { example: TRecord(TInteger) }          // { ada: 3, alan: 5 }

function assign(manager: ManagerEmail) {
  return manager == null ? 'unassigned' : `managed by ${manager}`
}
function reply(to: ReplyTo) {
  return to == null ? 'no reply address' : `reply to ${to}`
}
function addLine(entry: Entry) {
  return `${entry[1]} x ${entry[0]}`
}
function best(scores: Scores) {
  return Object.keys(scores).reduce((a, b) => (scores[a] >= scores[b] ? a : b))
}

console.log(assign(null), '|', assign('grace@example.com'))
console.log(reply(undefined), '|', reply('alan@example.com'))
console.log(addLine(['apples', 3]))
console.log(best({ ada: 3, alan: 5, grace: 4 }))

test 'Nullable allows null; Optional also allows undefined' {
  expect(assign(null)).toBe('unassigned')
  expect(isMonadicError(assign(undefined))).toBe(true)
  expect(reply(undefined)).toBe('no reply address')
  expect(isMonadicError(assign('grace'))).toBe(true)
}

test 'TPair checks both slots; TRecord checks every value' {
  expect(isMonadicError(addLine([3, 'apples']))).toBe(true)
  expect(isMonadicError(addLine(['apples', 3, 'extra']))).toBe(true)
  expect(isMonadicError(best({ ada: 3, alan: 'five' }))).toBe(true)
  expect(isMonadicError(best([3, 5]))).toBe(true)
}
```

It prints:

```text
unassigned | managed by grace@example.com
no reply address | reply to alan@example.com
3 x apples
alan
```

`Nullable` allows `null` and refuses `undefined`. The type check tells the two apart even
though TJS's `==` treats them as equal, which is why `assign` can still test
`manager == null`. `TRecord` checks every value of a plain object, and refuses an array.

`TArray(T)` (an array whose every item is a `T`) and `Union(A, B, …)` (any one of several
types) work the same way. (`Union` is also a declaration form,
`Union Direction 'a direction' 'north' | 'south'`, for a named set of values; see
[Declarations](/declarations/). The imported function combines types; the declaration lists
values.) The arguments may be built-in types, types you declared, or example values, and an
example value means what it always means: `TPair('', 0.0)` is the same type as
`TPair(TString, TNumber)`, while `TPair('', 0)` accepts only an integer in its second slot.

Built-in types also work inside a `Type` example's object. That is how you describe data
that arrives from outside your program, as JSON from an API or a file, before any of your
code touches it (the pipeline at the end of this page does this):

```tjs:inline
import { TEmail, TUrl } from 'tjs-lang'

Type Profile {
  example: {
    name: 'Ada',
    email: TEmail,
    homepage: TUrl | undefined,   // may be left out
  }
}

console.log(Profile({ name: 'Ada', email: 'ada@example.com' }))
console.log(Profile({ name: 'Ada', email: 'ada' }))
console.log(Profile({ name: 'Ada', email: 'ada@example.com', homepage: 'ada.dev' }))
```

It prints:

```text
true
false
false
```

The second has no valid email, the third no valid URL. A type you declare answers `true` or
`false`, never a reason string. (This example has no `test` block on purpose: from the
command line, a test of `Profile` would run before `TEmail` and `TUrl` are loaded, and pass
or fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the data.)

## Dates: two values and three types

A `.tjs` file refuses `new Date(…)`. A `Date` is a mutable object (`d.setMonth(…)` changes
it for everyone holding it), and it mixes a moment with a calendar date and the zone of
whatever machine runs the code; [What `.tjs` Refuses](/safer-code/) has the details.
`Date.now()` is allowed, because it returns a plain number. In place of the object are two
plain values:

- A **Timestamp** is a moment: a number of milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC, the number
  `Date.now()` returns. Use it for "when did this happen".
- A **LegalDate** is a calendar date with no time and no zone: a `'YYYY-MM-DD'` string. Use
  it for birthdays, due dates and contract dates.

Each has a module of functions to work with it (`Timestamp`, `LegalDate`), and there are
three types to check a parameter with:

| Type            | Accepts                                                               | Example value                |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `TimestampType` | a finite number (milliseconds since 1970 UTC)                         | `1705311000000`              |
| `TimestampISO`  | an ISO 8601 date-and-time string, the readable form of a Timestamp    | `'2024-01-15T09:30:00.000Z'` |
| `LegalDateType` | a `'YYYY-MM-DD'` string                                               | `'2024-01-15'`               |

Note the names. `Timestamp` and `LegalDate` are the modules; the types are `TimestampType`
and `LegalDateType`. Mixing them up fails silently: `t: Timestamp` compiles with no warning
and accepts any value, because the module is not a type and has nothing to check with.
Write `t: TimestampType` and `d: LegalDateType`.

```tjs:inline
import { Timestamp, LegalDate, TimestampType, TimestampISO, LegalDateType } from 'tjs-lang'

function hoursBetween(start: TimestampType, end: TimestampType) {
  return Timestamp.diffHours(end, start)
}
function received(at: TimestampISO) {
  return Timestamp.parse(at)
}
function dueAfter(issued: LegalDateType, days: 30) {
  return LegalDate.addDays(issued, days)
}

const start = Timestamp.from(2024, 3, 10, 14, 0) // months count from 1: 3 is March
const end = Timestamp.addHours(start, 36)

console.log(start, Timestamp.iso(start))
console.log(hoursBetween(start, end))
console.log(received('2024-01-15T09:30:00Z'))
console.log(dueAfter('2024-01-15', 30))

console.log(hoursBetween('2024-03-10', end).message)
console.log(received('2024-01-15').message)
console.log(dueAfter('15/01/2024', 30).message)

test 'the date types' {
  expect(TimestampType(Timestamp.now())).toBe(true)
  expect(TimestampType(NaN)).toBe(false)
  expect(TimestampISO('2024-01-15T09:30:00.000Z')).toBe(true)
  expect(TimestampISO('2024-01-15')).toBe(false)
  expect(LegalDateType('2024-01-15')).toBe(true)
  expect(LegalDateType('2024-1-15')).toBe(false)
}
```

It prints:

```text
1710079200000 2024-03-10T14:00:00.000Z
36
1705311000000
2024-02-14
Expected TimestampType for 'hoursBetween.start', got string
Expected TimestampISO for 'received.at', got string
Expected LegalDateType for 'dueAfter.issued', got string
```

`TimestampISO` exists for values that arrive as text (from JSON, an API, a form). Inside
your program, turn it into a Timestamp with `Timestamp.parse` and work with the number.

Two functions in the tables below throw rather than return an error: `Timestamp.parse` on
text that is not a date, and `LegalDate.from` (and `LegalDate.parse`) on a day that does not
exist. They are for values you have already checked, such as an argument that passed
`TimestampISO`. For text you have not checked, use `tryParse`, which returns `null` instead.

### The `Timestamp` module

Every function takes Timestamps (numbers) and returns a new value; nothing is changed in
place. All of them work in UTC unless they take a time zone.

| Group        | Functions                                                                                                                         |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| make         | `now()`, `from(year, month, day, hour?, minute?, second?, ms?)` (month 1–12), `parse(text)` (throws on bad text), `tryParse(text)` (returns `null`) |
| add          | `addMilliseconds`, `addSeconds`, `addMinutes`, `addHours`, `addDays`, `addWeeks`, `addMonths`, `addYears`                          |
| difference   | `diff(a, b)` (milliseconds), `diffSeconds`, `diffMinutes`, `diffHours`, `diffDays`: all `a - b`, rounded down                      |
| read a part  | `year`, `month` (1–12), `day`, `hour`, `minute`, `second`, `millisecond`, `dayOfWeek` (1 = Monday, 7 = Sunday)                     |
| boundaries   | `startOfDay`, `endOfDay`, `startOfMonth`, `endOfMonth`, `startOfYear`, `endOfYear`                                                 |
| compare      | `isBefore`, `isAfter`, `isEqual`, `min`, `max` (or just `<`, `>`, `==`: they are numbers)                                          |
| display      | `iso(ts)`, `toDate(ts)` (the UTC `'YYYY-MM-DD'`), `format(ts, zone?)`, `formatDate(ts, zone?)`, `formatTime(ts, zone?)`, `toLocal(ts, zone?, options?)` |
| check        | `isValid(v)`, `isValidISO(text)`                                                                                                  |

```tjs:inline
import { Timestamp } from 'tjs-lang'

const launch = Timestamp.parse('2024-01-31T23:30:00Z')

console.log(Timestamp.iso(Timestamp.addMonths(launch, 1)))  // clamps to the end of February
console.log(Timestamp.iso(Timestamp.startOfMonth(launch)))
console.log(Timestamp.iso(Timestamp.endOfDay(launch)))
console.log(Timestamp.dayOfWeek(launch), Timestamp.hour(launch))
console.log(Timestamp.toDate(launch))

// The same moment, displayed in two zones (the wording follows your locale)
console.log(Timestamp.format(launch, 'UTC'))
console.log(Timestamp.format(launch, 'Asia/Tokyo'))

test 'Timestamp arithmetic' {
  expect(Timestamp.iso(Timestamp.addMonths(launch, 1))).toBe('2024-02-29T23:30:00.000Z')
  expect(Timestamp.diffDays(Timestamp.addDays(launch, 10), launch)).toBe(10)
  expect(Timestamp.dayOfWeek(launch)).toBe(3)
  expect(Timestamp.tryParse('next Tuesday')).toBe(null)
}
```

The first five lines print:

```text
2024-02-29T23:30:00.000Z
2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z
2024-01-31T23:59:59.999Z
3 23
2024-01-31
```

The last two show the same moment as 31 January in UTC and as 1 February in Tokyo. In an
English (US) locale they read something like `Jan 31, 2024 at 11:30:00 PM` and
`Feb 1, 2024 at 08:30:00 AM`; the exact punctuation depends on the browser.
The formatting functions use the locale of whatever runs the code, so their output differs
between machines. So does anything that reads the clock (`now()`, `today()`) and, as the
trip-ups below explain, `parse` given a time with no zone.

### The `LegalDate` module

Every function takes and returns `'YYYY-MM-DD'` strings (or numbers, for the parts). A
LegalDate has no time and no zone, so the 15th is the 15th everywhere. Only "what is the
date today" depends on a zone, which is why there are both `today()` and `todayIn(zone)`.

| Group        | Functions                                                                                                         |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| make         | `today()` (in UTC), `todayIn(zone)`, `from(year, month, day)` (throws on a date that does not exist), `parse(text)`, `tryParse(text)` |
| add          | `addDays`, `addWeeks`, `addMonths`, `addYears` (month and year arithmetic clamp to the end of a short month)       |
| difference   | `diff(a, b)` (days), `diffMonths(a, b)`, `diffYears(a, b)`                                                         |
| read a part  | `year`, `month`, `day`, `dayOfWeek` (1 = Monday), `weekOfYear` (ISO week), `dayOfYear`, `quarter`                  |
| calendar     | `isLeapYear(year)`, `daysInMonth(year, month)`, `daysInYear(year)`                                                 |
| boundaries   | `startOfWeek`, `endOfWeek` (Monday to Sunday), `startOfMonth`, `endOfMonth`, `startOfQuarter`, `endOfQuarter`, `startOfYear`, `endOfYear` |
| compare      | `isBefore`, `isAfter`, `isEqual`, `isBetween(date, start, end)`, `min`, `max`                                      |
| convert      | `toTimestamp(date)` (midnight UTC), `toTimestampISO(date)`, `toUnix(date)` (seconds), `fromUnix(seconds)`          |
| display      | `format(date, options?)`, `formatLong(date)`, `formatShort(date)`                                                  |
| check        | `isValid(text)`: the right shape **and** a day that exists                                                         |

```tjs:inline
import { LegalDate } from 'tjs-lang'

const signed = '2024-02-29'

console.log(LegalDate.addYears(signed, 1))          // no 29 February in 2025
console.log(LegalDate.endOfQuarter(signed), LegalDate.quarter(signed))
console.log(LegalDate.startOfWeek(signed), LegalDate.dayOfWeek(signed))
console.log(LegalDate.weekOfYear('2024-12-30'))     // ISO week 1 of 2025
console.log(LegalDate.diff('2024-12-25', signed))   // days
console.log(LegalDate.isValid('2024-02-30'), LegalDate.tryParse('2024-02-30'))
console.log(LegalDate.toTimestamp(signed))

test 'LegalDate arithmetic' {
  expect(LegalDate.addMonths('2024-01-31', 1)).toBe('2024-02-29')
  expect(LegalDate.addYears('2024-02-29', 1)).toBe('2025-02-28')
  expect(LegalDate.isBetween('2024-03-01', '2024-01-01', '2024-12-31')).toBe(true)
  expect(LegalDate.daysInMonth(2023, 2)).toBe(28)
  expect(LegalDate.isValid('2023-02-29')).toBe(false)
}
```

It prints:

```text
2025-02-28
2024-03-31 1
2024-02-26 4
1
300
false null
1709164800000
```

### When a library needs a `Date`: `LegacyDate`

Some code you call wants a real `Date`: `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, a charting library, an older
API. `LegacyDate(…)` makes one. It needs no import, because the compiler provides it in
every `.tjs` file as a function that calls `new Date(…)`. Make the `Date` at the call, hand
it over, and come back to a Timestamp with `.getTime()`:

```tjs:inline
import { Timestamp } from 'tjs-lang'

const paid = Timestamp.parse('2024-01-15T09:30:00Z')

const asDate = LegacyDate(paid)
const label = new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-GB', { dateStyle: 'long', timeZone: 'UTC' })
console.log(label.format(asDate))

console.log(asDate.getTime() == paid)

test 'a Date goes out and a Timestamp comes back' {
  expect(LegacyDate(paid).getTime()).toBe(paid)
}
```

It prints:

```text
15 January 2024
true
```

Keep the `Date` at the edge, as here, rather than passing it around: the reasons `.tjs`
refuses `new Date` apply to a `LegacyDate` just as much.

## A date pipeline

Here is a small program of the kind dates usually appear in. Subscriptions arrive as JSON,
with the email to notify, the plan, the date the subscription started and the moment of the
last payment. For each one we want the next renewal date, how many days away it is, and
whether the last payment is overdue.

To copy it into your own project, keep the `test` blocks in mind: from the command line they
come out inconclusive, because they need the imports (see
[Reading the examples](#reading-the-examples)). They run here, on the page.

```tjs:inline
import { Timestamp, LegalDate, TEmail, LegalDateType, TimestampISO, TimestampType } from 'tjs-lang'

Type Subscription {
  example: {
    email: TEmail,
    plan: 'monthly' | 'yearly',
    started: LegalDateType,
    lastPaid: TimestampISO,
  }
}

const WEEKDAYS = ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri', 'Sat', 'Sun']

// The first renewal on or after `today`. Each candidate is counted from the start
// date, so a subscription started on the 31st renews on the last day of short months
// and on the 31st again when there is one. `plan` must be exactly one of the two.
function nextRenewal(started: LegalDateType, plan: 'monthly' | 'yearly', today: LegalDateType) {
  if (!LegalDate.isValid(started)) {
    return Error(`${started} is not a date`)
  }
  const step = plan == 'monthly' ? 1 : 12
  let n = 1
  while (LegalDate.isBefore(LegalDate.addMonths(started, n * step), today)) {
    n += 1
  }
  return LegalDate.addMonths(started, n * step)
}

function renewalNotice(sub: Subscription, today: LegalDateType, now: TimestampType) {
  const renews = nextRenewal(sub.started, sub.plan, today)
  if (renews instanceof Error) {
    return renews
  }
  const days = LegalDate.diff(renews, today)
  const paidHoursAgo = Timestamp.diffHours(now, Timestamp.parse(sub.lastPaid))
  const limit = (sub.plan == 'monthly' ? 31 : 366) * 24
  return {
    to: sub.email,
    renews: `${WEEKDAYS[LegalDate.dayOfWeek(renews) - 1]} ${renews}`,
    inDays: days,
    overdue: paidHoursAgo > limit,
  }
}

const incoming = JSON.parse(`[
  { "email": "ada@example.com", "plan": "monthly", "started": "2024-01-31", "lastPaid": "2024-03-29T08:00:00Z" },
  { "email": "alan@example.com", "plan": "yearly", "started": "2023-04-02", "lastPaid": "2023-04-02T10:15:00Z" },
  { "email": "grace", "plan": "monthly", "started": "2024-02-10", "lastPaid": "2024-03-10T12:00:00Z" },
  { "email": "kay@example.com", "plan": "monthly", "started": "2024-02-30", "lastPaid": "2024-03-01T12:00:00Z" }
]`)

// The clock is read once, at the edge. Everything above takes the date as an argument.
const today = '2024-04-10'                 // in a real program: LegalDate.today()
const now = Timestamp.parse('2024-04-10T09:00:00Z') // in a real program: Timestamp.now()

for (const sub of incoming) {
  const notice = renewalNotice(sub, today, now)
  console.log(notice instanceof Error ? `skipped ${sub.email}` : JSON.stringify(notice))
}

// Why the last two were skipped
console.log(TEmail(incoming[2].email))
console.log(LegalDate.isValid(incoming[3].started))

test 'a subscription started on the 31st keeps its day where it can' {
  expect(nextRenewal('2024-01-31', 'monthly', '2024-02-10')).toBe('2024-02-29')
  expect(nextRenewal('2024-01-31', 'monthly', '2024-03-01')).toBe('2024-03-31')
  expect(nextRenewal('2024-01-31', 'monthly', '2024-04-10')).toBe('2024-04-30')
}

test 'a plan is monthly or yearly, nothing else' {
  expect(isMonadicError(nextRenewal('2024-01-31', 'quarterly', '2024-02-10'))).toBe(true)
}

test 'yearly renewals and overdue payments' {
  const alan = renewalNotice(incoming[1], today, now)
  expect(alan.renews).toBe('Wed 2025-04-02')
  expect(alan.inDays).toBe(357)
  expect(alan.overdue).toBe(true)
  expect(renewalNotice(incoming[0], today, now).overdue).toBe(false)
}

test 'bad records are refused, not processed' {
  expect(isMonadicError(renewalNotice(incoming[2], today, now))).toBe(true)
  expect(renewalNotice(incoming[3], today, now) instanceof Error).toBe(true)
}
```

It prints:

```text
{"to":"ada@example.com","renews":"Tue 2024-04-30","inDays":20,"overdue":false}
{"to":"alan@example.com","renews":"Wed 2025-04-02","inDays":357,"overdue":true}
skipped grace
skipped kay@example.com
"grace" is not a valid email
false
```

### What to notice

- **Each kind of time has its own value.** `started` is a calendar date, so it is a
  `LegalDate` string and month arithmetic happens on the calendar. `lastPaid` is a moment,
  so it arrives as an ISO string, is turned into a Timestamp with `Timestamp.parse`, and
  the gap is measured in hours. The code makes no `Date` object, so the file needs no
  `TjsCompat` (the first-line marker that gives a file JavaScript's rules, `Date` included;
  see [Date Formatting](/date-formatting-with-import/)).
- **The clock is read in one place.** `nextRenewal` and `renewalNotice` take `today` and
  `now` as arguments, so the same input always gives the same answer, and the tests can
  name exact dates. A real program passes `LegalDate.today()` and `Timestamp.now()` at the
  call, once.
- **Renewals are counted from the start date.** `LegalDate.addMonths(started, n)` for
  `n = 1, 2, 3` gives 29 February, 31 March and 30 April. Adding one month to the previous
  renewal instead would drift: 31 January, 29 February, 29 March, 29 April.
- **The record is checked once, at the boundary.** `Subscription` is declared from the
  built-in types, so a record with a bad email is refused before any date arithmetic runs.
  The error names the type, not the member (`Expected Subscription for
  'renewalNotice.sub', got object`); call `TEmail(sub.email)` yourself, as the last lines
  do, when you want to tell the user which field is wrong.
- **`'monthly' | 'yearly'` is a set of two values.** A union of example strings does not
  widen to "any string": on the parameter and inside `Subscription`, `'quarterly'` is
  refused.
- **`LegalDateType` is not the whole check.** Whether it accepts `'2024-02-30'` depends on
  the browser (see below); `LegalDate.isValid` is what reliably knows February has no 30th.
  So `nextRenewal` checks too, and returns an `Error` of its own. `Error(…)` without `new`
  is ordinary JavaScript, and `.tjs` returns errors rather than throwing them. Either way the
  record is skipped: a `MonadicError` is an `Error`, so `instanceof Error` catches the type
  error and this one alike. That is why the loop prints the email rather than the message,
  which differs between browsers for this record.

## Things that trip people up

- **`t: Timestamp` checks nothing, and says nothing.** `Timestamp` is the module of
  functions, not the type, so a parameter annotated with it accepts any value, with no
  warning. Write `t: TimestampType` (and `d: LegalDateType`, not `d: LegalDate`).
- **`LegalDateType` checks the shape; the calendar is up to the browser.** It requires
  `'YYYY-MM-DD'` and then asks the platform's own date parser, which in Chrome, Safari, Node
  and Bun rolls `'2024-02-30'` and `'2023-02-29'` over to March and so accepts them. Other
  engines may refuse them. `LegalDate.isValid` checks that the day exists, the same way
  everywhere, and `LegalDate.from` and `LegalDate.parse` throw on one that does not.
- **A string or number type's failure is a string, and strings are truthy.**
  `if (TEmail(x))` is true for every `x`. Compare with `=== true`.
- **`p: TEmail | null` on a parameter currently checks only `TEmail`**, so `null` is
  refused. Declare `Type MaybeEmail { example: Nullable(TEmail) }` and use that. Inside a
  `Type` example, `TEmail | null` works as written.
- **A combinator needs a `Type` declaration to be a parameter type.**
  `p: MaybeEmail` where `const MaybeEmail = Nullable(TEmail)` is not checked; the compiler
  warns (see [Building types from other types](#building-types-from-other-types)).
- **`Optional(T)` in an object example does not make the member optional.** It allows the
  value `undefined`, but the key must still be there. To let a caller leave a member out,
  write `T | undefined`, as `Profile` does with `homepage`.
- **A time without a zone is local time.** `TimestampISO` accepts `'2024-01-15T09:30'`, and
  `Timestamp.parse` reads it as 9:30 where the code runs, so the Timestamp differs between
  machines. Data you store or send should carry its zone (`Z` or `+01:00`).
- **`LegalDate.today()` is today in UTC.** In the evening in America it is already
  tomorrow in UTC. Use `LegalDate.todayIn('America/New_York')` (or the user's zone) for a
  date the user sees.
- **`diffMonths` and `diffYears` count calendar boundaries.**
  `LegalDate.diffMonths('2024-03-01', '2024-02-29')` is `1`, though only a day has passed.
  For elapsed time, use `LegalDate.diff` (days). The `Timestamp.diff…` functions round down,
  so a gap of minus an hour and a half is `-2` hours.
- **Signature examples cannot see imports.** A function whose signature or body uses an
  imported type or module has an _inconclusive_ signature example, and from the command
  line its tests are inconclusive too (see [Reading the examples](#reading-the-examples)).
  A test of a `Type` built from imported types is worse: it can pass while checking
  nothing.
title: Built-in Types and Dates
description: The `tjs-lang` package ships ready-made types for values that come up in almost every program: email addresses, URLs, UUIDs, positive integers, non-empty strings, and dates. None of them is part of the language. A `.tjs` file sees them only after it imports them, and they all come from the package `'tjs-lang'`: | Import                                                    | What it is                                                                 | | --------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `TEmail`, `TUrl`, `TUuid`, `TNonEmptyString`              | types for strings                                                          | | `TInteger`, `TPositiveInt`                                | types for numbers                                                          | | `TimestampType`, `TimestampISO`, `LegalDateType`          | types for dates and times                                                  | | `Nullable`, `Optional`, `TPair`, `TRecord`, `TArray`, `Union` | functions that build a new type from other types (`Union` is also a declaration form; see below) | | `Timestamp`, `LegalDate`                                  | modules of date functions (`Timestamp.now()`, `LegalDate.addMonths(…)`, …) | ### Reading the examples Three things hold for every example on this page. - **A bad argument is answered, not thrown.** When an argument fails its parameter type, the function does not run; it returns an error value, a `MonadicError`, whose `.message` says what was expected. # Inline WASM

A `wasm { }` block inside a TJS function is compiled to WebAssembly when the file is
transpiled, and the bytes are embedded in the emitted JavaScript. This page covers how a block
gets its inputs, which numbers it works with, and what it may contain. It assumes you know
roughly what WebAssembly is; if you have never used it from TJS, the
**[WASM Quick Start](/WASM-QUICKSTART/)** is a shorter walk-through.

## When to use a block

When a profiler says a numeric inner loop is hot. Most code is fast enough written plainly,
and a call into WASM has its own cost. WASM pays off on tight loops over typed arrays, and
most of all with SIMD, which the next chapter covers.

Using WebAssembly from plain JavaScript means writing WAT (WebAssembly's text format) or
compiling C or Rust, shipping a separate `.wasm` file, instantiating it asynchronously, and
copying data between JavaScript and WASM memory. A `wasm { }` block does all of that for you.
There is no `.wasm` file and no build step beyond transpiling the file, and inline blocks
instantiate synchronously when the file loads, so the first call already runs in WASM.

## The shape of a block

```javascript
function square(! x: 0.0):! 0.0 {
  return wasm {
    return x * x
  }
}
```

The block returns a value with `return`, and the function returns that with `return wasm { … }`.
Two markers appear on every function on this page:

- **`!` at the start of the parameter list** turns off TJS's argument checks for the whole
  function, every parameter, not only the first.
- **`:!` on the return** makes the return annotation a type only, not a tested example.

Both are explained under "Why `!` and `:!`" below.

## An example

```tjs:inline
// --- Scalar math ---

function addNumbers(! a: 0, b: 0):! 0 {
  return wasm {
    return a + b
  }
}

function factorial(! n: 0):! 0 {
  return wasm {
    let result = 1.0          // f64: an i32 here would overflow at 13!
    for (let i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
      result = result * i
    }
    return result
  }
}

function lerp(! a: 0.0, b: 0.0, t: 0.0):! 0.0 {
  return wasm {
    return a + (b - a) * t
  }
}

// --- Array processing ---

function sumArray(! arr: Float32Array, len: 0):! 0.0 {
  return wasm {
    let sum = 0.0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
      sum = sum + arr[i]
    }
    return sum
  }
}

console.log('addNumbers(3, 4):', addNumbers(3, 4))       // 7
console.log('factorial(10):', factorial(10))             // 3628800
console.log('factorial(13):', factorial(13))             // 6227020800
console.log('lerp(0, 100, 0.25):', lerp(0.0, 100.0, 0.25)) // 25
console.log('sumArray([1,2,3,4]):', sumArray(new Float32Array([1, 2, 3, 4]), 4)) // 10
```

Things to notice:

- **Variables are captured, not declared.** `a`, `b`, `n`, `arr` and `len` are the outer
  function's parameters. The transpiler sees which ones the block uses and passes them in.
- **There is no implicit last-expression return.** A block whose last line is a bare
  expression such as `x * 2` does not compile; the error tells you to write `return x * 2`.
- **A `fallback` is optional.** None of these functions has one. When the runtime cannot run
  WASM, the block's own body runs as JavaScript instead. See
  [Checking the block against its fallback](#checking-the-block-against-its-fallback).
- **Typed arrays are read by index.** `arr[i]` reads an element of a parameter annotated
  `Float32Array`, `Float64Array`, `Int32Array` or `Uint8Array`. A block cannot read
  `arr.length`, so pass the length as its own parameter (`len` here).

## Numbers inside a block

A WASM block has no JavaScript numbers. It has two numeric types:

- **`f64`**, a 64-bit float: the same thing as a JavaScript number.
- **`i32`**, a 32-bit integer.

The rules:

- **Every captured number arrives as `f64`**, whatever its example. `a: 0` checks for an
  integer at the call when validation is on, but inside the block `a + b` is float addition.
- **A `let` takes the type of its initializer.** `let i = 2` is an `i32`, which suits a loop
  counter; `let sum = 0.0` is an `f64`.
- **Mixing the two gives `f64`.** `i <= n` compares as floats, and `result * i` is a float
  multiplication.
- **An `i32` wraps on overflow.** With `let result = 1`, the factorial above would be computed
  in 32 bits, and `factorial(13)` would return 1932053504 where JavaScript gives 6227020800.
  That is why the example writes `1.0`.
- **`/` is JavaScript's division**, even between two `i32` values: `7 / 2` is 3.5, never 3.
- **`%` and the bitwise operators (`|`, `&`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`, `>>>`) need `i32` operands.**
  WASM has no float remainder, so `x % 2` on a captured number is a compile error. For integer
  algorithms, use a [`wasm function`](/wasm-functions/), a standalone WASM function whose
  parameters you declare as `i32`.
- **A comparison is an `i32`, 1 or 0.** A block that returns `v != v` returns the number 1,
  not `true`.

## Why `!` and `:!`

- **`!` skips argument validation.** Without it, TJS checks the arguments on every call: a
  fractional `len` returns a `MonadicError` (TJS's returned error value) instead of running.
  A block exists to make a hot path fast, and checking each argument can cost more than the
  WASM saves. Drop the `!` when the function receives outside data and you want the check.
- **`:!` skips the signature test.** A plain return annotation is a worked example: the
  transpiler calls the function with the parameter examples and compares the result.
  `factorial(! n: 0): 0` would fail that test, because `factorial(0)` is 1, not 0. `:!` says
  only "returns a number".
- **A typed-array annotation is written by type name.** The colon value in TJS is normally an
  example, but there is no literal for a `Float32Array`, so the parameter names the type.
  Such a parameter is not checked at runtime even without `!`, and the transpiler warns that
  it is unchecked. The warning is expected; checking the array is up to the caller.

## Checking the block against its fallback

`fallback { }` is ordinary TJS that runs when the runtime cannot run WASM at all: no
`WebAssembly`, as in iOS Lockdown Mode, or a refused instantiation. When that happens the
runtime records it once per file in `__tjs.records({ source: 'wasm' })`, the
[flight recorder](/error-history/). Write an explicit fallback when the JavaScript version
should be different code, for example a library call the block cannot make; otherwise leave it
out and the block's body runs as JavaScript.

Setting `globalThis.__tjs_wasm_enabled = false` forces every block to run its fallback, even
though the WASM is loaded. Use it to test that the two paths agree, or to benchmark one
against the other.

```tjs:inline
function mean(! xs: Float32Array, len: 0):! 0.0 {
  return wasm {
    let sum = 0.0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
      sum = sum + xs[i]
    }
    return sum / len
  } fallback {
    return xs.reduce((total, x) => total + x, 0) / len
  }
}

const xs = new Float32Array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
const inWasm = mean(xs, 5)

globalThis.__tjs_wasm_enabled = false
const inFallback = mean(xs, 5)
delete globalThis.__tjs_wasm_enabled

console.log('in WASM:    ', inWasm)                  // 3
console.log('in fallback:', inFallback)              // 3
console.log('agree:      ', inWasm === inFallback)   // true
```

## Limits

A `wasm { }` body is a small, typed subset of JavaScript, not arbitrary code. Anything outside
it is a **compile error** that names the construct; it is never silently shipped as
JavaScript, because writing `wasm { }` is a request for WASM.

- **Allowed:** numeric `let`, `for` loops (nested), `if`/`else`, arithmetic and comparison,
  typed-array element access, the `f32x4_*` SIMD intrinsics, and the math intrinsics
  `Math.sqrt`, `Math.abs`, `Math.floor`, `Math.ceil`, `Math.trunc`, `Math.min` and `Math.max`.
- **Not allowed:** `while` (use `for`), `break` and `continue` (put the exit condition in the
  `for` test), `&&` and `||` (nest the `if`s), function calls other than those intrinsics,
  closures, objects, strings, `try`/`catch`, and any allocation.
- **Not yet supported:** the trigonometric functions (`Math.sin`, `Math.cos`, `Math.tan` and
  their inverses), `Math.exp`, `Math.log` and `Math.pow`. WebAssembly has no instruction for
  them, and a block that uses one does not compile.
- **`==` and `!=` are WASM's inside a block**, not TJS's. In TJS `NaN == NaN` is true; inside a
  block, as in plain JavaScript, `x != x` is true for NaN.
- **This subset is not AJS**, the agent language, which has `while` and no `for`.

<!-- tjs-doc: expect-error -->

```tjs:static
function wave(! t: 0.0):! 0.0 {
  return wasm {
    return Math.sin(t)  // compile error: Math.sin is not supported in a block
  }
}
```

[`DOCS-WASM.md`](/DOCS-WASM/) is the full reference.

# WASM SIMD

A `wasm { }` block inside a function is compiled to WebAssembly when the file is
transpiled. Its `fallback { }` is the same logic in plain JavaScript, used where WebAssembly
cannot run. There is no toolchain to install: the transpiler builds the module.

This page is about SIMD inside those blocks. Inside a `wasm { }` block, the `f32x4_*`
**intrinsics** (built-in functions that the compiler turns into a single SIMD instruction
rather than a function call) work on four 32-bit floats at once. An `f32x4` value holds four
floats, called **lanes**.

For more detail on `wasm { }` blocks themselves, see the
**[WASM Quick Start](/WASM-QUICKSTART/)** and [WASM Basics](/wasm-basics/). The full list of
intrinsics is in [DOCS-WASM, under "SIMD intrinsics"](/DOCS-WASM/#simd-intrinsics).

## The intrinsics used here

| Intrinsic                        | What it does                                                              |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `f32x4_splat(x)`                 | Makes a vector with `x` in all four lanes.                                |
| `f32x4_load(arr, byteOffset)`    | Reads four floats from `arr`, starting `byteOffset` bytes in.             |
| `f32x4_store(arr, byteOffset, v)`| Writes the four lanes of `v` into `arr`, starting `byteOffset` bytes in.  |
| `f32x4_extract_lane(v, n)`       | Reads lane `n` (0 to 3) of `v` as a single float.                         |
| `f32x4_add(a, b)`, `f32x4_mul(a, b)`, `f32x4_min`, `f32x4_max`, … | Lane-by-lane arithmetic: lane 0 with lane 0, and so on. |
| `f32x4_lt(a, b)`, `f32x4_gt`, …  | Lane-by-lane comparison, producing a mask (see below).                   |
| `f32x4_select(mask, a, b)`       | Takes each lane from `a` where the mask is set, from `b` where it is not. |

The rest of the list works the same way, in the same four groups: memory and lanes,
arithmetic, comparisons, and select.

## Reading the signatures

The examples below use TJS signatures, which are not TypeScript:

```javascript
function scale(! arr: Float32Array, len: 0, factor: 0.0) { … }
function dot(! a: Float32Array, b: Float32Array, len: 0):! 0.0 { … }
```

- **A colon value is an example, not a default.** `len: 0` means "a required integer";
  `factor: 0.0` means "a required float" (the `.0` is what makes it a float).
- **`!` at the start of the parameter list turns off runtime argument checks for every
  parameter of the function** ([Safety markers](/TJS-SYNTAX/#safety-markers)). Without it, a
  call such as `scale(xs, 'x', 2.0)` returns a type error instead of running. These functions
  are meant for hot loops whose callers already pass the right values, so the checks are
  switched off for speed.
- **`Float32Array` is not checked either way.** TJS cannot turn that name into a runtime
  check, so `arr` is unchecked even without `!`. A plain array passed in is silently ignored:
  no error, and its values do not change. Callers must pass a real `Float32Array`.
- **`:! 0.0` declares a float return value that is not checked or tested.** A plain `: 0.0`
  would be a worked example: TJS would call `dot` with example arguments and expect `0.0`
  back.

The examples below are live: each runs in its own scope, so names do not clash between them.

```tjs:inline
/#
## SIMD: Single Instruction, Multiple Data

Each step of these loops handles four floats with one instruction.
#/

// --- Scale an array by a constant (SIMD: 4 elements per step) ---

function scale(! arr: Float32Array, len: 0, factor: 0.0) {
  wasm {
    let s = f32x4_splat(factor)
    // Steps by 4, so len must be a multiple of 4
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4
      let v = f32x4_load(arr, off)
      f32x4_store(arr, off, f32x4_mul(v, s))
    }
  } fallback {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) arr[i] *= factor
  }
}

// --- Dot product (sum of element-wise products) ---

function dot(! a: Float32Array, b: Float32Array, len: 0):! 0.0 {
  return wasm {
    let acc = f32x4_splat(0.0)
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4
      let va = f32x4_load(a, off)
      let vb = f32x4_load(b, off)
      acc = f32x4_add(acc, f32x4_mul(va, vb))
    }
    // Sum the 4 lanes
    return f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 0)
      + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 1)
      + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 2)
      + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 3)
  } fallback {
    let sum = 0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) sum += a[i] * b[i]
    return sum
  }
}

// --- Demo ---

const SIZE = 1024

// Create test arrays
const arr = new Float32Array(SIZE)
const a = new Float32Array(SIZE)
const b = new Float32Array(SIZE)

for (let i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) {
  arr[i] = i + 1
  a[i] = 1.0
  b[i] = 2.0
}

// Scale
scale(arr, SIZE, 0.5)
console.log('scale([1..1024], 0.5) first 4:', arr[0], arr[1], arr[2], arr[3])
// → scale([1..1024], 0.5) first 4: 0.5 1 1.5 2

// Dot product: 1.0 * 2.0 * 1024 = 2048
const d = dot(a, b, SIZE)
console.log('dot([1,1,...], [2,2,...], 1024):', d)
// → dot([1,1,...], [2,2,...], 1024): 2048

// --- Benchmark ---
// Run until at least minMs of wall clock has elapsed, then divide. Timing a single
// sub-millisecond call does not work: some browsers clamp `performance.now()` to about
// 1ms, so a fast call reads as 0.
function timePerOp(fn, minMs = 25) {
  let iters = 0
  const start = performance.now()
  do {
    fn()
    iters++
  } while (performance.now() - start < minMs)
  return (performance.now() - start) / iters
}

function report(label, data) {
  // A factor near 1, so thousands of repeated calls don't drive the values to 0 or Infinity
  const simd = timePerOp(() => scale(data, SIZE, 1.001))
  // Switch every wasm block to its fallback, time the same calls, switch back
  globalThis.__tjs_wasm_enabled = false
  const js = timePerOp(() => scale(data, SIZE, 1.001))
  globalThis.__tjs_wasm_enabled = true
  console.log(`${label}: SIMD ${(simd * 1000).toFixed(2)}us, JS ${(js * 1000).toFixed(2)}us per call`)
}

// `arr` is an ordinary Float32Array: it is copied into WASM memory and back on every call
report('copied Float32Array', arr)

// A wasmBuffer array already lives in WASM memory, so nothing is copied
const shared = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, SIZE)
shared.set(arr)
report('wasmBuffer array    ', shared)
```

`/# … #/` is a TJS doc comment: its contents are markdown, which the playground and the doc
site render above the code ([Doc comments](/TJS-SYNTAX/#doc-comments-)).

## What the example shows

Every `f32x4_*` intrinsic works on all four lanes at once, so a loop that steps `i += 4` does
a quarter of the iterations a scalar loop would. That also means **the length must be a
multiple of 4**: the loop reads and writes four floats per step and has no tail loop.
`SIZE` is 1024, which is.

Read the loops with these things in mind:

- **Offsets are in bytes, indexes are in elements.** `f32x4_load(arr, off)` takes a byte
  offset, and a float is 4 bytes, hence `let off = i * 4`. Getting this wrong usually does not
  fail loudly: it reads the wrong floats.
- **`f32x4_splat` builds the constant once, outside the loop.** It copies `factor` into all
  four lanes of `s`, and `scale` multiplies every group of four by that same `s`.
- **A reduction ends with a horizontal sum.** `dot` accumulates four partial sums in one
  vector, then adds the four lanes with `f32x4_extract_lane`.
- **A `wasm { }` block can produce a value.** Write `return` inside the block (and inside
  `fallback`) to give the block its value, and put `return wasm { … }` in the function to pass
  that value out, as `dot` does. Without an inner `return` the block produces nothing, as in
  `scale`. A bare expression on the block's last line does not count; it is a compile error.
- **A lane index is a literal.** `f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 0)` works; passing a variable as the
  lane does not compile, because the lane is encoded into the instruction itself. It must be
  0, 1, 2 or 3.
- **The `fallback { }` is the same algorithm in plain JavaScript.** It runs only where WASM
  cannot (no `WebAssembly` at all, as in iOS Lockdown Mode) or when you switch WASM off. It
  is not a safety net for code that does not compile: a `wasm { }` block outside the
  supported subset is a build error, naming the construct.

### Reading the benchmark

A WebAssembly module has its own **memory**: a separate block of bytes that the module can
read and write directly. It cannot read a JavaScript array where it lies, so when `scale` is
given an ordinary `Float32Array`, the generated wrapper copies the array's bytes into WASM
memory, runs the loop, and copies them back.

`wasmBuffer(Type, length)` allocates a typed array *inside* WASM memory instead, so the
wrapper hands the module its address and copies nothing.

> **`wasmBuffer` allocations are never freed.** Allocate once and reuse the array; calling
> `wasmBuffer` on every call of a long-running program leaks. See
> [WASM Memory](/wasm-memory/).

The benchmark times `scale` twice for each array: once in WASM, and once with
`globalThis.__tjs_wasm_enabled = false`. That is a documented switch for "WASM vs JS"
comparisons: while it is `false`, every `wasm { }` block in the page (or process) runs its
`fallback`, even though the WASM is loaded. Set it back to `true` afterwards, as `report`
does.

One illustrative run (2026-11-06, Apple M5 Max, Bun 1.4.2; your numbers will differ):

```text
copied Float32Array: SIMD 0.73us, JS 0.29us per call
wasmBuffer array    : SIMD 0.24us, JS 0.28us per call
```

With an ordinary `Float32Array`, the SIMD version is *slower* than the JavaScript loop.
`scale` does one multiply per float, and each call first copies all 1024 floats into WASM
memory and then copies them back out. That copying costs more than the multiplies save. The
`wasmBuffer` array removes the copy, which makes the SIMD call about three times faster than
the copied one, and level with or a little faster than plain JavaScript. The general lesson:
SIMD pays when there is enough arithmetic per byte moved, or when the data stays in WASM
memory between calls.

The runtime tells you about the copy. The first time a function is handed a typed array
outside WASM memory, it adds a notice to `globalThis.__tjs.records({ source: 'wasm' })`
saying the array is being copied in and out on every call. `globalThis.__tjs` is the
runtime's flight recorder ([Error History](/error-history/)); read it through `globalThis`,
because a bare `__tjs` inside a `.tjs` file is that file's own runtime and does not see
these entries.

## Branch-free decisions: compare, mask, select

SIMD has no per-lane `if`. Instead a comparison produces a **mask**: in each lane where the
comparison is true, every bit is set, and in each lane where it is false, every bit is clear.
A set lane is not the number 1.0 (read as a float it is `NaN`), so a mask is not something to
log or multiply by. It is meant to be passed to `f32x4_select(mask, a, b)`, which takes each
lane from `a` where the mask is set and from `b` where it is not. For the common case of
clamping, `f32x4_min` and `f32x4_max` do the job without a mask.

```tjs:inline
// Clamp every value into [0, 1], four lanes at a time
function clamp01(! xs: Float32Array, len: 0) {
  wasm {
    let lo = f32x4_splat(0.0)
    let hi = f32x4_splat(1.0)
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4
      let v = f32x4_load(xs, off)
      f32x4_store(xs, off, f32x4_min(f32x4_max(v, lo), hi))
    }
  } fallback {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) xs[i] = Math.min(Math.max(xs[i], 0), 1)
  }
}

// Replace negatives with zero using a lane mask and select
function relu(! xs: Float32Array, len: 0) {
  wasm {
    let zero = f32x4_splat(0.0)
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4
      let v = f32x4_load(xs, off)
      let negative = f32x4_lt(v, zero)
      f32x4_store(xs, off, f32x4_select(negative, zero, v))
    }
  } fallback {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) if (xs[i] < 0) xs[i] = 0
  }
}

const clamped = new Float32Array([-0.5, 0.25, 0.75, 1.5, 2, -3, 0.5, 1])
clamp01(clamped, clamped.length)
console.log('clamp01:', Array.from(clamped).join(', '))
// → clamp01: 0, 0.25, 0.75, 1, 1, 0, 0.5, 1

const rectified = new Float32Array([-1, 2, -3, 4, 5, -6, 7, -8])
relu(rectified, rectified.length)
console.log('relu:   ', Array.from(rectified).join(', '))
// → relu:    0, 2, 0, 4, 5, 0, 7, 0

// Length 6 is not a multiple of 4: run SIMD on the first 4, finish the tail in JS
const ragged = new Float32Array([-1, 2, -3, 4, -5, 6])
const whole = ragged.length - (ragged.length % 4)
relu(ragged, whole)
for (let i = whole; i < ragged.length; i++) if (ragged[i] < 0) ragged[i] = 0
console.log('relu with a tail:', Array.from(ragged).join(', '))
// → relu with a tail: 0, 2, 0, 4, 0, 6
```

`relu` compares each value with zero, giving a mask that is set in the negative lanes, then
selects `zero` in those lanes and the original value everywhere else. The same pattern
handles any per-lane choice: saturating, or replacing out-of-range values.

## Limits

- **Lengths must be a multiple of 4, and no larger than the array.** A SIMD loop reads and
  writes four floats per step, and there is no automatic tail loop. Nothing checks `len`
  against the array, and getting it wrong does not fail loudly. With an ordinary typed array,
  the extra steps read and write past the end of the copy inside WASM memory; those writes are
  not copied back, so they are lost. With a `wasmBuffer` array, they can write into whatever
  was allocated next, which silently corrupts a neighbouring array. Either pad your arrays (zeros are harmless in a sum or a dot
  product) or finish the last one to three elements in JavaScript, as the last lines above
  do.
- **SIMD loads need a typed-array parameter, and should get a `Float32Array`.** A plain
  array, or a parameter typed by an example such as `[0.0]`, is not a pointer into WASM
  memory, and the build stops with "is not a typed array parameter". Other typed arrays
  (`Float64Array`, `Int32Array`, `Uint8Array`) compile, but `f32x4_load` reads their bytes as
  32-bit floats without converting them, so the results are wrong.
- **Only `f32x4`.** There are no integer or `f64x2` lane types yet.
- **The `'wasm'` records hold two kinds of entry.** A *warning* when a file's blocks fall back
  to JavaScript because WebAssembly is unavailable or the module failed to instantiate, and a
  *notice* the first time a function is handed a typed array outside WASM memory (see
  "Reading the benchmark"). All current browsers, Node and Bun support WebAssembly SIMD, so
  on a normal setup you will see only the notices. Read them with
  `globalThis.__tjs.records({ source: 'wasm' })`.

# WASM Memory

> New to WASM in TJS? Start with the **[WASM Quick Start](/WASM-QUICKSTART/)**.
> [`DOCS-WASM.md`](/DOCS-WASM/) is the reference; its "Memory discipline" section states the
> rules this chapter puts to work.

WebAssembly code can read and write only its own **linear memory**: one flat block of bytes,
separate from the rest of the JavaScript heap. Whatever a `wasm { }` block works on has to be
in that memory when the block runs. TJS moves values there for you, in one of three ways:

- **Numbers pass straight through.** A number parameter becomes a WASM parameter. Nothing is
  copied or allocated.
- **An ordinary typed array is copied.** The wrapper TJS generates copies it into WASM memory
  before the call and copies it back afterwards, so the block's changes reach your array.
- **A `wasmBuffer()` array is not copied.** `wasmBuffer(Float32Array, n)` allocates the array
  inside WASM memory, so JavaScript and WASM read and write the same bytes.

The first example shows both array paths, and what the runtime says about the first one.

```tjs:inline
// Adds 1 to the first len floats of arr, four at a time. len must be a multiple of 4.
// The ! turns off the parameter checks for this whole function (see below).
function addOne(! arr: Float32Array, len: 0) {
  wasm {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4 // f32x4 load/store take a BYTE offset: 4 bytes per float
      f32x4_store(arr, off, f32x4_add(f32x4_load(arr, off), f32x4_splat(1.0)))
    }
  } fallback {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) arr[i] += 1
  }
}

// WASM notices go to the global runtime's flight recorder, not to this file's own
// __tjs (see "Read it from globalThis.__tjs" below).
globalThis.__tjs.clearRecords()

// 1. An ordinary Float32Array: copied into WASM memory and back on every call.
const regular = new Float32Array([10, 20, 30, 40])
addOne(regular, 4)
addOne(regular, 4)
console.log('regular, after two calls:', Array.from(regular).join(', '))

// 2. A wasmBuffer array: its bytes ARE WASM memory, so nothing is copied.
const shared = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, 4)
shared.set([100, 200, 300, 400])
addOne(shared, 4)
console.log('shared, after one call:  ', Array.from(shared).join(', '))
console.log('shared is a Float32Array:', shared instanceof Float32Array)

// 3. The runtime noticed the copies, and wrote it down once.
for (const r of globalThis.__tjs.records({ source: 'wasm', severity: 'notice' })) {
  console.log(`[${r.severity}] copied param '${r.data.param}' (${r.data.bytes} bytes)`)
}
```

It prints:

```text
regular, after two calls: 12, 22, 32, 42
shared, after one call:   101, 201, 301, 401
shared is a Float32Array: true
[notice] copied param 'arr' (16 bytes)
```

## What the example shows

Both arrays end up changed, so from the outside the two paths look the same. The difference
is what happens on each call.

`addOne(regular, 4)` copies the 16 bytes of `regular` into WASM memory, runs the block, and
copies the 16 bytes back. It does that on every call. For 4 floats the cost is nothing; for a
large array called in a loop, two copies per call can cost more than the arithmetic.

`wasmBuffer(Float32Array, 4)` returns an ordinary `Float32Array` (it works with `set`,
`Array.from`, indexing and everything else), but its `.buffer` is WASM memory. When the
wrapper sees that, it passes the array's position in memory and copies nothing.

Inside the block, `f32x4_load` and `f32x4_store` take a **byte** offset into memory, not an
element index. The loop counts floats (`i += 4`), so the offset is `i * 4`.

The `!` at the start of the parameter list turns off every parameter check in the function,
not only the check on `arr`. Here that means `len` is no longer checked as an integer, which
a kernel called in a hot loop with known inputs does not need. `Float32Array` is not checked
at runtime in any case: in an ordinary signature it tells the `wasm` block that `arr` is a
typed array, and without the `!` TJS warns that it leaves that parameter unchecked. See
[Safety markers](/TJS-SYNTAX/#safety-markers).

These blocks are small, so they compile synchronously when the file loads and the first call
already runs in WASM. The exception is a browser main thread with a module over 4KB, which
runs the `fallback { }` until the module is ready; `await globalThis.__tjs_wasm_ready()`
waits for it (DOCS-WASM, "Runtime: readiness, failures, and the enable toggle").

### The flight recorder notices the copy

A copied array is not an error, so nothing throws and every test passes. That is why the
runtime writes it down: the first time a WASM block is handed an array outside WASM memory,
it adds a `notice` to the [Flight Recorder](/error-history/) with `source: 'wasm'`. The
record's `data` names the first copied parameter (`param`) and its size in bytes (`bytes`),
and its message says what to do: allocate the array with `wasmBuffer()`. The message and
`data.fn` name the block by an internal id (such as `__tjs_wasm_1anfoz_0`), not by the
function you wrote, which is why the example prints only `param` and `bytes`.

It records once per block, not once per call and not once per parameter. The example calls
`addOne(regular, 4)` twice and gets one record. A later call that copies a different
parameter of the same block adds nothing. A recorder that wrote on every call of a hot kernel
would become the slowdown it exists to report.

Two details matter when you look for this record:

- **Read it from `globalThis.__tjs`.** The WASM wrapper writes to the installed runtime.
  Inside a `.tjs` file, a bare `__tjs` is that file's own runtime instance, and its
  `records()` does not include the WASM notices.
- **The copy notice appears only when the WASM ran.** When a block runs its `fallback { }`
  nothing is copied, so there is no copy notice. Why it fell back decides whether anything
  else is recorded. A runtime with no WebAssembly, or a module that fails to instantiate,
  records one `warning` with the same `source: 'wasm'` (the example's `severity: 'notice'`
  filter leaves it out). A browser still compiling the module asynchronously records nothing.

## What a copy costs

The next example times one read-only kernel over 100,000 floats, once with an ordinary
`Float32Array` and once with a `wasmBuffer` array. The kernel only reads, so every call does
the same work and the only difference is the copy.

```tjs:inline
// Adds up the first len values of arr. It only reads, so every call does the same work.
// total starts at 0.0, not 0: inside a wasm block `let total = 0` would be an integer.
function sum(! arr: Float32Array, len: 0) {
  return wasm {
    let total = 0.0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) total += arr[i]
    return total
  } fallback {
    let total = 0.0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) total += arr[i]
    return total
  }
}

// Run fn until at least minMs of wall clock has passed, then divide. A single
// sub-millisecond call cannot be timed: some browsers round performance.now()
// to about 1ms, so it would read as zero.
function timePerOp(fn, minMs = 50) {
  let iters = 0
  const start = performance.now()
  do {
    fn()
    iters++
  } while (performance.now() - start < minMs)
  return (performance.now() - start) / iters
}

const SIZE = 100000
const plain = new Float32Array(SIZE)          // ordinary JavaScript memory
const shared = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, SIZE) // WASM memory
for (let i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) plain[i] = shared[i] = i % 10

console.log('plain sum: ', sum(plain, SIZE))
console.log('shared sum:', sum(shared, SIZE))

const plainUs = timePerOp(() => sum(plain, SIZE)) * 1000
const sharedUs = timePerOp(() => sum(shared, SIZE)) * 1000
console.log(`plain Float32Array: ${plainUs.toFixed(0)}µs per call (copied in and out)`)
console.log(`wasmBuffer:         ${sharedUs.toFixed(0)}µs per call (no copy)`)
```

`return wasm { ... }` hands the block's value back to the caller: a `wasm` block can be the
value of a `return`. The block returns a number; a block never returns an array (see the
limits below).

Both calls return the same total, 450000. The timings depend on your machine; in our runs the
plain array was the slower of the two. Under Bun, on the machine this chapter was written on
(November 2026), it was about 105µs against 68µs per call. The copied version moves 400KB in
and 400KB out on every call, and the copy back happens even though `sum` changed nothing.

## Allocate once, reuse forever

`wasmBuffer` is a **bump allocator with no free**. It keeps one pointer to the first unused
byte of WASM memory; each call hands out the slice starting there and moves the pointer past
it. Nothing ever moves the pointer back, so a slice is never given back. This is deliberate:
nobody has to decide who owns a buffer or when it dies, even across libraries. The price is
that a `wasmBuffer` call inside a loop, or once per request, uses up memory that never
returns.

So the pattern is: allocate the working buffers once, when the module loads, and refill them.
A kernel that produces an array takes an **output parameter** instead of allocating one, so
the caller decides where the result goes.

```tjs:inline
// Allocate the working buffers ONCE, when the module loads.
const LEN = 8
const src = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, LEN)
const dst = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, LEN)

// The kernel reads one buffer and writes another; it never allocates.
function squares(! input: Float32Array, output: Float32Array, len: 0) {
  wasm {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4 // byte offset: 4 bytes per float
      let v = f32x4_load(input, off)
      f32x4_store(output, off, f32x4_mul(v, v))
    }
  } fallback {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) output[i] = input[i] * input[i]
  }
}

// Each "request" refills the same buffers instead of allocating new ones.
for (const start of [1, 10, 100]) {
  for (let i = 0; i < LEN; i++) src[i] = start + i
  squares(src, dst, LEN)
  console.log(`squares from ${start}:`, Array.from(dst).join(', '))
}

// An ordinary Float32Array still works as the output: copied in, and copied back out.
const plainOut = new Float32Array(LEN)
squares(src, plainOut, LEN)
console.log('into a plain Float32Array:', Array.from(plainOut).join(', '))
```

The three "requests" reuse `src` and `dst`; the module allocates 64 bytes of WASM memory in
total, however many times the loop runs. The last call mixes the two kinds of array: `src` is
passed in place, and only `plainOut` is copied. That call is the first time `squares` copies
anything, so it adds the block's one copy notice to the flight recorder.

The copy path does not use up memory. An ordinary array is copied into scratch space past the
last `wasmBuffer` slice, and that space is reused by the next call.

## Limits

- **WASM never allocates.** Neither an inline block nor a `wasm function` can create an array;
  JavaScript allocates every byte. That is why one allocator on the JavaScript side is enough:
  there is no second allocator inside WASM for it to coordinate with.
- **The memory is finite.** All the WASM in one file shares one `WebAssembly.Memory` of
  64MB (1024 pages of 64KB), which never grows, and `wasmBuffer` slices are permanent. Budget
  for your largest working set, once. Running past the end **throws** a `RangeError` rather
  than returning an error value: from `wasmBuffer` when the slice does not fit, and from a
  call whose copied arrays do not fit after the last `wasmBuffer` slice.
- **A `wasmBuffer` array is zero-copy only in its own file.** Every file containing WASM has
  its own memory, and loading the file points the global `wasmBuffer` at that memory. A
  buffer allocated after file B loaded lives in B's memory; handed to a kernel in file A, it
  is copied (and recorded) like any ordinary array. Allocate buffers in the module whose
  kernels use them.
- **Only typed arrays can be shared.** A block accepts `Float32Array`, `Float64Array`,
  `Int32Array` and `Uint8Array` parameters (DOCS-WASM, "Parameter types"). A plain JavaScript
  array is not a typed array: `[1, 2, 3]`, or a parameter whose example is `[0.0]`, has no
  bytes to share. Annotate kernel parameters as typed arrays and pass typed arrays.
- **SIMD loops step by 4.** A kernel that uses `f32x4_*` instructions, like `addOne` and
  `squares`, processes four floats at a time, so its length must be a multiple of 4. Nothing
  checks this. With `i < len` the loop rounds up: `addOne(arr, 6)` on an 8-float array
  changes all 8 floats in WASM, while the fallback changes 6. Keep lengths a multiple of 4,
  or handle the last few elements with an ordinary loop.
- **No WASM, no shared memory.** In a runtime that cannot create WASM memory, `wasmBuffer`
  returns an ordinary typed array and every block runs its `fallback { }`. Code written with
  `wasmBuffer` still runs; it is no faster than plain JavaScript.

The copy path is not wrong, only slower. For a small array called rarely it is the simpler
choice. Reach for `wasmBuffer` when the array is large or the call is hot, and let the flight
recorder tell you which calls are paying for copies.
title: WASM Memory
description: > New to WASM in TJS? Start with the **[WASM Quick Start](/WASM-QUICKSTART/)**. > [`DOCS-WASM.md`](/DOCS-WASM/) is the reference; its "Memory discipline" section states the > rules this chapter puts to work. WebAssembly code can read and write only its own **linear memory**: one flat block of bytes, separate from the rest of the JavaScript heap. Whatever a `wasm { }` block works on has to be in that memory when the block runs. TJS moves values there for you, in one of three ways: - **Numbers pass straight through.** A number parameter becomes a WASM parameter. Nothing is copied or allocated. - **An ordinary typed array is copied.** The wrapper TJS generates copies it into WASM memory before the call and copies it back afterwards, so the block's changes reach your array. - **A `wasmBuffer()` array is not copied.** `wasmBuffer(Float32Array, n)` allocates the array inside WASM memory, so JavaScript and WASM read and write the same bytes. The first example shows both array paths, and what the runtime says about the first one.
